name: Sagbita
label: Sagbita
date: c. 815 BC (Encyclopaedia Iranica; the year of Shamshi-Adad V's Median campaign is uncertain)
place: Sagbita, royal city of Hanasiruka (unidentified, central Zagros), Iran
persian_force: The warriors of the Median chief Hanasiruka, including horsemen (140 were captured); the annals give no other detail.
iranian_note: The Assyrian text calls Hanasiruka and his people Medes (Matai), an Iranian-speaking people.
result_basis: Shamshi-Adad V's annals record 2,300 Medes killed, 140 of their horsemen captured and Hanasiruka's royal city taken; there is no other source.
borderline: an episode of an Assyrian campaign record, not a named battle in modern lists
doubt: Borderline: an episode of an Assyrian campaign record, not a named battle in modern lists.
sources: Inscriptions of Shamshi-Adad V (Grayson, RIMA 3); Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Media'
note: The annals also claim 1,200 nearby settlements destroyed and tribute imposed on the Median tribes. Sagbita lay in the district later called Sagbat, in the Assyrian province of Kishesim (Iranica).
qbasis: Media: an Iranian-led state

name: Harhar
label: Harhar
place: Harhar, renamed Kar-Sharrukin (unidentified, central Zagros, perhaps the Kermanshah area), Iran
commanders_b: unknown (the townsmen, who had driven out their lord Kibaba)
persian_force: The people of Harhar in revolt against their pro-Assyrian lord; no numbers or units are recorded.
iranian_note: Harhar lay among the Median chiefdoms of the central Zagros, but its population was mixed and the sources do not call its defenders Medes.
result_basis: Sargon besieged and took Harhar, which became the seat of the Assyrian province of Kar-Sharrukin.
borderline: a town of the Median borderland: whether its defenders counted as Medes is uncertain, and the siege is known only from Sargon's own texts
doubt: Borderline: a town of the Median borderland: whether its defenders counted as Medes is uncertain, and the siege is known only from Sargon's own texts.
sources: Annals of Sargon II; Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Media'
note: Iranica adds that Harhar revolted in 715 and the Assyrians had to conquer it again; no detail of that second capture survives, so it is not a separate entry.
qbasis: Media: an Iranian-led state

name: Kishesim (716 BC)
label: Kishesim (716 BC)
place: Kishesim, renamed Kar-Nergal (unidentified, central Zagros), Iran
persian_force: The townsmen and retainers of Bel-sharru-usur, lord of Kishesim; Sargon's texts give no numbers or units.
iranian_note: The central Zagros towns had mixed Median and older non-Iranian populations, and the lord's name is Akkadian, so the Median share is a guess.
result_basis: Kishesim fell to Sargon II, who captured its lord Bel-sharru-usur and made the town an Assyrian provincial seat under the name Kar-Nergal.
borderline: a town of the Median borderland: whether its lord and defenders counted as Medes is uncertain, and the capture is known only from Sargon's own texts
doubt: Borderline: a town of the Median borderland: whether its lord and defenders counted as Medes is uncertain, and the capture is known only from Sargon's own texts.
sources: Annals and Display Inscription of Sargon II; Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Media'; en.wikipedia Sargon II
note: Iranica treats Kishesim and Harhar, both made provinces in 716, as the start of the Assyrian conquest of Media; Sargon received tribute from 28 Median city lords in the same campaign. Wikipedia spells the town Kisheshim.
qbasis: Media: an Iranian-led state

name: Cimmerian defeat of Rusa I
label: Cimmerian defeat of Rusa I
date: c. 714-713 BCE (Assyrian intelligence letters to Sargon II; date approximate)
place: Urartu, eastern Anatolia (Uasi/Guriania region; exact site unknown)
result_basis: Assyrian reports say the Urartian army and its king were beaten by the Gimirrai, which left Rusa too weak to meet Sargon's 8th campaign (714).
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Assyrian state letters to Sargon II (State Archives of Assyria vols 1 and 5); Sargon's letter to the god Assur on the 8th campaign; Ivantchik, Les Cimmeriens au Proche-Orient (1993); Diakonoff, CHI 2 (1985)
note: The Cimmerians' language is unknown; many scholars call them Iranian-speaking, others Thracian or unclassified. The fight is known only from Assyrian secondhand reports and details are vague.

name: Halule
label: Halule
place: Halule on the Tigris (unidentified, perhaps near Samarra), Iraq
commanders_a: Humban-nimena III of Elam, Mushezib-Marduk of Babylon, Humban-undasha (Elamite commander, killed), Nabu-shuma-ishkun (captured)
persian_force: The contingents of Parsuash (the Persians) and Anzan (Anshan) among the allies of Elam listed by Sennacherib, beside Ellipi, Pashiru and the Chaldean and Aramaean tribes; no numbers are given.
iranian_note: Sennacherib names Parsuash (Persians) and Anzan; the Anzan troops may have been Elamite-speaking, so the Iranian share of this small contingent is uncertain.
result_basis: Sennacherib claims a crushing victory but the Babylonian Chronicle says the Elamite king forced an Assyrian retreat, and modern historians treat the battle as indecisive.
sources: Sennacherib's annals (Chicago and Taylor prisms); Babylonian Chronicle (ABC 1); en.wikipedia Battle of Halule; Encyclopaedia Iranica
note: Contingent: the Persians were a small part of Elam's coalition. Whether Parsuash here means the Persians of Fars or the Zagros Parsua, and whether Anzan was then Persian-ruled, is debated; Wikipedia's infobox names Achaemenes as a commander, an unproven modern identification, and gives an 'Assyrian victory' while its text calls the battle indecisive.
qbasis: Persians (Anshan): an Iranian-led state

name: Hubushna (Esarhaddon v Teushpa)
label: Hubushna
date: c. 679 BCE (early in Esarhaddon's reign; exact year uncertain)
place: Hubushna (Hupisna), on the Cilician/Cappadocian border near Eregli, Turkey
commanders_a: Esarhaddon (or a field commander in his name)
result_basis: Esarhaddon's prism inscriptions claim that he defeated Teushpa the Cimmerian in the land of Hubushna.
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Esarhaddon Nineveh Prism A (Borger, Die Inschriften Asarhaddons); Ivantchik 1993; Diakonoff, CHI 2 (1985)
note: Teushpa is the first Cimmerian leader named in cuneiform; the report is a royal claim, so the scale of the fighting is unknown. Cimmerian speech is unclassified (probably Iranian, perhaps not).

name: Esarhaddon v Ishpakaia (Scythians and Mannaeans)
label: Esarhaddon v Ishpakaia
date: c. 676-675 BCE (Assyrian dating; Schmitt gives c. 675)
war: Esarhaddon's wars on the north-eastern frontier
place: Mannaean country and the Hubuskia border, in the Median borderlands of north-western Iran (site unknown)
commanders_b: Ishpakaia the Scythian (killed); Ahsheri, king of the Mannaeans
result_basis: Esarhaddon's inscriptions say that he defeated the Ashkuzai (Scythian) force and killed Ishpakaia, who had joined the Mannaeans against Assyria.
sources: Esarhaddon Nineveh Prism A and the Babylon Prism; Assyrian oracle queries (SAA 4); Ivantchik 1993; Diakonoff 1985; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishpakaia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scythians
note: This is the first Scythian leader named in Assyrian sources. The Scythians were allies of the Mannaeans, with Cimmerians possibly on the same side; the fight itself is told only in royal inscriptions, and the place is given variously as Mannaean or Median territory.

name: Kishassu (c. 672 BC)
label: Kishassu (c. 672 BC)
date: c. 672 BC (the oracle queries are dated c. 672-669)
commanders_a: Kashtaritu (city lord of Kar-kashshi), Mamitiarshu (city lord of the Medes), Dusanni of Saparda
persian_force: Kashtaritu's Medes of Kar-kashshi and the Medes of Mamitiarshu, with Mannaean, Cimmerian and Saparda allies; no numbers survive.
iranian_note: The queries name Median leaders (Kashtaritu, Mamitiarshu) at the head of the coalition; the languages of the Mannaean, Cimmerian and Saparda allies are uncertain.
result_basis: Esarhaddon's oracle queries only ask whether Kashtaritu's coalition would take Kishassu and its neighbours and record no result, though the revolt as a whole freed the Medes from Assyrian rule (Iranica).
borderline: known only from oracle queries that name the threatened towns but record no fighting or result; not a named battle in modern lists
doubt: The sources consulted do not give the result, so the battle is listed but not scored. Borderline: known only from oracle queries that name the threatened towns but record no fighting or result; not a named battle in modern lists.
sources: Esarhaddon's oracle queries to Shamash (Starr, SAA 4); Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Media'; en.wikipedia Kashtariti
note: Kishassu is usually taken as the later spelling of Kishesim, whose Sagbat district held Kashtaritu's seat Kar-kashshi; Iranica says the rebels attacked the fortresses of Harhar and Kishesim. Kashtaritu has been identified with Herodotus' Phraortes, but many reject this. Wikipedia also counts Scythians in his alliance and mentions a planned raid on Kilman.
qbasis: Media: an Iranian-led state

name: Nineveh (Cyaxares, c. 653 BC)
label: Nineveh (Cyaxares, c. 653 BC)
date: c. 653 BC (shortly after Phraortes' death; some put it c. 625)
persian_force: Cyaxares' army, which Herodotus says he gathered from all his subjects and was the first to divide into separate units of spearmen, archers and horsemen.
iranian_note: Herodotus' Cyaxares led the Medes and their subject peoples, chiefly the Persians; no contingents are named.
result_basis: Herodotus says Cyaxares met and defeated the Assyrians and then sat down before Nineveh; the siege was broken off only when the Scythians arrived.
borderline: no conventional name; the field battle is recorded in a single clause of Herodotus
doubt: Traditional: Known only from Herodotus 1. Borderline: no conventional name; the field battle is recorded in a single clause of Herodotus.
sources: Herodotus 1.103; en.wikipedia Cyaxares
note: Herodotus makes the attack revenge for Phraortes. The siege that followed is not scored separately: it was abandoned because of the Scythian invasion, not an Assyrian defence (see the next entry).
qbasis: Media: an Iranian-led state

name: Nineveh (Phraortes, c. 653 BC)
label: Nineveh (Phraortes, c. 653 BC)
date: c. 653 BC (traditional dating of Phraortes' death; c. 625 if Herodotus' reign lengths are counted back from 550 without a separate Scythian interval)
commanders_a: unknown (the Assyrian king, Ashurbanipal by the usual dating)
persian_force: The Median army of Phraortes, who according to Herodotus had first subdued the Persians and other peoples of Asia; no units or numbers are given.
iranian_note: Herodotus' Median kingdom drew on the Medes and the subject Persians; nothing more is recorded.
losses_b: Phraortes and most of his army (Herodotus)
result_basis: Herodotus says Phraortes perished with most of his army in his campaign against the Assyrians of Nineveh.
borderline: no conventional name: Herodotus names the enemy (the Assyrians of Nineveh) but not the site
doubt: Traditional: Known only from Herodotus 1. Borderline: no conventional name: Herodotus names the enemy (the Assyrians of Nineveh) but not the site.
sources: Herodotus 1.102; en.wikipedia Phraortes
note: Wikipedia (Phraortes) gives his reign as c. 675-653 and says he was killed by the Assyrian king, generally taken to be Ashurbanipal.
qbasis: Media: an Iranian-led state

name: Scythian invasion of Media
label: Scythian invasion of Media
date: c. 653 BC (Wikipedia dates Scythian rule over Media c. 653-625; Iranica c. 653/635-625/615)
persian_force: Cyaxares' Median army, called back from the siege of Nineveh; Herodotus gives no detail.
iranian_note: The army was that of the Median kingdom, Medes with subject Persians; no units are named.
result_basis: Herodotus says the Medes met the Scythians, were beaten in the battle and lost their rule.
borderline: the name is Wikipedia's title for the war; the battle itself has no name or site
doubt: Traditional: Known only from Herodotus 1. Borderline: the name is Wikipedia's title for the war; the battle itself has no name or site.
sources: Herodotus 1.103-106; en.wikipedia Scythian invasion of Media; Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Media'
note: Herodotus says the Scythians, pursuing the Cimmerians, came upon Cyaxares while he was besieging Nineveh. Cyaxares later ended Scythian rule by murdering their leaders at a banquet (a massacre, not a battle; not an entry). Wikipedia's infobox result ('Medes victory') contradicts its own text.
qbasis: Media: an Iranian-led state

name: Sardis (Cimmerian capture, c. 652 BC)
label: Sardis
date: c. 652 BCE (other dates for Gyges' death and the sack: c. 644 or c. 637 BCE)
commanders_b: Gyges (killed in the war); his son Ardys
result_basis: Strabo says Lygdamis' Cimmerians took Sardis except the citadel; Ashurbanipal's inscriptions say that they killed Gyges.
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Strabo 1.3.21, 13.4.8; Herodotus 1.6, 1.15; Callinus fr. 5a; Ashurbanipal's prisms (Rassam cylinder, on Gyges); Ivantchik 1993
note: The Lydian king Gyges died fighting the Cimmerians; the Lydians kept the acropolis and the Cimmerians later withdrew or were driven out (Ardys, Alyattes). The Cimmerians' Iranian speech is uncertain, so this is a doubtful qualifier.

name: Arrapha
label: Arrapha
war: Medo-Babylonian conquest of the Assyrian Empire
persian_force: The Median army of Cyaxares; the chronicle gives no detail of units or numbers.
iranian_note: The Babylonian Chronicle names the attackers as Medes.
result_basis: The Medes took Arrapha and its region and used it as their base against Assyria in 614; the chronicle line itself is broken.
borderline: the chronicle breaks off after 'the Medes went down to Arrapha'; the capture is inferred and no fighting is described
doubt: Borderline: the chronicle breaks off after 'the Medes went down to Arrapha'; the capture is inferred and no fighting is described.
sources: Babylonian Chronicle ABC 3 (Fall of Nineveh Chronicle), year 11; en.wikipedia Sinsharishkun; Cyaxares; Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Media'
note: Not the Babylonian victory over the Assyrians at Madanu near Arrapha in 616, in which no Medes are recorded. Wikipedia (Sinsharishkun) dates the Median move to late 615 or 614.
qbasis: Media: an Iranian-led state

name: Assur (siege)
label: Assur (siege)
war: Medo-Babylonian conquest of the Assyrian Empire
persian_force: Cyaxares' Median army; the chronicle gives no numbers or units.
iranian_note: The chronicle says the Mede encamped against Assur and did battle against the city; the Babylonians took no part.
losses_b: heavy: the chronicle says the Medes 'inflicted a terrible defeat on a great people'
result_basis: Assur fell to the Medes, who stormed and sacked it; Nabopolassar's Babylonians arrived only after the city had fallen.
sources: Babylonian Chronicle ABC 3, year 12; en.wikipedia Fall of Assur; Sinsharishkun; Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Media'
note: Wikipedia titles it 'Fall of Assur'. Cyaxares and Nabopolassar met by the city and made their alliance, later sealed by the marriage of Nebuchadnezzar and Amytis.
qbasis: Media: an Iranian-led state

name: Tarbisu
label: Tarbisu
war: Medo-Babylonian conquest of the Assyrian Empire
place: Tarbisu (Sherif Khan, just north of Nineveh), Iraq
persian_force: Cyaxares' Median army; no units or numbers are recorded.
iranian_note: The Babylonian Chronicle names the attackers as Medes.
result_basis: The chronicle records that the Medes captured Tarbisu, a city in the district of Nineveh.
borderline: a capture recorded in one line of the chronicle; the fighting is not described
doubt: Borderline: a capture recorded in one line of the chronicle; the fighting is not described.
sources: Babylonian Chronicle ABC 3, year 12; en.wikipedia Sinsharishkun; Cyaxares; Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Media'
note: The broken line before it is usually restored as a Median march on Nineveh in the same month (Wikipedia's Sinsharishkun adds Nimrud; Cyaxares calls it a feint); Nineveh did not fall and that attack is not a separate entry. Wikipedia's article on the war misdates Tarbisu to 615.
qbasis: Media: an Iranian-led state

name: Nineveh (siege, 612 BC)
label: Nineveh (siege, 612 BC)
date: Simanu to Abu (June-August) 612 BC; the city fell in August
war: Medo-Babylonian conquest of the Assyrian Empire
persian_force: Cyaxares' Median army (the Umman-manda of the chronicle), which Iranica and Wikipedia say played the major part; whether Scythian or other steppe contingents served with it is debated.
iranian_note: The chronicle's Umman-manda here are the Medes under their king; a Scythian share, also Iranian-speaking, is possible but unproven.
losses_b: unknown; the city was sacked and burned
result_basis: Nineveh fell to the Medes and Babylonians in August 612 after a three-month siege.
sources: Babylonian Chronicle ABC 3, year 14; Herodotus 1.106; en.wikipedia Battle of Nineveh (612 BC); Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Media'
note: Wikipedia titles it 'Fall of Nineveh' and lists Scythians as allies of the Babylonians, without detail. Sinsharishkun is commonly held to have died in the defence; Ashur-uballit II then took the throne at Harran.
qbasis: Media: an Iranian-led state

name: Harran (siege)
label: Harran (siege)
date: Arahsamnu (November) 610 BC; the city was taken in 610 or early 609
war: Medo-Babylonian conquest of the Assyrian Empire
commanders_a: Nabopolassar; the Umman-manda (Medes; Wikipedia names Cyaxares)
persian_force: The Umman-manda (Medes), who came to help the king of Akkad and joined their army to his as a separate force; no numbers.
iranian_note: The chronicle names the Umman-manda, the Medes, as the Babylonians' partners.
result_basis: Ashur-uballit and his Egyptian allies abandoned Harran, which the Babylonians and Medes then captured and plundered.
borderline: the defenders fled before the main attack; one translation of the chronicle has the Babylonian king fight a battle before taking the city
doubt: Borderline: the defenders fled before the main attack; one translation of the chronicle has the Babylonian king fight a battle before taking the city.
sources: Babylonian Chronicle ABC 3, year 16; en.wikipedia Fall of Harran; Medo-Babylonian conquest of the Assyrian Empire; Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Media'
note: The Medes plundered the temple Ehulhul and went home (Iranica). In 609 Ashur-uballit and an Egyptian army besieged the Babylonian garrison of Harran until Ululu and failed; no Median force is recorded then, so that siege is not an entry. Wikipedia's 'Fall of Harran' treats 610-609 as one event.
qbasis: Media: an Iranian-led state

name: Scythian slaves' revolt (Herodotus)
label: Scythian slaves' revolt
date: c. 625-585 BCE (after the Scythians' return from Asia; no firm date)
place: the Scythian ditch between the Tauric mountains and Lake Maeotis, Crimea/steppe (site unknown)
result_basis: Herodotus says the Scythians failed with spears and bows but routed the slaves' sons by charging with whips.
doubt: Traditional: known only from a doubtful tradition.
sources: Herodotus 4.1-4
note: Told by Herodotus as a story of the Scythians' return from their 28 years in Asia. It is more legend than record, but it is a named engagement of Scythians against Scythians.

name: Halys
label: Halys
date: 28 May 585 BC (the date of the solar eclipse; alternatives 582 or 581 BC, or a lunar eclipse in 609 or 587)
place: near the Halys (Kizilirmak) river (site unknown), Turkey
persian_force: Cyaxares' army after the conquest of Assyria; Herodotus gives no composition, so presumably the Median spearmen, archers and horsemen with contingents of subject peoples.
iranian_note: The Median kingdom's army was raised from the Medes and their Iranian subjects, with Urartian and other conquered peoples; no source names the units.
result_basis: Herodotus says the fighting stopped when day turned to night and both sides at once made peace, with no victor.
doubt: Traditional: Known only from Herodotus 1.
sources: Herodotus 1.73-74; en.wikipedia Eclipse of Thales; Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Media'
note: Also called the Battle of the Eclipse. The war lasted five years with victories on both sides (Herodotus). Syennesis of Cilicia and Labynetus of Babylon mediated a peace fixing the Halys as the border, sealed by the marriage of Astyages and Aryenis, daughter of Alyattes. Herodotus does not name the site; the Halys is an assumption. Iranica gives 29 May.
qbasis: Media: an Iranian-led state

name: Hyrba
label: Hyrba
date: 552 BC (uncertain; Wikipedia gives winter-spring 552; some accounts put all the battles of the revolt in 550)
place: Hyrba (unidentified, on the road from Media into Persis), Iran
commanders_b: unnamed commander of Astyages' horsemen (Nicolaus); Harpagus in Herodotus' first battle
persian_force: Cyrus' side: the inhabitants of Hyrba, whom he armed, and Persian troops (1,000 horse and 5,000 foot were asked of his father); Astyages' side: 300 Median horsemen.
iranian_note: Both sides were Iranian: Persians of Hyrba and Persis against Median cavalry.
strength_a: 1,000 cavalry and 5,000 infantry requested from Persia (Nicolaus; whether they fought is uncertain)
result_basis: In Nicolaus' account Cyrus' men killed 250 of the 300 Median horsemen sent after him and the rest fled.
doubt: Traditional: Known only from Nicolaus of Damascus (after Ctesias), whose story of Cyrus' revolt is full of legendary elements; Herodotus has instead a first battle in which Harpagus and most of the Medes went over to Cyrus.
sources: Nicolaus of Damascus, FGrH 90 F66; Herodotus 1.127; en.wikipedia Battle of Hyrba; Medo-Persian conflict
note: Civil: Persians (Anshan) against Media. Ctesias (as summarised by Wikipedia) has Cyrus defeat the Medes near Hyrba before Astyages won the next fight. Iranica (Astyages) counts only three battles in Nicolaus and Justin, so Hyrba is the preliminary clash.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Persian Border
label: Persian Border
place: on the border of Media and Persis, on the road from Ecbatana to Pasargadae (site unknown), Iran
commanders_b: Cyrus, Oebares, Cyrus' father (Atradates in Nicolaus; Cambyses I in Wikipedia), who died of his wounds or in captivity
persian_force: Astyages' Median army, said to be enormous, against Cyrus' Persian tribal levy; no credible figures survive.
iranian_note: Both armies were Iranian: the Median royal army against the Persian tribes.
result_basis: After two days' fighting the Persians fell back to Pasargadae and Astyages took the town they had defended, so the Medes held the field (Nicolaus).
doubt: Traditional: Known only from Nicolaus of Damascus (after Ctesias); Polyaenus and Justin also speak of early Persian defeats, but the details are legendary and the battle is absent from the Babylonian sources.
sources: Nicolaus of Damascus, FGrH 90 F66; Polyaenus 7.6; Justin 1.6; en.wikipedia Battle of the Persian Border; Medo-Persian conflict; Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Astyages'
note: Civil: Media against the Persians (Anshan). Wikipedia's article on this battle gives a 'Persian victory' (a first-day success) and an infobox of 60,000 horse and 3,000 chariots for the Medes and 50,000 horse and 100 chariots for the Persians, figures of unclear origin; the Medo-Persian conflict article and Iranica (Cyrus lost the first two battles) support the Median victory followed here.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Ecbatana (550 BC)
label: Ecbatana (550 BC)
commanders_b: Astyages (already captured; in Ctesias hiding in the palace)
persian_force: Cyrus' Persian army with the Median troops who had gone over to him; nothing is known of any defenders.
iranian_note: Cyrus' army was the Persian tribal levy reinforced by Median deserters.
result_basis: Cyrus marched to Ecbatana and carried off its treasure to Anshan (Nabonidus Chronicle); no defence or fighting is recorded.
borderline: a capture after the Median army's collapse; no fighting is recorded (Wikipedia's Persian Revolt suggests the walls may have allowed some resistance)
doubt: Borderline: a capture after the Median army's collapse; no fighting is recorded (Wikipedia's Persian Revolt suggests the walls may have allowed some resistance).
sources: Nabonidus Chronicle (ABC 7) ii 1-4; Ctesias (Photius); en.wikipedia Medo-Persian conflict; Persian Revolt; Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Astyages'
note: Civil: Persians (Anshan) against Media. In Ctesias Astyages hid in the palace with his daughter Amytis and her husband Spitamas; Oebares carried the treasure to Persia. Ecbatana became an Achaemenid royal capital.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Pasargadae
label: Pasargadae
date: 550 BC (the Nabonidus Chronicle dates Astyages' fall to Nabonidus' sixth year, 550/549)
place: near Pasargadae (perhaps the Morghab plain), Iran
persian_force: Cyrus' Persian tribal levy (Herodotus 1.125: the Pasargadae, Maraphii and Maspii, the farming tribes and the nomad Dai, Mardi, Dropici and Sagartii) with Median deserters, against Astyages' Median royal army.
iranian_note: Both armies were Iranian: Herodotus names the Persian tribes Cyrus raised, and the Medes opposed them.
result_basis: On the second day the Persians, shamed by their women on the mountain, routed the Medes and took their camp (Nicolaus), and Strabo too places Cyrus' last victory over Astyages at Pasargadae.
doubt: Traditional: The battle story (two days, the women baring themselves to shame the fleeing men) comes from Nicolaus of Damascus after Ctesias, with echoes in Polyaenus, Justin and Plutarch, and is legendary; the decisive defeat and capture of Astyages c.
sources: Nicolaus of Damascus, FGrH 90 F66; Herodotus 1.127-128; Strabo 15.3.8; Polyaenus 7.6, 7.45; Justin 1.6; Nabonidus Chronicle (ABC 7) ii 1-4; Sippar cylinder of Nabonidus; en.wikipedia Medo-Persian conflict; Persian Revolt; Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Astyages'
note: Civil: Persians (Anshan) against Media. Herodotus (1.128) says Astyages armed the remaining Medes, was defeated and captured; the Nabonidus Chronicle says his army mutinied and handed him over to Cyrus; the Sippar cylinder that Cyrus 'scattered the large army of the Umman-manda with his small army'. Wikipedia's campaign box lists a 'Siege of Pasargadae Hill' (no article), apparently the mountain phase of this battle, which is not a separate entry here. Accounts differ on whether Astyages was taken in this battle, in a later fight or hiding at Ecbatana.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Pteria
label: Pteria
date: autumn 547 BC (traditional date; possibly later in the 540s)
place: Pteria (probably Kerkenes Dag, near Sorgun), Turkey
persian_force: Cyrus's Persians and Medes, joined by levies of 'all who dwelt in the lands between' gathered on the march (Herodotus 1.76); no numbers in the sources.
iranian_note: Herodotus names only Cyrus's own (Persian and Median) army and the peoples picked up on the march through Media, Armenia and Cappadocia.
losses_a: heavy (Herodotus: many fell on both sides)
result_basis: Night parted the armies with neither side victorious (Herodotus 1.76); Croesus marched back to Sardis the next day, which is a strategic matter.
sources: Herodotus 1.76-77; Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander; en.wikipedia Battle of Pteria
note: Pteria is usually identified with Kerkenes Dag (some prefer Bogazkoy). Wikipedia's 95,000 Lydians and 20,000 Persians are not in Herodotus. The 547 date rests on a now doubted reading of the Nabonidus Chronicle; many date the Lydian war c. 547-541.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Sardis (siege, 547 BC)
label: Sardis (siege, 547 BC)
date: late 547 BC or 546 BC (14 days; possibly later in the 540s)
commanders_a: Cyrus II; Hyroeades the Mardian led the escalade
persian_force: Cyrus's Persian and Median army after the victory before Sardis; the assault was led by Hyroeades of the Mardi, a Persian mountain tribe (Herodotus 1.84).
iranian_note: Herodotus speaks of Cyrus's Persians and names a Mardian (Persian tribesman) as first on the wall.
result_basis: Sardis fell to the besiegers on the fourteenth day, when Persians climbed an unguarded stretch of the acropolis cliff (Herodotus 1.84).
sources: Herodotus 1.80-87; Xenophon, Cyropaedia 7.2; Nabonidus Chronicle ii.15-18 (disputed); en.wikipedia Siege of Sardis (547 BC)
note: The Nabonidus Chronicle entry for 547 (Cyrus marched to 'Lu-...' and killed its king) was long read as Lydia; the reading is now doubted, so the fall of Sardis may date anywhere from 547 to c. 541. Herodotus has Croesus spared on the pyre.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Thymbra
label: Thymbra
date: late 547 BC (traditional date; possibly later in the 540s)
place: the plain before Sardis (Thymbra in Xenophon), near Sart, Turkey
persian_force: Persian infantry and cavalry with the baggage camels, mounted by men armed as horsemen, placed in front on Harpagus' advice (Herodotus 1.80); Xenophon adds Medes, Armenians, Hyrcanians, Arabs, scythed chariots and siege towers.
iranian_note: Herodotus's army is Cyrus's Persians; Xenophon's adds Armenian, Hyrcanian and Arab allies around a Persian and Median core.
result_basis: The Lydian cavalry was broken (by the smell of the camels, in Herodotus) and the Lydians fled into Sardis, leaving the field to the Persians.
doubt: Traditional: A battle on the plain before Sardis is told by Herodotus (1.
sources: Herodotus 1.79-80; Xenophon, Cyropaedia 6.2-7.1; en.wikipedia Battle of Thymbra
note: Modern estimates (Wikipedia) put the Persians at 20,000-50,000. Wikipedia lists Arab, Babylonian and Egyptian mercenaries with Croesus (Xenophon); Herodotus says Croesus had dismissed his mercenaries and fought with the Lydians alone. Xenophon's Egyptians later took service with Cyrus.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Phocaea (siege)
label: Phocaea (siege)
persian_force: Harpagus' army, the Persian and Median force left in Asia Minor after the Lydian war; it took the Ionian cities by mounds (Herodotus 1.162-164). Not described further.
iranian_note: Harpagus was a Mede commanding Cyrus's western army; Herodotus says Ionian and Aeolian levies were added only after Ionia was subdued.
result_basis: The city fell: under siege by a mound, the Phocaeans sailed away during a truce and Harpagus occupied the empty town (Herodotus 1.164).
borderline: a siege with siege works but no recorded assault; the city was abandoned
doubt: Borderline: a siege with siege works but no recorded assault; the city was abandoned.
sources: Herodotus 1.162-167; en.wikipedia Phocaea
note: Phocaea is the city in the Greek list; most Phocaeans went to Chios and then to Alalia in Corsica, later founding Elea (the battle of Alalia against Carthaginians and Etruscans involved no Persians).
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Sardis (siege, 546 BC)
label: Sardis (siege, 546 BC)
date: 546 BC or 545 BC (the year after the fall of Sardis)
commanders_a: Tabalus (commander of the acropolis); Mazares (relief army)
persian_force: Tabalus' Persian garrison shut in the acropolis, relieved by an army under the Mede Mazares sent by Cyrus (Herodotus 1.153-157).
iranian_note: The garrison commander was a Persian and the relief army was led by a Mede; neither force is described.
result_basis: The siege was abandoned: Pactyes fled to Cyme at the approach of Mazares' relief army, and Tabalus kept the acropolis (Herodotus 1.154-157).
borderline: a siege with little recorded fighting
doubt: Borderline: a siege with little recorded fighting.
sources: Herodotus 1.153-161
note: Pactyes, a Lydian in charge of Croesus's treasure, hired mercenaries on the coast and raised the coastal Greeks. Mazares then enslaved Priene and plundered the Maeander plain and Magnesia (Herodotus 1.161); no battle is recorded there.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Cyrus v Amorges (Saka)
label: Cyrus v Amorges
date: c. 545-540 BCE (Ctesias' story, no firm date)
war: Cyrus the Great's wars in Central Asia
place: Saka country east of the Caspian (site not given by Ctesias)
commanders_b: Amorges (Amorges, king of the Saka); his wife Sparethra
result_basis: Ctesias says that Cyrus took Amorges but that Sparethra then defeated the Persians and recovered him, and the two peoples made peace as allies.
doubt: Traditional: known only from a doubtful tradition.
sources: Ctesias, Persica (Photius' epitome; the Saka and Amorges episode); Polyaenus, Strategemata, book 7 (Cyrus); Lenfant, Ctesias de Cnide (2004); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saka
note: Ctesias is an unreliable source and Herodotus has no such war; the Saka here are the Haumavarga of Amorges, not the Massagetae of Tomyris. Included because the Saka are named opponents and Cyrus (Persian) leads the other side.

name: Teos (siege)
label: Teos (siege)
persian_force: Harpagus' Persian and Median army (not described).
iranian_note: Same army as at Phocaea; Herodotus does not describe it.
result_basis: Harpagus took the walls by a mound, and the Teians took ship and sailed off to found Abdera in Thrace (Herodotus 1.168).
borderline: fighting is implied (the wall taken by a mound) but not described
doubt: Borderline: fighting is implied (the wall taken by a mound) but not described.
sources: Herodotus 1.168-169
note: Herodotus adds that the other Ionians except Miletus fought Harpagus city by city and were defeated (1.169); those fights are unnamed and not listed.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Lide (siege)
label: Lide (siege)
place: Mount Lide, near Pedasa (Gokceler, near Bodrum), Turkey
persian_force: Harpagus' Persian and Median army with the Ionian and Aeolian levies he compelled to serve against the Carians, Caunians and Lycians (Herodotus 1.171).
iranian_note: Herodotus names Ionian and Aeolian Greek levies alongside Harpagus' Iranian army; the proportions are not recorded.
result_basis: The Pedasians held out for a long time on fortified Mount Lide but were finally subdued (Herodotus 1.175).
sources: Herodotus 1.171, 1.175
note: The Pedasians were the only Carians to resist; the site of Mount Lide is uncertain (near Pedasa on the Bodrum peninsula). Herodotus dates nothing in Harpagus' campaign; it is placed c. 546-540 BC.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Caunus (siege, 540 BC)
label: Caunus (siege, 540 BC)
persian_force: Harpagus' Persian and Median army with Ionian and Aeolian levies (Herodotus 1.171).
iranian_note: As at Xanthos: Iranian army with named Greek levies; proportions unknown.
losses_b: most of the defenders (Herodotus: 'for the most part' they did as the Lycians)
result_basis: The Caunians, like the Lycians of Xanthos, fought to the end and their city fell (Herodotus 1.176).
borderline: known from one sentence of Herodotus
doubt: Borderline: known from one sentence of Herodotus.
sources: Herodotus 1.172, 1.176
note: Herodotus treats the Caunians as distinct from the Carians (they claimed Cretan origin) though they spoke Carian; listed under Carians. The year in the name distinguishes it from any later Caunus entry (e.g. 396 BC).
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Xanthos (siege)
label: Xanthos (siege)
persian_force: Harpagus' Persian and Median army with Ionian and Aeolian levies (Herodotus 1.171, 1.176).
iranian_note: Herodotus names Ionian and Aeolian levies with Harpagus' Iranian army; proportions unknown.
losses_b: all the fighting men killed; only 80 families who were away survived (Herodotus 1.176)
result_basis: The Lycians were beaten on the Xanthian plain, burned their families in the acropolis and died in a last sally, and Xanthos fell (Herodotus 1.176).
sources: Herodotus 1.171, 1.176; en.wikipedia Xanthos
note: A field battle on the plain north of the city followed by a siege and last stand; one entry. Date c. 540 (Harpagus' campaign is undated, c. 546-540).
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Opis
label: Opis
date: month Tashritu (late September or early October) 539 BC, before 10 October
place: Opis, on the Tigris (perhaps Tell al-Mujailat, southeast of Baghdad), Iraq
commanders_a: Cyrus II; Ugbaru (Gobryas), governor of Gutium
persian_force: Cyrus's army of Persians and Medes, with the troops of Gutium under Ugbaru (Gobryas), a Babylonian governor who had gone over to Cyrus (Nabonidus Chronicle).
iranian_note: The Chronicle names only 'the army of Cyrus' and the army of Gutium; the royal army was Persian and Median.
result_basis: The Babylonian army was defeated at Opis and the town plundered (Nabonidus Chronicle iii.12-14); Sippar surrendered without battle a few days later.
sources: Nabonidus Chronicle iii.12-16; Cyrus Cylinder; en.wikipedia Battle of Opis; Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander
note: Translators disagree whether the Chronicle's massacre of 'the people of Akkad' was Cyrus's work or Nabonidus's. Wikipedia's 70,000 Persians attributed to Herodotus is not reliable (Herodotus does not mention Opis). The site of Opis is uncertain.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Babylon (siege, 539 BC)
label: Babylon (siege, 539 BC)
date: 12 October 539 BC (16 Tashritu); Cyrus entered on 29 October
persian_force: Cyrus's Persian and Median army with Ugbaru's troops of Gutium, who made the entry (Nabonidus Chronicle iii.15-16).
iranian_note: As at Opis; the Gutian contingent's language is unknown.
result_basis: Babylon fell: the army of Gutium under Ugbaru entered the city on 16 Tashritu (12 October 539) and Nabonidus was taken.
borderline: the Nabonidus Chronicle and Cyrus Cylinder say the city was taken 'without battle'; Herodotus and Xenophon tell of a siege and a night entry along the lowered Euphrates
doubt: Borderline: the Nabonidus Chronicle and Cyrus Cylinder say the city was taken 'without battle'; Herodotus and Xenophon tell of a siege and a night entry along the lowered Euphrates.
sources: Nabonidus Chronicle iii.15-18; Cyrus Cylinder; Herodotus 1.188-191; Xenophon, Cyropaedia 7.5; Daniel 5; en.wikipedia Fall of Babylon
note: Wikipedia title: Fall of Babylon. Briant doubts the 'without battle' claim as Persian court propaganda. Xenophon and Daniel have Belshazzar killed that night; unconfirmed.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Massagetae (530 BC)
label: Massagetae (530 BC)
date: 530 BC (between August and December, from the Babylonian dating of Cyrus's death)
place: beyond the Araxes (probably the Syr Darya), Kazakhstan
persian_force: Cyrus's royal army of Persians and Medes (not described beyond 'the Persians'; Herodotus 1.214).
iranian_note: No contingents are named; the royal army was Persian and Median at its core.
losses_b: most of the Persian army and Cyrus (Herodotus)
result_basis: In Herodotus's account the Massagetae won the field, destroying most of the Persian army and killing Cyrus (1.214).
doubt: Traditional: Herodotus says his version was the most credible of several; Ctesias has Cyrus mortally wounded fighting the Derbices and their Indians, Berossus has him fall against the Dahae, Xenophon has him die in bed.
sources: Herodotus 1.205-216; Ctesias, Persica (Photius' epitome); Berossus; Xenophon, Cyropaedia 8.7; en.wikipedia Tomyris, Cyrus the Great
note: In Ctesias the Derbices, with elephants and Indian allies, wound Cyrus, but the Saka of Amorges come to his aid and the Persians win; Cyrus dies three days later. Under Herodotus's version, which this entry follows, the Massagetae won. Site unknown (Araxes = Syr Darya, Amu Darya or Uzboy).
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Massagetae (camp ambush, 530 BC)
label: Massagetae (camp ambush, 530 BC)
place: beyond the Araxes (probably the Syr Darya), Kazakhstan
persian_force: Cyrus's royal army of Persians and Medes; the weakest part was left in the camp with the feast and was killed before the main body returned (Herodotus 1.207-211).
iranian_note: Herodotus speaks only of 'the Persians'; Cyrus's army was Persian and Median at its core.
strength_b: a third of the Massagetae army (Herodotus)
losses_a: the troops left in the camp
result_basis: The Persians returned on the drunken Massagetae in the captured camp, killed many and took Spargapises and many others prisoner (Herodotus 1.211).
borderline: an episode without a conventional name
doubt: Traditional: Known only from Herodotus, who tells a folktale-like ruse (a camp left with wine) in a campaign of which he admits several versions; Ctesias and Berossus tell Cyrus's last war differently. Borderline: an episode without a conventional name.
sources: Herodotus 1.205-211
note: Herodotus's Araxes has been taken as the Syr Darya, the Amu Darya or the Uzboy; the site is unknown. Spargapises was Tomyris' son.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Gaza (siege, 525 BC)
label: Gaza (siege, 525 BC)
date: probably 526-525 BC (Cambyses' march on Egypt); undated
persian_force: Presumably Cambyses' invasion army (Persians and Medes with subject levies); not described.
iranian_note: Inferred from the make-up of Cambyses' army; the source says nothing.
result_basis: Polybius says only that Gaza alone withstood a siege when the Persians invaded; it was under Persian rule afterwards, but whether it fell or came to terms is not recorded.
borderline: known only from a passing remark of Polybius; date, commander and outcome are not stated
doubt: The sources consulted do not give the result, so the battle is listed but not scored. Borderline: known only from a passing remark of Polybius; date, commander and outcome are not stated.
sources: Polybius 16.22a; Herodotus 3.5; en.wikipedia Battle of Pelusium
note: Gaza (Herodotus' Cadytis) was a Philistine city, so 'Philistines' is used as the opponent (a new name). Wikipedia's History of Gaza has a confused entry on a failed Persian attack in 529 BC; not used.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Memphis (siege, 525 BC)
label: Memphis (siege, 525 BC)
persian_force: Cambyses' Persian and Median army with Greek subjects and a river fleet (a Mytilenean ship carried the herald; Herodotus 3.13).
iranian_note: Same army as at Pelusium; the Mytilenean ship's crew were Greek subjects.
losses_a: a Persian herald and the 200 men of a Mytilenean ship, killed before the siege
losses_b: 2,000 young Egyptian nobles executed after the fall, ten for each Mytilenean (Herodotus 3.14)
result_basis: Memphis surrendered after a siege and Psamtik III was captured (Herodotus 3.13).
sources: Herodotus 3.13-15; en.wikipedia Battle of Pelusium, First Achaemenid conquest of Egypt
note: Wikipedia's conquest article calls it 'a long siege'. The later expeditions to the Ammonians (Siwa) and to Kush ended without battles (the army lost in the sand, the march abandoned for hunger) and are not listed.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Pelusium (525 BC)
label: Pelusium (525 BC)
persian_force: Cambyses' Persian and Median army with his Ionian and Aeolian Greek subjects (Herodotus 3.1), backed by a Phoenician, Cypriot and Ionian fleet; the Arab king of the desert road supplied water (Herodotus 3.4-9, 3.19).
iranian_note: Herodotus names Greek subjects and Phoenician and Cypriot ships, but the land army's core was the Persian and Median royal army; no proportions are given.
result_basis: After a hard fight with many dead on both sides the Egyptians broke and fled to Memphis, leaving the field to the Persians (Herodotus 3.11).
sources: Herodotus 3.1-13; Ctesias, Persica; Polyaenus 7.9; en.wikipedia Battle of Pelusium, First Achaemenid conquest of Egypt
note: Psamtik's Greek and Carian mercenaries killed the sons of the turncoat Phanes before the battle (Herodotus 3.11). Polyaenus' story of cats held before the Persian ranks is late and doubtful. The Arabs (Qedar) gave passage and water across Sinai; Herodotus does not say they fought.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Sikayauvati
label: Sikayauvati
place: the fortress of Sikayauvati, district of Nisaya, Media (unlocated), Iran
commanders_a: Darius I with Intaphernes, Otanes, Gobryas, Hydarnes, Megabyzus and Ardumanish
persian_force: Darius and six Persian nobles 'with a few men' (Behistun §13).
iranian_note: All seven conspirators were Persian nobles, named in the inscription and in Herodotus.
strength_a: seven nobles and a few men
losses_b: Gaumata and his foremost followers killed
result_basis: Darius and his fellow conspirators killed Gaumata and his foremost followers in the fortress (Behistun §13).
borderline: a palace coup and assassination rather than a battle
doubt: Borderline: a palace coup and assassination rather than a battle.
sources: Behistun (DB) §§10-13; Herodotus 3.61-79; Ctesias; Livius.org Behistun translation; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Bisotun iii
note: Herodotus (3.76-79) describes a fight in the royal apartments; Ctesias names the Magus Sphendadates. Whether Gaumata was an impostor or the real Bardiya, son of Cyrus, is disputed. Nisaya is often placed near Bisotun; the coordinates are regional.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Izala
label: Izala
place: Izala district (Mount Izla, Tur Abdin), 'in Assyria', Turkey
persian_force: An army under the Persian Vaumisa sent by Darius; not described (the royal army was Persian and Median).
iranian_note: Inferred: detached from Darius's Persian and Median army under a Persian commander.
result_basis: The inscription says Vaumisa's army defeated the rebels who came against him (Behistun §29).
sources: Behistun (DB) §29; Livius.org Behistun translation
note: Vaumisa afterwards waited in Armenia for Darius, which suggests the victory was not decisive. The rebels belong to the inscription's Armenian section, though the battle was fought in Assyria; Izala is the Tur Abdin (Mount Izla) near Mardin.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Kapishakanish
label: Kapishakanish
place: the fortress of Kapishakanish, Arachosia (unlocated), Afghanistan
faction_b: Vahyazdata (the army he sent to Arachosia)
persian_force: Vivana's satrapal army of Arachosia, loyal to Darius; not described (presumably Arachosian levies and Persian garrison troops).
iranian_note: A satrapal army raised in Arachosia, an Iranian-speaking land, under a Persian satrap.
result_basis: Vivana's army defeated the rebel army at the fortress (Behistun §45).
sources: Behistun (DB) §45; Livius.org Behistun translation; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Bisotun iii
note: Vahyazdata, who claimed to be Bardiya, son of Cyrus, had risen in Persis and sent this army east. Kapishakanish has been compared with Kapisa (Bagram), which lies outside Arachosia; unlocated.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Tigris (522 BC)
label: Tigris (522 BC)
place: a crossing of the Tigris (unlocated, probably near Opis), Iraq
persian_force: Darius's own army, which he calls 'the Persian and Median army which was with me' (Behistun §25); some crossed on skins, some on camels and horses (§18).
iranian_note: The inscription describes Darius's field army of 522-521 as Persian and Median.
result_basis: Darius crossed the river on inflated skins, camels and horses and routed the Babylonian army holding the bank (Behistun §18).
sources: Behistun (DB) §§16-18; Livius.org Behistun translation; en.wikipedia Nebuchadnezzar III
note: Nidintu-Bel claimed to be Nebuchadnezzar, son of Nabonidus; his troops held the reed thickets and boats on the river. The site of the crossing is not named.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Zazana
label: Zazana
place: Zazana, on the Euphrates (unlocated, probably near Sippar), Iraq
persian_force: Darius's Persian and Median field army (Behistun §§19, 25).
iranian_note: As at the Tigris.
result_basis: The Babylonians were routed and partly driven into the river; Nidintu-Bel fled to Babylon with a few horsemen (Behistun §19).
sources: Behistun (DB) §§19-20; Livius.org Behistun translation; en.wikipedia Nebuchadnezzar III
note: Darius then took Babylon and Nidintu-Bel (§20); the first Babylonian tablet dated by Darius is of 22 December 522, so the city fell within days and no separate siege entry is made. Herodotus' 19-month siege and the Zopyrus story (3.150-160) fit neither Babylonian revolt.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Sagartia
label: Sagartia
date: 521 BC (undated in the inscription; Chiçantakhma was a prisoner by mid-July 521)
persian_force: A Persian and Median army under the Mede Takhmaspada (Behistun §33).
iranian_note: The inscription names the force as Persian and Median.
result_basis: Takhmaspada's army defeated the rebels and captured Chiçantakhma, who was impaled at Arbela (Behistun §33).
borderline: the inscription names no site or date
doubt: Borderline: the inscription names no site or date.
sources: Behistun (DB) §33; Livius.org Behistun translation; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Bisotun iii; en.wikipedia Behistun inscription
note: Chiçantakhma claimed descent from Cyaxares. Iranica (after Borger's reading of the Babylonian version) puts his capture by 15 July 521. Sagartia is variously placed in the Zagros or eastern Media; coordinates regional.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Marush
label: Marush
persian_force: A detachment of Darius's small 'Persian and Median army' under the Persian Hydarnes (Behistun §25).
iranian_note: The inscription calls it part of the Persian and Median army with Darius.
result_basis: The only source, the inscription, says Hydarnes' army defeated the Median rebels (Behistun §25); he then halted at Kampanda to wait for Darius.
sources: Behistun (DB) §§24-25; Livius.org Behistun translation
note: Many historians judge Marush indecisive, since Hydarnes waited at Kampanda until Darius came; the field test follows the inscription. Fravartish claimed to be Khshathrita of the line of Cyaxares.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Gandutava
label: Gandutava
faction_b: Vahyazdata (the army he sent to Arachosia)
persian_force: Vivana's satrapal army of Arachosia (not described).
iranian_note: As at Kapishakanish.
result_basis: Vivana again routed the rebel army (Behistun §46); its commander fled to the fortress of Arshada, where Vivana caught and killed him.
sources: Behistun (DB) §§46-47; Livius.org Behistun translation
note: The capture of the rebel commander at Arshada (§47) is a pursuit and capture, not listed separately.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Vishpauzatish
label: Vishpauzatish
faction_b: Parthian and Hyrcanian rebels (partisans of Fravartish)
persian_force: Vishtaspa's loyal forces of Parthia, before the Persian reinforcement arrived (Behistun §35).
iranian_note: The loyal army of the Parthian satrapy under the king's father; the inscription does not describe it.
result_basis: The inscription says Vishtaspa defeated the rebels (Behistun §35), though he needed reinforcements before he could finish the revolt.
sources: Behistun (DB) §35; Livius.org Behistun translation; en.wikipedia Patigrabana
note: Parthia and Hyrcania rose for Fravartish of Media. Historians often treat this battle as indecisive because Vishtaspa waited for reinforcements.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Kunduru
label: Kunduru
persian_force: Darius's own field army, 'the Persian and Median army which was with me' (Behistun §§25, 31).
iranian_note: The inscription calls Darius's army Persian and Median.
result_basis: Darius routed Fravartish's army; Fravartish fled towards Raga with a few horsemen and was caught and impaled at Ecbatana (Behistun §§31-32).
sources: Behistun (DB) §§31-32; Livius.org Behistun translation; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Bisotun iii
note: The decisive battle of the Median revolt. The identification of Kundurush with Kangavar is a guess.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Rakha
label: Rakha
persian_force: Part of 'the Persian and Median army which was with me', detached under the Persian Artavardiya while the rest went with Darius to Media (Behistun §41).
iranian_note: The inscription names the force as Persian and Median.
result_basis: Artavardiya defeated Vahyazdata, who fled with a few horsemen to Paishiyauvada (Behistun §41).
sources: Behistun (DB) §§40-41; Livius.org Behistun translation
note: Vahyazdata claimed to be Bardiya, son of Cyrus, and rose at Tarava in Yautiya with Persian support.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Tigra
label: Tigra
place: the stronghold of Tigra, Armenia (unlocated), Turkey
persian_force: Dadarshi's army (not described; see Zuzahya).
iranian_note: As at Zuzahya.
result_basis: The inscription says Dadarshi's army defeated the rebels at the stronghold (Behistun §27).
sources: Behistun (DB) §27; Livius.org Behistun translation; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Dadarsis
note: A battle at a stronghold, not described as a siege.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Zuzahya
label: Zuzahya
commanders_a: Dadarshi, an Armenian in Darius's service
persian_force: An army sent with Dadarshi; the inscription does not describe it (presumably royal Persian and Median troops, perhaps with loyal Armenians).
iranian_note: Inferred from Darius's royal army; the commander himself was Armenian (or Urartian).
result_basis: The inscription says Dadarshi's army defeated the rebels (Behistun §26).
sources: Behistun (DB) §26; Livius.org Behistun translation; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Dadarsis
note: Achaemenid Armina lay around Lake Van and the upper Euphrates; Zuzahya is unlocated (coordinates regional). The rebels' names are Urartian rather than Armenian (Iranica).
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Autiyara
label: Autiyara
persian_force: Vaumisa's army (not described; the royal army was Persian and Median).
iranian_note: Inferred, as at Izala.
result_basis: The inscription says Vaumisa's army defeated the rebels (Behistun §30); the Babylonian version counts the rebel dead and prisoners.
sources: Behistun (DB) §30; Babylonian version lines 55-57 ('On the rocks: the unfinished story of the Babylonian version of the Bisotun inscription', Iraq, 2025); Livius.org Behistun translation
note: Vaumisa then waited in Armenia until Darius came to Media, suggesting the revolt was not yet over.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Uyama
label: Uyama
place: the fortress of Uyama, Armenia (unlocated), Turkey
persian_force: Dadarshi's army (not described; see Zuzahya).
iranian_note: As at Zuzahya.
result_basis: The inscription says Dadarshi's army defeated the rebels at the fortress (Behistun §28).
sources: Behistun (DB) §28; Livius.org Behistun translation; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Dadarsis
note: Dadarshi then waited in Armenia until Darius came to Media; Iranica calls Uyama the decisive defeat of the Armenian rebels.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Parga
label: Parga
place: Mount Parga, Persis (unlocated; perhaps Forg near Darab), Iran
persian_force: Artavardiya's Persian and Median detachment (Behistun §§41-42).
iranian_note: As at Rakha.
result_basis: Artavardiya routed Vahyazdata's second army and captured him; he was impaled at Uvadaicaya (Behistun §§42-43).
sources: Behistun (DB) §§42-43; Livius.org Behistun translation; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Bisotun iii
note: Vahyazdata had raised a new army at Paishiyauvada after Rakha. The Forg identification is old and uncertain; coordinates regional.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Patigrabana
label: Patigrabana
place: Patigrabana, Parthia (unlocated; Mashhad has been suggested), Iran
faction_b: Parthian and Hyrcanian rebels (partisans of Fravartish)
persian_force: Vishtaspa's Parthian loyalists reinforced by a Persian army that Darius sent from Raga (Behistun §36).
iranian_note: The inscription names the Persian reinforcement joined to the loyal Parthian forces.
result_basis: Vishtaspa, reinforced from Raga, routed the rebels and Parthia submitted (Behistun §36).
sources: Behistun (DB) §36; Livius.org Behistun translation; en.wikipedia Patigrabana
note: Wikipedia dates it 'around 520 BC'; the inscription's date converts to 11 July 521. The Mashhad identification is speculative.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Babylon (siege, 521 BC)
label: Babylon (siege, 521 BC)
persian_force: An army sent by Darius under the Persian Intaphernes, his bow-bearer; not described (Behistun §50).
iranian_note: Inferred from Darius's Persian and Median royal army; the force is not described.
losses_b: Arakha and 2,497 of his followers executed (Babylonian version)
result_basis: Babylon fell to Intaphernes on 22 Markazanash (27 November 521) and Arakha and his chief followers were taken (Behistun §50).
sources: Behistun (DB) §§49-50; Livius.org Behistun translation; en.wikipedia Nebuchadnezzar IV, Fall of Babylon
note: Arakha, son of Haldita, an 'Armenian' (Urartian), revolted on 25 August 521 claiming to be Nebuchadnezzar, son of Nabonidus. Herodotus' 19-month siege and Zopyrus' stratagem (3.150-160) are sometimes referred to this revolt but fit neither; his 3,000 impaled may echo it. Parts of the walls were pulled down after the capture.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Margiana
label: Margiana
date: 28 December 521 BC (23 Aciyadiya; 10 December 522 is the alternative)
persian_force: The army of the Bactrian satrapy under its satrap Dadarshi (Behistun §38).
iranian_note: A satrapal army raised in Bactria (Bactrian, an East Iranian language) under a Persian-named satrap; not described further.
losses_b: 55,243 killed and 6,972 captured (Aramaic version); 55,2[..] killed and 6,572 captured (Babylonian version)
result_basis: Dadarshi's army crushed the Margians (Behistun §38).
sources: Behistun (DB) §§38-39 with the Babylonian and Aramaic versions; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Frada and Dadarsis; Livius.org Behistun translation
note: No site is named beyond Margiana. Iranica prefers 28 December 521 because Frada is the last rebel on the relief. The casualty figures are generally thought inflated.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Elam (520 BC)
label: Elam (520 BC)
date: 520 or 519 BC (Darius's second or third year)
persian_force: An army under the Persian Gobryas; not described (the royal army was Persian and Median).
iranian_note: Inferred; the column V text does not describe the army.
result_basis: Gobryas defeated the Elamites and captured their leader Atamaita, who was brought to Darius and killed (Behistun col. V).
borderline: the inscription names no site
doubt: Borderline: the inscription names no site.
sources: Behistun (DB) col. V (§71); Encyclopaedia Iranica, Bisotun iii
note: The third Elamite revolt. The first two (Açina, Martiya, 522-521) ended without battles: Açina was handed over bound and the Elamites killed Martiya themselves.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Saka campaign of Darius I
label: Saka campaign of Darius I
place: beyond the 'sea' (draya): the Caspian, Aral, Amu Darya or Syr Darya, Central Asia
persian_force: Darius's royal army, not described in the inscription (normally a Persian and Median core).
iranian_note: Inferred from the make-up of the royal army; the text says only 'with all my army'.
result_basis: After crossing the 'sea' with all his army Darius routed the Saka and their chief Skunkha was captured and brought to him (Behistun col. V).
borderline: a campaign entry: the inscription records a victory but names no site
doubt: Borderline: a campaign entry: the inscription records a victory but names no site.
sources: Behistun (DB) col. V (§74) and relief; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Bisotun iii; en.wikipedia Skunkha
note: Against the Saka tigraxauda ('pointed caps'). A few scholars refer the 'sea' to the Bosporus and the campaign to the European Scythians. Polyaenus' tale of the herdsman Sirakes leading Darius's army into the desert (7.12) is legendary and not listed.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Samos (517 BC)
label: Samos (517 BC)
persian_force: Otanes' Persian army, carried by sea to install Syloson (Herodotus 3.141-147); the ships were presumably from the subject Ionians and Phoenicians.
iranian_note: Herodotus speaks of 'the Persians' (many of high rank among the dead); the ships' crews are not named.
losses_a: many Persians of high rank killed in the sortie (Herodotus 3.146)
result_basis: The Persians drove Charilaus' mercenaries back into the acropolis after their surprise sortie, then massacred the Samians and handed the island to Syloson (Herodotus 3.146-149).
sources: Herodotus 3.139-149; en.wikipedia Syloson
note: Herodotus calls Samos the first of all Greek and barbarian cities that Darius took. Maeandrius escaped by a secret passage and sailed to Sparta.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Barca (siege)
label: Barca (siege)
commanders_a: Amasis, a Maraphian (army); Badres, a Pasargadan (fleet); sent by Aryandes, satrap of Egypt
persian_force: 'All the army of Egypt, by land and sea' under two Persian commanders (Herodotus 4.167): the Persian garrison troops of Egypt with subject levies and a fleet; miners dug under the walls.
iranian_note: The army of the Egyptian satrapy had a Persian and Iranian core with Egyptian and other subject troops; Herodotus gives no proportions.
losses_b: the leaders impaled by Pheretime and the rest enslaved; some deported to Bactria (Herodotus 4.202-204)
result_basis: Barca fell after a nine-month siege, taken by a broken oath sworn over a plank-covered trench (Herodotus 4.200-202).
sources: Herodotus 4.145, 4.165-167, 4.200-205; en.wikipedia Barca (ancient city)
note: Sent at the request of Pheretime of Cyrene; Herodotus thinks the real aim was the conquest of Libya. The army went on to Euesperides, and Libyans harried it on the march home (4.203), unnamed skirmishes not listed. Herodotus puts it at the time of the Scythian campaign; Wikipedia's Barca article says 515.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Scythian campaign of Darius I
label: Scythian campaign of Darius I
place: the steppe north of the Danube towards the Oarus (southern Ukraine), Ukraine
persian_force: The royal army of all the subject nations, 700,000 men with 600 ships in Herodotus (4.87); the Ionian, Aeolian and Hellespontine Greeks guarded the Danube bridge while the land army marched into Scythia.
iranian_note: The field army beyond the Danube was levied from many nations around a Persian and Median core; the Greeks stayed at the bridge; no proportions are given.
strength_b: 700,000 men and 600 ships (Herodotus 4.87); 80,000 left with Megabazus afterwards (4.143)
losses_b: heavy; the sick and weak abandoned in the camp (Herodotus 4.135)
result_basis: No pitched battle was fought; after weeks of Scythian raids Darius withdrew by night, leaving his sick and his camp, and the Scythians held the field (Herodotus 4.128-136).
borderline: a campaign of raids and skirmishes without a pitched battle
doubt: Borderline: a campaign of raids and skirmishes without a pitched battle.
sources: Herodotus 4.1, 4.83-144; Ctesias; en.wikipedia Scythian campaign of Darius I
note: Wikipedia's infobox calls it a Persian victory, its text a costly stalemate; the field test gives it to the Scythians, whom the Sauromatae (listed as Sarmatians), Budini and Geloni joined. On the way the Getae resisted and were at once subdued (Herodotus 4.93), and the empty wooden town of Gelonus was burned (4.123); neither is listed. Herodotus' figures are impossible.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Perinthus
label: Perinthus
persian_force: Megabazus' army of 80,000 left in Europe by Darius after the Scythian campaign (Herodotus 4.143, 5.1-2).
iranian_note: Herodotus calls the force 'the Persians'; it was part of the royal army of the Scythian campaign, whose make-up is not given.
result_basis: The Perinthians fought bravely for their freedom but were overcome by the numbers of Megabazus' army and the city was subdued (Herodotus 5.2).
note: Same as Ancient Greek Battles: Perinthus, c. 512 BC, Persian victory; the opponent there is named 'Perinthus'. If Perinthus (siege, 340 BC) is also in this set, this entry should become 'Perinthus (512 BC)'. Megabazus then subdued Thrace and deported the Paeonians without a recorded battle.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Lemnos
label: Lemnos
persian_force: Otanes' Persian army carried on ships supplied by the Lesbians (Herodotus 5.26).
iranian_note: Herodotus names the Lesbian (Greek) ships that carried Otanes' Persians; proportions unknown.
result_basis: The Lemnians fought hard but were in time overcome, and the Persians set Lycaretus over the survivors (Herodotus 5.27).
borderline: known from two sentences of Herodotus
doubt: Borderline: known from two sentences of Herodotus.
sources: Herodotus 5.25-27
note: The Lemnians were then 'Pelasgians' (Tyrsenians), not Greeks; listed under Greek cities. In the same campaign Otanes took Constantinople, Chalcedon, Antandrus, Lamponium and Imbros (Herodotus 5.26) with no fighting described; not listed.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Naxos (siege, 499 BC)
label: Naxos (siege, 499 BC)
date: 499 BC (a siege of about four months)
commanders_a: unknown (the Naxian people, who had expelled their oligarchs)
commanders_b: Megabates (cousin of Darius), Aristagoras of Miletus; sent by the satrap Artaphernes
persian_force: A royal fleet of about 200 triremes raised by Artaphernes, carrying 'many Persians and other allies' (Herodotus 5.32), with Aristagoras' Milesians and the Naxian exiles; the ships were crewed by Aegean subjects (a ship of Myndus in Caria is named).
iranian_note: Herodotus says many Persians sailed, but the 200 ships' crews (some 30,000-40,000 rowers) were Ionian, Carian and other Aegean subjects, so Iranians were probably a small part of the force.
result_basis: An initial attack was repelled and after four months the besiegers ran out of money and sailed away without taking the town.
sources: Herodotus 5.28-34; en.wikipedia Siege of Naxos (499 BC); en.wikipedia Ionian Revolt
note: Allies_b 'Greek cities' = Miletus under Aristagoras and the exiled Naxian oligarchs. Herodotus' story that Megabates warned the Naxians after a quarrel with Aristagoras may be Aristagoras' later excuse. The failure set off the Ionian Revolt.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Ephesus (498 BC)
label: Ephesus (498 BC)
commanders_a: the Persian commanders west of the Halys (unnamed by Herodotus; Wikipedia gives Artaphernes)
persian_force: The Persians holding lands west of the Halys, who gathered to relieve Sardis and followed the Greeks to Ephesus (Herodotus 5.102); probably mostly cavalry (Holland).
iranian_note: Herodotus calls the relieving force Persians, i.e. the Iranian settlers and garrisons of western Anatolia, who would have been joined by local levies.
losses_b: many killed, among them Eualcides of Eretria (Herodotus 5.102)
result_basis: The Persians caught the Greeks retreating from Sardis outside Ephesus and routed them; the survivors scattered to their cities.
sources: Herodotus 5.102-103; en.wikipedia Battle of Ephesus (498 BC)
note: Name kept as in Ancient Greek Battles; Wikipedia: Battle of Ephesus (498 BC). Side_b 'Greek cities' = Eretria. Afterwards the Athenians left the revolt.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Sardis (siege, 498 BC)
label: Sardis (siege, 498 BC)
commanders_b: Charopinus (brother of Aristagoras) and Hermophantus (Milesians), Melanthius (Athenians)
persian_force: Artaphernes' garrison of the citadel and the Persians and Lydians of the city, who gathered in the agora by the Pactolus and fought the Greeks there (Herodotus 5.100-101).
iranian_note: Herodotus names Persians and Lydians fighting together; their proportions are not known.
strength_b: unknown (the Ionian army with the crews of 20 Athenian and 5 Eretrian ships)
result_basis: The attackers took and burned the lower city but failed to take the citadel held by Artaphernes and withdrew when the Persians and Lydians massed against them in the agora, so the place did not fall.
sources: Herodotus 5.97-105; en.wikipedia Siege of Sardis (498 BC)
note: Side_b 'Greek cities' = Eretria. Wikipedia's infobox reads 'Greek retreat, city burned'; the fire destroyed most of the lower city and the temple of Cybebe and moved Darius to vow vengeance on Athens (Herodotus 5.105).
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Labraunda
label: Labraunda
place: sanctuary of Zeus Stratios, Labraunda (near Milas), Turkey
persian_force: Daurises' army of Persians, as at the Marsyas.
iranian_note: Herodotus calls the attackers Persians; the satrapal army also included local levies.
result_basis: The Persians attacked the Carians and the Milesian relief army at the sanctuary and routed them, the Milesians losing most heavily.
borderline: no standalone Wikipedia article (treated as a battle in the Ionian Revolt article)
doubt: Borderline: no standalone Wikipedia article (treated as a battle in the Ionian Revolt article).
sources: Herodotus 5.119-120; en.wikipedia Ionian Revolt
note: Ionian rebels = the Milesians and their allies.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Marsyas River
label: Marsyas River
place: the White Pillars on the Marsyas (Cine river), near its confluence with the Maeander, Turkey
commanders_b: unnamed Carian leaders (Pixodarus son of Mausolus of Cindye proposed fighting with the river behind them)
persian_force: Daurises' army, fresh from retaking the Hellespontine towns; Herodotus calls its men Persians.
iranian_note: Herodotus counts 2,000 Persian dead, implying a strong Persian core, though satrapal armies also took in local levies.
result_basis: After a long fight the Carians were beaten and fled to Labraunda, leaving the field to the Persians.
borderline: no standalone Wikipedia article (treated as a battle in the Ionian Revolt article)
doubt: Borderline: no standalone Wikipedia article (treated as a battle in the Ionian Revolt article).
sources: Herodotus 5.117-119; en.wikipedia Ionian Revolt
note: The site of the White Pillars is unknown; coordinates are for the lower Marsyas valley. Most date the Carian battles to 497, some to 496.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Pedasus
label: Pedasus
place: the road to Pedasa (Gokceler, near Bodrum), Turkey
commanders_a: Heraclides son of Ibanollis of Mylasa
commanders_b: Daurises, Amorges, Sisimaces, Myrsus son of Gyges (all killed)
persian_force: Daurises' army of Persians marching on the Carian cities (Herodotus 5.121).
iranian_note: Herodotus calls the army Persians and names its Persian generals; its levies are not described.
losses_b: the army destroyed with its generals (Herodotus 5.121)
result_basis: The Carians ambushed the Persian army at night on the road to Pedasus and destroyed it with its generals.
borderline: no standalone Wikipedia article (a named ambush, treated as a battle in the Ionian Revolt article)
doubt: Borderline: no standalone Wikipedia article (a named ambush, treated as a battle in the Ionian Revolt article).
sources: Herodotus 5.121; en.wikipedia Ionian Revolt
note: Which Pedasus is meant is uncertain (the Lelegian Pedasa near Halicarnassus is usual); coordinates approximate. Wikipedia notes a 496 date would give the Carians time to regroup.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Salamis in Cyprus (497 BC)
label: Salamis in Cyprus (497 BC)
commanders_b: Onesilus of Salamis (killed), Aristocyprus of Soli (killed), Stesenor of Curium (changed sides)
persian_force: Artybius' 'great army of Persians' shipped over from Cilicia (Herodotus 5.108-112), probably with Cilician levies; the loyal Amathusians were on the Persian side.
iranian_note: Herodotus speaks of an army of Persians facing the picked Salaminians and Solians; the other troops are not named.
result_basis: The Cypriot line broke after Stesenor of Curium and the Salaminian chariots went over to the Persians, Onesilus fell, and the Persians held the field.
sources: Herodotus 5.104, 5.108-115; en.wikipedia Ionian Revolt
note: Side_b = Salamis, Soli, Curium and the other rebel Cypriot kingdoms. Fought the same day as the sea battle off Salamis, which the Ionians won.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Salamis in Cyprus (sea) (497 BC)
label: Salamis in Cyprus (sea) (497 BC)
persian_force: The Phoenician fleet that brought Artybius' army to Cyprus (Herodotus 5.108, 5.112).
iranian_note: The fleet was Phoenician; any Iranian commanders or marines aboard are not recorded.
result_basis: The Ionian fleet defeated the Phoenician fleet off Salamis (Herodotus 5.112).
sources: Herodotus 5.108-112; en.wikipedia Ionian Revolt
note: The victory was wasted by the defeat on land the same day; the Ionians sailed home.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Soli in Cyprus (siege, 497 BC)
label: Soli in Cyprus (siege, 497 BC)
commanders_b: unknown (King Aristocyprus had fallen at Salamis)
persian_force: The Persian army victorious at Salamis, with Phoenician naval support; its make-up at the siege is not recorded.
iranian_note: Inferred from Artybius' Persian army and the Phoenician fleet that served in Cyprus; not stated for the siege.
result_basis: Soli fell in the fifth month after the Persians undermined its wall (Herodotus 5.115).
borderline: no Wikipedia battle article; Herodotus describes the siege (mining) in one sentence
doubt: Borderline: no Wikipedia battle article; Herodotus describes the siege (mining) in one sentence.
sources: Herodotus 5.115-116
note: Herodotus says the other rebel cities were besieged and retaken within the year and Soli held out longest. The excavated Persian siege mound and Cypriot counter-mines at Old Paphos (Kouklia) belong to the same campaign, but no written account of that siege survives.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Lade
label: Lade
place: sea off the island of Lade (now silted up, near Balat), Turkey
commanders_a: unnamed Persian generals (Wikipedia suggests Datis may have commanded the fleet)
persian_force: A fleet of 600 ships from the Phoenicians (the keenest), the Cypriots, the Cilicians and the Egyptians (Herodotus 6.6, 6.9).
iranian_note: Herodotus names only Phoenician, Cypriot, Cilician and Egyptian contingents; Iranians served at most as commanders and marines.
losses_b: heavy, above all the Chians; 49 of 60 Samian ships and the Lesbians deserted (Wikipedia's infobox: 246 ships)
result_basis: The Ionian line collapsed when most of the Samians and the Lesbians fled, the Chians withdrew after heavy losses, and the Persian fleet held the sea off Miletus.
sources: Herodotus 6.6-17; en.wikipedia Battle of Lade
note: Some modern historians doubt Herodotus' Samian story of desertion, which he probably had from Samian sources.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Miletus (siege, 494 BC)
label: Miletus (siege, 494 BC)
persian_force: The Persian land armies of Asia Minor, combined into one army for the siege (Herodotus 6.6), with the victorious fleet blockading by sea.
iranian_note: Herodotus speaks only of 'the Persians'; the satrapal armies had a Persian core with Anatolian levies, and the blockading fleet was Phoenician, Cypriot, Cilician and Egyptian.
losses_b: most of the men killed, the women and children enslaved, the survivors deported to Ampe on the Persian Gulf (Herodotus 6.19-20)
result_basis: Miletus fell to the besiegers after they mined its walls and brought up engines, in the sixth year of the revolt (Herodotus 6.18).
sources: Herodotus 6.6, 6.18-21; en.wikipedia Ionian Revolt; en.wikipedia Battle of Lade
note: No standalone Wikipedia article for this siege. Phrynichus' play 'The Capture of Miletus' was staged at Athens soon after.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Malene
label: Malene
place: Malene, territory of Atarneus (near Dikili), Turkey
persian_force: A large Persian army under Harpagus; the Persian cavalry decided the battle (Herodotus 6.28-29).
iranian_note: Herodotus credits the Persian cavalry with the victory; the infantry is not described.
strength_b: unknown (Histiaeus' foragers, Ionians and Aeolians from Lesbos)
losses_b: many killed; Histiaeus captured and impaled at Sardis by Artaphernes
result_basis: After a long fight a Persian cavalry charge routed Histiaeus' men and he was captured in the flight.
sources: Herodotus 6.26-30; en.wikipedia Ionian Revolt
note: Histiaeus, the former tyrant of Miletus, was by then fighting as a freebooter with a Lesbian fleet; Wikipedia places the battle in 494-493 without a firm date.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Brygian night raid
label: Brygian night raid
war: First Persian invasion of Greece (Mardonius' campaign)
place: Mardonius' camp in Macedonia (site unknown), Greece
persian_force: Mardonius' land army that crossed the Hellespont in 492 (the fleet had been wrecked off Athos); its make-up is not recorded. Achaemenid field armies of the time were built round Persian and Median infantry and Iranian cavalry with subject levies.
iranian_note: Inferred from the usual make-up of a royal field army under a Persian general; Herodotus says nothing of its units.
result_basis: The Brygi killed many Persians and wounded Mardonius in their night attack but did not take the camp, which the Persians held (Herodotus 6.45); their later subjection is a separate matter.
borderline: a night raid told in one sentence by Herodotus; no Wikipedia battle article (named 'Brygian night raid' in the campaign article)
doubt: Borderline: a night raid told in one sentence by Herodotus; no Wikipedia battle article (named 'Brygian night raid' in the campaign article).
sources: Herodotus 6.43-45; en.wikipedia First Persian invasion of Greece
note: Side_b 'Thracians' = the Brygi (Bryges), whom Herodotus calls Thracians. Their homeland is placed near Mt Bermion or further north-west (Lake Ohrid, Pelagonia, now North Macedonia), so the site is uncertain. Judged by the raid alone, the Brygi inflicted the heavier recorded loss.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Eretria (siege, 490 BC)
label: Eretria (siege, 490 BC)
date: 490 BC (August or September, a week before Marathon)
war: First Persian invasion of Greece (Datis and Artaphernes)
commanders_b: unknown (Euphorbus son of Alcimachus and Philagrus son of Cyneas betrayed the city)
persian_force: Datis' expeditionary army, landed at Tamynae, Choereae and Aegilia (Herodotus 6.101), with cavalry; modern estimates about 25,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry.
iranian_note: Herodotus names Persians and Saka as the core of the same army at Marathon a week later; the Ionian and Aeolian contingents served in the fleet.
losses_b: heavy; the city sacked, its temples burned and its people deported to Arderikka in Kissia (Herodotus 6.101, 6.119)
result_basis: After six days of assaults with heavy losses on both sides, Eretria fell on the seventh when Euphorbus and Philagrus opened the gates.
sources: Herodotus 6.99-101, 6.119; en.wikipedia Siege of Eretria
note: Side_b 'Greek cities' = Eretria. The 4,000 Athenian cleruchs of Chalcis sent to help left before the siege (Herodotus 6.100-101).
