qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Karystos (siege, 490 BC)
label: Karystos (siege, 490 BC)
war: First Persian invasion of Greece (Datis and Artaphernes)
persian_force: Datis' expeditionary army (modern estimates about 25,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry), carried by a fleet with Ionian and Aeolian contingents (Herodotus 6.98).
iranian_note: Herodotus names Persians and Saka as the core of Datis' army at Marathon; the fleet's crews (not counted as the besieging army) were Ionians, Aeolians and Phoenicians.
strength_a: about 25,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry (modern estimate for the expedition)
result_basis: The Carystians, besieged and their land ravaged, submitted to the Persians (Herodotus 6.99).
borderline: Herodotus records a siege and the ravaging of the land but no assault; it ended in surrender
doubt: Borderline: Herodotus records a siege and the ravaging of the land but no assault; it ended in surrender.
sources: Herodotus 6.99; en.wikipedia First Persian invasion of Greece
note: Side_b 'Greek cities' = Karystos (Carystus).
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Lindos (siege, 490 BC)
label: Lindos (siege, 490 BC)
war: First Persian invasion of Greece (Datis and Artaphernes)
persian_force: Datis' expeditionary fleet and army on its way into the Aegean (600 triremes for the whole expedition, Herodotus 6.95); the force at Lindos is not described.
iranian_note: Inferred from Datis' expedition, whose soldiers were Persians and Saka (Herodotus 6.113) and whose crews were Phoenician and Ionian subjects.
result_basis: By the Lindian Chronicle, Datis ended the blockade with a pact of friendship while the town was still invested, after rain relieved its water shortage.
borderline: a blockade with no recorded fighting, known only from a temple chronicle
doubt: Traditional: Known only from a miracle story of Athena in the Lindian Chronicle (inscribed 99 BC), not from Herodotus; Datis' fleet may well have touched Rhodes, but the siege and its ending are temple legend. Borderline: a blockade with no recorded fighting, known only from a temple chronicle.
sources: Lindian Chronicle (Epiphany D); en.wikipedia First Persian invasion of Greece
note: Side_b 'Greek cities' = Lindos (and the country people of Rhodes who fled there). Wikipedia says the attempt 'failed'; under the siege test a siege ended by treaty is a draw.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Marathon
label: Marathon
war: First Persian invasion of Greece (Datis and Artaphernes)
commanders_a: Miltiades, Callimachus (killed), Aristides, Themistocles, Stesilaus (killed); Arimnestus (Plataeans)
commanders_b: Datis, Artaphernes (son of Artaphernes); the exiled tyrant Hippias as guide
persian_force: Datis' expeditionary army: the Persians and the Saka held the centre and broke through (Herodotus 6.113); the cavalry may not have been engaged.
iranian_note: Herodotus names Persians and Saka in the centre; the troops of the wings are not named and may have included subject levies.
strength_b: about 25,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry (modern estimates); 600 ships (Herodotus)
losses_b: 6,400 killed and 7 ships captured (Herodotus 6.115-117); modern estimates 1,000-2,000 killed
result_basis: The Athenian and Plataean wings routed the Persian wings and then the victorious Persian centre, driving the Persians to their ships and holding the field.
sources: Herodotus 6.102-117; Nepos, Miltiades 4-6; Pausanias 1.32; en.wikipedia Battle of Marathon
note: Allies_a 'Greek cities' = Plataea. The traditional date (Boeckh) is 12 September; some prefer August. The Persians then sailed round Sunium but found the Athenian army back at Athens and returned to Asia.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Olynthus (siege, 480 BC)
label: Olynthus (siege, 480 BC)
date: winter 480/479 BC (during the siege of Potidaea)
persian_force: Artabazus' corps of 60,000 picked from Mardonius' army (Herodotus 8.126).
iranian_note: As at Potidaea: a corps drawn from Mardonius' mainly Iranian picked army; its units are not recorded.
result_basis: Artabazus took Olynthus and massacred its Bottiaean defenders by a nearby lake (Herodotus 8.127).
borderline: Herodotus records the siege and capture but not the fighting
doubt: Borderline: Herodotus records the siege and capture but not the fighting.
sources: Herodotus 8.127; en.wikipedia Second Persian invasion of Greece
note: Side_b 'Greek cities' = Olynthus, then held by the Bottiaeans (a people driven out of Macedonia, not Greeks in the strict sense). Artabazus gave the town to Critobulus of Torone and the Chalcidians.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Potidaea (siege, 480 BC)
label: Potidaea (siege, 480 BC)
persian_force: Artabazus' 60,000 men picked from Mardonius' army to escort Xerxes to the Hellespont (Herodotus 8.126); in 480 Artabazus had led the Parthians and Chorasmians (Herodotus 7.66).
iranian_note: Mardonius kept the best Iranian contingents (Persians, Medes, Saka, Bactrians) and Artabazus' corps was drawn from that army; its exact make-up is not recorded.
losses_b: many drowned or killed in the flood (Herodotus 8.129)
result_basis: After three months Artabazus' attack across the shallows at low tide was caught by a great flood, many drowned or were killed by the Potidaeans in boats, and he raised the siege (Herodotus 8.129).
sources: Herodotus 8.126-129; en.wikipedia Second Persian invasion of Greece
note: Side_a 'Greek cities' = Potidaea, which had revolted with the other towns of Pallene (Herodotus 8.126). The flood is often read as a tsunami; Herodotus blamed Poseidon. Some date the end of the siege to early 479.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Artemisium
label: Artemisium
date: August or September 480 BC (three days, the same days as Thermopylae)
place: strait off Cape Artemisium, northern Euboea, Greece
commanders_b: Achaemenes, Ariabignes, Prexaspes, Megabazus (the four admirals), Artemisia I, Damasithymus
persian_force: The royal fleet (1,207 ships at Doriscus by Herodotus' count, reduced by storms): Phoenician, Egyptian, Cypriot, Cilician, Ionian, Hellespontine, Carian, Lycian, Pamphylian and other ships, each with 30 Persian, Median or Saka marines (Herodotus 7.89-96, 7.184).
iranian_note: Herodotus says each ship carried 30 Persian, Median or Saka marines besides a native crew of about 200, so Iranians were roughly an eighth of the men.
strength_b: 1,207 ships at the start of the campaign less storm losses (Herodotus); modern estimates far lower
losses_a: heavy; half the Athenian ships damaged (Herodotus 8.18); Wikipedia's infobox: 100 ships
losses_b: about 30 ships on day 1, a Cilician squadron on day 2 and more than the Greeks on day 3 (Herodotus); about 200 more wrecked in a storm off Euboea; Wikipedia's infobox: 400 ships
result_basis: On the third day the fleets broke off with heavy losses, the Persians having lost more ships (Herodotus 8.16) but the Greeks leaving the strait that night, so the ships lost and the sea area point opposite ways.
sources: Herodotus 8.1-23; Diodorus 11.12-13; en.wikipedia Battle of Artemisium
note: Outcome kept as a draw, as in Ancient Greek Battles; Wikipedia's infobox calls it a Persian victory (the Persians then took Euboea). The preliminary skirmish off Sciathus, where Persian scouts took two Greek guard ships, is counted within this battle. Allies_a 'Greek cities' = Corinth, Aegina, Megara, Chalcis, Sicyon, Epidaurus, Eretria, Troezen and others.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Thermopylae
label: Thermopylae
date: August or September 480 BC (Wikipedia gives 21-23 July, 20 August or 8-10 September; three days)
commanders_b: Leonidas I (killed), Demophilus of Thespiae (killed), Leontiades of Thebes
persian_force: Xerxes' land army: the Medes and Kissians attacked first, then the Immortals (the 10,000 Persian guard) under Hydarnes, then picked troops of every nation; the Immortals turned the pass (Herodotus 7.210-225).
iranian_note: The units Herodotus names in the assaults are Medes, Kissians (Elamite-speaking Susians) and the Persian Immortals; the rest of the multi-ethnic army joined later.
strength_a: 40,000-300,000 (modern estimates); Herodotus gives 2,641,610 fighting men for the whole army
result_basis: On the third day the Persians, having turned the pass by the Anopaea path, destroyed the Greek rearguard and held the pass.
sources: Herodotus 7.175-233; Diodorus 11.4-10; en.wikipedia Battle of Thermopylae
note: Allies_b 'Greek cities' = Thespiae, Phocis, Opuntian Locris, Tegea, Mantinea, Corinth, Phlius, Mycenae and other Peloponnesians. Fought on the same days as Artemisium; the date is disputed.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Athens (siege, 480 BC)
label: Athens (siege, 480 BC)
persian_force: Xerxes' land army: Persians posted on the Areopagus shot fire-arrows into the wooden barricade, and a party climbed the north face (Herodotus 8.52-53).
iranian_note: Herodotus calls the attackers Persians but uses the name loosely; Xerxes' land army was led by Persian, Median and other Iranian contingents among dozens of subject peoples.
strength_b: a few: the temple treasurers and poor Athenians behind a wooden barricade (Herodotus 8.51)
result_basis: The Persians took the Acropolis by climbing the cliff near the shrine of Aglauros and killed its defenders (Herodotus 8.53).
sources: Herodotus 8.50-55; en.wikipedia Achaemenid destruction of Athens; en.wikipedia Second Persian invasion of Greece
note: Wikipedia's article 'Achaemenid destruction of Athens' covers this siege and the burning of 480 and Mardonius' razing of 479, which saw no fighting and is not a separate entry. Exiled Pisistratids accompanied Xerxes and parleyed with the defenders.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Delphi (480 BC)
label: Delphi (480 BC)
place: below the sanctuary of Athena Pronaia, Delphi, Greece
persian_force: A detachment of Xerxes' army sent through Phocis to plunder Delphi; its units are not recorded.
iranian_note: Herodotus does not say which troops formed the detachment.
strength_a: unknown (60 Delphians stayed, the rest fled to Parnassus)
result_basis: Herodotus says the Persian detachment fled when thunderbolts and falling rocks struck it near the shrine of Athena Pronaia, and the Delphians pursued and killed many.
borderline: a miracle story; no Wikipedia battle article
doubt: Traditional: Known only from Herodotus' miracle story (8. Borderline: a miracle story; no Wikipedia battle article.
sources: Herodotus 8.35-39; Diodorus 11.14
note: Side_a 'Greek cities' = Delphi.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Salamis
label: Salamis
date: late September 480 BC (26 or 27 September per Wikipedia)
place: straits between Salamis and Attica, Greece
commanders_a: Themistocles, Eurybiades, Adeimantus of Corinth, Aristides (at Psyttaleia)
commanders_b: Xerxes I (watching from the shore), Ariabignes (killed), Achaemenes, Artemisia I of Halicarnassus, Damasithymus (killed)
persian_force: The royal fleet: Phoenicians on the west wing facing the Athenians, Ionians on the east facing the Spartans, with Egyptian, Cypriot, Cilician, Carian, Pamphylian and Lycian ships; Persian, Median and Saka marines aboard; and about 400 troops on Psyttaleia (Herodotus 8.85, 8.95).
iranian_note: As at Artemisium, the crews were Phoenician, Greek, Egyptian and Anatolian subjects, with 30 Iranian marines a ship (Herodotus 7.96, 7.184), roughly an eighth of the men.
result_basis: The Greeks broke the Persian fleet in the straits, sinking or taking some 200 ships, and held the sea; the Persian fleet fell back to Phaleron and then to Asia.
sources: Herodotus 8.40-96; Aeschylus, Persians; Diodorus 11.15-19; Plutarch, Themistocles 11-15; en.wikipedia Battle of Salamis
note: Allies_a 'Greek cities' = Aegina, Corinth, Megara, Chalcis, Sicyon, Epidaurus, Eretria, Troezen, Naxos, Leucas, Ambracia and others. The destruction of the Persian troops on Psyttaleia by Aristides' hoplites is counted within this battle.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Sestos (siege, 479 BC)
label: Sestos (siege, 479 BC)
war: Second Persian invasion of Greece (Greek counter-offensive)
persian_force: Artayctes' garrison: the Persians of Sestos and the neighbouring towns and Oeobazus' party from Cardia, with the Aeolian townspeople (Herodotus 9.115-118).
iranian_note: Herodotus names Persians and 'their other allies' in the town, whose people were Aeolian Greeks; no numbers are given.
losses_b: Artayctes and his son captured and executed; Oeobazus caught and sacrificed by the Apsinthian Thracians
result_basis: Sestos fell after the starving Persian garrison slipped out by night and the townspeople opened the gates to the Athenians (Herodotus 9.118).
sources: Herodotus 9.114-121; Thucydides 1.89; en.wikipedia Greco-Persian Wars
note: Allies_a = the Ionian and Hellespontine allies who stayed with the Athenians after Leotychides' Peloponnesians went home. Herodotus ends his history with this siege; the town fell in winter 479/478 or spring 478. Wikipedia has no standalone article (Siege of Sestos redirects to Greco-Persian Wars).
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Dryoskephalai
label: Dryoskephalai
date: August 479 BC (the eighth day of the stand-off on the Asopus)
war: Second Persian invasion of Greece (Plataea campaign)
place: Dryoskephalai pass over Mt Cithaeron (near Eleutherae), Greece
commanders_a: Mardonius (on the advice of Timagenidas of Thebes)
persian_force: Mardonius' cavalry, sent by night to the pass (Herodotus 9.39).
iranian_note: Herodotus does not say which squadrons rode; Mardonius' cavalry was Persian, Median, Bactrian, Indian and Saka, with Boeotian horse.
strength_b: a supply convoy of 500 pack animals with drivers
result_basis: The Persian cavalry caught a convoy of 500 pack animals coming down the pass, killed men and beasts and drove the rest back to the Persian camp (Herodotus 9.39).
borderline: a cavalry raid on a supply convoy within the Plataea campaign, named only by its pass
doubt: Borderline: a cavalry raid on a supply convoy within the Plataea campaign, named only by its pass.
sources: Herodotus 9.38-39; en.wikipedia Battle of Plataea
note: Side_b 'Greek cities' = the supply train of the Greek allied army. Wikipedia's Plataea article mentions the raid without naming the pass.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Erythrae (479 BC)
label: Erythrae (479 BC)
date: August 479 BC (about ten days before Plataea)
war: Second Persian invasion of Greece (Plataea campaign)
place: foothills of Cithaeron near Erythrae (near Erythres), Greece
commanders_a: Pausanias; Olympiodorus son of Lampon (300 Athenians and archers)
persian_force: The whole of Mardonius' cavalry attacking by squadrons under Masistius (Herodotus 9.20); his horse were Persians, Medes, Bactrians, Indians and Saka.
iranian_note: Herodotus names Persian, Bactrian, Indian and Saka horse in Mardonius' army (8.113, 9.31); Masistius himself was a Persian noble.
strength_a: 3,000 Megarians, relieved by 300 Athenian picked men and archers
result_basis: The Persian cavalry fell back after Masistius was killed and failed to recover his body, leaving the field to the Greeks (Herodotus 9.22-25).
borderline: a preliminary engagement of the Plataea campaign, described in the Plataea article but not separately named
doubt: Borderline: a preliminary engagement of the Plataea campaign, described in the Plataea article but not separately named.
sources: Herodotus 9.19-25; Plutarch, Aristides 14; en.wikipedia Battle of Plataea
note: Side_a 'Greek cities' = Megara. The Greeks then moved down from Erythrae to the Asopus ridge near Plataea.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Mycale
label: Mycale
date: August 479 BC (traditionally the same day as Plataea)
place: shore beneath Mt Mycale (near Priene), Turkey
persian_force: Tigranes' army left to guard Ionia (60,000 by Herodotus 9.96) with the marines and crews of the beached fleet; the Persians fought hardest, while the disarmed Samians, the Milesians and other Ionians turned on them (Herodotus 9.99-104).
iranian_note: Herodotus calls the land army Persians and says the Persians fought best (Tigranes had led the Medes in 480), but the force also held Ionian contingents that changed sides.
strength_a: the crews and marines of 110 ships (Herodotus 8.131)
losses_b: most of the army killed; the camp and ships burned (about 4,000 killed by a modern estimate)
result_basis: The Greeks broke the Persian shield-wall, stormed the stockaded camp and burned the beached fleet, holding the field.
sources: Herodotus 9.90-106; Diodorus 11.34-36; en.wikipedia Battle of Mycale
note: Allies_a: 'Greek cities' = Corinth, Sicyon, Troezen; 'Ionian rebels' = the Samians, Milesians and other Ionians who changed sides during the battle. The Phoenician ships had been sent away before the battle.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Plataea
label: Plataea
date: August 479 BC (27 or 28 August per Wikipedia)
war: Second Persian invasion of Greece (Plataea campaign)
commanders_b: Mardonius (killed), Artabazus; Theban leaders Attaginus and Timagenidas
persian_force: Mardonius' picked army: Persians (with the Immortals), Medes, Bactrians, Indians and Saka, foot and horse, with Phrygian, Thracian, Mysian, Paeonian, Ethiopian and Egyptian units and about 50,000 Medising Greeks (Herodotus 8.113, 9.31-32).
iranian_note: In Herodotus' line-up Persians, Medes, Bactrians and Saka fill most of the battle line and the cavalry, with the Medising Greeks facing the Athenians.
losses_b: all but 3,000 of those not with Artabazus (Herodotus 9.70); 100,000 (Diodorus)
result_basis: The Spartans and Tegeans killed Mardonius and routed the Persians, and the Greeks stormed the Persian stockade and held the field; Artabazus marched off with 40,000 men.
sources: Herodotus 9.12-89; Diodorus 11.29-33; Plutarch, Aristides 11-21; en.wikipedia Battle of Plataea
note: Allies_a 'Greek cities' = Tegea, Corinth, Megara, Sicyon, Plataea, Aegina, Phlius, Epidaurus, Troezen, Eretria, Chalcis and others. Allies_b 'Greek cities' = the other Boeotians, Thessalians, Locrians, Malians and Phocians; the Thebans fought the Athenians hard. Traditionally fought on the same day as Mycale.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Byzantium (siege, 478 BC)
label: Byzantium (siege, 478 BC)
commanders_a: Pausanias (with Aristides and Cimon leading the Athenians, per Plutarch)
persian_force: The Persian garrison of Byzantium ('held by the Medes'), which included Persian nobles who were kinsmen of the King (Thucydides 1.94, 1.128).
iranian_note: Thucydides calls the garrison 'the Medes' (i.e. Persians) and names royal kinsmen among the prisoners.
strength_a: 20 Peloponnesian ships, 30 Athenian and many other allied ships (Thucydides 1.94)
losses_b: the garrison captured, including kinsmen of the King (later released secretly by Pausanias)
result_basis: Constantinople fell to the besiegers and its Persian garrison was captured.
sources: Thucydides 1.94, 1.128; Plutarch, Aristides 23, Cimon 6; en.wikipedia Greco-Persian Wars, Wars of the Delian League
note: Thucydides puts it after Pausanias' campaign in Cyprus in the same year, where he 'subdued most of the island' (no named battle).
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Eion
label: Eion
place: Eion at the mouth of the Strymon (near Amphipolis), Greece
persian_force: The Persian garrison of the governor Boges, supplied by Thracian allies until Cimon drove them off (Herodotus 7.107; Plutarch, Cimon 7).
iranian_note: Herodotus and Plutarch speak of Boges' Persians and Thucydides of 'the Medes' holding Eion.
losses_b: the garrison destroyed; Boges killed himself; the inhabitants enslaved
result_basis: Cimon beat the Persians outside the walls and starved Eion into falling; the governor Boges burned himself rather than surrender.
sources: Herodotus 7.107; Thucydides 1.98; Plutarch, Cimon 7; en.wikipedia Wars of the Delian League
note: The battle outside the walls and the siege are one entry, as in Ancient Greek Battles.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Doriskos (siege)
label: Doriskos (siege)
place: Doriskos, near the mouth of the Hebrus (Evros), Greece
persian_force: The garrison of the governor Mascames, appointed by Xerxes in 480; its make-up is not recorded (an Achaemenid garrison was normally Persians with local troops).
iranian_note: Herodotus names only the Persian governor; the class is inferred from other Achaemenid garrisons in Thrace.
result_basis: Mascames held Doriskos against every Greek attempt and the fort was never taken (Herodotus 7.106).
borderline: several unsuccessful attempts mentioned in one sentence by Herodotus; no single described engagement
doubt: Borderline: several unsuccessful attempts mentioned in one sentence by Herodotus; no single described engagement.
sources: Herodotus 7.105-106; en.wikipedia Wars of the Delian League
note: Herodotus says 'the Greeks' tried; Wikipedia takes them to be Athenian attempts. The Persians probably withdrew the garrison around 465 BC, and the King sent gifts every year to Mascames' descendants for his defence.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Eurymedon
label: Eurymedon
place: banks of the Eurymedon (Koprucay) near Aspendos, Antalya, Turkey
commanders_b: Pherendates (army, per Ephorus); Ariomandes son of Gobryas (overall, per Callisthenes)
persian_force: The royal army gathered at Aspendos under Pherendates, joined by the crews of the beached Phoenician ships; no ancient source gives its size.
iranian_note: Plutarch speaks of the Persian foot; the crews who fled ashore were Phoenician, and Pamphylian and Cilician levies are likely but not attested.
strength_a: the hoplite marines of about 200 triremes (perhaps 5,000)
result_basis: Cimon's landed hoplites routed the Persian army after a hard fight and took its camp.
sources: Thucydides 1.100; Plutarch, Cimon 12-13; Diodorus 11.60-62; en.wikipedia Battle of the Eurymedon
note: Wikipedia's infobox marks Pherendates as killed. Diodorus puts the sea battle off Cyprus and the land battle at the Eurymedon the same day.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Eurymedon (sea)
label: Eurymedon (sea)
place: off the mouth of the Eurymedon (Koprucay), Antalya, Turkey
persian_force: The royal fleet of 200 Phoenician triremes (Thucydides; 350 per Ephorus, 600 per Phanodemus), waiting for 80 more Phoenician ships from Cyprus; marines probably Iranian, as in 480.
iranian_note: Thucydides calls the ships Phoenician; Iranian marines are inferred from the fleet of 480 (Herodotus 7.184).
result_basis: The Persian fleet was broken at the river mouth and 200 Phoenician triremes were taken or destroyed (Thucydides 1.100).
sources: Thucydides 1.100; Plutarch, Cimon 12-13; Diodorus 11.60-61; en.wikipedia Battle of the Eurymedon
note: Plutarch adds that Cimon then destroyed the 80 Phoenician ships coming from Cyprus; Thucydides is silent and some historians doubt it, so it is not entered separately.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Chersonese (465 BC)
label: Chersonese (465 BC)
persian_force: Persians who had stayed in the Chersonese with at least 13 ships, and Thracians from the interior whom they called in (Plutarch, Cimon 14).
iranian_note: Plutarch names Persians with Thracian helpers; their proportions are not given.
strength_b: at least 13 ships, with Thracian allies
result_basis: Cimon with four triremes took 13 Persian ships and drove the Persians out of the Chersonese (Plutarch, Cimon 14).
borderline: minor action known only from Plutarch, with no conventional name
doubt: Borderline: minor action known only from Plutarch, with no conventional name.
sources: Plutarch, Cimon 14.1; en.wikipedia Wars of the Delian League
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Nile
label: Nile
war: Wars of the Delian League (Egyptian revolt of Inaros)
persian_force: A royal fleet of 50 ships supporting Achaemenes' army, probably Phoenician (Ctesias calls them Persian ships; Wikipedia, Phoenician).
iranian_note: Achaemenid fleets were crewed by Phoenicians and other subject seafarers, with Iranian marines.
result_basis: Charitimides' 40 Athenian ships captured 20 of the 50 Persian ships with their crews and sank the other 30 (Ctesias).
sources: Ctesias, Persica (Photius' summary) 36; en.wikipedia Inaros II, Wars of the Delian League
note: Known only from Ctesias' summary; the site and exact date are unknown, but it belongs to the campaign of Achaemenes.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Papremis
label: Papremis
war: Wars of the Delian League (Egyptian revolt of Inaros)
place: Papremis, western Nile Delta (site unidentified), Egypt
persian_force: The army of the satrap Achaemenes, brother of Xerxes, raised from the empire: over 300,000 horse and foot (Diodorus 11.74) or 400,000 with 80 ships (Ctesias), figures much exaggerated.
iranian_note: Herodotus (3.12) saw the skulls of the Persians who fell with Achaemenes; the rest of the army came from the western satrapies and is not detailed.
strength_a: the Egyptian rebels and the Athenian expedition (200 ships came from Cyprus)
losses_b: Achaemenes and, by Ctesias' figure, 100,000 men killed
result_basis: Inaros' Egyptians and the Athenians broke Achaemenes' army, which fled to Memphis; Achaemenes was killed.
sources: Herodotus 3.12, 7.7; Thucydides 1.104; Diodorus 11.74; Ctesias (Photius) 36; en.wikipedia Inaros II, Wars of the Delian League
note: Thucydides does not name the battle; Herodotus and Ctesias do. Some date it to 459.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Memphis
label: Memphis
date: c. 456 BC (relief of the White Castle, besieged since c. 459)
war: Wars of the Delian League (Egyptian revolt of Inaros)
persian_force: The White Castle garrison (Persians and Medes, with the Egyptians who had not joined the revolt, Thucydides 1.104) and Megabyzus' relief army, drilled for a year in Cilicia (300,000 per Diodorus, 200,000 per Ctesias; modern estimate about 25,000), with Phoenician, Cilician and Cypriot ships.
iranian_note: Thucydides names Persians and Medes in the White Castle; the relief army came from the western satrapies and its fleet from Phoenicia, Cilicia and Cyprus.
strength_a: 300,000 men and 300 triremes (Diodorus 11.75); 200,000 men and 300 ships under Oriscus (Ctesias); modern estimate about 25,000
result_basis: Megabyzus beat the Egyptians and Athenians in battle and drove them from Memphis, raising their siege of the White Castle.
sources: Thucydides 1.104, 1.109; Diodorus 11.74-77; Ctesias (Photius) 37; en.wikipedia Inaros II, Megabyzus, Wars of the Delian League
note: One entry for the siege of the White Castle (c. 459-456, at least three years) and the relief battle, as in Ancient Greek Battles.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Prosopitis (siege)
label: Prosopitis (siege)
war: Wars of the Delian League (Egyptian revolt of Inaros)
place: island of Prosopitis, western Nile Delta (near Nikiou), Egypt
persian_force: Megabyzus' army and the Phoenician fleet (Thucydides 1.109-110).
iranian_note: Megabyzus' army had a Persian core with levies from Syria and Cilicia; the ships were Phoenician.
strength_b: the Athenian expedition's remaining fleet and the Egyptian rebels
losses_b: the fleet burned or taken; the whole Egyptian expedition cost Athens about 250 ships (modern estimate)
result_basis: After 18 months Megabyzus drained the channel round the island, took it and destroyed the Athenian fleet; only a few Athenians escaped through Libya to Cyrene (Thucydides 1.109-110).
sources: Thucydides 1.109-110; Diodorus 11.77; Ctesias (Photius) 37-38; en.wikipedia Inaros II, Wars of the Delian League
note: Diodorus says the Egyptians went over and the Athenians left under a truce; Ctesias says Megabyzus took Inaros and the Greeks at Byblos on terms. Either way the place fell. Not in Ancient Greek Battles.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Mendesian mouth
label: Mendesian mouth
war: Wars of the Delian League (Egyptian revolt of Inaros)
place: Mendesian mouth of the Nile (Lake Manzala area), Egypt
persian_force: The Phoenician fleet attacking from the sea and Persian infantry from the shore (Thucydides 1.110).
iranian_note: Thucydides names the Phoenician fleet and the land army; the army had a Persian core.
result_basis: The Phoenician fleet and the Persian land army destroyed most of the 50 relief triremes; only a few escaped (Thucydides 1.110).
sources: Thucydides 1.110; en.wikipedia Inaros II, Wars of the Delian League
note: The squadron arrived unaware that Prosopitis had fallen.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Kition (siege, 450 BC)
label: Kition (siege, 450 BC)
war: Wars of the Delian League (Cimon's Cyprus campaign)
persian_force: The Phoenician kingdom of Kition defending its city as a subject of the King; Persian royal forces (Artabazus' fleet, Megabyzus' army) were in the region (Diodorus 12.3) but none is said to have been inside.
iranian_note: Kition was a Phoenician city on Cyprus; no Iranian troops are attested in the siege.
strength_b: 200 ships at the start, less 60 sent to Amyrtaeus in Egypt (Thucydides 1.112)
losses_b: Cimon died (of sickness or a wound)
result_basis: The Athenians gave up the siege for lack of food after Cimon's death and sailed away (Thucydides 1.112).
borderline: the defenders were the Phoenician kingdom of Kition, a Persian vassal; no Persian troops are named in the siege
doubt: Borderline: the defenders were the Phoenician kingdom of Kition, a Persian vassal; no Persian troops are named in the siege.
sources: Thucydides 1.112; Plutarch, Cimon 18-19; Diodorus 12.3; en.wikipedia Wars of the Delian League
note: Diodorus (12.3) says Cimon took Kition and Marion by storm; Thucydides, followed here, says the siege was abandoned. Not in Ancient Greek Battles.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Salamis in Cyprus (450 BC)
label: Salamis in Cyprus (450 BC)
date: c. 450 BC (about 30 days after the Athenians left Kition)
war: Wars of the Delian League (Cimon's Cyprus campaign)
persian_force: Phoenicians, Cyprians and Cilicians (Thucydides 1.112); Diodorus places the royal army of Megabyzus (300,000) in Cilicia.
iranian_note: Thucydides names only Phoenicians, Cyprians and Cilicians; Persians would have been officers and marines.
strength_a: the fleet of about 140 ships and its troops (200 less 60 sent to Egypt)
result_basis: The Athenians beat the Phoenicians, Cyprians and Cilicians on land as well as at sea and then sailed home unhindered (Thucydides 1.112).
sources: Thucydides 1.112; Diodorus 12.3-4; Plutarch, Cimon 18-19; en.wikipedia Wars of the Delian League
note: Diodorus tells the campaign differently: Cimon took 100 of Artabazus' 300 ships off Cyprus, then landed in Cilicia and beat Megabyzus' army, before besieging Salamis.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Salamis in Cyprus (sea) (450 BC)
label: Salamis in Cyprus (sea) (450 BC)
war: Wars of the Delian League (Cimon's Cyprus campaign)
persian_force: The royal fleet of Phoenicians, Cyprians and Cilicians (Thucydides 1.112); 300 ships under Artabazus (Diodorus 12.3).
iranian_note: The crews were Phoenician, Cypriot and Cilician; Iranians would only have been commanders and marines.
losses_b: 100 ships taken with their crews, many sunk (Diodorus)
result_basis: The Athenians defeated the Phoenician, Cyprian and Cilician fleet off Salamis (Thucydides 1.112); Diodorus says they took 100 ships.
sources: Thucydides 1.112; Diodorus 12.3-4; en.wikipedia Wars of the Delian League
note: The Peace of Callias, if historical, followed; Thucydides does not mention it.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Megabyzus' revolt (Menostanes)
label: Megabyzus' revolt (Menostanes)
date: c. 448-445 BC (after the defeat of Usiris; date uncertain)
persian_force: Megabyzus' Syrian army against a second royal army under the King's nephew Menostanes; no numbers given.
iranian_note: Megabyzus' army was raised in Syria (Ctesias); the royal army's make-up is not stated.
result_basis: Ctesias says Megabyzus wounded Menostanes and the royal army fled.
borderline: no conventional name; known only from Ctesias
doubt: Traditional: Known only from Ctesias (Photius' summary 41), whose account of the revolt is a court romance; modern historians doubt the details and some the battles themselves. Borderline: no conventional name; known only from Ctesias.
sources: Ctesias, Persica (Photius' summary) 41; en.wikipedia Megabyzus
note: Megabyzus then submitted on terms negotiated by Artarius, Amytis and Artoxares and was pardoned.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Megabyzus' revolt (Usiris)
label: Megabyzus' revolt (Usiris)
date: c. 448-445 BC (some years after the execution of Inaros; date uncertain)
persian_force: Megabyzus' army of 150,000 foot raised in his satrapy of Syria against Usiris' royal army of 200,000 (Ctesias), both figures incredible.
iranian_note: Megabyzus' army was raised in Syria, so mostly Aramaic-speaking levies under Persian officers; the royal army's make-up is not stated.
result_basis: Ctesias says Megabyzus routed Usiris' royal army after the two generals wounded each other, and took Usiris prisoner.
borderline: no conventional name; known only from Ctesias
doubt: Traditional: Known only from Ctesias' romantic court history (Photius' summary 40), with incredible numbers and a duel of generals; Wikipedia's Megabyzus article treats the encounters as duels rather than pitched battles. Borderline: no conventional name; known only from Ctesias.
sources: Ctesias, Persica (Photius' summary) 40; en.wikipedia Megabyzus
note: Usiris is called an Egyptian by Ctesias.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Arsites' revolt (first battle)
label: Arsites' revolt (first battle)
date: c. 420 BC (early in the reign of Darius II; date uncertain)
persian_force: Artyphius' army with Greek mercenaries against the royal army of Artasyras; no numbers given (Ctesias).
iranian_note: Ctesias names only Artyphius' Greek mercenaries; the rest of both armies is not described.
result_basis: Ctesias says the royal general Artasyras was defeated by Artyphius.
borderline: no name or place; one of three battles known only from one sentence of Ctesias' summary
doubt: Borderline: no name or place; one of three battles known only from one sentence of Ctesias' summary.
sources: Ctesias, Persica (Photius' summary) 52
note: Arsites was a full brother of Darius II. The site is unknown; Syria is a guess because Artyphius' father Megabyzus had been satrap there.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Arsites' revolt (second battle)
label: Arsites' revolt (second battle)
persian_force: Artyphius' army with Greek mercenaries against the royal army of Artasyras; no numbers given (Ctesias).
iranian_note: Ctesias names only Artyphius' Greek mercenaries.
result_basis: Ctesias says Artasyras was defeated a second time.
borderline: no name or place; known only from one sentence of Ctesias' summary
doubt: Borderline: no name or place; known only from one sentence of Ctesias' summary.
sources: Ctesias, Persica (Photius' summary) 52
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Arsites' revolt (third battle)
label: Arsites' revolt (third battle)
persian_force: The royal army of Artasyras against Artyphius, whose Greek mercenaries had been bought off (Ctesias).
iranian_note: Ctesias names only the Greek mercenaries; the royal army is not described.
result_basis: Ctesias says Artasyras won the third battle after bribing Artyphius' Greek mercenaries, all but three Milesians, and Artyphius surrendered.
borderline: no name or place; known only from one sentence of Ctesias' summary
doubt: Borderline: no name or place; known only from one sentence of Ctesias' summary.
sources: Ctesias, Persica (Photius' summary) 52
note: Artyphius and later Arsites surrendered on promises of safety and were put to death in the ashes at Parysatis' urging.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Iasos
label: Iasos
war: Peloponnesian War (Ionian War); revolt of Amorges
persian_force: The rebel Amorges, bastard son of the satrap Pissouthnes, with his mercenaries, mostly Peloponnesian, and the people of Iasos (Thucydides 8.28).
iranian_note: Thucydides says Amorges' mercenaries were mostly Peloponnesians; the Iasians were Greeks and Carians.
strength_a: the Peloponnesian and Syracusan fleet of 55 ships
losses_b: Amorges captured; his mercenaries taken into Peloponnesian service; the town sacked
result_basis: The Peloponnesian and Syracusan fleet took Iasos by a surprise assault, captured Amorges and handed him and the town to Tissaphernes (Thucydides 8.28).
borderline: the Persian side was a rebel against the King; the attackers acted at the urging and in the pay of the loyal satrap Tissaphernes, who received the town (could be treated as civil or left out)
doubt: Borderline: the Persian side was a rebel against the King; the attackers acted at the urging and in the pay of the loyal satrap Tissaphernes, who received the town (could be treated as civil or left out).
sources: Thucydides 8.5, 8.26-28 (no Wikipedia article)
note: Amorges had held Caria in revolt since about 414 with Athenian support; Syracusans were with the Peloponnesians (Greek cities).
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Miletus (412 BC)
label: Miletus (412 BC)
commanders_b: Tissaphernes; Milesian and Peloponnesian commanders unnamed
persian_force: Tissaphernes in person with his cavalry and a body of foreign mercenaries (Thucydides 8.25); no numbers given.
iranian_note: Thucydides names Tissaphernes' cavalry, Persian in western Asia Minor, and his mercenaries, probably Greek and Anatolian.
strength_b: 800 Milesian hoplites, the Peloponnesians of Chalcideus' fleet, Tissaphernes' mercenaries and cavalry
result_basis: The Athenians routed the Peloponnesians and Tissaphernes' troops, set up a trophy and began to wall off Miletus, though the Milesians beat the Argives on the other wing (Thucydides 8.25).
sources: Thucydides 8.25-27
note: Miletus (Greek cities) and the Peloponnesians led the defending side. The Athenians withdrew to Samos when a Peloponnesian and Syracusan fleet of 55 ships arrived (a strategic matter). No Wikipedia article; Persian role could be judged a contingent.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Abydos (411 BC)
label: Abydos (411 BC)
place: off Abydos (Nara Burnu), Dardanelles, Canakkale, Turkey
persian_force: Pharnabazus' army of cavalry and foot, which he led down to the beach, riding into the sea himself, to protect the Peloponnesian ships (Xenophon, Hellenica 1.1.6).
iranian_note: The satrap's cavalry in Hellespontine Phrygia was Persian; his foot were local Anatolian levies and Greek mercenaries (inferred).
strength_b: 97 ships (as given in Wikipedia's infobox), with Pharnabazus' army
result_basis: Alcibiades' arrival turned the day; the Peloponnesians fled to Abydos and lost 30 ships, while Pharnabazus' troops on the shore saved the rest (Xenophon, Hellenica 1.1.4-7).
sources: Xenophon, Hellenica 1.1.4-7; Diodorus 13.45-46; en.wikipedia Battle of Abydos
note: Wikipedia's infobox lists only Athens and Sparta; the Persian role rests on Xenophon and Diodorus. The land battle of 409/408 at the same place keeps its set-12 name 'Abydos' below; the merged list may need years on both.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Cyzicus
label: Cyzicus
date: spring 410 BC (usually May or June; one view March)
place: off Cyzicus and on the shore near Cleri, Sea of Marmara (near Erdek), Turkey
persian_force: Pharnabazus' satrapal army, foot and an important cavalry force, drawn up on the beach where Mindarus ran his ships ashore (Xenophon, Hellenica 1.1.14-18; Diodorus 13.49-51).
iranian_note: Pharnabazus' cavalry was Persian; his foot were mainly local levies and mercenaries (inferred).
losses_b: the entire fleet (the Syracusans burned their own); Mindarus killed
result_basis: The Athenians destroyed or took the whole Peloponnesian fleet and beat the Spartans and Pharnabazus' troops on the beach, killing Mindarus; Cyzicus surrendered the next day.
sources: Xenophon, Hellenica 1.1.11-18; Diodorus 13.49-51; Plutarch, Alcibiades 28; en.wikipedia Battle of Cyzicus
note: Syracusan ships fought with the Peloponnesians (Greek cities).
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Abydos
label: Abydos
place: near Abydos (Nara Burnu), Dardanelles, Canakkale, Turkey
persian_force: Pharnabazus with a large force of cavalry and foot from his satrapy of Hellespontine Phrygia.
iranian_note: Xenophon stresses Pharnabazus' horsemen, who in this satrapy were Persians and Iranian settlers.
strength_a: the combined army of Thrasyllus and Alcibiades (30 ships with Thrasyllus)
result_basis: Pharnabazus came to the relief of Abydos with many horsemen and was routed; Alcibiades pursued with his cavalry and 120 hoplites until dark (Xenophon, Hellenica 1.2.15-17).
sources: Xenophon, Hellenica 1.2.15-17; Plutarch, Alcibiades 29; en.wikipedia Thrasyllus
note: Name and date as in Ancient Greek Battles; the sea battle of 411 at the same place is entered as 'Abydos (411 BC)'. The Athenians did not take Abydos; the Abydenes (Greek cities) fought with Pharnabazus.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Ephesus (409 BC)
label: Ephesus (409 BC)
place: before Ephesus, near Koressos and the marsh (near Selcuk), Turkey
commanders_a: Tissaphernes; the Syracusan and Selinuntine captains (unnamed)
persian_force: The troops Tissaphernes mustered to save the shrine of Artemis, with his Persian cavalry and the levy of the countryside (Xenophon, Hellenica 1.2.6).
iranian_note: Tissaphernes' cavalry was Persian; the levies he summoned were Lydians and Ionians (inferred).
strength_b: 1,000 hoplites, 100 cavalry and 50 triremes, with 5,000 sailors armed as peltasts (Xenophon, Hellenica 1.2.1)
losses_b: several hundred killed (Xenophon and Diodorus give different figures)
result_basis: The Ephesians, Tissaphernes' troops and the Syracusan and Selinuntine crews routed both Athenian landing forces, at Koressos and at the marsh, and set up two trophies (Xenophon, Hellenica 1.2.6-10).
sources: Xenophon, Hellenica 1.2.6-10; Diodorus 13.64; en.wikipedia Thrasyllus
note: Ancient Greek Battles lists Ephesus, Persia and Syracuse as the winners; Ephesus had been under Tissaphernes since 412. The Ionian revolt's battle of 498 BC at Ephesus may require a year in the merged list.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Chalcedon
label: Chalcedon
place: before the Athenian siege wall at Chalcedon (Kadikoy, across the Bosporus from Constantinople), Turkey
persian_force: Pharnabazus' army of foot and a large cavalry force, which came up to the Heracleion of Chalcedon to relieve the town (Xenophon, Hellenica 1.3.5).
iranian_note: Pharnabazus' cavalry was Persian; his foot were local levies (inferred).
losses_b: Hippocrates and many of his men killed
result_basis: Thrasyllus beat Hippocrates' sortie and killed him while Alcibiades held off Pharnabazus, who could not break through the siege wall and fell back to his camp at the Heracleion (Xenophon, Hellenica 1.3.4-7).
sources: Xenophon, Hellenica 1.3.4-7; Diodorus 13.66; Plutarch, Alcibiades 30
note: The siege then ended in an agreement with Pharnabazus: Chalcedon to pay tribute to Athens again, and Pharnabazus to escort Athenian envoys to the King.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Centrites
label: Centrites
war: Revolt of Cyrus the Younger (retreat of the Ten Thousand)
place: the Centrites (Botan) near its confluence with the Tigris, Siirt, Turkey
persian_force: Cavalry on the far bank and infantry on the bluffs: the troops of Orontas and Artuchas, Armenians, Mardians and Chaldaean mercenaries (Xenophon, Anabasis 4.3.3-4).
iranian_note: Xenophon names Armenians, Mardians (an Iranian people) and Chaldaean mercenaries under Persian commanders.
result_basis: The Greeks forced the ford after a feint; the Persian cavalry on the bank and the infantry on the bluffs fled, and the rearguard beat off the Carduchians (Xenophon, Anabasis 4.3).
borderline: an episode of the Anabasis with no battle article
doubt: Borderline: an episode of the Anabasis with no battle article.
sources: Xenophon, Anabasis 4.3; en.wikipedia Ten Thousand (Greek mercenaries)
note: Kentrites in Greek; usually identified with the Botan (Bohtan) Su. The Carduchians who attacked the rear were not Persian allies.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Tiribazus' camp
label: Tiribazus' camp
war: Revolt of Cyrus the Younger (retreat of the Ten Thousand)
place: western Armenia, between the Teleboas and the Euphrates (north-west of Lake Van), Turkey
persian_force: Tiribazus, hyparch of western Armenia, with his own troops and Chalybian and Taochian mercenaries (Xenophon, Anabasis 4.4.18).
iranian_note: Xenophon names only the Chalybian and Taochian mercenaries; the governor's own troops would be Persian and Armenian.
losses_b: a few killed; camp, tent and household taken
result_basis: The Greeks fell on Tiribazus' camp before he could spring his ambush in the pass, routed his men and took his tent with its silver-footed couches and his household (Xenophon, Anabasis 4.4.18-22).
borderline: camp raid of the retreat with no conventional name
doubt: Borderline: camp raid of the retreat with no conventional name.
sources: Xenophon, Anabasis 4.4.4-22; en.wikipedia Ten Thousand (Greek mercenaries)
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Tissaphernes' attacks (Tigris valley)
label: Tissaphernes' attacks (Tigris valley)
war: Revolt of Cyrus the Younger (retreat of the Ten Thousand)
place: Tigris valley north of Mespila (Nineveh, at Mosul) and the hills beyond, Iraq
persian_force: Tissaphernes' own cavalry, the army of Orontas (satrap of Armenia, the King's son-in-law), Cyrus' former Asian troops and troops given by the King, with many archers and slingers (Xenophon, Anabasis 3.4.13).
iranian_note: Xenophon names Persian cavalry, Orontas' Armenian levies and Cyrus' old Asian troops; no proportions.
result_basis: The Greek slingers and archers outranged Tissaphernes' missile troops near Mespila and the Greeks won the race for the summit in the hills, so Tissaphernes drew off each time without stopping the march (Xenophon, Anabasis 3.4.13-49).
borderline: several days of skirmishing grouped as one entry; no conventional name
doubt: Borderline: several days of skirmishing grouped as one entry; no conventional name.
sources: Xenophon, Anabasis 3.4.13-3.5.1; en.wikipedia Ten Thousand (Greek mercenaries), Anabasis (Xenophon)
note: Tissaphernes then burned the villages and the Greeks entered the Carduchian mountains, where no Persian forces fought them.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Zapatas
label: Zapatas
date: autumn 401 BC (a few days after the arrest of the Greek generals)
war: Revolt of Cyrus the Younger (retreat of the Ten Thousand)
place: beyond the Great Zab (Zapatas) near its confluence with the Tigris, Iraq
persian_force: Mithradates' force: on the first day about 200 horse and 400 archers and slingers, on the second 1,000 horse and 4,000 archers and slingers lent by Tissaphernes (Xenophon, Anabasis 3.3.6, 3.4.2).
iranian_note: Xenophon gives no peoples; Persian cavalry and missile troops of a satrapal army are inferred.
strength_a: the Ten Thousand, with 200 Rhodian slingers and 50 horsemen newly formed
losses_b: some foot killed in the ravine; 18 horsemen captured
result_basis: On the second day the Greek slingers and new cavalry charged Mithradates' horse and missile troops at a ravine and routed them, taking 18 horsemen alive (Xenophon, Anabasis 3.4.1-5).
borderline: a skirmish of the retreat with no conventional name; named after the river
doubt: Borderline: a skirmish of the retreat with no conventional name; named after the river.
sources: Xenophon, Anabasis 3.3.6-3.4.5; en.wikipedia Ten Thousand (Greek mercenaries)
note: On the first day (Anabasis 3.3.6-11) Mithradates harassed the Greeks without loss and drew off; this entry scores the second day.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Cunaxa
label: Cunaxa
place: Cunaxa, on the Euphrates north of Babylon (near Baghdad), Iraq
persian_force: Royal army: Tissaphernes' cavalry, 6,000 horse under Artagerses, wicker-shield infantry, Egyptian heavy infantry, archers and 200 scythed chariots. Cyrus' army: 10,400 Greek hoplites and 2,500 peltasts, about 1,000 Paphlagonian horse, his 600 Persian horsemen, Ariaeus' Asian levies and 20 scythed chariots (Xenophon, Anabasis 1.7-8).
iranian_note: Both armies were Persian-led and largely Iranian; Cyrus' Greek mercenaries (about 13,000) were a minority of the combined forces.
strength_a: 900,000 present of a nominal 1,200,000, with 200 scythed chariots (Xenophon); 400,000 (Ctesias); about 40,000 (modern estimate in Wikipedia)
strength_b: 10,400 Greek hoplites, 2,500 peltasts, 100,000 Asian troops and 20 scythed chariots (Xenophon); modern estimates of the Asian troops 10,000-20,000
result_basis: Cyrus was killed and his Asian troops fled the field with Ariaeus; only the Greek mercenaries held their ground, and they withdrew to their plundered camp at nightfall.
sources: Xenophon, Anabasis 1.7-10; Plutarch, Artaxerxes 7-13; Diodorus 14.22-24; Ctesias (Photius) 63-64; en.wikipedia Battle of Cunaxa
note: Xenophon and Ctesias stress that the Greeks were victorious on their wing; under the test the royal side won, as the rebel army left the field and its claimant was dead. Abrocomas' 300,000 arrived five days late.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Calpe
label: Calpe
commanders_a: Xenophon and the generals of the Ten Thousand
commanders_b: Bithynian chiefs; commanders of Pharnabazus' cavalry (not named)
persian_force: The cavalry of Pharnabazus, satrap of Hellespontine Phrygia, sent to help the Bithynian Thracians keep the Greeks out of Phrygia; the day before it had cut up a Greek foraging party under Neon (Anabasis 6.4.23-24).
iranian_note: Xenophon does not describe the horsemen; the satrapal cavalry of Hellespontine Phrygia was drawn from the Persian nobility and Iranian settlers of the satrapy.
strength_a: the Ten Thousand, reunited (several thousand hoplites and peltasts)
losses_a: about 500 of Neon's foragers killed the day before (Xenophon)
result_basis: The Greeks routed the Bithynian infantry and Pharnabazus' horsemen and held the field (Xenophon, Anabasis 6.5).
borderline: no conventional battle name; a minor battle known from Xenophon
doubt: Borderline: no conventional battle name; a minor battle known from Xenophon.
sources: Xenophon, Anabasis 6.4.23-6.5.32
note: Persia is listed as the Bithynians' ally: Pharnabazus sent his cavalry to their aid. Calpe Harbour was the Ten Thousand's base on the Black Sea coast.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Cyme (siege)
label: Cyme (siege)
date: late 400 BC (raised at the onset of winter 400/399)
war: Persian-Spartan War (prelude: Tissaphernes against the Ionian and Aeolian cities)
persian_force: Tissaphernes' satrapal army; the source gives no composition. Western satrapal armies then combined Persian and other Iranian cavalry with Anatolian (Carian, Lydian) levies and Greek mercenaries (said here, not in the source).
iranian_note: Inferred from the satrapal armies of western Asia Minor, an Iranian cavalry core with Anatolian levies and Greek mercenaries (Diodorus 14.80.1 gives Tissaphernes 10,000 horse and 50,000 foot in 395).
losses_a: many captives taken in the countryside, later ransomed
result_basis: Tissaphernes ravaged Cyme's territory but could not take the city and raised the siege as winter came on, releasing his captives for ransom (Diodorus 14.35.7).
borderline: a minor siege known only from Diodorus
doubt: Borderline: a minor siege known only from Diodorus.
sources: Diodorus 14.35.6-7
note: Tissaphernes' attacks on the Greek cities led them to appeal to Sparta, which sent Thibron (399).
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Asidates' tower (raid)
label: Asidates' tower (raid)
war: Persian-Spartan War (the Ten Thousand join Thibron)
place: Plain of the Caicus near Pergamum (Bergama), Turkey
persian_force: Asidates' household defending his tower, then the relief forces: Itabelius with his own troops, Assyrian hoplites and about 80 Hyrcanian horsemen in the King's pay from Comania, about 800 peltasts, and men from Parthenium and Apollonia, including horsemen (Anabasis 7.8.15).
iranian_note: Xenophon names a Persian lord's household and Hyrcanian horsemen beside Assyrian hoplites; the peltasts were probably local Mysians.
strength_a: the tower garrison and relief forces (above)
strength_b: a picked force of a few hundred of Xenophon's men, with more horse and peltasts sent after them
result_basis: The night assault failed to take Asidates' fortified tower, and the Greeks withdrew with their booty under attack from the Persian relief forces, leaving the field to them (Xenophon, Anabasis 7.8.12-19).
borderline: a raid on a Persian noble's estate; no conventional name
doubt: Borderline: a raid on a Persian noble's estate; no conventional name.
sources: Xenophon, Anabasis 7.8.8-23
note: Xenophon's account ends with Asidates captured with his family and goods in a second sortie soon afterwards, so the raid as a whole ended in the Greeks' favour; the fight at the tower is scored as above.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Larisa (siege)
label: Larisa (siege)
place: Larisa 'the Egyptian' (probably Larisa Phrikonis, near Buruncuk), Turkey
persian_force: The townsmen of Larisa, held for the King; Xenophon (Cyropaedia 7.1.45) says their ancestors were Egyptian soldiers settled there by Cyrus.
iranian_note: The defenders were the town's own military colonists, of Egyptian descent according to Xenophon; no Persian troops are named.
result_basis: The defenders filled Thibron's water-shaft and burned his siege shed in sorties, and he abandoned the siege when ordered to Caria (Xenophon, Hellenica 3.1.7).
borderline: a Persian-held town defended by its own colonists; no Persian army present
doubt: Borderline: a Persian-held town defended by its own colonists; no Persian army present.
sources: Xenophon, Hellenica 3.1.7; Cyropaedia 7.1.45
note: Dercylidas took Larisa without a fight later in 399.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Magnesia (399 BC)
label: Magnesia (399 BC)
place: Magnesia on the Maeander (near Tekin), Turkey
persian_force: The town's defenders under Tissaphernes' rule; no Persian troops are named.
iranian_note: Diodorus says only that the town was subject to Tissaphernes; any garrison is unrecorded.
strength_a: Thibron's army: about 5,000 Peloponnesians and neodamodeis, 2,000 Asiatic Greeks and the Cyreans (Xenophon, Hellenica 3.1.4-6)
result_basis: Thibron took Magnesia, a town subject to Tissaphernes, at the first assault (Diodorus 14.36.2).
borderline: a Persian-held Greek town taken at the first assault; no Persian army is named
doubt: Borderline: a Persian-held Greek town taken at the first assault; no Persian army is named.
sources: Diodorus 14.36.2-3
note: Thibron then moved the unwalled town to the hill Thorax. Xenophon's account of 399 does not mention Magnesia or Tralles.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Tralles (siege)
label: Tralles (siege)
persian_force: The garrison of a town held for Tissaphernes; composition not given. Tissaphernes' cavalry soon forced Thibron back to Ephesus.
iranian_note: Diodorus gives no detail of the defenders.
result_basis: Thibron could achieve nothing against the strong town and abandoned the siege (Diodorus 14.36.3).
borderline: a siege known only from Diodorus; no fighting described
doubt: Borderline: a siege known only from Diodorus; no fighting described.
sources: Diodorus 14.36.3
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Caunus (siege)
label: Caunus (siege)
persian_force: Conon's 40 triremes of the King's fleet (raised in Cyprus, Cilicia and Phoenicia) and the land forces of Pharnabazus and Artaphernes.
iranian_note: The fleet's crews were Cypriot, Cilician and Phoenician; Iranians were only in the satraps' relieving forces and the command.
strength_a: 40 triremes, then land forces of two satraps
result_basis: Pharax raised his blockade of Conon at Caunus when Artaphernes and Pharnabazus came up with strong forces, and sailed back to Rhodes (Diodorus 14.79.5).
borderline: a blockade raised without recorded fighting
doubt: Borderline: a blockade raised without recorded fighting.
sources: Diodorus 14.79.4-5; Hellenica Oxyrhynchia 9 (Conon at Caunus)
note: Rhodes revolted from Sparta soon afterwards and received Conon.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Gordium (siege)
label: Gordium (siege)
persian_force: The garrison of Gordium under the Persian Rathines; its composition is not given (Phrygian strongholds were normally held by Persian officers with local troops).
iranian_note: Only the Persian commander is named; the garrison's make-up is unrecorded.
result_basis: Agesilaus attacked the well-provisioned hill fortress for several days without success and marched away (Hellenica Oxyrhynchia).
borderline: known only from the Hellenica Oxyrhynchia
doubt: Borderline: known only from the Hellenica Oxyrhynchia.
sources: Hellenica Oxyrhynchia (Agesilaus' march through Phrygia, autumn 395)
note: On the same march Agesilaus also failed against the fortresses of Leonton Kephalai and Miletou Teichos before going on to Paphlagonia.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Kaue
label: Kaue
place: Kaue, a village in Hellespontine Phrygia (site unknown, in the region of Dascylium), Turkey
persian_force: Pharnabazus' field camp with his household troops and outposts; Xenophon gives no numbers. Earlier that winter the satrap had attacked Greek foragers with two scythed chariots and about 400 horsemen (Hellenica 4.1.17-19).
iranian_note: Inferred: a satrap's mobile force was his Iranian household cavalry with local troops.
strength_a: a picked force of hoplites and peltasts with Spithridates' cavalry
result_basis: Herippidas' dawn attack overran Pharnabazus' camp; the satrap fled and the Greeks took the camp and its booty (Xenophon, Hellenica 4.1.20-26).
borderline: a raid on a camp; no conventional name
doubt: Borderline: a raid on a camp; no conventional name.
sources: Xenophon, Hellenica 4.1.20-27; Plutarch, Agesilaus 11
note: The quarrel over the booty made Spithridates and the Paphlagonians desert Agesilaus. The village is Kaue in Xenophon (translated 'Cave').
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Sardis (395 BC)
label: Sardis (395 BC)
place: plain near the Pactolus, outside Sardis (Sart), Turkey
commanders_a: Agesilaus II (Xenocles led the ambush in the Hellenica Oxyrhynchia and Diodorus)
commanders_b: Tissaphernes (in Sardis during the battle, according to Xenophon)
persian_force: Tissaphernes' Persian cavalry, fighting without its infantry, which had not come up (Xenophon); Diodorus gives the satrap 10,000 horse and 50,000 foot shadowing Agesilaus.
iranian_note: Xenophon says only the Persian cavalry fought, a force drawn from the Iranian nobility and settlers of Lydia; the infantry (Anatolian levies and mercenaries) was absent.
strength_a: Agesilaus' army: 30 Spartiates, 2,000 neodamodeis, 6,000 allies, with the Cyreans and Asiatic Greeks (Xenophon)
strength_b: 10,000 cavalry and 50,000 infantry with Tissaphernes (Diodorus 14.80.1); only the cavalry engaged
losses_b: over 6,000 killed (Diodorus 14.80.4); much lower in the Hellenica Oxyrhynchia
result_basis: Agesilaus routed the Persian cavalry by the Pactolus and took its camp; the Spartans held the field.
sources: Xenophon, Hellenica 3.4.20-25; Hellenica Oxyrhynchia 11-12; Diodorus 14.80; Pausanias 3.9.6; en.wikipedia Battle of Sardis (395 BC)
note: Ancient Greek Battles calls it 'Sardis'; the year is added because the Persian set has other Sardis entries (547, 498 BC). Xenophon describes a set battle by the Pactolus, the Hellenica Oxyrhynchia and Diodorus an ambush by Xenocles on the march. Tissaphernes was executed soon afterwards.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Cnidus
label: Cnidus
date: August 394 BC (shortly before the eclipse of 14 August)
persian_force: The King's fleet of more than 90 triremes (Diodorus): Phoenician squadrons under Pharnabazus and the Greek squadron under Conon, largely Cypriot (Evagoras of Salamis), with Cilician ships.
iranian_note: The crews were Phoenician, Cypriot Greek and Cilician; Iranians were only the satrap's staff and probably some marines.
losses_b: 50 triremes and about 500 men captured (Diodorus 14.83.7); Peisander killed
result_basis: The royal fleet routed Peisander's fleet, captured 50 triremes (Diodorus) and held the sea off Cnidus.
sources: Xenophon, Hellenica 4.3.10-12; Diodorus 14.83.4-7; Isocrates, Evagoras 56; Pausanias 1.1.3; en.wikipedia Battle of Cnidus
note: Ancient Greek Battles lists Salamis (Cyprus) as Persia's ally; here 'Cypriot kingdoms' (Evagoras of Salamis supplied most of Conon's ships).
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Cythera
label: Cythera
persian_force: The royal fleet after Cnidus, Phoenician and Cypriot Greek ships with the troops they carried, under Pharnabazus and Conon.
iranian_note: A fleet manned mainly by Phoenicians and Greeks, with Iranians only in the satrap's suite.
result_basis: Conon took the town of Cythera at the first assault and sent the Cytherians to Laconia under truce (Diodorus 14.84.5).
borderline: a capture with little recorded fighting
doubt: Borderline: a capture with little recorded fighting.
sources: Diodorus 14.84.4-5; Xenophon, Hellenica 4.8.7-8
note: On the same cruise the fleet raided the Laconian coast (Pherae, Phoenicus). A garrison under the Athenian Nicophemus was left on Cythera.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Maeander (Thibron)
label: Maeander (Thibron)
persian_force: Struthas' cavalry, which Xenophon makes the only arm engaged.
iranian_note: A satrapal cavalry force of Lydia, drawn from the Persian nobility and Iranian settlers.
losses_b: Thibron, Diphilas and most of the force killed (Xenophon)
result_basis: Struthas' cavalry caught Thibron's disorderly raiding force, killed Thibron and most of his men and drove the rest off the field (Xenophon, Hellenica 4.8.18-19).
sources: Xenophon, Hellenica 4.8.17-19; Diodorus 14.99.1-3
note: Diodorus dates it 390/389. The survivors were taken over by Diphridas.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Egypt (invasion, 385-383 BC)
label: Egypt (invasion, 385-383 BC)
persian_force: The royal army of Abrocomas, Tithraustes and Pharnabazus; no composition survives. Royal armies of the time joined Persian and other Iranian troops with levies of the western satrapies and Greek mercenaries (said here, not in the source).
iranian_note: Inferred from the make-up of later royal armies against Egypt (373, 343).
result_basis: Isocrates says the King's generals suffered more harm than they did in three years of fighting in Egypt and then withdrew, leaving Hakor in possession (Panegyricus 140); no single battle is described.
borderline: a campaign known only in outline; no named battle
doubt: Borderline: a campaign known only in outline; no named battle.
sources: Isocrates, Panegyricus 140-141; en.wikipedia Battle of Pelusium (373 BC) (background)
note: The Athenian Chabrias served Hakor in these years, but his part in this war is uncertain.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Citium
label: Citium
persian_force: The royal fleet of about 300 triremes under Glos, raised in Ionia, Cilicia and Phoenicia (the army assembled at Phocaea and Cyme), with marines of the royal army.
iranian_note: The crews came from the Greek, Cilician and Phoenician coastlands; Iranians were few aboard.
result_basis: Glos' fleet defeated Evagoras' fleet off Citium, destroying or taking many ships, and Evagoras fled to Salamis (Diodorus 15.3.4-6).
sources: Diodorus 15.2-4; Isocrates, Evagoras 60-64; en.wikipedia Evagoras I
note: Evagoras' Salamis is 'Cypriot kingdoms' (Ancient Greek Battles: Salamis (Cyprus)). Glos was the son of Tamos, an Egyptian of Memphis in Persian service. Cimon's siege of Kition (450/449 BC) is a separate entry.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Salamis in Cyprus (siege, 381 BC)
label: Salamis in Cyprus (siege, 381 BC)
persian_force: The royal army of Tiribazus and Orontes, put by Diodorus at 300,000 men, with Glos' fleet: Persian and other Iranian troops with levies of the western satrapies and Greek mercenaries.
iranian_note: Inferred from royal armies of the time; Diodorus gives only the total.
result_basis: Salamis was still invested by land and sea when Orontes ended the war by treaty: Evagoras kept his city as a tribute-paying vassal king (Diodorus 15.8-9).
sources: Diodorus 15.4, 15.8-9; Isocrates, Evagoras 64; en.wikipedia Evagoras I
note: Egypt (Hakor) gave Evagoras some help during the siege. Wikipedia's Evagoras article keeps an older chronology (invasion 385, peace 376).
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Pelusium (373 BC)
label: Pelusium (373 BC)
place: Pelusium (Tell el-Farama) and the Mendesian mouth of the Nile, Egypt
persian_force: Pharnabazus' royal army, given as 200,000 'barbarians' with 20,000 Greek mercenaries under Iphicrates, 300 triremes and 200 thirty-oared ships (Diodorus 15.41.3).
iranian_note: Diodorus separates the Greek mercenaries (about a tenth) from the 'barbarians', who were Persian troops and levies of the western satrapies.
losses_a: many killed and taken at the Mendesian fort
result_basis: In the one battle described, the Persians and Iphicrates' mercenaries routed the Egyptian force that came out against their landing at the Mendesian mouth and stormed the fort (Diodorus 15.42.4-5); the halt short of Memphis and the withdrawal when the Nile rose are strategic matters.
sources: Diodorus 15.41-43; Nepos, Iphicrates 2; en.wikipedia Battle of Pelusium (373 BC)
note: Wikipedia also calls it the Battle of Mendes. Pelusium was too strongly fortified to attack, so the fleet entered the Mendesian mouth, where the fort was stormed (a Persian success); Pharnabazus refused Iphicrates' plan to march on Memphis. Coordinates are for the Mendesian mouth (approximate). Wikipedia's 'Port Said' for Pelusium is wrong.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Assos (siege)
label: Assos (siege)
persian_force: Both sides Persian: Ariobarzanes' satrapal troops and mercenaries, helped by Agesilaus' mercenaries; the besiegers were the satrapal army of Lydia under Autophradates and Mausolus' Carian forces, with 100 ships (Xenophon).
iranian_note: Inferred: satrapal armies with Iranian cavalry, Anatolian levies and Greek mercenaries; Mausolus' fleet was Carian and Greek.
result_basis: Autophradates raised the siege on Agesilaus' approach and Mausolus sailed away, so the defender won (Xenophon, Agesilaus 2.26).
borderline: a siege raised without recorded fighting
doubt: Borderline: a siege raised without recorded fighting.
sources: Xenophon, Agesilaus 2.26-27; en.wikipedia Ariobarzanes of Phrygia (as Adramyttium); en.wikipedia Revolt of the Satraps
note: Xenophon names Assos; Wikipedia and the Cambridge History of Iran place the siege of Ariobarzanes at Adramyttium. Cotys of Thrace besieged Sestos at the same time.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Datames against Autophradates
label: Datames against Autophradates
place: a defile in Cappadocia near the Cilician Gates, Turkey
persian_force: Both sides Persian. Autophradates' royal army (Nepos, Datames 8): 20,000 horse and 100,000 Cardaces infantry, 3,000 slingers, with Cappadocian, Armenian, Paphlagonian, Phrygian, Lydian, Aspendian and Pisidian, Cilician and Captianian contingents, 3,000 Greek mercenaries and many light troops; Datames' army, mainly Cappadocians, was 'not a twentieth part' as large.
iranian_note: Nepos lists Iranian cavalry and the Cardaces beside many Anatolian, Armenian and Greek contingents; the Cardaces' origin is debated and the figures are inflated.
strength_a: under a twentieth of the royal army (Nepos)
result_basis: Datames caught the royal army in a narrow defile, killed many thousands for the loss of about 1,000, set up a trophy on the field, and Autophradates made a truce and withdrew to Phrygia (Nepos, Datames 8).
borderline: an unnamed campaign known only from Nepos; date uncertain
doubt: Borderline: an unnamed campaign known only from Nepos; date uncertain.
sources: Nepos, Datames 7-8; en.wikipedia Revolt of the Satraps; en.wikipedia Datames
note: Nepos alone tells it; the chronology of Datames' revolt is obscure.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Samos (siege, 366 BC)
label: Samos (siege, 366 BC)
war: Satraps' Revolt (Athens against the King's garrison in Samos)
persian_force: The garrison put into Samos by Cyprothemis with the backing of Tigranes, the King's hyparch (Demosthenes 15.9); probably mercenaries.
iranian_note: Garrisons of this kind were mostly Greek mercenaries under Persian authority.
strength_a: 8,000 peltasts and 30 ships (Isocrates 15.111, for the expedition)
result_basis: Samos fell to Timotheus after a ten-month siege.
sources: Isocrates, Antidosis 108-111; Demosthenes 15.9; Nepos, Timotheus 1; en.wikipedia Timotheus (general)
note: Timotheus was sent to aid Ariobarzanes but, finding him in open revolt, attacked Samos instead. Athens then settled cleruchs on Samos.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Bosporus (Leucon v Heracleots)
label: Bosporus
sources: Polyaenus 6.9.3–4
note: The Heracleots landed from a large fleet and raided. Leucon posted Scythian archers behind his hoplites to cut down anyone who fled, then defeated the invaders. Date and site are uncertain.
qbasis: Scythians among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans

name: Datames against Artabazus
label: Datames against Artabazus
persian_force: Both sides Persian: Datames' Cappadocian cavalry and mercenary infantry against the royal army of Artabazus; no breakdown is given.
iranian_note: Inferred: Anatolian satrapal armies of Iranian cavalry with local and mercenary infantry.
result_basis: Datames pursued his father-in-law's cavalry as it deserted to Artabazus and cut it down beside the royal army, which was defeated and withdrew (Diodorus 15.91.2-7).
borderline: an unnamed battle
doubt: Borderline: an unnamed battle.
sources: Diodorus 15.91.2-7; Nepos, Datames 6; en.wikipedia Datames; en.wikipedia Artabazus II
note: Nepos (Datames 6) tells the same stratagem against Mithrobarzanes' desertion, but in a war against the Pisidians; the two may be versions of one event.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Chares' victory over the satraps
label: Chares' victory over the satraps
persian_force: Both sides Persian: Artabazus' own small force, with Chares' Athenian mercenary army doing most of the fighting, against the royal satraps' army of 70,000 (Diodorus).
iranian_note: The winning side was mostly Greek mercenaries; the royal army was a satrapal levy of Iranian cavalry and Anatolian infantry.
strength_a: Artabazus' few troops and Chares' army
result_basis: Chares' mercenary army and Artabazus defeated the royal satraps' army (Diodorus 16.22.1).
borderline: an unnamed battle; Athens fought as Artabazus' paid ally
doubt: Borderline: an unnamed battle; Athens fought as Artabazus' paid ally.
sources: Diodorus 16.22.1-2; Demosthenes 4.24 and scholia; en.wikipedia Chares of Athens; en.wikipedia Artabazus II
note: Artaxerxes III's protest and threat to aid Athens' rebel allies made Athens recall Chares and end the Social War.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Pammenes' victories over the satraps
label: Pammenes' victories over the satraps
persian_force: Both sides Persian: Artabazus' forces with 5,000 Theban troops under Pammenes, against the royal satraps' armies.
iranian_note: Inferred: satrapal armies of Iranian cavalry and Anatolian infantry on both sides, with Greek allies and mercenaries.
result_basis: Pammenes' Thebans and Artabazus defeated the satraps in two great battles (Diodorus 16.34.1-2).
borderline: two unnamed battles combined in one entry
doubt: Borderline: two unnamed battles combined in one entry.
sources: Diodorus 16.34.1-2; en.wikipedia Artabazus II
note: Artabazus later fell out with Pammenes; the revolt collapsed and Artabazus fled to Philip II with Memnon.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Halicarnassus (c. 352 BC)
label: Halicarnassus (c. 352 BC)
war: Wars of the Hecatomnids (Caria against Rhodes)
persian_force: The fleet and troops of the Hecatomnid satrapy of Caria under Artemisia, using Mausolus' secret harbour.
iranian_note: The Hecatomnid forces were Carian and Greek; no Iranians are attested.
losses_b: the Rhodian landing party killed, the fleet captured (Vitruvius)
result_basis: In Vitruvius' story Artemisia's men seized the Rhodian ships in the harbour, killed the Rhodians who had landed, and then took Rhodes with the captured fleet.
borderline: a Carian satrap's own war; counted as Persian because the Hecatomnids were the King's satraps
doubt: Traditional: Known only from Vitruvius (2. Borderline: a Carian satrap's own war; counted as Persian because the Hecatomnids were the King's satraps.
sources: Vitruvius 2.8.14-15; Demosthenes 15; en.wikipedia Artemisia II of Caria
note: The Rhodian oligarchs were backed by Caria; Demosthenes' speech On the Liberty of the Rhodians (351) shows Rhodes under Carian control.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Egypt (invasion, 351 BC)
label: Egypt (invasion, 351 BC)
commanders_a: Nectanebo II; Diophantus of Athens and Lamius of Sparta
persian_force: Artaxerxes III's royal army; no composition survives. It will have been like the army of 343: Persian and other Iranian troops, imperial levies and Greek mercenaries (said here, not in the sources).
iranian_note: Inferred from the royal army of 343 (Diodorus 16.47).
result_basis: The Egyptians, led by their Greek generals Diophantus and Lamius, repulsed the royal invasion and the King withdrew without reconquering Egypt (Diodorus 16.40.3, 16.48.2; Isocrates, Philippus 101).
borderline: a campaign; no named battle known
doubt: Borderline: a campaign; no named battle known.
sources: Diodorus 16.40.3-6, 16.44.1, 16.48.1-2; Isocrates, Philippus 101; en.wikipedia Second Achaemenid conquest of Egypt
note: The failure set off the revolts of Phoenicia (Sidon) and Cyprus.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Mentor's victory over the satraps
label: Mentor's victory over the satraps
date: c. 346 BC (date uncertain; Diodorus narrates the revolt under 351/350)
commanders_a: Tennes of Sidon; Mentor of Rhodes
commanders_b: Belesys (satrap of Syria), Mazaeus (satrap of Cilicia)
persian_force: The satrapal armies of Syria (Belesys) and Cilicia (Mazaeus); no figures. Such armies combined Persian cavalry and garrison troops with Syrian, Cilician and mercenary infantry (said here, not in the source).
iranian_note: Inferred; Diodorus gives no detail of the satraps' armies.
strength_a: the Sidonians with 4,000 Greek mercenaries sent by Nectanebo II (Diodorus)
result_basis: Tennes and Mentor's 4,000 Greek mercenaries defeated the two satraps and drove them out of Phoenicia (Diodorus 16.42.1-2).
borderline: an unnamed battle
doubt: Borderline: an unnamed battle.
sources: Diodorus 16.41-42; en.wikipedia Tennes; en.wikipedia Mentor of Rhodes
note: The mercenaries were lent by Nectanebo II of Egypt, hence Egypt as ally.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Sidon (siege)
label: Sidon (siege)
commanders_a: Artaxerxes III; Mentor of Rhodes (after changing sides)
persian_force: Artaxerxes III's royal army (Diodorus: 300,000 foot, 30,000 horse, 300 triremes, 500 transports) with about 10,000 Greek mercenaries (1,000 Thebans under Lacrates, 3,000 Argives under Nicostratus, 6,000 Asiatic Greeks), joined by Mentor's 4,000.
iranian_note: The royal field army was built on Persian and other Iranian infantry and cavalry with imperial levies and Greek mercenaries; Diodorus gives only totals for the Asiatic troops.
losses_b: over 40,000 dead in the fire (Diodorus 16.45); 100 leading citizens and 500 suppliants killed
result_basis: Sidon fell to Artaxerxes III when Tennes and Mentor betrayed it; the Sidonians burned the city with themselves inside (Diodorus 16.45).
borderline: taken by betrayal, with little fighting at the walls
doubt: Borderline: taken by betrayal, with little fighting at the walls.
sources: Diodorus 16.41-45; en.wikipedia Tennes
note: The Sidonians had burned their own ships to prevent flight. Tennes was executed afterwards.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Salamis in Cyprus (siege, 344 BC)
label: Salamis in Cyprus (siege, 344 BC)
commanders_a: Evagoras II and Phocion of Athens (for Idrieus, satrap of Caria)
persian_force: The force sent by Idrieus, satrap of Caria, on the King's orders: 40 triremes and 8,000 mercenaries under Evagoras II and Phocion (Diodorus 16.42.7).
iranian_note: Diodorus describes Greek mercenaries and a Carian fleet; no Iranian troops are mentioned.
result_basis: Besieged by land and sea, Pnytagoras surrendered Salamis by submitting to the King and was left as his vassal (Diodorus 16.46.1-3).
sources: Diodorus 16.42.3-9, 16.46.1-3; Plutarch, Phocion
note: The other Cypriot kingdoms were reduced in the same campaign; Evagoras II, who hoped to recover Salamis, was set aside. Pnytagoras' submission is treated as a surrender (the place fell); if read as a negotiated peace the result would be a draw.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Pelusium (343 BC)
label: Pelusium (343 BC)
commanders_a: Artaxerxes III; Lacrates of Thebes and Rhosaces; Nicostratus of Argos and Aristazanes; Mentor of Rhodes and Bagoas
commanders_b: Nectanebo II; Philophron (garrison of Pelusium); Cleinius of Cos (killed)
persian_force: Artaxerxes III's royal army (Diodorus: 300,000 foot, 30,000 horse) with about 14,000 Greeks in three divisions, each under a Greek and a Persian commander: Lacrates' Thebans with Rhosaces' cavalry and Asiatic infantry, Nicostratus' Argives with Aristazanes and 80 triremes, Mentor's mercenaries with Bagoas.
iranian_note: Diodorus names Persian commanders and 'barbarian' cavalry and infantry beside the Greek divisions, which were about a tenth of the army.
strength_b: about 100,000: 20,000 Greek mercenaries, 20,000 Libyans, 60,000 Egyptians (Diodorus 16.47); 5,000 Greeks in Pelusium
losses_a: part of the army lost earlier in the Barathra marshes
losses_b: Cleinius and over 5,000 of his men killed (Diodorus)
result_basis: Pelusium surrendered to Lacrates on terms after Nicostratus' division crossed the Nile and destroyed Cleinius' counterattack and Nectanebo fell back on Memphis (Diodorus 16.48-49).
sources: Diodorus 16.46.4-16.51; en.wikipedia Battle of Pelusium (343 BC) (archived); en.wikipedia Second Achaemenid conquest of Egypt
