note: Wikipedia has merged the battle article into 'Second Achaemenid conquest of Egypt', which dates the conquest 340/339. Bubastis and the other Delta towns then surrendered, and Nectanebo fled south.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Perinthus (siege)
label: Perinthus (siege)
commanders_a: Apollodorus (commander of the force sent by Arsites); the Perinthians
persian_force: Mercenaries, money, grain and missiles sent by the coastal satraps on Artaxerxes III's orders (Diodorus 16.75.1-2); Pausanias (1.29.10) names Apollodorus as commander of the mercenaries sent by Arsites, satrap of Hellespontine Phrygia.
iranian_note: The Persian contribution was a body of Greek mercenaries with supplies and money.
strength_b: unknown (larger than the defenders, with siege engines)
result_basis: Philip failed to take Perinthus and broke off the siege to attack Byzantium (Diodorus 16.74-77).
borderline: the size of the Persian force is unknown; it may have been only a contingent
doubt: Borderline: the size of the Persian force is unknown; it may have been only a contingent.
sources: Diodorus 16.74-77; Pausanias 1.29.10; Arrian 2.14.5; en.wikipedia Siege of Perinthus
note: Constantinople also sent troops and artillery. 'Greek cities' = Perinthus and Constantinople.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Ateas (Scythians)
label: Ateas
place: Dobruja, south of the Danube delta
sources: Justin 9.2; Frontin. Str. 2.8.14; Strabo 7.3.18; Lucian Macr. 10
note: About 20,000 women and children reportedly captured. Site unknown.
qbasis: Scythians among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans

name: Magnesia (336 BC)
label: Magnesia (336 BC)
war: Macedonian advance force in Asia Minor (Parmenion and Attalus)
place: near Magnesia (probably on the Maeander), Turkey
persian_force: Memnon's mercenary army of about 4,000 men (Polyaenus 5.44.4), Greek mercenaries in Persian pay.
iranian_note: Memnon commanded Greek mercenaries; any Persian horse with him is unrecorded.
result_basis: Memnon surprised the Macedonians at their evening meal, killed or captured many and drove the survivors into Magnesia (Polyaenus 5.44.4).
sources: Polyaenus 5.44.4; Diodorus 17.7.8-10 (the campaign); en.wikipedia Memnon of Rhodes; Livius, Memnon of Rhodes
note: Ancient Greek Battles calls it 'Magnesia'; the year is added because of the separate entry for Thibron's capture of Magnesia (399 BC). Polyaenus places it near Magnesia held by Parmenion and Attalus; Memnon's later actions (Cyzicus, Pitane, the Troad) belong to 335.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Cyzicus (335)
label: Cyzicus (335)
date: 335 BC (Diodorus' year; some date it to 336)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Macedonian advance force in Asia Minor)
persian_force: Memnon's 5,000 Greek mercenaries (Diodorus 17.7.3).
iranian_note: Diodorus names only Memnon's mercenaries, who were Greeks.
result_basis: Memnon's surprise attack narrowly failed to take the city, and he withdrew after ravaging its territory (Diodorus 17.7.3).
borderline: a failed surprise attack on a city; the fighting is barely described
doubt: Borderline: a failed surprise attack on a city; the fighting is barely described.
sources: Diodorus 17.7.3; livius.org Memnon of Rhodes
note: Cyzicus was on the Macedonian side. Diodorus narrates the operations of Memnon and Parmenion under 335; Livius dates them to 336.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Pitane (siege)
label: Pitane (siege)
date: 335 BC (Diodorus' year; some date it to 336)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Macedonian advance force in Asia Minor)
persian_force: Memnon's relief army, not described; earlier that year he led 5,000 Greek mercenaries (Diodorus 17.7.3), and the Persian forces of the north-west were then mercenaries with the satrapal cavalry of Hellespontine Phrygia.
iranian_note: Memnon's field force in 335 was built round Greek mercenaries; any Persian cavalry with him is not mentioned.
result_basis: Parmenion raised the siege when Memnon's relief army appeared (Diodorus 17.7.10).
borderline: a siege raised when a relief army approached; no fighting is recorded
doubt: Borderline: a siege raised when a relief army approached; no fighting is recorded.
sources: Diodorus 17.7.9-10; livius.org Memnon of Rhodes
note: Just before, Parmenion stormed Grynium and enslaved its people (Diodorus 17.7.9); no Persian force is recorded there, so it is not listed.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Troad
label: Troad
date: 335 BC (Diodorus' year; some date it to 336)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Macedonian advance force in Asia Minor)
persian_force: A Persian army many times larger than Calas' force (Diodorus), not described; the western satraps then fielded Persian cavalry with Greek mercenaries and local levies.
iranian_note: Inferred from the satrapal armies of Asia Minor, whose cavalry was Persian and whose foot were mercenaries and levies; Diodorus gives no detail.
result_basis: Calas, far outnumbered, was beaten and withdrew to Rhoeteum (Diodorus 17.7.10).
sources: Diodorus 17.7.10; livius.org Memnon of Rhodes
note: Name, year and site as in Ancient Greek Battles. Diodorus does not name the Persian commander; Memnon is often assumed.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Halicarnassus (siege)
label: Halicarnassus (siege)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (conquest of the Achaemenid Empire)
commanders_b: Memnon of Rhodes, Orontobates, Ephialtes (killed), Thrasybulus
persian_force: Orontobates' Persian and Carian troops and Greek mercenaries (among them Athenian exiles under Ephialtes and Thrasybulus), supported by the Persian fleet (Arrian 1.20-23; Diodorus 17.24-27).
iranian_note: The sources stress Memnon's Greek mercenaries and Carian troops; only Orontobates' own Persians were Iranian.
losses_a: about 40 killed in the last sortie (Arrian 1.22.7); 16 killed and 300 wounded in an earlier fight
losses_b: about 1,000 killed in the last sortie (Arrian 1.22.7); 170 in an earlier fight
result_basis: After their sorties were beaten back, Memnon and Orontobates set fire to the town and withdrew to the citadels and Cos, and the town fell.
sources: Arrian 1.20-23; Diodorus 17.23-27; en.wikipedia Siege of Halicarnassus
note: Ancient Greek Battles lists this as 'Halicarnassus (sortie)', autumn 334, because it counts a siege only through a battle fought in it (here Ephialtes' sortie from the Tripylon gate); this entry covers the whole siege, the sorties included, and the result is the same. The citadels Salmakis and Zephyrion held out into 333 (see 'Caria').
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Miletus (siege, 334)
label: Miletus (siege, 334)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (conquest of the Achaemenid Empire)
persian_force: Hegesistratus' garrison of Greek mercenaries with the Milesians; the Persian fleet of 400 ships, mainly Phoenician and Cypriot, lay off Mycale but could not intervene (Arrian 1.18-19).
iranian_note: The defenders named are Greek mercenaries and Milesians, and the fleet was crewed mainly by Phoenicians and Cypriots.
strength_b: garrison unknown (Wikipedia: 300 Milesians); 400 ships offshore, not engaged
losses_b: heavy; 300 mercenaries who fled to an islet were taken into Alexander's service (Arrian 1.19.6)
result_basis: Miletus was stormed after Nicanor's fleet at Lade cut it off from the Persian fleet.
sources: Arrian 1.18-19; Diodorus 17.22; en.wikipedia Siege of Miletus
note: A raid by five Persian ships on the Macedonian anchorage was beaten off (Arrian 1.19.9-11); it is counted here as part of the siege. Not in Ancient Greek Battles, which counts sieges only through a battle fought in them.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Granicus
label: Granicus
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (conquest of the Achaemenid Empire)
commanders_b: Arsites, Spithridates (killed), Arsames, Rheomithres, Memnon of Rhodes, Omares (killed), Mithrobuzanes (killed), Mithridates (killed)
persian_force: The cavalry of the western satraps along the river (Persian horse, 1,000 Medes, 2,000 Bactrians, Hyrcanians under Spithridates, Paphlagonians under Arsites) with Greek mercenary infantry under Omares behind; Arrian gives 20,000 horse and nearly 20,000 mercenary foot.
iranian_note: The cavalry was mostly Iranian (Persian landholders of Asia Minor, Medes, Bactrians, Hyrcanians) with Paphlagonians, while the foot were Greek mercenaries (and perhaps local levies), so roughly half the army spoke Iranian languages (Arrian 1.14).
strength_a: about 18,000 engaged (modern estimate); the whole expedition about 32,000 foot and 5,100 horse (Diodorus 17.17)
strength_b: 20,000 horse and nearly 20,000 mercenary foot (Arrian); 10,000 horse and 100,000 foot (Diodorus); modern estimate about 14,000-15,000 (Devine)
losses_b: about 1,000 cavalry killed, most of the mercenaries killed and 2,000 captured (Arrian 1.16.2); Diodorus: over 10,000 foot and 2,000 horse killed, over 20,000 captured
result_basis: The Persian cavalry broke and fled and the Greek mercenaries were surrounded and cut down; the Macedonians held the field.
sources: Arrian 1.13-16; Diodorus 17.18-21; Plutarch, Alexander 16; en.wikipedia Battle of the Granicus
note: Macedon's allies were the Thessalian cavalry and the Hellenic League contingents (Ancient Greek Battles lists 'Thessaly'). Arsites killed himself after the battle.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Caria
label: Caria
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (conquest of the Achaemenid Empire)
persian_force: Orontobates' satrapal army of Caria, not described; it held the citadels of Halicarnassus and would have been Persian, Carian and Greek mercenary troops.
iranian_note: Inferred from the Persian forces in Caria in 334 (Carians and Greek mercenaries under Persian officers).
losses_b: about 700 foot and 50 horse killed, at least 1,000 captured (Arrian 2.5.7)
result_basis: Ptolemy and Asander defeated Orontobates in battle, killing about 700 foot and 50 horse (Arrian 2.5.7).
sources: Arrian 2.5.7
note: Afterwards the Macedonians took Myndus, Caunus, Thera, Callipolis, Cos and Triopium (Arrian 2.5.7). Name, year and site as in Ancient Greek Battles.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Memphis (333)
label: Memphis (333)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (after Issus)
persian_force: The Persian garrison of Memphis under the satrap Mazaces; not described, but the Achaemenid garrisons of Egypt were Persian troops with Aramaean, Jewish and other soldiers.
iranian_note: Curtius calls the garrison 'Persians'; the make-up of the Egyptian garrisons (Persians with Aramaic-speaking troops) is inferred.
strength_b: about 4,000 mercenaries (Diodorus 17.48.2; Arrian 2.13.2 has 8,000 escape from Issus with Amyntas and others) and Egyptian supporters
losses_b: Amyntas and most of his men killed
result_basis: Amyntas first beat the garrison before Memphis, but Mazaces' sally caught his men scattered for plunder and killed him and most of them (Curtius 4.1.30-33; Diodorus 17.48.3-5).
borderline: no conventional name; it is the fight of Amyntas' mercenaries with the Persian garrison before Memphis
doubt: Borderline: no conventional name; it is the fight of Amyntas' mercenaries with the Persian garrison before Memphis.
sources: Curtius 4.1.27-33; Diodorus 17.48.2-5; Arrian 2.13.2-3; en.wikipedia Amyntas (son of Antiochus)
note: Amyntas, a Macedonian exile in Persian service, fled from Issus with Greek mercenaries via Tripolis and Cyprus to Pelusium, claimed to act for Darius, and tried to take Egypt for himself; Arrian says only that he was killed by the Egyptians. New entity: 'Greek mercenaries'.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Mytilene (siege, 333)
label: Mytilene (siege, 333)
date: spring-summer 333 BC (Memnon died during the siege)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Memnon's Aegean campaign)
commanders_a: Memnon of Rhodes (died during the siege), Pharnabazus, Autophradates
commanders_b: unknown (the Mytileneans and Alexander's mercenary garrison)
persian_force: The Persian fleet (about 300 ships, mainly Phoenician and Cypriot: Diodorus 17.29.2) and Memnon's Greek mercenaries, who shut the city in with a double stockade and five camps (Arrian 2.1.1-2).
iranian_note: The fleet was Phoenician and Cypriot and the troops Greek mercenaries; the Persians were the commanders and marines.
result_basis: Mytilene, walled off by land and blockaded by sea, capitulated to Pharnabazus and Autophradates and took a Persian garrison (Arrian 2.1).
sources: Arrian 2.1; Diodorus 17.29; livius.org Memnon of Rhodes
note: Mytilene was allied to Alexander. The terms expelled his mercenaries and restored the exiles; Lycomedes of Rhodes commanded the Persian garrison and Diogenes became tyrant (Arrian 2.1.4-5). Before this Memnon took Chios by betrayal and most of Lesbos without a battle.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Siphnos
label: Siphnos
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Memnon's Aegean campaign)
persian_force: Datames' squadron of 10 ships detached from the Persian fleet of Pharnabazus and Autophradates (Arrian 2.2.4-5); its crews are not described.
iranian_note: The Persian fleet was crewed mainly by Phoenicians, Cypriots and Greeks under Persian officers.
result_basis: Proteas surprised Datames' squadron at dawn and captured eight of its ten ships.
sources: Arrian 2.2.4-5
note: Name, year and site as in Ancient Greek Battles.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Issus
label: Issus
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (conquest of the Achaemenid Empire)
place: river Pinarus (Payas or Deli Çay) near Issus, Turkey
commanders_b: Darius III, Nabarzanes, Arsames (killed), Rheomithres (killed), Atizyes (killed), Sabaces (killed), Thymondas
persian_force: Darius' royal army: Greek mercenary hoplites (Arrian 30,000; modern estimates about 10,000-12,000), the Cardaces (Persian infantry), the Persian guard (Immortals, the kinsmen cavalry), the Persian, Median and Hyrcanian heavy cavalry under Nabarzanes on the seaward wing, and light-armed levies (Arrian 2.8; Curtius 3.9).
iranian_note: Apart from the Greek mercenaries the named units (Cardaces, guards, Persian, Median and Hyrcanian cavalry) were Iranian; the eastern levies of Gaugamela were not present.
strength_b: 600,000 (Arrian, Plutarch), 400,000 (Diodorus, Justin), 250,000 (Curtius); modern estimates mostly under 100,000
losses_a: 182 killed, 504 wounded, 302 missing (Curtius 3.11.27); 300 foot and 150 horse killed (Diodorus 17.36.6)
losses_b: 100,000 foot and 10,000 horse killed (Arrian 2.11.8; Diodorus); modern estimates far lower (Wikipedia: 20,000-40,000)
result_basis: Darius fled and his army broke and was pursued off the field; the Macedonians took his camp and family.
sources: Arrian 2.6-11; Curtius 3.8-11; Diodorus 17.32-36; Plutarch, Alexander 20; en.wikipedia Battle of Issus
note: The day (5 November) is a modern calculation and is not in the ancient sources. Macedon's allies were the Thessalian cavalry and Hellenic League troops.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Gaza (siege, 332)
label: Gaza (siege, 332)
date: autumn 332 BC (about two months; Wikipedia: October)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (conquest of the Achaemenid Empire)
persian_force: Batis' garrison of Persian troops and the Arab mercenaries he had hired (Arrian 2.25.4; Curtius 4.6.7-30).
iranian_note: Curtius counts Persians and Arabs among the dead; the Arab mercenaries were probably the larger part (Arrian 2.25.4), so the Iranian share is a guess.
losses_b: about 10,000 Persians and Arabs killed (Curtius 4.6.30); the men killed and the women and children enslaved (Arrian 2.27.7)
result_basis: Gaza was stormed at the fourth assault and its defenders were killed.
sources: Arrian 2.25-27; Curtius 4.6.7-30; Diodorus 17.48.7; en.wikipedia Siege of Gaza (332 BC)
note: Ancient Greek Battles lists this as 'Gaza (sortie)', autumn 332 (the defenders' sally against the siege works, in which Alexander was wounded: Arrian 2.26.4-27.2); this entry covers the whole siege, the sortie included, with the same result. Curtius (4.6.29) says Batis was dragged behind a chariot.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Hellespont
label: Hellespont
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (after Issus)
commanders_a: the Macedonian fleet summoned from Greece (commanders not named)
persian_force: Aristomenes' squadron, not described; the Persian fleet was then crewed mainly by Phoenicians, Cypriots and Greeks.
iranian_note: Inferred from the make-up of the Persian fleet in the Aegean.
result_basis: The Macedonian fleet defeated Aristomenes, sent by Darius to recover the Hellespont coast, and took or sank his ships (Curtius 4.1.36).
sources: Curtius 4.1.36
note: Known only from Curtius' short notice. The Macedonian Hellespont fleet raised in 333 was under Amphoterus and Hegelochus. Name, year and site as in Ancient Greek Battles.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Lydia
label: Lydia
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (after Issus)
place: Lydia and neighbouring regions (three battles, sites unknown), Turkey
commanders_b: Persian generals who escaped from Issus (not named)
persian_force: The commanders and troops who escaped from Issus, reinforced with Cappadocian and Paphlagonian recruits (Curtius 4.1.34).
iranian_note: Curtius names Persian survivors of Issus and Cappadocian and Paphlagonian levies; the Paphlagonians and most Cappadocians spoke Anatolian languages.
result_basis: Antigonus defeated the Persian generals in three battles in different places (Curtius 4.1.35).
note: One entry for three battles, as in Ancient Greek Battles. Heckel identifies the three as Antigonus in Lycaonia, Calas in Paphlagonia and Balacrus at Miletus (Curtius 4.5.13), so this entry may overlap 'Miletus (332)'.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Miletus (332)
label: Miletus (332)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (after Issus)
persian_force: Hydarnes' force, not described; the Persian counter-offensive of 332 used Issus survivors, Anatolian levies and mercenaries.
iranian_note: Curtius names only the commander.
result_basis: Balacrus defeated Hydarnes, Darius' general, and recovered Miletus (Curtius 4.5.13).
sources: Curtius 4.5.13
note: Ancient Greek Battles calls this 'Miletus'; the year is added here because of 'Miletus (siege, 334)'. See also 'Lydia'.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Mytilene (siege, 332)
label: Mytilene (siege, 332)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (after Issus)
persian_force: About 2,000 troops 'of the Persians' (Arrian 3.2.6) under the Athenian Chares, probably mostly mercenaries in Persian pay.
iranian_note: Arrian calls the garrison Persians, but under an Athenian commander it was probably largely mercenary.
result_basis: Hegelochus besieged Mytilene and Chares surrendered it on terms and left with his men (Arrian 3.2.6).
borderline: a blockade ended by capitulation; no assault is recorded
doubt: Borderline: a blockade ended by capitulation; no assault is recorded.
sources: Arrian 3.2.3-7; Curtius 4.5.14-22
note: In the same campaign Hegelochus recovered Tenedos, Chios (where the citizens let him in and Pharnabazus was captured) and Cos without battles; those captures are not listed.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Scythia
label: Scythia
place: Scythia, north-west of the Black Sea (site unknown)
note: Zopyrion, Alexander's governor in Thrace ('Pontus' in Justin), invaded Scythia with 30,000 men and besieged Olbia (Macrobius). He then perished with his whole army. Justin dates it c. 331; Curtius puts the news in 325. No details of the battle survive.
qbasis: Scythians among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans

name: Gaugamela
label: Gaugamela
date: 1 October 331 BC (fixed by the Babylonian astronomical diaries)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (conquest of the Achaemenid Empire)
place: Gaugamela (probably Tel Gomel, near Erbil), Iraq
persian_force: The levy of the whole empire: Persian guards (Immortals, kinsmen) and about 2,000 Greek mercenaries in the centre; Bactrian, Sogdian, Dahae, Saka, Arachosian, Persian, Susian and Cadusian horse under Bessus on the left; Median, Parthian, Hyrcanian, Tapurian, Syrian, Mesopotamian, Armenian, Cappadocian and Albanian horse under Mazaeus on the right; Indians, Mardian archers, scythed chariots and 15 elephants (Arrian 3.8, 3.11).
iranian_note: Arrian's order of battle (from a captured Persian document) is dominated by Iranian peoples: Persians, Medes, Parthians, Hyrcanians, Bactrians, Sogdians, Saka, Dahae and Arachosians.
strength_b: 1,000,000 foot and 40,000 horse (Arrian 3.8.6); 800,000 foot and 200,000 horse (Diodorus 17.53.3); 200,000 foot and 45,000 horse (Curtius); modern estimates about 50,000-120,000
result_basis: Darius fled, the Persian centre and left broke and Mazaeus' wing withdrew; the Macedonians held the field and pursued to Arbela.
sources: Arrian 3.8-15; Curtius 4.12-16; Diodorus 17.53-61; Plutarch, Alexander 31-33; en.wikipedia Battle of Gaugamela
note: Arrian (3.8.3) says the Saka came not as Bessus' subjects but as allies of Darius. Macedon's allies were the Thessalian cavalry and Hellenic League troops.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Uxian Defile
label: Uxian Defile
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (conquest of the Achaemenid Empire)
place: the Uxian pass on the road from Susa to Persis (site disputed), Iran
persian_force: The Uxian hillmen (Arrian) or Madates' garrison holding the pass and his town for Darius (Curtius 5.3); numbers not given.
iranian_note: The Uxians' language is unknown (perhaps descended from Elamite); Madates' own men were presumably Persians.
result_basis: Alexander turned the pass, and the Uxians, caught between his column and Craterus on the heights, were routed and sued for terms (Arrian 3.17).
borderline: Persian role depends on the source: Arrian's Uxians were independent hillmen who took tolls even from the Persian kings, while Curtius makes it a stand by Darius' kinsman Madates, governor of the Uxians
doubt: Borderline: Persian role depends on the source: Arrian's Uxians were independent hillmen who took tolls even from the Persian kings, while Curtius makes it a stand by Darius' kinsman Madates, governor of the Uxians.
sources: Arrian 3.17; Curtius 5.3.1-16; Diodorus 17.67; en.wikipedia Battle of the Uxian Defile
note: Curtius has Madates besieged in his town and pardoned at Sisygambis' plea. The tribute imposed was 100 horses, 500 cattle and 30,000 sheep a year (Arrian 3.17.6). Wikipedia's coordinates are those of Susa; the pass was in the Zagros east of Susa. New entity: 'Uxians'.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Artacoana (siege)
label: Artacoana (siege)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Bessus' war)
persian_force: Arian rebels who had risen for Satibarzanes when he went over to Bessus (Curtius: 13,000 armed men on the rock).
iranian_note: The defenders were Arians of the Herat region, an Iranian people.
result_basis: Alexander took the rebels' wooded rock by setting fire to it, and those who had joined the revolt were killed or enslaved (Curtius 6.6.23-34; Diodorus 17.78.1-2).
borderline: a minor siege known from Curtius and Diodorus; Arrian mentions only the pursuit and punishment of the rebels
doubt: Borderline: a minor siege known from Curtius and Diodorus; Arrian mentions only the pursuit and punishment of the rebels.
sources: Curtius 6.6.20-34; Diodorus 17.78.1-2; Arrian 3.25.5-7
note: Satibarzanes, satrap of Aria, submitted to Alexander and then revolted for Bessus, who had taken the title Artaxerxes V; hence 'Achaemenid Empire'.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Persian Gate
label: Persian Gate
date: January 330 BC (some date it to December 331)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (conquest of the Achaemenid Empire)
place: the Persian Gates pass (north of Yasuj), Iran
commanders_a: Alexander the Great, Craterus, Philotas, Ptolemy
persian_force: Ariobarzanes' army of Persis behind a wall across the pass: 40,000 foot and 700 horse (Arrian 3.18.2), 25,000 foot (Curtius; Diodorus, with 300 horse); modern estimates are far lower.
iranian_note: Ariobarzanes was satrap of Persis and his men were Persians of the homeland defending the road to Persepolis.
strength_a: Alexander's division (Wikipedia: about 17,000); Parmenion took the rest by the wagon road
strength_b: 40,000 foot and 700 horse (Arrian); 25,000 foot and 300 horse (Diodorus 17.68.1); modern estimates as low as 700-2,000 (Wikipedia)
losses_a: unknown; heavy in the first frontal attack
result_basis: Alexander's flanking column came down behind the Persian wall while Craterus attacked from the front, and the defenders were destroyed or scattered.
sources: Arrian 3.18; Curtius 5.3.17-5.4.34; Diodorus 17.68; en.wikipedia Battle of the Persian Gate
note: Arrian says Ariobarzanes escaped with a few horsemen; Curtius (5.4.33-34) that he broke out, was refused entry at Persepolis and died fighting. The modern Iranian story of his sister Youtab is not in the ancient sources.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Aria
label: Aria
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Bessus' war)
persian_force: Satibarzanes' Arian rebels with 2,000 horsemen sent by Bessus (Arrian 3.28.2).
iranian_note: Arians and Bessus' Bactrian horse, both Iranian peoples.
strength_a: 6,000 Greek foot and 600 horse, with Phrataphernes' troops (Arrian 3.28.2)
strength_b: 2,000 horse from Bessus and the Arian rebels
result_basis: Satibarzanes was killed in single combat by Erigyius and his army fled (Arrian 3.28.3; Curtius 7.4.33-40).
note: Bessus (Artaxerxes V) was still free, so this counts as 'Achaemenid Empire'. The Persian nobles Artabazus and Phrataphernes fought on Alexander's side. Name, year and site as in Ancient Greek Battles.
qbasis: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Cyropolis (siege)
label: Cyropolis (siege)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Sogdian and Bactrian revolt)
persian_force: About 15,000 Sogdian fighters, the best of the region (Arrian 4.3.4).
iranian_note: The defenders were Sogdians.
result_basis: The Macedonians got in by a dry watercourse and opened the gates, and the citadel surrendered for lack of water (Arrian 4.3.1-4).
sources: Arrian 4.2-3; Curtius 7.6.16-23; en.wikipedia Siege of Cyropolis
note: Ptolemy said the town surrendered, Aristobulus that it was stormed (Arrian 4.3.5). Curtius' siege of the city of the Memaceni is probably the same. Wikipedia's coordinates (40.28, 69.63) are those of Khujand (Alexandria Eschate).
qbasis: Iranian resistance: an Iranian-led state

name: Gaza (Sogdiana)
label: Gaza (Sogdiana)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Sogdian and Bactrian revolt)
place: Gaza (perhaps Nau, south-west of Khujand), Tajikistan
persian_force: Sogdian townsmen and the rebels of the region gathered in the seven Jaxartes towns (Arrian 4.2.1-2).
iranian_note: The defenders were Sogdians.
result_basis: Alexander stormed the town with ladders on the first day; the men were killed and the women and children enslaved (Arrian 4.2.3-4).
borderline: the first of seven towns taken in a few days; a minor assault
doubt: Borderline: the first of seven towns taken in a few days; a minor assault.
sources: Arrian 4.2.2-4
note: Arrian says five of the seven towns fell within two days; Cyropolis is entered separately. Site identification uncertain.
qbasis: Iranian resistance: an Iranian-led state

name: Jaxartes (329 BC)
label: Jaxartes
place: north bank of the Jaxartes (Syr Darya) opposite Alexandria Eschate (Khujand), Tajikistan/Uzbekistan
commanders_b: no commander named (a Saka king and his brother Carmanes are mentioned in Curtius)
result_basis: Alexander crossed the river under a catapult barrage, routed the Scythian horse (Saka) and pursued them into the steppe (Arrian 4.4).
sources: Arrian, Anabasis 4.2.1-4.4.9; Curtius 7.6.1-7.9.17; Plutarch, Alexander 45; Bosworth, Conquest and Empire (1988); Ancient Greek Battles ('Jaxartes')
note: The Saka (the 'Asiatic Scythians' of Arrian) had helped the Sogdian rebels. Alexander fell ill from the river water; the fight was a quick cavalry victory that kept the frontier on the Jaxartes.

name: Maracanda (siege)
label: Maracanda (siege)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Sogdian and Bactrian revolt)
commanders_a: the garrison of the citadel (commander not named)
persian_force: Spitamenes' Sogdian rebels, joined in the second blockade by Scythian (Saka) horsemen (Arrian 4.5-6).
iranian_note: Sogdians and Saka, both East Iranian speakers.
result_basis: Spitamenes twice gave up the blockade of the citadel, first when Pharnuches' relief column approached and again when Alexander came (Arrian 4.5.2-3, 4.6.3-4).
note: In the first blockade the garrison made a sortie and then withdrew into the citadel (Arrian 4.5.2).
qbasis: Iranian resistance: an Iranian-led state

name: Polytimetus
label: Polytimetus
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Sogdian and Bactrian revolt)
persian_force: Spitamenes' Sogdians with about 600 Scythian horse archers (Arrian 4.5.4), probably Massagetae or Dahae.
iranian_note: Sogdians and Saka horsemen, both East Iranian speakers.
strength_b: about 2,360: 60 Companions, 800 mercenary horse, 1,500 mercenary foot (Arrian 4.3.7); Curtius: 3,000 foot and 800 horse
result_basis: Spitamenes' horse archers surrounded the Macedonian column at a river crossing and destroyed it; only about 300 foot and 40 horse escaped (Arrian 4.5.4-4.6.2).

name: Gabai
label: Gabai

result_basis: Coenus routed Spitamenes' horsemen, killing over 800, and the Sogdian and Bactrian rebels deserted him (Arrian 4.17.4-7).
sources: Arrian 4.17.4-7; en.wikipedia Wars of Alexander the Great
note: Afterwards the Massagetae killed Spitamenes and sent his head to Alexander (Arrian 4.17.7); Curtius (8.3) says his wife killed him. Name, year and site as in Ancient Greek Battles.

label: Xenippa

place: Xenippa (site unknown, perhaps the Baysun area), Uzbekistan
persian_force: About 2,500 Bactrian exiles, all horsemen, driven out of Xenippa (Curtius 8.2.15).
iranian_note: The rebels were Bactrians.
result_basis: After a long and even fight the Bactrian exiles broke, losing 700 killed and 300 captured (Curtius 8.2.16-17).
borderline: known only from Curtius
doubt: Borderline: known only from Curtius.

name: Zariaspa
label: Zariaspa

persian_force: Spitamenes' raiders: the Massagetae with over 1,000 other horsemen (Arrian 4.17.1); Curtius calls them Dahae.
iranian_note: Massagetae and Dahae (Saka) with Sogdian and Bactrian exiles, all East Iranian speakers.
strength_b: the Massagetae and over 1,000 other horse
result_basis: Craterus caught the raiders at the edge of the desert and beat them; about 150 were killed and the rest escaped into the desert (Arrian 4.17.1).

label: Zariaspa (ambush)

persian_force: Spitamenes and the Sogdian exiles with about 600 Massagetae horsemen (Arrian 4.16.4).
iranian_note: Sogdian exiles and Massagetae, both East Iranian speakers.
strength_a: about 600 Massagetae horse with the Sogdian exiles

borderline: no conventional name; Arrian's account of the sortie from Zariaspa

name: Paraetacene (327)
label: Paraetacene (327)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Sogdian and Bactrian revolt)
place: Paraetacene (the Hissar region, site unknown), Tajikistan
persian_force: The rebels of Paraetacene, horse and foot, under the local lords Catanes and Austanes (Arrian 4.22.1-2).
iranian_note: The rebels were Sogdians and Bactrians of Paraetacene.
result_basis: Craterus won a hard-fought battle in which Catanes fell and Austanes was captured (Arrian 4.22.2).
sources: Arrian 4.22.1-2; Curtius 8.5.2
note: The last fight of the Sogdian and Bactrian revolt; the year is added to the name to keep it apart from the Diadochi battle of Paraitacene (317).

name: Rock of Chorienes (siege)
label: Rock of Chorienes (siege)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Sogdian and Bactrian revolt)
place: Rock of Chorienes (probably Kuh-e Nur on the Vakhsh), Tajikistan
persian_force: Chorienes' Sogdian followers in Paraetacene (numbers not given).
iranian_note: The defenders were Sogdians of Paraetacene.
losses_b: unknown (Curtius: many killed by slings and arrows)
result_basis: Chorienes surrendered after the Macedonians filled the ravine and brought the rock within bowshot (Arrian 4.21; Curtius 8.2.19-33).
sources: Arrian 4.21; Curtius 8.2.19-33; iranicaonline.org Chorienes
note: Encyclopaedia Iranica takes Arrian's Chorienes and Curtius' Sisimithres to be the same man (Bosworth thought them different) and places the rock at Kuh-e Nur by the Vakhsh. Chorienes was restored as governor.
qbasis: Iranian resistance: an Iranian-led state

name: Sogdian Rock (siege)
label: Sogdian Rock (siege)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Sogdian and Bactrian revolt)
place: Sogdian Rock, or Rock of Ariamazes (site disputed, perhaps near Derbent in the Baysun range), Uzbekistan
persian_force: Ariamazes' Sogdians (Curtius 7.11.1: 30,000 armed men), sheltering the family of the Bactrian lord Oxyartes, Roxane among them.
iranian_note: Sogdians and Bactrians.
losses_b: none in fighting; Curtius says Ariamazes and his kin were crucified
result_basis: The defenders surrendered when 300 climbers reached the heights above them (Arrian 4.18.4-4.19.4).
sources: Arrian 4.18.4-4.19.6; Curtius 7.11; en.wikipedia Siege of the Sogdian Rock
note: Wikipedia places the rock at 40.4 N, 69.4 E (near Khujand); most modern proposals are in the south, in the Baysun-Hissar ranges. The coordinates are a regional guess.
qbasis: Iranian resistance: an Iranian-led state

name: Hydaspes
label: Hydaspes
place: left bank of the Hydaspes (Jhelum), Punjab, Pakistan
result_basis: Alexander's cavalry, opened by the Dahae mounted archers, drove Porus' horse back on his infantry and the Macedonian phalanx finished it (Arrian 5.14-18).
sources: Arrian, Anabasis 5.12.2, 5.14-18 (the Bactrian, Sogdian and Scythian horse and 1,000 Dahae horse archers); Curtius 8.13-14; Diodorus 17.87-89; Plutarch, Alexander 60; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Hydaspes
note: Alexander's cavalry included Bactrian, Sogdian and Scythian (Saka) squadrons and about 1,000 Dahae horse archers, who began the fight by harassing the Indian right wing. The Iranian horse formed a large part of the cavalry but a small part of the whole army, so this counts as a named unit rather than a fifth.

name: Cappadocia (322)
label: Cappadocia (322)
war: Wars of the Diadochi (Perdiccas' conquest of Cappadocia)
persian_force: Ariarathes' army, mainly Cappadocian: 30,000 foot and 15,000 horse (Diodorus 18.16.2).
iranian_note: Cappadocia had a Persian landed nobility, which would have supplied much of the cavalry, over a native Anatolian population; the sources give no breakdown.
result_basis: Perdiccas defeated Ariarathes in battle, killing about 4,000 and capturing 5,000 with the king (Diodorus 18.16.2).
borderline: Ariarathes was the Achaemenid satrap of Cappadocia and never submitted to Alexander, but Cappadocia is not one of this set's Persian states and this set counts the Iranian resistance only to 327: probably out
doubt: Borderline: Ariarathes was the Achaemenid satrap of Cappadocia and never submitted to Alexander, but Cappadocia is not one of this set's Persian states and this set counts the Iranian resistance only to 327: probably out.
sources: Diodorus 18.16.1-3; Appian, Mithridatic Wars 8; Plutarch, Eumenes 3
note: His nephew Ariarathes II recovered Cappadocia about 301 with Armenian help (Diodorus 31.19.5); that fight is not listed.
qbasis: Iranian resistance: an Iranian-led state

name: Paraitacene
label: Paraitacene
result_basis: As in Ancient Greek Battles: Eumenes' phalanx routed Antigonus' and Antigonus lost far more men, but Antigonus' cavalry broke Eumenes' left and Antigonus camped on the field and claimed victory. Wikipedia infobox: Eumenes victory
sources: Diod. 19.26–32; Plut. Eum. 15; Nep. Eum. 8
note: Peucestas brought 10,000 Persian archers and slingers and 3,000 Persians armed in the Macedonian manner, besides the levies of the upper satraps (Diod. 19.14, 19.27-28)
qbasis: Peucestas brought 10,000 Persian archers and slingers and 3,000 Persians armed in the Macedonian manner, besides the levies of the upper satraps (Diod. 19.14, 19.27-28)

name: Parthia (Peithon v the upper satraps)
label: Parthia
result_basis: As in Ancient Greek Battles: Peucestas and the satraps of the upper provinces defeated Peithon, satrap of Media, after he had killed Philip of Parthia. Both sides Macedonian.
note: The upper satraps (Peucestas of Persis and others) drove Peithon out of Parthia with their native levies (Diod. 19.14)
qbasis: The upper satraps (Peucestas of Persis and others) drove Peithon out of Parthia with their native levies (Diod. 19.14)

name: Gabiene
label: Gabiene

sources: Diod. 19.39–43; Plut. Eum. 16–17; Nep. Eum. 10; Polyaen. 4.6.13
note: Peucestas' Persians and the upper satraps' levies in Eumenes' army (Diod. 19.40-43)
qbasis: Peucestas' Persians and the upper satraps' levies in Eumenes' army (Diod. 19.40-43)

label: Callatis
war: Third War of the Diadochi (Lysimachus v Pontic cities)
note: Pitched battle against the Scythians who came to help rebel Callatis; the Thracians changed sides before the fighting. Followed by a siege of Callatis.
qbasis: Scythians among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans

name: Tigris
label: Tigris
place: marshes by the Tigris, east of Babylonia (site unknown)
commanders_b: Nicanor (satrap of Media), Evagoras (satrap of Aria, killed)
result_basis: As in Ancient Greek Battles: Night attack from concealment in the marshes; Evagoras killed, most of Nicanor's army went over to Seleucus.
note: Nicanor, satrap of Media, led a force raised in Media and the upper satrapies (Diod. 19.92)
qbasis: Nicanor, satrap of Media, led a force raised in Media and the upper satrapies (Diod. 19.92)

name: Aripharnes' fortress (siege, 310 BC)
label: Aripharnes' fortress
date: 310/309 BCE (after the battle on the Thates)
war: Bosporan civil war (Satyrus II v Eumelus)
place: the stronghold of Aripharnes, king of the Siraces, across the Thates (Kuban), Taman/Kuban region (site unknown)
result_basis: Satyrus II was wounded in the assaults and died; his son Prytanis raised the siege and withdrew, so the fortress held (Diodorus 20.23).
sources: Diodorus Siculus 20.22.3-23; Ancient Greek Battles (note to 'Thates River'); Minns, Scythians and Greeks (1913); Rostovtzeff, Iranians and Greeks (1922)
note: Satyrus' army was mostly Scythian; Aripharnes' Siraces were Sarmatian-type nomads. The siege followed Satyrus' victory at the Thates and ended the war in Eumelus' favour.

name: Thates River
label: Thates River
place: across the Thates river, Asian Bosporus (Kuban; site unknown)
commanders_b: Eumelus; Aripharnes, king of the Siraces
note: Satyrus' army was mostly Scythian (c. 20,000 foot, 10,000 horse); Eumelus' mostly the Siraces (Sarmatians) of Aripharnes. Satyrus was killed soon afterwards besieging Aripharnes' fortress (siege, not listed). Diodorus spells the river Thates (often 'Thatis').
qbasis: Scythians among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans

note: Ariarathid dynasty of Cappadocia, of Persian descent (Ariarathes I a Persian satrap; Diod. 31.19)
qbasis: Ariarathid dynasty of Cappadocia, of Persian descent (Ariarathes I a Persian satrap; Diod. 31.19)

name: Ancyra
label: Ancyra
commanders_a: Antiochus Hierax; Mithridates II of Pontus
result_basis: As in Ancient Greek Battles: Trogus credits the Gauls with the victory; Eusebius says it was against Mithridates and that about 20,000 of Seleucus' men fell. Seleucus barely escaped, and Asia Minor west of the Taurus was left to
sources: Trogus Prol. 27; Justin 27.2.10–11; Porphyry FGrH 260 F32.8

name: Parni conquest of Parthia
label: Parni conquest of Parthia
date: c. 238 BC (dates between c. 247 and 238 BC are proposed)
place: Parthia (Astabene and Parthyene; site unknown), Iran
commanders_a: Arsaces I, Tiridates (his brother, in Arrian's version)
persian_force: The Parni, a tribe of the Dahae steppe horsemen from the Ochus (Tejen) region, led by Arsaces (Strabo 11.9.2-3; Justin 41.4); no numbers.
iranian_note: Strabo calls the Parni a branch of the Dahae, Iranian-speaking (Scythian) nomads, who soon took up the Parthian language of the province they conquered.
result_basis: Arsaces overpowered and killed the satrap Andragoras and took Parthia (Justin 41.4.7); no battle is described, so the result rests on the conquest itself.
borderline: a conquest campaign rather than a named battle: Andragoras was killed, but no battle is described
doubt: Borderline: a conquest campaign rather than a named battle: Andragoras was killed, but no battle is described.
sources: Justin 41.4.6-7; Strabo 11.9.2-3; Arrian, Parthica (in Photius and Syncellus); en.wikipedia Parni conquest of Parthia; Seleucid-Parthian Wars
note: Andragoras had probably made himself independent of Seleucus II before the invasion (his coins), so the opponent is a breakaway Seleucid satrapy. Arrian's version (via Syncellus) has Arsaces and Tiridates kill a satrap called Pherecles or Agathocles instead. Hyrcania was taken soon after.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Parthia (Arsaces I v Seleucus II)
label: Parthia (Arsaces I v Seleucus II)
persian_force: Arsaces' Parni and Parthian horsemen, perhaps reinforced from the Apasiacae, the steppe nomads to whom he had first withdrawn (Strabo 11.8.8); no figures.
iranian_note: The early Arsacid army was the Parni tribal horse with the Parthian and Hyrcanian population of the conquered provinces, all Iranian-speaking.
result_basis: Justin reports that Arsaces defeated Seleucus in battle, a day the Parthians kept ever after as the beginning of their liberty; Seleucus withdrew.
borderline: known only from Justin; no site or conventional name
doubt: Borderline: known only from Justin; no site or conventional name.
sources: Justin 41.4.8-10; Strabo 11.8.8; Athenaeus 4.153a (Posidonius); en.wikipedia Seleucid-Parthian Wars
note: Strabo says only that Arsaces fled from Seleucus to the Apasiacae, and some historians doubt a pitched battle; a report that Seleucus was captured (Posidonius in Athenaeus 4.153a) is disputed and may refer to a later Seleucus. Seleucus was recalled west by a rising (Justin). Date disputed (c. 235-227 BC).
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Sinope (siege, c. 220 BC)
label: Sinope
date: c. 220 BCE (Polybius 4.56, in his narrative of 220)
war: Pontic-Sinopean war (Mithridates of Pontus against Sinope)
commanders_b: not recorded (the Sinopeans, with a general sent from Rhodes)
result_basis: Sinope, supplied by Rhodes, was not taken and stayed independent until Pharnaces I took it in 183 BCE (Polybius 4.56; Strabo 12.3.11).
sources: Polybius 4.56; Strabo 12.3.11; Wikipedia 'Mithridates III of Pontus'
note: The Pontic king belonged to the Mithridatid house of Persian descent; Polybius gives only the blockade and the Rhodian relief, not an assault, and the king's numbering (II or III) varies between scholars. Weak entry: a blockade with no recorded fighting.

name: Raphia
label: Raphia
place: Raphia (Rafah), on the Egyptian-Palestinian border, Gaza Strip
commanders_a: Ptolemy IV, Arsinoe III, Echecrates, Andromachus
commanders_b: Antiochus III; Aspasianus the Mede, Byttacus, Menedemus
result_basis: Ptolemy's phalanx broke the Seleucid left and centre after Antiochus' wing had routed the Ptolemaic left, and Antiochus withdrew.
sources: Polybius 5.79-86; Walbank, Commentary on Polybius vol. 1; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Raphia
note: The Seleucid order of battle lists 5,000 Medes, Cissians, Cadusians and Carmanians under Aspasianus the Mede, 5,000 light-armed Dahae, Carmanians and Cilicians under Byttacus, and 2,000 Persian and Agrianian archers and slingers: perhaps a seventh of the army, and several named units. The Dahae are the steppe element.

name: Arsamosata (siege, c. 212 BC)
label: Arsamosata
date: c. 212 or 211 BCE (Polybius 8.23-25; the year is inferred from his narrative order)
war: Antiochus III's Armenian expedition (submission of Xerxes of Armenia and Sophene)
place: Arsamosata (Haraba, near Elazig), Turkey; site approximate
result_basis: Shut up in Arsamosata, Xerxes came to terms: he paid tribute, kept his kingdom and married Antiochus' sister Antiochis (Polybius 8.25).
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Polybius 8.23-25; Wikipedia 'Xerxes of Sophene' and 'Arsamosata'; Strabo 11.14.15
note: Xerxes belonged to the Orontid (Eruandid) house, of Iranian origin that claimed Achaemenid descent (uncertain; some regard the Orontids as only Iranianised). Polybius calls him king of Armenia; modern historians place him as ruler of Sophene (and Commagene). The siege ended by agreement rather than assault, so the 'result' is the Seleucid gain of submission and tribute.

name: Mount Labus
label: Mount Labus
place: pass over Mount Labus (Elburz range), between Hecatompylos and Hyrcania, Iran
commanders_a: Antiochus III; Diogenes, Nicomedes of Cos, Nicolaus the Aetolian, Polyxenidas
commanders_b: Arsaces II (overall command; Polybius names no commander at the pass)
persian_force: The 'barbarians' sent by Arsaces II to hold the pass with ambushes and rolled stones: Parthian and Hyrcanian light troops and mountaineers (Polybius 10.29-31); no numbers.
iranian_note: Polybius calls the defenders only barbarians; they were Arsaces' Parthian subjects and the Hyrcanian highlanders of the Elburz, both Iranian-speaking.
result_basis: After a day-long fight the Parthian defenders of the pass were outflanked by Seleucid light troops at night and abandoned the summit to Antiochus (Polybius 10.29-31).
sources: Polybius 10.28-31; en.wikipedia Battle of Mount Labus; Seleucid-Parthian Wars
note: en.wikipedia (Seleucid-Parthian Wars) describes the fight as a stalemate turned into a Seleucid success by the night flank attack. Arsaces II later accepted Seleucid suzerainty (208 BC).
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Syrinx (siege)
label: Syrinx (siege)
place: Syrinx (Sirynx), Hyrcania (site unknown, in the Gorgan plain), Iran
persian_force: The Parthian garrison and the Hyrcanian 'barbarians' who had gathered in Syrinx after the loss of the Labus pass (Polybius 10.31); no numbers.
iranian_note: The defenders were Hyrcanian and Parthian subjects of Arsaces II, Iranian-speaking; the Greek townsmen were massacred by them before the fall.
result_basis: Antiochus filled the ditches, mined the walls and took Syrinx by assault after the defenders had killed its Greek inhabitants (Polybius 10.31).
sources: Polybius 10.31; en.wikipedia Seleucid-Parthian Wars; List of wars involving Iran (before 1979)
note: Polybius calls the defenders only barbarians; en.wikipedia says the city held a Parthian garrison while Arsaces II was at Nisa. Tambrax, a nearby unwalled city with a palace, fell without a fight.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Arius
label: Arius

note: Euthydemus' 10,000 horse at the Arius were Bactrian cavalry (Polyb. 10.49)

name: Magnesia
label: Magnesia

note: Antiochus III's right wing, where he commanded, included 1,200 Dahae horse archers (Livy), with Cyrtian slingers and Elymaean archers; the Dahae are a named unit, far below a fifth of the army. Also in Ancient Greek Battles and Battles of the Romans.

name: Elymais (death of Antiochus III)
label: Elymais (death of Antiochus III)
war: Seleucid wars in the east (Antiochus III's raid on the temple of Bel)
place: temple of Bel in Elymais (site unknown, in the Zagros foothills of Khuzestan), Iran
commanders_a: unknown (the Elymaeans of the temple district)
persian_force: The Elymaean highlanders around the temple, who rose against the plunderers (Strabo's 'neighbouring barbarians'); no numbers or leaders recorded.
iranian_note: Nothing is known of the Elymaean language; the population probably descended from the Elamites and wrote in Aramaic, so an Iranian share cannot be stated.
losses_b: Antiochus III and his force killed
result_basis: The Seleucid force that attacked the temple by night was overwhelmed by the local Elymaeans and Antiochus III was killed with his men (Diodorus 28.3, 29.15; Strabo 16.1.18; Justin 32.2.1-2).
borderline: a fight over a temple raid, not a named battle; Elymais was still a Seleucid province, so whether it 'fought on its own account' is a judgment
doubt: Borderline: a fight over a temple raid, not a named battle; Elymais was still a Seleucid province, so whether it 'fought on its own account' is a judgment.
sources: Diodorus 28.3, 29.15; Strabo 16.1.18; Justin 32.2.1-2; en.wikipedia Elymais
note: Elymais counts here only because the Elymaeans fought on their own account against the king; Elymais became an independent kingdom only under Kamnaskires I (c. 147 BC). A similar attempt by Antiochus IV in 164 BC was foiled without a recorded battle (Polybius 31.9; 1 Maccabees 6.1-4).
qbasis: Elymais: an Iranian-led state

name: Sinope (siege, 183 BC)
label: Sinope
war: Pharnaces I's expansion on the Black Sea (Pontic capture of Sinope)
result_basis: Pharnaces took Sinope and made it his capital; Rhodes' protest to Rome came to nothing (Polybius 23.9; Strabo 12.3.11).
sources: Polybius 23.9.2 and 24.1; Strabo 12.3.11; Wikipedia 'Pharnaces I of Pontus' (fetched 1 Nov 2026)
note: Pharnaces I belonged to the Mithridatid house of Pontus, of Persian descent (claimed Achaemenid ancestry; Wikipedia: 'of Persian and Greek ancestry'). Sinope fell to a sudden attack and the details of the fighting are not recorded, so this is a thin 'siege'; the war with Eumenes II and Ariarathes IV that followed (181-179 BCE) has no named battle.

name: Media (capture of Demetrius II)
label: Media (capture of Demetrius II)
place: mountains of Media (exact site unknown), Iran
commanders_a: Mithridates I (his general Bagasis had held the Seleucids for a year)
persian_force: Mithridates I's Parthian army, chiefly cavalry, with the forces of his governor in Media, Bagasis; no figures.
iranian_note: Parthian armies of this time were raised from the Parthian nobility and their retainers, with levies from newly conquered Media, all Iranian-speaking.
result_basis: Demetrius' army was destroyed and he himself was captured (Justin 36.1, 38.9; Josephus Ant. 13.186; Babylonian astronomical diaries).
sources: Justin 36.1.2-6, 38.9.2; Josephus Ant. 13.184-186; 1 Maccabees 14.1-3; Appian, Syriaca 67; en.wikipedia Seleucid-Parthian Wars
note: Justin says Demetrius was taken by a ruse during peace talks after winning several fights; the Babylonian diaries date the capture to summer 138 BC. Justin says the Persians (of Persis), Elymaeans and Bactrians aided Demetrius in the war, not necessarily in this battle; Persis and Elymais are thus on the Seleucid side here, as allies only.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Lycus (Great Zab)
label: Lycus (Great Zab)
place: river Lycus (Great Zab), northern Mesopotamia, Iraq
commanders_a: Antiochus VII Sidetes; John Hyrcanus (Jewish contingent)
persian_force: Indates' Parthian field army in Mesopotamia; the sources give no details, and it was presumably Parthian cavalry with local levies.
iranian_note: Inferred only: Parthian field armies were built on the Parthian nobles' horse; Mesopotamian (Aramaic-speaking) levies may have served too.
strength_a: about 80,000 armed men for the whole campaign (Justin 38.10)
result_basis: Antiochus defeated the Parthian general Indates and set up a trophy by the Lycus (Nicolaus of Damascus in Josephus, Ant. 13.251-252).
sources: Josephus Ant. 13.249-253 (Nicolaus of Damascus); Justin 38.10; Diodorus 34/35.15-17; en.wikipedia Battle of Ecbatana
note: One of three Seleucid victories in 130 BC (Justin 38.10); the other two are unnamed. The army halted two days at the river at Hyrcanus' request for a Jewish festival.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Ecbatana (129 BC)
label: Ecbatana (129 BC)
persian_force: Phraates II's Parthian army, chiefly cavalry, supported by the Median towns that rose against the Seleucid troops billeted on them (Justin 38.10; Diodorus 34/35.17).
iranian_note: Phraates' army was the Parthian royal and noble cavalry; the rising Median townsmen who joined it spoke Iranian dialects.
strength_b: Antiochus' own column small (probably the royal guard); the whole army about 80,000 armed men with 300,000 camp followers (Justin 38.10)
losses_b: Antiochus killed; his guard destroyed; most of the army in winter quarters killed or captured
result_basis: Antiochus' column was destroyed and he was killed (or killed himself); the Seleucid troops in their Median winter quarters were killed or captured.
sources: Justin 38.10, 39.1; Diodorus 34/35.15-17; Appian, Syriaca 68; Josephus Ant. 13.253; en.wikipedia Battle of Ecbatana
note: The sources place the battle only in Media; 'Ecbatana' is the conventional label. Antiochus' son Seleucus was captured. The Seleucid prisoners were drafted into Phraates' army and deserted him against the Saka.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Phraates II v Saka
label: Phraates II v Saka
war: Parthian wars with the Saka and Yuezhi
persian_force: Phraates II's Parthian army, with the Greek soldiers captured from Antiochus VII's army, who deserted in the battle (Justin 42.1).
iranian_note: Justin names the Parthian army and the Greek ex-Seleucid prisoners serving in it; the Greeks' share is not known, but the army was the Parthian host.
losses_b: the army destroyed; Phraates II killed
result_basis: When the Parthian line wavered the Greek prisoners in Phraates' army went over to the Saka; the Parthian army was cut to pieces and the king killed (Justin 42.1.4-5).
borderline: no conventional name or site; known only from Justin
doubt: Borderline: no conventional name or site; known only from Justin.
sources: Justin 42.1.1-5; en.wikipedia Phraates II
note: The Saka had been hired for the war against Antiochus VII, arrived too late, were refused pay and ravaged Parthia; Phraates left Himerus in charge of Babylonia when he marched east. Date 128 or 127 BC.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Artabanus I v Tocharians
label: Artabanus I v Tocharians
war: Parthian wars with the Saka and Yuezhi
place: eastern frontier of Parthia (site unknown), Turkmenistan

iranian_note: Inferred only: the Parthian royal army of the time was raised from Parthian nobles and their retainers.
result_basis: Justin says only that Artabanus was wounded in the arm in the war with the Tochari and died of it at once; the outcome of the fight is not reported.

name: Yucheng (siege, 104 BC)
label: Yucheng
commanders_a: Li Guangli; Wang Shensheng and Hu Chongguo
result_basis: A Han detachment of about 1,000 was routed by a 3,000-man sortie and Li Guangli's main army, weakened by the march, withdrew to Dunhuang.
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Shiji 123 (Dayuan liezhuan); Hanshu 61; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Heavenly_Horses
note: Whether the Dayuan were Iranian-speaking is doubtful: Sima Qian says that from Dayuan to Anxi (Parthia) the languages differed but were close, which points to a Saka or Sogdian-type speech; Tocharian and Greek-descended elites have also been proposed. Yucheng fell to Shangguan Jie in 102 and its king fled to the Kangju.

name: Guishan/Ershi (siege, 102-101 BC)
label: Guishan/Ershi
place: Guishan, capital of Dayuan (Ferghana; the 'Ershi' of the Han sources; site uncertain), Uzbekistan
result_basis: The Han cut the city's water, broke the outer wall and captured Jianmi; the Dayuan nobles killed Wugua and gave horses for a Han withdrawal.
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Shiji 123; Hanshu 61; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Heavenly_Horses
note: The Dayuan cavalry sortie was beaten by Han crossbowmen before the siege. Li took about 3,000 horses and enthroned the noble Meicai. Whether the Dayuan were Iranian-speaking is doubtful (see the note on Yucheng); the earlier note about a Saka king of Ferghana named Mauakes is a modern guess at the name Wugua.

name: Cappadocia (Sulla)
label: Cappadocia
result_basis: As in Ancient Greek Battles: Sulla killed many Cappadocians of Gordius' pro-Pontic regime and more Armenians who came to help them, and installed Ariobarzanes I. Date of Sulla's mission disputed (96 or 92).
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Plut. Sulla 5.3; App. Mith. 10, 57
note: Gordius and the Armenian troops of Tigranes II (Artaxiad); Orontid line (Commagene; Artaxiad Armenia as its branch) widely described as of Iranian origin, but disputed

losses_b: the whole army surrendered; Demetrius captured

note: Named 'Beroea' in Ancient Greek Battles; the year is added because Khosrow I attacked Beroea in AD 540. A camp besieged in the field, treated as a field battle.
