iranian_note: Surena's army was Parthian and Saka horse from his estates; the defenders included the Greek and Aramaic-speaking townsmen of Seleucia.
result_basis: Surena took Seleucia by storm, being himself the first man on the wall (Plutarch, Crassus 21.6).
sources: Plutarch, Crassus 21.6; Justin 42.4.1-4; en.wikipedia Mithridates IV of Parthia
note: en.wikipedia (after Bivar) puts the siege in 54 BC and has Mithridates offer battle and lose; Justin has him surrender at Babylon after a long siege. Older numbering calls him Mithridates III. Gabinius had brought him to the Euphrates in 55 BC before turning to Egypt.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Babylon (siege, 54 BC)
label: Babylon (siege, 54 BC)
war: Parthian civil war (Mithridates IV against Orodes II)
persian_force: Orodes' Parthian army against Mithridates' remaining partisans in Babylon; no details.
iranian_note: Inferred only: both armies were Parthian, the defenders with townsmen of Babylon.
result_basis: Mithridates, besieged in Babylon for a long time, surrendered because of famine and was put to death (Justin 42.4.2-4).
borderline: a siege ended by famine; no fighting is described
doubt: Borderline: a siege ended by famine; no fighting is described.
sources: Justin 42.4.2-4; en.wikipedia Mithridates IV of Parthia
note: Some modern accounts merge this with the fall of Seleucia (above) and have Mithridates defeated in battle near Seleucia.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Ichnae
label: Ichnae
place: near Ichnae, on the Balikh south of Carrhae, Syria
commanders_b: Silaces (Dio's Talymenus Ilaces), satrap of Mesopotamia
persian_force: The satrap Silaces with a few horsemen (Dio 40.12); no figures.
iranian_note: A Parthian satrap's mounted retinue; local Mesopotamian levies may have been present.
result_basis: The satrap's small force was beaten and Silaces fled wounded to Orodes; the Romans held the field (Dio 40.12).
sources: Cassius Dio 40.12-13; Plutarch, Crassus 17; en.wikipedia Battle of Carrhae
note: After the fight Crassus stormed Zenodotium, a Greek town whose people had killed his soldiers; no Parthian force fought there.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Carrhae
label: Carrhae
date: 9 June 53 BC (Republican calendar; day by tradition, Ovid Fasti 6.465)
place: the plain south of Carrhae (Harran), near the Balikh, Turkey
commanders_b: Marcus Licinius Crassus, Publius Crassus (killed), Gaius Cassius Longinus
persian_force: Surena's household army of no fewer than 10,000 horsemen, his vassals and slaves: about 1,000 mail-clad cataphracts and the rest horse archers, supplied with arrows by a train of 1,000 camels (Plutarch, Crassus 21, 24-25).
iranian_note: Surena's retainers were Parthian and Saka horsemen from his family's domains in Sakastan (Plutarch; Encyclopaedia Iranica 'Carrhae').
strength_b: about 42,000: seven legions (about 34,000), 4,000 cavalry and 4,000 light troops (Plutarch)
result_basis: The Parthians held the field; the Roman army abandoned it at night, leaving 4,000 wounded, and was destroyed in the retreat.
sources: Plutarch, Crassus 17-33; Cassius Dio 40.16-27; en.wikipedia Battle of Carrhae; Encyclopaedia Iranica 'Carrhae' (Shahbazi)
note: The Arab chief of Osroene (Plutarch's Ariamnes, probably Abgar II), a Parthian client, guided Crassus while in Parthian pay and is not counted as a Roman ally; Crassus had Gallic cavalry under Publius, and Artavasdes II of Armenia, who had promised troops, stayed away. Crassus was killed a few days later in a scuffle at a parley near Sinnaca, and Varguntius' detachment was destroyed in the retreat. Orodes II was meanwhile in Armenia with the main army.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Antioch (siege, 51 BC)
label: Antioch (siege, 51 BC)
date: autumn 51 BC (the Parthians besieged Antioch again in 50 BC)
war: Roman-Parthian Wars (Parthian invasion of Syria, 51-50 BC)
place: Antioch on the Orontes (Antakya), and the ambush near Antigonea, Turkey
persian_force: A large Parthian cavalry raiding army under the general Osaces with the young prince Pacorus (Dio 40.28-29; Cicero, Ad Familiares 15.1-4); no figures.
iranian_note: Dio and Cicero describe a Parthian cavalry army led by Parthian nobles; no other contingents are named.
strength_a: unknown (the remnants of Crassus' army and local levies)
losses_b: many killed in the ambush; Osaces mortally wounded
result_basis: The Parthians failed to take Antioch and withdrew, and their force was ambushed near Antigonea, where Osaces was mortally wounded (Dio 40.29; Cicero).
sources: Cassius Dio 40.28-30; Cicero, Ad Atticum 5.20-21 and Ad Familiares 2.10, 15.1-4; en.wikipedia Siege of Antioch (51 BC)
note: Named 'Antioch (siege)' in Battles of the Romans; the year is added because the Sasanians besieged Antioch later. The Parthians wintered in Cyrrhestica and besieged Bibulus in Antioch in 50 BC without success before leaving Syria. A small Parthian raid of 52 BC had also been repelled by Cassius (Dio 40.28).
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Nicopolis
label: Nicopolis
result_basis: As in Ancient Greek Battles: Pharnaces II, king of the Cimmerian Bosporus, fighting to recover his father's Pontic kingdom (counted as Pontus). Two of Calvinus' four legions were Deiotarus' Galatians; Ariobarzanes III of Cappadoc
sources: [Caes.] B. Alex. 34–40; App. Mith. 120; Dio 42.46
note: Mithridatid dynasty of Pontus, Persian in the male line (founder Mithridates I Ktistes of a Persian noble house; App. Mith. 9, 112) and Greek through its Seleucid queens: Mithridates VI's mother Laodice VI was a Seleucid, and Justin 38.7 has him claim Cyrus and Darius on his father's side and Alexander and Seleucus on his mother's; his kingdom was Greek, and its battles are Greek battles in Ancient Greek Battles and Battles of the Romans
qbasis: Mithridatid dynasty of Pontus, Persian in the male line (founder Mithridates I Ktistes of a Persian noble house; App. Mith. 9, 112) and Greek through its Seleucid queens: Mithridates VI's mother Laodice VI was a Seleucid, and Justin 38.7 has him claim Cyrus and Darius on his father's side and Alexander and Seleucus on his mother's; his kingdom was Greek, and its battles are Greek battles in Ancient Greek Battles and Battles of the Romans

name: Pelusium (siege, 47 BC)
label: Pelusium
war: Alexandrian War (Caesar's relief army from Syria)
commanders_b: Egyptian garrison of Ptolemy XIII (commander not recorded)
result_basis: Mithridates stormed Pelusium on the day he arrived (Bellum Alexandrinum 26; Josephus, BJ 1.187-190).
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Caesar (Bellum Alexandrinum) 26; Josephus BJ 1.187-192, AJ 14.127-136; Appian BC 2.89; Wikipedia 'Mithridates of Pergamon' (fetched)
note: Mithridates of Pergamon was reputed a son of Mithridates VI by the Galatian Adobogiona (Wikipedia accepts it; Strabo 13.4.3 records the claim as a report), so a Mithridatid of Persian-Greek descent (uncertain). His army was Levantine, so the Iranian part is only the leader.

name: Pharnaces II v Asander (47 BC)
label: Pharnaces II v Asander
place: European Bosporus, near Panticapaeum (Kerch), Crimea (site unknown)
result_basis: Pharnaces, who had retaken Theodosia and Panticapaeum with Scythian and Sarmatian troops, was beaten and killed by his governor Asander.
sources: Appian, Mithridatica 120; Dio 42.47.5; Strabo 13.4.3
note: Appian says Pharnaces raised Scythian and Sarmatian troops for the reconquest, and also lists him as a Mithridatid of claimed Persian descent. Ancient Greek Battles has the fight as 'Bosporus (Pharnaces v Asander)'; Scythian and Sarmatian numbers are not given.

name: Zela
label: Zela
result_basis: As in Ancient Greek Battles: 'Veni, vidi, vici.' Pharnaces II (king of the Bosporus) counted as Pontus.
sources: [Caes.] B. Alex. 72–77; Plut. Caes. 50; Suet. Caes. 35, 37; App. BC 2.91, Mith. 120; Dio 42.47
note: Mithridatid dynasty of Pontus, Persian in the male line (founder Mithridates I Ktistes of a Persian noble house; App. Mith. 9, 112) and Greek through its Seleucid queens: Mithridates VI's mother Laodice VI was a Seleucid, and Justin 38.7 has him claim Cyrus and Darius on his father's side and Alexander and Seleucus on his mother's; his kingdom was Greek, and its battles are Greek battles in Ancient Greek Battles and Battles of the Romans
qbasis: Mithridatid dynasty of Pontus, Persian in the male line (founder Mithridates I Ktistes of a Persian noble house; App. Mith. 9, 112) and Greek through its Seleucid queens: Mithridates VI's mother Laodice VI was a Seleucid, and Justin 38.7 has him claim Cyrus and Darius on his father's side and Alexander and Seleucus on his mother's; his kingdom was Greek, and its battles are Greek battles in Ancient Greek Battles and Battles of the Romans

name: Nile (47 BC)
label: Nile
place: Nile Delta, between the Jewish Camp (Tell el-Yahudiya) and Alexandria, Egypt; exact site unknown
side_a: Rome and the relief army of Mithridates of Pergamon
persian_state: Rome and the relief army of Mithridates of Pergamon
commanders_a: Julius Caesar; Mithridates of Pergamon (commanding the relief army)
result_basis: The Egyptian army was routed, Ptolemy XIII drowned and Alexandria passed to Caesar (Bellum Alexandrinum 28-31).
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Caesar (Bellum Alexandrinum) 26-31; Appian BC 2.90; Dio 42.43; Josephus BJ 1.187-192; Wikipedia 'Mithridates of Pergamon' (fetched)
note: Mithridates of Pergamon commanded the relief army that joined Caesar; his descent from Mithridates VI (uncertain) is what qualifies the battle. The army was Levantine, so the Iranian part is only the leader.

name: Apamea (siege, 45 BC)
label: Apamea (siege, 45 BC)
date: 45-44 BC (to 43 BC in Battles of the Romans)
war: Roman civil wars (Caecilius Bassus' revolt in Syria)
place: Apamea on the Orontes (Qalaat al-Mudiq), Syria
commanders_a: Quintus Caecilius Bassus (Pompeians); Pacorus (Parthian force); Alchaudonius the Arab
commanders_b: Gaius Antistius Vetus; then Lucius Staius Murcus and Quintus Marcius Crispus (Caesarians); Antipater
persian_force: A Parthian force (under the prince Pacorus, per en.wikipedia) that came at Bassus' invitation but left because of winter without achieving anything important (Dio 47.27); size unknown.
iranian_note: A detachment of the Parthian royal army; its size and make-up are not recorded.
strength_a: Bassus' two legions with slaves and levies, Arab archers
strength_b: three legions (Murcus) and three (Crispus), with a Jewish force from Antipater
result_basis: Apamea never fell: the first Caesarian siege was given up and the second ended in 43 BC when both armies went over to Cassius.
borderline: Dio says the Parthians came but left for the winter without doing anything important; en.wikipedia says Pacorus and Alchaudonius drove off Antistius' army. Parthian fighting is uncertain, hence 'contingent'
doubt: Borderline: Dio says the Parthians came but left for the winter without doing anything important; en.wikipedia says Pacorus and Alchaudonius drove off Antistius' army. Parthian fighting is uncertain, hence 'contingent'.
sources: Cassius Dio 47.26-28; Appian, Civil Wars 3.77-78, 4.58-59; Strabo 16.2.10; Josephus Ant. 14.268-272; en.wikipedia Siege of Apamea
note: A Roman civil siege in Battles of the Romans ('Apamea (siege)', civil); not civil here, since only one Persian side took part. The year is added because the Sasanians took Apamea in 540 and 573. Dio credits the archery of Alchaudonius' Arabs with Bassus' success in the first fighting.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Philippi
label: Philippi
commanders_b: Marcus Junius Brutus, Gaius Cassius Longinus (Liberators)
persian_force: Parthian and Median horse archers in the Liberators' cavalry: Cassius had 4,000 mounted bowmen, Arabs, Medes and Parthians, and Brutus 2,000 'Parthian and Thessalian' horse (Appian, Civil Wars 4.88).
iranian_note: Appian names Parthians and Medes, with Arabs, among Cassius' 4,000 mounted archers; the Iranian share within that body is not given.
losses_b: about 8,000 in the first battle; the army surrendered after the second
result_basis: In the second battle (23 October) Brutus' army was routed and then surrendered; the first battle (3 October) was indecisive, each side taking one enemy camp.
borderline: the Parthian horse archers joined Cassius drawn by his reputation (Appian 4.59) and may not have been a force of the Parthian state
doubt: Borderline: the Parthian horse archers joined Cassius drawn by his reputation (Appian 4.59) and may not have been a force of the Parthian state.
sources: Appian, Civil Wars 4.59, 4.88, 4.105-131; Plutarch, Brutus 38-52; Cassius Dio 47.35-49; en.wikipedia Battle of Philippi; Roman-Parthian Wars
note: en.wikipedia lists a 'Parthian Empire (cavalry force)' among the Liberators. Labienus had been sent to Orodes II to ask for help, but no royal army arrived before the battle. One entry for both engagements; Cassius killed himself after the first.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Decidius Saxa's defeat
label: Decidius Saxa's defeat
persian_force: Orodes II's Parthian cavalry army under Pacorus and the Roman renegade Quintus Labienus, joined by Roman garrison troops in Syria who had served Brutus and Cassius (Dio 48.24-25).
iranian_note: Dio describes a large Parthian army given to Labienus and Pacorus, with Roman deserters from the Syrian garrison (Latin and Greek speakers) joining it.
strength_a: Parthian cavalry, about 14,000-20,000 for the whole invasion (modern estimates on en.wikipedia)
strength_b: unknown (Saxa's remaining troops, most having gone over)
losses_b: army destroyed or gone over; standards taken
result_basis: Saxa was beaten in the field and fled to Antioch and then Cilicia, where he was caught and killed (Dio 48.25).
sources: Cassius Dio 48.24-26; Plutarch, Antony 30; Livy, Periochae 127; Florus 2.19; en.wikipedia Parthian invasion of 40 BC; Quintus Labienus
note: Persian role principal: Labienus commanded a Parthian army in Orodes' service. Apamea first repulsed Labienus, then surrendered on a false report of Saxa's death; Antioch surrendered too.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Stratonicea (siege)
label: Stratonicea (siege)
persian_force: Labienus' army in Asia: Parthian troops given him by Orodes with Roman deserters and local levies (Dio 48.24-26, 48.39).
iranian_note: Dio says Labienus took Parthian forces into Asia but was left with local levies once they withdrew; the share at Stratonicea is not known.
result_basis: Labienus besieged Stratonicea for a long time but could not take it (Dio 48.26); the siege ended with Ventidius' advance in 39 BC.
borderline: a minor siege with no conventional name; the Persian role is through Labienus' Parthian-backed army
doubt: Borderline: a minor siege with no conventional name; the Persian role is through Labienus' Parthian-backed army.
sources: Cassius Dio 48.26; Tacitus, Annals 3.62; en.wikipedia Quintus Labienus
note: Stratonicea's resistance was later rewarded by Rome (Tacitus, Annals 3.62). Labienus took Alabanda and razed the deserted Mylasa after both had killed his garrisons; no battle is recorded there.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Amanus Pass
label: Amanus Pass
war: Roman-Parthian Wars (Parthian invasion of 40 BC; Ventidius' counter-offensive)
place: Amanus pass (Belen pass, the Syrian Gates), between Cilicia and Syria, Turkey
persian_force: A Parthian force under Pacorus' lieutenant Pharnapates holding the pass: horse archers and cataphracts; no figures.
iranian_note: Dio calls the force simply Parthian, under a Parthian commander.
result_basis: Pharnapates' Parthians, who were getting the better of Silo's advance guard, were routed when Ventidius came up, and Pharnapates was killed (Dio 48.41).
sources: Cassius Dio 48.41; Plutarch, Antony 33; en.wikipedia Battle of Amanus Pass
note: After the defeat Pacorus withdrew beyond the Euphrates and Syria was recovered.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Cilician Gates (39 BC)
label: Cilician Gates (39 BC)
war: Roman-Parthian Wars (Parthian invasion of 40 BC; Ventidius' counter-offensive)
place: Cilician Gates (Gulek pass), Taurus mountains, Turkey
commanders_b: Quintus Labienus; Parthian cavalry commanders (Pharnapates, per en.wikipedia)
persian_force: Parthian cavalry (horse archers and cataphracts) sent to Labienus, with Labienus' Roman and locally levied infantry camped apart (Dio 48.39-40).
iranian_note: Dio separates the Parthian cavalry, which did the fighting, from Labienus' Roman deserters and local levies; their proportions are not given.
strength_a: unknown (light troops ahead of the main legions)
losses_b: heavy; Labienus' army dispersed or went over
result_basis: The Parthian cavalry charged Ventidius' camp on high ground without waiting for Labienus and was thrown back with heavy loss; Labienus' army then broke up in Ventidius' night ambushes (Dio 48.39-40).
sources: Cassius Dio 48.39-40; Plutarch, Antony 33; en.wikipedia Battle of the Cilician Gates; Quintus Labienus
note: Dio places the fight near the Taurus; en.wikipedia names it the Cilician Gates. Labienus fled, was found in Cilicia and killed (other sources have him die in battle).
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Samosata (siege)
label: Samosata
result_basis: As in Battles of the Romans: The assaults failed and Antony withdrew on terms, taking 300 talents (Plutarch). Commagene was a Hellenistic kingdom with a Greek-speaking court under an Iranian (Orontid) dynasty.
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Plutarch Antony 34; Cassius Dio 49.20-22; Josephus BJ 1.321-322, AJ 14.439-447
note: Antiochus I of Commagene, who claimed descent from Darius I on his father's side and from Alexander and the Seleucids on his mother's (his mother Laodice Thea was a Seleucid; the two ancestor galleries at Nemrut Dag); Orontid line (Commagene; Artaxiad Armenia as its branch) widely described as of Iranian origin, but disputed
qbasis: Antiochus I of Commagene, who claimed descent from Darius I on his father's side and from Alexander and the Seleucids on his mother's (his mother Laodice Thea was a Seleucid; the two ancestor galleries at Nemrut Dag); Orontid line (Commagene; Artaxiad Armenia as its branch) widely described as of Iranian origin, but disputed

name: Mount Gindarus
label: Mount Gindarus
date: 9 June 38 BC (by tradition, the anniversary of Carrhae)
war: Roman-Parthian Wars (Pacorus' second invasion of Syria)
persian_force: Pacorus' Parthian army of horse archers and cataphracts (Dio 49.20); no figures.
iranian_note: The sources describe a Parthian cavalry army led by the crown prince and his guards.
losses_b: very heavy; Pacorus killed with his guard
result_basis: The Parthians charged the Roman camp on high ground, were routed by the legionaries and slingers, and Pacorus fell (Dio 49.20; Plutarch, Antony 34).
sources: Cassius Dio 49.19-21; Plutarch, Antony 34; Strabo 16.2.8; Frontinus, Strategemata 1.1.6, 2.2.5; Justin 42.4.7-10; en.wikipedia Battle of Mount Gindarus
note: Ventidius lured Pacorus across the Euphrates at an unexpected point by a deliberate leak (Frontinus; Dio 49.19). The date on the anniversary of Carrhae is a tradition (Dio 49.21; Eutropius).
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Phraaspa (siege)
label: Phraaspa (siege)
place: Phraaspa (Praaspa), royal city of Media Atropatene (perhaps Maragheh), Iran
commanders_a: Phraates IV; Artavasdes I of Media Atropatene
persian_force: The garrison of the Median royal city, which made sorties (Plutarch, Antony 39), and Phraates IV's Parthian cavalry with the horse of Atropatene, about 24,000 (2,000 cataphracts and 22,000 horse archers) by the estimate given on en.wikipedia.
iranian_note: The defenders were the Median (Atropatenian) garrison and Parthian and Median cavalry, all Iranian-speaking.
strength_b: about 100,000: 60,000 Roman infantry, 10,000 Spanish and Celtic horse and 30,000 allies (Plutarch, Antony 37)
result_basis: Antony failed to take Phraaspa and abandoned the siege in October, his siege train lost and his foragers harassed by the Parthian cavalry.
sources: Plutarch, Antony 38-40; Cassius Dio 49.25-28; Strabo 11.13.3-4; en.wikipedia Antony's Atropatene campaign
note: In a foraging battle before the walls Antony put the Parthians to flight but killed only 80 and took 30 (Plutarch, Antony 39). The site of Phraaspa is disputed (Maragheh, or less likely Takht-e Soleyman).
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Statianus' convoy (ambush)
label: Statianus' convoy (ambush)
place: on the road to Phraaspa, Media Atropatene, Iran
commanders_a: Phraates IV or his general Monaeses; Artavasdes I of Media Atropatene
commanders_b: Oppius Statianus (killed), Polemon I of Pontus (captured)
persian_force: Phraates IV's Parthian cavalry with the horse of his ally Artavasdes I of Media Atropatene (Dio 49.25); no figures.
iranian_note: Dio names the Parthian and Median kings' horsemen; both peoples were Iranian-speaking.
strength_b: two legions (about 10,000) escorting 300 wagons of siege engines (Plutarch)
losses_b: 10,000 killed (Plutarch); Polemon captured; the siege train destroyed
result_basis: The Parthian and Median cavalry destroyed the baggage train and its two legions, killing Statianus and burning the siege engines (Plutarch, Antony 38; Dio 49.25).
sources: Plutarch, Antony 38; Cassius Dio 49.25; Velleius 2.82; en.wikipedia Antony's Atropatene campaign; Artavasdes I of Media Atropatene
note: Artavasdes II of Armenia left with his cavalry before the attack, so the Armenian role is nominal. Media Atropatene, itself a Persian state in this set, fought as Phraates' ally. Kelly makes Phraates himself the commander.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Zhizhi (36 BC)
label: Zhizhi
place: Zhizhi's fortress on the Talas river near Taraz, Kazakhstan
result_basis: Han and allied troops stormed the fortress, killed Zhizhi and about 1,500 of his men after repelling Kangju cavalry attacks.
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Hanshu 70 (Chen Tang biography) and 94b; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zhizhi; Hill, Through the Jade Gate
note: Zhizhi's father-in-law, the Kangju king, sent several thousand horse (10,000 in one count). The Kangju (north of Sogdiana) were perhaps Iranian-speaking (Saka or Sogdian type) but this is uncertain, so the entry qualifies only if they are counted. Zhizhi's own Xiongnu are not Iranian.

name: Antony's retreat from Phraaspa
label: Antony's retreat from Phraaspa
place: the mountain road from Phraaspa to the Araxes, Media Atropatene, Iran
persian_force: Phraates IV's Parthian horse archers and cataphracts with Median (Atropatenian) cavalry (Plutarch; Dio 49.28-31); no figures.
iranian_note: The pursuers were the Parthian and Median cavalry named by Plutarch and Dio.
losses_b: about 20,000 foot and 4,000 horse, more than half by disease (Plutarch, Antony 50)
result_basis: In 27 days and 18 engagements the Parthian cavalry harried an army that left the field to them each day until it crossed the Araxes, having lost about 20,000 foot and 4,000 horse (Plutarch, Antony 40-50).
borderline: a fighting retreat of many engagements, not a single battle
doubt: Borderline: a fighting retreat of many engagements, not a single battle.
sources: Plutarch, Antony 40-51; Cassius Dio 49.28-31; Velleius 2.82; en.wikipedia Antony's Atropatene campaign
note: The best known engagement is the destruction of Flavius Gallus' force (3,000 killed, 5,000 wounded; Plutarch, Antony 42-43), which Antony's legions finally checked. A Mardian guide led the army by a mountain road. Antony lost about 8,000 more in the winter march through Armenia (Plutarch, Antony 51).
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Artavasdes I of Media v Phraates IV
label: Artavasdes I of Media v Phraates IV
date: c. 32 BC (between Antony's treaty with the Mede in 33 BC and Actium)
side_b: Phraates IV, with Artaxias II of Armenia
faction_b: Phraates IV (Parthia), with Artaxias II of Armenia
commanders_b: unknown (forces of Phraates IV and Artaxias II)
persian_force: Artavasdes' Median (Atropatenian) cavalry with Roman troops lent by Antony, against the Parthian army and Artaxias' Armenians.
iranian_note: Inferred: Atropatene's army was its Median nobility and horse, with an unknown number of Roman legionaries; the Parthian side was Parthian with Armenian allies.
result_basis: Dio says only that the Median king, with Roman soldiers lent by Antony, defeated the Parthians and Artaxias (Dio 49.44).
borderline: no named battle; known only from a summary sentence of Dio
doubt: Borderline: no named battle; known only from a summary sentence of Dio.
sources: Cassius Dio 49.33, 49.44; Plutarch, Antony 52-53; en.wikipedia Artavasdes I of Media Atropatene
note: Civil because two states of the list (Atropatene and Parthia) fought each other; en.wikipedia says only that the Roman reinforcements helped Artavasdes repel a Parthian attack.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Artaxias II v Artavasdes I of Media
label: Artaxias II v Artavasdes I of Media
place: Media Atropatene or Armenia (site unknown), Iran
side_a: Phraates IV and Artaxias II of Armenia
faction_a: Phraates IV (Parthia) and Artaxias II of Armenia
persian_force: The Parthian army with Artaxias II's Armenians against Artavasdes' Median forces, left without their Roman auxiliaries; no details.
iranian_note: Inferred only: the victors were Parthian and Armenian forces, the losers Median; the proportions are unknown.
result_basis: After Antony recalled his Roman troops the Median king was defeated and captured (Dio 49.44.4).
borderline: no named battle; known only from a summary sentence of Dio, and the Parthian share of the victors' army is unclear (en.wikipedia names only Artaxias)
doubt: Borderline: no named battle; known only from a summary sentence of Dio, and the Parthian share of the victors' army is unclear (en.wikipedia names only Artaxias).
sources: Cassius Dio 49.44.4, 51.16.2; Res Gestae 32-33; en.wikipedia Artavasdes I of Media Atropatene
note: If Artaxias fought without Parthian forces this would be a defeat of Atropatene by Armenia rather than a civil battle. Artavasdes later escaped during a Parthian civil war and took refuge with Octavian, who gave him Lesser Armenia.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Artabanus' first defeat
label: Artabanus' first defeat
war: Parthian succession war (Vonones I against Artabanus II)
place: probably near the borders of Media, Iran (site unknown)
faction_b: Artabanus II (then king of Media Atropatene)
persian_force: Parthian noble cavalry on both sides: Vonones had the retinues of the nobles (the Karin and Suren factions) who had brought him from Rome; Artabanus came with forces from Media Atropatene and, Tacitus says, had grown up among the Dahae.
iranian_note: Both claimants relied on the cavalry of the Parthian and Median nobility, and Artabanus's Dahae links suggest East Iranian steppe horsemen as well.
result_basis: Artabanus was routed in the first clash and fell back to the borders of Media (Tacitus; Josephus).
borderline: no conventional name: an unnamed battle of the succession war, known only in outline
doubt: Borderline: no conventional name: an unnamed battle of the succession war, known only in outline.
sources: Tacitus, Annals 2.3; Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 18.46-50; en.wikipedia Vonones I; en.wikipedia Artabanus II of Parthia
note: The dates rest on coins: Vonones reigned c. 8-12 and Artabanus struck coins from c. 10/11.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Sagala (Rajuvula v Strato II, c. 10 CE)
label: Sagala
date: c. 10 CE (the date is drawn from coins and the Mathura Lion Capital; uncertain by a decade)
result_basis: Strato II's coinage ends and Rajuvula takes over Sagala, the Indo-Greek capital of the Punjab.
sources: Mathura Lion Capital inscription; coin evidence (Bopearachchi, Monnaies gréco-bactriennes et indo-grecques, 1991); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-Scythians
note: No fighting is described; the conquest is inferred from coin overstrikes and the end of Strato's coinage, so the entry is a marker for the end of Greek rule in the Punjab.

name: Vonones' defeat
label: Vonones' defeat
war: Parthian succession war (Vonones I against Artabanus II)
persian_force: Artabanus' rebuilt army of Median and Parthian nobles, perhaps with Dahae horse, against Vonones' following among the Parthian nobility (no details survive).
iranian_note: Parthian armies of the early first century were the retinues of the Iranian nobility; Artabanus had been raised among the Dahae (Tacitus).
result_basis: Artabanus beat Vonones, who fled from the field with a few horsemen to Seleucia and then to Armenia (Josephus).
borderline: no conventional name: the decisive but unnamed battle of the succession war
doubt: Borderline: no conventional name: the decisive but unnamed battle of the succession war.
sources: Tacitus, Annals 2.3-4; Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 18.46-52; en.wikipedia Vonones I
note: Vonones became king of Armenia in 12 and was later held by the Romans in Syria and Cilicia, where he was killed in 19.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Orodes' defeat
label: Orodes' defeat
place: Armenia, probably in the Araxes plain (site unknown), Armenia
commanders_a: Pharasmanes I of Iberia, his brother Mithridates (the Roman candidate for Armenia)
persian_force: Orodes' Parthian army, mostly horse archers and noble cavalry; Tacitus contrasts it with the Iberian and Albanian foot and the Sarmatian horse of Pharasmanes, and says Orodes failed to hire Sarmatians because the Iberians held the passes.
iranian_note: Tacitus calls Orodes' troops Parthians and describes them fighting as mounted archers.
result_basis: Pharasmanes wounded Orodes in single combat and the Parthians, believing their prince dead, fled the field (Tacitus).
borderline: no conventional name: the one pitched battle of the Iberian invasion of Armenia
doubt: Borderline: no conventional name: the one pitched battle of the Iberian invasion of Armenia.
sources: Tacitus, Annals 6.33-35; en.wikipedia Iberian invasion of Armenia; en.wikipedia List of wars involving Iran (before 1979)
note: Rome backed the invasion but sent no troops; Mithridates of Iberia took the Armenian throne.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Seleucia (siege, 40-42)
label: Seleucia (siege, 40-42)
war: Revolt of Seleucia (c. 35-42) and the war of Vardanes I and Gotarzes II
place: Seleucia on the Tigris (near al-Mada'in), Iraq
persian_force: Vardanes' Parthian royal army; the sources give no details (Parthian armies of the time were noble cavalry, cataphracts and horse archers, with levies).
iranian_note: Inferred from the usual make-up of Parthian royal armies, levied from the Iranian nobility.
result_basis: Seleucia submitted to Vardanes in 42, in the seventh year of its revolt, after a siege interrupted by Gotarzes' return.
borderline: a siege known only in outline; the fighting is not described
doubt: Borderline: a siege known only in outline; the fighting is not described.
sources: Tacitus, Annals 11.8-9; en.wikipedia Vardanes I; en.wikipedia Gotarzes II
note: Seleucia, the Greek city opposite Ctesiphon, revolted c. 35. Gotarzes used the long siege to raise an army and drive Vardanes east; after the two brothers came to terms, Vardanes took the city's surrender and its right to coin (Wikipedia: June 42).
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Erindes
label: Erindes
date: c. 45 (between 43 and 46; Tacitus tells it under AD 47)
war: Parthian succession war (Vardanes I against Gotarzes II)
place: the river Erindes (Charinda), on the border of Media and Hyrcania (unidentified), Iran
persian_force: Vardanes' Parthian royal cavalry against Gotarzes' army from Hyrcania; in the earlier round of the war Gotarzes had called on the Dahae and Hyrcanians (Tacitus 11.8).
iranian_note: Both armies came from the Iranian nobility of Parthia, Media and Hyrcania, and Gotarzes leaned on Dahae steppe horsemen.
result_basis: Vardanes won the fierce fight for the river crossing and Gotarzes withdrew (Tacitus).
sources: Tacitus, Annals 11.10; en.wikipedia Vardanes I; en.wikipedia Gotarzes II
note: The manuscripts and translations give the river as Erindes or Charinda; Vardanes then subdued the peoples as far as the river Sindes, between the Dahae and the Arians, in unnamed fights.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Corma
label: Corma
date: 49 (Tacitus tells it under AD 49; some date it 50 or 51)
war: Parthian succession war (Gotarzes II against Meherdates)
place: near Mount Sanbulos, across the river Corma (perhaps near Bisotun, Kermanshah), Iran
commanders_b: Meherdates, Carenes (of the house of Karen)
persian_force: Gotarzes' Parthian royal army against Meherdates' Parthian partisans led by Carenes; the contingents of Abgar of Edessa and Izates of Adiabene deserted Meherdates before the battle.
iranian_note: Once the Edessan and Adiabenian allies had left, both armies were the cavalry of Parthian noble houses (Tacitus).
result_basis: Meherdates' army broke after Carenes pursued too far, and Meherdates was betrayed by Parraces and handed to Gotarzes, who cut off his ears (Tacitus).
sources: Tacitus, Annals 12.10-14; en.wikipedia Meherdates; livius.org (Behistun, Parthian relief of Gotarzes II defeating Meherdates)
note: Meherdates, a son of Vonones I raised in Rome, was escorted to the Euphrates by Cassius Longinus but had no Roman troops in the battle. Neither Mount Sanbulos nor the Corma is securely identified; Gotarzes' victory relief is at Bisotun.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Panda River (Aorsi and Romans v Dandarii, 49 CE)
label: Panda River
date: 49 CE (summer?); the fight is an episode of the campaign that ends at Uspe
war: Bosporan war of Mithridates VIII v Cotys I
place: River Panda, in the land of the Dandarii (Kuban/Taman region, Russia; exact river unknown)
persian_state: Bosporan kingdom of Cotys I v Mithridates VIII
faction_a: Bosporan kingdom of Cotys I, Aorsi
commanders_a: Eunones (king of the Aorsi); Cotys I; C. Julius Aquila (Roman prefect)
commanders_b: Mithridates VIII (deposed Bosporan king); Zorsines (king of the Siraces, until he changed sides at Uspe)
result_basis: Tacitus has the Aorsi cavalry and Roman foot beat the Dandarii and cross the Panda, after which Soza falls and the army goes on to Uspe.
sources: Tacitus, Annals 12.15-21; Rostovtzeff, Iranians and Greeks in South Russia (1922); Minns, Scythians and Greeks (1913)
note: Tacitus does not give the fight a name and may be summarising a running cavalry action; check that it is not already counted inside the Uspe siege. Whether Zorsines' Siraces fought here (as opposed to at Uspe) is not certain.

name: Uspe (siege)
label: Uspe
place: Uspe, town of the Siraces beyond the river Panda (site unknown, Kuban region)
commanders_a: Gaius Julius Aquila, Cotys I, Eunones
sources: Tacitus Ann. 12.15-17; en.wikipedia Roman–Bosporan War
note: Opponent: the Siraces, allies of the deposed Mithridates of the Bosporus; allies_a Sarmatians = the Aorsi. The town was stormed after its offer of 10,000 slaves was refused, and Zorsines submitted.
qbasis: Sarmatians among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans

name: Vannius' defeat (50 CE)
label: Vannius' defeat
date: c. 50 CE (Tacitus places it in the 12th book under 50)
war: Revolt against Vannius, king of the Danubian Suebi
place: Danube frontier of the Suebic kingdom of Vannius (Moravia / western Slovakia); exact site unknown
commanders_a: Vibilius (king of the Hermunduri); Vangio and Sido (Vannius' nephews)
commanders_b: Vannius (king of the Suebi); the Iazyges chiefs (not named)
result_basis: Tacitus says Vannius' Iazyges horsemen would not be shut in the forts, so he fought in the open, was beaten and fled to the Danube fleet; Claudius settled him in Pannonia.
sources: Tacitus, Annals 12.29-30; Wolfram, The Roman Empire and Its Germanic Peoples (1997)
note: The Iazyges are the first Sarmatians named in the Middle Danube. Their share of Vannius' army is not given, but Tacitus makes them the decisive part (the cavalry).

name: Artaxata
label: Artaxata
result_basis: As in Battles of the Romans: The en.wikipedia list calls it the Sack of Artaxata. Its 'Capture of Tigranocerta' (59) was a surrender without fighting and is not entered; the resistance of Legerda is entered separately.
sources: Tacitus Ann. 13.39-41; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles (Sack of Artaxata)
note: Tiridates I of Armenia, brother of the Parthian king Vologases I (Tac. Ann. 13.37-41)
qbasis: Tiridates I of Armenia, brother of the Parthian king Vologases I (Tac. Ann. 13.37-41)

name: Volandum (siege)
label: Volandum
result_basis: As in Battles of the Romans: Stormed within a day, with three smaller forts; Artaxata surrendered soon after.
sources: Tacitus Ann. 13.39; en.wikipedia Roman–Parthian War of 58–63
note: Partisans of the Arsacid Tiridates I (Tac. Ann. 13.39)
qbasis: Partisans of the Arsacid Tiridates I (Tac. Ann. 13.39)

name: Suoju (Yarkand), 61 CE
label: Suoju, 61 CE
date: 61 CE (Hou Hanshu: the 4th year of Yongping)
war: Khotan's wars against the oasis states of the Tarim basin
result_basis: The Hou Hanshu says Guangde of Khotan attacked and killed Xian and Suoju was ruled by Khotan, with thirteen states submitting.
sources: Hou Hanshu 88 (Western Regions: Yutian); Hill, The Western Regions according to the Hou Hanshu (2009); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Khotan
note: Khotanese is an eastern Iranian (Saka) language; the Hou Hanshu records only the result. Dates in the tradition differ by a year or two.

name: Tigranocerta (siege)
label: Tigranocerta (siege)
commanders_a: Tigranes VI of Armenia with the Roman garrison (Corbulo in overall command)
commanders_b: Monaeses, Monobazus II of Adiabene (Vologases I at Nisibis)
persian_force: Monaeses' picked Parthian cavalry, with the infantry of Monobazus of Adiabene, who carried the scaling ladders (Tacitus).
iranian_note: Tacitus names Monaeses' Parthian horse and the Adiabenian foot; their proportions are unknown.
strength_a: unknown (Tigranes' Armenians and a Roman garrison)
losses_b: Adiabenians cut down in the sally (Tacitus)
result_basis: The Parthian assault was beaten off by a sally and the siege was given up for want of fodder; Tigranocerta held.
sources: Tacitus, Annals 15.1-6; Cassius Dio 62.20; en.wikipedia Roman-Parthian War of 58-63; en.wikipedia Battle of Rhandeia
note: Tigranes' raid into Adiabene provoked the siege. The site of Tigranocerta is disputed (Arzan near Batman or Silvan/Mayafarqin).
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Chersonesus (siege, c. 62 CE)
label: Chersonesus
date: c. 62-66 CE (the inscription falls under Silvanus' governorship, c. 60-67)
war: Scythian (Crimean) attack on Chersonesus and its relief by Rome
commanders_b: Ti. Plautius Silvanus Aelianus (governor of Moesia)
result_basis: Silvanus' inscription says he compelled the king of the Scythians to raise the siege of Chersonesus, beyond the Borysthenes.
sources: CIL XIV 3608 (Silvanus Aelianus' elogium from Tibur); Vinogradov and Zolotarev, Chersonesus and Rome (1990); Minns, Scythians and Greeks (1913)
note: Silvanus's Roman force and the Bosporan fleet are said to have been used. The Scythians are the late (Crimean) Scythians, an Iranian people by the usual account.

name: Rhandeia
label: Rhandeia
place: Paetus' winter camp at Rhandeia, on the Arsanias (Murat) near Arsamosata, Turkey
commanders_a: Vologases I, Tiridates I of Armenia
persian_force: Vologases' Parthian royal army of cavalry with Tiridates' Armenians; on the way it destroyed the Roman detachments that Paetus had posted in the Taurus passes.
iranian_note: The army was the Parthian king's own levy of noble cavalry, joined by the Armenian forces of his brother Tiridates.
strength_b: two legions (IV Scythica, XII Fulminata) with auxiliaries
losses_b: the army capitulated; the forts and stores were surrendered
result_basis: Paetus, blockaded in his camp, capitulated and the Romans left Armenia before Corbulo's relief arrived.
sources: Tacitus, Annals 15.7-17; Cassius Dio 62.21; en.wikipedia Battle of Rhandeia; en.wikipedia Roman-Parthian War of 58-63
note: Wikipedia's infobox coordinates (39.40 N, 43.80 E) do not fit its own text; the Roman-set site on the Arsanias is kept. The Romans had to bridge the Arsanias for Vologases; the treaty of Rhandeia (63/64) made Tiridates king of Armenia, crowned by Nero.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Moesia
label: Moesia
place: Moesia, south of the lower Danube (site not given)
sources: Tacitus, Histories 1.79
note: Roxolani (Sarmatians).
qbasis: Sarmatians among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans

name: Alan invasion of Media and Armenia
label: Alan invasion of Media and Armenia
date: 72 CE (Josephus dates it to the 4th year of Vespasian, after the Commagene war)
war: Alan raid through the Caucasus (called in by the king of Hyrcania)
place: Media Atropatene and Armenia (Iranian Azerbaijan, Armenia)
commanders_b: Pacorus (king of Media, brother of Vologases I); Tiridates I of Armenia (also a brother of Vologases)
result_basis: Josephus says the Alans routed Pacorus (who fled and later ransomed his wife and concubines for 100 talents) and defeated Tiridates in a battle in which he was nearly lassoed, then went home with plunder.
sources: Josephus, Jewish War 7.244-251; Cassius Dio 66.15; Bivar, 'The Political History of Iran under the Arsacids', CHI 3(1) (1983)
note: Both sides were Iranian (the Arsacid brothers of Vologases I were Parthians). Josephus gives no place name for the fight with Tiridates.

name: Commagene
label: Commagene
place: Commagene, near Samosata on the Euphrates
commanders_b: Epiphanes and Callinicus, sons of Antiochus IV
result_basis: As in Battles of the Romans: The battle lasted a whole day without decision; the princes then fled to Parthia and Commagene, a Hellenistic kingdom with a Greek court, was annexed.
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Josephus, Jewish War 7.219-243
note: Sons of Antiochus IV of Commagene; Orontid line (Commagene; Artaxiad Armenia as its branch) widely described as of Iranian origin, but disputed
qbasis: Sons of Antiochus IV of Commagene; Orontid line (Commagene; Artaxiad Armenia as its branch) widely described as of Iranian origin, but disputed

name: Gumo (Ban Chao, 78 CE)
label: Gumo
war: Ban Chao's reconquest of the Western Regions
commanders_b: the king of Gumo (name not preserved)
result_basis: Ban Chao led the troops of Khotan, Shule and other states against Gumo and cut off about 700 heads, according to the Hou Hanshu.
sources: Hou Hanshu 47 (Ban Chao biography); Hill (2009); Yu Taishan, Sino-Platonic Papers 131 (2004)
note: The troop numbers and the part played by the Khotanese are from Chinese sources; the summary of the campaign is brief. Khotan is named among the allied states.

name: Shache (Ban Chao, 87 CE)
label: Shache
date: 87 CE (Zhanghe 1); Wikipedia's Ban Chao article has the Yarkand fight in 88
war: Ban Chao's reconquest of the Western Regions
commanders_a: Ban Chao; the king of Khotan (Guangde or his successor)
commanders_b: the marshals of Kucha (about 50,000 men); the king of Shache
result_basis: Ban Chao ambushed the 50,000-strong Kucha relief force on the night it marched past, killed 5,000, and Shache surrendered.
sources: Hou Hanshu 47 (Ban Chao biography); Hill (2009); Yu Taishan (2004)
note: Ban Chao drew his 25,000 men from Khotan and other allied states; the share of the Khotanese is not given, but Khotan is the first named and the chief ally of the Han in this region. The date is not identical in all modern accounts.

name: Ban Chao's defeat of the Kushan army (90 CE)
label: Ban Chao's defeat of the Kushan army
date: 90 CE (second year of Yongyuan; month not given)
place: Shule (Kashgar) region, western Tarim Basin, Xinjiang
commanders_a: Xie (Kushan deputy king); Kushan king (probably Vima Takto)
result_basis: Xie's army, short of supplies and robbed of its couriers to Kucha, asked leave to withdraw and the Kushans later sent tribute (Hou Hanshu 47).
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Hou Hanshu 47 (biography of Ban Chao) and 88 (Western Regions); Hill, J. E., Through the Jade Gate to Rome (2009); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ban_Chao
note: The Han text gives 70,000 Kushans, almost certainly inflated; Ban Chao won by scorched-earth defence and by intercepting envoys sent to the king of Kucha, with little actual fighting. The Kushans ruled Bactria and wrote Bactrian (an Eastern Iranian language), but the dynasty came from the Yuezhi, whose own language is disputed (Tocharian or Iranian), so the identification is uncertain.
qbasis: A Kushan army led by the deputy king Xie (Hou Hanshu 47) fought Ban Chao; the Kushans are uncertain Iranians (see note).

name: Destruction of Legio XXI Rapax (92 CE)
label: Destruction of Legio XXI Rapax
date: 92 CE (spring or early summer; the year is certain, the month is not)
place: Pannonia, on the middle Danube (exact site unknown; between Carnuntum and Brigetio is the usual guess)
commanders_b: the legate of Legio XXI Rapax (name not preserved), killed with the legion
result_basis: Suetonius says the Sarmatians cut a legion and its legate to pieces; the legion is not heard of again.
sources: Suetonius, Domitian 6.1; Cassius Dio 67.5-7; Jones, The Emperor Domitian (1992); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iazyges
note: Suetonius names the Sarmatians as the destroyers; Dio blames the Marcomanni and Quadi, and some modern accounts add Dacians. The identification of the legion as XXI Rapax rests on its disappearance from the record after 92.

name: Yanqi (Ban Chao, 94 CE)
label: Yanqi
war: Ban Chao's reconquest of the Western Regions
commanders_b: Guang (king of Yanqi, captured and executed)
result_basis: Ban Chao's army of Han officers and troops of the Tarim states took Yanqi; King Guang was captured and executed.
sources: Hou Hanshu 47 (Ban Chao biography); Hill (2009); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ban_Chao
note: Khotan is among the allied states named; the Khotanese share of the 70,000 is not given. Ban Chao's earlier defeat of the Kushans (90) is left out, since the Kushans are an uncertain case.

name: Adamclisi
label: Adamclisi
sources: Trajan's Column; Tropaeum Traiani; en.wikipedia Battle of Adamclisi; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles
note: Dacians with Roxolani (Sarmatians) and Bastarnae. The Tropaeum Traiani (109) commemorates the victory; the altar may instead commemorate Fuscus' or Oppius Sabinus' dead.
qbasis: Sarmatians among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans

name: Nicopolis ad Istrum
label: Nicopolis ad Istrum
place: Near the later city of Nicopolis ad Istrum, on the Yantra
sources: Trajan's Column; Jordanes, Getica 101; en.wikipedia Trajan's Dacian Wars; en.wikipedia Battle of Adamclisi
note: en.wikipedia's Adamclisi article calls the night battle near Nicopolis indecisive; its Dacian Wars article calls it a Roman victory.
qbasis: Sarmatians among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans

name: Ctesiphon (116)
label: Ctesiphon (116)
place: Ctesiphon, on the Tigris (near Salman Pak), Iraq
persian_force: Whatever garrison Osroes I left in his capital; no Parthian field army is recorded (the empire was split between Osroes and Vologases III).
iranian_note: Inferred only: the royal guard of the Parthian capital would have been Iranian, the townspeople Aramaic- and Greek-speaking.
result_basis: Trajan took Ctesiphon with Osroes' daughter and golden throne; the king had fled and no defence is described.
borderline: capture without described fighting; kept to agree with Battles of the Romans
doubt: Borderline: capture without described fighting; kept to agree with Battles of the Romans.
sources: Cassius Dio 68.28; en.wikipedia Trajan's Parthian campaign
note: Trajan took the title Parthicus in February 116, which is why some put the capture in late 115; Wikipedia's campaign article dates it to 115.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Maximus' defeat
label: Maximus' defeat
commanders_a: probably Sanatruces, nephew of Osroes I
persian_force: Parthian cavalry under Sanatruces, perhaps with Saka archers, acting with the rebellious cities of Mesopotamia.
iranian_note: Dio speaks of 'the rebels': the Parthian horse of Sanatruces fought alongside Aramaic-, Greek- and Jewish-populated cities in revolt.
result_basis: Maximus' army was defeated in battle and he was killed (Cassius Dio).
borderline: no place name; kept to agree with Battles of the Romans
doubt: Borderline: no place name; kept to agree with Battles of the Romans.
sources: Cassius Dio 68.30; John Malalas, Chronicle 11; en.wikipedia Trajan's Parthian campaign
note: Dio says Maximus was sent 'against the rebels'; Battles of the Romans credits the victory to the Parthians, and Wikipedia does not say whether Parthian troops took part.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Sanatruces' defeat
label: Sanatruces' defeat
commanders_a: Trajan, Lusius Quietus, Erucius Clarus, Julius Alexander (with Parthamaspates, who deserted Sanatruces)
persian_force: The Parthian cavalry that Sanatruces had kept together, perhaps reinforced with Saka archers (Wikipedia, after Malalas).
iranian_note: A Parthian prince's cavalry army, perhaps with Saka archers; no units are named.
result_basis: Sanatruces' army was beaten and he was killed after Parthamaspates went over to the Romans (Malalas).
borderline: no place name; known mainly from Malalas
doubt: Borderline: no place name; known mainly from Malalas.
sources: John Malalas, Chronicle 11; Cassius Dio 68.30; en.wikipedia Trajan's Parthian campaign
note: Trajan then crowned Parthamaspates at Ctesiphon; Dio credits Erucius Clarus and Julius Alexander with retaking and burning rebel Seleucia.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Quadratus Bassus' defeat (117 CE)
label: Quadratus Bassus' defeat
date: 117 CE (the end of Trajan's reign and the first months of Hadrian's)
place: Roman Dacia and Lower Moesia, along the Danube/Banat frontier (exact site unknown)
commanders_b: C. Julius Quadratus Bassus (governor of Dacia, killed); Q. Marcius Turbo sent to restore the frontier
result_basis: The Roman governor of Dacia, Quadratus Bassus, was killed in the fighting, and Hadrian had to hurry to the Danube and make terms; the Roxolani were soon won over by a tribute adjustment.
sources: Historia Augusta, Hadrian 5-6; the honorific inscription for Quadratus Bassus from Pergamon; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iazyges
note: That Bassus died fighting the Sarmatians is attested; the circumstances of the fight are not. Treat as a minor, thinly sourced defeat.

name: Uttamabhadras relief (Ushavadata v Malavas, c. 120 CE)
label: Uttamabhadras relief
date: c. 120 CE (Nashik Cave 10 inscription, year 42 of the Saka era)
war: Western Satrap (Kshaharata) wars in Rajasthan and Malwa
place: Pushkar region (Pokkhara), Rajasthan, India; exact site unknown
commanders_a: Ushavadata (son-in-law of Nahapana and his viceroy; son of Dinika)
result_basis: The Nashik Cave 10 inscription says the Malayas fled 'at the mere roar' of Ushavadata's approach, and the Uttamabhadras they had besieged were freed.
sources: Nashik Cave 10 inscription of Ushavadata (Epigraphia Indica 8); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Satraps
note: Ushavadata (Rishabhadatta) is an Indian-named relative of the Saka Nahapana; the inscription is a boast, and the fight, if any, is not described.

name: Gautamiputra Satakarni v Nahapana (c. 124 CE)
label: Gautamiputra Satakarni v Nahapana
date: c. 124 CE (range c. 105-130; Gautamiputra's inscriptions are dated by regnal years 18-19)
war: Satavahana reconquest of Maharashtra from the Western Satraps (Kshaharatas)
place: Nashik / Govardhana region, western Deccan (exact site unknown)
commanders_b: Nahapana (Kshaharata satrap); Ushavadata (his son-in-law and viceroy)
result_basis: Gautamiputra's inscriptions (through his mother Gautami Balasri) say he 'rooted out the Khakharata family' and destroyed Sakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas; the Jogalthembi hoard of Nahapana's coins overstruck by Gautamiputra shows the recovery of Nashik.
sources: Nashik (Pandavleni) Cave 3 inscription of Gautami Balasri; Jogalthembi coin hoard; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India (2008); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Satraps
note: No battle is described; the war is known from inscriptions and the overstruck coin hoard. The Kshaharatas are called Saka or Pahlava (Parthian) in different accounts; either way they are Iranian.

name: Saketa (Khotan and Kanishka, c. 127)
label: Saketa
date: c. 127 CE (the date is that of Kanishka's accession in the Khotan tradition; uncertain)
war: Khotanese-Kushan campaign in the Ganges plain (Tibetan Khotan annals)
result_basis: The Tibetan Li yul lung bstan pa says the Khotanese king Vijaya Kirti and Kanishka took Saketa together.
doubt: Traditional: known only from a doubtful tradition.
sources: Li yul lung bstan pa (Prophecy of the Li Country), as in Emmerick, Tibetan Texts Concerning Khotan (1967); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Khotan
note: Known only from a late Tibetan Buddhist tradition about Khotan; no independent source. Included because the Khotanese king is named as a leader.

name: Salut
label: Salut
date: 130 (traditional; modern guesses range from the 2nd to the 3rd century)
place: Salut, near Bisya and Bahla, Oman
commanders_a: Malik ibn Fahm al-Azdi, Amr ibn Fahm
commanders_b: the Persian marzban of Oman (named in the tradition Bara son of Dara son of Bahman)
persian_force: In the tradition, the Persian garrison and settlers of Oman under their marzban; no reliable details.
iranian_note: The tradition speaks of a Persian governor and garrison holding the Omani interior.
result_basis: In the Omani tradition the Azd won the battle and the Persians left the interior of Oman.
borderline: a traditional battle of uncertain date and Persian state
doubt: Traditional: Known only from Omani and Arab traditions written down many centuries later; modern scholars read it as a memory of the Azd migration rather than a documented event, and the date given by Wikipedia (130) is not explained. Borderline: a traditional battle of uncertain date and Persian state.
sources: Omani tradition (al-Awtabi, Ansab al-Arab; the Kashf al-Ghumma); en.wikipedia Battle of Salut (Ulrich 2008, 2019; Wilkinson)
note: Wikipedia's infobox says Parthian forces, its text 'Persian'; if the battle is historical but later, it belongs to the Sasanian period.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Kashgar's victory over Khotan (132 CE)
label: Kashgar's victory over Khotan
war: Khotan's wars against Keriya and the Han governors
place: Khotan / Keriya area, southern Tarim basin (Xinjiang, China)
commanders_a: Chenpan (king of Kashgar), with about 20,000 men
result_basis: The Hou Hanshu says Chenpan's army of 20,000 beat the Khotanese, cut off several hundred heads, and the king of Keriya was replaced.
sources: Hou Hanshu 88 (Yutian); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Khotan
note: Fangqian had killed the king of Keriya (129) and kept it against Han orders; this is the Han reply. Details of the fight are thin.

name: Kanishka's war with Parthia
label: Kanishka's war with Parthia
place: west of the Kushan realm, perhaps Aria or Bactria (site unknown), Afghanistan
commanders_b: the Parthian king (unnamed; perhaps Vologases III)
persian_force: In the Buddhist account the Parthian king led mounted bowmen, armoured troops, foot archers and spearmen.
iranian_note: A Parthian army in the east would have been raised from Parthian, Arian and Margian nobles and their followers.
result_basis: The only source says Kanishka won after a great slaughter of the Parthian army.
borderline: a war known from one Buddhist text; no battle or site is named
doubt: Traditional: Attested only in the Fu fazang yinyuan zhuan, a Buddhist text translated into Chinese in the 470s, as a moral tale of Kanishka's remorse; the Parthian king is unnamed and the date is a modern inference. Borderline: a war known from one Buddhist text; no battle or site is named.
sources: Fu fazang yinyuan zhuan (Taisho 2058); en.wikipedia Kanishka's war with Parthia
note: Wikipedia's List of wars involving Iran also lists a first Parthian-Kushan war (45-50s), fought mainly by the Indo-Parthians, with no named battle.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Rudradaman v Vasishthiputra Satakarni (c. 140-150 CE)
label: Rudradaman v Vasishthiputra Satakarni
date: before 150 CE (the Junagadh inscription is dated Saka year 72 = 150 CE); the fights are undated
place: Dakshinapatha (northern Deccan and the Konkan); exact sites unknown
result_basis: The Junagadh inscription says Rudradaman twice completely defeated the lord of Dakshinapatha, Satakarni, but spared him because of their close relationship.
sources: Junagadh (Girnar) rock inscription of Rudradaman (Epigraphia Indica 8); Kanheri inscription of Vasishthiputra Satakarni's queen; Sircar, Select Inscriptions (2005); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Satraps
note: Two battles are implied; entered as one event. Rudradaman's dynasty (Kardamaka, descended from Chashtana) is Saka by the usual account.

name: Rudradaman v the Yaudheyas (c. 150 CE)
label: Rudradaman v the Yaudheyas
date: c. 150 CE (the Junagadh inscription of Saka year 72)
place: Yaudheya country (Haryana / eastern Rajasthan); exact site unknown
result_basis: The Junagadh inscription says Rudradaman 'forcibly uprooted' the Yaudheyas, who were proud of their title 'heroes among all Kshatriyas' and would not submit.
sources: Junagadh (Girnar) rock inscription of Rudradaman, line 11; Sircar (2005); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Satraps
note: Known only from a royal inscription's boast; the place and the fighting are not described.

name: Elegeia
label: Elegeia
place: Elegeia, beyond the Cappadocian frontier near the headwaters of the Euphrates (probably Ilica, near Erzurum), Turkey
persian_force: The Parthian army that Vologases IV sent into Armenia under Osroes; the sources say only 'the Parthians', i.e. the usual horse archers and cataphracts of the noble levy.
iranian_note: Parthian field armies of the second century were the cavalry of the Iranian nobility; no units are named.
strength_b: one legion (perhaps IX Hispana) with auxiliaries
result_basis: Severianus' army was trapped and destroyed within three days, and he killed himself.
sources: Cassius Dio 71.2; Lucian, How to Write History and Alexander 27; en.wikipedia Roman-Parthian War of 161-166
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Cornelianus' defeat
label: Cornelianus' defeat
commanders_b: Lucius Attidius Cornelianus, governor of Syria
persian_force: The Parthian army that invaded Syria in 161-162; no details survive (normally the noble cavalry levy).
iranian_note: Inferred from the usual make-up of Parthian field armies.
result_basis: The governor's army was beaten and fled in disorder (Historia Augusta).
borderline: no place name; known only from brief mentions
doubt: Borderline: no place name; known only from brief mentions.
sources: Historia Augusta, Marcus 8.6; Fronto; en.wikipedia Roman-Parthian War of 161-166
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Artaxata
label: Artaxata
place: Artaxata, the Armenian capital on the Araxes (near Artashat), Armenia
persian_force: Parthian troops supporting the Parthian-installed king Pacorus, with Armenian forces; no details survive.
iranian_note: Inferred only; the Armenian share of the defence is unknown.
strength_a: including I Minervia and V Macedonica
result_basis: Statius Priscus captured and destroyed Artaxata.
sources: Historia Augusta, Marcus 9.1; Fronto; en.wikipedia Roman-Parthian War of 161-166
note: The Romans founded a new capital, Kaine Polis, in 164 and made Sohaemus king of Armenia.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Edessa (siege, 163)
label: Edessa (siege, 163)
persian_force: A Parthian army of Vologases IV, with the Edessan partisans of Wa'el; no details survive.
iranian_note: Inferred: a Parthian royal force with local Aramaic-speaking supporters.
result_basis: The Parthians took Edessa and installed Wa'el son of Sahru as their client king.
borderline: the siege is known from coins and the Edessan king list; the fighting is not described
doubt: Borderline: the siege is known from coins and the Edessan king list; the fighting is not described.
sources: Wa'el's coins with the Parthian king's portrait; Edessan king list; en.wikipedia Siege of Edessa (163)
note: Ma'nu VIII fled to the Romans; Wa'el ruled Edessa as a Parthian client from 163 to 165.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Sura (163)
label: Sura (163)
place: Sura, on the right bank of the Euphrates (near Mansoura), Syria
persian_force: Parthian forces holding the south bank of the Euphrates; nothing more is known.
iranian_note: Inferred from the usual make-up of Parthian field armies.
result_basis: Lucian mentions a battle at Sura only in passing and no source says who won; the Parthians still held the right bank there in 163.
doubt: The sources consulted do not give the result, so the battle is listed but not scored.
sources: Lucian, How to Write History; en.wikipedia Roman-Parthian War of 161-166
note: The year is added to the Roman-set name because Khosrow I's capture of Sura (540) is another entry.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Ctesiphon (165)
label: Ctesiphon (165)
place: Ctesiphon and Seleucia, on the Tigris (near Salman Pak), Iraq
persian_force: The defenders of the Parthian capital under Vologases IV's officers; no details survive.
iranian_note: Inferred only: the royal troops would have been Iranian, the twin cities' people Aramaic- and Greek-speaking.
result_basis: Avidius Cassius took Ctesiphon and burned the royal palace; Seleucia opened its gates and was sacked.
sources: Cassius Dio 71.2; Historia Augusta, Verus 8; en.wikipedia Battle of Ctesiphon (165); en.wikipedia Roman-Parthian War of 161-166
note: Wikipedia names it the Battle of Ctesiphon (165) but describes a siege and capture. Avidius Cassius went on into Media in 166 without a recorded battle.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Dura-Europos (165)
label: Dura-Europos (165)
place: Dura-Europos, on the middle Euphrates (near Salhiyeh), Syria
persian_force: The Parthian army on the middle Euphrates and the garrison of Dura, a Parthian-held town of Greek and Aramaic speakers; no units are named.
iranian_note: Parthian field troops fought beside the local levies of a mixed Greek and Aramaic city.
losses_a: 2 killed, 7 wounded (a historian mocked by Lucian)
result_basis: Lucian reports a great Roman victory at Europos, and Dura passed into Roman hands.
sources: Lucian, How to Write History; en.wikipedia Roman-Parthian War of 161-166
note: The year is added to the Roman-set name because Shapur I's siege of Dura (256) is another entry.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Edessa (siege, 165)
label: Edessa (siege, 165)
commanders_a: Lucius Verus (nominal), probably Martius Verus or Avidius Cassius; Ma'nu VIII
commanders_b: Wa'el son of Sahru and the Parthian garrison
persian_force: The Parthian garrison of Edessa with the Edessan partisans of Wa'el.
iranian_note: A Parthian garrison backed by local Aramaic-speaking supporters of Wa'el; their numbers are unknown.
result_basis: The citizens killed the Parthian garrison and opened the gates, so Edessa fell to the Roman besiegers.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Edessa (165); en.wikipedia Roman-Parthian War of 161-166
note: Ma'nu VIII was restored with the title Philorhomaios.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Nisibis (siege, 165)
label: Nisibis (siege, 165)
persian_force: The Parthian army that fell back from Edessa to Nisibis under Osroes; no units are named.
iranian_note: Inferred: a Parthian field army with the garrison of an Aramaic-speaking city.
result_basis: Nisibis was besieged and taken; the Parthian army dispersed and Osroes escaped by swimming the Tigris (Lucian).
sources: Lucian, How to Write History; en.wikipedia Roman-Parthian War of 161-166
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Death of Fronto (170 CE)
label: Death of Fronto
date: 170 CE (the year is certain; Fronto died early in the Marcomannic invasion of Dacia)
place: Roman Dacia (the Alburnus Maior and Banat approaches; exact site unknown)
commanders_b: M. Claudius Fronto (governor of the Dacias, killed)
result_basis: Fronto's tomb inscription says he fell fighting 'against the Germans and the Iazyges' after earlier successes; it does not say who held the field.
doubt: The sources consulted do not give the result, so the battle is listed but not scored.
sources: CIL VI 1377 (Fronto's monument inscription); Historia Augusta, Marcus Aurelius 22.1; Birley, Marcus Aurelius (1987); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iazyges
note: The Iazyges hold Dacia's western edge, so they were the natural party in the attack; the inscription names them alongside the Germans.

name: Frozen Danube
label: Frozen Danube
place: On the frozen middle Danube (site unknown)
sources: Cassius Dio 71.7
note: Iazyges (Sarmatians).
qbasis: Sarmatians among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans

name: Sauromates II's defeat of the Scythians (c. 180-210)
label: Sauromates II's defeat of the Scythians
war: Bosporan wars against the Crimean Scythians
result_basis: The Wikipedia summary of the Bosporan kingdom says Sauromates II inflicted a critical defeat on the Scythians and brought the whole Crimean peninsula into his state.
sources: Bosporan inscriptions (CIRB); Mielczarek, The Army of the Bosporan Kingdom (1999); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosporan_Kingdom
note: Known from inscriptions and brief summaries; no named battle. Bosporan kings after Sauromates I (93-124) are of mixed (Thracian, Greek and Sarmatian) descent, so only the Scythians are counted here.

name: Nisibis (siege, 197)
label: Nisibis (siege, 197)
persian_force: Vologases V's royal army, a seasonal levy of the nobles' cavalry; the sources give no breakdown.
iranian_note: Inferred from the usual make-up of Parthian royal armies, raised from noble contingents for each campaign.
result_basis: Laetus held Nisibis and the Parthians raised the siege as Severus approached.
sources: Cassius Dio 76(75).9; en.wikipedia Septimius Severus' Parthian campaigns
note: The earlier siege of Nisibis (194) was by Abgar VIII of Osrhoene, Adiabene and Hatra without Parthian forces, and is left out.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Ctesiphon (198)
label: Ctesiphon (198)
date: late 197 or January 198 (Severus took the title Parthicus Maximus on 28 January 198)
place: Ctesiphon, on the Tigris (near Salman Pak), Iraq
persian_force: The garrison and people of the Parthian capital under Vologases V; the sources give no breakdown.
iranian_note: Inferred only: the royal troops would have been Iranian, the townspeople largely Aramaic-speaking.
result_basis: Severus stormed and sacked Ctesiphon after strong resistance, and Vologases fled.
sources: Cassius Dio 76(75).9; Herodian 3.9; en.wikipedia Battle of Ctesiphon (198); en.wikipedia Septimius Severus' Parthian campaigns
note: Severus failed twice before Hatra (198 and 199), which was defended by the Hatrene army without recorded Parthian troops; those sieges are left out.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Nisibis (217)
label: Nisibis (217)
persian_force: Artabanus IV's great levy: horse archers, cataphracts, and armoured lancers mounted on camels (Herodian 4.14-15).
iranian_note: Herodian names mounted archers and armoured lancers on horses and camels: the camel troops were probably Arab, the rest the Iranian noble cavalry.
result_basis: Cassius Dio, a contemporary, says Macrinus was beaten in the three days of fighting before Nisibis, and Herodian, who makes the slaughter even, does not have the Parthians leave the field; the 200 million sesterces Macrinus then paid for peace is a strategic matter.
sources: Cassius Dio 79(78).26-27; Herodian 4.15; en.wikipedia Battle of Nisibis (217); en.wikipedia Parthian war of Caracalla
note: Kept as a Parthian victory as in Battles of the Romans and Wikipedia; Caracalla had been murdered on 8 April 217. His surprise attack on Artabanus' court in 216 (Herodian) was a massacre, not a battle, and is left out.
qbasis: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Ardashir's conquest of Kerman
label: Ardashir's conquest of Kerman
persian_force: Ardashir's army from Persis, the Persian nobility and their mounted retainers, against the local Iranian levy of Kerman.
iranian_note: Both sides were Iranian provincial armies of southern Iran.
result_basis: Ardashir defeated and captured the king of Kerman and took the province (al-Tabari).
borderline: no conventional name: an unnamed battle of Ardashir's rise, known from al-Tabari; date uncertain
doubt: Borderline: no conventional name: an unnamed battle of Ardashir's rise, known from al-Tabari; date uncertain.
sources: al-Tabari, History (tr. Noldeke 1879; tr. Bosworth vol. V); en.wikipedia Ardashir I
note: Al-Tabari's account comes from Sasanian royal tradition; modern historians accept the conquest but not every detail. Ardashir made his son, also named Ardashir, king of Kerman.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Ardashir's conquest of Isfahan
label: Ardashir's conquest of Isfahan
persian_force: Ardashir's army of Persian nobles and their retainers, against the levy of the Parthian vassal of Isfahan.
iranian_note: Both sides were Iranian provincial armies.
result_basis: Ardashir defeated and killed Shadh-Shapur, ruler of Isfahan (al-Tabari).
borderline: no conventional name: an unnamed battle of Ardashir's rise, known from al-Tabari; date uncertain
doubt: Borderline: no conventional name: an unnamed battle of Ardashir's rise, known from al-Tabari; date uncertain.
sources: al-Tabari, History (tr. Noldeke 1879; tr. Bosworth vol. V); en.wikipedia Ardashir I
note: The sequence Kerman, Isfahan, Khuzestan, Mesene, Hormozdgan follows al-Tabari; the dates are approximations.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Ardashir's conquest of Khuzestan
label: Ardashir's conquest of Khuzestan
place: Khuzestan (al-Ahwaz or Susa; site unknown), Iran
persian_force: Ardashir's army of Persian nobles and their retainers, against the forces of the Parthian vassal of Khuzestan (Elymais/Susiana).
iranian_note: Ardashir's army was Persian; the Khuzestan levy was mixed Iranian and Aramaic-speaking.
result_basis: Ardashir defeated and killed the ruler of Khuzestan and annexed the province (al-Tabari).
borderline: no conventional name: an unnamed battle of Ardashir's rise, known from al-Tabari; date uncertain
doubt: Borderline: no conventional name: an unnamed battle of Ardashir's rise, known from al-Tabari; date uncertain.
sources: al-Tabari, History (tr. Noldeke 1879; tr. Bosworth vol. V); en.wikipedia Ardashir I
note: Wikipedia calls the slain ruler the governor of Susa; al-Tabari names Nirufar, king of al-Ahwaz, whom Artabanus had ordered to march against Ardashir.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Ardashir's conquest of Mesene
label: Ardashir's conquest of Mesene
place: Mesene, at the head of the Persian Gulf (near Charax Spasinou), Iraq
faction_b: Bandu, king of Mesene (Characene, a Parthian vassal)
persian_force: Ardashir's army of Persian nobles and their retainers, against the forces of the vassal kingdom of Characene.
iranian_note: Ardashir's army was Persian; the Characene forces were mainly Aramaic- and Arabic-speaking.
result_basis: Ardashir killed the king of Mesene with his own hand and annexed Characene (al-Tabari).
borderline: no conventional name: known from al-Tabari; Characene was a Parthian vassal kingdom, treated here as Parthian (civil); date uncertain
doubt: Borderline: no conventional name: known from al-Tabari; Characene was a Parthian vassal kingdom, treated here as Parthian (civil); date uncertain.
sources: al-Tabari, History (tr. Noldeke 1879; tr. Bosworth vol. V); en.wikipedia Ardashir I
note: Ardashir founded Astarabadh-Ardashir (Karkh Maysan) there. Characene had been ruled by Parthian princes since Vologases IV's conquest of 151.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Hormozdgan
label: Hormozdgan
war: Sasanian overthrow of the Parthians (rise of Ardashir I)
place: plain of Hormozdgan, probably near Ram-Hormoz (Khuzestan), Iran
commanders_b: Artabanus IV (killed), the chief secretary Dad-windad
persian_force: Ardashir's army of Persis, about 10,000 horse (later tradition), partly in mail, with his sons and the lords of Persis, Kerman and Elymais; Artabanus led the larger Parthian army of noble cavalry in lamellar armour.
iranian_note: Both armies were Iranian noble cavalry, Ardashir's from Persis and its neighbours and Artabanus' from the Parthian houses (Tabari; the Firuzabad relief).
losses_b: heavy; Artabanus IV killed, Dad-windad taken or killed
result_basis: Artabanus IV was killed and his army broke; Ardashir held the field.
sources: Tabari 1.818-819; Nihayat al-arab; Bal'ami; Firuzabad relief; Iranica, Ardasir I; en.wikipedia Battle of Hormozdgan
note: Also spelled Hormozgan or Hormizdagan. The site is disputed: Ram-Hormoz (Bal'ami) is usually preferred; Iranica puts the plain in Media and Widengren at Golpayegan.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Hatra (siege, 227)
label: Hatra (siege, 227)
war: Ardashir I's western campaigns (first Mesopotamian campaign)
commanders_a: the king of Hatra (probably Sanatruq II)
persian_force: Ardashir's new royal army, the Persian and Parthian noble cavalry that had joined him after Hormozdgan, with levied foot; the sources name no units.
iranian_note: Ardashir's early armies were the noble cavalry of Persis and of the Parthian houses that had gone over to him (Iranica, Ardasir I).
result_basis: Ardashir failed to take Hatra and marched away to Media (Cassius Dio 80.3.2).
sources: Cassius Dio 80.3.2; Iranica, Ardasir I; en.wikipedia First Mesopotamian campaign of Ardashir I; en.wikipedia Fall of Hatra
note: Iranica dates the attempt c. 226-227, the Wikipedia campaign article c. 229. Dio says Ardashir breached the wall but lost many men in an ambush. Hatra, an Arab kingdom, was then probably a Roman ally.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Nisibis (siege, 230)
label: Nisibis (siege, 230)
persian_force: Ardashir's invading army, which also sent cavalry raids into Syria and Cappadocia; no units named. It was a levy of Persian and Parthian nobles fighting mainly as horse archers and armoured cavalry.
iranian_note: Herodian describes Ardashir's army as nobles and their followers levied for each campaign, mounted archers above all.
result_basis: The Persians besieged Nisibis but failed to take it and withdrew.
sources: Zonaras 12.15; Herodian 6.2; Cassius Dio 80.4; Iranica, Ardasir I; en.wikipedia Sasanian campaign of Severus Alexander
note: Called Nisibis (siege) in Battles of the Romans.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Severus Alexander's southern column
label: Severus Alexander's southern column
place: lower Mesopotamia, on the march towards Ctesiphon (site unknown), Iraq
commanders_b: unknown (Severus Alexander led the campaign with the central column)
persian_force: Ardashir's whole field army of mounted archers and armoured cavalry; the Historia Augusta's 120,000 cataphracts, 700 elephants and 1,800 scythed chariots (Alex. 55-56) are not credible.
iranian_note: Herodian describes a levy of Persian and Parthian nobles and their followers fighting with bow and horse; no peoples are named.
strength_a: very large (Herodian); 120,000 cataphracts, 700 elephants, 1,800 scythed chariots (Historia Augusta)
result_basis: Ardashir's main army caught the southern column on its own and destroyed most of it (Herodian 6.5).
borderline: no conventional name (Battles of the Romans's descriptive name)
doubt: Borderline: no conventional name (Battles of the Romans's descriptive name).
sources: Herodian 6.5-6; Historia Augusta, Alexander 55-56; en.wikipedia Sasanian campaign of Severus Alexander
note: Herodian says the Persians won by numbers; the Historia Augusta instead claims a great Roman victory, which modern historians reject. The northern column was checked by Ardashir in Media and wrecked by the Armenian winter, without a named battle.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Nisibis (siege, 237)
label: Nisibis (siege, 237)
war: Second Mesopotamian campaign of Ardashir I
persian_force: Ardashir's and Shapur's royal army, which took Carrhae next and later Hatra; no units named.
iranian_note: No units are recorded; the early Sasanian army was a levy of Persian and Parthian noble cavalry with infantry and siege workers.
result_basis: Nisibis fell to the Persians.
sources: Syncellus p. 681; Zonaras 12.18; Iranica, Ardasir I; en.wikipedia Siege of Nisibis (237)
note: Called Nisibis (siege) in Battles of the Romans. The Cambridge Ancient History dates the capture of Nisibis and Carrhae to 237 and 238.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Carrhae (siege, 238)
label: Carrhae (siege, 238)
war: Second Mesopotamian campaign of Ardashir I
persian_force: Ardashir's and Shapur's royal army; no units named.
iranian_note: No units are recorded; the early Sasanian army was a levy of Persian and Parthian noble cavalry with infantry and siege workers.
result_basis: Carrhae fell to the Persians.
sources: Syncellus p. 681; Zonaras 12.18; Iranica, Ardasir I; en.wikipedia Second Mesopotamian campaign of Ardashir I
note: Called Carrhae (siege) in Battles of the Romans. Nothing is known of the fighting.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Dura-Europos (siege, 239)
label: Dura-Europos (siege, 239)
war: Second Mesopotamian campaign of Ardashir I
commanders_b: Ardashir I and Shapur I (as rulers; field commander unknown)
persian_force: A Sasanian raiding army; no units named.
iranian_note: No units are recorded; the early Sasanian army was a levy of Persian and Parthian noble cavalry.
result_basis: The Persian attack on Dura was beaten off and the town stayed Roman until 256.
borderline: known mainly from a graffito saying the Persians 'came down upon us'; perhaps a raid or short attack rather than a full siege
doubt: Borderline: known mainly from a graffito saying the Persians 'came down upon us'; perhaps a raid or short attack rather than a full siege.
sources: graffito SEG VII 743b; Iranica, Ardasir I; en.wikipedia Sasanian campaign of Gordian III; en.wikipedia Second Mesopotamian campaign of Ardashir I
