name: Hatra (siege, 240)
label: Hatra (siege, 240)
war: Second Mesopotamian campaign of Ardashir I
commanders_b: Sanatruq II of Hatra (probably killed); a Roman garrison (cohors IX Maurorum Gordiana)
persian_force: Ardashir's and Shapur's royal army with siege engineers; no units named.
iranian_note: No units are recorded; the army was the Sasanian royal levy of Persian and Parthian nobles.
losses_b: the city destroyed; the Roman garrison probably wiped out
result_basis: Hatra fell after a long siege and was plundered and abandoned.
sources: Cologne Mani Codex; Tabari 1.827-830 (legend of al-Nadira); Iranica, Ardasir I; en.wikipedia Fall of Hatra
note: Called Hatra (siege) in Battles of the Romans. Iranica dates the fall between April and September 240; the Cologne Mani Codex points to April 241. The siege lasted one year (or two, Tabari). The tale of the princess al-Nadira betraying the city to Shapur is legend. Hatra's own army bore most of the defence.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Resaena
label: Resaena
persian_force: Shapur I's royal army; no units named. Normally Persian and Parthian noble cavalry (armoured lancers and horse archers) with levied foot.
iranian_note: No units are recorded; Shapur's army was the Sasanian noble levy.
result_basis: The Romans routed the Persian army, which withdrew from Roman Mesopotamia (Ammianus 23.5.17).
sources: Ammianus 23.5.17; Historia Augusta, Gordian 26-27; Iranica, Shapur I; en.wikipedia Battle of Resaena
note: The Romans then recovered Carrhae, Nisibis and Singara without recorded battles.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Misiche
label: Misiche
place: Misiche (later Peroz-Shapur, al-Anbar near Fallujah), Iraq
commanders_b: Gordian III (died), Philip the Arab, Gaius Julius Priscus
persian_force: Shapur I's royal army; the inscription (ŠKZ) names no units. Normally Persian and Parthian noble cavalry with levied foot.
iranian_note: No units are recorded; the army was the Sasanian noble levy.
result_basis: Shapur's inscription records a great frontal battle in which the Roman army was beaten; Gordian died and Philip bought peace.
sources: Shapur I's inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam (ŠKZ) 3-4; Zosimus 3.32; Oracula Sibyllina 13; en.wikipedia Battle of Misiche
note: Roman sources hide the defeat and blame Philip for Gordian's death; some modern scholars think Gordian died later near Zaitha. Shapur renamed the place Peroz-Shapur ('victorious is Shapur').
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Nisibis (siege, 252)
label: Nisibis (siege, 252)
persian_force: Shapur I's royal army; no units named.
iranian_note: No units are recorded; the army was the Sasanian noble levy.
result_basis: Shapur took Nisibis.
sources: Tabari; Chronicle of Seert; Liber Caliphorum; en.wikipedia Siege of Nisibis (252)
note: Not mentioned in Shapur's own inscription; dated to his 11th year (252, Potter) by Syriac and Arabic sources. Nothing is known of the siege itself.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

label: Antioch (siege, 253)

iranian_note: No units are recorded; the army was the Sasanian noble levy.
losses_b: the city sacked and many deported

doubt: Borderline: Ammianus says the city was taken by surprise while the people sat in the theatre: little fighting is recorded.
sources: Ammianus 23.5.3; Shapur I's inscription (ŠKZ); Malalas 12; en.wikipedia Siege of Antioch (253)

name: Barbalissos
label: Barbalissos
place: Barbalissos (Qal'at Balis), on the Euphrates, Syria
persian_force: Shapur I's royal army; the inscription names no units.
iranian_note: No units are recorded; the army was the Sasanian noble levy of Persian and Parthian cavalry.
result_basis: Shapur's inscription says a Roman force of 60,000 was destroyed at Barbalissos.
sources: Shapur I's inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam (ŠKZ) 4-5; Iranica, Shapur I; en.wikipedia Battle of Barbalissos
note: Known only from Shapur's inscription; Wikipedia dates it 252.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Emesa (253)
label: Emesa (253)

iranian_note: No units are recorded; it was part of the Sasanian royal army.

sources: Malalas 12; Domninus of Antioch; Baldus; en.wikipedia Siege of Emesa (253)

qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

label: Dura-Europos (siege, 256)

iranian_note: No units are recorded; the besiegers were the Sasanian royal army.

result_basis: Dura fell to the Persians after mining and assaults, and was abandoned.
sources: excavations at Dura (du Mesnil du Buisson; S. James 2011); Iranica, Dura-Europos; en.wikipedia Siege of Dura-Europos (256)
note: Called Dura-Europos (siege) in Battles of the Romans. Dated by a coin of 256 found with the dead in the countermine; some prefer 257.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Antioch (siege, 260)
label: Antioch (siege, 260)
persian_force: Shapur I's royal army after Edessa; no units named.
iranian_note: No units are recorded; the army was the Sasanian noble levy.
losses_b: the city sacked and its people deported

qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Caesarea (siege, 260)
label: Caesarea (siege, 260)

losses_b: the garrison killed; the city sacked
result_basis: The Persians took Caesarea by a night attack along a way into the city revealed by a tortured captive (Zonaras 12.23).

qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

label: Edessa

sources: Shapur I's inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam (ŠKZ) 9-11; Zosimus 1.36; Zonaras 12.23; Lactantius, De mortibus 5; en.wikipedia Battle of Edessa

qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Odaenathus' attack on Shapur's retreat
label: Odaenathus' attack on Shapur's retreat
place: on the Euphrates during Shapur's withdrawal (site unknown), Turkey or Syria
persian_force: The rear and baggage train of Shapur I's army returning from Syria and Asia Minor with booty and captives.
iranian_note: No units are recorded; it was the Sasanian royal army.
losses_b: baggage, booty and some of the royal women
result_basis: Odaenathus fell on the Persians as they recrossed the Euphrates and took baggage, booty and some of the king's women; the Persians went on retreating.

doubt: Borderline: no conventional name; scholars of the Persian side treat it as a minor raid on the baggage train, exaggerated by Roman writers.
sources: Historia Augusta, Gallieni 10, Tyranni triginta 15; Festus 23; Zosimus 1.39; en.wikipedia Odaenathus' Sasanian campaigns

qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Pompeiopolis
label: Pompeiopolis
place: near Pompeiopolis (Soli, near Mersin), and Sebaste (Elaiussa), Turkey

persian_force: Persian raiding columns besieging the Cilician coast towns, laden with booty and captives; no units named.
iranian_note: No units are recorded; the raiders were detachments of the Sasanian royal army.

sources: Zonaras 12.23; Syncellus p. 716; Historia Augusta, Gallieni 3; en.wikipedia Odaenathus' Sasanian campaigns
note: Battles of the Romans dates this to 260. Balista used ships along the coast, but the fighting was on land.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Ctesiphon (siege, 263)
label: Ctesiphon (siege, 263)
persian_force: The garrison of the capital and the forces of Asoristan; Shapur avoided a field battle. No units named.
iranian_note: No units are recorded; the defenders were Sasanian troops with the townspeople of the Aramaic-speaking capital region.
result_basis: Odaenathus ravaged the country round Ctesiphon but could not take it and withdrew.
sources: Historia Augusta, Gallieni 10; Zosimus 1.39; Festus 23; en.wikipedia Siege of Ctesiphon (263)
note: Called Ctesiphon (siege) in Battles of the Romans. Roman sources say Odaenathus beat Shapur's lieutenants in several engagements and sent prisoners to Rome for Gallienus' triumph.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Ctesiphon (siege, 266)
label: Ctesiphon (siege, 266)
persian_force: The garrison of the capital; no units named.
iranian_note: No units are recorded; the defenders were Sasanian troops with the townspeople.

sources: Historia Augusta, Gallieni 12; en.wikipedia Odaenathus' Sasanian campaigns

label: Carus' victory over the Sarmatians

label: Satala (298)

persian_force: Shapur II's royal army of armoured cavalry, archers and infantry with a fortified camp (Julian, Oration 1; Libanius, Oration 59); no peoples named.

label: Nisibis (siege, 346)
persian_force: Shapur II's royal army; no units named.

iranian_note: No peoples are named for 360; the army was the Sasanian royal levy.
losses_b: the garrison and people taken captive to Persia
result_basis: A ram brought down a newly repaired tower and Singara fell after a few days.
sources: Ammianus 20.6; en.wikipedia Siege of Singara (360)
note: Called Singara (siege) in Battles of the Romans.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Virta (siege)
label: Virta (siege)
place: the fortress of Virta (Birtha, probably Tikrit), Iraq
persian_force: Shapur II's army returning from Bezabde; no peoples named.
iranian_note: No peoples are named; the army was the Sasanian royal levy.
result_basis: The garrison beat off the assaults and Shapur withdrew across the Tigris.
sources: Ammianus 20.7.17-18; en.wikipedia Perso-Roman wars of 337-361
note: The identification of Virta with Tikrit is probable but not certain.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Ganzak (363)
label: Ganzak (363)
place: Ganzak in Atropatene (near Takab or Leylan), Iran
commanders_a: Vasak Mamikonian, for King Arshak II
persian_force: Shapur II's army gathering in Atropatene for the invasion of Armenia; no units named.
iranian_note: No units are recorded; a Sasanian royal army.
result_basis: Vasak surprised the Persian army before it had assembled; it broke and fled, and he pursued it (Buzandaran).
doubt: Traditional: Known only from the Buzandaran (Faustus of Byzantium), whose stories of Vasak Mamikonian's victories over Shapur are exaggerated and loosely dated; the year 363 and Shapur's presence are uncertain.
sources: Buzandaran Patmut'iwnk' IV; en.wikipedia Battle of Ganzak (363); en.wikipedia Armeno-Sasanian Wars of 363-371
note: Wikipedia lists the Romans with the Armenians in the war box; the Buzandaran account is Armenian only.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Pirisabora (siege)
label: Pirisabora (siege)
persian_force: A strong Persian garrison under Mamersides with the townspeople; about 2,500 people in all (Wikipedia, after Zosimus).
iranian_note: Ammianus calls the defenders a detachment of Persians; the townspeople of Asoristan spoke Aramaic.
losses_b: the garrison surrendered; the city burned
result_basis: After two days of fighting the defenders gave up the walls and then surrendered the citadel.
sources: Ammianus 24.2.9-22; Zosimus 3.17-18; Libanius, Oration 18; en.wikipedia Siege of Pirisabora
note: Called Pirisabora (siege) in Battles of the Romans. Soon after, Surena surprised three Roman squadrons of scouts nearby, an unnamed skirmish.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Ctesiphon (363)
label: Ctesiphon (363)
place: the east bank of the Tigris before Ctesiphon (near Salman Pak), Iraq
persian_force: Ranks of mailed cataphract cavalry, close-order infantry with oblong wicker shields behind them, and elephants in the rear (Ammianus 24.6.8).
iranian_note: Ammianus describes troop types, not peoples; the army was Shapur II's royal levy left to guard the capital.
result_basis: The Romans forced the river crossing and drove the Persians into Ctesiphon with about 2,500 dead to 70 Roman.
sources: Ammianus 24.6; Zosimus 3.24-25; Libanius, Oration 18; en.wikipedia Battle of Ctesiphon (363)
note: Called Ctesiphon in Battles of the Romans. Shapur II and his main army were away; Julian then decided not to besiege the city and burned his fleet.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Maiozamalcha (siege)
label: Maiozamalcha (siege)
persian_force: A Persian garrison under Nabdates (he and 80 of his men were taken alive) with the armed townspeople; a sally hit the Roman cattle.
iranian_note: Ammianus speaks of a Persian garrison; the townspeople of Asoristan spoke Aramaic.
losses_b: the inhabitants massacred; Nabdates and 80 men captured
result_basis: The Romans broke into the city through a mine and took it.
sources: Ammianus 24.4.1-27; Zosimus 3.20-22; Libanius, Oration 18; en.wikipedia Siege of Maiozamalcha
note: Called Maiozamalcha (siege) in Battles of the Romans.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Maranga
label: Maranga
place: Maranga, on the Tigris north of Ctesiphon, Iraq
commanders_b: Merena, commander of the cavalry, two sons of Shapur II and many satraps (Ammianus 25.1.11)
persian_force: Mail-clad cataphracts in close order, archers, and elephants (Ammianus 25.1.12-14).
iranian_note: Ammianus describes troop types, not peoples; the army was Shapur II's royal levy.
strength_a: Julian's main army (about 65,000 at the start, Zosimus)
result_basis: The Persian attack was beaten off and the Persians withdrew, leaving the Romans the field.
sources: Ammianus 25.1.11-19; Zosimus 3.28; en.wikipedia Battle of Maranga
note: A three-day truce followed.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Samarra (363)
label: Samarra (363)
place: on the Tigris south of Samarra, Iraq
persian_force: Cavalry with elephants attacking the Roman rear and left flank (Ammianus 25.3); fifty nobles and satraps fell.
iranian_note: Ammianus describes troop types, not peoples; the army was Shapur II's royal levy.
strength_a: Julian's main army (about 65,000 at the start, Zosimus)
losses_b: heavy; two commanders and fifty nobles and satraps killed (Ammianus)
result_basis: The Romans drove off the Persian attack on their column with heavy loss, Merena and Nohodares among the dead, and held the field at nightfall; Julian's mortal wound is not a battlefield result (Ammianus 25.3).
sources: Ammianus 25.3; Zosimus 3.28-29; Libanius, Oration 18; en.wikipedia Battle of Samarra (363)
note: Called Samarra in Battles of the Romans, which scores it a draw because of Julian's death; here the battlefield result decides: the Romans held the field. Wikipedia's campaign article misdates it to 26 July. Jovian's retreat after it brought further unnamed fighting (Sumere, Charcha, four days at Dura) and the peace of 363, ceding Nisibis and Singara.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Artogerassa (siege)
label: Artogerassa (siege)
date: winter 367/368 - spring 368 (some date the fall to 369 or 370)
place: Artogerassa (Artagers), in Arsharunik on the Araxes; probably near Kagizman, Turkey
commanders_a: Shapur II; at first the Armenian renegades Cylaces (Glak) and Artabannes (Vahan)
commanders_b: Queen Pharandzem (Parandzem), wife of Arsaces II
persian_force: First a siege corps under the Armenian renegades Cylaces and Artabannes (who went over to the queen and let her sortie rout their camp), then Shapur II's main army (Ammianus 27.12.5-12). No composition given.
iranian_note: Shapur's royal army was a Persian cavalry army; the first besieging corps was led by Armenian nobles in Persian service and probably held Armenian troops.
losses_b: most of the garrison died of disease and hunger (Faustus)
result_basis: The fortress fell to Shapur's blockade and assaults and the queen and the royal treasure were taken; the night sortie that routed the first besiegers did not end the siege.
sources: Ammianus 27.12.5-12; Faustus of Byzantium (Buzandaran) book 4; Lenski, Failure of Empire (2002); en.wikipedia Siege of Artogerassa
note: Faustus says the siege lasted 13 months. It followed the capture of Arsaces II by treachery.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Bagavan
label: Bagavan
place: near Bagavan (Vagabanta), in Bagrevand, at the foot of Mount Npat near the source of the Arsanias (Murat), Turkey
commanders_a: Traianus and Vadomarius; Mushegh Mamikonian (Armenian sparapet), with King Pap watching from Mount Npat
commanders_b: Shapur II's generals; King Urnayr of Albania (wounded), Meruzhan Artsruni
persian_force: The army sent by Shapur II, with the contingent of his ally King Urnayr of Caucasian Albania and Armenian renegades under Meruzhan Artsruni (Faustus 5.4).
iranian_note: A Persian cavalry army with an allied Caucasian Albanian contingent of unknown size.
result_basis: After answering a Persian cavalry attack the Romans and Armenians routed the Persians, who withdrew with heavy losses (Ammianus 29.1.3).
sources: Ammianus 29.1.2-4; Faustus of Constantinople 5.4-5; Movses Khorenatsi; en.wikipedia Battle of Bagavan
note: Also called Dzirav (Movses Khorenatsi), which Manandian and Garsoian regard as an error or a conflation with Faustus' battle of Gandzak (a Faustus-only battle with Shapur present, not listed separately). A truce followed.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Moesia Prima (Theodosius v Sarmatians, 374)
label: Moesia Prima
date: 374 CE (autumn; Theodosius the Younger was dux of Moesia Prima)
war: Sarmatian and Quadi invasions under Valentinian I
place: Moesia Prima, on the Danube (Viminacium region, Serbia); exact site unknown
commanders_a: Theodosius (later Theodosius I), dux of Moesia Prima
result_basis: Ammianus says Theodosius, as dux of Moesia, beat off a Sarmatian invasion with heavy losses to the invaders.
sources: Ammianus Marcellinus 29.6.15; Zosimus 4.16; Pacatus, Panegyric of Theodosius; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodosius_I
note: The best-attested fight of Theodosius before his accession, but brief and undated in detail. The invaders may have included Quadi.

name: Tanais (Huns v Alans, c. 374)
label: Tanais
date: c. 370-375 CE (Ammianus gives no year; modern dates run c. 370 to 375)
place: Steppe between the Don (Tanais) and the Volga, the land of the Tanaite Alans (Russia)
result_basis: Ammianus says the Huns killed and plundered many Alans and joined the rest to themselves by treaty.
sources: Ammianus Marcellinus 31.3.1-3; Jordanes, Getica 123-126; Maenchen-Helfen, The World of the Huns (1973); Thompson, The Huns (1996); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alans
note: This is the opening of the Hun westward move that led to the Gothic crossing of the Danube in 376. Several fights are summarised in one sentence; entered as one event.

name: Vithimiris' last battle (c. 376)
label: Vithimiris' last battle
date: c. 375-376 CE (after the death of Ermanaric)
place: Gothic steppe north of the Black Sea, between the Dniester and the Don (exact site unknown)
commanders_b: Vithimiris (Greuthungian king, killed); Alatheus and Saphrax (regents for his son Viderichus)
result_basis: Ammianus says Vithimiris held out for a while with Alan hirelings but was beaten and killed in battle.
sources: Ammianus Marcellinus 31.3.3; Heather, The Goths (1996); Wolfram, History of the Goths (1988)
note: Whether the hired force was Alan or Hun is a textual problem in Ammianus; most editors read Alans. The Alan share is unknown.

name: Dibaltum
label: Dibaltum
place: outside Dibaltum (Deultum, Debelt), near the Black Sea coast of Thrace
sources: Ammianus 31.8.9-10; en.wikipedia Battle of Dibaltum
qbasis: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans

name: Constantinople
label: Constantinople
commanders_a: unknown; the empress Dominica paid volunteers (Socrates)
sources: Ammianus 31.16.4-7; Socrates, Ecclesiastical History 5.1; Sozomen 7.1; Zosimus 4.22; en.wikipedia Gothic War (376-382)
note: Ammianus tells of a Saracen who drank the blood of a slain Goth, which unnerved the Goths.
qbasis: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans

name: Adrianople
label: Adrianople
place: north of Adrianople (Edirne), at the Gothic wagon laager
sources: Ammianus 31.12-13; Zosimus 4.24; Orosius 7.33; Socrates, Ecclesiastical History 4.38; en.wikipedia Battle of Adrianople
note: Valens' body was never found. The Greuthungi and Alans under Alatheus and Saphrax decided the battle.
qbasis: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans

name: Poetovio
label: Poetovio
war: Civil war of Theodosius I and Magnus Maximus
sources: Panegyrici Latini 2(12).35-36; Orosius 7.35.4; Zosimus 4.46; en.wikipedia Battle of Poetovio
note: Maximus was handed over at Aquileia and executed on 28 August 388.
qbasis: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans

name: Save
label: Save
war: Civil war of Theodosius I and Magnus Maximus
place: on the Save near Siscia (Sisak), Pannonia Savia
sources: Panegyrici Latini 2(12).32-34; Orosius 7.35.3-4; Zosimus 4.46; en.wikipedia Battle of Poetovio
note: Also called the battle of Siscia.
qbasis: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans

name: Frigidus (Theodosius v Eugenius, 394)
label: Frigidus
war: War of Theodosius against Eugenius and Arbogast
place: River Frigidus (Vipava), Julian Alps, Slovenia (exact field disputed)
allies_a: Gothic, Iberian, Hunnic and Alan federates
commanders_a: Theodosius I; Timasius; Stilicho; Gainas; Saul; Bacurius the Iberian (killed); Alaric (Gothic contingent)
result_basis: Theodosius' army, aided by the bora wind on the second day, broke Arbogast's; Eugenius was captured and executed and Arbogast killed himself.
sources: Zosimus 4.57-58; Orosius 7.35; Rufinus (via Socrates 5.25, Sozomen 7.24); Claudian, III Cons. Honorii; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Frigidus
note: Zosimus names Gainas, Saul and Bacurius as the federate commanders; Saul is described as a pagan barbarian of uncertain nation, an Alan in some accounts (the Saul of Pollentia, 402). The Wikipedia article does not mention Alans, so the Alan element rests on Saul and is weak.

name: Hunnic raid of 395
label: Hunnic raid of 395
place: the Tigris-Euphrates lands near Ctesiphon, Iraq
commanders_a: the Sasanian army of Bahram IV (no general named)
persian_force: The Sasanian royal army; no composition recorded (normally the asawaran cavalry of the Iranian nobility with infantry levies).
iranian_note: Inferred: a home army raised in the Iranian lands and Mesopotamia under the Persian nobility.
losses_b: part of one column killed; 18,000 captives freed
result_basis: The Huns fled before the Persian army; one column was overtaken and partly destroyed and the Persians recovered the booty and 18,000 captives.
borderline: a pursuit during a raid; known as an engagement only from a campaign article, not a named battle
doubt: Borderline: a pursuit during a raid; known as an engagement only from a campaign article, not a named battle.
sources: Priscus; Greatrex and Greatrex, Byzantion 69 (1999) 65-75; Maenchen-Helfen, The World of the Huns 54; en.wikipedia Hunnic raid of 395
note: The Huns came through the Caucasus, raided Roman Armenia and Syria and then went down the Euphrates; the second column escaped through the Derbent pass.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Pollentia
label: Pollentia
sources: Claudian, De bello Getico; Orosius 7.37; Prudentius, Contra Symmachum 2; Jordanes, Getica 154-155; en.wikipedia Battle of Pollentia
note: Result disputed: Roman sources claim a clear victory (the Gothic camp, with Alaric's wife, was taken), Jordanes a Gothic one; Alaric withdrew in good order.
qbasis: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans

name: Chandragupta II v Rudrasimha III (c. 395-410 CE)
label: Chandragupta II v Rudrasimha III
date: c. 395-410 CE (Rudrasimha III's reign is given as c. 388-415; Chandragupta's Udayagiri inscription of 401 and Sanchi inscription of 412-413 show him holding Malwa)
war: Gupta conquest of the Western Satraps
place: Malwa and Gujarat (Ujjain region); exact site unknown
commanders_b: Rudrasimha III (last Western Satrap, killed in the later tradition)
result_basis: The Satrap coinage ends and Gupta silver coins imitating it appear in Gujarat and Malwa; Chandragupta's Sanchi and Udayagiri inscriptions record his conquest of the region.
doubt: Traditional: known only from a doubtful tradition.
sources: Udayagiri and Sanchi inscriptions of Chandragupta II (401-413); Visakhadatta, Devichandragupta (fragments quoted in the Natyadarpana and Shringaraprakasha); Upinder Singh (2008); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Satraps
note: The conquest is attested by coins and inscriptions; the story of Chandragupta killing the Saka king in disguise is from the lost play and is a doubtful tradition. Dates in the range 395-415 are all argued.

name: Florence (siege)
label: Florence
sources: Zosimus 5.26; Orosius 7.37; Paulinus, Vita Ambrosii 50; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles; en.wikipedia Stilicho
note: Stilicho's arrival ended the siege and drove Radagaisus onto the hills of Faesulae (next entry); Florence was nearly lost.
qbasis: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans

name: Rhine frontier (Franks v Vandals and Alans, 406)
label: Rhine frontier
date: summer-autumn 406 CE (before the Rhine crossing of 31 December 406)
war: Vandal, Alan and Suebic invasion of Gaul
place: Rhine frontier, probably near Mainz (Germany; exact site unknown)
result_basis: The Franks killed Godigisel and about 20,000 Vandals, until Respendial's Alans came up and routed the Franks, saving the Vandals.
sources: Renatus Profuturus Frigeridus, in Gregory of Tours, Histories 2.9; Orosius 7.38; Prosper (Chronicle, 406); MacDowall, Germanic Warrior AD 236-568 (2016); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Respendial
note: Likely several actions summarised as one. Respendial's Alans decided the day; the other Alan group under Goar had already gone over to the Romans.

name: Faesulae
label: Faesulae
place: The hills of Faesulae (Fiesole), above Florence
sources: Zosimus 5.26; Orosius 7.37; Augustine, De civitate Dei 5.23; Olympiodorus fr. 9; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles
note: Radagaisus' host (Goths with others) was surrounded and starved rather than beaten in a pitched battle; 12,000 of his best men were taken into Roman service. Radagaisus was executed on 23 August 406.
qbasis: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans

name: Wallia's war on the Alans and Silings (Spain, 416-418)
label: Wallia's war on the Alans and Silings
date: 416-418 CE (Hydatius puts the final defeat of the Alans in 418; some scholars 426)
war: Visigothic campaigns in Spain for Honorius
place: Baetica and Lusitania (Andalusia and Portugal); exact sites unknown
commanders_b: Addac or Attaces (Alan king, killed); Fredbal (Siling king, captured)
result_basis: Hydatius says Wallia annihilated the Silingi, and the Alans were so cut up that Addac fell and the survivors, leaderless, joined the Asding king Gunderic.
sources: Hydatius, Chronicle (years 416-418); Orosius 7.43; Kulikowski, Late Roman Spain and Its Cities (2004); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alans
note: The campaign spans several years and several fights that the sources do not separate. After it the Alans fought as part of the Vandal kingdom.

name: Nervasos Mountains
label: Nervasos Mountains
place: The Nervasian mountains (Nerbasii montes), Gallaecia; site unknown
sources: Hydatius 71, 74; en.wikipedia Battle of the Nervasos Mountains
note: The Vandals lifted their siege of the Suebi when Asterius approached, but on their retreat they killed some of Maurocellus's men at Bracara (Braga); the usurper Maximus, backed by barbarians, was put down at the same time.
qbasis: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans

name: Arzanene
label: Arzanene
place: Arzanene, east of the Tigris, Turkey
persian_force: Narses' frontier army; no composition recorded (the Sasanian field army of the period was built around the asawaran heavy cavalry and horse archers of the Iranian nobility, with infantry levies).
iranian_note: Inferred from the normal make-up of Sasanian field armies (cavalry of the Persian and Parthian nobility and their retainers).
result_basis: Ardabur defeated Narses' army, which retreated (Socrates 7.18).
sources: Socrates, Historia Ecclesiastica 7.18; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Roman-Sasanian War of 421-422
note: Narses then tried to strike into Roman Mesopotamia but was intercepted by Ardabur.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Nisibis (siege, 421)
label: Nisibis (siege, 421)
commanders_a: the garrison of Nisibis; Bahram V (relief army); al-Mundhir I (Lakhmid)
persian_force: The Persian garrison of Nisibis and Bahram V's relief army, with the Lakhmid Arabs of al-Mundhir I (Socrates 7.18).
iranian_note: A Persian royal army and garrison with Lakhmid Arab allies of unknown number.
result_basis: Ardabur raised the siege and withdrew when Bahram V's relief army approached; the Persians kept Nisibis.
sources: Socrates, Historia Ecclesiastica 7.18; Malalas; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Roman-Sasanian War of 421-422
note: Socrates also tells how al-Mundhir's Arabs panicked and drowned in the Euphrates and how the Persian 'Immortals' were ambushed; neither is a separately named battle. Battles of the Romans lists the Lakhmids as 'Arabs'.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Theodosiopolis (siege, 421)
label: Theodosiopolis (siege, 421)
place: Theodosiopolis, probably in Armenia (Erzurum), Turkey; possibly Resaina in Osrhoene
commanders_b: Bahram V's army (a vassal king was killed by a stone-thrower)
persian_force: 'Many thousands' of soldiers with siege engines including a helepolis (Theodoret); composition not given.
iranian_note: Inferred: a Sasanian royal army under vassal kings; no units are named.
result_basis: The Persians lifted the siege after about 30 days, when a stone-thrower killed one of their vassal kings (Theodoret 5.37).
sources: Theodoret, Historia Ecclesiastica 5.37.6-10; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Siege of Theodosiopolis
note: The town is usually taken to be Theodosiopolis in Armenia (Erzurum); some identify it with Theodosiopolis-Resaina (Ras al-Ayn) in Osrhoene. Theodoret's account is hagiographic.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Tarraco
label: Tarraco
sources: Hydatius 77; Prosper s.a. 422; Salvian 7.11; en.wikipedia Battle of Tarraco
note: The battle was fought in Baetica; the name Tarraco comes from a modern addition to an online translation of Hydatius (Castinus may have retreated to Tarraco). The Vandals kept Baetica.
qbasis: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans

name: Ravenna (425)
label: Ravenna
war: War of the Eastern Empire against the usurper Joannes
commanders_a: Aspar (Alan by descent); Ardabur (Aspar's father, an Alan); Candidianus
commanders_b: Joannes; Castinus; Aetius (arrived after the fall)
result_basis: Aspar's cavalry crossed the marsh by an unguarded path and took Ravenna; Joannes was captured and killed.
sources: Socrates, Church History 7.23; Philostorgius 12.13; Prosper (425); Martindale, PLRE 2, 'Fl. Ardabur Aspar'
note: Counted by the leader rule: Aspar is described as of Alanic (or Alanic-Gothic) descent. His troops were Eastern Roman, so the contingent is not Alan.

name: Merv (427)
label: Merv (427)
commanders_b: the Kidarite king ('khaqan of the Turks' in Tabari), killed
persian_force: A picked force of the Persian nobility's cavalry, raised partly in Armenia and Azerbaijan while Mihr Narseh stayed as regent (Tabari).
iranian_note: A Persian noble cavalry force with troops recruited in Armenia (Tabari).
result_basis: In the tradition Bahram surprised and routed the invaders near Merv, killing their king and capturing his wife.
doubt: Traditional: Known only from Tabari, Dinawari, Thaalibi and the Shahnameh, which draw on the Sasanian royal tradition and the romance of Bahram Gur; modern historians accept a Persian success against the Kidarites about 427 but not the details.
sources: Tabari (tr. Bosworth, vol. 5, 95-96); Daryaee (2000); en.wikipedia Bahram V; en.wikipedia Sasanian-Kidarite wars
note: A general then pursued the enemy into Transoxiana and defeated them again (Tabari). The enemy is called Turks or Hephthalites in the Arabic sources; modern historians identify them as Kidarites.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Mérida (Vandals and Alans v Suebi, 428)
label: Mérida
date: 428 CE (Wikipedia; Hydatius' sequence puts it in 428-429, shortly before the Vandal crossing to Africa)
war: Vandal and Suebic wars in Gallaecia and Lusitania
commanders_a: Gaiseric (king of the Vandals and Alans)
commanders_b: Heremigarius (Suevic leader, drowned in the Guadiana)
result_basis: Hydatius says Gaiseric turned back, caught the Suebi near Mérida and drove them into the Guadiana, where Heremigarius drowned.
sources: Hydatius, Chronicle (years 428-429); Thompson, Romans and Barbarians (1982); Kulikowski (2004)
note: Hydatius and the standard accounts name the Vandals only; no source says Alans fought here. After 418 the Alans were part of the Vandal kingdom (Gaiseric is 'king of the Vandals and Alans'), so an Alan contingent is likely but not recorded.

name: Hippo Regius (siege)
label: Hippo Regius
sources: Possidius, Vita Augustini 28-29; Procopius, Wars 3.3.30-36; en.wikipedia Siege of Hippo Regius
note: Augustine died in the besieged city on 28 August 430. The Vandals raised the siege after about 14 months (a technical Roman success), but occupied the abandoned city after the battle of 431/432.
qbasis: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans

name: Africa (Boniface and Aspar's defeat by the Vandals, 431)
label: Africa
date: 431 (Procopius places it after the long siege of Hippo; some date it 432)
war: Vandal conquest of Africa (Roman relief expedition from the East)
place: near Hippo Regius (Annaba), Algeria; site not recorded
side_b: Western Roman army and the Eastern relief army of Aspar
persian_state: Western Roman army and the Eastern relief army of Aspar
result_basis: The combined Roman army was defeated, Boniface sailed for Italy and Hippo was abandoned (Procopius, Vand. 3.3.35-36; Prosper Tiro).
sources: Procopius, Wars 3.3.35-36; Prosper Tiro, Chronicle s.a. 431; Hydatius; Wikipedia 'Aspar'
note: Aspar, magister militum of the Eastern army, was of Alan descent (his father Ardabur and his own name are Alan); the Eastern army that he brought is not described as Alan, so the qualification is the commander. Procopius gives no place or numbers and the Vandals' own Alan element is not counted here. Weak: a defeat known only from short notices.

name: Avarayr
label: Avarayr
place: the plain of Avarayr, in Artaz (near Chors, Chaypareh County), Iran
persian_force: Mushkan's army of asawaran cavalry with the royal 'Immortals' and war elephants, joined by the Armenian loyalists of Vasak Siwni (Elishe; his 300,000 is rhetorical).
iranian_note: Elishe describes a Persian royal army with elephants and the Immortals, three times the Armenian army, plus Vasak's Armenian loyalists.
losses_b: 1,036 killed (Elishe), including Vardan and eight generals
result_basis: The Persians broke the Armenian army and held the field, killing Vardan and eight other generals; the later religious concessions are a strategic matter.
sources: Elishe, History of Vardan and the Armenian War; Lazar Parpetsi; Hewsen, 'Avarayr', Encyclopaedia Iranica; en.wikipedia Battle of Avarayr
note: A revolt of a Persian-ruled province (Persarmenia), hence opponent group 'Rebels'. Yazdegerd II afterwards dismissed Vasak and eased religious pressure.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Catalaunian Plains
label: Catalaunian Plains
place: The Catalaunian Plains (Campus Mauriacus), Champagne; site unknown
commanders_a: Flavius Aetius; Theodoric I (killed); Thorismund; Sangiban
sources: Jordanes, Getica 190-218; Hydatius 150; Prosper s.a. 451; en.wikipedia Battle of the Catalaunian Plains
note: Wikipedia's infobox calls it inconclusive; Attila was driven back to his laager and then withdrew from Gaul. Date 20 June after Bury (others: early July or 27 September). Proposed sites: Montgueux near Troyes, Méry-sur-Seine, La Cheppe. Attila's allies included Ostrogoths and Gepids.
qbasis: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans

name: Orléans (siege)
label: Orléans
commanders_a: Bishop Anianus (in the city); Flavius Aetius and Theodoric I (relief)
sources: Jordanes, Getica 194-195; Gregory of Tours 2.7; Vita Aniani; en.wikipedia Battle of the Catalaunian Plains
note: Attila broke off his final assault when the relief army approached; some historians see the defence of Orléans as the real turning point of 451.
qbasis: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans

name: Skandagupta's war with the Hunas (c. 455-457)
label: Skandagupta's war with the Hunas
date: c. 455-457 CE (Bhitari pillar, undated; Junagadh inscription of 457-458 mentions the mlecchas)
place: North-western frontier of the Gupta empire (battlefield not named; Punjab and Indus approaches), India/Pakistan
result_basis: The Bhitari pillar claims Skandagupta's arms made the earth tremble in the clash and the Gupta heartland stayed intact.
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Bhitari pillar inscription of Skandagupta; Junagadh rock inscription of Skandagupta (year 138); Bakker, H., The Alkhan (2020); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skandagupta
note: The only evidence is a vague royal praise-inscription and the identification of the mlecchas and Hunas is inferred; the site, scale and even the date within 455-467 are unknown. The Huna enemy is called Kidarite or Alchon depending on the scholar; both are of disputed Iranian identity.
qbasis: The Bhitari pillar says Skandagupta met the Hunas in battle; the Hunas of c. 456 are identified as Kidarites or Alchon Huns, both of uncertain Iranian identity.

name: Ossetians (Vakhtang I's first campaign, c. 455-459)
label: Ossetians
date: c. 455-459 (the Life of Vakhtang puts it in his sixteenth year; a reconstruction)
war: Wars of Vakhtang I Gorgasali (Ossetian raid on Iberia)
place: Dvaleti and the Darial approaches, north Georgia / North Ossetia; approximate
commanders_a: Vakhtang I Gorgasali (then a youth, with his father Mirdat)
result_basis: Vakhtang won the single combat with the enemy champion and freed his sister Mirandukht; the raiders were beaten (Life of Vakhtang Gorgasali).
doubt: Traditional: known only from a doubtful tradition. Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Juansher, Life of Vakhtang Gorgasali (Georgian Chronicles); Wikipedia 'Vakhtang I of Iberia' (fetched 1 Nov 2026); Suny, The Making of the Georgian Nation
note: Vakhtang belonged to the Chosroid house, which the Georgian Chronicles trace to the Persian Mihranids (Mirian III), and his mother Sagdukht is called Persian; 'Ossetians' (Ovsi) is the Georgian name for the Alans, though Wikipedia says they may have been Huns. Known only from the Life of Vakhtang; the date is reconstructed.

name: Arelate
label: Arelate
sources: Sidonius, Carmen 5; Hydatius 197; Gregory of Tours 2.11; en.wikipedia Battle of Arelate; en.wikipedia Majorian
note: Also called the Battle of Arles (458). Theodoric II had been besieging Aegidius in Arles; after the defeat the Visigoths returned to federate status and gave up Septimania.
qbasis: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans

name: Cartagena
label: Cartagena
place: Portus Ilicitanus (Santa Pola), bay of Alicante
sources: Hydatius 200; Marius of Avenches s.a. 460; en.wikipedia Battle of Cartagena (461)
note: Despite the name it was fought near Elche (Ilici), not at Cartagena; 13 May 460 is sometimes given. Majorian made peace and was deposed and killed in 461.
qbasis: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans

name: Bergamo
label: Bergamo
sources: Fasti Vindobonenses priores s.a. 464; Marcellinus Comes s.a. 464; Jordanes, Getica 236; en.wikipedia Battle of Bergamo
note: The day is flagged as uncertain on Wikipedia.
qbasis: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans

name: Peroz I's defeat of the Kidarites (c. 466)
label: Peroz I's defeat of the Kidarites
date: c. 466 CE (war began c. 464; victory announced at Constantinople in 467)
commanders_a: Peroz I; Mehama (Hephthalite or Alchon lord of Kadag)
result_basis: Peroz briefly took Tokharistan, minted gold at Balkh on Kidarite models and sent victory embassies in 467-468.
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Priscus fr. 41 (Blockley); Sims-Williams, N., Bactrian Documents from Northern Afghanistan; Rezakhani, K., ReOrienting the Sasanians (2017); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peroz_I; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kidarites
note: No battle narrative survives: the war is known from Priscus (Peroz's trick marriage offer and the 300 Persian officers maimed at Balaam), the victory embassy and Peroz's Balkh coinage. The Kidarites are Huns of disputed Iranian identity.
qbasis: Peroz I, a Persian king, led the Sasanian army with Hunnic allies against the Kidarite king Kunkhas (Priscus fr. 41; Bactrian documents).

name: Bolia (Ostrogoths v Suebi and allies, 468)
label: Bolia
war: Ostrogothic wars on the middle Danube
place: River Bolia, south of the Danube in Pannonia (Hungary; proposals include Pilismarot and Csem)
commanders_a: Theodemir (Valamir had already fallen); the young Theodoric
commanders_b: Hunimund (king of the Suebi); Beuca (named with the coalition, apparently the Sarmatian king); Hunulf (Sciri)
result_basis: Jordanes says the Goths beat the coalition of Suebi, Sarmatians, Gepids, Rugi and Sciri, though the Wikipedia article notes that Hyun Jin Kim argues the Goths lost and left for the south.
sources: Jordanes, Getica 53 (277-279); Wolfram, History of the Goths (1990); Gracanin and Skrgulja (2014); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Bolia
note: Jordanes lists Sarmatae among the coalition. By this date 'Sarmatians' of the Pannonian plain were remnants of the Iazyges and Limigantes mixed with Goths and Huns, so their Iranian character is doubtful; the Sarmatian leader's name is not certain.

name: Peroz I's first defeat by Akhshunwar (c. 474)
label: Peroz I's first defeat by Akhshunwar
date: c. 469-474 CE (Wikipedia gives c. 474; sources are vague)
place: Hephthalite frontier near Gurgan (Gorgan), north-eastern Iran/Turkmenistan
result_basis: Peroz was captured and had to be ransomed (Procopius says by the emperor Zeno) and to swear to keep the peace.
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.3-4; al-Tabari; Pseudo-Joshua the Stylite; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peroz_I
note: The Procopius account (the prostration to the rising sun, the concealed ditch) is anecdotal and the ditch trick is also told of the 484 battle, so which war it belongs to is disputed; some scholars count only two Hephthalite wars before 484. Not to be confused with the 484 battle (Herat), already in the dataset.
qbasis: Peroz I (a Persian king) led the Sasanian army against the Hephthalite king Akhshunwar and was ambushed and captured (Procopius, Wars 1.3-4; Tabari).

name: Akori
label: Akori
place: Akori (Arguri), on the northern slope of Mount Ararat, Turkey
persian_force: The marzban's army of about 7,000 horsemen (Lazar Parpetsi), Persian cavalry with some Armenian loyalists.
iranian_note: Lazar calls the marzban's force Persian cavalry; Armenian loyalists probably served with it.
result_basis: Vahan's rebels routed the marzban's army and killed Adhur Gushnasp (Lazar Parpetsi).
sources: Lazar Parpetsi, History of the Armenians; en.wikipedia Vahan Mamikonian
note: A revolt of a Persian-ruled province, hence opponent group 'Rebels'.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Akesga
label: Akesga
commanders_b: Vahan Mamikonian; Vasak Mamikonian and Sahak II Bagratuni (both killed)
persian_force: Shapur Mihran's army sent against the Iberian and Armenian rising; no composition recorded.
iranian_note: A Persian field army led by Shapur of the Parthian house of Mihran.
losses_b: unknown; Vasak Mamikonian and Sahak Bagratuni killed
result_basis: The Armenians, left without the Iberian help they expected from Vakhtang, were routed and two of their leaders killed.
sources: Lazar Parpetsi, History of the Armenians; en.wikipedia Vahan Mamikonian
note: Wikipedia does not name the Persian commander at Akesga; Shapur Mihran led the Persian army in the area (Lazar Parpetsi).
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Nersehapat
label: Nersehapat
commanders_b: commander of the Persian reinforcements (not named in Wikipedia)
persian_force: Persian reinforcements sent by Peroz I; no numbers or units given.
iranian_note: Inferred: a Persian field force sent from Iran against the rebels.
result_basis: Vahan defeated the Persian reinforcements and held the field (Lazar Parpetsi).
sources: Lazar Parpetsi, History of the Armenians; en.wikipedia Vahan Mamikonian
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Herat (484)
label: Herat (484)
place: near Balkh or Herat (the site is uncertain), Afghanistan
persian_force: Peroz's 'enormous' royal army of the asawaran and the great houses (a Mihran among the commanders); no numbers or units given.
iranian_note: Inferred: the royal army of the Persian and Parthian nobility; no foreign contingents are recorded.
losses_b: the whole army; Peroz and four of his sons and brothers killed, his daughter and treasure captured
result_basis: The Persian army was ambushed and destroyed (in Procopius' account in a hidden trench) and Peroz was killed.
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.4; Joshua the Stylite; Tabari; Schindel, 'Kawad I', Encyclopaedia Iranica; en.wikipedia Hephthalite-Sasanian War of 484
note: Wikipedia's article is titled 'Hephthalite-Sasanian War of 484' and places Peroz's last camp near Balkh after an advance from Herat; the battle is often called after Herat. Khonsarinejad and Khorashadi (2021) doubt the trench story. Peroz had earlier been defeated and captured by the Hephthalites (c. 474-481) in battles that have no name.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Sukhra's Hephthalite campaign
label: Sukhra's Hephthalite campaign
commanders_a: Sukhra (Zarmihr) of the house of Karen
persian_force: The remnant of the Sasanian army rallied by Sukhra ('the majority of the Sasanian army', Tabari).
iranian_note: Inferred: Sukhra was of the Parthian house of Karen and led the Persian home army.
result_basis: In Tabari's account Sukhra heavily defeated the Hephthalites and made Khushnavaz return Peroz's treasure, his daughter and the chief priest.
borderline: a campaign rather than a named battle
doubt: Traditional: Known only from Tabari and the later Perso-Arabic tradition, which glorifies the Karen family; the Roman and Syriac sources know only that Persia then paid tribute to the Hephthalites, and modern historians treat the victory as doubtful or as a negotiated return of the captives. Borderline: a campaign rather than a named battle.
sources: Tabari; Pourshariati, Decline and Fall of the Sasanian Empire (2008); Schindel, 'Kawad I', Encyclopaedia Iranica; Rezakhani, ReOrienting the Sasanians (2017); en.wikipedia Sukhra's Hephthalite campaign
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Iberia (Vakhtang I's last battle against the Iranians, c. 502 or 522)
label: Iberia
date: c. 502 (Javakhishvili) or c. 522-527 (Sanadze); undated in the Life
war: Persian invasion of Iberia under Kavadh I (death of Vakhtang I)
place: Kartli near Mtskheta, Georgia; the Life names Mtskheta as his burial place
commanders_b: Vakhtang I Gorgasali (died of his wounds)
result_basis: Vakhtang died fighting the invaders and an Iranian viceroy governed Tiflis by 518 (Wikipedia; Life of Vakhtang).
doubt: Traditional: known only from a doubtful tradition.
sources: Juansher, Life of Vakhtang Gorgasali; Wikipedia 'Vakhtang I of Iberia' (fetched 1 Nov 2026); Suny, The Making of the Georgian Nation
note: Vakhtang is said to have refused Kavadh's summons to join the war against Rome; the Iranian army that invaded Iberia fought him (the Life says he died at the hands of a renegade slave). Sasanian side Persian; Vakhtang's Chosroid house is of Persian Mihranid descent by the Georgian tradition (uncertain). Known only from the Life; no place or date is firm.

name: Amida (siege, 502)
label: Amida (siege, 502)
commanders_b: Cyrus (governor of Mesopotamia), Leontius, Paul bar Zainab
persian_force: Kavad I's royal army with Armenian and Arab (Lakhmid) allies (Joshua the Stylite, Zacharias); Hunnic troops are mentioned in some accounts.
iranian_note: A Persian royal army; the Armenian and Arab allies are named but not counted.
strength_b: no regular troops; the citizens defended the walls
losses_b: 80,000 dead including civilians (Wikipedia infobox, from the Syriac sources)
result_basis: Amida fell to Kavad's assault in January 503 after a three-month siege.
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.7; Joshua the Stylite; Zacharias of Mytilene book 7; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Siege of Amida (502-503)
note: Kavad had earlier taken Theodosiopolis (by betrayal) and Martyropolis (by surrender) in 502; those captures without real fighting are not listed.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Amida (siege, 503)
label: Amida (siege, 503)
persian_force: A garrison of 3,000 Persians under Glones (Joshua the Stylite); Patricius also defeated a Persian relief force.
iranian_note: Joshua the Stylite calls the garrison Persians.
losses_b: Glones and many of the garrison killed
result_basis: After a blockade of more than a year the starving Persian garrison gave Amida back to the Romans.
sources: Joshua the Stylite; Procopius, Wars 1.9; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Anastasian War
note: The garrison surrendered the city in early 505 in return for payment under the truce (Procopius gives 1,000 lb of gold); scored as a besieger's success as in Battles of the Romans.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Constantia (siege, 503)
label: Constantia (siege, 503)
date: 503 (before the attack on Edessa in September)
commanders_a: the garrison and citizens of Constantia
persian_force: Kavad's main army; no composition recorded.
iranian_note: Inferred from the normal make-up of the Sasanian royal army.
result_basis: Kavad failed to take Constantia and moved on to Edessa.
borderline: the fighting was slight; the townspeople even supplied Kavad's army
doubt: Borderline: the fighting was slight; the townspeople even supplied Kavad's army.
sources: Joshua the Stylite; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Anastasian War
note: Constantia and Constantina are the same city (Viransehir).
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Nisibis (503)
label: Nisibis (503)
persian_force: Kavad's main army at Nisibis; no composition recorded (asawaran cavalry with levies).
iranian_note: Inferred from the normal make-up of the Sasanian royal army.
strength_b: about 12,000 (Areobindus' division of the 52,000-man Roman army)
result_basis: After an early Roman success Kavad's counter-attack drove Areobindus' army back westward.
sources: Joshua the Stylite; Procopius, Wars 1.8; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Anastasian War
note: Asouades was probably a Kindite chief (Battles of the Romans lists 'Arabs').
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Tell Beshme
label: Tell Beshme
place: between Apadna (Opadna) and Tell Beshme, between Amida and Nisibis, Turkey
persian_force: Kavad's main army (no composition recorded), which had just plundered Areobindus' fort at Apadna.
iranian_note: Inferred from the normal make-up of the Sasanian royal army.
strength_b: about 40,000 (the divisions of Hypatius and Patricius)
result_basis: Hypatius and Patricius were routed and fled to Samosata, losing much of their cavalry in the retreat.
sources: Joshua the Stylite; Procopius, Wars 1.8; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Anastasian War
note: Also called the battle of Apadna (Opadna).
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Edessa (siege, 503)
label: Edessa (siege, 503)
persian_force: Kavad's army with Lakhmid Arab allies, who overran much of Osrhoene (Joshua the Stylite).
iranian_note: A Persian royal army with Lakhmid Arab auxiliaries of unknown number.
result_basis: The Persian assaults on Edessa failed and Kavad withdrew to Persia.
sources: Joshua the Stylite; Procopius, Wars 1.8; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Anastasian War
note: A Hunnic raid into Persian Armenia helped persuade Kavad to withdraw.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Second Battle of Eran (c. 510)
label: Second Battle of Eran
date: c. 510 CE or slightly earlier (the Eran pillar of Goparaja is dated Gupta year 191 = 510 CE and records the battle as past; the 29 June date in some summaries is the date of the pillar, not of the fight)
place: Eran (ancient Airikina), Sagar district, Madhya Pradesh, India
result_basis: The Eran inscription records a great battle in which Goparaja died but does not say who won; Toramana's boar inscription shows him ruling Eran soon after.
doubt: The sources consulted do not give the result, so the battle is listed but not scored. Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Eran inscription of Goparaja (Gupta year 191); Eran boar inscription of Toramana; Bakker, H., The Alkhan (2020); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Battle_of_Eran
note: Wikipedia's infobox says Gupta victory, but Bakker notes the inscription is silent on the outcome and Goyal argues the battle may precede Toramana's conquest of eastern Malwa. The opponent is not named in the text; the identification with Toramana's Huns is inferred.
qbasis: Toramana, king of the Alchon Huns (of disputed Iranian identity), is the probable enemy of the Gupta army in the Eran inscription of Goparaja; the inscription does not name him.

name: Rishtal (Aulikara-Huna war, c. 515)
label: Rishtal
war: Gupta-Huna wars (Aulikara-Hunnic war, end of the First Hunnic War)
place: Rishtal near Sitamau/Mandsaur (Dasapura), Madhya Pradesh, India (site approximate)
result_basis: The Rishtal inscription claims Prakashadharma ambushed the Huns, routed them and sacked Toramana's camp.
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Rishtal inscription of Prakashadharma (discovered 1983; edited by Salomon); Bakker, H., The Alkhan (2020); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aulikara%E2%88%92Hunnic_War
note: A single victory inscription gives the only account; the fight at Rishtal is as the inscription says, the identification of the Huna with Toramana is by the editors. Toramana's death at Varanasi is a later and weak claim.
qbasis: Toramana, Alchon Hun king (disputed Iranian identity), is named as the defeated Huna overlord in the Rishtal inscription of Prakashadharma.

name: Persarmenia
label: Persarmenia
persian_force: Persian forces in Persarmenia under the Armenian brothers Narses and Aratius (Kamsarakan), then in Persian service; no numbers given.
iranian_note: The commanders were Armenian nobles; the force was probably Persarmenian levies with Persian garrison troops.
result_basis: Narses and Aratius defeated the second Roman raid into Persarmenia (Procopius 1.12.20-22).
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.12.20-22; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Iberian War
note: The first Roman raid had plundered Persarmenia unopposed. Narses and Aratius later went over to Rome (530).
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Thebetha (siege)
label: Thebetha (siege)
place: Nisibis, then the Persian fortress of Thebetha, fifteen parasangs from Dara, Turkey
commanders_a: the garrisons of Nisibis and Thebetha
persian_force: Persian frontier garrisons; no composition recorded.
iranian_note: Inferred: Persian garrison troops of the Nisibis frontier.
result_basis: Libelarius' attacks on Nisibis and Thebetha achieved nothing and he withdrew in the summer heat; the Persian strongholds held.
borderline: little fighting is described
doubt: Borderline: little fighting is described.
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.12.23-24; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Iberian War
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Mindouos
label: Mindouos
place: Mindouos (Melebasa, modern Ogunduk), north of Nisibis, Turkey
commanders_a: Persian army (commander not named by Procopius)
persian_force: A Persian field army; no composition recorded (asawaran cavalry with levies).
iranian_note: Inferred from the normal make-up of Sasanian field armies.
result_basis: The Persians defeated the Roman army building a fort at Mindouos and the survivors fled to Dara (Procopius 1.13.1-8).
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.13.1-8; Zacharias of Mytilene book 9; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Battle of Thannuris
note: Possibly the same engagement as Thannuris (Hughes); kept separate as in Wikipedia and Battles of the Romans.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Sondani (Yashodharman v Mihirakula, c. 528)
label: Sondani
place: Sondani (Sondni), near Mandsaur (Dasapura), Madhya Pradesh, India
result_basis: The Mandasor pillar says Yashodharman made Mihirakula bow his head and the Huns lost their Indian possessions soon after.
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Mandasor (Sondani) pillar inscriptions of Yashodharman and Vishnuvardhana; Xuanzang, Records of the Western Regions (Baladitya); Bakker, H., The Alkhan (2020); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Sondani
note: No battle narrative: the 'battle' is inferred from a victory pillar that says Mihirakula submitted. The alliance with the Guptas and Mihirakula's capture are later tradition.
qbasis: Mihirakula, the Alchon Hun king (disputed Iranian identity), is the defeated opponent in the Mandasor pillar inscription of Yashodharman.

name: Thannuris
label: Thannuris
place: Thannuris (Tell Tuneinir), on the Khabur, south of Dara, Syria
commanders_b: Belisarius, Bouzes, Coutzes (captured or killed), Proclianus (killed), Sebastian, Basil; Jabala (Ghassanid, killed)
persian_force: A Persian army of about 30,000 (Zacharias), its cavalry decisive, under Xerxes and Peroz of the house of Mihran.
iranian_note: A Sasanian cavalry army under Persian and Parthian (Mihran) commanders; no foreign contingents recorded.
strength_b: presumably larger (Syvanne: about 30,000 cavalry and 10,000 infantry)
losses_b: heavy: most of the infantry killed or captured
result_basis: A feigned retreat drew the Roman cavalry into hidden ditches; the Roman army was routed, the unfinished fort destroyed and Belisarius fled to Dara.
sources: Zacharias of Mytilene book 9; Procopius, Wars 1.13.1-8; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Battle of Thannuris
note: Wikipedia and Battles of the Romans treat Thannuris and Mindouos as separate battles; Hughes argues Procopius compressed them into one.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Baladitya's capture of Mihirakula (Xuanzang's tradition, c. 530)
label: Baladitya's capture of Mihirakula
date: c. 530 CE (undated; Xuanzang's story written c. 645)
war: Gupta-Huna wars (Second Hunnic War, traditional account)
place: Magadha (a narrow pass or island refuge, site not named), Bihar, India
result_basis: Xuanzang says Baladitya captured Mihirakula and spared his life at his mother's request.
doubt: Traditional: known only from a doubtful tradition. Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Xuanzang, Datang Xiyu ji; Upinder Singh, Political Violence in Ancient India (2017); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mihirakula
note: Known only from a Buddhist pilgrim's report a century later; modern writers call it fanciful and may be a doublet of the Sondani victory. Included as a traditional entry.
qbasis: Mihirakula, Alchon Hun king (disputed Iranian identity), is the defeated enemy in Xuanzang's story.

name: Dara (530)
label: Dara (530)
place: before the walls of Dara (Anastasiopolis; Oguz), Turkey
commanders_a: Belisarius, Hermogenes; Bouzes, Pharas, John son of Nicetas, Sunicas and Aigan
persian_force: Perozes' 40,000 cavalry and infantry, reinforced by 10,000 from the Nisibis garrison: asawaran cavalry on the wings, the 'Immortals' in reserve and poorly armed levy infantry in the centre (Procopius 1.13-14).
iranian_note: Procopius names the Immortals and the levies but no foreign contingents; the commander was of the Parthian Mihran house.
losses_b: about 8,000 (3,000 cavalry, then 5,000 in the rout)
result_basis: The Persian army broke and fled on the third day with about 8,000 dead, leaving the field to the Romans.
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.13-14; Zacharias of Mytilene book 9; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Battle of Dara
note: The Roman army included Hunnic and Herul units (listed as allies in Battles of the Romans); they were in Roman service and are not given as allies here.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Satala (530)
label: Satala (530)
persian_force: About 30,000: Persarmenian levies, Sunitae from the Caucasus and 3,000 Sabir Huns, under Mihr-Mihroe (Procopius 1.15.1-2).

name: Martyropolis (siege, 531)
label: Martyropolis (siege, 531)
persian_force: A large Persian army under three generals; no composition recorded. Sabir Huns hired by Persia raided Roman territory at the same time (Procopius 1.21).
iranian_note: Inferred from the normal make-up of Sasanian field armies.
result_basis: The Persians abandoned the siege after Kavad's death and agreed an armistice; the town held.
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.21; Malalas; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Siege of Martyropolis (531)
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Callinicum (531)
label: Callinicum (531)
place: on the Euphrates opposite Callinicum (Raqqa), Syria
commanders_b: Belisarius, Hermogenes, Sunicas, Simmas; al-Harith ibn Jabalah (Ghassanid)
persian_force: Azarethes' 15,000 asawaran cavalry with about 5,000 Lakhmid Arab horse under al-Mundhir III (Procopius 1.17-18).

losses_b: heavy; Ascan, Longinus and Stephanacius killed
result_basis: The Persians broke the Roman right and held the field; the Roman infantry escaped across the Euphrates at nightfall.
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.17-18; Malalas; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Battle of Callinicum
note: A costly victory: Azarethes was disgraced by Kavad for his losses.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

label: Beroea (siege, 540)

iranian_note: Inferred from the normal make-up of the Sasanian royal army.
losses_b: town burned; garrison went over to the Persians
result_basis: The Persians took and burned the town, and the garrison of the acropolis, out of water, went over to Khosrow (Procopius 2.7).
borderline: a ransom dispute with brief fighting at the acropolis; not a named battle in Wikipedia

label: Dara (siege, 540)

note: Battles of the Romans scores it a Roman defensive success; here a siege bought off while the place was still invested counts as a draw.

label: Antioch (540)

iranian_note: Inferred from the normal make-up of the Sasanian royal army.

note: Battles of the Romans types it as a land battle; it was an assault on the city, so siege is set true here.
qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Nisibis (541)
label: Nisibis (541)

strength_a: unknown (the Army of the East with Gothic and Ghassanid troops)
result_basis: Nabedes' midday sally routed Peter's division, but Belisarius' main body drove the Persians back inside the walls with the loss of 150 men and held the field.
sources: Procopius, Wars 2.18; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Battle of Nisibis (541)

sources: Procopius, Wars 2.19; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Siege of Sisauranon (541)

name: Sergiopolis (siege)

label: Hippis

qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

name: Phasis River
label: Phasis River

qbasis: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state

label: Petra (siege, 550)

label: Avaze (siege)

doubt: Traditional: Told only in the Perso-Arabic tradition (Tabari, Dinawari, Balami, the Shahnameh), which follows a romance of Bahram Chobin; the place is unidentified and modern historians accept only the general course of the war.

iranian_note: Bahram's eastern army of Persian cavalry, probably with the Daylamites of his Turkic war.

label: Nahrawan Canal

persian_force: Bahram Chobin's veteran army of the eastern and northern fronts against Khosrow II's much smaller following of court troops and nobles.
iranian_note: Both armies were Sasanian forces led by Persian and Parthian nobles; no foreign contingents are recorded.
losses_b: unknown; Khosrow fled with about 30 nobles

name: Blarathon
label: Blarathon

persian_force: Khosrow II's side: about 8,000 Persian loyalists under his uncles Bindoe and Vistahm, with about 40,000 Romans and 12,000 Armenian cavalry as allies; Bahram's side: his veteran Sasanian field army from the Turkish war and the troops who had followed him from Ctesiphon.
iranian_note: Both Persian factions were Sasanian troops (Bahram was a Mihranid Parthian dynast); the Roman and Armenian allies of Khosrow, who formed most of his army, are not counted here.
result_basis: Bahram Chobin's army broke and he fled the field to the Turks, leaving Khosrow II and his Roman allies in possession.
sources: Theophylact Simocatta 5.9-11; Sebeos 11; en.wikipedia Battle of Blarathon
note: Also in Battles of the Romans as a Roman victory with Khosrow's loyalists as allies. Most of the winning army was Roman.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

label: Constantina

result_basis: Khosrow II's army defeated Phocas' general Germanus, who was mortally wounded, and the Romans withdrew.

sources: Theophanes AM 6096; Chronicle of Khuzistan; Greatrex and Lieu 2002, 184-185
