sources: al-Tabari; al-Baladhuri; en.wikipedia Persian revolts against the Rashidun Caliphate
note: Rashidun Caliphate (Ali). The Wikipedia article says Khulayd besieged both Nishapur and Merv until the rebels made peace.
qbasis: Iranian resistance: an Iranian-led state

name: Defeat of Masqala ibn Hubayra
label: Defeat of Masqala ibn Hubayra
date: during the reign of Mu'awiya I (661-680); year uncertain, placed here at c. 670
place: the passes of Ruyan, Tabaristan (Mazandaran), Iran
commanders_a: the lords of Tabaristan (commander not named in the sources used)
persian_force: Mountain levies of Tabaristan and Ruyan under their native lords; the sources give no numbers.
iranian_note: Tabaristan's armies were raised from its Caspian-speaking highlanders under a Persian-speaking Sasanian-descended aristocracy.
losses_b: Masqala and nearly all his army
result_basis: The Tabaristanis held the mountain passes and destroyed Masqala's army, which never returned.
borderline: no conventional battle name (named here by the defeated commander); not verified online
doubt: Borderline: no conventional battle name (named here by the defeated commander); not verified online.
sources: al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan (Tabaristan); Ibn Isfandiyar, History of Tabaristan
note: Umayyad Caliphate. The disaster gave rise to the Arabic proverb 'until Masqala returns from Tabaristan'. Date and numbers differ between the sources.
qbasis: Tabaristan: an Iranian-led state

name: Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad's raid on Bukhara (Baykand and Ramitan)
label: Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad's raid on Bukhara
war: Muslim conquest of Transoxiana (Umayyad raids of 673-676)
place: Baykand and Bukhara region, Zarafshan oasis (modern Bukhara Region)
allies_b: Turkic horse of Transoxiana called in by Khatun
result_basis: Ubayd Allah beat the Bukharan and Turkic army, took Baykand and Ramitan and forced Khatun to pay tribute (about a million dirhams in the Wikipedia summary of Tabari).
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); Narshakhi, History of Bukhara (trans. R. N. Frye, 1954); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim conquest of Transoxiana
note: First Arab crossing of the Oxus to reach Bukhara. Bukhara's ruler was a Sogdian queen-regent, so the Iranian side was both led and manned by Sogdians, with Turkic allies. Details of the actual fighting are thin and partly from Narshakhi's later retelling.

name: Bukhara (Sa'id ibn Uthman, 676)
label: Bukhara
war: Muslim conquest of Transoxiana (Umayyad raids of 673-676)
result_basis: Sa'id invested Bukhara, fought off its Bukharan and Turkic relief and Khatun bought peace and gave tribute (Tabari; Gibb).
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim conquest of Transoxiana
note: Same expedition as the Samarkand entry that follows. Tabari's account of the first stage is brief; some retellings make Bukhara a negotiated submission rather than a siege with fighting.

name: Samarkand (Sa'id ibn Uthman, 676)
label: Samarkand
date: 676 (56 AH); the city fell in three days
war: Muslim conquest of Transoxiana (Umayyad raids of 673-676)
result_basis: After a hard fight against the Sogdians and Turks the Arabs took Samarkand in three days and took Sogdian hostages (Tabari; Wikipedia summary).
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923); Kh. Y. Blankinship, The End of the Jihad State (1994); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim conquest of Transoxiana
note: The fate of the Sogdian hostages and slaves at Medina is told differently in the sources. The Arabs did not hold Samarkand, so the conquest did not last.

name: Umayya ibn Abdallah's defeat at Bukhara (c. 696)
label: Umayya ibn Abdallah's defeat at Bukhara
war: Muslim conquest of Transoxiana (Umayyad raids; second Fitna aftermath)
place: Beyond the Oxus, at or near Bukhara (modern Bukhara Region)
commanders_a: Umayya ibn Abdallah ibn Khalid; Bukayr ibn Wishah (second in command, who quit)
commanders_b: Bukharan nobles (names not given in the summaries)
result_basis: Abandoned by his lieutenant Bukayr, Umayya's army was encircled and made a humiliating peace with the Bukharans (Tabari; Wikipedia).
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim conquest of Transoxiana
note: A minor episode known only from one or two lines of Tabari. Included because Bukharans, not Turks alone, are named as the enemy; the Sogdian share of the force is not stated.

name: Zunbil's destruction of Ubayd Allah's army (698)
label: Zunbil's destruction of Ubayd Allah's army
war: Arab conquest of Zabulistan (Umayyad wars with the Zunbils)
result_basis: Rutbil trapped the Arab army in the mountains, forced Ubayd Allah to pay a large tribute and give hostages, and he promised not to invade again.
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; al-Tabari; Bosworth, C. E., Sistan under the Arabs (1968); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zunbils
note: The Arab army was called the 'army of destruction'; the better-known 'Army of Peacocks' of Ibn al-Ash'ath (c. 699-700) reached a settlement with the Zunbils and then rebelled. The Zunbils' ethnic origin (Hephthalite, Turk Shahi kin or local) is debated.
qbasis: The Zunbils are said to be of Hephthalite origin (Wink); the Hephthalite identification is uncertain.

name: Badghis (Yazid ibn al-Muhallab against Nezak, c. 703)
label: Badghis
date: c. 703 (Wikipedia, 'Nezak Tarkhan'); not found in the Transoxiana summary
side_b: Nezak Tarkhan of Badghis and his allies
persian_state: Nezak Tarkhan of Badghis and his allies
result_basis: Wikipedia states that Yazid ibn al-Muhallab defeated Nezak at Badghis in 703; I did not see this in Tabari's text.
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nezak_Tarkhan; al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.)
note: Nezak is called a Hephthalite ruler of Badghis (sometimes the last one); the Hephthalites' Iranian identity is debated and 'Nezak' may be a title. Weakest entry: the battle may be conflated with Nezak's alliance of 701-704.

name: Tirmidh (Musa ibn Abd Allah ibn Khazim, 704)
label: Tirmidh
date: 704 (Wikipedia); Musa's rebel rule at Tirmidh c. 689-704
war: Muslim conquest of Transoxiana (Arab rebel Musa ibn Khazim and the Tokharian princes)
side_b: Musa ibn Abd Allah ibn Khazim
allies_b: Native princes of Tokharistan and Hephthalite lords
persian_state: Musa ibn Abd Allah ibn Khazim
commanders_b: Musa ibn Abd Allah ibn Khazim
result_basis: Musa was killed and Tirmidh taken by Uthman ibn Mas'ud (Wikipedia summary of Tabari).
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim conquest of Transoxiana; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nezak_Tarkhan
note: The leader on the Tirmidh side was an Arab rebel; the Tokharian and Hephthalite princes were his allies (the 701-704 alliance with Nezak and Thabit and Hurayth ibn Qutba), and the share cannot be measured. Included as uncertain.

name: Balkh (Qutayba's recovery, 705)
label: Balkh
date: spring 705 (Wikipedia); sources disagree whether it surrendered or was stormed
war: Muslim conquest of Transoxiana (Qutayba ibn Muslim)
side_b: Balkh and the lords of Tokharistan
persian_state: Balkh and the lords of Tokharistan
commanders_b: Nezak Tarkhan (Hephthalite) and local lords of Balkh
result_basis: Qutayba retook Balkh in spring 705 and then took the submission of Tish of Chaghaniyan and of Nezak (Wikipedia, 'Qutayba ibn Muslim').
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qutayba_ibn_Muslim; al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923)
note: Little real fighting is certain; Nezak and Tish submitted. Kept because Wikipedia calls it a battle.

name: Baykand (Paykand), siege of 706
label: Baykand, siege of 706
war: Muslim conquest of Transoxiana (Qutayba ibn Muslim)
place: Baykand (Paykand), the 'city of merchants', south-west of Bukhara, Uzbekistan
result_basis: Qutayba took Baykand after a siege of about two months; it rose again and was sacked, its men killed and others enslaved (Narshakhi; Tabari).
sources: Narshakhi, History of Bukhara (trans. R. N. Frye, 1954); al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qutayba_ibn_Muslim
note: Narshakhi and Tabari say the Baykandis fought and called in help, which is the evidence that townsmen counted. The booty (arms, merchants' goods) financed the later campaigns.

name: Tumushkath and Ramitan (Qutayba, 707)
label: Tumushkath and Ramitan
war: Muslim conquest of Transoxiana (Qutayba ibn Muslim)
place: Tumushkath and Ramitan (Ramithana), north of Bukhara, Uzbekistan
side_b: Sogdian princes of Bukhara, Kish and Nasaf
persian_state: Sogdian princes of Bukhara, Kish and Nasaf
result_basis: Qutayba took the two towns and scattered the coalition, but then withdrew behind the Oxus to avoid a united Sogdian army (Tabari; Wikipedia).
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim conquest of Transoxiana; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qutayba_ibn_Muslim
note: The Sogdian princes were principals; the Turkic prince Kur Maghayun commanded the allied cavalry. The next year's (708) campaign failed against the united Sogdians but no named engagement is recorded.

name: Bukhara (Qutayba's capture, 709)
label: Bukhara
war: Muslim conquest of Transoxiana (Qutayba ibn Muslim)
result_basis: Qutayba defeated the relief army, stormed Bukhara, imposed a 200,000-dirham tribute and a garrison, and Tarkhun of Samarkand became his vassal (Tabari; Narshakhi; Wikipedia).
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); Narshakhi, History of Bukhara (trans. R. N. Frye, 1954); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qutayba_ibn_Muslim
note: The conquest of Bukhara after three years of campaigning. Narshakhi adds that the Arabs settled in Bukharan houses and built the first mosque.

name: Nezak's revolt in Tokharistan (709-710)
label: Nezak's revolt in Tokharistan
date: autumn 709 to spring 710 (91 AH); Nezak's capture and execution in 710 (one source says 709)
war: Muslim conquest of Transoxiana (revolt of Nezak Tarkhan)
place: Lower Tokharistan: Talaqan, Faryab, Balkh and Baghlan area, Afghanistan (Nezak's last stronghold not securely located)
side_b: Nezak Tarkhan and the princes of Tokharistan
persian_state: Nezak Tarkhan and the princes of Tokharistan
commanders_a: Qutayba ibn Muslim; Abd al-Rahman ibn Muslim
result_basis: Abd al-Rahman and Qutayba crushed the revolt; Nezak was captured and executed on al-Hajjaj's orders despite a promise of pardon, and the Yabghu was sent to Damascus (Tabari; Wikipedia).
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923); Kh. Y. Blankinship, The End of the Jihad State (1994); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nezak_Tarkhan; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qutayba_ibn_Muslim
note: Nezak is a Hephthalite ruler of Badghis; the princes of Tokharistan were Bactrian-speaking local lords, so the Iranian side is well attested though the Hephthalite identity is debated. The sources do not give one named battle.

name: Shuman and Akharun (Qutayba, c. 710)
label: Shuman and Akharun
war: Muslim conquest of Transoxiana (Qutayba ibn Muslim)
place: Shuman and Akharun, upper Oxus valley, Tokharistan (modern Surkhandarya / southern Tajikistan)
commanders_b: The king of Shuman and Akharun (name not recorded)
result_basis: Qutayba stormed the king's citadel and the king was killed (Wikipedia, 'Qutayba ibn Muslim'; Tabari).
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qutayba_ibn_Muslim; al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.)
note: A minor Tokharian principality; location approximate.

name: Khwarazm (Qutayba's intervention, 711-712)
label: Khwarazm
date: 711-712 (92-93 AH); the sources are unclear on the order of events
war: Muslim conquest of Transoxiana (Qutayba ibn Muslim)
place: Khwarazm (Kath and Hazarasp area), Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan
side_b: Khurrazadh and the king of Khamjird
allies_b: Khwarazmian rebels who later killed the Khwarazmshah
persian_state: Umayyad Caliphate v Khurrazadh and the king of Khamjird
faction_a: Umayyad Caliphate, Khwarazmshah Jigan as Arab client
faction_b: Khurrazadh and the king of Khamjird
commanders_a: Qutayba ibn Muslim; Abd al-Rahman ibn Muslim; Khwarazmshah Jigan
result_basis: Abd al-Rahman defeated the king of Khamjird's troops and Khurrazadh and his followers were executed; a later Khwarazmian rising was put down by al-Mughira ibn Abdallah (Tabari; Wikipedia, 'Qutayba ibn Muslim').
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qutayba_ibn_Muslim; al-Biruni, Chronology of Ancient Nations (on the killing of the Khwarazmian scholars)
note: Khwarazmian princes fought on both sides: the Afrighid shah as Arab ally against his own brother. Al-Biruni's story that Qutayba killed Khwarazm's scholars and burned their books is tradition. Place is the region only.

name: Samarkand (Qutayba's siege, 712)
label: Samarkand
war: Muslim conquest of Transoxiana (Qutayba ibn Muslim)
allies_a: Native levies of Bukhara, Kish, Nasaf and Khwarazm
allies_b: Relief force of the princes of Shash and Ferghana
result_basis: Qutayba ambushed the Shash relief force, breached the walls with siege engines and Ghurak made terms; 30,000 slaves and 2,200,000 dirhams were taken (Tabari; Wikipedia).
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923); Kh. Y. Blankinship, The End of the Jihad State (1994); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qutayba_ibn_Muslim; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim conquest of Transoxiana
note: Ghurak had overthrown Tarkhun and took the throne. He was left on it under Arab terms and later founded Farankath. Native Sogdian, Bukharan and Khwarazmian levies served in Qutayba's army (Tabari), so Iranians stood on both sides.

name: Khujand and Minak (Qutayba, 713)
label: Khujand and Minak
date: 713 (94 AH); the order and detail of the actions are uncertain
war: Muslim conquest of Transoxiana (Qutayba's Jaxartes campaign)
place: Khujand on the Jaxartes (Tajikistan) and Minak in Ushrusana
side_b: Princes of Shash, Ferghana and Ushrusana with their levies
persian_state: Princes of Shash, Ferghana and Ushrusana with their levies
result_basis: Qutayba's army fought before Khujand and at Minak and advanced to Shash; the Arabs held the field (Wikipedia, 'Qutayba ibn Muslim'; Tabari).
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qutayba_ibn_Muslim; al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923)
note: Merged because the sources give only the places. The Ushrusanans were Iranian; Ferghana and Shash only partly so.

name: Namangan (Chinese restoration of the Ikhshid of Ferghana, 715)
label: Namangan
persian_state: Tang China v Arab occupation force
faction_a: Tang China, the deposed Ikhshid of Ferghana
commanders_a: Zhang Xiaosong; the Ikhshid of Ferghana (name not given)
result_basis: The Chinese force defeated Alutar's Arab-backed army and put the Ikhshid back on the throne (Wikipedia; Chinese annals, Cefu Yuangui).
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim conquest of Transoxiana; Cefu Yuangui and Xin Tangshu (Tang annals), as summarised in Gibb 1923 and Beckwith 1987
note: The Ikhshid bore an Iranian title; Ferghana's ruling house and speech were probably partly Iranian but the sources do not settle it, so qualifies is uncertain.

name: Defeat of Yazid ibn al-Muhallab in Tabaristan
label: Defeat of Yazid ibn al-Muhallab in Tabaristan
place: the mountain passes of Tabaristan (Mazandaran), Iran
persian_force: Farrukhan's Tabaristani forces with allies he recruited from Daylam and Gilan.
iranian_note: The sources name Daylamite and Gilite allies alongside Farrukhan's own Tabaristanis, all Caspian Iranian peoples.
strength_b: part of an army given as about 100,000 for the whole campaign
losses_b: not heavy in the fighting, but many killed in the ravines during the retreat
result_basis: After losing on the plain, the Tabaristanis ambushed the Arab army in the mountain passes and drove it back in a chaotic retreat; Yazid then made a tributary peace and withdrew.
borderline: no conventional battle name (named here by the defeated commander)
doubt: Borderline: no conventional battle name (named here by the defeated commander).
sources: al-Tabari (year 98); Ibn Isfandiyar; en.wikipedia Yazid ibn al-Muhallab; Farrukhan the Great; Dabuyid dynasty
note: Umayyad Caliphate. Yazid had first beaten the Tabaristanis on the plain; the Wikipedia articles describe the result as Farrukhan's successful containment of the invasion. Tabaristan stayed independent until 760.
qbasis: Tabaristan: an Iranian-led state

name: Jurjan (siege, 717)
label: Jurjan (siege, 717)
war: Yazid ibn al-Muhallab's Caspian campaign (revolt of Jurjan)
commanders_b: the rebel leaders of Jurjan (not named)
persian_force: The Iranian townsmen and lords of Jurjan who had risen, encouraged by Farrukhan, and massacred the Arab garrison; no numbers are given.
iranian_note: The Wikipedia article calls the rebels the Iranian population of Jurjan.
losses_b: many killed and executed after the fall (al-Tabari)
result_basis: Al-Tabari says Yazid besieged the rebels in their stronghold for months and took it by a mountain path, so the place fell to the besiegers.
borderline: the siege is told by al-Tabari, but the Wikipedia articles (after Kennedy) mention only the revolt and Yazid's escape by diplomacy
doubt: Borderline: the siege is told by al-Tabari, but the Wikipedia articles (after Kennedy) mention only the revolt and Yazid's escape by diplomacy.
sources: al-Tabari (year 98); en.wikipedia Yazid ibn al-Muhallab; Farrukhan the Great
note: Umayyad Caliphate. The revolt nearly trapped Yazid's army in the Caspian lands.
qbasis: Iranian resistance: an Iranian-led state

name: Revolt of the Six Hu Prefectures (Kang Daibin, 721)
label: Revolt of the Six Hu Prefectures
date: 721 (the rising began in 720-721; Kang Daibin captured by Wang Jun and sent to Xuanzong)
war: Rising of the Six Hu Prefectures (Tang)
place: Six Hu Prefectures, the Ordos (Lanchi and Yanchi region), Ningxia-Inner Mongolia
side_b: Hu rebels of the Six Hu Prefectures
persian_state: Hu rebels of the Six Hu Prefectures
commanders_a: Zhang Yue; Wang Jun; Wang Maozhong
result_basis: Wang Jun captured Kang Daibin soon after the Tang commanders took the field and delivered him to the emperor.
sources: Zizhi Tongjian, juan 212; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhang_Yue_(Tang_dynasty); Rong Xinjiang, Zhonggu Hu zu shi yanjiu (2001), on the Six Hu Prefectures; de la Vaissiere, Sogdian Traders (2005)
note: A major rising of a Sogdian-Turkic settler community in the Tang Ordos; the Tang forces were under Zhang Yue, Wang Jun and Wang Maozhong. A second Hu rising under Kang Yuanzi in 722 was separate. Individual battles and places are not itemised in the sources used, so this is a campaign-level entry.
qbasis: Leader by descent: Kang Daibin, who led the Hu of the Six Hu Prefectures, bears the Sogdian surname Kang (Samarkand) and the prefectures were settled with Sogdians and Turks (Rong Xinjiang, de la Vaissière), so his people were Sogdian-Turkic mixed; the Turkic side of the community is large.

name: Khujand (Sa'id al-Harashi against the Sogdian rebels, 721-722)
label: Khujand
result_basis: At-Tar of Ferghana betrayed the Sogdians' camp; al-Harashi defeated them and massacred more than 3,000 Sogdians (Tabari; Wikipedia, 'Divashtich').
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923); Kh. Y. Blankinship, The End of the Jihad State (1994); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divashtich; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim conquest of Transoxiana
note: The Sogdian nobles had fled to Khujand from Samarkand and Panjikent. Some retellings put the massacre at the end of the fight, some after surrender.

name: Mount Mugh and Panjikent (Divashtich, 722)
label: Mount Mugh and Panjikent
date: 722 (autumn, Wikipedia); the defeat of Divashtich near the Zarafshan and his flight to Mount Mugh
place: Panjikent and the fortress of Kal'ai Mug on Mount Mugh, Tajikistan
side_b: Divashtich, ruler of Panjikent, and the Sogdian rebels
allies_b: Ferghanan and Turkic hopes of help that did not arrive
persian_state: Divashtich, ruler of Panjikent, and the Sogdian rebels
result_basis: Al-Harashi won the battle by the Zarafshan, Divashtich fled to Mug, surrendered and was crucified on a Zoroastrian dakhma (Tabari; Wikipedia, 'Divashtich').
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divashtich; Mugh Documents (Livshits, Smirnova, Bogolyubov)
note: The Mugh archive of Sogdian documents, found at the fortress in 1933, comes from Divashtich's court. The Wikipedia article does not describe a long siege, only the flight and surrender.

name: Day of Thirst (724)
label: Day of Thirst
date: 724 (106 AH); season uncertain (Tabari has it in the summer)
place: On the Jaxartes near Khujand, after the retreat from Ferghana (Tajikistan)
commanders_a: Muslim ibn Sa'id al-Kilabi; Abd al-Rahman ibn Na'im al-Ghamidi
result_basis: The Arabs were trapped between the Turgesh and the Transoxianian forces, burned their baggage, broke through to Khujand with heavy losses (Wikipedia; Tabari).
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923); Kh. Y. Blankinship, The End of the Jihad State (1994); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day_of_Thirst
note: Turgesh-led, with Sogdian, Shashi and Ferghanan allies; the Wikipedia article does not mention Alutar, so his presence is from the Divashtich and Namangan material. Muslim ibn Sa'id's expedition was against Ferghana.

name: Baykand (729)
label: Baykand
place: Baykand, about 30 km south of Bukhara, Uzbekistan
commanders_a: Ashras ibn Abdallah al-Sulami; Qatan ibn Qutayba; Thabit Qutnah
result_basis: The Arabs broke through the Turgesh encirclement with a narrow victory and reached Bukhara (Wikipedia).
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); Kh. Y. Blankinship, The End of the Jihad State (1994); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Baykand
note: Turgesh-led with Sogdian allies, among them the rulers of Bukhara, who had risen against Ashras's tax policy. Ghurak is listed in the infobox as a commander, but the text says only that he went over to the rebels.

name: Kamarja (siege, 729)
label: Kamarja
place: Kamarja, a fortress about 42 km west of Samarkand, Uzbekistan
allies_b: Contingents of Ferghana, al-Taraband, Afshinah, Nasaf and Bukhara
result_basis: The Arab garrison held out 58 days and was allowed to leave for Dabusiyya under a negotiated agreement (Wikipedia).
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); Kh. Y. Blankinship, The End of the Jihad State (1994); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Kamarja
note: Turgesh-led siege with Sogdian contingents named in the sources. The Sasanian prince Khosrau, a grandson of the last king, accompanied the Turgesh. Arab rule in Sogdia collapsed afterwards.

name: Defile (731)
label: Defile
place: Takhtakaracha Pass between Samarkand and Kish, Uzbekistan
allies_b: Troops of the rulers of Sogdia, Shash and Ferghana
commanders_a: Junayd ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Murri; Sawra ibn al-Hurr al-Abani (killed)
result_basis: The Turgesh destroyed Sawra's 12,000 and cut up Junayd's army, which escaped to Samarkand with very heavy losses (Wikipedia; Tabari; Blankinship).
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); Kh. Y. Blankinship, The End of the Jihad State (1994); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Defile
note: Turgesh-led with Sogdian, Shashi and Ferghanan allies; Ghurak advised the Turgesh to set the grass on fire. Tokharistan was also in revolt, which drew off about 28,000 of Junayd's men.

name: Baggage (Battle of the Baggage, 737)
label: Baggage
place: Upper Oxus, in or near Khuttal, Tajikistan or northern Afghanistan
allies_a: Contingent of al-Saghaniyan in the baggage escort
commanders_a: Asad ibn Abdallah al-Qasri; Ibrahim ibn Asim al-Uqayli
result_basis: The Turgesh captured most of Asad's baggage train and the Khuttal campaign failed (Wikipedia; Tabari).
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); Kh. Y. Blankinship, The End of the Jihad State (1994); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Baggage
note: Turgesh-led, with Sogdians and Khuttal. The Saghan Khudah, a Tokharian prince, was killed with his contingent fighting for the Arabs, so Iranians stood on both sides. Khuttal's ruling house was Hephthalite or Turkic, which Wikipedia does not settle.

name: Kharistan (737)
label: Kharistan
place: Kharistan in Juzjan, near Maymana, Afghanistan
allies_a: The Juzjan prince and his retinue
allies_b: Contingents of the princes of Sughd, Shash, Usrushana and Khuttal and of the Yabghu of Tokharistan
result_basis: Asad surprised the scattered Turgesh, took their camp and spoils, and Suluk and Ibn Surayj fled (Wikipedia; Tabari).
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); Kh. Y. Blankinship, The End of the Jihad State (1994); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Kharistan
note: Turgesh-led, with Sogdian, Ushrusanan, Shashi, Khuttali and Tokharian contingents named, and the Juzjan prince on the Arab side. About 4,000 Turgesh against 7,000 Arabs; the allied total of about 30,000 had dispersed to raid.

name: Jaxartes (Nasr ibn Sayyar against Shash and the Turgesh, c. 740)
label: Jaxartes
date: c. 739-741 (the sources do not date it exactly)
war: Nasr ibn Sayyar's reconquest of Transoxiana
place: On the Jaxartes, in Shash territory (modern Uzbekistan or Kazakhstan)
result_basis: Nasr drove off the Turgesh and killed the chief of one of their detachments, and the ruler of Shash then came to terms (Wikipedia, 'Nasr ibn Sayyar'; Tabari).
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); Kh. Y. Blankinship, The End of the Jihad State (1994); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasr_ibn_Sayyar
note: About 15,000 Shashi troops are reported. Shash's population was partly Sogdian-speaking but its rulers had Turkic titles, so the Iranian share is unproven.

name: Tus (748)
label: Tus (748)
date: spring 748, after the occupation of Merv
result_basis: Nasr's son Tamim was defeated at Tus and Nasr then gave up Nishapur to Qahtaba.
sources: al-Tabari, History vol. 27 (The Abbasid Revolution, Williams); Daniel, The Political and Social History of Khurasan under Abbasid Rule 747-820 (1979); Shaban, The Abbasid Revolution (1970); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Revolution; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasr_ibn_Sayyar
note: Qahtaba was an Arab (Tayyi'); Iranian mawali in the Khurasani army cannot be quantified, and Wikipedia stresses a heavily Arab core. This entry also stands for the fall of Nishapur, which followed without a separate battle that I could confirm.

name: Merv (748)
label: Merv
result_basis: The Hashimiyya army occupied Merv on 14 February 748 and Nasr fled to Nishapur.
sources: al-Tabari, History vol. 27 (The Abbasid Revolution, Williams); Daniel, The Political and Social History of Khurasan under Abbasid Rule 747-820 (1979); Shaban, The Abbasid Revolution (1970); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Revolution; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Muslim; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasr_ibn_Sayyar
note: Abu Muslim's origin is debated: Wikipedia says 'most likely Persian' (born at Merv or near Isfahan) but calls the accounts doubtful. His forces were Khurasani Arab settlers plus native (Iranian) converts and officers of mixed origin; this was more a seizure of Merv after months of skirmishing than a pitched battle.

name: Jurjan
label: Jurjan
commanders_b: Nubata ibn Hanzala (killed, per Tabari; unnamed in the Wikipedia article)
result_basis: The Abbasid army defeated an Umayyad force of about 10,000.
sources: al-Tabari, History vol. 27 (The Abbasid Revolution, Williams); Daniel, The Political and Social History of Khurasan under Abbasid Rule 747-820 (1979); Shaban, The Abbasid Revolution (1970); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Revolution
note: Arab leader; Iranian share of the Khurasani army unquantified (see Tus). Included because the Khurasani army is a named body with a documented Iranian element.

name: Nahavand (siege, 749)
label: Nahavand
commanders_a: Qahtaba ibn Shabib al-Ta'i; Al-Hasan ibn Qahtaba
commanders_b: Umayyad commanders (Syrian relief force defeated first)
result_basis: Nahavand fell after Qahtaba beat the Syrian relief army; the Syrians were spared and the Khurasani units of the garrison executed.
sources: al-Tabari, History vol. 27 (The Abbasid Revolution, Williams); Daniel, The Political and Social History of Khurasan under Abbasid Rule 747-820 (1979); Shaban, The Abbasid Revolution (1970); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Revolution
note: Arab leaders; Iranian share of the besiegers unquantified. The Umayyad garrison also had Khurasani units.

name: Isfahan (749)
label: Isfahan
commanders_b: Amir ibn Dubara (per Tabari; unnamed in the Wikipedia article)
result_basis: The Abbasid army defeated an Umayyad force put at 50,000, opening the way to Nahavand.
sources: al-Tabari, History vol. 27 (The Abbasid Revolution, Williams); Daniel, The Political and Social History of Khurasan under Abbasid Rule 747-820 (1979); Shaban, The Abbasid Revolution (1970); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Revolution
note: Arab leader; Iranian contingent unquantified. The site (Jabalaq near Isfahan) and the Umayyad commander's name are from memory of Tabari.

name: Euphrates crossing (749)
label: Euphrates crossing
place: Euphrates near Karbala and Kufa, Iraq
commanders_a: Qahtaba ibn Shabib al-Ta'i (killed); Al-Hasan ibn Qahtaba
commanders_b: Yazid ibn Umar ibn Hubayra al-Fazari
result_basis: The Abbasids surprised Ibn Hubayra's forces at night; Qahtaba died but Ibn Hubayra fled to Wasit and Al-Hasan entered Kufa on 2 September 749.
sources: al-Tabari, History vol. 27 (The Abbasid Revolution, Williams); Daniel, The Political and Social History of Khurasan under Abbasid Rule 747-820 (1979); Shaban, The Abbasid Revolution (1970); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Revolution
note: Arab leaders; the Kufa entry was without a major battle. Iranian share unquantified.

name: Wasit (siege, 749-750)
label: Wasit
commanders_b: Yazid ibn Umar ibn Hubayra al-Fazari
result_basis: Ibn Hubayra surrendered on promise of amnesty after the fall of the Umayyad dynasty and was then executed.
sources: al-Tabari, History vol. 27 (The Abbasid Revolution, Williams); Daniel, The Political and Social History of Khurasan under Abbasid Rule 747-820 (1979); Shaban, The Abbasid Revolution (1970); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Revolution
note: Arab leaders; the Iranian element of the Khurasani army is again unquantified.

name: Chach (Tashkent), Tang capture by Gao Xianzhi (750)
label: Chach, Tang capture by Gao Xianzhi
war: Tang-Arab conflict in Central Asia (preceding Talas)
result_basis: Gao Xianzhi took the city after agreeing terms and then plundered it and sent the king to Chang'an (Tang annals).
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gao_Xianzhi; Jiu Tangshu and Xin Tangshu (biography of Gao Xianzhi)
note: Almost no real fighting: Gao is said to have taken Chach by a breach of the truce. Chach had a large Sogdian population but its king's title was Turkic. Qualifies is doubtful. The Chach prince's flight to the Arabs led to Talas (751).

name: Zab
label: Zab
date: 25 January 750 (the Abbasid Revolution article gives 16 January)
place: Greater Zab (left bank, near its mouth), northern Iraq
commanders_a: Abdallah ibn Ali; Abu Awn Abd al-Malik ibn Yazid
result_basis: Marwan II's army was completely destroyed and he fled to Egypt.
sources: al-Tabari, History vol. 27 (The Abbasid Revolution, Williams); Daniel, The Political and Social History of Khurasan under Abbasid Rule 747-820 (1979); Shaban, The Abbasid Revolution (1970); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Revolution
note: Abdallah ibn Ali was an Abbasid prince (Arab) and Abu Awn a Khurasani commander of unclear descent. The Iranian share of the Khurasani army is not given in the sources I read.

name: Damascus (siege, 750)
label: Damascus
result_basis: Abdallah took the city by storm after a brief siege and killed the governor.
sources: al-Tabari, History vol. 27 (The Abbasid Revolution, Williams); Daniel, The Political and Social History of Khurasan under Abbasid Rule 747-820 (1979); Shaban, The Abbasid Revolution (1970); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Revolution; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_Allah_ibn_Ali
note: Arab leader; Iranian share of the army unquantified.

name: Bukhara (revolt of Sharik ibn Shaykh al-Mahri, 751)
label: Bukhara
war: Abbasid consolidation in Transoxiana (revolt against Abu Muslim)
persian_state: Abbasid army of Abu Muslim v Sharik ibn Shaykh al-Mahri's rebels
result_basis: Ziyad ibn Salih defeated and killed Sharik at Bukhara (Narshakhi; Tabari).
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Narshakhi, History of Bukhara (trans. R. N. Frye, 1954); al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.)
note: An Arab-led rising, not a native one. I could not confirm that Bukharan citizens fought for Sharik, nor give the share of Khurasani Persians in Ziyad's army. Weak entry.

name: Tuhe (An Lushan v the Khitan, 751)
label: Tuhe
date: late summer 751 (8th lunar month in ZZTJ, about Aug-Sept, Julian)
place: Tuhuzhen River, probably the Xar Moron (Xilamulun) basin, Inner Mongolia
commanders_b: Khitan chief (name not given in the sources used)
result_basis: An Lushan's army, worn down by a long march in rain and heat, was destroyed by the Khitan and he escaped with a handful of riders.
sources: Zizhi Tongjian, juan 216; Old Book of Tang, juan 200A (An Lushan); Pulleyblank 1955; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan
note: Before the rebellion; An Lushan, military governor of Pinglu and Fanyang, marched with about 60,000 men and Xi horse and was routed; the defeat and his later restoration to favour are part of the background of 755. Place and some details (the Xi desertion) are from ZZTJ memory and not rechecked.
qbasis: Leader by descent: An Lushan, ruler of Yan, was Sogdian on his father's side (New Book of Tang: 'a mixed Hu of Yingzhou, originally surnamed Kang'; his name is the Sogdian Roxshan; Pulleyblank 1955, Rong Xinjiang), but his mother was a Turk of the Ashide (Ashina) clan, his stepfather the Turk An Yanyan, and he grew up among the Turks, so the Turkic side of his family is at least as strong; here he commanded a Tang frontier army.

name: Talas
label: Talas
commanders_a: Ziyad ibn Salih; Abu Muslim (governor of Khurasan, directed from Samarkand)
result_basis: The Karluks went over to the Abbasids and the Tang army was routed.
sources: Bai Shouyi / Gibb on Talas (from memory); Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (from memory)
note: Weak candidate: the field commander Ziyad ibn Salih was an Arab and I found no source stating the Iranian share of the Abbasid army; Abu Muslim (most likely Persian, origin disputed) governed the province that raised it.

name: Nisibis (754)
label: Nisibis
war: Revolt of Abdallah ibn Ali against al-Mansur
result_basis: Abdallah suspected treachery on all sides and fled before the battle developed, to Basra.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_Allah_ibn_Ali; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Muslim; al-Tabari, History vol. 28 (Abbasid Authority Affirmed, Kennedy); Daniel, Khurasan under Abbasid Rule
note: Abu Muslim's origin is debated (probably Persian). Abdallah's army also had Khurasanis, many reluctant to fight Abu Muslim (one account says he had 17,000 of them killed).

name: Defeat of Sunpadh
label: Defeat of Sunpadh
date: 755 (the revolt lasted about 70 days after Abu Muslim's murder)
persian_force: Sunpadh's followers, mostly from Jibal and Tabaristan: former partisans of Abu Muslim, Zoroastrians and others; no reliable numbers.
iranian_note: The sources say most of his supporters came from Jibal and Tabaristan.
losses_b: very heavy (Ibn Isfandiyar says the bones were still visible in 912)
result_basis: Sunpadh's army was routed and he fled to Tabaristan, where he was killed.
borderline: a rising, not a state; no conventional battle name (named here by the defeated leader)
doubt: Borderline: a rising, not a state; no conventional battle name (named here by the defeated leader).
sources: al-Tabari (year 137); Nizam al-Mulk; Ibn Isfandiyar; en.wikipedia Sunpadh
note: Abbasid Caliphate. Sunpadh had taken Nishapur, Qumis and Rayy (with Abu Muslim's treasury) before the battle.
qbasis: Iranian risings: an Iranian-led state

name: Changshan (Yan Gaoqing's defence, 756)
label: Changshan
date: early 756 (about the 1st lunar month; Julian January-February); the town fell about a week after Yan Gaoqing's defection
allies_a: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
commanders_b: Yan Gaoqing (prefect of Changshan); Yuan Lüqian
result_basis: Shi Siming and Cai Xide took Changshan and captured Yan Gaoqing, who was sent to Luoyang and executed.
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shi_Siming; Old Book of Tang, juan 187B (Yan Gaoqing)
note: Yan Gaoqing and his cousin Yan Zhenqing (at Pingyuan) turned much of Hebei against the rebels in the winter of 755-756; Changshan, cut off and short of arms, fell after a siege of days. Li Guangbi later recaptured the town (spring 756), so Changshan changed hands twice. Dating is approximate.
qbasis: Leader by descent: Shi Siming has the surname Shi, that of the Sogdian city of Kesh, and modern scholars take his family as Turkicised Sogdian, but the Tang histories call him a 'mixed Turkic Hu' of Ningyi (Old Book of Tang 200), so his Sogdian descent is probable rather than certain and the Turkic side of his family is strong; An Lushan, ruler of Yan, was likewise Sogdian on his father's side but half Turkic (Turkic mother and stepfather).

name: Chentao Xie (Fang Guan's defeat, 756)
label: Chentao Xie
date: 21st day of the 10th lunar month 756 (about Oct-Nov 756, Julian); the Qingqu fight two days later
allies_a: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
commanders_a: An Shouzhong; Li Guiren (Yan generals before Chang'an)
result_basis: Fang Guan's centre column, moving ox-carts into the Yan cavalry, was burned and routed with very heavy losses, and his other columns failed at Qingqu two days later.
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; Old Book of Tang, juan 111 (Fang Guan)
note: A famous Tang disaster in which the chancellor Fang Guan, trying an antique ox-cart formation, lost 40,000 to 50,000 men; the Yan commanders are named An Shouzhong and Li Guiren (the An surname may point to Sogdian origin, unverified). An Lushan himself was at Luoyang, so this counts only through his role as ruler of the army. Date given loosely because the 10th lunar month of 756 straddles two Julian months.
qbasis: Leader by descent: An Lushan, ruler of Yan, was Sogdian on his father's side (New Book of Tang: 'a mixed Hu of Yingzhou, originally surnamed Kang'; his name is the Sogdian Roxshan; Pulleyblank 1955, Rong Xinjiang), but his mother was a Turk of the Ashide (Ashina) clan, his stepfather the Turk An Yanyan, and he grew up among the Turks, so the Turkic side of his family is at least as strong; the Chang'an front was held by his generals under his authority.

name: Jiashan (756)
label: Jiashan
date: about May-June 756 (4th-5th lunar month; ZZTJ), exact day not fixed here
allies_a: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
result_basis: Guo Ziyi and Li Guangbi routed Shi Siming's army, which lost (by ZZTJ) about 40,000 dead, and Shi fled.
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; Old Book of Tang, juan 120 (Guo Ziyi) and 110 (Li Guangbi)
note: The best Tang victory of the first campaign: Shi Siming, who had besieged Li Guangbi in Changshan, was caught in the open as Guo Ziyi's army joined Li Guangbi, and escaped on foot. The victory was thrown away when Xuanzong forced Geshu Han out of Tong Pass and the two armies had to fall back. Date and numbers are from ZZTJ and approximate.
qbasis: Leader by descent: Shi Siming has the surname Shi, that of the Sogdian city of Kesh, and modern scholars take his family as Turkicised Sogdian, but the Tang histories call him a 'mixed Turkic Hu' of Ningyi (Old Book of Tang 200), so his Sogdian descent is probable rather than certain and the Turkic side of his family is strong; An Lushan was ruler of Yan and the Yan army was his.

name: Yongqiu (siege, 756-757)
label: Yongqiu
date: Feb 756 (Linghu Chao's siege) to Jan 757 (Yin Ziqi's siege, over 60 days; Zhang Xun then withdrew to Ningling and Suiyang)
allies_a: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
result_basis: Zhang Xun, with about 2,000 to 3,000 men, repulsed Linghu Chao's 40,000 and held out against repeated assaults through 756, leaving only in January 757 to move his survivors to Suiyang.
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; Old Book of Tang, juan 187B (Zhang Xun)
note: Yongqiu stood across the rebels' road to the Huai and the Yangzi. The 'borrowing arrows with straw men' story is told of this siege. Linghu Chao was a defecting Tang prefect, not a Hu; Yin Ziqi's origin is not recorded in the sources used. The result is for the whole 756 siege and is the least certain part: whether the town was lost or simply abandoned in early 757 is told differently.
qbasis: Leader by descent: An Lushan, ruler of Yan, was Sogdian on his father's side (New Book of Tang: 'a mixed Hu of Yingzhou, originally surnamed Kang'; his name is the Sogdian Roxshan; Pulleyblank 1955, Rong Xinjiang), but his mother was a Turk of the Ashide (Ashina) clan, his stepfather the Turk An Yanyan, and he grew up among the Turks, so the Turkic side of his family is at least as strong (and after January 757 his son An Qingxu, Sogdian through his father).

name: Luoyang (An Lushan's march and capture, 755-756)
label: Luoyang
date: 16 Dec 755 (rising at Fanyang) to 18 Jan 756 (fall of Luoyang), Julian dates; An Lushan took the imperial title there on 5 Feb 756
place: Luoyang (the Eastern Capital), Henan, reached by the Yellow River crossing at Lingchang and by Chenliu, Xingyang and Wuniu
allies_a: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
commanders_b: Feng Changqing; Li Cheng (killed); Lu Yi (killed)
result_basis: Feng Changqing's newly raised levies were beaten in a running fight from Wuniu to the city gates and Luoyang fell, whereupon An Lushan proclaimed the Great Yan there.
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; Old Book of Tang, juan 104 (Feng Changqing)
note: The rebel army was about 150,000 (claimed 200,000) from the Fanyang, Pinglu and Hedong garrisons, many of them Khitan, Xi, Tongra and Shiwei horse; Feng Changqing, with about 60,000 untrained recruits, withdrew to Shan and joined Gao Xianzhi at Tong Pass. The Chinese Wikipedia's date of 12 Dec 755 falls before the rising and is a calendar-conversion error; 18 Jan 756 follows the English Wikipedia. The 'march' stands for the Fanyang rising itself, which saw no fighting.
qbasis: Leader by descent: An Lushan, ruler of Yan, was Sogdian on his father's side (New Book of Tang: 'a mixed Hu of Yingzhou, originally surnamed Kang'; his name is the Sogdian Roxshan; Pulleyblank 1955, Rong Xinjiang), but his mother was a Turk of the Ashide (Ashina) clan, his stepfather the Turk An Yanyan, and he grew up among the Turks, so the Turkic side of his family is at least as strong.

name: Tong Pass (Lingbao, 756)
label: Tong Pass
date: 7 Jul 756 (Julian; Lingbao fighting on the 4th day of the 6th lunar month, the pass lost within days)
place: Lingbao West Plain, east of Tong Pass (Tongguan), Henan-Shaanxi border
allies_a: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
allies_b: Tibetan, Tuyuhun and other frontier troops
commanders_a: Cui Qianyou (in the field); An Lushan (ruler, at Luoyang)
result_basis: Cui Qianyou's feigned weakness drew Geshu Han's army out of the pass into an ambush at Lingbao and it was destroyed; Tong Pass and then Chang'an fell.
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; Old Book of Tang, juan 104 (Geshu Han)
note: Geshu Han had been forced out of a strong position by Xuanzong and Yang Guozhong against his own judgement; Tang numbers are given as 80,000 to 200,000. Side note on the Tang commander: the Old Book of Tang makes Geshu Han a Turk of the Tuqishi (Turgesh) Geshu clan on his father's side with a mother who was a daughter of the king of Khotan; the Khotanese were Saka (Eastern Iranian), so on a strict descent reading the Tang commander was half Iranian too and iranian_sides could be 'both'. Not used here to qualify the battle.
qbasis: Leader by descent: An Lushan, ruler of Yan, was Sogdian on his father's side (New Book of Tang: 'a mixed Hu of Yingzhou, originally surnamed Kang'; his name is the Sogdian Roxshan; Pulleyblank 1955, Rong Xinjiang), but his mother was a Turk of the Ashide (Ashina) clan, his stepfather the Turk An Yanyan, and he grew up among the Turks, so the Turkic side of his family is at least as strong.

name: Suiyang (siege, 757)
label: Suiyang
date: late Jan-Feb 757 (first assaults) to 24 Nov 757 (fall, 9th day of the 10th lunar month; Julian); the last siege began in the 7th month
allies_a: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
commanders_a: Yin Ziqi; Yang Chaozong; An Qingxu (ruler)
commanders_b: Zhang Xun; Xu Yuan; Nan Jiyun
result_basis: After about ten months the starving garrison could hold no longer; Suiyang fell and Zhang Xun, Xu Yuan and Nan Jiyun were executed.
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Suiyang
note: Zhang Xun and Xu Yuan, with about 6,800 men, kept Yin Ziqi's army (put at 130,000) from the Huai and Yangzi valleys; the defenders ate horses, then people, and relief commanders such as Helan Jinming stood aside. The Yan army is said to have lost about 120,000 men in over 400 fights. An Lushan had been killed by his own son on 29 Jan 757, so An Qingxu was Yan ruler for most of the siege.
qbasis: Leader by descent: An Qingxu, ruler of Yan from January 757 to April 759, was An Lushan's son and so Sogdian by descent through his father (An Lushan's own family was half Turkic: Turkic mother and stepfather).

name: Taiyuan (siege, 756-757)
label: Taiyuan
date: winter 756-57 (Dec 756 to Feb 757 or later; over a month under Shi Siming, the siege then lingered under Cai Xide)
allies_a: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
result_basis: Li Guangbi, with under 10,000 soldiers, held the city by countermining and sorties against Shi Siming's 100,000 (Wikipedia, Shi Siming), and the besiegers withdrew.
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shi_Siming; Old Book of Tang, juan 110 (Li Guangbi)
note: Shi Siming left for Fanyang when An Lushan's death became known (late Jan 757); Cai Xide stayed and the siege was finally broken by Li Guangbi's sorties. The siege marks the decisive refusal of Tang Hedong to collapse. Dates are approximate.
qbasis: Leader by descent: Shi Siming has the surname Shi, that of the Sogdian city of Kesh, and modern scholars take his family as Turkicised Sogdian, but the Tang histories call him a 'mixed Turkic Hu' of Ningyi (Old Book of Tang 200), so his Sogdian descent is probable rather than certain and the Turkic side of his family is strong; the army was that of Yan, ruled by An Lushan and then An Qingxu.

name: Xindian and the recapture of Luoyang (757)
label: Xindian and the recapture of Luoyang
date: late Nov to early Dec 757 (10th lunar month, Julian; Luoyang entered about 18th day, c. 3 Dec)
place: Xindian near Shan (Sanmenxia), and Luoyang, Henan
allies_a: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
commanders_a: Yan Zhuang; Zhang Tongru; An Qingxu (ruler)
commanders_b: Guo Ziyi; Li Chu; Pugu Huaien
result_basis: The Yan army broke at Xindian on sight of the Uyghur cavalry on the Tang flank, and An Qingxu abandoned Luoyang and fled to Ye.
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion
note: Xindian (west of Shan) was the last pitched battle for the Eastern Capital in 757; Luoyang was handed over to the Uyghurs for plunder as agreed with their prince. An Qingxu executed about 30 captive Tang officers before leaving. Whether the fight at Xindian was one day or several is not clear in the sources used; dates approximate.
qbasis: Leader by descent: An Qingxu, ruler of Yan from January 757 to April 759, was An Lushan's son and so Sogdian by descent through his father (An Lushan's own family was half Turkic: Turkic mother and stepfather).

name: Xiangji Temple (757)
label: Xiangji Temple
date: 13 Nov 757 (Julian, 9th lunar month, renyin day, computed from the sexagenary date in ZZTJ); Chang'an recovered the next day
place: Plain by Xiangji Temple, south of Chang'an (Xi'an), Shaanxi
commanders_a: An Shouzhong; Li Guiren; Zhang Tongru (Chang'an)
commanders_b: Li Chu; Guo Ziyi; Li Siye; Wang Siyi; Pugu Huaien
result_basis: The Tang army, with a Uyghur cavalry ambush, destroyed the Yan army (about 60,000 beheaded) and Chang'an was retaken the next day.
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/香积寺之战
note: About 150,000 Tang against about 100,000 Yan; the Anxi and Beiting troops under Li Siye were nearly wiped out in the centre before the Uyghurs and Pugu Huaien struck the Yan rear. Chinese Wikipedia lists Khotanese troops among the Tang auxiliaries; Khotanese were Saka (Eastern Iranian), so a second Iranian contingent may sit on the Tang side, size unknown and probably under a fifth. The Gregorian date is computed (renyin = 13 Nov 757); some books give October.
qbasis: Leader by descent: An Qingxu, ruler of Yan from January 757 to April 759, was An Lushan's son and so Sogdian by descent through his father (An Lushan's own family was half Turkic: Turkic mother and stepfather); the Yan army before Chang'an acted for him.

name: Ye (siege of Xiangzhou, 758-759)
label: Ye (siege of Xiangzhou, 758-759)
date: winter 758 (Oct-Nov 758) to 7 Apr 759 (Shi Siming's relief battle, ended by a storm)
allies_a: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
commanders_a: An Qingxu; Shi Siming (relief army); Cai Xide; Tian Chengsi; Ashina Chengqing; Wu Lingxun
commanders_b: Guo Ziyi; Li Guangbi; Li Siye (died in the siege); Lu Jiong; Xu Shuji
result_basis: A sudden storm panicked both armies on 7 Apr 759; the Tang forces fled south and lifted the siege, and Shi Siming then took Ye and killed An Qingxu (10 Apr).
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shi_Siming; https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/安史之乱
note: The Tang gathered nine jiedushi (200,000 or more; later sources say 600,000) with no supreme commander, only the eunuch Yu Chao'en as overseer; An Qingxu reached Ye with only about 1,300 men (Wikipedia) before reinforcements, including Shi Siming's, raised the garrison above 60,000. Ashina Chengqing was a Turk. The Yan victory left Shi Siming master of the rebellion and he murdered An Qingxu three days later.
qbasis: Leader by descent: An Qingxu, ruler of Yan from January 757 to April 759, was An Lushan's son and so Sogdian by descent through his father (An Lushan's own family was half Turkic: Turkic mother and stepfather); the relief army was led by Shi Siming, probably Sogdian by descent (surname Shi; the Tang histories call him a 'mixed Turkic Hu', so the Turkic side is strong).

name: Heyang (759-760)
label: Heyang
date: autumn 759 to spring 760 (several actions around the Heyang bridgehead)
place: Heyang (Mengzhou), on the Yellow River north of Luoyang, Henan
allies_a: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
result_basis: Li Guangbi held the Heyang bridgehead and rebuffed Shi Siming's attacks, leaving a stalemate (Wikipedia, Shi Siming).
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shi_Siming; Old Book of Tang, juan 110 (Li Guangbi)
note: After losing Luoyang Li Guangbi kept Shi Siming from the Guanzhong by holding Heyang, an obstacle on the Yellow River crossing, for about a year; the individual engagements are not itemised here. Treated as a single entry because the sources used do not separate the actions.
qbasis: Leader by descent: Shi Siming has the surname Shi, that of the Sogdian city of Kesh, and modern scholars take his family as Turkicised Sogdian, but the Tang histories call him a 'mixed Turkic Hu' of Ningyi (Old Book of Tang 200), so his Sogdian descent is probable rather than certain and the Turkic side of his family is strong.

name: Luoyang (Shi Siming's capture, 759)
label: Luoyang
date: autumn 759 (about the 9th-10th lunar month, Oct-Nov; English Wikipedia's summary puts it in April)
place: Luoyang (the Eastern Capital), Henan, after Bianzhou (Kaifeng)
allies_a: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
commanders_b: Li Guangbi; Xu Shuji (changed sides at Bianzhou)
result_basis: Li Guangbi judged the Yan army stronger, evacuated Luoyang and fell back on Heyang, and Shi Siming entered the city.
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shi_Siming
note: Shi Siming declared himself emperor of Yan at Fanyang in spring 759 and marched south in autumn, taking Bianzhou when Xu Shuji went over to him. This is mostly manoeuvre with a rearguard fight rather than a set battle, hence the low confidence. The English Wikipedia (An Lushan Rebellion) lumps Bian and Luoyang under April 759; the ZZTJ narrative has the march after the Ye affair in the autumn, which is followed here.
qbasis: Leader by descent: Shi Siming has the surname Shi, that of the Sogdian city of Kesh, and modern scholars take his family as Turkicised Sogdian, but the Tang histories call him a 'mixed Turkic Hu' of Ningyi (Old Book of Tang 200), so his Sogdian descent is probable rather than certain and the Turkic side of his family is strong.

name: al-Taq (siege)
label: al-Taq (siege)
place: the fortress of al-Taq, Tabaristan (Mazandaran), Iran
commanders_a: Abu al-Khasib Marzuq, Khazim ibn Khuzayma, Rawh ibn Hatim (and Umar ibn al-Ala)
commanders_b: the garrison of Khurshid (Khurshid himself had withdrawn to Daylam)
persian_force: Khurshid's garrison and household troops in his treasure fortress; no numbers are given.
iranian_note: The Dabuyid garrison was drawn from Tabaristan under a Persian-speaking ruling house.
losses_b: the defenders were killed and the children taken captive
result_basis: After a long siege the gate was opened by Abu al-Khasib's ruse, the fortress fell and Khurshid's family was captured.
sources: al-Tabari; Ibn Isfandiyar; en.wikipedia Abbasid conquest of Tabaristan; Khurshid of Tabaristan; Khazim ibn Khuzayma al-Tamimi
note: Abbasid Caliphate. The Abbasid conquest article describes Umar ibn al-Ala taking al-Taq after prolonged fighting and, separately, Abu al-Khasib's ruse at Khurshid's fortress; they may be one siege or two.
qbasis: Tabaristan: an Iranian-led state

name: Defeat of Khurshid
label: Defeat of Khurshid
persian_force: An army of mountain levies that Khurshid raised in Daylam and Gilan, given as 50,000 men.
iranian_note: The sources say Khurshid raised his army among the mountain peoples of Daylam and Gilan.
result_basis: Khurshid's counter-invasion from Daylam was repulsed and he withdrew to Daylam, where he took poison the next year.
borderline: no conventional battle name; whether a pitched battle was fought is not clear (the Abbasid conquest article says cholera was decisive)
doubt: Borderline: no conventional battle name; whether a pitched battle was fought is not clear (the Abbasid conquest article says cholera was decisive).
sources: al-Tabari; Ibn Isfandiyar; en.wikipedia Khurshid of Tabaristan; Abbasid conquest of Tabaristan; Tabaristan
note: Abbasid Caliphate. The end of the Dabuyid dynasty; Tabaristan became an Abbasid province.
qbasis: Tabaristan: an Iranian-led state

name: Fanyang (Gao Juren's rising and the massacre of the Hu, 761)
label: Fanyang
date: after April 761 (spring-summer 761; month not given in the sources used)
allies_a: Turkic and Sogdian 'Hu' of the garrison
result_basis: Gao Juren's party defeated the Turkic and Hu forces under Ashina Chengqing and held Fanyang until Li Huaixian killed Gao and took over.
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; Zizhi Tongjian, juan 222-223
note: A garrison fight inside Yan after Shi Siming's murder, in which the Hu (Sogdians and Turks) of Fanyang were the victims; it is the clearest attested slaughter of a Sogdian community in the rebellion. Very thinly sourced here: the date, the numbers and who commanded the Hu side are all unclear, and Gao Juren acted against, not for, Shi Chaoyi's order.
qbasis: Shi Chaoyi's order to kill Shi Siming's favoured son Shi Chaoqing in Fanyang set the garrisons against each other, and Gao Juren defeated the Yan force under the Turk Ashina Chengqing and killed the Sogdians of the city (Wikipedia, An Lushan Rebellion), but no source seen says the Sogdians were organised as a fighting unit or names a Sogdian commander (the Shi family, if Sogdian by descent, is the link; Turkic side strong).

name: Mangshan (761)
label: Mangshan
date: Feb-Mar 761 (2nd lunar month, Julian), exact day not fixed here
place: Mount Mang (Beimang), north of Luoyang, Henan
allies_a: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
result_basis: The Tang army, sent against Luoyang over Li Guangbi's objection, was beaten below Mount Mang and withdrew.
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; Old Book of Tang, juan 110 (Li Guangbi)
note: The court, under pressure from the eunuch Yu Chao'en, forced Li Guangbi to attack Luoyang though he wanted to wait; Pugu Huaien's wing, badly placed, gave way. It was Shi Siming's last victory: he was strangled by his son within weeks. Details of the battle are from memory of the ZZTJ narrative and were not rechecked.
qbasis: Leader by descent: Shi Siming has the surname Shi, that of the Sogdian city of Kesh, and modern scholars take his family as Turkicised Sogdian, but the Tang histories call him a 'mixed Turkic Hu' of Ningyi (Old Book of Tang 200), so his Sogdian descent is probable rather than certain and the Turkic side of his family is strong.

name: Shan Prefecture (Shi Chaoyi's attacks, 761)
label: Shan Prefecture
date: spring 761 (about Mar-Apr), ended by Shi Siming's death on 18 Apr 761
allies_a: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
result_basis: Wei Boyu repeatedly threw back Shi Chaoyi's assaults on Shan, and the failure led Shi Siming to quarrel with his son and be killed.
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shi_Chaoyi; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shi_Siming
note: Shi Siming ordered his son to take a fort at Shan; after repeated failures he threatened to execute him, and the generals Luo Yue and Cai Wenjing seized and strangled the father (18 Apr 761 per Wikipedia). Included because it is a named siege that decided the dynasty's fate.
qbasis: Leader by descent: Shi Siming has the surname Shi, that of the Sogdian city of Kesh, and modern scholars take his family as Turkicised Sogdian, but the Tang histories call him a 'mixed Turkic Hu' of Ningyi (Old Book of Tang 200), so his Sogdian descent is probable rather than certain and the Turkic side of his family is strong; Shi Chaoyi led the attack as his son.

name: Luoyang (Tang-Uyghur recapture, 762)
label: Luoyang
date: late autumn 762 (10th lunar month of Baoying 1; about Nov 762)
place: Luoyang (the Eastern Capital) and the plain before it, Henan
allies_a: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
commanders_b: Li Kuo (Prince of Yong, later Emperor Dezong; nominal commander); Pugu Huaien; Dengli Khan
result_basis: The Tang-Uyghur army defeated Shi Chaoyi's army in front of the city and took Luoyang, which the Uyghurs plundered.
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shi_Chaoyi; https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/安史之乱
note: The second Tang-Uyghur recapture of the Eastern Capital (the first was in 757); Dengli Khan came in person and Pugu Huaien (a Turk of the Pugu tribe) commanded the Tang side. Shi Chaoyi fled north with his generals already wavering. Details of the battle (numbers, sub-fights) are not given in the sources used here.
qbasis: Leader by descent: Shi Chaoyi, ruler of Yan from April 761 to 763, was Shi Siming's son, so Sogdian by descent through his father if Shi Siming's family was Sogdian (disputed; the Tang histories call the Shis 'mixed Turkic Hu').

name: Shi Chaoyi's last campaign (Weizhou-Mozhou-Fanyang, 762-763)
label: Shi Chaoyi's last campaign
date: Nov 762 to Feb 763 (Shi Chaoyi's flight from Luoyang to Mozhou and Fanyang; he died before 17 Feb 763)
place: Mozhou (Renqiu), Hebei, and the road to Fanyang
allies_a: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
result_basis: Pursued by Pugu Huaien and abandoned by his generals (Tian Chengsi, Li Huaixian and others went over), Shi Chaoyi was cut off and hanged himself.
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shi_Chaoyi
note: A chain of defeats and defections, not one battle: after Luoyang the Yan generals Zhang Xiancheng, Xue Song, Zhang Zhongzhi, Tian Chengsi, Li Huaixian and Li Baozhong each went over to the Tang; Li Huaixian's men intercepted Shi Chaoyi when he tried to reach the Xi or Khitan. The dates and the sequence of the fights could not be pinned down with the sources used, so place and day are only indicative.
qbasis: Leader by descent: Shi Chaoyi, ruler of Yan from April 761 to 763, was Shi Siming's son, so Sogdian by descent through his father if Shi Siming's family was Sogdian (disputed; the Tang histories call the Shis 'mixed Turkic Hu').

name: Defeat of al-Ajtham
label: Defeat of al-Ajtham
persian_force: Ustadh Sis's peasant followers from Badghis, Herat and Sistan, many of them former followers of Bihafarid; he claimed 300,000 fighting men.
iranian_note: The sources describe his followers as villagers of eastern Khorasan (Badghis, Herat, Sistan).
losses_b: al-Ajtham and many of his men killed
result_basis: Ustadh Sis's followers defeated the Abbasid army of Marw al-Rudh and killed its commander.
borderline: a rising, not a state; no conventional battle name (named here by the defeated commander)
doubt: Borderline: a rising, not a state; no conventional battle name (named here by the defeated commander).

note: Abbasid Caliphate.

name: Defeat of Ustadh Sis
label: Defeat of Ustadh Sis
persian_force: The peasant army of Ustadh Sis from eastern Khorasan (Badghis, Herat, Sistan).
iranian_note: The sources describe his followers as villagers of eastern Khorasan.
result_basis: Ustadh Sis lost a bloody battle and fled to the mountains, where Khazim besieged and captured him.
borderline: a rising, not a state; no conventional battle name (named here by the defeated leader)
doubt: Borderline: a rising, not a state; no conventional battle name (named here by the defeated leader).
sources: al-Tabari (years 150-151); en.wikipedia Ustadh Sis; Khazim ibn Khuzayma al-Tamimi
note: Abbasid Caliphate. Al-Mahdi is said to have pardoned 30,000 captives, a figure that does not match the 14,000.

name: Narshakh (battle)
label: Narshakh (battle)
commanders_a: Husayn ibn Mu'adh (amir of Bukhara), with the qadi Amir ibn Imran
commanders_b: the White-clothed of Bukhara (leaders not named for this fight)
persian_force: Al-Muqanna's 'White-clothed' followers from the villages of the Bukhara oasis.
iranian_note: Narshakhi says most villages of Bukhara and Sughd joined al-Muqanna; their people spoke Sogdian.
losses_a: unknown (the Arab Na'im ibn Sahl killed)
result_basis: The Bukharan force killed about 700 of the White-clothed and the survivors asked for amnesty.
borderline: a rising, not a state
doubt: Borderline: a rising, not a state.
sources: Narshakhi, History of Bukhara (tr. Frye); al-Tabari
note: Abbasid Caliphate. The survivors signed a treaty, then broke it and fortified Narshakh (see Narshakh (siege)).

name: Narshakh (siege)
label: Narshakh (siege)
commanders_a: Jibra'il ibn Yahya, Husayn ibn Mu'adh
commanders_b: Hakim ibn Ahmad (killed), Khishwi (killed), Baghi (killed), Kirdik
persian_force: The White-clothed of the Bukhara oasis under Hakim ibn Ahmad and the village chiefs Khishwi, Baghi and Kirdik.
iranian_note: Narshakhi names the leaders as men of Bukharan villages (Fudail castle, Ghijduvan), Sogdian-speaking.
losses_a: heavy losses in a night sortie
result_basis: After four months a mine brought down part of the wall, the defenders came out to treat and were killed or defeated, and Narshakh fell.
borderline: a rising, not a state
doubt: Borderline: a rising, not a state.
sources: Narshakhi, History of Bukhara (tr. Frye); al-Tabari
note: Abbasid Caliphate. The headwoman of Narshakh was executed; Kirdik fled to al-Muqanna.

label: Sanam (siege)
date: 779 or 780 (AH 163, al-Tabari); Narshakhi and others give 783 (AH 167)
place: al-Muqanna's fortress of Sanam near Kesh (Shahrisabz), Uzbekistan
commanders_a: Sa'id al-Harashi (for the governor Mu'adh ibn Muslim and the caliph al-Mahdi)
persian_force: Al-Muqanna's last followers from Kesh and Sughd, who earlier had Turkic allies from beyond the Jaxartes.
iranian_note: The movement drew on the Sogdian villagers of Kesh, Nakhshab and Sughd, with Turkish allies who joined for plunder (Narshakhi).

borderline: a rising, not a state; no Wikipedia article; the fortress name (Sanam, Narshakhi's 'Mount Sam') varies

sources: al-Tabari (year 163); Narshakhi, History of Bukhara; en.wikipedia Al-Muqanna

label: Defeat of Farasha

iranian_note: The princes led the highland levies of Tabaristan, Caspian Iranian speakers.
result_basis: The rebels defeated the relief army and captured and executed its commander.

label: Defeat of Salm al-Farghani

iranian_note: The princes led the highland levies of Tabaristan, Caspian Iranian speakers.

label: Defeat of Vandad Hormozd
commanders_a: Yazid ibn Mazyad al-Shaybani and Sa'id al-Harashi (under the heir Musa al-Hadi)
persian_force: The forces of the Tabaristan princes under Vandad Hormozd (Qarinvandid) and Sharwin I (Bavandid).
iranian_note: The princes led the highland levies of Tabaristan, Caspian Iranian speakers.
result_basis: Yazid ibn Mazyad defeated Vandad Hormozd, who was wounded and then surrendered to Musa al-Hadi at Gurgan.
borderline: no conventional battle name (named here by the defeated leader); place not recorded

label: Samarkand
side_b: Rafi ibn al-Layth and his supporters
allies_b: Persian and Sogdian supporters of Rafi
persian_state: Rafi ibn al-Layth and his supporters

name: Asadabad Pass (811-812)

note: Named in the Wikipedia article on the siege of Baghdad but not in the Tahir biography; dating and sequence relative to Hamadan are uncertain.

name: Hamadan (811)
label: Hamadan
result_basis: After hard-fought engagements Abd al-Rahman's 20,000 abna were pushed back into Hamadan and blockaded, and he left seeking terms.

note: Several actions around Hamadan rather than one pitched battle; precise dating is loose. Tahir's Persian descent as at Rayy.

name: Rayy (811)
label: Rayy
place: Rayy (Shahr-e Rey, south of Tehran), Iran
result_basis: Tahir's 4,000-5,000 men routed Ali's army of about 40,000 abna; Ali was killed.

note: Tahir, a Persian dehqan of Pushang near Herat (great-grandson of a mawla of the Khuza'a), commanded for al-Ma'mun. The battle opened the Khurasani advance on Baghdad.

name: Ahwaz (812)
label: Ahwaz
commanders_a: Tahir ibn Husayn; Harthama ibn A'yan (reinforcements)
result_basis: Tahir defeated and killed the Muhallabid governor and the Muhallabids of Basra then submitted.

note: The Tahir article says 'Khuzistan' and the siege article 'al-Ahwaz'; the exact site is uncertain.

name: Baghdad (siege, 812-813)
label: Baghdad

sources: al-Tabari, History vol. 31 (Fishbein); Kennedy, The Early Abbasid Caliphate (1981); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Baghdad_(812%E2%80%93813); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tahir_ibn_al-Husayn
note: Tahir (Persian dehqan family) was the field commander, with Harthama ibn A'yan; Harthama was a mawla of the Banu Dabba born in Balkh, and Wikipedia does not say whether he was Arab or Persian, so he is not counted. Al-Ma'mun was in Merv.

Whether Theophobos had an independent command at the sack is not stated, and a second Khurramite group (about 16,000) arrived only in September 837.

name: Anzen
label: Anzen

note: Afshin was a hereditary Sogdian (Iranian) prince of Ushrusana; on the Roman side the Khurramite 'Persian' tourma of about 14,000 (Wikipedia: about 30,000 Persians in all by autumn 837) under Theophobos, with a Kurdish element, fought. Theophobos and Manuel urged a night attack.

note: Afshin (Sogdian prince of Ushrusana) was one of three major divisional commanders under the caliph, not the overall commander, so the leader link is secondary. Persian Khurramites were not among the defenders.

name: Sari (874)
label: Sari (874)

iranian_note: Both armies were overwhelmingly Iranian (both sides): Sistani and Khurasani Persians against Daylamite and Tabari highlanders.
result_basis: Ya'qub defeated the Zaydid forces at Sari and al-Hasan fled to the Daylam mountains; Ya'qub's later withdrawal in rain and sickness is a separate matter.

qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: al-Baida
label: al-Baida

iranian_note: Ya'qub's army was recruited mainly in Sistan and Khorasan, with a ghulam guard (Bosworth, 'The armies of the Saffarids').
result_basis: Muhammad ibn Wasil's larger army was defeated and he fled; Ya'qub then sacked his stronghold of Sa'idabad and took Fars.

qbasis: Saffarids: an Iranian-led state

result_basis: The Zanj routed al-Hisn's force, killing many and taking their horses; al-Hisn fled to Askar Mukram and the Zanj plundered the town.
borderline: a minor engagement of the Zanj war, told only by al-Tabari
doubt: Borderline: a minor engagement of the Zanj war, told only by al-Tabari.

persian_force: Mardavij's Daylamite and Gilite infantry with his Turkish ghulam cavalry.
iranian_note: Mardavij's army was built on Daylamite and Gilite foot, with Turkish slave cavalry who later murdered him (en.wikipedia Mardavij).
result_basis: Mardavij stormed Hamadan, where his nephew had been killed, and drove off the caliphal army sent to the Jibal.
borderline: the battle with Harun ibn Gharib is told briefly; the sources checked confirm the sack of the Jibal towns in 931 but not every detail
doubt: Borderline: the battle with Harun ibn Gharib is told briefly; the sources checked confirm the sack of the Jibal towns in 931 but not every detail.
sources: Ibn Miskawayh; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Mardavij; en.wikipedia Dinavar
note: Abbasid Caliphate (al-Muqtadir). Mardavij then took Dinavar, Kashan and Isfahan.
qbasis: Ziyarids: an Iranian-led state

name: Defeat of Yaqut (934)
label: Defeat of Yaqut (934)
place: on the road east from Shiraz towards Kerman, Fars, Iran (site not named)
persian_force: About 900 Daylamite infantry under Ali ibn Buya, probably with some local volunteers.
iranian_note: Kennedy and Busse give Ali's force as about 900 Daylamites.
result_basis: Yaqut's men fled in disorder and the road to Shiraz lay open (Kennedy).
borderline: no conventional name; the battlefield is not named in the sources checked
doubt: Borderline: no conventional name; the battlefield is not named in the sources checked.
sources: Kennedy, The Prophet and the Age of the Caliphates, ch. 10; en.wikipedia Imad al-Dawla; en.wikipedia Buyid dynasty; Ibn Miskawayh
