qbasis: Buyids: an Iranian-led state

name: Gorgan (siege, 939)
label: Gorgan (siege, 939)
place: Gorgan (medieval Jurjan, near Gonbad-e Kavus), Iran
persian_force: Samanid side: the Khurasan army of Abu Ali Chaghani (Turkish ghulams and Iranian levies). Makan's side: his Daylamite troops, with aid sent by Vushmgir.
iranian_note: Daylamite defenders against a mixed Turkish and Khurasani Samanid army (both sides).
result_basis: After a seven-month siege Makan abandoned Gorgan and fled to Rayy, and the city passed to the Samanids.
sources: en.wikipedia Makan ibn Kaki; en.wikipedia Vushmgir; Ibn Miskawayh
note: Makan, a Daylamite warlord, had broken with the Samanids and allied himself with the Ziyarid Vushmgir.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Iskhabad
label: Iskhabad
persian_force: Samanid side: Abu Ali Chaghani's Khurasan army of Turkish ghulams and Iranian levies. Ziyarid side: Daylamite and Gilite infantry, Makan's elite Daylamite units.
iranian_note: Daylamite officers were captured and sent to Bukhara; the Samanid army was led by the Iranian prince of Chaghaniyan (both sides).
losses_b: more than half killed, the rest captured or wounded (Wikipedia)
result_basis: Vushmgir fled early, Makan's elite units were destroyed and Makan was shot and beheaded; the Samanids held the field.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Iskhabad; en.wikipedia Vushmgir; Ibn Miskawayh
note: The Wikipedia infobox says 'Samanid-Buyid victory', but the Buyids are not described as taking part.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Tabriz (siege, 942)
label: Tabriz (siege, 942)
side_b: Daysam ibn Ibrahim and his Kurdish allies
faction_b: Daysam ibn Ibrahim (ruler of Azerbaijan) and his Kurdish allies
persian_force: Sallarid side: Marzuban's Daylamites, joined by Daysam's Daylamites who had deserted. Daysam's side: Kurdish tribesmen.
iranian_note: Daylamites against Kurds, both named in the sources (both sides).
result_basis: Marzuban's Daylamites beat Daysam's Kurds and besieged Tabriz, which fell after Daysam slipped away to Ardabil.
borderline: Daysam's Azerbaijan-seated principality is treated as an Iranian state; he was a Kurdish former Sajid officer
doubt: Borderline: Daysam's Azerbaijan-seated principality is treated as an Iranian state; he was a Kurdish former Sajid officer.
sources: en.wikipedia Marzuban ibn Muhammad; en.wikipedia Sallarid dynasty; Ibn Miskawayh; Minorsky, Studies in Caucasian History
note: Ardabil then surrendered after Daysam's vizier was bribed.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Barda'a (943)
label: Barda'a (943)
persian_force: The Sallarid garrison of Daylamites with local volunteers (ghazis) and Kurds.
iranian_note: Ibn Miskawayh names the Daylamite troops and the volunteers of Arran.
strength_b: unknown (a few hundred Daylamites and some thousands of volunteers)
result_basis: The Rus routed the governor's Daylamites and volunteers within a short fight and took Barda'a.
sources: Ibn Miskawayh, Tajarib al-umam; en.wikipedia Sallarid dynasty; en.wikipedia Marzuban ibn Muhammad; Kennedy (2004)
note: The Rus came up the Kura. Marzuban's army then lost several engagements before the ambush (next entry).
qbasis: Sallarids: an Iranian-led state

name: Rayy (943)
label: Rayy (943)
persian_force: Both sides: Daylamite infantry with Turkish cavalry.
iranian_note: Rayy's army was 'composed almost entirely of Daylamites' (Kennedy) (both sides).
result_basis: Vushmgir was defeated when his officers Shir Mardi and Gurigir went over to Rukn al-Dawla, and the Buyids occupied Rayy.
sources: en.wikipedia Rukn al-Dawla; en.wikipedia Vushmgir; Ibn Miskawayh
note: Rayy had been held for the Samanids; Vushmgir lost it for good.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Baghdad (944)
label: Baghdad (944)
date: 944 (AH 332); Mu'izz retreated to Ahvaz on 28 July
place: the approaches of Baghdad (near al-Mada'in), Iraq
persian_force: Ahmad ibn Buya's Daylamite infantry with some Turkish cavalry.
iranian_note: Mu'izz al-Dawla's army was built on Daylamite foot (Kennedy; en.wikipedia Mu'izz al-Dawla).
result_basis: Tuzun repelled Ahmad ibn Buya's attack on the approaches of Baghdad and Ahmad fell back to Ahvaz; the modern accounts (Kennedy; en.wikipedia Tuzun) have Tuzun beat him off, against the Mu'izz al-Dawla article's claim that Ahmad won the fight.
sources: Kennedy, The Prophet and the Age of the Caliphates, ch. 10; en.wikipedia Mu'izz al-Dawla; Ibn Miskawayh
note: Abbasid Caliphate under the Turkish amir al-umara Tuzun. The Wikipedia article on Mu'izz al-Dawla instead says Ahmad won the battle near al-Mada'in but retreated after Tuzun cut the bridge; Kennedy's verdict is followed.
qbasis: Buyids: an Iranian-led state

name: Barda'a (siege, 944)
label: Barda'a (siege, 944)
persian_force: Marzuban's Daylamite infantry, Kurdish horse and many volunteers (Ibn Miskawayh gives his army as about 30,000).
iranian_note: Daylamites were the core of Marzuban's forces, with Kurds and volunteers (Ibn Miskawayh; Madelung).
losses_b: about 700 killed in the ambush; many dead of disease
result_basis: After Marzuban's ambush killed about 700 Rus and the survivors were hemmed in and wasted by dysentery, they evacuated Barda'a, which returned to Sallarid control.
borderline: the Rus left with their loot and prisoners; the siege had been thinned when Marzuban marched against the Hamdanids
doubt: Borderline: the Rus left with their loot and prisoners; the siege had been thinned when Marzuban marched against the Hamdanids.
sources: Ibn Miskawayh, Tajarib al-umam; en.wikipedia Marzuban ibn Muhammad; en.wikipedia Sallarid dynasty
note: Dated 943-944 by most; one Wikipedia article dates the raid to 945.
qbasis: Sallarids: an Iranian-led state

name: Salmas (944)
label: Salmas (944)
date: 944 (during the siege of Barda'a; one account gives winter 945-946)
persian_force: Marzuban's Daylamite army (the rest having been left before Barda'a).
iranian_note: Daylamites were the core of Marzuban's forces (Madelung); the Hamdanid invader had Kurdish support.
result_basis: Marzuban defeated al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, who was soon recalled by Nasir al-Dawla.
borderline: site and date uncertain; the fighting is told briefly
doubt: Borderline: site and date uncertain; the fighting is told briefly.
sources: en.wikipedia Marzuban ibn Muhammad; Ibn Miskawayh
note: Hamdanids of Mosul (Nasir al-Dawla).
qbasis: Sallarids: an Iranian-led state

name: Baghdad (946)
label: Baghdad (946)
date: April to August 946; decisive crossing on the night of 1 August 946
commanders_a: Mu'izz al-Dawla; Abu Ja'far al-Saymari; Ispahdost
commanders_b: Nasir al-Dawla; Muhammad ibn Shirzad; al-Husayn ibn Sa'id
persian_force: Mu'izz al-Dawla's Daylamite infantry, the core of his army, with a fleet of zabzab river-boats; handpicked Daylamites made the crossing.
iranian_note: The sources name the Daylamites as the Buyid core; the Turks were mostly on the Hamdanid side.
result_basis: Saymari's Daylamites won the fight on the river and crossed, the Hamdanid army collapsed and Nasir al-Dawla fled Baghdad.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Baghdad (946); en.wikipedia Mu'izz al-Dawla; Ibn Miskawayh
note: Hamdanids of Mosul with Turkish mercenaries; allied Arab tribes blockaded western Baghdad. Peace followed at Ukbara.
qbasis: Buyids: an Iranian-led state

name: Qazvin (948)
label: Qazvin (948)
persian_force: Both sides: Daylamite infantry with Turkish cavalry (Buyids) and Kurds (Sallarids).
iranian_note: Both were Daylamite dynasties whose armies were largely Daylamite (both sides).
result_basis: Marzuban's army, marching on Rayy, was defeated and he was taken prisoner.
sources: en.wikipedia Rukn al-Dawla; en.wikipedia Marzuban ibn Muhammad; en.wikipedia Sallarid dynasty; Ibn Miskawayh
note: The Sallarid dynasty article places Marzuban's defeat at Samiran castle; the other accounts place it near Qazvin. Marzuban escaped from prison in 952-953.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Batiha (950)
label: Batiha (950)
place: the Batiha marshes between Wasit and Basra, Iraq
persian_force: A Buyid army of Daylamite infantry under the vizier al-Muhallabi and the Daylamite officer Ruzbahan.
iranian_note: Mu'izz al-Dawla's forces in southern Iraq were largely Daylamite (Kennedy).
result_basis: Ruzbahan held back and fled, and Imran's ambushes in the marshes destroyed much of al-Muhallabi's army; al-Muhallabi escaped by swimming.
sources: en.wikipedia Mu'izz al-Dawla; Ibn Miskawayh
note: Imran ibn Shahin ruled the marshes (Batiha) as an independent chief; Mu'izz made peace and appointed him governor. An earlier Buyid attack under Ruzbahan (949-950) had also failed.
qbasis: Buyids: an Iranian-led state

name: Isfahan (955)
label: Isfahan (955)
faction_b: Muhammad ibn Makan (Daylamite commander in Samanid service)
persian_force: Both sides: Daylamite troops; Adud's army from Fars also had Turkish cavalry.
iranian_note: Ibn Makan was a Daylamite officer; Buyid armies were largely Daylamite (both sides).
result_basis: Adud al-Dawla defeated Muhammad ibn Makan and recovered Isfahan.
borderline: the course of the fighting is not described in the sources checked
doubt: Borderline: the course of the fighting is not described in the sources checked.
sources: en.wikipedia 'Adud al-Dawla; en.wikipedia Mu'ayyad al-Dawla; Ibn Miskawayh
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Defeat of Ruzbahan (957)
label: Defeat of Ruzbahan (957)
war: Revolt of Ruzbahan (Daylamite mutiny in Buyid Iraq)
persian_force: Mu'izz al-Dawla's side: his Turkish ghulam cavalry. Rebel side: Ruzbahan's mutinous Daylamite infantry.
iranian_note: The sources describe the fight as Daylamite rebels against Mu'izz al-Dawla's Turks (both sides).
result_basis: Ruzbahan came close to winning but was defeated and captured, thanks to Mu'izz al-Dawla's personal bravery and his loyal Turks (Kennedy).
borderline: no conventional name; site not given
doubt: Borderline: no conventional name; site not given.
sources: Kennedy, The Prophet and the Age of the Caliphates, ch. 10; en.wikipedia Mu'izz al-Dawla
note: While Mu'izz was busy, the Hamdanid Nasir al-Dawla briefly retook Baghdad.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Ghazni (siege, 962)
label: Ghazni (siege, 962)
war: Revolt of Alp-Tegin (foundation of the Ghaznavid state)
persian_force: Alp-Tegin's Turkish ghulams with Iranian ghazi volunteers.
iranian_note: Wikipedia names his Turkish slave guard and Iranian ghazis; their proportions are unknown.
result_basis: Alp-Tegin took Ghazni from Abu Bakr Lawik and settled there as its ruler.
borderline: Wikipedia says only that he 'seized' Ghazna; Bosworth describes a siege of some four months
doubt: Borderline: Wikipedia says only that he 'seized' Ghazna; Bosworth describes a siege of some four months.
sources: en.wikipedia Alp-Tegin; en.wikipedia Samanid Empire; Bosworth, The Ghaznavids
note: Lawik dynasty of Ghazni, kinsmen of the Kabul Shahis. Alp-Tegin defeated the rulers of Bamiyan and Kabul on the way. He received Samanid investiture afterwards.
qbasis: Wikipedia names his Turkish slave guard and Iranian ghazis; their proportions are unknown.

name: Balkh (962)
label: Balkh (962)
faction_a: Alp-Tegin (rebel Samanid commander, founder of the Ghaznavid line)
persian_force: Alp-Tegin's side: his guard of Turkish ghulams with Iranian ghazis. Samanid side: the Samanid army of Transoxiana and Khorasan.
iranian_note: Wikipedia names Alp-Tegin's Turkish slave guard and Iranian ghazis; the Samanid army was mixed Turkish and Iranian (both sides).
result_basis: Alp-Tegin defeated the army sent against him by Mansur I and went on towards Ghazni.
sources: en.wikipedia Alp-Tegin; en.wikipedia Sabuktigin; Bosworth, The Ghaznavids; Barthold, Turkestan
note: Alp-Tegin had been Samanid commander-in-chief of Khorasan.

iranian_note: Kennedy describes the war as Turks against Daylamites (both sides).
result_basis: Bakhtiyar held out in Wasit and the Turks raised the siege as Adud al-Dawla's relief army approached.
borderline: the mutinous Turkish guard of the Buyid army is treated as a Persian-side faction
doubt: Borderline: the mutinous Turkish guard of the Buyid army is treated as a Persian-side faction.
sources: en.wikipedia Izz al-Dawla; Kennedy, The Prophet and the Age of the Caliphates, ch. 10; Ibn Miskawayh

doubt: Borderline: the mutinous Turkish guard of the Buyid army is treated as a Persian-side faction.

label: Ahvaz (977)

persian_force: Adud's side: Daylamite infantry and Turkish cavalry of Fars. Bakhtiyar's side: his Daylamites and Arab allies.
iranian_note: Buyid armies were Daylamite foot with Turkish horse; Bakhtiyar had lost most of his Turks in 975 (both sides).
result_basis: Adud al-Dawla defeated his cousin, who retreated to Wasit.

qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

persian_force: Adud al-Dawla's army of Daylamites and Turks; composition not recorded for this siege.
iranian_note: Adud al-Dawla's armies were Daylamite foot and Turkish horse (Kennedy).
result_basis: Mayyafariqin was taken by Adud al-Dawla's forces and Abu Taghlib fled to al-Rahba.

label: Defeat of Qabus (981)
persian_force: Buyid side: Mu'ayyad al-Dawla's Daylamites with troops sent by Adud al-Dawla. Ziyarid side: Qabus's Daylamite and Gilite army.
iranian_note: Both armies were Daylamite-based (both sides).

persian_force: Buyid side: Mu'ayyad's Daylamites and Turks. Samanid side: the Khurasan army under the Turkish generals Tash and Fa'iq and the Simjurid governor.

name: First Battle of Laghman
label: First Battle of Laghman
place: near Ghuzak, between Ghazni and Laghman, Afghanistan
persian_force: Sabuktigin's Ghaznavid army: Turkish ghulams with Afghan and Khalaj tribesmen and local levies.
iranian_note: Sabuktigin's armies combined a Turkish ghulam core with Afghan and Khalaj tribal levies (Bosworth, The Ghaznavids).

name: Battle of Balad (death of Badh ibn Dustak, 990)
label: Balad
date: 990 (the Hamdanid article gives 990, the Badh ibn Dustak article 991; exact date unknown)
war: Marwanid conquest of Diyar Bakr and wars with the Hamdanids and Uqaylids of Mosul
place: Balad (Eski Mosul), on the Tigris north of Mosul, Iraq (approximate)
side_a: Marwanid Kurds of Badh ibn Dustak
persian_state: Marwanid Kurds of Badh ibn Dustak
commanders_b: Abu Abdallah al-Husayn ibn Nasir al-Dawla (Hamdanid, an Arab), leading the Uqaylid forces

sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Abdallah_al-Husayn_ibn_Nasir_al-Dawla ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badh_ibn_Dustak ; Ibn al-Athir; Canard, Histoire de la dynastie des H'amdanides (1953); Ibn al-Azraq al-Fariqi, Ta'rikh Mayyafariqin

name: Amida (Hamdanid campaign against the Marwanids, c. 990-991)
label: Amida
date: c. 990-991 (soon after Balad; exact date unknown)
war: Marwanid conquest of Diyar Bakr and wars with the Hamdanids and Uqaylids of Mosul

commanders_b: Abu Abdallah al-Husayn ibn Nasir al-Dawla (Hamdanid, an Arab)

label: Second Battle of Laghman
persian_force: Sabuktigin's army in squadrons of 500, of Afghans and Khalaj with the Turkish ghulam cavalry.

result_basis: Sabuktigin's squadrons of 500 broke Jayapala's confederate army, which was pursued with great slaughter beyond the Indus.
sources: en.wikipedia Second Battle of Laghman; en.wikipedia Sabuktigin; Utbi, Tarikh-i Yamini; Bosworth, The Ghaznavids
note: Hindu Shahis with chiefs of Delhi, Ajmer, Kalinjar and Kannauj. Sabuktigin took the land between Laghman and Peshawar.
qbasis: Wikipedia (Sabuktigin) says his army in this campaign was of Afghans and Khalaj; the ghulam core was Turkish.

name: Defeat of Nuh II's army (991)
label: Defeat of Nuh II's army (991)
commanders_b: Nuh II's commanders (not named in the sources checked)
persian_force: The Samanid army of Transoxiana, largely Turkish ghulams with Iranian levies; composition not recorded.
iranian_note: Late Samanid armies were led and largely manned by Turkish ghulams (Treadwell, Barthold).
result_basis: Bughra Khan destroyed the Samanid army sent against him and went on to take Bukhara in the spring of 992.
borderline: no conventional name; site and commander not given in the sources checked
doubt: Borderline: no conventional name; site and commander not given in the sources checked.
sources: en.wikipedia Nuh II; Barthold, Turkestan; Treadwell, EIr 'Simjurids' (summary)
note: Bughra Khan withdrew from Bukhara and died in 992; Nuh returned.
qbasis: Samanids: an Iranian-led state

name: Herat (994)
label: Herat (994)
date: 23 October 994 (15 Ramadan 384); the Wikipedia article on Nuh II gives August 994
side_a: Nuh II with Sabuktigin and Mahmud
faction_a: Nuh II (Samanids) with Sabuktigin and Mahmud (Ghaznavids)
faction_b: Abu Ali Simjuri and Fa'iq (Samanid rebels)
persian_force: Loyalist side: Sabuktigin's Ghaznavid Turkish ghulams with war elephants, Nuh II's palace ghulams and vassal contingents. Rebel side: the Simjurid army of Khorasan and Fa'iq's ghulams, with the Ziyarid Dara's men (who deserted).
iranian_note: Both armies were led by Turkish ghulams, with Khurasani Iranian and Daylamite contingents (both sides).
result_basis: When the Ziyarid prince Dara went over to Sabuktigin, Abu Ali's winning attack collapsed and he and Fa'iq fled towards Gorgan.
sources: en.wikipedia Sabuktigin; en.wikipedia Nuh II; en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghaznavid Empire; Utbi; Barthold, Turkestan
note: Sabuktigin was rewarded with Balkh and Mahmud with the command of Khorasan.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Nishapur (995)
label: Nishapur (995)
faction_a: Abu Ali Simjuri and Fa'iq (Samanid rebels)
faction_b: Mahmud (Ghaznavids, governor of Khorasan for the Samanids)
persian_force: Rebel side: the Simjurid army and Fa'iq's Turkish ghulams. Ghaznavid side: Mahmud's army of Khorasan with elephants.
iranian_note: Turkish ghulam armies with Khurasani Iranian troops on both sides.
result_basis: Abu Ali and Fa'iq drove Mahmud out of Nishapur and took his elephants and treasure.
sources: en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni; en.wikipedia Ghaznavid-Samanid war; Utbi; Barthold, Turkestan
note: The Wikipedia article on Sabuktigin merges this battle with the battle of Tus that followed.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Tus (995)
label: Tus (995)
faction_b: Abu Ali Simjuri and Fa'iq (Samanid rebels)
persian_force: Ghaznavid side: Sabuktigin's Turkish ghulams with war elephants and Mahmud's army of Khorasan. Rebel side: the Simjurid army and Fa'iq's ghulams.
iranian_note: Turkish ghulam armies with Khurasani and Afghan troops (both sides).
losses_b: many soldiers and commanders crushed by elephants
result_basis: Sabuktigin refused terms and attacked, his elephants crushing many of the rebels; Abu Ali and Fa'iq fled.
sources: en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni; en.wikipedia Nuh II; en.wikipedia Sabuktigin; Utbi; Barthold, Turkestan
note: Abu Ali was handed to Sabuktigin in 996 and executed in 997.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Ghazni (998)
label: Ghazni (998)
persian_force: Both sides: Ghaznavid Turkish ghulams with Afghan and Khalaj levies; Isma'il's army had elephants.
iranian_note: The Ghaznavid army was a Turkish ghulam core with Afghan, Khalaj and Khurasani troops (Bosworth) (both sides).
result_basis: Mahmud's charge broke Isma'il's centre; Isma'il retreated into the fort and surrendered.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Ghazni (998); en.wikipedia Ghaznavid-Samanid war; Utbi; Bosworth, The Ghaznavids
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Merv (999)
label: Merv (999)
side_b: Abd al-Malik II with Begtuzun, Fa'iq and Abu'l-Qasim Simjuri
faction_b: Abd al-Malik II (Samanids) with Begtuzun, Fa'iq and Abu'l-Qasim Simjuri
commanders_b: Abd al-Malik II; Begtuzun; Fa'iq; Abu'l-Qasim Simjuri
persian_force: Ghaznavid side: 32,000 cavalry and 170 elephants in three divisions (Turkish ghulams, Khurasani and Afghan troops). Samanid side: the Turkish ghulam armies of Begtuzun and Fa'iq and the Simjurid troops.
iranian_note: Both armies were led by Turkish ghulams; Iranian Khurasanis served on both sides (both sides).
result_basis: Mahmud defeated the allies; Abu'l-Qasim fled to Kuhistan and Begtuzun withdrew towards Nishapur.
sources: en.wikipedia Ghaznavid-Samanid war; en.wikipedia Abd al-Malik II (Samanid emir); en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni; Utbi
note: The battle followed an attack on Mahmud's baggage incited by the Ziyarid Dara. Mahmud then took all the Samanid land south of the Oxus.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Ispahbud (siege)
label: Ispahbud (siege)
place: the fortress of Ispahbud, Sistan (site not identified), Afghanistan
persian_force: Ghaznavid side: Mahmud's Turkish ghulams and Khurasani troops. Saffarid side: Khalaf's Sistani garrison.
iranian_note: A Turkish-led Ghaznavid army against Sistani Persians (both sides).
result_basis: Khalaf ended the siege by submitting and paying tribute while the fortress was still invested; the sources count it as Mahmud's success.
borderline: the fighting during the siege is not described in the sources checked
doubt: Borderline: the fighting during the siege is not described in the sources checked.
sources: en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni; Bosworth, The History of the Saffarids of Sistan; Utbi
note: Mahmud returned in 1002-1003 and ended Khalaf's rule. Sistan straddles Iran and Afghanistan; the country is a guess.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Qum Rabat Padshahim (Imam Shakir's ambush)
label: Qum Rabat Padshahim
date: End of the 10th century (legend; no firm date)
place: Qum Rabat Padshahim, near Khotan, Xinjiang (China); site not fixed
result_basis: The Tazkirah legend says the Khotanese ambushed the Muslim force and the general Imam Shakir died there.
doubt: Traditional: known only from a doubtful tradition.
sources: Tazkirah-i Tort Imam-i Zabihlar (legend collection, 12th to 18th century); Iranica, 'Khotan iv, history in the Islamic period'
note: Known only from hagiographic legend, which also tells of a 1026 defeat of seven imams by the Buddhist leaders Choqti Rashid and Noqti Rashid. Flagged traditional.

name: Nishapur (February 1001)
label: Nishapur (February 1001)
date: 25 February 1001 (some accounts place Muntasir's taking of Nishapur in late 1000)
commanders_a: Isma'il al-Muntasir; his general Arslan Balu
persian_force: Samanid side: the remnant Samanid guard and Khurasani supporters of the last Samanid; Ghaznavid side: Nasr's garrison of Turkic ghulams and Khurasani troops. The sources give no breakdown.
iranian_note: Both armies were Khorasani forces with Turkic ghulam cores; the Samanid loyalists were largely Persian-speaking Khorasanis and Transoxianans (Barthold, Bosworth).
result_basis: Muntasir's force beat Nasr outside Nishapur and Nasr withdrew to Herat, leaving the field and the city.
borderline: named only by place in the narrative histories
doubt: Borderline: named only by place in the narrative histories.
sources: Utbi, Ta'rikh al-Yamini; Gardizi; Bosworth, The Ghaznavids (1963); en.wikipedia Ghaznavid-Samanid war; en.wikipedia Isma'il Muntasir
note: Mahmud then came up with reinforcements and Muntasir fled to Gurgan without a battle.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Nishapur (September 1001)
label: Nishapur (September 1001)
persian_force: Ghaznavid side: Nasr's Khorasan army reinforced by Altuntash's Turkic ghulams; Samanid side: Muntasir's Khorasani followers, perhaps with Ziyarid help from Gurgan. No breakdown in the sources.
iranian_note: Ghaznavid ghulam cavalry fought Muntasir's mainly Persian-speaking Khorasani partisans.
result_basis: The reinforced Ghaznavid army defeated Muntasir, who fled the field to Gurgan.
borderline: named only by place in the narrative histories
doubt: Borderline: named only by place in the narrative histories.
sources: Utbi; Gardizi; Bosworth, The Ghaznavids; en.wikipedia Ghaznavid-Samanid war
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Peshawar
label: Peshawar
persian_force: About 15,000 picked cavalry (the Turkic ghulam core and Khurasani horse) and 10,000 ghazi volunteers, many of them Afghans (Utbi, as cited by Wikipedia).
iranian_note: The sources name a large corps of ghazis and Afghans beside the Turkic ghulam cavalry; the ghazis were mostly Persian-speaking Khorasanis.
losses_b: 5,000-15,000 killed; Jayapala and 15 of his sons and grandsons captured
result_basis: Jayapala's army broke under Mahmud's cavalry charges and Jayapala was captured on the field.
sources: Utbi, Ta'rikh al-Yamini; Gardizi; Bosworth, The Ghaznavids; en.wikipedia Battle of Peshawar (1001)
note: 'Indian kingdoms': the Hindu Shahis of Jayapala. Chronology of the capture of Jayapala and of his later self-immolation follows Utbi; Satish Chandra doubts the story of his capture and release.
qbasis: The sources name a large corps of ghazis and Afghans beside the Turkic ghulam cavalry; the ghazis were mostly Persian-speaking Khorasanis.

name: Sarakhs (1002)
label: Sarakhs (1002)
persian_force: Ghaznavid side: Nasr's Khorasan army of ghulams and Khurasani troops; Samanid side: Muntasir's followers and Simjurid retainers.
iranian_note: Khorasani armies on both sides, the Ghaznavid one with a Turkic ghulam core.
result_basis: Nasr defeated Muntasir's force at Sarakhs and captured Abu'l-Qasim Simjuri; Muntasir fled.
borderline: named only by place in the narrative histories
doubt: Borderline: named only by place in the narrative histories.
sources: Utbi; Bosworth, The Ghaznavids; en.wikipedia Ghaznavid-Samanid war
note: Year uncertain (late 1001 or 1002).
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Hund
label: Hund
persian_force: The army of Peshawar: Turkic ghulam cavalry, Khurasani horse and Afghan and ghazi volunteers.
iranian_note: Same army as at Peshawar, where the sources name ghazis and Afghans beside the ghulams.
result_basis: Mahmud defeated the Shahi forces before the capital and took Waihind by assault.
sources: Utbi; en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni (campaign table); en.wikipedia Ghaznavid-Hindu Shahi Wars; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghaznavid Empire
note: Jayapala then made peace for 250,000 dinars and 50 elephants and later burned himself.
qbasis: Same army as at Peshawar, where the sources name ghazis and Afghans beside the ghulams.

name: Taq (siege, 1002)
label: Taq (siege, 1002)
place: fortress of Taq, Sistan (site not securely identified), Afghanistan
persian_force: Ghaznavid side: Mahmud's ghulam cavalry, infantry and war elephants; Saffarid side: Khalaf's Sistani garrison.
iranian_note: The defenders were Persian-speaking Sistanis; the Ghaznavid army mixed Turkic ghulams with Khurasani and Afghan troops.
result_basis: Mahmud's troops filled the ditch, elephants broke the gates and Khalaf surrendered the fortress.
sources: Utbi; Ta'rikh-i Sistan; Bosworth, The History of the Saffarids of Sistan (1994); en.wikipedia Ghaznavid-Saffarid war
note: Khalaf's first stand at the fortress of Ispahbud (December 999) is a separate entry. Taq has seven walls and a deep ditch in the sources.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Uk
label: Uk
place: fort of Uk, Sistan (site not identified), Afghanistan
commanders_a: Mahmud of Ghazni, Nasr, Altuntash, Abu Abdallah Muhammad al-Ta'i
persian_force: Ghaznavid side: about 10,000 men including Hindu troops (who sacked the mosque of Zaranj), under Nasr, Altuntash and the Arab commander al-Ta'i; rebel side: Sistani partisans of the Saffarids.
iranian_note: The rebels were Persian-speaking Sistanis; the Ghaznavid force had Turkic, Indian and Arab elements (Bosworth).
result_basis: The Ghaznavids took the rebel-held fort in a night surprise attack.
borderline: a revolt in Sistan, counted as civil
doubt: Borderline: a revolt in Sistan, counted as civil.
sources: Ta'rikh-i Sistan; Bosworth, The Ghaznavids; en.wikipedia Ghaznavid-Saffarid war
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Bhatiya (siege)
label: Bhatiya (siege)
place: Bhatiya (probably Bhera; Uch, Bhatinda and Bhatnair also proposed), Pakistan
persian_force: Mahmud's standing army of Turkic ghulam cavalry with Khurasani, Afghan and ghazi troops; the sources give no breakdown.
iranian_note: Bosworth describes Mahmud's army as a Turkic ghulam core with Khurasani, Afghan, Daylamite, Kurdish and Arab units and Persian-speaking volunteers.
result_basis: Mahmud broke Baji Rai's army in a four-day field battle and then took his fortress; Baji Rai killed himself.
sources: Utbi; al-Biruni; en.wikipedia Siege of Bhatiya
note: One entry for the field battle and the siege that followed. Site disputed.
qbasis: Bosworth describes Mahmud's army as a Turkic ghulam core with Khurasani, Afghan, Daylamite, Kurdish and Arab units and Persian-speaking volunteers.

name: Fall of Khotan to the Karakhanids
label: Fall of Khotan to the Karakhanids
date: About 1006 (the conquest was complete by 1016-17, when Yusuf Qadir Khan struck coins at Khotan)
commanders_b: Khotanese king (Visa' Sagemayi, r. 999-1006, per the Kingdom of Khotan article)
result_basis: Khotan ceased to be an independent Buddhist kingdom; Yusuf Qadir Khan ruled it and called himself Khan of Khotan.
sources: Abu Nasr Utbi, Kitab-i Yamini (Yusuf Qadir Khan, Khan of Khotan, 1006-7); Iranica, 'Khotan iv, history in the Islamic period'; Millward, Eurasian Crossroads (2007); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Khotan
note: Known as a conquest after decades of war; no field battle or siege of the city is described in the sources read. The Khotanese were Saka (an East Iranian language) but the royal house used Indic names; Emmerick thinks the king was an Iranian speaker. Whether the city was besieged is unknown.

name: Hulwan (1006)
label: Hulwan
result_basis: Badr dislodged Abu'l-Fath from Hulwan and he retired to Baghdad; the Annazid recovered his position within a few years.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annazids ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasanwayhids ; Ibn al-Athir; Minorsky, 'Hasanwayhids' and 'Annazids', EI2
note: A clash between two Kurdish dynasts; the Annazid article says only that Badr 'temporarily dislodged' Abu'l-Fath, so the scale of the fighting is unclear.

name: Multan (siege, 1006)
label: Multan (siege, 1006)
commanders_b: Abu'l-Fath Dawud, Ismaili amir of Multan
persian_force: Mahmud's field army: Turkic ghulam cavalry, Khurasani and Afghan troops and ghazi volunteers (no breakdown in the sources).
iranian_note: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).
result_basis: After seven days Dawud bought off the siege with an annual tribute of 20,000 dirhams and kept Multan; a siege ended by treaty while the place was still invested is a draw under the test.
sources: Gardizi; Utbi; en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni; en.wikipedia Ghaznavid-Hindu Shahi Wars
note: Wikipedia lists it as a Ghaznavid victory; the city was annexed only in 1010. 'Indian kingdoms' here is the Ismaili emirate of Multan. Mahmud broke off to meet the Qarakhanid invasion of Khorasan.
qbasis: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).

name: Indus (1006)
label: Indus (1006)
place: near the Indus crossing above Peshawar, Pakistan
persian_force: Mahmud's field army on its way to Multan: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Khurasani, Afghan and ghazi troops (no breakdown in the sources).
iranian_note: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).
result_basis: Anandapala, who tried to bar Mahmud's road to Multan, was defeated and fled towards Kashmir.
borderline: the site is not given precisely
doubt: Borderline: the site is not given precisely.
sources: Utbi; en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni (campaign table: Battle of the Indus, March-April 1006); en.wikipedia Ghaznavid-Hindu Shahi Wars
note: Anandapala was pursued to Sodra on the Chenab.
qbasis: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).

name: Balkh (1008)
label: Balkh (1008)
place: plain of Katar, about 12 miles from Balkh, Afghanistan
commanders_a: Mahmud of Ghazni; Altuntash (right), Arslan Jadhib (left), Nasr, Abu Nasr Farighuni of Guzgan and Abu Abdallah Muhammad al-Ta'i (centre)
commanders_b: Ilig Nasr Khan, Yusuf Qadir Khan of Khotan, Chaghartigin
persian_force: Mahmud's whole army with a front line of 500 elephants: Turkic ghulams, the Farighunid prince of Guzgan with his levies, Arab horse under al-Ta'i, Khurasani and Indian troops.
iranian_note: The Farighunid ruler of Guzgan (an Iranian local dynasty) and Khurasani levies fought beside the Turkic ghulams and al-Ta'i's Arabs.
result_basis: The Qarakhanid army panicked and fled before Mahmud's elephants, many drowning in the Oxus.
sources: Utbi; Gardizi; Barthold, Turkestan; Bosworth, The Ghaznavids; en.wikipedia Kara-Khanid invasion of Khorasan
note: Also called the battle of Katar (or Sharkhiyan in some modern accounts).
qbasis: The Farighunid ruler of Guzgan (an Iranian local dynasty) and Khurasani levies fought beside the Turkic ghulams and al-Ta'i's Arabs.

name: Chach
label: Chach
place: plain of Chach near Hazro, between Waihind and the Indus, Pakistan
commanders_a: Mahmud of Ghazni; Arslan Jadhib and Abdallah al-Ta'i in the pursuit
commanders_b: Anandapala and his son Trilochanapala (Hindu Shahi), with allied rajas
persian_force: 6,000 archers, 6,000 cavalry and 10,000 infantry with the sultan's elite guard (Firishta via Wikipedia).
iranian_note: The sources give arms, not peoples; inferred from the Ghaznavid recruitment of Turkic ghulams, Khurasanis and Afghans (Bosworth).
result_basis: After a Khokhar/Gakhar onslaught on his camp, Mahmud's guards counter-attacked and the Shahi army fled in rout, leaving 30 elephants.
sources: Utbi; Firishta; en.wikipedia Battle of Chach; en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni
note: Often called the battle of Waihind. Firishta's figures are late.
qbasis: The sources give arms, not peoples; inferred from the Ghaznavid recruitment of Turkic ghulams, Khurasanis and Afghans (Bosworth).

name: Nagarkot (siege, 1009)
label: Nagarkot (siege, 1009)
commanders_b: Hindu Shahi refugees and the temple garrison (not named)
persian_force: The army of Chach in pursuit: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Khurasani and Afghan troops.
iranian_note: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).
result_basis: The fort capitulated after three days and its temple treasure was taken.
borderline: short siege; how much fighting is unclear
doubt: Borderline: short siege; how much fighting is unclear.
sources: Utbi; en.wikipedia Battle of Chach; en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni
qbasis: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).

name: Multan (1010)
label: Multan (1010)
commanders_b: Abu'l-Fath Dawud, Ismaili amir of Multan (captured)
persian_force: Mahmud's standing army (no breakdown in the sources).
iranian_note: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).
result_basis: Mahmud defeated Dawud, took Multan and carried him off a prisoner.
borderline: details of the fighting are thin
doubt: Borderline: details of the fighting are thin.
sources: Gardizi; en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni (campaign table: Battle of Multan, 1010)
note: 'Indian kingdoms' here is the Ismaili emirate of Multan.
qbasis: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).

name: Ahangaran
label: Ahangaran
place: Ahangaran, the Ghurid seat on the upper Hari Rud, Ghor, Afghanistan
commanders_a: Mahmud of Ghazni; Altuntash and Arslan Jadhib (advance guard)
commanders_b: Muhammad ibn Suri (captured), his son Shith (captured)
persian_force: Ghaznavid side: Mahmud's army with an advance guard of Turkic ghulam cavalry under Altuntash and Arslan Jadhib; Ghurid side: about 10,000 Ghuri highlanders.
iranian_note: The Ghurid force was Persian-speaking (Tajik) highlanders; the Ghaznavid army had a Turkic ghulam core with Khurasani and Afghan troops.
losses_b: unknown; Ibn Suri and his son captured
result_basis: After the advance guard was checked, Mahmud feigned a retreat, drew the Ghurids onto open ground and routed them, capturing Ibn Suri.
borderline: the Ghurid chiefs of Mandesh long before the Ghurid state of Firuzkuh; counted civil only because the Ghurids are on the list of Persian states
doubt: Borderline: the Ghurid chiefs of Mandesh long before the Ghurid state of Firuzkuh; counted civil only because the Ghurids are on the list of Persian states.
sources: Utbi; Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri; en.wikipedia Ghaznavid campaign of Ghur; en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni
note: If the early Ghurid chiefdom is not treated as a listed state, this is a Ghaznavid victory over the Ghuris (not civil).
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Shamkir (siege, 1012)
label: Shamkir
date: 1012 (Georgian chronicle date as given by Rayfield; exact month unknown)
commanders_b: the Shaddadid emir (Fadl I ibn Muhammad, a Kurd)
result_basis: Bagrat besieged the town and the Shaddadids bought him off with tribute, which they paid until his death in 1014.
sources: Rayfield, Edge of Empires: A History of Georgia (2012) p. 74; Minorsky, Studies in Caucasian History (1953) and 'Shaddadids', Encyclopaedia of Islam 2nd ed.; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgian%E2%80%93Shaddadid_wars
note: A minor siege known from one line in a modern history; the Shaddadid emir is not named in the Wikipedia summary and Fadl I is the likely ruler. Kurdish by descent as the sources describe the dynasty.

name: Sutlej (1012)
label: Sutlej (1012)
place: on a river crossing on the road to Thanesar (the Sutlej in the campaign table), India
persian_force: Mahmud's standing army (no breakdown in the sources): Turkic ghulam cavalry with Khurasani, Afghan and Indian troops and ghazi volunteers.
iranian_note: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).
result_basis: Rama's army, posted behind the river, was driven off and Mahmud went on to sack Thanesar.
borderline: date and site uncertain; the sack of Thanesar itself was not a battle
doubt: Borderline: date and site uncertain; the sack of Thanesar itself was not a battle.
sources: Utbi; en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni (campaign table: Battle of the Sutlej, 1012)
qbasis: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).

name: Tausi
label: Tausi
place: River Tausi (Poonch or Tohi river), India
commanders_b: Trilochanapala (Hindu Shahi); Tunga, Jayasimha, Srivardhana and Vibhramarka of Kashmir
persian_force: The army of Nandana: Turkic ghulam cavalry, Daylamite and Afghan foot, archers.
iranian_note: Same army that fought at Nandana, where Daylamites and Afghans are named.
result_basis: Mahmud's main army routed Tunga's Kashmiris the day after their skirmish success and Trilochanapala failed to rally his men.
sources: Kalhana, Rajatarangini; Utbi; en.wikipedia Battle of the River Tausi
note: 'Indian kingdoms': the Hindu Shahis with the Lohara kingdom of Kashmir.
qbasis: Same army that fought at Nandana, where Daylamites and Afghans are named.

name: Nandana
label: Nandana
commanders_a: Mahmud of Ghazni, Altuntash (centre), Amir Nasr (right), Arslan Jadhib (left), Abu Abdallah Muhammad al-Ta'i (advance guard, wounded)
commanders_b: Bhimapala (Hindu Shahi), Kashmiri contingent under Tunga
persian_force: Cavalry in three divisions with Daylamite warriors and Afghan spearmen deployed to encircle the enemy, and archers against the elephants (Utbi via Wikipedia).
iranian_note: The sources name Daylamite and Afghan foot beside the Turkic ghulam cavalry and al-Ta'i's Arabs.
result_basis: Bhimapala's force was lured into the open and routed, his elephant charge broke under archery, and Mahmud then took the fort.
sources: Utbi; Gardizi; en.wikipedia Battle of Nandana; en.wikipedia Ghaznavid-Hindu Shahi Wars
note: Also called the battle of Nardin or Nazin. One entry for the battle and the capture of the fort.
qbasis: The sources name Daylamite and Afghan foot beside the Turkic ghulam cavalry and al-Ta'i's Arabs.

name: Kermanshah (Shams al-Dawla against the Annazids, c. 1014-1016)
label: Kermanshah
date: c. 1014-1016 (the Annazid article dates the whole sequence from 1014; Avicenna entered Shams al-Dawla's service about 1015)
commanders_a: Abu'l-Shawk Faris ibn Muhammad (Annazid, a Kurd)
commanders_b: Shams al-Dawla (Buyid emir of Hamadan, of Daylamite origin)
result_basis: The Annazid article says Shams al-Dawla marched on the Annazids and was defeated near Kermanshah; Avicenna, in his service, reportedly saw the battle.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annazids ; Ibn al-Athir; Minorsky, 'Annazids', EI2; Gohlman, The Life of Ibn Sina (1974)
note: The sequence in the sources is confused (Hilal ibn Badr was killed in 1014, Tahir ibn Hilal killed by Abu'l-Shawk, then Shams al-Dawla's campaign), and I have no second source for the date of the battle. Both sides are Iranian: Kurds against a Daylamite Buyid army.

name: Khwabin (siege)
label: Khwabin (siege)
place: fortress of Khwabin, western Ghur, Afghanistan
persian_force: Ghaznavid side: a detachment of Mahmud's army under the prince Mas'ud; Ghurid side: the Ghuri garrison.
iranian_note: Persian-speaking Ghuri defenders against a Ghaznavid force with a Turkic core.
result_basis: The defenders' chief was killed by an arrow shot by Mas'ud and the garrison surrendered.
borderline: a small siege; the Ghuri chiefs counted as Ghurids (see Ahangaran)
doubt: Borderline: a small siege; the Ghuri chiefs counted as Ghurids (see Ahangaran).
sources: Bayhaqi; en.wikipedia Ghaznavid campaign of Ghur
note: Mas'ud's further sieges in Ghur in 1020 (Bartar, Shan, Tur) are not entered separately.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Lohkot (siege, 1015)
label: Lohkot (siege, 1015)
place: Lohkot (Loharkot, near Loran, Tosa Maidan route), India
persian_force: Mahmud's field army (no breakdown in the sources).
iranian_note: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).
losses_b: heavy, mostly in the winter retreat
result_basis: Mahmud abandoned the siege at the onset of winter and retreated with heavy losses.
sources: Kalhana, Rajatarangini; Gardizi; en.wikipedia Siege of Lohkot (1015)
note: Wikipedia calls the result inconclusive; under the test a raised siege is a win for the defender.
qbasis: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).

name: Hazarasp
label: Hazarasp
place: near Hazarasp, on the road to Gurganj, Uzbekistan
faction_b: Khwarazm (the Ma'munid regime of the army that killed Ma'mun II)
commanders_a: Mahmud of Ghazni, Abu Abdallah Muhammad al-Ta'i, Altuntash, Arslan Jadhib
persian_force: Ghaznavid side: Mahmud's main army, claimed at 100,000 horse with elephants; Khwarazmian side: about 50,000, the Turkic ghulam army of the Khwarazmshahs (with a Bukharan garrison under Alptegin) and Khwarazmian levies.
iranian_note: Both armies had Turkic ghulam cores; the Khwarazmians spoke an East Iranian language and the Ghaznavid army had Khurasani and Afghan troops.
strength_a: 100,000 cavalry and 500 elephants (Wikipedia infobox; certainly exaggerated)
result_basis: The Khwarazmian army was decisively beaten and scattered and Mahmud marched on to Gurganj.
borderline: counted civil because the Ma'munid Khwarazmshahs were a local Iranian dynasty seated in Khwarazm
doubt: Borderline: counted civil because the Ma'munid Khwarazmshahs were a local Iranian dynasty seated in Khwarazm.
sources: Bayhaqi (after al-Biruni); Gardizi; Bosworth, CHI 4; en.wikipedia Ghaznavid conquest of Khwarazm
note: Wikipedia's battle article names no site and its Mahmud article calls it the battle of Gurganj; Bosworth places the decisive battle near Hazarasp. Earlier Khumartash had routed al-Ta'i's vanguard before being beaten and captured by the sultan's guard.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Kannauj (1018)
label: Kannauj (1018)
date: 20 December 1018 (the body of the Wikipedia article says January 1019)
persian_force: Mahmud's regulars and some 20,000 volunteers from Transoxiana (Utbi); Firishta's 100,000 horse and 20,000 foot is a late exaggeration.
iranian_note: Utbi names some 20,000 Transoxianan ghazi volunteers beside the Turkic ghulam regulars.
strength_a: 11,000 regulars (Sibt ibn al-Jawzi); 20,000 volunteers (Utbi); 100,000 horse and 20,000 foot (Firishta)
result_basis: Rajyapala fled without battle and Mahmud took the seven forts of Kannauj in a single day.
borderline: the Pratihara king fled; how much fighting there was at the forts is unclear
doubt: Borderline: the Pratihara king fled; how much fighting there was at the forts is unclear.
sources: Utbi; Sibt ibn al-Jawzi; Firishta; en.wikipedia Ghaznavid invasions of Kannauj
note: The minor actions of the same march (Baran/Bulandshahr surrendered, Mathura plundered, Asi abandoned) are not entered.
qbasis: Utbi names some 20,000 Transoxianan ghazi volunteers beside the Turkic ghulam regulars.

name: Mahaban
label: Mahaban
place: Mahaban, on the Yamuna near Mathura, India
persian_force: The Kannauj expedition: Mahmud's regulars (11,000 per Sibt ibn al-Jawzi) with about 20,000 volunteers from Transoxiana (Utbi).
iranian_note: Utbi names some 20,000 ghazi volunteers from Transoxiana, mostly Persian-speaking, beside the Turkic ghulam regulars.
result_basis: Kulchand's army was routed and driven into the Yamuna, and Kulchand killed himself.
sources: Utbi; Nazim, The Life and Times of Sultan Mahmud of Ghazna (1931); en.wikipedia Ghaznavid invasions of Kannauj; en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni
note: Utbi's casualty figure is typical of the panegyric sources.
qbasis: Utbi names some 20,000 ghazi volunteers from Transoxiana, mostly Persian-speaking, beside the Turkic ghulam regulars.

name: Munj (siege)
label: Munj (siege)
persian_force: The Kannauj expedition: Turkic ghulam regulars and Transoxianan volunteers.
iranian_note: Same army as at Kannauj, with many Persian-speaking volunteers (Utbi).
result_basis: The fort was stormed and taken.
borderline: obscure fort; site not identified
doubt: Borderline: obscure fort; site not identified.
sources: Utbi; en.wikipedia Ghaznavid invasions of Kannauj; en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni
qbasis: Same army as at Kannauj, with many Persian-speaking volunteers (Utbi).

name: Sharwa
label: Sharwa
place: near Sharwa (perhaps near Meerut or Sirsawa), India
persian_force: The Kannauj expedition: Turkic ghulam regulars and Transoxianan volunteers.
iranian_note: Same army as at Kannauj, with many Persian-speaking volunteers (Utbi).
result_basis: Mahmud overtook Chand Rai's retreating army and defeated it, taking his elephants and baggage.
borderline: site uncertain
doubt: Borderline: site uncertain.
sources: Utbi; en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni (campaign table: Battle of Sharwa)
qbasis: Same army as at Kannauj, with many Persian-speaking volunteers (Utbi).

name: Ramganga
label: Ramganga
date: late 1019 (410 AH); Wikipedia's articles give October 1019, October or 15 December 1020
place: Ramganga river (the Rahib of the sources) near Afzalgarh, India
persian_force: Mahmud's mounted army, crossing on horseback and on inflated skins (no breakdown by people in the sources).
iranian_note: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).
result_basis: Eight of Mahmud's guards swam the river, the army crossed on horses and skins, and Trilochanapala's entrenched army fled with heavy loss.
sources: Utbi; Gardizi; en.wikipedia Battle of the Ramganga; en.wikipedia Ghaznavid-Hindu Shahi Wars
note: Also called the battle of the Rahib. Mahmud then faced the Chandela Vidyadhara, whose army withdrew in the night without battle (not entered).
qbasis: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).

name: Lohkot (siege, 1021)
label: Lohkot (siege, 1021)
persian_force: Mahmud's field army (no breakdown in the sources).
iranian_note: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).
result_basis: Mahmud again gave up the siege before winter and withdrew.
sources: Gardizi; en.wikipedia Siege of Lohkot (1015); en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni
qbasis: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).

name: Gwalior (siege, 1022)
label: Gwalior (siege, 1022)
commanders_b: the Kachchhapaghata ruler of Gwalior, vassal of the Chandelas
persian_force: Mahmud's field army (no breakdown in the sources).
iranian_note: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).
result_basis: The ruler submitted after four days and gave 35 elephants, and Mahmud moved on without taking the fort; a siege ended by treaty is a draw under the test.
borderline: short siege ended by submission; fighting not described
doubt: Borderline: short siege ended by submission; fighting not described.
sources: Utbi; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni (campaign table)
note: Wikipedia lists the 1022 sieges as Ghaznavid victories.
qbasis: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).

name: Kalinjar (siege, 1022)
label: Kalinjar (siege, 1022)
persian_force: Mahmud's field army (no breakdown in the sources).
iranian_note: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).
result_basis: Vidyadhara bought peace with tribute and elephants while the fort was invested and kept Kalinjar; a siege ended by treaty is a draw under the test.
borderline: siege ended by submission; fighting not described
doubt: Borderline: siege ended by submission; fighting not described.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Utbi; en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni (campaign table)
note: Mahmud returned fifteen forts to Vidyadhara in exchange for his submission (as usually told).
qbasis: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).

name: Modhera
label: Modhera
place: Mundher of the sources (probably Modhera), Gujarat, India
persian_force: The Somnath expedition: about 30,000 cavalry with volunteers (see Somnath).
iranian_note: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).
result_basis: About 20,000 Hindu fighters who barred the road were defeated and dispersed.
borderline: identification of the site uncertain; known only from the Muslim chroniclers
doubt: Borderline: identification of the site uncertain; known only from the Muslim chroniclers.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Sack of Somnath; en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni ('Battle of Kathiawar')
qbasis: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).

name: Shamkir (siege, 1026)
label: Shamkir
commanders_b: Fadl I ibn Muhammad (a Kurd), emir of Ganja
result_basis: Frye (and the Wikipedia summary of the Georgian-Shaddadid wars) says George I launched the siege and was defeated.
sources: Frye ed., Cambridge History of Iran vol. 4 (1975) p. 241; Minorsky, Studies in Caucasian History (1953) and 'Shaddadids', Encyclopaedia of Islam 2nd ed.; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgian%E2%80%93Shaddadid_wars
note: Known from a single sentence; details of the fighting are not given. The Shaddadid ruler is inferred (Fadl I).

name: Somnath
label: Somnath
date: 6-8 January 1026 (the town seized 6 January, assault 7 January, the temple taken 8 January)
commanders_b: Mandalika (Abhira overseer of the fort); Bhima I (Chaulukya) had fled to Kanthkot
persian_force: About 30,000 cavalry and an unknown number of volunteers, each man with two camels (Ibn al-Athir via Wikipedia); the usual Ghaznavid mixture of Turkic ghulams, Khurasanis, Afghans and Indians.
iranian_note: The sources give totals only; inferred from the Ghaznavid recruitment of ghulams and Persian-speaking volunteers (Bosworth).
result_basis: After three days of assaults and counter-attacks the Ghaznavids stormed the walls and the shrine, and the temple was sacked.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Gardizi; al-Biruni; Thapar, Somanatha (2004); en.wikipedia Sack of Somnath
note: The account rests on Muslim sources; Thapar and others doubt its scale. 'Indian kingdoms': the Chaulukyas and the Abhira lord of the fort.
qbasis: The sources give totals only; inferred from the Ghaznavid recruitment of ghulams and Persian-speaking volunteers (Bosworth).

name: Nahavand (1028)
label: Nahavand (1028)
war: Wars of Ala al-Dawla Muhammad (Kakuyid expansion in Jibal)
side_b: Bavandids of Tabaristan and allied rivals
faction_b: Bavandids of Tabaristan and allied rivals
commanders_b: Abu Ja'far Muhammad, Bavandid ispahbad (captured with his two sons)
persian_force: Kakuyid side: Ala al-Dawla's Daylamite and Turkish troops; opposing side: Tabaristani (Mazandarani) levies of the Bavandid ispahbad and Kurdish allies.
iranian_note: Both sides were raised mainly from Daylamites, Tabaristanis and Kurds, with Turkish ghulams in the Kakuyid army.
losses_b: unknown; the Bavandid ruler and his sons captured
result_basis: Ala al-Dawla won a great victory and captured the Bavandid ruler and his sons on the field.
borderline: named only by place; details thin
doubt: Borderline: named only by place; details thin.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Bosworth, 'Kakuyids', Encyclopaedia Iranica; en.wikipedia Muhammad ibn Rustam Dushmanziyar
note: The Bavandids, an Iran-seated dynasty of Tabaristan, are treated as a Persian state.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Ribat-i Farawa
label: Ribat-i Farawa
war: Ghaznavid-Seljuk wars (the Turkmen of Arslan Isra'il in Khorasan)
place: Ribat-i Farawa (near Serdar, formerly Gyzylarbat), Turkmenistan
commanders_b: Turkmen chiefs of the Seljuk clan of Arslan Isra'il
persian_force: Mahmud's army in Khorasan (no breakdown in the sources): Turkic ghulam cavalry and Khurasani troops.
iranian_note: Inferred from the usual recruitment of the Ghaznavid army in Khorasan (Bosworth).
result_basis: Mahmud defeated the Turkmen bands that had beaten his governor of Tus, and drove them out towards the Balkhan mountains.
borderline: details thin
doubt: Borderline: details thin.
sources: Bayhaqi; Gardizi; Bosworth, The Ghaznavids; en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni (campaign table)
note: 'Oghuz': the Turkmen followers of Arslan Isra'il, kinsmen of Tughril and Chaghri, whom Mahmud had let into Khorasan in 1025.
qbasis: Inferred from the usual recruitment of the Ghaznavid army in Khorasan (Bosworth).

name: Maragha (Wahsudan against the Oghuz, 1029)
label: Maragha
date: 1029 (as given in the Rawwadid article; month unknown)
commanders_a: Wahsudan ibn Muhammad (Rawwadid, of Arab descent but Kurdicised and reckoned a Kurdish dynasty)
result_basis: The Rawwadid article says Wahsudan, with the Hadhbani Kurds, defeated the Oghuz invaders at Maragha.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rawadid_dynasty ; Minorsky, 'Rawwadids', EI2 and Studies in Caucasian History (1953); Ibn al-Athir
note: The Rawwadids were of Arab (Azd) origin but Kurdicised; the Hadhbani Kurds are the named unit that qualifies the battle regardless of how the dynasty is classed.

name: Sarjahan (siege)
label: Sarjahan (siege)
place: Sarjahan castle, near Soltaniyeh, Zanjan, Iran
commanders_a: Mas'ud, with the Daylamite Marzuban ibn Hasan
persian_force: Ghaznavid side: Mas'ud's army with Daylamite chiefs who had come over to him; Sallarid side: Daylamite and Gilaki troops of the Musafirid ruler of Tarom.
iranian_note: The defenders were Daylamites and Mas'ud fought alongside Daylamite chieftains; his own army had a Turkic ghulam core.
result_basis: Mas'ud besieged the fort, Ibrahim came out to fight and was defeated and captured, and his son submitted.
sources: Bayhaqi; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Ghaznavid campaigns in Persia
note: Mahmud had entered Rayy without resistance on 26 May 1029 (not entered: a capture without fighting).
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Defeat of Fadl I in Georgia (1030)
label: Defeat of Fadl I in Georgia
place: a place on the Georgian-Armenian route home to Ganja (site not given); Georgia or northern Armenia
result_basis: Fadl I, returning from a successful raid into Georgia, was ambushed and his army reportedly lost about 10,000 men.
sources: Minorsky, Studies in Caucasian History (1953) p. 43; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgian%E2%80%93Shaddadid_wars ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaddadids
note: Not a named battle in the sources; entered under a descriptive name because it is a real engagement with a specific loss. Location unknown.

name: Isfahan (1030)
label: Isfahan (1030)
persian_force: Ghaznavid side: Mas'ud's western army of Turkic ghulams and Khurasani troops; Kakuyid side: Ala al-Dawla's Daylamite and Turkish soldiers with Kurdish allies.
iranian_note: Kakuyid armies were Daylamite with Turkish ghulams; Ghaznavid armies had a Turkic core with Iranian units (Bosworth).
result_basis: Mas'ud defeated Ala al-Dawla, who fled to the Buyids at Ahvaz, and occupied Isfahan.
borderline: the fighting is thinly reported; may have been more submission than battle
doubt: Borderline: the fighting is thinly reported; may have been more submission than battle.
sources: Bayhaqi; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Ghaznavid campaigns in Persia; en.wikipedia Muhammad ibn Rustam Dushmanziyar
note: Ala al-Dawla was then left as a tributary; Mas'ud left for Ghazni on Mahmud's death (April 1030).
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Makran
label: Makran
commanders_a: Yariq-Toghmish (Ghaznavid commander), with the claimant Abu'l-Askar
commanders_b: Isa ibn Ma'dan, ruler of Makran (killed)
persian_force: Selected officers (muqaddams) and 2,000 branded (ghulam) cavalry sent by Mas'ud, with Abu'l-Askar's local followers.
iranian_note: The Ghaznavid detachment was ghulam cavalry; the claimant's men were local Makranis, who spoke Iranian languages.
strength_a: 2,000 branded cavalry and officers, plus the claimant's men
result_basis: Isa's much larger army was beaten and Isa killed, and Abu'l-Askar was installed as ruler.
sources: Bayhaqi; Bosworth, The Ghaznavids; en.wikipedia Ghaznavid campaigns in Persia; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghaznavid Empire
note: 'Makran' (new entity name): the Ma'danid amirate of Makran, seated at Kiz in present-day Pakistan.
qbasis: The Ghaznavid detachment was ghulam cavalry; the claimant's men were local Makranis, who spoke Iranian languages.

name: Edessa (Bal's expedition, 1032)
label: Edessa
side_b: Arab tribes backed by the Roman Empire
commanders_a: Nasr al-Dawla Ahmad ibn Marwan (a Kurd), directing; his general Bal with 5,000 horse
commanders_b: an Arab tribal chief (killed; name not given in the source consulted)
result_basis: Bal took the city and killed the Arab chief, then asked Nasr al-Dawla for reinforcements; the Romans recovered Edessa in 1033.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marwanids_(Diyar_Bakr) ; Ibn al-Azraq al-Fariqi; Canard, 'Marwanids', EI2
note: The page gives few details and the Roman and Arab sides (Maniakes, Banu Numayr) are not named in it. The Marwanid army is said to rely on Kurdish tribesmen, but Bal's ethnicity is not stated.

name: Dabusiyya
label: Dabusiyya
place: near Dabusiyya, between Bukhara and Samarkand, Uzbekistan
commanders_a: Altuntash, Khwarazmshah (mortally wounded); his vizier Ahmad ibn Abd al-Samad
commanders_b: Ali Tegin Bughra Khan, with Seljuk Turkmen allies
persian_force: Altuntash's army of Khwarazm (Turkic ghulams and Khwarazmian troops) reinforced by Ghaznavid regulars sent by Mas'ud.
iranian_note: The Khwarazm army combined Turkic ghulams with Khwarazmian levies, who spoke an East Iranian language.
result_basis: The bloody battle had no clear victor: Ali Tegin's army fell back, Altuntash was mortally wounded, and his vizier hid his death and led the army home under a truce.
sources: Bayhaqi; Bosworth, The Ghaznavids; en.wikipedia Battle of Dabusiyya; en.wikipedia Altuntash (khwarazmshah)
note: Wikipedia calls it a stalemate/indecisive.
qbasis: The Khwarazm army combined Turkic ghulams with Khwarazmian levies, who spoke an East Iranian language.

name: Sarsuti (siege)
label: Sarsuti (siege)
place: fortress of Sarsuti (identified either with Sarsawa near Saharanpur or a fort on the road to Kashmir), India
persian_force: Mas'ud's army (no breakdown in the sources): Turkic ghulams, Indian troops and Khurasani soldiers.
iranian_note: Mas'ud's army had a Turkic core with large Indian contingents and Iranian units (Bosworth).
result_basis: Mas'ud took the fortress.
borderline: site and details uncertain
doubt: Borderline: site and details uncertain.
sources: Gardizi; Bayhaqi; en.wikipedia Mas'ud I of Ghazni; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghaznavid Empire ('Siege of Sarsawa')
qbasis: Mas'ud's army had a Turkic core with large Indian contingents and Iranian units (Bosworth).

name: Kerman (1034)
label: Kerman (1034)
commanders_a: Bahram ibn Mafinna, vizier of Abu Kalijar
commanders_b: the Ghaznavid governor of Kerman (not named)
persian_force: Buyid side: about 10,000 Daylamite and Turkish troops of Fars; Ghaznavid side: 4,000 cavalry, 2,500 infantry and 5 elephants.
iranian_note: Buyid armies of Fars were Daylamite foot and Turkish horse; the Ghaznavid garrison had a Turkic core.
result_basis: The Buyid army defeated the Ghaznavid garrison force, which retreated to Nishapur.
borderline: named only by province
doubt: Borderline: named only by province.
sources: Bayhaqi; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Ghaznavid campaigns in Persia; en.wikipedia Mas'ud I of Ghazni (dates it c. 1037)
note: An earlier Ghaznavid invasion of Kerman (1031) also failed; it is not entered for lack of detail.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Nasa
label: Nasa
date: June or July 1035 (the army left for Nasa on 19 June 1035)
place: near Nasa (Nisa, by Bagir near Ashgabat), Turkmenistan
persian_force: About 15,000 regulars under the chamberlain Begtoghdi: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Indian, Kurdish, Arab and Khurasani units in the usual Ghaznavid mixture (no breakdown in the sources).
iranian_note: Inferred from the Ghaznavid recruitment under Mas'ud: a Turkic ghulam core with Indian, Daylamite, Kurdish, Arab and Khurasani units (Bosworth).
result_basis: The Seljuks drew Begtoghdi's army on with a feigned retreat, then fell on it and routed it.
sources: Bayhaqi; Bosworth, The Ghaznavids; en.wikipedia Battle of Nasa (1035)
note: 'Oghuz': the Seljuk Turkmen under Tughril and Chaghri, not yet a state seated in Iran. Mas'ud then ceded Nasa, Farawa and Dihistan to them. The List of battles places Nasa in Tabaristan, which is wrong.
qbasis: Inferred from the Ghaznavid recruitment under Mas'ud: a Turkic ghulam core with Indian, Daylamite, Kurdish, Arab and Khurasani units (Bosworth).

name: Hansi (siege)
label: Hansi (siege)
commanders_b: the Tomara garrison of Hansi (commander not named)
persian_force: Mas'ud's army (no breakdown in the sources): Turkic ghulams, Indian troops and Khurasani soldiers.
iranian_note: Mas'ud's army had a Turkic core with large Indian contingents and Iranian units (Bosworth).
result_basis: Mas'ud stormed Hansi after a short siege.
sources: Bayhaqi; Gardizi; en.wikipedia Mas'ud I of Ghazni; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghaznavid Empire
note: Mas'ud then took Sonipat (not entered).
qbasis: Mas'ud's army had a Turkic core with large Indian contingents and Iranian units (Bosworth).

name: Rayy (1038)
label: Rayy (1038)
persian_force: Kakuyid side: Ala al-Dawla's Daylamite and Turkish troops; Ghaznavid side: the garrison of Rayy (1,500 in one infobox figure).
iranian_note: Kakuyid armies were Daylamite with Turkish ghulams; the Ghaznavid garrison was mainly ghulam cavalry.
result_basis: The Kakuyids defeated the Ghaznavid garrison, whose commander was killed, and the Ghaznavids abandoned Rayy.
borderline: thinly reported; Wikipedia's Kakuyid article speaks only of an occupation of Rayy
doubt: Borderline: thinly reported; Wikipedia's Kakuyid article speaks only of an occupation of Rayy.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Ghaznavid campaigns in Persia; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghaznavid Empire
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Sarakhs (1038)
label: Sarakhs (1038)
commanders_b: Subashi (commander in Khorasan), with Begtoghdi and the civil governor Abu'l-Fadl Suri
persian_force: The Ghaznavid army of Khorasan (15,000-25,000 in an unsourced estimate): Turkic ghulam cavalry, Indian, Kurdish and Arab units and Khurasani foot.
iranian_note: Inferred from the Ghaznavid recruitment under Mas'ud (Bosworth).
result_basis: Subashi's army was routed and many were taken prisoner; Nishapur opened its gates to the Seljuks soon after.
sources: Bayhaqi; Bosworth, The Ghaznavids; en.wikipedia Battle of Sarakhs (1038)
note: 'Oghuz': the Seljuk Turkmen, not yet a state seated in Iran. The 'Battle of Nishapur (1038)' article describes what was in fact the surrender of Nishapur after this battle (excluded).
qbasis: Inferred from the Ghaznavid recruitment under Mas'ud (Bosworth).

name: Battle of Tashir (1040)
label: Tashir
commanders_a: the Kiurikid Armenian king of Tashir-Dzoraget (David Anhoghin); Georgian auxiliary commander sent by Bagrat IV
result_basis: The Wikipedia article on the Georgian-Shaddadid wars says the allied Armenian and Georgian force defeated Abu'l-Aswar.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgian%E2%80%93Shaddadid_wars (no source cited there); Minorsky, Studies in Caucasian History (1953) and 'Shaddadids', Encyclopaedia of Islam 2nd ed.
note: Weakly sourced: one line in Wikipedia without a citation. Included as a named battle with a Shaddadid commander.

name: Dandanaqan
label: Dandanaqan
place: Dandanaqan, between Sarakhs and Merv, Turkmenistan
commanders_a: Tughril, Chaghri Beg, Ibrahim Inal, Musa Yabghu
persian_force: Mas'ud's main army, reportedly about 50,000 with 100-300 elephants: the Turkic palace ghulams, Indian (Hindu) cavalry and infantry, Daylamite, Kurdish, Arab and Khurasani units (Bayhaqi); part of the ghulams went over to the Seljuks.
iranian_note: Bayhaqi's narrative names Turkic ghulams, Indians, Kurds, Arabs and Daylamite and Khurasani foot; Bosworth treats the army as a Turkic-led multi-ethnic force.
result_basis: Mas'ud's army, worn down by thirst and harassment, broke when part of the ghulam cavalry deserted, and the sultan fled the field.
sources: Bayhaqi, Ta'rikh-i Mas'udi; Gardizi; Bosworth, The Ghaznavids and CHI 4; en.wikipedia Battle of Dandanaqan
note: 'Oghuz': the Seljuk Turkmen, who became a Persian state only by this victory (not civil). Khorasan passed to the Seljuks; Mas'ud was deposed and killed in 1041.
qbasis: Bayhaqi's narrative names Turkic ghulams, Indians, Kurds, Arabs and Daylamite and Khurasani foot; Bosworth treats the army as a Turkic-led multi-ethnic force.

name: Zaranj (siege, 1040)
label: Zaranj (siege, 1040)
commanders_b: Abu'l-Fadl Nasr, Nasrid amir of Sistan under Ghaznavid rule
persian_force: Seljuk side: Turkmen cavalry under Ertash; defenders: the Sistani forces of the Nasrid amir.
iranian_note: Persian-speaking Sistani defenders against Turkmen besiegers.
result_basis: Abu'l-Fadl went over to the Seljuks and Zaranj was occupied.
borderline: ended by the defender's change of side; fighting not described
doubt: Borderline: ended by the defender's change of side; fighting not described.
sources: Ta'rikh-i Sistan; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghaznavid Empire; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Seljuk Empire
note: Civil because after Dandanaqan the Seljuks held a seat in Khorasan.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Sarab (Rawwadids against the Ghuzz, 1041-1042)
label: Sarab
date: 1041-1042 (the Rawwadid article gives the desert of Sarab, 1041-42)
place: the desert of Sarab, East Azerbaijan, Iran
commanders_b: Wahsudan ibn Muhammad (Rawwadid, reckoned a Kurdish dynasty)
result_basis: The Rawwadid article calls it a Rawwadid defeat by a Ghuzz band that had reached Azerbaijan.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rawadid_dynasty ; Minorsky, 'Rawwadids', EI2; Ibn al-Athir
note: Known from one line in the Rawwadid article; the Oghuz had already been killed or driven off in 1037-1041, so this is a second wave. The Iranian criterion rests on Wahsudan's leadership of a dynasty reckoned Kurdish.

name: Nangrahar
label: Nangrahar
place: Dinur in Nangrahar, near Jalalabad, Afghanistan
faction_b: Muhammad (brother of Mas'ud) and his sons
commanders_b: Muhammad ibn Mahmud, his sons Ahmad and others
persian_force: Both sides were parts of the Ghaznavid army: Mawdud's Ghazni troops against the mutinous army that had deposed Mas'ud, Turkic ghulams and Indian units on both sides.
iranian_note: Inferred from the Ghaznavid recruitment: Turkic ghulams, Indians, Khurasanis and Afghans (Bosworth).
result_basis: Mawdud defeated his uncle's army, captured Muhammad and his sons and put them to death in revenge for Mas'ud.
sources: Gardizi; Ibn al-Athir; Bosworth, The Later Ghaznavids (1977); en.wikipedia Mawdud of Ghazni; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghaznavid Empire
note: Also called the battle of Dinur.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Dvin
label: Dvin
commanders_a: Abu'l-Aswar Shavur, Shaddadid emir of Dvin
commanders_b: Michael Iasites, the magistros Constantine the Alan
result_basis: As in Battles of the Romans: The Shaddadids were a Kurdish dynasty, counted here with the Muslim emirates under 'Arabs'.
sources: Skylitzes, Constantine IX 15; Aristakes 12; en.wikipedia Abu'l-Aswar Shavur ibn Fadl
note: Abu'l-Aswar Shavur, Shaddadid (Kurdish) emir of Dvin, against an imperial army in which Constantine the Alan was one of the commanders (Skylitzes)
qbasis: Abu'l-Aswar Shavur, Shaddadid (Kurdish) emir of Dvin, against an imperial army in which Constantine the Alan was one of the commanders (Skylitzes)

name: Sirwan (siege, 1045-1047)
label: Sirwan
date: 1045-1047 (Abu'l-Shawk held out and died in April 1046; the castle fell in or about 1047)
war: Seljuk conquest of the Annazid lands
place: Sirwan castle, in the Zagros between Hulwan and Shahrizur (Iran-Iraq borderland, site uncertain)
commanders_a: Ibrahim Yinal (Tughril Beg's half-brother, a Turk)
commanders_b: Abu'l-Shawk Faris ibn Muhammad (Annazid, a Kurd), who died in April 1046; then his son Sa'adi
result_basis: The Annazid article says Abu'l-Shawk held the castle until his death in 1046 and Sirwan, the last Annazid stronghold, fell soon after.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annazids ; Minorsky, 'Annazids', EI2; Ibn al-Athir
note: The Annazids are Kurdish by descent; the defence of a hill fortress by Kurdish clans against the Seljuk Turkmen. Dates are given only by year in the source.

name: Isfahan (siege, 1047)
label: Isfahan (siege, 1047)
persian_force: Seljuk side: Turkmen cavalry and the sultan's ghulams; Kakuyid side: Daylamite and Turkish garrison troops and the townsmen behind Ala al-Dawla's walls.
iranian_note: Turkmen besiegers against a Daylamite-led Iranian garrison.
result_basis: Tughril could not enter the city and lifted the siege for tribute and the khutba; a siege ended by treaty is a draw under the test.
borderline: how much fighting there was is not reported
doubt: Borderline: how much fighting there was is not reported.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Tughril
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Kapetron
label: Kapetron
date: 18 September 1048 (perhaps beginning on the evening of 17 September)
war: Seljuk-Roman wars (Ibrahim Inal's invasion of Armenia)
commanders_a: Ibrahim Inal; Aspan Salarios (centre); Chorosantes (left, killed); Qutalmish
commanders_b: Aaron and Katakalon Kekaumenos (Roman wings); Liparit IV of Kldekari (centre, captured)
persian_force: Seljuk Turkmen and newly arrived Oghuz tribes, with Daylamites and 'Kabeiroi' (probably Khurasani Iranians); the left wing was led by 'Chorosantes', perhaps the Khurasani commander, and the centre by an ispahsalar (Skylitzes).
iranian_note: Skylitzes names Daylamite and Khurasani ('Kabeiroi') contingents, the Khurasanis apparently forming a whole wing beside the Turkmen.
result_basis: The Roman wings drove the Turks opposite them from the field and pursued them till morning, while the Seljuk centre captured Liparit and Ibrahim withdrew with his captives; the sources disagree on who held the field and modern scholarship gives no verdict.
sources: Skylitzes; Aristakes Lastivertsi; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Battle of Kapetron
note: Ibn al-Athir and Aristakes treat it as a Seljuk victory; Skylitzes stresses the Roman pursuit. 'Georgia': Liparit's duchy of Kldekari.
qbasis: Skylitzes names Daylamite and Khurasani ('Kabeiroi') contingents, the Khurasanis apparently forming a whole wing beside the Turkmen.

name: Isfahan (siege, 1050)
label: Isfahan (siege, 1050)
date: 1050 to May 1051 (about a year; Tughril entered in Muharram 443; Wikipedia's Tughril article gives 1051-52)
persian_force: Seljuk side: Turkmen cavalry and the sultan's ghulams with siege engines; Kakuyid side: Daylamite and Turkish garrison troops and the citizens.
iranian_note: Turkmen besiegers against a Daylamite-led Iranian garrison and Persian townsmen.
result_basis: After a siege of about a year the city surrendered and Tughril made it his capital.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Nasir-i Khusraw; Bosworth, CHI 5; en.wikipedia Tughril
note: Faramurz was compensated with Yazd and Abarquh.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Sarmaj (siege)
label: Sarmaj (siege)
place: fortress of Sarmaj, near Bisotun, Kermanshah, Iran
persian_force: Both sides were Seljuk Turkmen cavalry with ghulams; Ibrahim's force was his own Turkmen following in Jibal.
iranian_note: A war between Turkmen armies of the Seljuk family.
result_basis: Tughril beat Ibrahim in the field and after a four-day siege of Sarmaj Ibrahim surrendered.
borderline: one entry for a field action and a short siege
doubt: Borderline: one entry for a field action and a short siege.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Tughril
note: Ibrahim was pardoned and returned to service.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Hupyan
label: Hupyan
persian_force: Ghaznavid side: Turkic ghulam cavalry under Toghrul with Indian and Afghan troops; Seljuk side: Alp Arslan's Turkmen horse from Tokharistan.
iranian_note: Both armies were led and largely manned by Turks; the later Ghaznavid army relied on ghulams and Indians (Bosworth).
result_basis: Toghrul defeated Alp Arslan's invading army in the Hindu Kush.
sources: Gardizi; Bosworth, The Later Ghaznavids; en.wikipedia Toghrul of Ghazna; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghaznavid Empire
note: Civil: both the Ghaznavids and the Great Seljuks were seated in the eastern Iranian world by then.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Taq (siege, 1051)
label: Taq (siege, 1051)
place: fortress of Taq, Sistan (site not securely identified), Afghanistan
side_a: Sistan with a Seljuk relief army
faction_a: Sistan (Nasrid-Saffarid amirs, Seljuk vassals) with a Seljuk relief army
commanders_a: Hilal Daraqi, commandant of Taq; Payghu (Musa Yabghu) with the relief army
persian_force: Defenders: the Sistani garrison of the Nasrid amirs and a Seljuk Turkmen relief force; besiegers: Toghrul's Ghaznavid ghulam army.
iranian_note: A Persian-speaking Sistani garrison and Turkic ghulam and Turkmen troops on the other sides.
result_basis: Toghrul beat the Seljuk relief army but could not take Taq and gave up the siege.
sources: Ta'rikh-i Sistan; Bosworth, The Later Ghaznavids; en.wikipedia Toghrul of Ghazna; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghaznavid Empire
note: Toghrul's victory over Payghu's relief army during the siege is not separately named. Toghrul then usurped the throne at Ghazni (1052) and was murdered after some weeks (not a battle).
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Anbar (1055)
label: Anbar (1055)
war: Buyid-Uqaylid wars (last campaigns of the Buyids in Iraq)
commanders_a: Arslan al-Basasiri, Turkish commander-in-chief of the Buyid al-Malik al-Rahim; Dubays I of the Mazyadids
commanders_b: Abu'l-Ghana'im ibn al-Muhallaban, client of Quraysh the Uqaylid (captured)
persian_force: Al-Basasiri's Turkish mamluks of the Buyid army of Iraq with the Mazyadid Arabs of Dubays.
iranian_note: By the 1050s the Buyid army in Iraq was mainly Turkish ghulams, with few Daylamites left.
result_basis: Al-Basasiri retook Anbar and captured its commander with about 100 Khafaja soldiers.
borderline: a minor action; the Buyid regime was weeks from its end
doubt: Borderline: a minor action; the Buyid regime was weeks from its end.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Al-Basasiri
note: 'Arab tribes': the Uqaylids and Khafaja (opponents) and the Mazyadids (allies). Quraysh had taken Anbar in November 1054.
qbasis: Buyids: an Iranian-led state

name: Rayy (1059)
label: Rayy (1059)
date: summer 1059 (Jumada II 451; Wikipedia's Alp Arslan article gives 3 August 1059, its Tughril article 1060)
side_a: Tughril, with his nephews Alp Arslan, Yaquti and Qavurt
side_b: Ibrahim Inal and his nephews Muhammad and Ahmad
faction_a: Tughril, with his nephews Alp Arslan, Yaquti and Qavurt
faction_b: Ibrahim Inal and his nephews Muhammad and Ahmad
persian_force: Both sides were Seljuk Turkmen armies; Ibrahim's was swollen by Turkmen discontented with Tughril's turn to settled rule, Tughril's reinforced by Chaghri's sons from Khorasan.
iranian_note: A war between Turkmen armies of the Seljuk family.
result_basis: Ibrahim's army was defeated and he was captured by Alp Arslan and executed with his nephews.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Bosworth, CHI 5; en.wikipedia Tughril; en.wikipedia Alp Arslan
note: Earlier in the revolt Tughril was hemmed in at Hamadan but avoided battle.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Damghan (1063)
label: Damghan (1063)
date: late November or early December 1063 (Qutalmish died on 7 December 1063)
war: Seljuk succession war (Alp Arslan against Qutalmish)
place: Dihinemek, near Damghan (in the flooded Milh valley), Iran
side_b: Qutalmish, with his brother Resul and his son Suleiman
faction_b: Qutalmish, with his brother Resul and his son Suleiman
commanders_b: Qutalmish (died in the flight), Resul and Suleiman (captured)
persian_force: Alp Arslan's army of Khorasan (Turkmen, ghulams and Khurasani troops) against Qutalmish's Turkmen following.
iranian_note: Both armies were mainly Turkmen and Turkish ghulam cavalry.
result_basis: After a vanguard success Qutalmish's army fled when the main armies met, and Qutalmish died after falling from his horse in the flight.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Bundari; en.wikipedia Battle of Damghan (1063); en.wikipedia Alp Arslan
note: Some accounts place the battle nearer Rayy, which Qutalmish had been besieging since 15 November 1063.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Herat (siege, 1064)
label: Herat (siege, 1064)
war: Seljuk succession war (Alp Arslan against Musa Yabghu)
persian_force: Seljuk Turkmen armies on both sides; Musa held Herat with its garrison and townsmen.
iranian_note: Turkmen armies, though Herat's townsmen were Persian-speaking.
result_basis: Alp Arslan defeated Musa Yabghu and took him prisoner at Herat.
borderline: whether there was a battle or only a siege and surrender is unclear
doubt: Borderline: whether there was a battle or only a siege and surrender is unclear.
