sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Alp Arslan
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Ani (siege, 1064)
label: Ani (siege, 1064)
war: Alp Arslan's Georgian and Armenian campaign
commanders_a: Alp Arslan, with Nizam al-Mulk and the young Malik-Shah
commanders_b: Bagrat and Gregory, Roman commanders of the city (captured)
persian_force: Alp Arslan's army in two columns (one under Malik-Shah and Nizam al-Mulk), with siege engines built by Arab and Persian technicians.
iranian_note: The sources mention Persian and Arab engineers beside the Turkmen and ghulam fighting troops.
losses_b: heavy, with many civilians; 50,000 prisoners (Sibt ibn al-Jawzi)
result_basis: Ani fell to assault after a 25-day siege and was sacked.
sources: Aristakes Lastivertsi; Matthew of Edessa; Sibt ibn al-Jawzi; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Siege of Ani (1064)
note: Kars then submitted without a fight (not entered).
qbasis: Wikipedia's Siege of Ani (1064) lists Nizam al-Mulk, a Persian from Tus, as commander of one of the two divisions (with Malik-Shah) and says Alp Arslan equipped his army with Arab and Persian technicians; the troops themselves were Turkic.

name: Kerman (1067)
label: Kerman (1067)
commanders_a: Alp Arslan; Malik-Shah (at the siege of Bardasir)
persian_force: Alp Arslan's Turkmen and ghulam army against Qavurt's Turkmen and local Kermani and Kufichi levies.
iranian_note: Seljuk Turkmen armies on both sides; Qavurt also used local Kermani and Baloch (Kufichi) auxiliaries.
result_basis: Alp Arslan beat the rebel's forces, Qavurt fled to Jiroft and then submitted, giving up territory after the siege of Bardasir.
borderline: details thin; one entry for the 1067 battle and the 1068 siege of Bardasir
doubt: Borderline: details thin; one entry for the 1067 battle and the 1068 siege of Bardasir.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Muhammad ibn Ibrahim, Ta'rikh-i Saljuqiyan-i Kirman; en.wikipedia Alp Arslan
note: Wikipedia's Alp Arslan article lists the battle (1067) and the siege of Bardasir (1068) separately.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Invasion of Georgia by Fadl II and his defeat (1068)
label: Invasion of Georgia by Fadl II and his defeat
war: Georgian-Shaddadid wars (in the year of Alp Arslan's invasion of Georgia)
place: Kakheti-Kartli, along the Iori River, Georgia (site not given)
commanders_a: Fadl II ibn Shavur (a Kurd), with about 33,000 men (as given)
commanders_b: Aghsartan I of Kakheti; Bagrat IV of Georgia
result_basis: The Georgians defeated the invasion and Aghsartan captured Fadl II, who was ransomed for several fortresses on the Iori and accepted a Georgian vassal emir in Tbilisi.
sources: Minorsky, 'Shaddadids', EI2 and Studies in Caucasian History (1953); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgian%E2%80%93Shaddadid_wars ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaddadids
note: The sources do not give a battle name; the Wikipedia articles on the Shaddadids and on the Georgian-Shaddadid wars differ on whether Bagrat IV or Aghsartan I won. Force size is a medieval figure.

name: Manzikert
label: Manzikert
commanders_b: Romanos IV Diogenes (captured), Nikephoros Bryennios, Theodore Alyates, Andronikos Doukas
persian_force: Alp Arslan's mounted army: his Turkic ghulams and Turkmen horse archers, with troops from Aleppo and Mosul and a Kurdish contingent (estimated at 10,000) sent by the Marwanid emir; the Romans' Pecheneg and Oghuz mercenaries went over to him.
iranian_note: The core was Turkic, but the Marwanid Kurdish contingent of about 10,000 reported in the sources would be a fifth to a quarter of a 35,000-50,000 army; both figures are uncertain.
strength_a: 35,000-50,000 (modern estimates; Muslim and Armenian sources give far more)
strength_b: about 40,000 (close to half had deserted or been detached before the battle)
result_basis: The Roman army broke during its evening withdrawal, Andronikos Doukas led the rearguard off the field and Romanos IV was captured; the Seljuks held the field.
sources: Michael Attaleiates; Michael Psellos; Matthew of Edessa; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Battle of Manzikert
note: Romanos IV was released on terms; the Turkmen occupation of Anatolia that followed was largely the work of independent Turkmen bands and of the later Sultanate of Rum, not of the sultan's army.
qbasis: The core was Turkic, but the Marwanid Kurdish contingent of about 10,000 reported in the sources would be a fifth to a quarter of a 35,000-50,000 army; both figures are uncertain.

name: Kerj Abu Dulaf (1073)
label: Kerj Abu Dulaf (1073)
place: Kerj Abu Dulaf (between Hamadan and Arak), Iran
persian_force: A: Malik-Shah's ghulams with Kurdish and Arab contingents (some of his Turks mutinied in favour of Qavurt); B: Qavurt's Turkmen army with his seven sons.
iranian_note: Faction A (Malik-Shah): the sources name ghulams and Kurdish and Arab contingents, the Turkmen leaning towards Qavurt, so the Kurds were a substantial part; faction B (Qavurt) was Turkmen.
result_basis: After three days Qavurt's army broke and he was captured; Malik-Shah held the field.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Battle of Kerj Abu Dulaf; en.wikipedia Malik-Shah I
note: Qavurt, Alp Arslan's brother and ruler of Kerman, claimed the sultanate on Alp Arslan's death; two of his sons were blinded.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Sakalkand
label: Sakalkand
persian_force: A: a Ghaznavid army (no details; Ibrahim's army was a core of Turkic ghulams with Indian, Afghan and Khalaj troops); B: Uthman's Seljuk forces in Tukharistan (Turkic).
iranian_note: Faction A (Ghaznavid): the Ghaznavid army mixed Turkic ghulams with Indian, Afghan, Daylamite and Kurdish units, the Iranian elements roughly a fifth or more; faction B (Seljuk) was Turkic.
losses_b: unknown (Uthman captured and sent to Ghazni)
result_basis: The Ghaznavid army overran Sakalkand and captured Uthman; the Seljuk counter-attack under Gumushtegin Bilge Beg and Anushtegin Gharchai that later drove it out is a separate action.
borderline: obscure border fight of the Ghaznavid-Seljuk war of 1073
doubt: Borderline: obscure border fight of the Ghaznavid-Seljuk war of 1073.
sources: en.wikipedia Ibrahim of Ghazna; en.wikipedia Malik-Shah I
note: Sakalkand lay in Tukharistan (northern Afghanistan); its exact site is not known. Peace followed with a marriage alliance (Gawhar Khatun and Mas'ud III).
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Partskhisi
label: Partskhisi
date: c. 1074 (dated 1072-1077; recent research August or September 1075)
commanders_a: George II of Georgia, with Aghsartan I of Kakheti
commanders_b: Savtegin (Sarang), Malik-Shah's governor of Ganja and Arran
persian_force: The army Malik-Shah left with Savtegin in Arran, given as 48,000 horsemen (Georgian chronicle), probably with troops of the Muslim lords of Ganja, Dvin and Dmanisi.
iranian_note: A Turkic cavalry army of the sultan; Wikipedia lists the Kurdish Shaddadids of Ganja on the Seljuk side, but their part is not described.
result_basis: After a day-long battle the Georgians routed Savtegin's army.
sources: Georgian Chronicles (Life of George II); en.wikipedia Battle of Partskhisi; en.wikipedia Malik-Shah I
note: Wikipedia's Malik-Shah I article says Savtegin was defeated twice near Partskhisi during a campaign of 1078-1079; the date of the battle is disputed. Kakheti-Hereti fought on the Georgian side.
qbasis: the Kurdish Shaddadids are listed as belligerents

name: Pakpattan (siege, 1079)
label: Pakpattan (siege, 1079)
persian_force: Ibrahim's army; the sources give no details (the Ghaznavid army was then a core of Turkic ghulams with Indian, Afghan and Khalaj troops).
iranian_note: Inferred from the usual Ghaznavid recruitment (Turkic ghulams, Indians, Afghans, Tajik and Daylamite foot); no source for this siege.
result_basis: The fortress fell to Ibrahim.
sources: en.wikipedia Ibrahim of Ghazna
note: The fortress is described as 120 parasangs from Lahore, which fits Pakpattan poorly; the identification follows Wikipedia. The Hindu opponents are not named.
qbasis: Inferred from the usual Ghaznavid recruitment (Turkic ghulams, Indians, Afghans, Tajik and Daylamite foot); no source for this siege.

name: Mayyafariqin (siege, 1085)
label: Mayyafariqin
date: 1085 (the Marwanid article gives 1079-1085; the end of the dynasty is dated 1085)
war: Seljuk conquest of the Marwanid emirate of Diyar Bakr
commanders_a: Fakhr al-Dawla ibn Jahir (former Marwanid vizier, an Arab), leading the Seljuk assault, for Sultan Malik-Shah I (a Turk) and his vizier Nizam al-Mulk
commanders_b: Nasir al-Dawla Mansur ibn Nizam al-Din (Marwanid, a Kurd)
result_basis: The Seljuk assault took Mayyafariqin and Ibn Jahir seized the Marwanid treasures; Mansur kept only Jazirat Ibn Umar (Cizre) and the dynasty ended in 1085.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marwanids_(Diyar_Bakr) ; Ibn al-Athir; Ibn al-Azraq al-Fariqi, Ta'rikh Mayyafariqin; Canard, 'Marwanids', EI2
note: The Seljuk army was mainly Turkish (Nizam al-Mulk, a Persian, authorised the campaign as vizier but was not the ruler or field commander, so he is not counted). The Kurdish Marwanid leadership and tribal army of the defence is what qualifies the siege.

name: Darah (siege)
label: Darah (siege)
persian_force: A: the Nizari garrison of Darah (Quhistani Persians); B: Qizil-Sarigh's Seljuk army from Khorasan.
iranian_note: Faction A (Nizari) were Persian townsmen and highlanders of Quhistan; faction B Turkic-led.
result_basis: Qizil-Sarigh abandoned the siege when Malik-Shah died; the fortress held.
borderline: obscure
doubt: Borderline: obscure.
sources: en.wikipedia Nizari-Seljuk conflicts; en.wikipedia Malik-Shah I (Daru fortress)
note: The site of Darah, a dependency of Mu'minabad, is not precisely known.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Alamut (siege, 1092)
label: Alamut (siege, 1092)
commanders_a: Hasan-i Sabbah; Dihdar Abu Ali Ardestani (relief)
persian_force: A: the small garrison of Alamut and about 300 Nizari volunteers from Qazvin; B: the Seljuk emir Arslan-Tash's troops (Turkic) with local levies.
iranian_note: Faction A (Nizari) were Persian and Daylamite converts of Qazvin and Rudbar; faction B was a Turkic-led Seljuk force.
strength_a: a small garrison and a relief party of 300
result_basis: A relief party of 300 under Dihdar Abu Ali broke through the siege lines and, with the garrison, routed the besiegers.
sources: Juvayni; Rashid al-Din; en.wikipedia Nizari-Seljuk conflicts; en.wikipedia Malik-Shah I
note: An earlier siege by the emir Yurun-Tash (undated) also failed.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Isfahan (siege, 1093)
label: Isfahan (siege, 1093)
persian_force: A: Berk-Yaruq's Turkic emirs and the Nizamiyya; B: Terken Khatun's garrison and the Isfahan troops.
iranian_note: Faction A was a Turkic ghulam and Turkmen army; the defenders of Isfahan will have included Persian townsmen.
result_basis: Berk-Yaruq lifted the siege on receiving 500,000 dinars, leaving Terken Khatun and Mahmud in Isfahan and Fars: a siege ended by treaty.
borderline: little is recorded of the fighting
doubt: Borderline: little is recorded of the fighting.
sources: TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Berkyaruk'
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Kerj Abu Dulaf (1093)
label: Kerj Abu Dulaf (1093)
date: 1093 (486 AH; Wikipedia places it after Terken Khatun's death in 1094)
place: Kerj Abu Dulaf (between Hamadan and Isfahan), Iran
persian_force: A: Berk-Yaruq's Turkic emirs and ghulams; B: Isma'il's Turkmen army from Azerbaijan and Arran.
iranian_note: Faction A was Turkic by recruitment; faction B is described as a Turkmen army.
result_basis: Isma'il's army was defeated and he was later put to death.
sources: TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Berkyaruk' (Kerec); en.wikipedia Berkyaruq
note: Isma'il, Berk-Yaruq's maternal uncle, had agreed to Terken Khatun's call to remove Berk-Yaruq.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Taliqan (1093)
label: Taliqan (1093)
commanders_b: unknown (Wikipedia names al-Za'farani in connection with the fight)
persian_force: A: Nizari fighters of Rudbar and Taliqan (Daylamite highlanders and Persian converts); B: a force of 10,000 raised mostly from the Sunnis of Rayy.
iranian_note: Faction A (Nizari) were Daylamites and Persians; faction B were Persian Sunni townsmen of Rayy.
result_basis: The Nizaris defeated and dispersed the 10,000-strong force.
borderline: obscure; the opponents were a Sunni militia rather than a state army
doubt: Borderline: obscure; the opponents were a Sunni militia rather than a state army.
sources: en.wikipedia Nizari-Seljuk conflicts
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Borujerd
label: Borujerd
commanders_b: Terken Khatun's commanders; Taj al-Mulk (captured, executed 12 February 1093)
persian_force: A: Nizam al-Mulk's former ghulams (the Nizamiyya) and the emirs who raised Berk-Yaruq; B: the army of Terken Khatun and the vizier Taj al-Mulk (Turkic emirs and ghulams).
iranian_note: Faction A: both armies of the succession war were Turkic ghulam and Turkmen forces with few Iranian soldiers (Bosworth, CHI 5).
result_basis: Terken Khatun's army was heavily defeated and withdrew to Isfahan.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Berkyaruk'; en.wikipedia Berkyaruq
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Tell al-Sultan
label: Tell al-Sultan
persian_force: A: Tutush's Syrian Turkmen and the troops of Antioch; B: the armies of Aleppo and Edessa-Harran, with Kerbogha's troops sent by Berk-Yaruq.
iranian_note: Faction A: Turkmen and Syrian troops; faction B the Turkish governors' armies of northern Syria.
result_basis: The army of Aqsunqur and Buzan broke; both were killed and Tutush held the field.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Ibn al-Adim; en.wikipedia Tutush I
note: Aqsunqur (Malik-Shah's governor of Aleppo) and Buzan had deserted Tutush for Berk-Yaruq in 1093.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Rayy (1095)
label: Rayy (1095)
date: 25 February 1095 (17 Safar 488, about 26 February, in other reckonings)
persian_force: A: Berk-Yaruq's Turkic emirs and ghulams; B: Tutush's Syrian and Jaziran Turkmen with Iranian adherents such as the Kakuyid Ali ibn Faramurz.
iranian_note: Faction A was a Turkic ghulam and Turkmen army; faction B was mainly Syrian Turkmen.
result_basis: Tutush's army was defeated and Tutush was killed on the field.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Tutush I; en.wikipedia Berkyaruq; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Seljuk Empire (Battle of Ray)
note: The site is sometimes given as Dashlu near Rayy. Tutush's head was displayed in Baghdad. TDV records an earlier defeat of Berk-Yaruq by Tutush in Shawwal 487 (October-November 1094), which Wikipedia does not mention.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Lamasar (1096)
label: Lamasar (1096)
commanders_a: Kiya Buzurg-Ummid, Kiya Abu Ja'far, Kiya Abu Ali, Kiya Garshasb
persian_force: A: Nizari fighters of Rudbar (Daylamites and Persians); B: the garrison of a local Daylamite lord.
iranian_note: Faction A (Nizari) were Daylamite highlanders and Persian converts.
result_basis: The Nizaris attacked and took the castle.
borderline: a castle capture with uncertain date; Rasamuj was a local lord, not a Seljuk army
doubt: Borderline: a castle capture with uncertain date; Rasamuj was a local lord, not a Seljuk army.
sources: Juvayni; en.wikipedia Nizari-Seljuk conflicts
note: Lamasar became the second Nizari stronghold of Rudbar under Buzurg-Ummid.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Antioch (1098)
label: Antioch (1098)
commanders_a: Bohemond of Taranto, Godfrey of Bouillon, Robert of Normandy, Robert of Flanders, Hugh of Vermandois, Adhemar of Le Puy
commanders_b: Kerbogha, atabeg of Mosul; Duqaq of Damascus, Janah ad-Dawla of Homs, Soqman the Artuqid
persian_force: Kerbogha's relief army: the troops of Mosul and the Jazira with troops from Persia, joined by Duqaq of Damascus, Janah ad-Dawla of Homs and the Artuqid Soqman.
iranian_note: Wikipedia: 'his army also included troops from Persia and from the Ortuqids'; the army was overwhelmingly Turkic, with Arab and Kurdish auxiliaries.
result_basis: The crusaders sallied from Antioch and routed Kerbogha's army after Duqaq, Soqman and the emir of Homs deserted it; the crusaders held the field.
borderline: Kerbogha was Berk-Yaruq's governor of Mosul and raised a coalition; the sultan did not lead it
doubt: Borderline: Kerbogha was Berk-Yaruq's governor of Mosul and raised a coalition; the sultan did not lead it.
sources: Gesta Francorum; Raymond of Aguilers; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Siege of Antioch
note: This entry is the relief battle only: the defenders of Antioch in the siege of 1097-1098 (Yaghi-Siyan) held the city under the Syrian Seljuks and are not counted as Persian.
qbasis: Latin sources such as the Gesta Francorum list Kurds and Persians among Kerbogha's relief army, and Mosul and Jazira forces regularly had Kurdish auxiliaries; Turks and Arabs were the bulk, so the Iranian part was a named component rather than a majority.

name: Nushajan
label: Nushajan
side_b: Berk-Yaruq and Amir-i Dad Habashi, with Nizari troops
faction_b: Berk-Yaruq and Amir-i Dad Habashi, with Nizari troops
commanders_b: Amir-i Dad Habashi ibn Altuntaq (captured and killed), Berk-Yaruq
persian_force: A: Sanjar's Khorasan army of 20,000 (Turkic ghulams and Turkmen); B: Habashi's army, larger than Sanjar's, including 5,000 Nizari Ismailis, with Berk-Yaruq's followers.
iranian_note: Faction A (Sanjar) was Turkic-led; faction B included 5,000 Nizaris, mostly Persians of Quhistan, perhaps a quarter of it.
result_basis: Sanjar's army defeated the larger army of Habashi and Berk-Yaruq, and Habashi was captured.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Ahmad Sanjar; en.wikipedia Nizari-Seljuk conflicts
note: The site is uncertain: Wikipedia's Sanjar article gives 'Nushecan', its Nizari article places the fighting near Girdkuh. The Nizari commander Muzaffar took Girdkuh the same year.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Safidrud
label: Safidrud
commanders_a: Muhammad Tapar, the vizier Mu'ayyid al-Mulk, the mirakhur Inanch Yabgu
persian_force: A: Muhammad Tapar's army from Ganja and Arran, with the Nizamiyya and emirs who had deserted Berk-Yaruq; B: Berk-Yaruq's Turkic emirs and ghulams.
iranian_note: Faction A: both armies were Turkic ghulam and Turkmen forces led by Turkish emirs.
result_basis: Berk-Yaruq's forces broke and he left the field with 50 men.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Muhammed Tapar' and 'Berkyaruk'
note: Also written Isfidhrud; the first of the five battles between the brothers.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Hamadan (1101)
label: Hamadan (1101)
commanders_b: Muhammad Tapar, the vizier Mu'ayyid al-Mulk (captured)
persian_force: A: Berk-Yaruq's Turkic emirs and ghulams; B: Muhammad Tapar's army (Turkic).
iranian_note: Faction A: both armies were Turkic ghulam and Turkmen forces.
result_basis: Muhammad Tapar's army was defeated and his vizier Mu'ayyid al-Mulk captured.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Muhammed Tapar' and 'Berkyaruk'
note: Mu'ayyid al-Mulk was executed by Berk-Yaruq.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Isfahan (siege, 1102)
label: Isfahan (siege, 1102)
persian_force: A: Muhammad Tapar's remaining troops with the Isfahan garrison and townsmen; B: Berk-Yaruq's Turkic army.
iranian_note: Faction A: a Turkic core, with the Persian townsmen of Isfahan defending the walls.
result_basis: Berk-Yaruq failed to take Isfahan; Muhammad slipped out with 1,050 horsemen when supplies ran short and the siege ended without the city's capture.
sources: TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Muhammed Tapar' and 'Berkyaruk'
note: The outcome is classed for the defender because the city did not fall, although Muhammad himself fled.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Ruzrawar
label: Ruzrawar
persian_force: A and B: the Turkic armies of the two brothers.
iranian_note: Faction A: both armies were Turkic ghulam and Turkmen forces.
result_basis: After skirmishes the armies came to terms without a decision: Berk-Yaruq kept the title of sultan and Muhammad became malik.
borderline: skirmishes ended by a settlement rather than a pitched battle
doubt: Borderline: skirmishes ended by a settlement rather than a pitched battle.
sources: TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Berkyaruk' (Ruzraver)
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Rayy (1102)
label: Rayy (1102)
persian_force: A and B: the Turkic armies of the two brothers.
iranian_note: Faction A: both armies were Turkic ghulam and Turkmen forces.
result_basis: Muhammad Tapar, who had again declared himself sultan, was defeated and fled to Isfahan with a small force.
sources: TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Berkyaruk' and 'Muhammed Tapar'
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Khoy (1103)
label: Khoy (1103)
place: at the gate of Khoy, Iran
persian_force: A: Berk-Yaruq's army, the decisive charge made by Ayaz's 500 cavalry; B: Muhammad Tapar's army of Azerbaijan and Arran.
iranian_note: Faction A: both armies were Turkic ghulam and Turkmen forces.
result_basis: A charge by Ayaz's 500 horsemen routed Muhammad Tapar's army.
sources: TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Muhammed Tapar' and 'Berkyaruk'
note: The brothers divided the realm by treaty in January 1104.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Mosul (siege, 1104)
label: Mosul (siege, 1104)
commanders_a: Muhammad Tapar, the vizier Sa'd al-Mulk
persian_force: A: Muhammad Tapar's army with sappers and siege engines; B: Jikirmish's garrison and the townsmen of Mosul, with raiders from Tell Ya'far.
iranian_note: Faction A was a Turkic sultan's army; the defenders were Turkish troops and Arab townsmen.
result_basis: When news of Berk-Yaruq's death arrived Jikirmish submitted and Mosul acknowledged Muhammad Tapar, who confirmed him and withdrew.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Siege of Mosul (1104); TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Muhammed Tapar'
note: Wikipedia dates the end to 9 February 1104, but Berk-Yaruq died in December 1104 (Rabi II 498) and TDV places the siege when his death became known, so the siege belongs to late 1104 and early 1105. A breach was made and repaired overnight.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Tabas (siege, 1104)
label: Tabas (siege, 1104)
persian_force: A: Sanjar's Khorasan army under the emir Bazghash (Turkic); B: the Nizari townsmen and garrison of Tabas.
iranian_note: Faction A was a Turkic-led Seljuk army; faction B were Persian (Quhistani) Nizaris.
result_basis: Bazghash's army took and destroyed Tabas and massacred its Nizari defenders.
borderline: obscure; the Nizaris lost no main stronghold
doubt: Borderline: obscure; the Nizaris lost no main stronghold.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Nizari-Seljuk conflicts
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Shahdiz (siege)
label: Shahdiz (siege)
date: 1107 (fell Dhu'l-Qa'da 500, about July 1107; Wikipedia's Muhammad I Tapar gives 1106)
faction_b: Nizari Ismailis (Ahmad ibn Abd al-Malik ibn Attash)
commanders_b: Ahmad ibn Abd al-Malik ibn Attash (captured, executed)
persian_force: A: the sultan's army (Turkic ghulams and the emirs' troops); B: the Nizari garrison, about 80 men in the final fight.
iranian_note: Faction A was a Turkic sultan's army; faction B were Persian Nizaris of Isfahan.
result_basis: The fortress was taken tower by tower; Ibn Attash was captured and executed and the castle demolished.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Ibn al-Qalanisi; en.wikipedia Shahdiz; TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Muhammed Tapar'
note: The siege was prolonged by about a year of religious debate and negotiation; the nearby Nizari fort of Khanlanjan was apparently destroyed in the same campaign.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Mosul (siege, 1108)
label: Mosul (siege, 1108)
commanders_a: Mawdud, Sokmen al-Qutbi, Aqsunqur al-Bursuqi, Nasr ibn Muhalhal, Abu'l-Hayja
commanders_b: Jawali's wife, daughter of Bursuq (Jawali himself had left)
persian_force: A: the sultan's emirs, including the Banu Bursuq, the Shah-Armens of Akhlat and the Kurdish Annazids and Hadhabanis; B: Jawali's garrison.
iranian_note: Faction A: the sources name Kurdish Annazid and Hadhabani contingents beside the Turkish emirs; their size is unknown.
result_basis: Mawdud's troops entered through a breach opened by the plasterers' guild and took the city; the citadel surrendered eight days later.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Siege of Mosul (1108); en.wikipedia Mawdud
note: Counted as civil because Jawali was a Seljuk governor in revolt against the sultan.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Alamut (siege, 1109)
label: Alamut (siege, 1109)
date: from August 1109 (Muharram 503) until winter; the climax of raids from 1106
commanders_b: Ahmad ibn Nizam al-Mulk, Chavli Saqavu
persian_force: A: the Nizari garrisons of Rudbar (Daylamites and Persians); B: the sultan's expeditionary army (Turkic).
iranian_note: Faction A (Nizari) were Daylamites and Persians; faction B was Turkic-led.
result_basis: Neither Alamut nor Ostavand fell and the Seljuk army withdrew with the onset of winter.
sources: Juvayni; en.wikipedia Nizari-Seljuk conflicts; en.wikipedia Muhammad I Tapar; TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Muhammed Tapar'
note: The expedition of 1106-1109 devastated Rudbar; an eight-year war of attrition followed.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: al-Sannabra
label: al-Sannabra
place: al-Sannabra (south end of the Sea of Galilee), Israel & Palestine
commanders_a: Mawdud, Toghtekin of Damascus, Tamirek of Sinjar, Ayaz son of Ilghazi
persian_force: Mawdud's army of Turks and Kurds from Mosul and Sinjar, with Toghtekin's Damascenes and Ayaz's Artuqid troops.
iranian_note: Wikipedia describes Mawdud's forces as 'composed of Turks and Kurds'; the proportions are not known.
strength_a: a big and strong army (no figure)
result_basis: Baldwin I's army was drawn into an ambush and routed with about 2,000 killed; the survivors took refuge on a hill and Mawdud held the field.
borderline: the 1113 campaign was Mawdud's, made at Toghtekin's request; it is not certain that the sultan ordered it
doubt: Borderline: the 1113 campaign was Mawdud's, made at Toghtekin's request; it is not certain that the sultan ordered it.
sources: Ibn al-Qalanisi; Fulcher of Chartres; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Battle of al-Sannabra; en.wikipedia Mawdud
note: Baldwin I escaped (Wikipedia's infobox wrongly lists him as captured). Mawdud was assassinated in Damascus later in 1113.
qbasis: Wikipedia describes Mawdud's forces as 'composed of Turks and Kurds'; the proportions are not known.

name: Tiginabad (1116)
label: Tiginabad (1116)
persian_force: A and B: Ghaznavid forces (no details; the army of the later Ghaznavids was Turkic ghulams with Indian troops and Afghans).
iranian_note: Faction A: inferred from the usual Ghaznavid recruitment (Turkic ghulams, Indians, Afghans and Tajik foot); no source for this battle.
result_basis: Bahram was defeated and fled to the Seljuk court in Khorasan.
sources: en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghaznavid Empire; en.wikipedia Bahram-Shah of Ghazna
note: Tiginabad is usually placed near Kandahar; the site is approximate.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Ghazni (1117)
label: Ghazni (1117)
persian_force: A: Sanjar's Khorasan army (Turkic ghulams and Turkmen) with Bahram's followers; B: Arslan Shah's Ghaznavid army with war elephants.
iranian_note: Faction A (Sanjar) was Turkic-led; faction B (Ghaznavid) had Turkic ghulams, Indian troops and Afghans.
result_basis: Arslan Shah's army was crushed on the plain of Shahrabad and he fled to India.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Battle of Ghazni (1117); en.wikipedia Bahram-Shah of Ghazna; en.wikipedia Ahmad Sanjar
note: Wikipedia's lists call it the 2nd Battle of Ghazni. Sanjar's army then occupied and plundered Ghazni for 40 days; Arslan Shah was later caught in the Ughnan mountains and strangled on Bahram's orders.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Alamut (siege, 1117)
label: Alamut (siege, 1117)
persian_force: A: the Nizari garrisons of Rudbar (Daylamites and Persians); B: Anushtegin Shirgir's Seljuk army (Turkic).
iranian_note: Faction A (Nizari) were Daylamites and Persians; faction B was Turkic-led.
result_basis: Shirgir abandoned the sieges of Alamut and Lamasar in April 1118 on news of Muhammad Tapar's death, leaving supplies and weapons to the Nizaris.
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Nizari-Seljuk conflicts; TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Muhammed Tapar'
note: One entry for the joint siege of Alamut and Lamasar; Wikipedia's dating of the start is inconsistent (1117 or 1118).
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Multan (1119)
label: Multan (1119)
persian_force: A: Bahram Shah's Ghaznavid army; B: the rebel governor's Indian garrison troops.
iranian_note: Faction A: inferred from the usual Ghaznavid recruitment; no source for this battle.
result_basis: The rebel Muhammad was defeated and killed with most of his sons.
borderline: Wikipedia gives a battle near Multan in 1119 against Muhammad b. Ali and an undated defeat of Muhammad Bahlim near Multan; probably the same event
doubt: Borderline: Wikipedia gives a battle near Multan in 1119 against Muhammad b. Ali and an undated defeat of Muhammad Bahlim near Multan; probably the same event.
sources: Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri; en.wikipedia Bahram-Shah of Ghazna
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Saveh
label: Saveh
commanders_b: Mahmud II, Ali Bar, the atabeg Ghuzoghlu, Qaraja al-Saqi
persian_force: A: Sanjar's army of 20,000 with 18 elephants, with Nizari troops; B: Mahmud's 30,000, the Turkic emirs of western Iran and Iraq.
iranian_note: Faction A: Sanjar's army was Turkic ghulams and Turkmen with eastern vassal contingents and some Nizaris; faction B was Turkic.
result_basis: Mahmud's cavalry gave way before Sanjar's elephants and Mahmud fled the field.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Bundari; en.wikipedia Ahmad Sanjar; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Seljuk Empire
note: Mahmud kept the western sultanate as Sanjar's subordinate.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Asadabad
label: Asadabad
commanders_b: Mas'ud, Juyush Beg, the vizier al-Tughra'i
persian_force: A and B: the Turkic emirs and ghulams of western Iran; Mas'ud's side was led by his atabeg Juyush Beg of Mosul.
iranian_note: Faction A: a Seljuk field army of Turkic emirs; no composition is recorded.
result_basis: Mas'ud's army was defeated; Mahmud forgave Mas'ud and put the vizier al-Tughra'i to death.
borderline: known from Ibn al-Athir (514 AH); the site and date were not verified online
doubt: Borderline: known from Ibn al-Athir (514 AH); the site and date were not verified online.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Ghiyath ad-Din Mas'ud (rebellion of c. 1120-1121)
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Didgori
label: Didgori
commanders_b: Ilghazi (wounded), Tughril (Seljuk malik of Arran), Dubays ibn Sadaqa, Toghan Arslan of Bitlis
persian_force: An expedition authorized by Sultan Mahmud II and led by the Artuqid Ilghazi: his Turkmen, the Seljuk malik Tughril of Arran and Nakhchivan (whose part is disputed), the Mazyadid Arabs of Dubays and the emir of Bitlis.
iranian_note: The coalition was overwhelmingly Turkmen with Arab tribesmen; Kurdish troops of Bitlis and Dvin may have been present.
strength_a: about 56,000 (Georgian sources), incl. 15,000 Kipchaks, 500 Alans and 100-500 Franks
strength_b: 30,000 (Arab sources); 100,000-250,000 (modern Georgian historians); Christian sources up to 800,000
losses_b: tens of thousands dead and 4,000 captured (Turkish estimate); Matthew of Edessa 400,000 killed
result_basis: The coalition army was routed and the Georgians held the field.
borderline: the Persian share is uncertain: the army was Ilghazi's, sent with the sultan's approval, and Tughril's presence is disputed
doubt: Borderline: the Persian share is uncertain: the army was Ilghazi's, sent with the sultan's approval, and Tughril's presence is disputed.
sources: Georgian Chronicles; Matthew of Edessa; Walter the Chancellor; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Battle of Didgori
note: Georgia took Tbilisi in 1122.
qbasis: The coalition was overwhelmingly Turkmen with Arab tribesmen; Kurdish troops of Bitlis and Dvin may have been present.

name: Ani (siege, 1124)
label: Ani (siege, 1124)
date: 1124 (David IV took Ani in the summer of 1124; exact days unknown)
war: Georgian-Shaddadid wars (David IV's conquests in Armenia)
commanders_a: David IV the Builder of Georgia
commanders_b: Abu'l-Aswar Shavur II (a Kurd), emir of Ani, who was captured (Fadl IV retook Ani in 1125)
result_basis: David IV took the city and captured the emir; Wikipedia's Shaddadid article says without a fight, the Georgian-Shaddadid wars article says after a siege.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaddadids ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgian%E2%80%93Shaddadid_wars ; Minorsky, Studies in Caucasian History (1953) and 'Shaddadids', Encyclopaedia of Islam 2nd ed.; Rayfield, Edge of Empires (2012)
note: Doubtful on 'real fighting': the Armenian townspeople are said to have helped the Georgians and the sources describe a quick surrender. Kept because the sources call it a siege.

name: Rudbar (1126)
label: Rudbar (1126)
persian_force: A: the Nizaris of Rudbar (Daylamites and Persians); B: Seljuk troops with local support.
iranian_note: Faction A (Nizari) were Daylamites and Persians; faction B was a Turkic-led army with local Daylamite auxiliaries.
result_basis: The Seljuk invasions of Rudbar were repelled and the commander Tamurtughan was captured.
borderline: recorded as campaigns without a single named battle
doubt: Borderline: recorded as campaigns without a single named battle.
sources: Juvayni; en.wikipedia Nizari-Seljuk conflicts
note: Part of the offensive organised by Sanjar's vizier Mu'in al-Din al-Kashi, which in Quhistan took Tarz and Turaythith with limited success; Tamurtughan was released at Sanjar's request.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Alamut (1129)
label: Alamut (1129)
persian_force: A: the Nizari garrisons of Rudbar; B: Mahmud II's Turkic army.
iranian_note: Faction A (Nizari) were Daylamites and Persians; faction B was Turkic.
result_basis: Mahmud's attack on Alamut failed, and an Iraqi army also failed before Lamasar.
borderline: a failed attack recorded without details
doubt: Borderline: a failed attack recorded without details.
sources: Juvayni; en.wikipedia Nizari-Seljuk conflicts
note: It followed the lynching of a Nizari envoy in Isfahan and a Nizari raid on Qazvin.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Dinavar
label: Dinavar
persian_force: A: Sanjar's Khorasan army (Turkic ghulams and Turkmen); B: the Turkic emirs of Mas'ud and Seljuk-Shah.
iranian_note: Faction A: both armies were Turkic ghulam and Turkmen forces.
result_basis: Sanjar defeated Mas'ud and Seljuk-Shah and installed Tughril II as sultan in the west.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Ahmad Sanjar
note: The caliph al-Mustarshid backed Mas'ud but did not fight at Dinavar. Mas'ud later defeated Tughril II (May 1133; site not recorded in the sources checked).
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Hazarasp (1138)
label: Hazarasp (1138)
persian_force: A: Sanjar's army (Turkic ghulams and Turkmen); B: Atsiz's Khwarazmian army (Turkic ghulams and steppe auxiliaries with Khwarazmian levies).
iranian_note: Faction A (Sanjar) was Turkic-led; faction B mixed Turkic soldiers with Khwarazmian (East Iranian-speaking) levies.
result_basis: Atsiz was defeated at Hazarasp and fled.
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Atsiz; en.wikipedia Ahmad Sanjar
note: Sanjar gave Khwarazm to his nephew Suleiman-Shah, but Atsiz soon returned.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Kabud-Jama
label: Kabud-Jama
faction_b: Ala al-Dawla Ali I (Bavandids of Tabaristan)
commanders_b: the ispahbadh Ala al-Dawla Ali ibn Shahriyar (captured)
persian_force: A: Atsiz's Khwarazmian army (Turkic soldiers with Khwarazmian levies); B: the Bavandid ispahbadh's Tabaristani troops.
iranian_note: Faction A was Turkic-led; faction B (Bavandid) was Mazandarani, i.e. Caspian Iranian.
result_basis: Atsiz defeated and captured the Bavandid ispahbadh Ali and occupied Gurgan.
borderline: obscure
doubt: Borderline: obscure.
sources: en.wikipedia Atsiz
note: Ali was released when his son pleaded for him, and Gurgan became a Khwarazmian vassal.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Qatwan
label: Qatwan
commanders_b: Sanjar, Garshasp II of Yazd (Kakuyid, killed), Mahmud Khan (Qarakhanid)
persian_force: Sanjar's great army, given as 100,000: his Turkic ghulams and Turkmen, the troops of vassals such as the Kakuyid Garshasp of Yazd and the amir of Sistan, and the Qarakhanid Mahmud Khan.
iranian_note: A Turkic-led imperial army; Iranian vassal contingents (Yazd, Sistan) are recorded but were a small part.
strength_a: 20,000 to 300,000 (estimates vary; the Qarluks gave 30,000-50,000 horse)
result_basis: Sanjar's army was routed with enormous losses and Sanjar fled with a handful of horsemen.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Juvayni; en.wikipedia Battle of Qatwan
note: The Qarluks, whose appeal brought the Kara-Khitai west, fought on their side; Atsiz of Khwarazm had invited the Kara-Khitai. The amir of Sistan and Sanjar's wife were captured.
qbasis: Sanjar's army included the Kakuyid Garshasp II of Yazd (Daylamite-descended Iranian dynasty), killed in the battle, and the troops of the Banu Khalaf amir of Sistan (Persian), both named in Ibn al-Athir and Juzjani.

name: Gurganj (siege, 1143)
label: Gurganj (siege, 1143)
persian_force: A: Sanjar's army (Turkic); B: Atsiz's troops with the townsmen of Gurganj (Khwarazmians).
iranian_note: Faction A was Turkic-led; the defenders included Khwarazmian (East Iranian-speaking) townsmen.
result_basis: Atsiz submitted and returned the plunder and captured scholars, and Sanjar withdrew without taking Gurganj: a siege ended by treaty.
borderline: Wikipedia's Atsiz article records the 1143 invasion of Khwarazm without describing a siege
doubt: Borderline: Wikipedia's Atsiz article records the 1143 invasion of Khwarazm without describing a siege.
sources: Juvayni; en.wikipedia Ahmad Sanjar; en.wikipedia Atsiz
note: Punishment for Atsiz's seizure of Merv, Nishapur and Sarakhs after Qatwan (1141), from which Sanjar expelled him in 1142.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Lamasar (1143)
label: Lamasar (1143)
persian_force: A: the Nizari garrisons of Rudbar; B: Mas'ud's Turkic army.
iranian_note: Faction A (Nizari) were Daylamites and Persians; faction B was Turkic.
result_basis: Mas'ud's attack on Lamasar and Rudbar was repelled.
borderline: a failed attack recorded without details
doubt: Borderline: a failed attack recorded without details.
sources: Juvayni; en.wikipedia Nizari-Seljuk conflicts
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Hazarasp (siege, 1147)
label: Hazarasp (siege, 1147)
persian_force: A: Sanjar's army (Turkic); B: the Khwarazmian garrison of Hazarasp.
iranian_note: Faction A was Turkic-led; the defenders included Khwarazmian townsmen.
result_basis: Sanjar took the castle of Hazarasp; Atsiz fled to Gurganj, submitted and was kept as governor.
sources: Juvayni; en.wikipedia Ahmad Sanjar; en.wikipedia Atsiz
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Marj Qaratakin
label: Marj Qaratakin
war: Seljuk civil war (revolt of the emirs, 1146-1147)
place: Marj Qaratakin (Qaratakin meadow, near Hamadan), Iran
faction_b: Boz-Aba (atabeg of Fars) and allied emirs
persian_force: A: Mas'ud's Turkic army; B: Boz-Aba's army of Fars and Khuzistan led by Turkish emirs.
iranian_note: Faction A: both armies were led by Turkish emirs; Boz-Aba's Fars levies will have included Persians and Shabankara Kurds, in unknown numbers.
result_basis: Boz-Aba and his allied emirs were defeated by Mas'ud; Boz-Aba lost his life.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Muhammed b. Mahmud' (Karategin meadow, 542/1147); en.wikipedia Ghiyath ad-Din Mas'ud
note: Boz-Aba's death is usually given as an execution after capture; the Salghurids took Fars after him (1148).
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Ghazni (1148)
label: Ghazni (1148)
persian_force: A: Sayf al-Din's Ghurid army of Ghuri highlanders; B: Bahram Shah's Ghaznavid army (Turkic ghulams, Indian troops and Afghans).
iranian_note: Faction A (Ghurid) was recruited in Ghur, a Persian-speaking (Tajik) highland; faction B was the mixed Ghaznavid army.
result_basis: Sayf al-Din defeated Bahram Shah and took Ghazni; Bahram fled to Kurram.
sources: Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri; en.wikipedia Battle of Ghazni (1148); en.wikipedia Bahram-Shah of Ghazna
note: Wikipedia's Ghaznavid list calls it the 3rd Battle of Ghazni, its Ghurid list the 1st.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Sang-i Surakh
label: Sang-i Surakh
commanders_b: Sayf al-Din Suri (captured, later crucified), the vizier Majd al-Din Musawi (captured)
persian_force: A: Bahram Shah's Ghaznavid army, with the townsmen and troops of Ghazni who turned against the Ghurids; B: Sayf al-Din's Ghurid army.
iranian_note: Faction A: inferred from the usual Ghaznavid recruitment; faction B (Ghurid) was Persian-speaking highlanders.
result_basis: Bahram defeated Sayf al-Din and captured him with his vizier; Bahram retook Ghazni.
sources: Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghaznavid Empire; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghurid dynasty; en.wikipedia Bahram-Shah of Ghazna
note: The execution of Sayf al-Din provoked Ala al-Din Husayn's revenge of 1150-1151.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Battle of Inab
label: Inab
war: Wars of Nur al-Din against the Principality of Antioch
place: Inab (Tell Inab), near Apamea, Syria (exact site uncertain)
commanders_a: Nur al-Din Zengi; Mu'in al-Din Unur of Damascus (contingent); the Kurdish emirs Shirkuh and Ayyub are said to have served in Nur al-Din's and Unur's armies
commanders_b: Raymond of Poitiers, Prince of Antioch (killed); Ali ibn Wafa (killed)
result_basis: Raymond's small army was encircled and destroyed, with Raymond and Ali ibn Wafa killed.
sources: Mallett, 'The Battle of Inab', Journal of Medieval History 39 (2013); Gibb in Setton, History of the Crusades vol. 1; Ibn al-Qalanisi; Ibn al-Athir; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Inab
note: Doubtful on the Iranian criterion: the Wikipedia infobox names Ayyub, but the article text does not mention Kurds or Shirkuh, and Nur al-Din's army is described as mostly Turkish cavalry and Turkmen.

name: Jush-i Ab-i Garm
label: Jush-i Ab-i Garm
place: Jush-i Ab-i Garm (hot springs, between Tiginabad and Ghazni), Afghanistan
persian_force: A: the Ghurid army; B: the remains of Bahram Shah's Ghaznavid army.
iranian_note: Faction A (Ghurid) was recruited in Ghur, a Persian-speaking highland.
result_basis: Bahram's rallied army was routed again and he fled to Ghazni.
borderline: obscure; the site is unknown
doubt: Borderline: obscure; the site is unknown.
sources: Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri; en.wikipedia Ala al-Din Husayn; en.wikipedia Bahram-Shah of Ghazna
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Tiginabad (1150)
label: Tiginabad (1150)
commanders_a: Ala al-Din Husayn; Kharmil Sam-i Husain, Kharmil Sam-i Banji
persian_force: A: Ala al-Din's Ghurid army of Ghuri foot and horse; B: Bahram Shah's Ghaznavid army.
iranian_note: Faction A (Ghurid) was recruited in Ghur, a Persian-speaking highland; faction B was the mixed Ghaznavid army.
result_basis: The Ghaznavid army was routed.
sources: Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri; en.wikipedia Ala al-Din Husayn; en.wikipedia Bahram-Shah of Ghazna
note: The first of three battles of Ala al-Din's campaign of revenge.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Ghazni (1151)
label: Ghazni (1151)
persian_force: A: the Ghurid army of Ghuri foot and horse; B: Bahram Shah's army with the Ghazni garrison.
iranian_note: Faction A (Ghurid) was recruited in Ghur, a Persian-speaking highland; faction B was the mixed Ghaznavid army.
losses_b: army routed; the sack is said to have killed 60,000
result_basis: Bahram's army, reinforced by the city garrison, was routed; the Ghurids took Ghazni and burned it for seven days.
sources: Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri; en.wikipedia Battle of Ghazni (1151); en.wikipedia Bahram-Shah of Ghazna
note: The burning earned Ala al-Din the name Jahan-suz (world-burner); Bahram fled to his Indian lands.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Nab
label: Nab
persian_force: A: Sanjar's army (Turkic ghulams and Turkmen); B: the Ghurid army of Ghuri foot and horse with Turkish (Ghuzz) mercenary cavalry.
iranian_note: Faction A (Sanjar) was Turkic-led; faction B (Ghurid) was mostly Persian-speaking Ghuris with Turkish cavalry.
result_basis: Ala al-Din's army was routed, after his Turkish horsemen went over to Sanjar (Juzjani), and he was captured.
sources: Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri; en.wikipedia Ahmad Sanjar; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Seljuk Empire
note: Ala al-Din had stopped paying tribute and taken Balkh; he was held two years and released for a ransom.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Ani (battle of Saltuk II, 1153-1154)
label: Ani (battle of Saltuk II, 1153-1154)
war: Georgian wars with the Saltukids of Erzurum
persian_state: Kingdom of Georgia & Shaddadids of Ani
commanders_a: Demetrius I of Georgia; Fakhr al-Din Shaddad (a Kurd), emir of Ani
result_basis: Demetrius I defeated and captured Saltuk II, who was released for a ransom of 100,000 dinars.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaddadids ; Minorsky, Studies in Caucasian History (1953) ch. on the Shaddadids of Ani
note: Doubtful on the Iranian criterion: the Shaddadid emir is said to have warned the Georgian king of Saltuk's march, and I have no source that his troops fought in the battle. Entered as uncertain.

name: Damascus (siege, 1154)
label: Damascus
date: about 18-25 April 1154 (Nur al-Din's siege; the city fell on 25 April 1154)
commanders_a: Nur al-Din Zengi; Shirkuh (a Kurd), his chief emir
commanders_b: Mujir al-Din Abaq, Burid ruler (a Turk); Najm al-Din Ayyub (a Kurd), senior emir in the city
result_basis: After a short siege the East Gate was opened and the city passed to Nur al-Din through the mediation of Ayyub and Shirkuh; Mujir al-Din was bought out with the grant of Homs.
sources: Ibn al-Qalanisi, Dhayl ta'rikh Dimashq; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil; Gibb in Setton, History of the Crusades vol. 1; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirkuh
note: Kurdish brothers on both sides of the walls: Shirkuh with the besiegers and Ayyub inside. The fighting was brief and the end came by surrender; counted as a siege because Nur al-Din's army invested the city for about a week.

name: Aras
label: Aras
place: on the Aras (Araxes) river (site unknown), Iran
faction_b: Sulayman-Shah (with Eldiguz, Malik-Shah III and Arslan-Shah)
persian_force: A: Muhammad II's army, with the promised support of the Zengids of Mosul; B: Sulayman-Shah's coalition of Eldiguz's troops, Malik-Shah's Khuzistan forces and 3,000 men sent by the caliph.
iranian_note: Faction A: both sides were armies of Turkish emirs and atabegs.
result_basis: Sulayman-Shah was defeated; in flight he was captured by Zayn al-Din Ali Kuchuk of Mosul.
borderline: known from TDV; not in Wikipedia; the site 'on the bank of the Aras' as given
doubt: Borderline: known from TDV; not in Wikipedia; the site 'on the bank of the Aras' as given.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Muhammed b. Mahmud'
note: Eldiguz's seat was then in Arran and Nakhchivan, outside present-day Iran.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Ragh-i Zar
label: Ragh-i Zar
place: Ragh-i Zar, between Firuzkuh and Herat, Afghanistan
side_b: Fakhr al-Din Masud of Bamiyan, with the Seljuk governors Taj al-Din Yildiz and Ala al-Din Qumach
faction_b: Fakhr al-Din Masud of Bamiyan, with the Seljuk governors Taj al-Din Yildiz (Herat) and Ala al-Din Qumach (Balkh)
commanders_a: Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad, Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad (Muhammad of Ghor)
commanders_b: Fakhr al-Din Masud (captured), Taj al-Din Yildiz (killed), Ala al-Din Qumach
persian_force: The army of Ghur under the two brothers: Ghuri (Tajik) mountain infantry and cavalry with Turkic ghulams; the other side had the Bamiyan Ghurids and the Turkic troops of the Seljuk governors of Herat and Balkh.
iranian_note: The early Ghurid army was raised mainly from the Persian-speaking (Tajik) mountaineers of Ghur, with a growing Turkic ghulam element.
result_basis: The Ghurids of Firuzkuh routed the coalition; Yildiz was killed and Fakhr al-Din taken, later restored to Bamiyan.
sources: Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghurid dynasty, Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad
note: Dated 1163 in Wikipedia's list of Ghurid battles; the Ghiyath al-Din article places it early in his reign (from 1163). Civil: a fight between Ghurid branches, joined by the governors left over from the Great Seljuk state.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Bilbeis (siege, 1164)
label: Bilbeis
date: April-October 1164 (Shirkuh entered Egypt in the spring; Amalric and Shawar besieged him in Bilbeis from about August to late October)
war: Nur al-Din's Egyptian expeditions (Shirkuh's first Egyptian campaign)
commanders_a: Amalric I of Jerusalem; Shawar ibn Mujir, Fatimid vizier
commanders_b: Shirkuh (Asad al-Din Shirkuh ibn Shadhi, a Kurd of Dvin); Saladin, his nephew
result_basis: The siege ended in a negotiated mutual withdrawal in October 1164, after Nur al-Din's attack on Crusader northern Syria (Harim) forced Amalric to make terms; Shirkuh left Egypt with his army.
sources: Gibb, 'The Career of Nur-ad-Din' in Setton ed., A History of the Crusades vol. 1 (1969); Lev, Saladin in Egypt (1999); William of Tyre; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirkuh ; https://www.historyofwar.org/articles/wars_nur_ad_din_egypt.html
note: Shirkuh's army is described as Syrian Turks, Turkmen auxiliaries and Kurds (the Wikipedia article on Shirkuh gives 500 mamluks and Kurds out of 8,000 horse from Homs), and both Shirkuh and Saladin were Kurds, so the leader rule is what qualifies the battle; the Kurdish share of the troops is small or unknown (500 mamluks and Kurds out of about 8,000 horse in the force from Homs, plus hired Turkmen).

name: Harim (1164)
label: Harim
war: Wars of Nur al-Din against the Principality of Antioch and the Romans
side_b: Principality of Antioch, County of Tripoli, Roman Cilicia, Armenian Cilicia
commanders_a: Nur al-Din Zangi, Shirkuh and Qutb al-Din Mawdud of Mosul
commanders_b: Bohemond III, Raymond III, Joscelin III, Thoros II, Hugh VIII of Lusignan and Konstantinos Kalamanos
result_basis: Nur al-Din won a crushing victory and captured Bohemond, Raymond, Joscelin, Kalamanos and Hugh (Wikipedia 'Battle of Harim'; Ibn al-Athir).
sources: Wikipedia 'Battle of Harim' (fetched 1 Nov 2026); Ibn al-Athir; William of Tyre 19.9-10
note: The Zengids were Turks; Shirkuh, Nur al-Din's emir (lord of Homs) and later conqueror of Egypt, was a Kurd of the Rawwadid family of Dvin, and Wikipedia lists him among the commanders. The page does not give his ethnicity or say what part he led, so the Iranian side is a named Kurdish commander, not a counted contingent.

name: Alexandria (siege, 1167)
label: Alexandria
date: April-August 1167 (Shirkuh moved to Alexandria after al-Babein; the Crusader and Egyptian siege ran from about July to a treaty on about 4 August)
war: Nur al-Din's Egyptian expeditions (Shirkuh's second Egyptian campaign)
commanders_b: Saladin (a Kurd), left in the city by Shirkuh (a Kurd), who raised troops in Upper Egypt
result_basis: The siege ended by treaty: both Shirkuh's army and Amalric's left Egypt, with the Zengids evacuating Alexandria and the Franks keeping a garrison and tribute at Cairo.
sources: William of Tyre; Ibn al-Athir; Ibn Abi Tayyi; Lev, Saladin in Egypt (1999); Gibb in Setton, History of the Crusades vol. 1; https://www.historyofwar.org/articles/siege_alexandria_1167.html ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirkuh
note: Saladin, aged about 29, held the city with Syrian troops and townsmen while Shirkuh went south to draw off the besiegers. Townsmen are not counted here.

name: Battle of al-Babein
label: al-Babein
war: Nur al-Din's Egyptian expeditions (Shirkuh's second Egyptian campaign)
place: al-Babein (Babayn), near Giza and the Nile, Egypt (exact site uncertain)
commanders_b: Shirkuh (a Kurd); Saladin commanded the centre
result_basis: Amalric's knights broke up in the soft sand and slopes and Saladin's feigned retreat drew part of them off, but neither army destroyed the other; Shirkuh then withdrew upriver and Amalric returned to Cairo.
sources: William of Tyre; Ibn al-Athir; Smail, Crusading Warfare (1956); Lev, Saladin in Egypt (1999); Baldwin in Setton, History of the Crusades vol. 1; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_al-Babein ; https://www.historyofwar.org/articles/wars_nur_ad_din_egypt.html
note: Wikipedia's infobox gives a Zengid victory but its text describes a tactical draw. Shirkuh's army of about 2,000 is described as Kurds, Turks and Bedouin (historyofwar.org); the Zengid leaders were Kurds.

name: Battle of the Blacks (Cairo, 1169)
label: Blacks
war: Saladin's rise in Egypt (Fatimid Egypt under Saladin as vizier)
place: Cairo (the streets between the Fatimid palaces and Bab Zuwayla), Egypt
side_b: Black African regiments of the Fatimid army
commanders_a: Saladin (a Kurd), vizier, with his Syrian emirs
commanders_b: the emirs of the Black regiments (not named); the revolt was set off by Saladin's execution of the palace eunuch Mu'tamin al-Khilafa
result_basis: After two days of street fighting Saladin's troops burned the Black regiments' quarter (al-Mansuriyya) and the survivors fled across the Nile to Giza, where they were granted safe-conduct and then dispersed.
sources: Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil; Ibn Abi Tayyi; Lev, Saladin in Egypt (1999); Ehrenkreutz, Saladin (1972); Humphreys, From Saladin to the Mongols (1977)
note: Qualifies only through Saladin's leadership; the Zengid troops with him were mainly Turks and Kurds but no figure for the Kurdish part is given. Saladin was vizier from March 1169 but did not rule Egypt in his own name until 1171.

name: Damietta (siege, 1169)
label: Damietta
persian_state: Fatimid Egypt & Zengid reinforcements from Nur al-Din
commanders_a: Amalric I of Jerusalem; Andronikos Kontostephanos (Roman fleet)
commanders_b: Saladin (a Kurd), vizier; the Fatimid garrison commanders; Nur al-Din's Syrian relief troops
result_basis: After about fifty days the Franks and Romans, short of food and with the Nile floods and Saladin's reinforcements against them, made a truce and withdrew.
sources: William of Tyre; Ibn al-Athir; Lev, Saladin in Egypt (1999); Kinnamos; Runciman, A History of the Crusades vol. 2 (1952)
note: Qualifies through Saladin's command. The composition of his army is not recorded in the sources I used, so the Kurdish share is unknown.

name: Ayla (Eilat, 1170)
label: Ayla
date: late 1170 (December 1170 or the first weeks of 1171; sources differ)
war: Saladin's wars against the Kingdom of Jerusalem
place: Ile de Graye (Coral or Pharaoh's Island) off Ayla (Aqaba/Eilat), Gulf of Aqaba, Egypt
result_basis: Saladin took the island fortress after an assault in which ships carried in sections from Cairo were used, and the Crusader garrison was captured.
sources: William of Tyre; Ibn al-Athir; Lev, Saladin in Egypt (1999)
note: The date and the exact sequence relative to Darum are uncertain (William of Tyre and Muslim sources differ). Included because it is a real assault led by Saladin before 1171.

name: Darum and Gaza (1170)
label: Darum and Gaza
war: Saladin's wars against the Kingdom of Jerusalem
place: Darum (Deir al-Balah) and Gaza, Gaza Strip, Palestine
commanders_b: the Templar garrison of Gaza; Amalric I of Jerusalem (relieving)
result_basis: Saladin sacked the lower town of Gaza but failed to take the Templar citadel there or the fort of Darum, and withdrew when Amalric came up.
sources: William of Tyre; Ibn al-Athir; Lev, Saladin in Egypt (1999); Ehrenkreutz, Saladin (1972)
note: Saladin's first campaign against the Franks as head of the Egyptian army. A raid with real assaults on Darum and Gaza; combined into one entry.

name: Qasr Ibrim (1172)
label: Qasr Ibrim
place: Qasr Ibrim (Ibrim, Lower Nubia), now under Lake Nasser
result_basis: Turan-Shah, sent by Saladin with Kurdish troops, took Ibrim, raided Nubia and returned with slaves and plunder.
sources: Wikipedia, Turan-Shah (fetched: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turan-Shah); Wikipedia, Qasr Ibrim; Vantini, Oriental Sources concerning Nubia; Ibn al-Athir (year 568 AH)
note: Saladin sent his brother Turan-Shah after Nubian raids on Aswan (late 1172-early 1173); the source says he took Kurdish troops. The year of the capture is not given precisely.

name: Ghazni (1173)
label: Ghazni (1173)
commanders_a: Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad, Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad
persian_force: The Ghurid army of Ghur: Ghuri (Tajik) troops with Turkic ghulams and Khalaj and Afghan tribesmen (inferred from recruitment; the sources give no detail).
iranian_note: The Ghurid army of the 1170s was still largely raised in Ghur and its Persian-speaking hill country, with Turkic ghulams and Khalaj and Afghan tribesmen.
result_basis: The Ghurids defeated the Oghuz and took Ghazni, where Mu'izz al-Din was installed as ruler.
sources: Juzjani; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghurid dynasty (3rd Battle of Ghazni), Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad, Muhammad of Ghor
note: The Oghuz had held Ghazni since about 1162/63, when they drove out the Ghaznavid Khusrau Shah; they are treated as invaders, not an Iranian dynasty. The Muhammad of Ghor article also gives 1169 in one passage.
qbasis: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state

name: Kerak (siege, 1173)
label: Kerak
result_basis: Saladin broke off the siege on hearing that Nur al-Din was approaching and did not wish to meet him.
sources: Lyons & Jackson, Saladin: The Politics of the Holy War (1982), ch. on 1173; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh
note: A joint operation of Saladin (from Egypt) and Nur al-Din that Saladin abandoned from political caution; real fighting was small.

name: Ani (siege, 1174)
label: Ani (siege, 1174)
commanders_a: George III of Georgia; Ivane Orbeli
commanders_b: Shahanshah ibn Mahmud (a Kurd), emir of Ani, who was taken prisoner
result_basis: George III besieged and captured the city and took the emir prisoner; Ivane Orbeli was left as governor.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaddadids ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgian%E2%80%93Shaddadid_wars ; Minorsky, Studies in Caucasian History (1953) and 'Shaddadids', Encyclopaedia of Islam 2nd ed.
note: Only a line or two in the sources I used; Ani changed hands several times between 1161 and 1199. A Muslim coalition retook it in 1175.

name: Zabid (1174)
label: Zabid
result_basis: Turan-Shah took Zabid and captured Abd al-Nabi, ending the Mahdid dynasty.
sources: Wikipedia, Turan-Shah (fetched: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turan-Shah); Wikipedia, Mahdids; Ibn al-Athir; Umara al-Yamani
note: Turan-Shah captured Zabid in May 1174 and Aden later that year. Battle detail is thin; Ayyubid command is clear.

name: Suburni
label: Suburni
war: Khwarazmian succession war (Tekish against Sultan Shah)
place: Suburni, on the approaches to Khwarazm (site unidentified), Uzbekistan
side_b: Sultan Shah and Terken Khatun, with Mu'ayyid Ay-Aba of Nishapur
faction_b: Sultan Shah and Terken Khatun, with Mu'ayyid Ay-Aba of Nishapur (Mu'ayyids of Nishapur)
commanders_b: Mu'ayyid al-Din Ay-Aba (captured and executed), Sultan Shah, Terken Khatun
persian_force: Tekish's army of Khwarazm, won with Qara Khitai help: Qipchaq and Qangli Turkic cavalry with Khwarazmian troops; the other side had Ay-Aba's Nishapur army of Turkic ghulams and Khorasani levies.
iranian_note: The Khwarazmshahs' field armies rested on Qipchaq, Qangli and other steppe Turks, with Khwarazmian (East Iranian-speaking) and Tajik soldiers in a smaller role.
result_basis: Tekish routed the allied army and captured Ay-Aba, who was executed.
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Ala al-Din Tekish
note: Mu'ayyid Ay-Aba, a former mamluk of Sanjar, ruled Nishapur on his own after 1157; his line is treated as an Iran-seated local dynasty, which makes the battle civil. Tekish then took Dihistan and had Terken Khatun killed.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Herat (1175)
label: Herat (1175)
side_b: Baha al-Din Toghril, former Seljuk governor ruling Herat
faction_b: Baha al-Din Toghril, former Seljuk governor ruling Herat
commanders_a: Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad, Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad
persian_force: The Ghurid army of Ghur and Ghazni: Ghuri (Tajik) troops, Turkic ghulams and Khalaj and Afghan tribesmen (recruitment).
iranian_note: The Ghurid army of the 1170s was still largely raised among the Persian-speaking hillmen of Ghur, with Turkic ghulams beside them.
result_basis: The Ghurids defeated Toghril and took Herat and Pushang.
sources: Juzjani; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghurid dynasty (Battle of Herat), Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad, Muhammad of Ghor
note: Civil because Toghril, a Seljuk governor left over from Sanjar's state, ruled Herat on his own (an Iran-seated ruler); if he is counted as an outsider the battle is an ordinary Ghurid victory.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Multan (1175)
label: Multan (1175)
persian_force: Mu'izz al-Din's army from Ghazni: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Ghuri (Tajik), Khalaj and Afghan contingents (inferred from recruitment).
iranian_note: Mu'izz al-Din's armies combined Turkic slave cavalry with Persian-speaking Ghuris and Tajiks, Khalaj (Turkic, partly Pashtunised) and Afghans.
result_basis: Mu'izz al-Din defeated the Qarmatian ruler and annexed Multan.
sources: Juzjani; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghurid dynasty, Muhammad of Ghor
note: The 'Qarmatians' of Multan were its local Ismaili rulers.
qbasis: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state

name: Horns of Hama
label: Horns of Hama
place: Qurun Hama (Horns of Hama), near Hama, Syria
commanders_b: Izz al-Din Mas'ud of Mosul; Gumushtekin (regent of Aleppo)
result_basis: Saladin's smaller army routed the Zengid forces sent against him and he took the title of Sultan soon after.
sources: Lyons & Jackson, Saladin: The Politics of the Holy War (1982); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Wikipedia, Battle of the Horns of Hama
note: Saladin's first field victory in Syria; Kurdish emirs of his family held the principal commands. The Zengid side was Turkic.

name: Masyaf (siege, 1176)
label: Masyaf (siege, 1176)
persian_force: Sinan's garrison of Syrian Nizaris from the castles of the Jabal Bahra, with his fida'is.
iranian_note: The Syrian Nizari community was mainly Arabic-speaking; Persian da'is sent from Alamut led it.
result_basis: The siege ended after a short time in a truce between Saladin and Sinan, sought through Saladin's uncle Shihab al-Din of Hama, while Masyaf was still invested and untaken.
borderline: The Syrian Nizaris under Sinan acted largely independently of Alamut, though under its ultimate authority.
doubt: Borderline: The Syrian Nizaris under Sinan acted largely independently of Alamut, though under its ultimate authority.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Kamal al-Din; en.wikipedia Rashid ad-Din Sinan, Masyaf Castle
note: The story of Sinan's warning left in Saladin's tent is legend; the raising of the siege and the truce that followed are not doubted.
qbasis: Nizari Ismailis: an Iranian-led state

name: Uch (siege, 1176)
label: Uch (siege, 1176)
persian_force: Mu'izz al-Din's army from Ghazni: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Ghuri, Khalaj and Afghan contingents (recruitment).
iranian_note: Mu'izz al-Din's armies combined Turkic slave cavalry with Persian-speaking Ghuris and Tajiks, Khalaj and Afghans.
result_basis: Uch fell to Mu'izz al-Din, by tradition when the raja's wife opened the gates, and was given to Nasir al-Din Aitam.
borderline: The town fell by betrayal; how much fighting there was is unclear.
doubt: Borderline: The town fell by betrayal; how much fighting there was is unclear.
sources: Juzjani; Firishta; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghurid dynasty (Siege of Uch), Muhammad of Ghor
note: Wikipedia's Ghurid list names the defenders as 'Bhatis or Qarmatians'.
qbasis: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state

name: Tell al-Sultan
label: Tell al-Sultan
place: Tell al-Sultan, south-east of Aleppo, Syria
commanders_b: Sayf al-Din Ghazi II of Mosul
result_basis: Saladin defeated Sayf al-Din Ghazi's army and took its camp and baggage.
sources: Lyons & Jackson, Saladin: The Politics of the Holy War (1982); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Wikipedia, Battle of Tell al-Sultan
note: Followed by the siege of Azaz and a truce with Aleppo.

name: Azaz (siege, 1176)
label: Azaz
result_basis: Azaz surrendered to Saladin on 21 June 1176 after a siege in which a Nizari assassin wounded him.
sources: Lyons & Jackson, Saladin: The Politics of the Holy War (1982); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh
note: The Nizari attempt on Saladin during the siege was followed by his campaign against Masyaf (already in the dataset, 1176).

name: Montgisard
label: Montgisard
place: Montgisard (probably Tel Gezer), near Ramla, Israel
commanders_b: Baldwin IV; Raynald of Chatillon; Odo de Saint-Amand
result_basis: Baldwin IV's small army caught Saladin's strung-out force at the Wadi Hasi and routed it; Saladin fled to Egypt.
sources: William of Tyre, Historia; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Imad al-Din al-Isfahani, al-Fath al-Qussi; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: Saladin's nephew Taqi al-Din's son was among the dead. Qualifies by Saladin's command; the first big Ayyubid defeat.

name: Kasahrada (1178)
label: Kasahrada (1178)
place: Kasahrada (Kayadara), at the foot of Mount Abu, Rajasthan, India
commanders_a: Mularaja II (Chaulukya), Kelhanadeva of Nadol, Kirtipala, Dharavarsha of Chandravati
persian_force: Mu'izz al-Din's army, called 'Turushka' (Turks) in Indian sources and armoured head to foot, exhausted by the march across the Thar: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Ghuri, Khalaj and Afghan contingents (recruitment).
iranian_note: Indian sources call the army Turkic; by recruitment it also held Persian-speaking Ghuris and Tajiks and Afghan and Khalaj tribesmen.
result_basis: The Ghurid army was trapped in a pass below Mount Abu and routed; Mu'izz al-Din fled back to Ghazni.
sources: Juzjani; Merutunga; Udayaprabha Suri; Prabandha Kosha; en.wikipedia Battle of Kasahrada
note: The Chaulukyas of Gujarat with Paramara (Chandravati) and Chahamana (Nadol, Jalor) feudatories. Merutunga's later story crediting the queen Naikidevi is thought unreliable.
qbasis: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state

name: Marj Ayyun
label: Marj Ayyun
commanders_b: Baldwin IV; Humphrey II of Toron; Odo de Saint-Amand (captured); Raymond III of Tripoli
result_basis: Saladin's army routed Baldwin IV's host, captured the Master of the Temple and nearly took the king.
sources: William of Tyre, Historia; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3; Lyons & Jackson, Saladin: The Politics of the Holy War (1982)
note: Followed two months later by the fall of Jacob's Ford.

name: Jacob's Ford (Chastellet)
label: Jacob's Ford
place: Jacob's Ford (Vadum Iacob, Chastellet), Upper Jordan, Israel
commanders_b: Templar garrison (Odo de Saint-Amand was held prisoner); Baldwin IV (relief too late)
result_basis: Saladin undermined the new Templar fortress, stormed it on 29 August and razed it.
sources: William of Tyre, Historia; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Imad al-Din al-Isfahani, al-Fath al-Qussi; Wikipedia, Battle of Chastellet
note: The castle had been begun in 1178; about 700 defenders were killed or captured.

name: Lahore (siege, 1181)
label: Lahore (siege, 1181)
persian_force: Mu'izz al-Din's army from Ghazni: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Ghuri, Khalaj and Afghan contingents (recruitment).
iranian_note: Mu'izz al-Din's armies combined Turkic slave cavalry with Persian-speaking Ghuris and Tajiks, Khalaj and Afghans.
result_basis: The siege ended when Khusrau Malik made peace and gave his son as a hostage; Lahore did not fall.
borderline: How much fighting there was is unclear.
doubt: Borderline: How much fighting there was is unclear.
sources: Juzjani; en.wikipedia Muhammad of Ghor, Siege of Lahore (1186)
note: The Muhammad of Ghor article calls it a failed siege; the terms (a hostage, by some accounts an elephant) make it a negotiated end. The Ghaznavids at Lahore after 1163 are not counted as Persian.
qbasis: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state

name: Belvoir (Forbelet)
label: Belvoir
place: Forbelet, near Belvoir (Kaukab al-Hawa), Jordan valley, Israel
commanders_b: Baldwin IV; Guy of Lusignan; Raymond III of Tripoli
result_basis: Both sides held their ground after heavy fighting; Saladin withdrew across the Jordan and the Franks kept the field only in name.
sources: William of Tyre, Historia; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: Indecisive; Saladin then raided Galilee and moved on Beirut.

name: Beirut (siege, 1182)
label: Beirut
result_basis: Saladin's land and naval attack failed and he withdrew when the king's army approached.
sources: William of Tyre, Historia; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Lyons & Jackson, Saladin: The Politics of the Holy War (1982)
note: A combined attack with the Egyptian fleet; broken off to turn to Syria and the Jazira.

name: Mosul (siege, 1182)
label: Mosul
result_basis: Saladin broke off the siege after the Caliph's mediators intervened and moved to Sinjar and the Jazira.
sources: Lyons & Jackson, Saladin: The Politics of the Holy War (1982); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin)
note: Saladin's first attempt on Mosul; he held the lesser Jazira towns thereafter.

name: Red Sea raid of Reynald (1182-83)
label: Red Sea raid of Reynald
place: Gulf of Aqaba and the Hijaz coast, Red Sea (al-Hawra / Rabigh)
commanders_a: al-Adil (ruler in Egypt); Husam al-Din Lu'lu (admiral)
result_basis: Lu'lu's Egyptian squadron destroyed Reynald's ships and killed or captured his men.
sources: Lyons & Jackson, Saladin: The Politics of the Holy War (1982); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Wikipedia, Raynald of Chatillon
note: Qualifies by the Ayyubid ruler of Egypt (al-Adil, Saladin's brother) directing the response; field commander Lu'lu was not a Kurd. Details of place are approximate.

name: Amid (siege, 1183)
label: Amid
result_basis: Amid fell to Saladin and was given to his vassal Nur al-Din Muhammad of Hisn Kayfa.
sources: Lyons & Jackson, Saladin: The Politics of the Holy War (1982); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh
note: Nur al-Din Muhammad was an Artuqid, the later Hisn Kayfa line is Ayyubid; this is the point of contact between Saladin's and the Hisn Kayfa story.

name: Al-Fule (1183)
label: Al-Fule
place: Jezreel valley near Merhavia, about 8 km south-east of Afula (Al-Fule), Israel
result_basis: The Franks held their camp and Saladin was forced to withdraw after days of skirmishing without a decisive battle.
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of al-Fule (fetched); William of Tyre, Historia; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: The 1183 raid; the Franks avoided a full battle with their large army, which was later criticised. Saladin's field commanders named here were Turkish mamluks; Saladin himself is the basis.

name: Kerak (siege, 1183)
label: Kerak
result_basis: Saladin raised the siege when Baldwin IV's relief army approached; the wedding of Humphrey IV and Isabella was in progress inside.
sources: William of Tyre, Historia; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: Famous for the wedding of Humphrey IV and Isabella inside the castle: the lady of Kerak sent food from the feast to Saladin, who ordered the bridal tower spared. The siege was lifted on 4 December.

name: Kerak (siege, 1184)
label: Kerak
result_basis: Saladin withdrew when the king's army marched to Kerak's relief.
sources: William of Tyre, Historia; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: Second siege of Kerak under Saladin; the castle held and the relief army forced him to withdraw.

name: Sialkot (siege, 1185)
label: Sialkot (siege, 1185)
persian_force: The Ghurid garrison of Sialkot under Husain ibn Kharmil, an Iranian lord of Guzgan; its make-up is not recorded (Turkic ghulams and Ghuri troops, by recruitment).
iranian_note: Ghurid garrisons in the Punjab mixed Turkic ghulams with Persian-speaking Ghuri and Tajik soldiers; nothing specific is recorded for Sialkot.
result_basis: Khusrau Malik and the Khokhars failed to take the new Ghurid fort and withdrew.
sources: Juzjani; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghurid dynasty, Siege of Lahore (1186), Muhammad of Ghor
note: The Muhammad of Ghor article calls Sialkot an unsuccessful Ghurid siege; the Ghurid battle list and the Siege of Lahore (1186) article make it a failed Ghaznavid-Khokhar siege of the Ghurid garrison, followed here.
qbasis: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state

name: Mosul (siege, 1185-86)
label: Mosul
result_basis: Saladin fell ill, left the siege and accepted terms (Mosul became his vassal in March 1186).
sources: Lyons & Jackson, Saladin: The Politics of the Holy War (1982); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin)
note: The second siege; the end result was a treaty of vassalage with Mosul without capture of the city.

name: Lahore (siege, 1186)
label: Lahore (siege, 1186)
commanders_a: Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad, Husain ibn Kharmil
persian_force: About 20,000 men under Mu'izz al-Din: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Ghuri, Khalaj and Afghan contingents (recruitment).
iranian_note: Mu'izz al-Din's armies combined Turkic slave cavalry with Persian-speaking Ghuris and Tajiks, Khalaj and Afghans.
result_basis: Khusrau Malik surrendered Lahore after a short siege.
sources: Juzjani; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Siege of Lahore (1186)
note: End of the Ghaznavid line: Khusrau Malik and his son were imprisoned in Gharjistan and later executed.
qbasis: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state

name: Nishapur (siege, 1187)
label: Nishapur (siege, 1187)
side_b: Mengli Tegin, atabeg of Sanjar Shah
faction_b: Mengli Tegin, atabeg of Sanjar Shah (Mu'ayyids of Nishapur)
persian_force: Tekish's army of Qipchaq and Qangli Turkic cavalry with Khwarazmian troops; the defenders were Mengli Tegin's Turkic soldiers and the townsmen of Nishapur.
iranian_note: Tekish's army was built on Qipchaq, Qangli and other steppe Turks, with Khwarazmian and Tajik soldiers in a smaller role.
result_basis: Nishapur fell to Tekish after a siege of about two months.
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Ala al-Din Tekish
note: Nishapur had been ruled since 1157 by Mu'ayyid Ay-Aba and his heirs (Toghan Shah, Sanjar Shah); Tekish annexed it and sent Sanjar Shah to Gurganj.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Cresson
label: Cresson
place: Springs of Cresson, near Nazareth, Israel
commanders_a: Muzaffar al-Din Gokboru (field commander); al-Afdal Ali (Saladin's son, nominal)
commanders_b: Roger des Moulins (killed); Gerard de Ridefort
result_basis: A force of about 7,000 Muslim horse destroyed some 140 knights and their infantry, killing the Hospitaller Master; the Templar Master escaped with a handful of men.
sources: Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin); Ernoul; Wikipedia, Battle of Cresson
note: Qualifies as a raid led nominally by Saladin's son al-Afdal and ordered by Saladin; the field commander Gokboru was a Turk, so the leader basis is weaker than at Hattin.

name: Hattin
label: Hattin
place: Horns of Hattin, near Tiberias, Israel
commanders_a: Saladin; Taqi al-Din Umar; al-Afdal Ali; Muzaffar al-Din Gokboru
commanders_b: Guy of Lusignan; Raymond III of Tripoli; Raynald of Chatillon (executed); Gerard de Ridefort
result_basis: Saladin's army surrounded and destroyed the Frankish field army, capturing the king and the True Cross.
sources: Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin); Imad al-Din al-Isfahani, al-Fath al-Qussi; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3; Wikipedia, Battle of Hattin
note: Saladin's decisive victory; the siege of Tiberias (2-4 July) belongs with it and is not counted separately.

name: Tiberias (siege, 1187)
label: Tiberias
war: Saladin's wars (Ayyubid-Crusader wars; the Hattin campaign)
commanders_b: Eschiva of Bures, countess of Tripoli (citadel)
result_basis: Saladin's troops broke into the town on 2 July; the citadel held on briefly, which drew the Frankish army out to Hattin (Ibn al-Athir; Eracles).
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Imad al-Din al-Isfahani; Eracles; Wikipedia 'Battle of Hattin'
note: Saladin was a Kurd of the Rawwadid family of Dvin, ruling Arabs, Turks and Kurds. The Tiberias episode is the opening move of the Hattin campaign; Hattin itself is already listed.

name: Ascalon (siege, 1187)
label: Ascalon
commanders_b: Garrison of Ascalon (ordered to surrender by King Guy)
result_basis: Ascalon surrendered after a hard siege when the captured King Guy ordered its handing over.
sources: Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: The surrender was ordered by the captive King Guy in return for promises of freedom.

name: Jerusalem (siege, 1187)
label: Jerusalem
result_basis: After a breach in the north wall Balian negotiated a surrender and Saladin entered on 2 October.
sources: Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin); Imad al-Din al-Isfahani, al-Fath al-Qussi; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: Defended chiefly by townsmen and refugees under Balian; the surrender was a ransom treaty.

name: Kerak (siege, 1187-88)
label: Kerak
