result_basis: The castle held out for about a year and surrendered through famine.
sources: Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: Date of capitulation (c. November 1188) is approximate in the sources.

name: Tyre (siege, 1187-88)
label: Tyre
result_basis: Saladin lifted the siege on 1 January 1188 after Conrad's sorties and the loss of his fleet in a naval action on 30 December.
sources: Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: Saladin's chief failure of 1187; Tyre became the base of the Third Crusade.

name: Montreal (Shawbak, siege, 1188-1189)
label: Montreal
date: late 1188 to May 1189 (a siege of about a year)
war: Saladin's wars (Ayyubid-Crusader wars; reduction of the Transjordan castles)
result_basis: The starving garrison surrendered in 1189 (Ibn Shaddad; Wikipedia 'Montreal (Shobak)').
sources: Ibn Shaddad, Nawadir; Ibn al-Athir; Wikipedia 'Montreal (castle)'
note: Saladin and his brother al-Adil were Kurds ruling Egypt and Syria. Kerak and Montreal were the Frankish castles that cut the road from Egypt to Damascus; Kerak's sieges are already listed.

name: Saone (siege, 1188)
label: Saone
result_basis: Saladin's mangonels took the lower castle and the garrison surrendered on 29 July.
sources: Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh
note: One of the castles taken in Saladin's 1188 northern campaign (Latakia, Saone, Bourzey).

name: Belvoir (siege, 1188-89)
label: Belvoir
result_basis: The garrison, after a long siege with mining, surrendered on terms in early January 1189.
sources: Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: The last major fortress of Galilee to fall to Saladin.

name: Safed (siege, 1188)
label: Safed
result_basis: After a month's bombardment the Templars surrendered on terms.
sources: Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh
note: Part of Saladin's reduction of the remaining Galilean castles.

name: Acre (siege, 1189-91)
label: Acre
commanders_a: Saladin; al-Adil; Taqi al-Din; Baha' al-Din Qaraqush (garrison)
commanders_b: Guy of Lusignan; Philip II of France; Richard I of England; Conrad of Montferrat
result_basis: Acre capitulated to the Crusaders on 12 July 1191 after a two-year siege.
sources: Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin); Imad al-Din al-Isfahani, al-Fath al-Qussi; Itinerarium Peregrinorum; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: The Ayyubid relief army under Saladin besieged the besiegers for two years; Qualifies by Saladin's command and Ayyubid princes (al-Adil, Taqi al-Din) in the field.

name: Acre (battle, 4 October 1189)
label: Acre
commanders_b: Guy of Lusignan; Gerard de Ridefort (killed)
result_basis: The Frankish attack on Saladin's camp was repulsed after initial success and the Templar Master was killed, but the siege lines remained.
sources: Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin); Itinerarium Peregrinorum; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: The first big battle of the Acre siege; the field was held by Saladin but the Crusaders kept their siege lines.

name: Beaufort (siege, 1189-90)
label: Beaufort
result_basis: Reynald of Sidon's stalling failed and the castle fell to Saladin's forces in April 1190.
sources: Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Wikipedia, Beaufort Castle
note: Dates are approximate; Reynald was arrested for his ruse.

name: Marw al-Rudh (1190)
label: Marw al-Rudh (1190)
place: on the Murghab near Marw al-Rudh (Bala Murghab), Afghanistan
side_a: Ghiyath al-Din and Mu'izz al-Din, with the rulers of Bamiyan and Sistan
side_b: Sultan Shah, Khwarazmian ruler of Merv
faction_a: Ghiyath al-Din and Mu'izz al-Din (Ghurids), with the rulers of Bamiyan and Sistan
faction_b: Sultan Shah, Khwarazmian ruler of Merv
commanders_a: Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad, Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad
persian_force: The combined Ghurid armies of Firuzkuh and Ghazni with the Bamiyan Ghurids and the Nasrid malik of Sistan: Turkic ghulams, Ghuri troops and Sistani contingents; Sultan Shah had Turkic troops of Merv.
iranian_note: Ghuri and Sistani contingents were Persian-speaking; the Ghurid cavalry core was Turkic ghulams.
result_basis: Sultan Shah was defeated on the Murghab and fled to Merv; the Ghurids annexed most of his Khorasan lands.
sources: Juzjani; Juvayni; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghurid dynasty (Battle of Merv), Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad, Muhammad of Ghor, Ala al-Din Tekish
note: Listed as 'Battle of Merv' (1190) in Wikipedia's list of Ghurid battles; the Muhammad of Ghor article puts it on the Murghab and also gives 1192. Sultan Shah, Tekish's brother, ruled Merv, Sarakhs and Tus as a rival Khwarazmshah.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Tabarhindah (siege, 1191)
label: Tabarhindah (siege, 1191)
date: 1191-1192 (thirteen months, after the first battle of Tarain)
persian_force: A Ghurid garrison of about 2,000 under Qazi Zia al-Din Tulaki; its make-up is not recorded (Turkic and Tajik soldiers, by recruitment).
iranian_note: A Persian-speaking qazi commanded; the garrison was presumably the usual Ghurid mix of Turkic ghulams and Tajik and Ghuri soldiers.
result_basis: The Ghurid garrison surrendered the fort after holding out for thirteen months.
borderline: No separate article; described in the Tarain and Muhammad of Ghor articles.
doubt: Borderline: No separate article; described in the Tarain and Muhammad of Ghor articles.
sources: Juzjani; en.wikipedia First Battle of Tarain, Muhammad of Ghor
note: Tabarhindah is usually identified with Bathinda (some prefer Sirhind). Mu'izz al-Din had taken it shortly before the first battle of Tarain.
qbasis: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state

name: Tarain (1191)
label: Tarain (1191)
commanders_b: Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad (wounded), Qutb al-Din Aibak, Bahauddin Tughril
persian_force: Mu'izz al-Din's cavalry army: mounted Turkic ghulam archers with Ghuri, Khalji and Afghan emirs and their men (Juzjani names the Ghurid, Khalji and Afghan emirs who fled); a Khalji horseman carried the wounded sultan away.
iranian_note: Juzjani names Ghurid (Persian-speaking), Khalji (Turkic) and Afghan (Pashto) emirs beside the Turkic slave archers.
strength_a: unknown (100,000 cavalry per Roy, an unreliable figure)
result_basis: The Chahamana counter-attack drove the Ghurids off after Mu'izz al-Din was wounded and carried away; the Rajputs held the field.
sources: Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri; Hasan Nizami; Firishta; en.wikipedia First Battle of Tarain
note: Wikipedia title: 'First Battle of Tarain'. The Chahamanas of Shakambhari (Prithviraj III) with allied Rajput chiefs.
qbasis: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state

name: Arsuf
label: Arsuf
commanders_b: Richard I; Robert of Leicester; James of Avesnes (killed)
result_basis: Richard's counter-charge routed the Muslim army, which withdrew with the road to Jaffa open.
sources: Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin); Imad al-Din al-Isfahani, al-Fath al-Qussi; Itinerarium Peregrinorum; Ambroise; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: Saladin tried to break up the crusader column on its march to Jaffa and lost the field.

name: Tarain (1192)
label: Tarain (1192)
commanders_a: Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad, Qutb al-Din Aibak, Taj al-Din Yildiz, Nasir al-Din Qubacha, Husain ibn Kharmil, Kharbak, Mukalba, Ilah
persian_force: Mu'izz al-Din's army of 120,000 armoured men (Minhaj): 40,000 elite horse under the sultan, 10,000 mounted archers in four divisions and a reserve of 12,000, with the commands of the Turkic slave generals Aibak, Yildiz and Qubacha and of the Ghazni lords Kharbak, Kharmil, Ilah and Mukalba, and Khalji and Afghan troops.
iranian_note: The striking arm was Turkic slave cavalry, but the Ghurid lords' contingents, Tajiks and Afghans brought many Iranian-language speakers.
result_basis: Ghurid dawn attacks and feigned retreats broke the Rajput army, which fled; Prithviraj was captured near Sursuti.
sources: Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri; Hasan Nizami, Taj al-Ma'athir; Firishta; en.wikipedia Second Battle of Tarain
note: Wikipedia title: 'Second Battle of Tarain'. It opened northern India to the Ghurids; Prithviraj was later executed.
qbasis: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state

name: Jaffa (1192)
label: Jaffa
result_basis: Saladin stormed Jaffa on 28 July but Richard's relief force retook it and repulsed a Muslim surprise attack on 5 August.
sources: Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin); Itinerarium Peregrinorum; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: The final battle of the Third Crusade, fought shortly before the Treaty of Ramla; Richard's small force repulsed Saladin's army.

name: Bagar
label: Bagar
war: Ghurid campaigns in India (rebellion of Jatwan)
persian_force: Aibak's Ghurid army in India: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Ghuri and Khalji contingents (recruitment).
iranian_note: Aibak's armies were led by Turkic ghulams but drew on Ghuri, Tajik and Afghan soldiers as well.
result_basis: Jatwan raised his siege of Hansi, was beaten near Bagar and was killed.
sources: Hasan Nizami; en.wikipedia Rebellion of Jatwan, List of battles involving the Ghurid dynasty (Battle of Bagar)
note: Includes the relief of Hansi, where Jatwan, a former Chahamana subordinate, had besieged the Ghurid commander Nasrat al-Din.
qbasis: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state

name: Ajmer (1194)
label: Ajmer (1194)
persian_force: Aibak's Ghurid army in India: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Ghuri and Khalji contingents (recruitment).
iranian_note: Aibak's armies were led by Turkic ghulams but drew on Ghuri, Tajik and Afghan soldiers as well.
result_basis: Aibak defeated Hariraja, who burned himself, and the Ghurids reoccupied Ajmer.
borderline: No separate article; listed in Wikipedia's list of Ghurid battles.
doubt: Borderline: No separate article; listed in Wikipedia's list of Ghurid battles.
sources: Hasan Nizami; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghurid dynasty (Battle of Ajmer), Muhammad of Ghor, Battle of Kasahrada (1197)
note: Hariraja, Prithviraj's brother, had driven out the Ghurid vassal Govindaraja IV.
qbasis: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state

name: Chandawar
label: Chandawar
place: Chandawar (Chandwar), near Firozabad, Uttar Pradesh, India
commanders_a: Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad, Qutb al-Din Aibak
persian_force: Mu'izz al-Din's army of 50,000 horsemen with Aibak's vanguard: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Ghuri, Khalji and Afghan contingents (recruitment).
iranian_note: Mu'izz al-Din's armies combined Turkic slave cavalry with Persian-speaking Ghuris and Tajiks, Khalaj and Afghans.
result_basis: The battle was hotly contested until Jayachandra was killed and his army routed.
sources: Hasan Nizami; Juzjani; en.wikipedia Battle of Chandawar, Muhammad of Ghor
note: The Gahadavalas of Kannauj and Varanasi. Some date it to winter 1193-94.
qbasis: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state

name: Rayy (1194)
label: Rayy (1194)
date: March 1194 (19 March in the Toghrul III article; 4 March in the Tekish article)
side_a: Tekish, with the Eldiguzid Qutlugh Inanch
faction_a: Tekish (Khwarazmshah), with the Eldiguzid Qutlugh Inanch
persian_force: Tekish's Khwarazmian army of Qipchaq and Qangli Turkic cavalry, with the troops of the Eldiguzid claimant Qutlugh Inanch; Toghrul's side was his mamluks and Turkmen-backed amirs, most of whom did not fight.
iranian_note: Tekish's army drew on Qipchaq, Qangli and Uran Turks through his Qipchaq marriage; Iranian troops were a small part.
result_basis: Toghrul III charged with about 60 guards while his amirs held back and was killed; the Khwarazmians held the field.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Juvayni; Rawandi; en.wikipedia Toghrul III, Ala al-Din Tekish, List of battles involving the Seljuk Empire, Al-Nasir
note: End of the Seljuk sultanate of Iraq; Toghrul's head was sent to the caliph al-Nasir, who had encouraged Tekish.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Shamkor
label: Shamkor
war: Georgian-Seljuk wars (Georgian intervention in the Eldiguzid succession)
persian_force: Abu Bakr's Eldiguzid army of Azerbaijan and Arran, reinforced by his client Muslim emirs: Turkic mamluks and Turkmen cavalry with Kurdish and local troops (recruitment).
iranian_note: The Eldiguzid armies were Turkic mamluks and Turkmen tribesmen, with Kurdish and Iranian auxiliaries in a smaller role.
result_basis: Soslan's flank march broke Abu Bakr's army, which fled to Ganja; the Georgians took Shamkor and then Ganja.
sources: Georgian Chronicles (Histories and Eulogies of the Sovereigns); en.wikipedia Battle of Shamkor, Georgian-Seljuk wars
note: Abu Bakr's brother Amir Amiran (Mihran) sided with Georgia and the Shirvanshah; the Georgians took the caliph's standard. Some accounts date the battle to the early 1190s.
qbasis: The Georgian army was commanded by Queen Tamar's consort David Soslan, an Ossetian (Alan) prince of the Bagatar royal family (Georgian Chronicle of Queen Tamar; Wikipedia, Battle of Shamkor, for his command).

name: Ajmer (siege, 1196)
label: Ajmer (siege, 1196)
commanders_b: the Mer chiefs, with Bhima II's Chaulukyas
persian_force: Aibak's Ghurid troops in Ajmer, relieved by an army sent by Mu'izz al-Din: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Ghuri and Khalji contingents (recruitment).
iranian_note: Aibak's armies were led by Turkic ghulams but drew on Ghuri, Tajik and Afghan soldiers as well.
result_basis: A relief army from Ghazni reached Ajmer and the besiegers withdrew.
borderline: No separate article; described in the Battle of Kasahrada (1197) article.
doubt: Borderline: No separate article; described in the Battle of Kasahrada (1197) article.
sources: Hasan Nizami; Firishta; en.wikipedia Battle of Kasahrada (1197)
note: The Mers had driven the Ghurid garrison out of the Ajmer country while Aibak was in Delhi.
qbasis: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state

name: Bayana (siege)
label: Bayana (siege)
commanders_a: Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad, Qutb al-Din Aibak, Bahauddin Tughril
persian_force: Mu'izz al-Din's army with Aibak's: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Ghuri, Khalji and Afghan contingents (recruitment).
iranian_note: Mu'izz al-Din's armies combined Turkic slave cavalry with Persian-speaking Ghuris and Tajiks, Khalaj and Afghans.
result_basis: Kumarapala surrendered the fort and Bayana was put under Bahauddin Tughril.
borderline: No separate article; listed in Wikipedia's list of Ghurid battles.
doubt: Borderline: No separate article; listed in Wikipedia's list of Ghurid battles.
sources: Hasan Nizami; Juzjani; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghurid dynasty (Siege of Bayana), Muhammad of Ghor
qbasis: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state

name: Damascus (siege, 1196)
label: Damascus
war: Ayyubid succession war (sons of Saladin v. al-Adil)
persian_state: Ayyubids of Egypt v Ayyubids of Damascus
result_basis: Al-Adil allied with al-Aziz, took Damascus and let al-Afdal retire to Salkhad.
sources: Humphreys, From Saladin to the Mongols: The Ayyubids of Damascus 1193-1260 (1977); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayyubid_dynasty (fetched); Wikipedia, Al-Afdal ibn Salah ad-Din (fetched)
note: A war inside the Ayyubid family, with Ayyubid princes leading both sides; sources differ on how much fighting there was before the settlement. Exact dates are uncertain.

name: Gwalior (siege, 1196)
label: Gwalior (siege, 1196)
commanders_a: Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad, Qutb al-Din Aibak, Bahauddin Tughril
persian_force: Aibak's and Tughril's Ghurid forces: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Ghuri and Khalji troops (recruitment).
iranian_note: Aibak's armies were led by Turkic ghulams but drew on Ghuri, Tajik and Afghan soldiers as well.
result_basis: After a long siege Sulakshanapala surrendered and accepted Ghurid rule (Wikipedia: Gwalior annexed).
sources: Juzjani; Firishta; en.wikipedia Siege of Gwalior (1196), Muhammad of Ghor
note: Kachchhapaghata (Parihar) ruler. Some accounts have the raja only pay tribute in 1196 and hand over the fort in 1200 after Tughril's blockade; if so the 1196 siege was a draw.
qbasis: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state

name: Kasahrada (1197)
label: Kasahrada (1197)
place: Kasahrada (Kayadara), at the foot of Mount Abu, Rajasthan, India
commanders_a: Qutb al-Din Aibak, Asad al-Din Arslan Qulij, Jahan Pahlavan, Nasir al-Din Husain
commanders_b: Bhima II's commanders: Jayatasimha (killed), Dharavarsha, Prahladana
persian_force: Aibak's Indian army reinforced from Ghazna: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Khalji and Ghuri contingents (recruitment).
iranian_note: Aibak's armies were led by Turkic ghulams but drew on Ghuri, Tajik and Afghan soldiers as well.
result_basis: The Rajputs came down into the plain and the Ghurid cavalry routed them; Aibak then sacked Anhilwara.
sources: Hasan Nizami, Taj al-Ma'athir; Firishta; en.wikipedia Battle of Kasahrada (1197)
note: Chaulukyas with Paramara and Naddula Chahamana allies. Wikipedia title: 'Battle of Kasahrada (1197)'.
qbasis: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state

name: Jaffa (1197)
label: Jaffa
commanders_b: Henry of Champagne (died during the siege); garrison of Jaffa
result_basis: Al-Adil took Jaffa by storm before the German crusaders arrived.
sources: Humphreys, From Saladin to the Mongols: The Ayyubids of Damascus 1193-1260 (1977); Wikipedia, Al-Adil I (fetched)
note: Henry of Champagne fell from a window to his death in the same days. The date within September 1197 is approximate.

name: Toron (siege, 1197-98)
label: Toron
side_b: German Crusaders and Kingdom of Jerusalem
commanders_b: Henry of Brabant; Conrad of Querfurt
result_basis: The Crusaders raised the siege when al-Adil's relief army approached and news came of the death of Henry VI.
sources: Humphreys, From Saladin to the Mongols: The Ayyubids of Damascus 1193-1260 (1977); Wikipedia, Al-Adil I (fetched); Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: Date-range as given in standard accounts of the German Crusade.

name: Guzgan (1198)
label: Guzgan (1198)
commanders_a: the Ghurid amirs of Guzgan and Balkh, for Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad
persian_force: The Ghurid forces of Guzgan and Balkh (Husain ibn Kharmil's lordship): Turkic ghulams with Ghuri and local Tajik troops (recruitment).
iranian_note: Provincial Ghurid forces in Guzgan were raised from local Persian-speaking lords and their men alongside Turkic ghulams.
result_basis: The Ghurids routed a large Qara Khitai army that had invaded Guzgan.
borderline: No conventional name; a pitched battle in Juzjani and Juvayni.
doubt: Borderline: No conventional name; a pitched battle in Juzjani and Juvayni.
sources: Juzjani; Juvayni; en.wikipedia Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad, Ala al-Din Tekish
note: The Qara Khitai invaded at Tekish's request; the Ghurids took Balkh the same year.
qbasis: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state

name: Arslan-Gusha (siege)
label: Arslan-Gusha (siege)
persian_force: Tekish's Khwarazmian army (Qipchaq and Qangli Turkic troops); the defenders were Nizari garrison troops of the Alamut state.
iranian_note: Tekish's army drew on Qipchaq, Qangli and Uran Turks; Iranian troops were a small part.
result_basis: The fortress fell to Tekish after a four-month siege.
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Ala al-Din Tekish
note: Wikipedia's Tekish article also says he attacked Alamut the same year without success (not listed here).
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Damascus (siege, 1199)
label: Damascus
war: Ayyubid succession war (sons of Saladin v. al-Adil)
persian_state: Ayyubids of Damascus v Ayyubids of Egypt and Aleppo
result_basis: Al-Adil split the brothers' vassals and the siege ended when al-Kamil's reinforcements arrived in December 1199.
sources: Wikipedia, Al-Adil I (fetched); Humphreys, From Saladin to the Mongols: The Ayyubids of Damascus 1193-1260 (1977)
note: Ayyubid princes led both sides; al-Adil prevailed.

name: Sack of Magadha
label: Sack of Magadha
war: Ghurid campaigns in India (Bakhtiyar Khalji in Bihar)
persian_force: Bakhtiyar Khalji's band of Khalaj and other Muslim horsemen from Awadh, about 200 at the start.
iranian_note: Bakhtiyar's followers were mainly Khalaj, a Turkic people of the Garmsir, with some Tajik and Afghan adventurers.
result_basis: Bakhtiyar took the fortified monastery of Odantapuri and defeated and killed its ruler in the field outside.
borderline: Bakhtiyar acted largely on his own as a Ghurid officer under Aibak; a raid on a fortified monastery.
doubt: Borderline: Bakhtiyar acted largely on his own as a Ghurid officer under Aibak; a raid on a fortified monastery.
sources: Juzjani; Taranatha; en.wikipedia Sack of Magadha
note: The destruction of Nalanda and Vikramashila attributed to Bakhtiyar is disputed.
qbasis: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state

name: Turshiz (siege)
label: Turshiz (siege)
faction_a: Qutb al-Din Muhammad (later Muhammad II), for Tekish
persian_force: Qutb al-Din Muhammad's Khwarazmian army (Turkic cavalry and Khorasani troops); the defenders were the Nizari garrison of Quhistan.
iranian_note: Khwarazmian field armies were mainly Qipchaq and Qangli Turks.
result_basis: The siege ended in a truce, the Nizaris paying 100,000 dinars, with the fort still untaken.
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Ala al-Din Tekish, Muhammad II of Khwarazm
note: Muhammad broke off the siege on hearing of Tekish's death (July 1200); the Tekish article dates it 1199.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Bilbeis (1200)
label: Bilbeis
war: Ayyubid succession war (sons of Saladin v. al-Adil)
persian_state: Ayyubids of Damascus v Ayyubids of Egypt
result_basis: Al-Adil pursued al-Afdal into Egypt and defeated him at Bilbeis; al-Afdal fled to Cairo and gave up Egypt.
sources: Wikipedia, Al-Adil I (fetched); Humphreys, From Saladin to the Mongols: The Ayyubids of Damascus 1193-1260 (1977)
note: Ayyubid princes on both sides; al-Adil proclaimed himself Sultan on 17 February 1200.

name: Damascus (siege, 1201)
label: Damascus
war: Ayyubid succession war (sons of Saladin v. al-Adil)
result_basis: Quarrels between al-Afdal and al-Zahir broke up the siege and al-Adil retained Damascus.
sources: Wikipedia, Al-Adil I (fetched); Humphreys, From Saladin to the Mongols: The Ayyubids of Damascus 1193-1260 (1977)
note: The last attempt by Saladin's sons to retake Damascus; exact dates uncertain.

name: Nishapur (Ghurid siege, 1201)
label: Nishapur (Ghurid siege, 1201)
date: April 1201 (fell about 7 April after a few days; Ghurid list: 1200/1)
faction_b: Muhammad II of Khwarazm (garrison under Taj al-Din Ali Shah)
commanders_a: Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad, Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad
persian_force: The combined Ghurid armies of Ghiyath al-Din and Mu'izz al-Din, with war elephants brought from India: Turkic ghulams, Ghuri and Afghan contingents (recruitment).
iranian_note: The Ghurid armies combined Turkic slave cavalry with Persian-speaking Ghuris and Tajiks and Afghans.
result_basis: The Khwarazmian garrison surrendered Nishapur after a few days' siege.
sources: Juzjani; Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Muhammad II of Khwarazm, Ghurid conquest of Khorasan, List of battles involving the Ghurid dynasty (Battle of Nishapur)
note: Part of the Ghurid conquest of Khorasan (1200-1201), in which Merv, Sarakhs and Tus also fell.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Nishapur (Khwarazmian siege, 1201)
label: Nishapur (Khwarazmian siege, 1201)
side_b: Ghurid garrison under Diya al-Din Muhammad al-Ghuri
faction_b: Ghurid garrison under Diya al-Din Muhammad al-Ghuri
persian_force: Muhammad II's Khwarazmian army of Qipchaq and Qangli Turkic cavalry with Khorasani troops; the defenders were the Ghurid garrison of Ghuri and Turkic soldiers.
iranian_note: Muhammad II's armies rested on Qipchaq and Qangli Turks; Iranian troops were a smaller element.
result_basis: The Ghurid garrison surrendered after a two-month siege and the walls were razed.
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Muhammad II of Khwarazm
note: Muhammad retook Merv the same month.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Herat (siege, 1202)
label: Herat (siege, 1202)
side_a: Ghurid garrison of Herat, relieved by Husain ibn Kharmil
faction_a: Ghurid garrison of Herat, relieved by Husain ibn Kharmil
commanders_a: Umar al-Marghani, Alp Ghazi, Husain ibn Kharmil
persian_force: The Ghurid garrison of Herat under Umar al-Marghani and Alp Ghazi, with Husain ibn Kharmil's field force from Guzgan (Turkic ghulams and Ghuri and Tajik troops, by recruitment).
iranian_note: The Ghurid forces in Khorasan were led by Iranian lords such as Kharmil and al-Marghani alongside Turkic ghulams.
result_basis: Muhammad lifted the siege of Herat, and Ibn Kharmil destroyed a Khwarazmian detachment.
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Muhammad II of Khwarazm
note: In the spring of 1202 Mu'izz al-Din fought Muhammad near Merv with heavy losses on both sides (not listed separately).
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Kalinjar (siege, 1203)
label: Kalinjar (siege, 1203)
date: 1202 to 12 April 1203 (some scholars date the fall to 1202)
place: Kalinjar fort, Banda, Uttar Pradesh, India
persian_force: Aibak's 'huge army' with Iltutmish: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Ghuri and Khalji troops (recruitment).
iranian_note: Aibak's armies were led by Turkic ghulams but drew on Ghuri, Tajik and Afghan soldiers as well.
result_basis: With its reservoirs dry, the garrison surrendered the fort on terms and withdrew to Ajaigarh.
sources: Hasan Nizami, Taj al-Ma'athir; Firishta; en.wikipedia Siege of Kalinjar (1203)
note: The Chandelas of Jejakabhukti. The Taj al-Ma'athir claims 50,000 people were enslaved; Kalpi and Mahoba also fell.
qbasis: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state

name: Basiani
label: Basiani
date: About 1203 (scholars range 1202-1204; Ibn Bibi gives 598 AH, 1201-02)
place: Basiani valley, near modern Pasinler, east of Erzurum (Turkey)
commanders_a: David Soslan (commander of the army); Zakaria II Mkhargrdzeli (vanguard); Ivane Mkhargrdzeli
result_basis: Georgian Chronicle: the Georgians routed the sultan, who fell back on Erzurum, and took the Emir of Erzincan prisoner.
sources: Georgian Chronicle of Queen Tamar; Ibn Bibi; Rayfield (2012); Mikaberidze; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Basian; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Soslan
note: As at Shamkor, the Iranian element is the commander David Soslan, an Alan (Ossetian) prince; no Alan unit is named.

name: Gurganj (siege, 1204)
label: Gurganj (siege, 1204)
war: Ghurid-Khwarazmian wars (Mu'izz al-Din's invasion of Khwarazm)
side_a: Muhammad II of Khwarazm and Terken Khatun
faction_a: Muhammad II of Khwarazm and Terken Khatun
commanders_a: Muhammad II, Terken Khatun, Shihab al-Din al-Khivaqi; relief under Tayangu, Uthman ibn Ibrahim and Taj al-Din Bilge Khan
commanders_b: Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad, Husain ibn Kharmil
persian_force: Gurganj's defenders: the citizen militia raised by Terken Khatun and the Shafi'i leader Shihab al-Din al-Khivaqi (70,000 claimed) and the Khwarazmshah's Turkic troops; the relief army was Qara Khitai and Qarakhanid.
iranian_note: The sources stress the townsmen's militia of Gurganj, who spoke Khwarazmian, beside the Khwarazmshah's Qipchaq and Qangli troops.
strength_a: about 40,000 with a militia of 70,000 (claimed); Qara Khitai relief 10,000-40,000
result_basis: Mu'izz al-Din abandoned the siege when the Qara Khitai relief army approached.
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Siege of Gurganj (1204)
note: Civil because the Khwarazmshah's own forces held Gurganj; the Qara Khitai and Uthman of Samarkand came as allies.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Kakadadaha
label: Kakadadaha
persian_force: The Ghurid forces of the Kalinjar region; nothing is recorded (Turkic ghulams and their Ghuri and Khalji followers, by recruitment).
iranian_note: Ghurid garrison forces in India mixed Turkic ghulams with Persian-speaking soldiers; nothing specific is recorded here.
result_basis: A Chandela inscription records Trailokyavarman's victory over the 'Turushkas' at Kakadadaha.
borderline: Known only from a Chandela copper-plate inscription; no Persian-language source mentions it.
doubt: Borderline: Known only from a Chandela copper-plate inscription; no Persian-language source mentions it.
sources: Garra copper-plate inscription; Ajaygarh inscription of Viravarman; en.wikipedia Trailokyavarman, List of wars involving Iran (before 1979)
note: Wikipedia's list of Iranian wars dates it 1205. Trailokyavarman's recovery of Kalinjar rests on the same inscriptions.
qbasis: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state

name: Nadia
label: Nadia
persian_force: Bakhtiyar Khalji's Khalaj and Turkic horsemen; he rode in with 18 men disguised as horse dealers while the main body waited in a nearby forest.
iranian_note: Bakhtiyar's army was mainly Khalaj (Turkic) cavalry with some Tajik and Afghan followers.
strength_a: 18 horsemen in the raid, the main army nearby
result_basis: Bakhtiyar's raiders seized the palace, Lakshmana Sena fled east, and the Ghurid army held Nadia.
borderline: Bakhtiyar acted largely on his own as a Ghurid officer; a raid on a capital rather than a pitched battle.
doubt: Borderline: Bakhtiyar acted largely on his own as a Ghurid officer; a raid on a capital rather than a pitched battle.
sources: Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri; en.wikipedia Ghurid conquest of Bengal
note: Sena kingdom. Wikipedia title: 'Ghurid conquest of Bengal'; a footnote there identifies Nadiya with Naoda in Rajshahi District, Bangladesh. Bakhtiyar then made Lakhnauti his capital.
qbasis: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state

name: Qarasu
label: Qarasu
war: Ghurid-Khwarazmian wars (Mu'izz al-Din's invasion of Khwarazm)
place: the Qarasu canal, east of Gurganj, Turkmenistan
side_b: Muhammad II of Khwarazm, with Uthman of Samarkand
faction_b: Muhammad II of Khwarazm, with Uthman of Samarkand
persian_force: Mu'izz al-Din's invasion army with war elephants: Turkic ghulam cavalry, Ghuri, Khalji and Afghan contingents and Indian troops (recruitment); the Khwarazmians had Qipchaq and Qangli Turks.
iranian_note: The Ghurid armies combined Turkic slave cavalry with Persian-speaking Ghuris and Tajiks, Khalaj and Afghans.
result_basis: The Ghurids won a costly fight at the canal and the Khwarazmshah fell back on Gurganj.
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Battle of Qarasu, Muhammad II of Khwarazm
note: Called a Pyrrhic Ghurid victory; the Ghurids killed their Khwarazmian prisoners. The Khwarazmshah had flooded the approaches by breaching dikes, holding the Ghurids for about 40 days.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Herat (siege, 1204)
label: Herat (siege, 1204)
side_b: Alp Ghazi, Ghurid governor of Herat
faction_b: Alp Ghazi, Ghurid governor of Herat
persian_force: Muhammad II's Khwarazmian army of Qipchaq and Qangli Turkic cavalry; the defenders were the Ghurid garrison of Herat.
iranian_note: Muhammad II's armies rested on Qipchaq and Qangli Turks.
result_basis: The siege ended in an agreement by which Alp Ghazi paid an indemnity, and the Khwarazmshah turned back when Mu'izz al-Din invaded Khwarazm.
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Muhammad II of Khwarazm, Siege of Gurganj (1204)
note: Wikipedia's wording ('Alp Ghazi surrendered for an indemnity') is ambiguous; if Herat was handed over, the besieger won. This siege provoked Mu'izz al-Din's invasion of Khwarazm.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Andkhud
label: Andkhud
date: 28-29 September 1204 (date per the Muhammad II article)
war: Ghurid-Qara Khitai conflicts (Mu'izz al-Din's retreat from Khwarazm)
commanders_a: Tayangu, Uthman ibn Ibrahim of Samarkand, Taj al-Din Bilge Khan
commanders_b: Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad (wounded), Husain ibn Kharmil, Nasir al-Din Aitam (killed), Aibak Yogi, Aibak Beg
persian_force: Mu'izz al-Din's army, about 20,000 horse worn out by the retreat from Gurganj: his Turkic slave commanders (Aibak Yogi, Aibak Beg), provincial governors such as Nasir al-Din Aitam, and Ghuri and Afghan troops.
iranian_note: The Ghurid army combined Turkic slave cavalry with Persian-speaking Ghuris and Tajiks and Afghans; the named commanders here are mostly Turkic ghulams.
result_basis: The Qara Khitai and Qarakhanids routed the Ghurids and besieged Mu'izz al-Din in Andkhud fort until he paid a ransom.
sources: Juzjani; Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Battle of Andkhud, Muhammad II of Khwarazm
note: Wikipedia also lists the Khwarazmians as belligerents (they had harried the Ghurid retreat at Hazar Saf); the battle itself was fought by the Qara Khitai and Uthman of Samarkand, so it is not counted as civil. The Ghurids lost Khorasan except Herat and Balkh.
qbasis: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state

name: Tirmidh (siege, 1205)
label: Tirmidh (siege, 1205)
persian_force: The Ghurid forces of Balkh (the Bamiyan Ghurid sphere): Turkic ghulams with Ghuri and local Tajik troops (recruitment).
iranian_note: Provincial Ghurid forces in Balkh drew on local Persian-speaking troops beside Turkic ghulams.
result_basis: The Ghurids took Tirmidh and destroyed its Qara Khitai garrison.
sources: Juzjani; en.wikipedia Muhammad of Ghor
qbasis: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state

name: Jhelum (1206)
label: Jhelum (1206)
place: between the Chenab and the Jhelum, Punjab, Pakistan
commanders_a: Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad, Qutb al-Din Aibak, Iltutmish
persian_force: Mu'izz al-Din's main army from Ghazna with Aibak's contingent from Delhi and Iltutmish's from Badaun: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Ghuri, Khalji and Afghan troops (recruitment).
iranian_note: The Ghurid armies combined Turkic slave cavalry with Persian-speaking Ghuris and Tajiks, Khalaj and Afghans.
result_basis: After a fight from morning to sunset, the arrival of Aibak and Iltutmish broke the Khokhars, who were routed and massacred.
sources: Juzjani; Hasan Nizami; Firishta; en.wikipedia Battle of Jhelum (1206)
note: Wikipedia's list of Ghurid battles has the same campaign as 'Revolt of Khokars', February-March 1205. Mu'izz al-Din was assassinated at Dhamiak on 15 March 1206 on his way back.
qbasis: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state

name: Bakhtiyar Khalji's Tibet campaign
label: Bakhtiyar Khalji's Tibet campaign
war: Ghurid campaigns in India (Bakhtiyar Khalji's Tibet expedition)
place: Chumbi Valley, Tibet, and the Teesta crossing on the retreat, China
commanders_a: Tibetan tribal leaders; the raja of Kamrup
persian_force: Bakhtiyar's Bengal army of about 10,000 cavalry, mostly Khalaj and other Turks, with local (Deshi) Muslims, guided by Ali Mech.
iranian_note: The sources describe a Turkic cavalry army with local Bengali Muslims; Iranian speakers can only have been a few.
result_basis: The Tibetans trapped and drove back the army, and at the broken bridge on the retreat it was destroyed; only about 100 horsemen returned.
borderline: A campaign rather than a single battle; Bakhtiyar ruled Lakhnauti as an autonomous Ghurid officer, and Mu'izz al-Din was killed (15 March 1206) as it began.
doubt: Borderline: A campaign rather than a single battle; Bakhtiyar ruled Lakhnauti as an autonomous Ghurid officer, and Mu'izz al-Din was killed (15 March 1206) as it began.
sources: Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri; en.wikipedia Bakhtiyar Khalji's Tibet campaign, Muslim invasions of Assam
note: The forces of Kamarupa (Kamrup) destroyed the bridge on the retreat. Accounts of Bakhtiyar's death (illness, or murder by Ali Mardan Khalji) differ.
qbasis: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state

name: Herat (siege, 1207-1208)
label: Herat (siege, 1207-1208)
war: Khwarazmian conquest of the Ghurid lands (revolt of Husain ibn Kharmil)
side_b: Herat rebels under Khwaja al-Sahib, pledged to the Ghurid Ghiyath al-Din Mahmud
faction_b: Herat rebels under Khwaja al-Sahib (after Husain ibn Kharmil's capture), pledged to the Ghurid Ghiyath al-Din Mahmud
commanders_a: Emir Jaldik, Taj al-Din Abu Bakr, Kuzlik Khan, Muhammad II
commanders_b: Husain ibn Kharmil (captured, executed), Khwaja al-Sahib (executed)
persian_force: Khwarazmian cavalry: Jaldik's 2,000 and then about 10,000 under Kuzlik Khan and Taj al-Din Abu Bakr (Turkic troops, by recruitment); the defenders were Herat's garrison and townsmen.
iranian_note: Muhammad II's armies rested on Qipchaq and Qangli Turks; the defenders of Herat were mainly Persian-speaking townsmen.
result_basis: The Khwarazmians breached the walls and took Herat in July 1208 (or 1209).
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Revolt of Husain ibn Kharmil, Muhammad II of Khwarazm
note: Wikipedia title: 'Revolt of Husain ibn Kharmil'. The Khwarazmians also tried to flood the city by damming its water.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Khilat (siege, 1208)
label: Khilat
date: 1208 (Georgian sources put the capture of Ivane Mkhargrdzeli in 1210)
result_basis: The Georgian siege failed and their general Ivane was taken prisoner, released under the truce of 1210.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayyubid_dynasty (fetched); Georgian Chronicles; Humphreys, From Saladin to the Mongols: The Ayyubids of Damascus 1193-1260 (1977)
note: Dates differ between the Arabic and Georgian sources; the Ayyubid ruler of Khilat was al-Awhad, al-Adil's son.

name: Ganja (siege, 1213)
label: Ganja (siege, 1213)
persian_force: Uzbek's Eldiguzid garrison of Ganja, which sortied 10,000 strong: Turkic mamluks and Turkmen troops with the townsmen (recruitment).
iranian_note: The Eldiguzid armies were Turkic mamluks and Turkmen tribesmen; Ganja's townsmen were Persian-speaking.
result_basis: The garrison's sortie was beaten but Ganja did not fall; the siege ended in a treaty by which Uzbek resumed tribute to Georgia.
sources: Georgian Chronicles; en.wikipedia Siege of Ganja (1213)
note: Wikipedia calls it a Georgian victory; under the siege test a treaty with the place still invested is a draw.
qbasis: Ganja's townsmen joined the sortie

name: Karaj (1215)
label: Karaj (1215)
war: Revolt of Mengli in Persian Iraq
place: near Karaj (Karaj of Abu Dulaf), Markazi, Iran
side_a: Uzbek with Hasan III's Nizaris and the caliph's army
side_b: Mengli, ruler of Hamadan, Isfahan and Rayy
faction_a: Uzbek (Eldiguzids) with Hasan III's Nizaris and the caliph's army
faction_b: Mengli, ruler of Hamadan, Isfahan and Rayy
commanders_a: Muzaffar al-Din Uzbek; Muzaffar al-Din Sunqur (Wajh al-Sab', for the caliph); the troops of Jalal al-Din Hasan III of Alamut
persian_force: Uzbek's Eldiguzid army of Azerbaijan (Turkic mamluks and Turkmens) with Nizari troops sent by Hasan III; the caliph's army from Baghdad fought beside them; Mengli had his own mamluks and the troops of Persian Iraq.
iranian_note: The Eldiguzid troops were mainly Turkic, but the Nizari contingent from Alamut and Quhistan was Iranian.
result_basis: Mengli's army was beaten on a mountain slope near Karaj and he fled to Saveh, where he was killed.
borderline: No conventional name; a pitched battle in Ibn al-Athir.
doubt: Borderline: No conventional name; a pitched battle in Ibn al-Athir.
sources: Ibn al-Athir (year 612); Juvayni; en.wikipedia Muzaffar al-Din Uzbek, Al-Nasir
note: Mengli, a mamluk of the Eldiguzids, had seized Persian Iraq; his lands were divided between Hasan III and Aghlamish. Karaj is taken to be Karaj of Abu Dulaf, not modern Karaj near Tehran.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Miyaneh (1217)
label: Miyaneh (1217)
war: Muhammad II's campaign in western Iran
side_b: Nusrat al-Din Pish-Tegin, for the Eldiguzid Uzbek
faction_b: Nusrat al-Din Pish-Tegin, for the Eldiguzid Uzbek
persian_force: A Khwarazmian army of Qipchaq and Qangli Turkic cavalry; the Eldiguzid force was Turkic mamluks and Turkmens of Azerbaijan.
iranian_note: Both armies were mainly Turkic.
result_basis: The Eldiguzid force was beaten and Pish-Tegin and Uzbek's vizier were captured.
borderline: No conventional name; a minor engagement known from the narrative of Muhammad's 1217 campaign.
doubt: Borderline: No conventional name; a minor engagement known from the narrative of Muhammad's 1217 campaign.
sources: Nasawi; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Muhammad II of Khwarazm, Muzaffar al-Din Uzbek
note: Uzbek then accepted Muhammad as overlord. Muhammad's march on Baghdad was stopped by snow at the Asadabad pass (not a battle).
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Rayy (1217)
label: Rayy (1217)
war: Muhammad II's campaign in western Iran
faction_b: Sa'd I ibn Zangi (Salghurids of Fars)
commanders_a: Muhammad II, Taj al-Din Abu Bakr of Zuzan
persian_force: Muhammad II's army, put at 100,000: Qipchaq and Qangli Turkic cavalry with Khorasani troops; Sa'd's Fars army was Salghurid Turkmens with Persian and Shabankara Kurdish troops.
iranian_note: Muhammad II relied on Turkic troops by 1217; the Salghurid army had more Iranians.
result_basis: Sa'd nearly routed the Khwarazmian vanguard but was beaten and captured.
borderline: No conventional name.
doubt: Borderline: No conventional name.
sources: Nasawi; Ibn al-Athir; Juvayni; en.wikipedia Muhammad II of Khwarazm, Muzaffar al-Din Uzbek
note: Sa'd had seized much of Persian Iraq after the murder of Aghlamish (1217); he was released as a Khwarazmian vassal.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Mount Tabor (siege, 1217)
label: Mount Tabor
commanders_b: Andrew II of Hungary; Templars and Hospitallers (second attack)
result_basis: A Hungarian-led attack on 3 December was abandoned and a renewed attack by the Templars and Hospitallers met Greek fire and was given up on 7 December.
sources: Wikipedia, Fifth Crusade (fetched); Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3; Oliver of Paderborn; Humphreys, From Saladin to the Mongols: The Ayyubids of Damascus 1193-1260 (1977)
note: Al-Mu'azzam's fortress; the attack ended the Syrian campaign of the first Fifth Crusade army.

name: Aleppo (1218)
label: Aleppo
commanders_b: Seljuk army of Kaykaus I (commander not named)
result_basis: Al-Ashraf routed a Seljuk army at Aleppo in 1218.
sources: Wikipedia, Fifth Crusade (fetched; one-line mention); Humphreys, From Saladin to the Mongols (1977)
note: I could find only the one-line statement in the fetched page; place within the Aleppo region, month and Seljuk commander not confirmed.

name: Damietta (siege, 1218-19)
label: Damietta
commanders_b: John of Brienne; Cardinal Pelagius; Leopold VI of Austria; William I of Holland
result_basis: Damietta fell to the Crusaders on 5 November 1219 after famine and disease had reduced the defenders.
sources: Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3; Oliver of Paderborn; James of Vitry; Ibn Wasil, Mufarrij al-Kurub; al-Maqrizi, Suluk (Kitab al-Suluk li-Ma'rifat Duwal al-Muluk)
note: The Chain Tower fell on 25 August 1218 and al-Adil died on 31 August; al-Kamil led the defence and his brother al-Mu'azzam brought the Syrian army.

name: Fariskur (1219)
label: Fariskur
place: Ayyubid camp at Fariskur, south of Damietta, Egypt
commanders_b: Cardinal Pelagius (his faction); John of Brienne and Ranulf of Chester (covered the retreat)
result_basis: The Crusader attack on the sultan's camp was a disaster: the Hospitaller Marshal Aymar de Lairon and many Templars were killed.
sources: Wikipedia, Fifth Crusade (fetched); Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3; Oliver of Paderborn; James of Vitry; Ibn Wasil, Mufarrij al-Kurub
note: Pelagius's faction forced the attack against the advice of John of Brienne; al-Kamil moved to Mansurah before the Crusaders took Damietta in November.

name: Khujand (siege, 1220)
label: Khujand (siege, 1220)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
persian_force: Timur Malik's garrison, at the end about 1,000 picked men in the island fortress, with the townsmen of Khujand.
iranian_note: Khujand was a Persian-speaking (Tajik) town; Timur Malik and his professional troops were probably Turks.
result_basis: The town and finally the island fortress were given up; Timur Malik broke out down the Syr Darya by boat and the Mongols held the place.
sources: Juvayni; Barthold, Turkestan; en.wikipedia Siege of Khujand (1220)
qbasis: Khujand was a Persian-speaking (Tajik) town; Timur Malik and his professional troops were probably Turks.

name: Qazvin (1220)
label: Qazvin (1220)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire (raid of Jebe and Subutai)
persian_force: The townsmen of Qazvin; the Khwarazmian field forces of Iraq-e Ajam had scattered.
iranian_note: Ibn al-Athir describes the defence as the townsmen's, in a Persian-speaking city.
result_basis: The Mongols stormed Qazvin, whose people fought on in the streets with knives until they were killed.
borderline: defenders were townsmen, not the Shah's army; no Wikipedia article
doubt: Borderline: defenders were townsmen, not the Shah's army; no Wikipedia article.
sources: Ibn al-Athir, year 617; Juvayni
qbasis: Ibn al-Athir describes the defence as the townsmen's, in a Persian-speaking city.

name: Termez (siege)
label: Termez (siege)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
persian_force: The garrison and townsmen of Termez; the sources give no units or numbers.
iranian_note: The defence was carried by the Persian-speaking townsmen with a small Turkic garrison, as in the other Oxus towns.
result_basis: Termez was stormed on the eleventh day of the siege and its people massacred.
borderline: a town siege known from Juvayni, with no Wikipedia article
doubt: Borderline: a town siege known from Juvayni, with no Wikipedia article.
sources: Juvayni; Rashid al-Din; Barthold, Turkestan
qbasis: The defence was carried by the Persian-speaking townsmen with a small Turkic garrison, as in the other Oxus towns.

name: Samarkand (siege, 1220)
label: Samarkand (siege, 1220)
date: March 1220 (town surrendered 16-17 March; citadel about a month later)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
commanders_a: Genghis Khan, Chagatai, Ogedei, Jebe, Subutai
persian_force: Qangli Turkish troops (30,000-60,000 in the medieval figures) and about 50,000 local Tajik troops with 20 war elephants; modern estimates put the garrison near 10,000.
iranian_note: The medieval figures set the Turks at 30,000-60,000 against 50,000 local Tajik troops, so Iranian speakers were roughly 45-60%.
losses_b: about 1,000 in the sortie; about 3,000 surrendered troops executed
result_basis: A sortie with war elephants was destroyed, the town surrendered and the citadel fell about a month later.
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; Rashid al-Din; en.wikipedia Siege of Samarkand (1220)
qbasis: The medieval figures set the Turks at 30,000-60,000 against 50,000 local Tajik troops, so Iranian speakers were roughly 45-60%.

name: Gurganj (siege)
label: Gurganj (siege)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
commanders_b: Khumar Tegin (proclaimed sultan; went over to the Mongols)
persian_force: Khumar Tegin's Turkic troops and the citizens of the Khwarazmian capital, who fought quarter by quarter after the commanders gave up (Ibn al-Athir, Juvayni).
iranian_note: The long street fighting was done by the citizens, who still spoke Khwarazmian (East Iranian); the Turkic commanders deserted early.
losses_a: higher than usual for the Mongols
losses_b: heavy; Juvayni's 1.2 million dead is a gross exaggeration
result_basis: Gurganj fell to the besiegers after months of street fighting, and the dams were broken to flood the city.
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; Rashid al-Din; en.wikipedia Siege of Gurganj
qbasis: The long street fighting was done by the citizens, who still spoke Khwarazmian (East Iranian); the Turkic commanders deserted early.

name: Bamyan (siege)
label: Bamyan (siege)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
persian_force: The inhabitants and garrison of Bamyan, fighting with archers and catapults.
iranian_note: Bamyan, a former Ghurid capital, was defended by its Persian-speaking people.
result_basis: Bamyan was stormed and razed after Genghis Khan's grandson Mutukan was killed by an arrow before its walls.
sources: Juvayni; Juzjani; en.wikipedia Siege of Bamyan
qbasis: Bamyan, a former Ghurid capital, was defended by its Persian-speaking people.

name: Hamadan (1221)
label: Hamadan (1221)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire (raid of Jebe and Subutai)
commanders_b: the notables of Hamadan (the ra'is and a jurist, per Ibn al-Athir)
persian_force: The townsmen of Hamadan under their notables, with remnants of the Khwarazmian troops of Iraq-e Ajam.
iranian_note: Ibn al-Athir describes the defence as the townspeople's, in a Persian-speaking city.
result_basis: After the townsmen rose and killed the Mongol governor, the Mongols returned, beat their sorties and stormed the city.
borderline: defenders were townsmen; no Wikipedia article
doubt: Borderline: defenders were townsmen; no Wikipedia article.
sources: Ibn al-Athir, year 618; Juvayni
qbasis: Ibn al-Athir describes the defence as the townspeople's, in a Persian-speaking city.

name: Kandahar (1221)
label: Kandahar (1221)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
persian_force: Jalal al-Din's following on the march from Bust to Ghazni, Khwarazmian Turks with local troops.
iranian_note: Before Parwan his following was a mix of Khwarazmian Turks and local Iranian and Afghan troops; no figures survive.
result_basis: Jalal al-Din drove off the Mongol force besieging the town after two or three days of fighting.
borderline: a minor action named only in the background of the Parwan article; the site may not be modern Kandahar
doubt: Borderline: a minor action named only in the background of the Parwan article; the site may not be modern Kandahar.
sources: al-Nasawi; Juvayni; en.wikipedia Battle of Parwan; en.wikipedia Jalal al-Din Mangburni
qbasis: Before Parwan his following was a mix of Khwarazmian Turks and local Iranian and Afghan troops; no figures survive.

name: Nasa (siege, 1221)
label: Nasa (siege, 1221)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
persian_force: The townsmen and local garrison of Nasa (al-Nasawi's home town).
iranian_note: The defence was by the Persian-speaking townsmen of a Khorasan town.
result_basis: Nasa was taken after a siege of about fifteen days with mangonels and its people were massacred.
borderline: a town siege known from al-Nasawi, with no Wikipedia article
doubt: Borderline: a town siege known from al-Nasawi, with no Wikipedia article.
sources: al-Nasawi; Juvayni; Barthold, Turkestan; en.wikipedia Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
qbasis: The defence was by the Persian-speaking townsmen of a Khorasan town.

name: Taliqan (siege, 1221)
label: Taliqan (siege, 1221)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
persian_force: The garrison of the Nusrat-Kuh fortress; the sources give no units.
iranian_note: A local Tajik garrison with Khwarazmian officers is assumed; the sources say nothing.
result_basis: The fortress of Nusrat-Kuh was stormed after Tolui's army arrived, following a siege of some six months.
sources: Juvayni; Rashid al-Din; en.wikipedia Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
note: Talaqan is identified by some with the Talaqan of Guzganan (near Maymana) rather than Taloqan in Tokharistan.
qbasis: A local Tajik garrison with Khwarazmian officers is assumed; the sources say nothing.

name: Merv (siege, 1221)
label: Merv (siege, 1221)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
commanders_b: Mujir al-Mulk (Wikipedia names the governor Dawud)
persian_force: About 12,000 garrison troops and the townsmen of Merv, crowded with refugees.
iranian_note: The defenders were mainly the Persian-speaking townsmen and local militia with a Khwarazmian garrison.
losses_b: the population massacred (700,000 in Ibn al-Athir, 1,300,000 in Juvayni, both exaggerated)
result_basis: After a seven-day assault and two failed sorties the town surrendered on terms, which Tolui broke.
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Siege of Merv (1221)
note: A second massacre followed a revolt in November 1221 (Shigi Qutuqu).
qbasis: The defenders were mainly the Persian-speaking townsmen and local militia with a Khwarazmian garrison.

name: Maragha (1221)
label: Maragha (1221)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire (raid of Jebe and Subutai)
commanders_b: unknown (the town was ruled by a woman, per Ibn al-Athir)
persian_force: The townsmen of Maragha; no field army defended it.
iranian_note: The defenders were the townsmen of an Iranian-speaking city of Azerbaijan (Persian and Old Azari).
result_basis: The Mongols stormed Maragha, driving Muslim prisoners ahead of them against the walls, and massacred its people.
borderline: defenders were townsmen; the ruler is identified as the last of the Ahmadili house of Maragha only by inference
doubt: Borderline: defenders were townsmen; the ruler is identified as the last of the Ahmadili house of Maragha only by inference.
sources: Ibn al-Athir, year 618; Juvayni
qbasis: The defenders were the townsmen of an Iranian-speaking city of Azerbaijan (Persian and Old Azari).

name: Nishapur (siege, 1221)
label: Nishapur (siege, 1221)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
persian_force: The townsmen and militia of Nishapur under the governor, with archers, crossbows and mangonels on the walls (12,000 archers at each of four gates, by one account).
iranian_note: The sources describe a defence by the people of Nishapur, a Persian-speaking city.
losses_b: heavy; Juvayni's 1,747,000 dead is a gross exaggeration (modern estimates 100,000-200,000)
result_basis: The walls were breached on 9 April and the city fell on 10 April 1221.
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; Juzjani; en.wikipedia Siege of Nishapur (1221)
note: Genghis Khan's son-in-law Toghachar had been killed in an earlier attack on the city (November 1220).
qbasis: The sources describe a defence by the people of Nishapur, a Persian-speaking city.

name: Herat (siege, 1221)
label: Herat (siege, 1221)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
persian_force: The governor's Khwarazmian garrison (12,000 in later accounts) and the townsmen.
iranian_note: The garrison was the Shah's (partly Turkic, partly Ghurid-Tajik) and the townsmen Persian-speaking; the proportions are not known.
result_basis: Herat surrendered after an eight-day assault; the garrison was killed and the townsmen spared.
sources: Juzjani; Juvayni; Sayfi Haravi; en.wikipedia Siege of Herat (1221)
qbasis: The garrison was the Shah's (partly Turkic, partly Ghurid-Tajik) and the townsmen Persian-speaking; the proportions are not known.

name: Mansurah (1221)
label: Mansurah
place: Barmun, near Mansurah, Nile Delta, Egypt
result_basis: On 26 August the Egyptians attacked the Crusaders' night march, al-Kamil opened the sluices and Pelagius sued for peace on 28 August, yielding Damietta.
sources: Wikipedia, Fifth Crusade (fetched); Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3; Oliver of Paderborn; Ibn Wasil, Mufarrij al-Kurub; al-Maqrizi, Suluk (Kitab al-Suluk li-Ma'rifat Duwal al-Muluk)
note: The end of the Fifth Crusade. Al-Mu'azzam and al-Ashraf had sent troops to Egypt (their presence in the final action is not confirmed in the summary seen); al-Kamil is the Ayyubid basis.

name: Parwan
label: Parwan
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
place: Parwan (near Jabal Saraj, north of Kabul), Afghanistan
commanders_a: Jalal al-Din, Amin Malik, Saif al-Din Ighraq, Timur Malik
persian_force: About 10,000 Turks (Qangli) under Amin Malik on the right, Khalaj and Afghan contingents under Saif al-Din Ighraq on the left, Khwarazmian and Ghurid loyalists; many archers fought dismounted.
iranian_note: Juvayni and al-Nasawi name the Turks of Amin Malik and the Khalaj, Afghan and Ghurid contingents; the Khalaj were Turkic, the Afghans Pashto-speaking and the Ghurids Persian-speaking.
result_basis: On the second day Shigi Qutuqu's army broke and fled, leaving the field to Jalal al-Din.
sources: Juvayni; al-Nasawi; Juzjani; en.wikipedia Battle of Parwan
note: The first defeat of a Mongol army in a pitched battle by a Muslim ruler; the Khalaj and Afghans deserted over the spoils soon after.
qbasis: Juvayni and al-Nasawi name the Turks of Amin Malik and the Khalaj, Afghan and Ghurid contingents; the Khalaj were Turkic, the Afghans Pashto-speaking and the Ghurids Persian-speaking.

name: Valiyan (1221)
label: Valiyan (1221)
date: autumn 1221, about a week before Parwan
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
persian_force: Jalal al-Din's army newly gathered at Ghazni: Khwarazmian Turks, Qangli, Khalaj, Afghan and Ghurid contingents.
iranian_note: The same army as at Parwan, with Afghan (Pashto) and Ghurid (Persian) contingents beside the Turks.
result_basis: Jalal al-Din attacked the Mongols besieging Valiyan, killed about 1,000 and drove the rest back across the river.
borderline: a preliminary action named in the Parwan article
doubt: Borderline: a preliminary action named in the Parwan article.
sources: Juvayni; al-Nasawi; en.wikipedia Battle of Parwan
qbasis: The same army as at Parwan, with Afghan (Pashto) and Ghurid (Persian) contingents beside the Turks.

name: Beylagan (1221)
label: Beylagan (1221)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire (raid of Jebe and Subutai)
persian_force: The townsmen of Beylagan, in the realm of the Eldiguzid atabeg Ozbeg.
iranian_note: An urban defence in an Iranian-speaking town of Arran; no troops of the atabeg are mentioned.
result_basis: After the townsmen killed the Mongol envoy, Beylagan was stormed and its people massacred.
borderline: defenders were townsmen; no Wikipedia article
doubt: Borderline: defenders were townsmen; no Wikipedia article.
sources: Ibn al-Athir, year 618
qbasis: An urban defence in an Iranian-speaking town of Arran; no troops of the atabeg are mentioned.

name: Indus
label: Indus
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
place: west bank of the Indus (near Kalabagh or Nilab), Pakistan
commanders_b: Jalal al-Din, Amin Malik (killed), Timur Malik
persian_force: Jalal al-Din's 700 guards in the centre, Turkish troops under Amin Malik on the right and Afghan troops on the left: about 30,000 after the desertions following Parwan.
iranian_note: The sources name a Turkish right wing and an Afghan left wing; the Khalaj under Ighraq had already left.
result_basis: Genghis Khan's army destroyed Jalal al-Din's army against the river; the Sultan escaped by riding into the Indus and swimming across.
sources: Juvayni; al-Nasawi; Juzjani; en.wikipedia Battle of the Indus
note: Wikipedia lists Timur Malik as killed; other accounts have him survive. The date is also given as autumn (August-September) 1221.
qbasis: The sources name a Turkish right wing and an Afghan left wing; the Khalaj under Ighraq had already left.

name: Herat (siege, 1221-1222)
label: Herat (siege, 1221-1222)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire (risings after Parwan)
commanders_b: Malik Mubariz al-Din (of the Firuzkuh fort), Khwaja Fakhr al-Din Abd al-Rahman
persian_force: The townsmen of Herat, who had risen for Jalal al-Din after Parwan and killed the Mongol governors, with Ghurid hillmen from Firuzkuh.
iranian_note: Juzjani and Sayfi describe a defence by the people of Herat and the Ghurid hill forts, all Persian-speaking.
losses_b: a seven-day massacre (1.6-2.4 million in the chronicles, impossibly high)
result_basis: Herat fell to the besiegers on 14 June 1222 after a siege of six to eight months.
borderline: a rising in Jalal al-Din's name rather than his army
doubt: Borderline: a rising in Jalal al-Din's name rather than his army.
sources: Juzjani; Sayfi Haravi; en.wikipedia Siege of Herat (1221)
note: Wikipedia treats both Herat sieges in one article.
qbasis: Juzjani and Sayfi describe a defence by the people of Herat and the Ghurid hill forts, all Persian-speaking.

name: Mongol defeat of the Alans and Cumans (North Caucasus)
label: Mongol defeat of the Alans and Cumans
date: Winter 1221-22 or early 1222 (Ibn al-Athir under 617 AH; the year is uncertain by about one)
place: Foothills of the North Caucasus, Terek-Kuban steppe (Russia); exact field unknown
allies_b: Cuman khans, who withdrew after Mongol bribes
result_basis: Ibn al-Athir: after one indecisive fight the Mongols detached the Cumans with gifts and then crushed the isolated Alans, then turned on the Cumans.
sources: Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil (year 617 AH); Kouznetsov and Lebedynsky, Les Alains (2005); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongol_invasion_of_Alania; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alania
note: First Mongol-Alan clash. The Alans led the coalition and bore the final defeat; the Cuman part of the coalition left the field beforehand.

name: Tabriz (siege, 1225)
label: Tabriz (siege, 1225)
faction_b: Eldiguzids (Atabeg Ozbeg's capital, held by his wife)
commanders_b: Malika Khatun (Ozbeg's wife); Ozbeg had fled to Ganja
persian_force: Jalal al-Din's Khwarazmian army (Turkic cavalry with Iranian levies) against the townsmen and garrison of the Eldiguzid capital.
iranian_note: The besiegers were mostly Turkic; the defenders were Tabriz townsmen (Persian and Old Azari speakers) and the atabeg's Turkic guards.
result_basis: Tabriz surrendered to Jalal al-Din after a short siege.
borderline: a short siege ending in surrender; Wikipedia treats it as a seizure
doubt: Borderline: a short siege ending in surrender; Wikipedia treats it as a seizure.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; al-Nasawi; Juvayni; en.wikipedia Jalal al-Din Mangburni
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Bolnisi
label: Bolnisi
persian_force: Jalal al-Din's Khwarazmian army of Qipchaq and Turkmen cavalry.
iranian_note: No units are named for his side; his army was built on Turkic horsemen.
result_basis: The Kipchaks of the Georgian coalition went over or withdrew at Jalal al-Din's appeal, and the Georgian army was beaten from the field.
sources: al-Nasawi; Georgian Chronicles; en.wikipedia Battle of Bolnisi
note: The Georgian coalition included Kipchaks, Alans, Lezgins, Svans and Vainakhs.
qbasis: No units are named for his side; his army was built on Turkic horsemen.

name: Damascus (siege, 1229)
label: Damascus
war: Ayyubid succession war (al-Kamil v. an-Nasir Dawud)
result_basis: After nearly two months of fighting Damascus surrendered to al-Ashraf and an-Nasir Dawud was compensated with Transjordan.
sources: Wikipedia, Al-Kamil (fetched); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayyubid_dynasty (fetched); Humphreys, From Saladin to the Mongols: The Ayyubids of Damascus 1193-1260 (1977)
note: A war inside the Ayyubid family; al-Ashraf took Damascus for himself.

name: Yassıçemen
label: Yassıçemen
place: Yassicemen, between Sivas and Erzincan, Turkey
commanders_b: Jalal al-Din, Jahan Shah ibn Tughril (Seljuk ruler of Erzurum)
persian_force: Jalal al-Din's Khwarazmian army (10,000-40,000), Turkic cavalry with the troops of his ally Jahan Shah of Erzurum.
iranian_note: No units are named; both the Khwarazmian army and the Erzurum troops were mainly Turkic.
result_basis: After the allies seized part of their position the Khwarazmians abandoned the field by night and Jalal al-Din fled.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Ibn Bibi; al-Nasawi; en.wikipedia Battle of Yassicemen
note: On 10 August a Khwarazmian detachment of 700 beat an allied detachment of 3,000. Wikipedia also lists the Empire of Trebizond on Jalal al-Din's side.
qbasis: The Ayyubid ruler al-Ashraf Musa, of the Kurdish Rawadi dynasty (Arabic-speaking by this date), personally led the Ayyubid army with Kayqubad I of Rum against Jalal al-Din (Nasawi; Humphreys).

name: Gaza (1239)
label: Gaza
commanders_a: Rukn al-Din al-Hijawi (field commander; nisba of the Hakkari Kurdish emirs, not verified)
commanders_b: Henry II of Bar (killed); Amaury VI of Montfort (captured); Hugh of Burgundy; Walter of Brienne
result_basis: The Egyptian force destroyed the Crusader raiding party near Gaza; the Count of Bar was killed and Amaury of Montfort and several hundred others captured.
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Gaza (1239) (fetched); Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3; Matthew Paris, Chronica Majora; Humphreys, From Saladin to the Mongols: The Ayyubids of Damascus 1193-1260 (1977)
note: Qualifies only by the Ayyubid ruler of Egypt (al-Adil II, as-Salih Ayyub being then Dawud's prisoner) directing the army; the Wikipedia article does not name the sender or any Kurdish troops. The field commander's nisba al-Hijawi may be Kurdish (Hakkari), which I could not confirm.

name: Siege of Maghas
label: Siege of Maghas
date: Nov/Dec 1239 to Feb 1240 (Yuanshi: 11th lunar month 1239 to 2nd lunar month 1240); older works give 1238-39
war: Mongol invasion of Alania (Batu's western campaign)
place: Maghas, capital of Alania; site disputed (Ingushetia, North Ossetia, Arkhyz or the Kuban; modern Magas, Ingushetia, is named after it) (Russia)
allies_a: a group of Alans allied to the Mongols
commanders_a: Batu (overall); Mongke and Buri (Rashid al-Din; the Alania article names Mongke and Guyuk); Shiri-gambu (Yuanshi)
commanders_b: Ajis (Alan leader, captured, per the Alania article)
result_basis: Juvaini and the Yuanshi: the Mongols took the walled capital after about three months and massacred its people.
sources: Juvaini, Tarikh-i Jahangushay; Rashid al-Din, Jami al-tawarikh; Yuanshi (Song Zi, Shiri-gambu); Latham-Sprinkle, 'The Alan capital Magas: a preliminary identification of its location', BSOAS (2015); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maghas; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongol_invasion_of_Alania
note: The fall of the Alan capital ended the Alan kingdom. Alans stood on both sides (defenders, and a small allied group in the final assault); the main Iranian side is the defenders. The location is unsettled, so the coordinates give only the Ingush candidate.

name: Jerusalem (siege, 1239)
label: Jerusalem
date: autumn 1239; the Tower of David fell about 7 December 1239
commanders_b: Garrison of the Tower of David
result_basis: An-Nasir Dawud's troops took the Tower of David after a siege of about three weeks and destroyed it.
sources: Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3; Matthew Paris; Humphreys, From Saladin to the Mongols: The Ayyubids of Damascus 1193-1260 (1977)
note: Ended the Frederick II truce for Jerusalem; the garrison surrendered the citadel.

name: La Forbie (Hirbiya)
label: La Forbie
war: Ayyubid civil war; Crusader alliance of 1244
place: Hirbiya (La Forbie), north-east of Gaza, Palestine (Gaza Strip)
side_b: Ayyubids of Damascus, Homs and Kerak
Kingdom of Jerusalem and the military orders
persian_state: Ayyubids of Egypt v Ayyubids of Damascus, Homs and Kerak
faction_b: Ayyubids of Damascus, Homs and Kerak, Kingdom of Jerusalem and the military orders
commanders_a: Rukn al-Din Baybars al-Salihi; as-Salih Ayyub (ruler directing from Cairo)
commanders_b: al-Mansur Ibrahim of Homs; an-Nasir Dawud of Kerak (allied); Walter IV of Brienne
result_basis: The Egyptians and Khwarazmians destroyed the allied army; over 5,000 Crusaders were killed and Walter of Brienne captured.
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of La Forbie (fetched); Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3; Matthew Paris; Ibn Wasil, Mufarrij al-Kurub
note: Ayyubid princes led both sides: al-Mansur Ibrahim of Homs in person on the Syrian side, as-Salih Ayyub directing the Egyptian side.

name: Damascus (siege, 1245)
label: Damascus
war: Ayyubid civil war (as-Salih Ayyub v. as-Salih Ismail)
persian_state: Ayyubids of Egypt v Ayyubids of Damascus
commanders_a: as-Salih Ayyub's army (Mu'in al-Din ibn al-Shaykh); Khwarazmians
result_basis: Damascus fell to as-Salih Ayyub's forces in 1245, ending Ismail's rule there.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayyubid_dynasty (fetched); Wikipedia, Al-Salih Ayyub (fetched); Humphreys, From Saladin to the Mongols: The Ayyubids of Damascus 1193-1260 (1977)
note: Ayyubid princes on both sides; starting date of the siege uncertain.

name: Lake Homs (1246)
label: Lake Homs
result_basis: Al-Mansur Ibrahim's army scattered the Khwarazmians and killed their leader.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayyubid_dynasty (fetched); Wikipedia, Al-Salih Ayyub (fetched); Ibn Wasil, Mufarrij al-Kurub
note: Which army carried the day (Homs and Aleppo or Egypt) is differently told; Ayyubid command is not in doubt.

name: Ascalon (siege, 1247)
label: Ascalon
commanders_a: Fakhr al-Din ibn al-Shaykh; as-Salih Ayyub (ruler directing)
result_basis: Fakhr al-Din stormed Ascalon on 24 October 1247 and razed it.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayyubid_dynasty (fetched); Ibn Wasil, Mufarrij al-Kurub; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: Qualifies by the Ayyubid ruler directing the army; Fakhr al-Din was of a Khurasani shaykh family.

name: Damietta (1249)
label: Damietta
commanders_a: Fakhr al-Din ibn al-Shaykh; as-Salih Ayyub (ill, directing from Mansurah)
commanders_b: Louis IX; Charles of Anjou; Robert of Artois
result_basis: Louis IX landed on 5 June; the garrison and Fakhr al-Din's force withdrew and Damietta was occupied intact.
sources: Wikipedia, Seventh Crusade (fetched); Joinville; Ibn Wasil, Mufarrij al-Kurub; al-Maqrizi, Suluk (Kitab al-Suluk li-Ma'rifat Duwal al-Muluk)
note: Qualifies by the Ayyubid Sultan as-Salih Ayyub directing; the Kinana Bedouin garrison was not Kurdish. Fakhr al-Din's family (Banu Hamawayh) is of Khurasani origin.

name: Mansurah (1250)
label: Mansurah
commanders_a: Fakhr al-Din ibn al-Shaykh (killed); Baybars al-Bunduqdari; Qutuz; Aybak
commanders_b: Louis IX; Robert of Artois (killed); William Longespee (killed)
result_basis: The Egyptians killed Fakhr al-Din in the first surprise but Baybars and Qutuz rallied them and destroyed the vanguard, killing Robert of Artois.
sources: Wikipedia, Seventh Crusade (fetched); Joinville; Ibn Wasil, Mufarrij al-Kurub; al-Maqrizi, Suluk (Kitab al-Suluk li-Ma'rifat Duwal al-Muluk)
note: As-Salih Ayyub had died on 22 November 1249 and his death was concealed; Turan-Shah arrived only on 28 February. The Ayyubid basis is thus indirect, via the dynasty's rule, and the leaders in the field were mamluks and Fakhr al-Din.

name: Fariskur (1250)
label: Fariskur
commanders_b: Louis IX (captured); Hugh XI of Lusignan (killed)
result_basis: The Egyptians surrounded the retreating Crusader army, killed or captured it and took King Louis.
sources: Wikipedia, Seventh Crusade (fetched); Joinville; Ibn Wasil, Mufarrij al-Kurub; al-Maqrizi, Suluk (Kitab al-Suluk li-Ma'rifat Duwal al-Muluk)
note: Turan-Shah, Saladin's great-nephew and the reigning Ayyubid sultan, commanded in person; he was murdered on 2 May 1250 by the Bahri mamluks.

name: Al-Abbasa (1251)
label: Al-Abbasa
war: Ayyubid war with the Mamluks of Egypt
commanders_a: an-Nasir Yusuf of Aleppo and Damascus
result_basis: Yusuf's larger Syrian army was first successful but a Mamluk regiment deserted mid-battle and Yusuf fled to Damascus.
sources: Wikipedia, Seventh Crusade (fetched); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayyubid_dynasty (fetched); Ibn Wasil, Mufarrij al-Kurub; al-Maqrizi, Suluk (Kitab al-Suluk li-Ma'rifat Duwal al-Muluk)
note: The Ayyubid prince invaded Egypt to restore Ayyubid rule; peace in April 1253 recognised Aybak. Whether Shahrazuriyya Kurds fought in Yusuf's army is not confirmed in the sources seen.

name: Girdkuh (siege)
label: Girdkuh (siege)
commanders_a: Kitbuqa, Buri (killed December 1253); later the Ilkhans' commanders
persian_force: The Nizari garrison of Girdkuh, reinforced from Alamut in 1254; its night sortie of December 1253 killed about 100 Mongols and their commander.
iranian_note: Nizari garrisons were drawn from the Ismaili communities of Qumis, Daylam and Quhistan.
strength_a: part of Kitbuqa's 5,000 horse and 5,000 foot
result_basis: Girdkuh surrendered to the besiegers on 15 December 1270, short of clothing, after a siege of seventeen years.
sources: Juvayni; Rashid al-Din; en.wikipedia Mongol campaign against the Nizaris
note: Begun by Mongke's commanders (so the besiegers are the Mongol Empire, as for all of Hulagu's Nizari campaign) and completed under the Ilkhan Abaqa.
qbasis: Nizari Ismailis: an Iranian-led state

name: Tun (siege, 1256)
label: Tun (siege, 1256)
persian_force: The Nizari townsmen and garrison of Tun in Quhistan.
iranian_note: Quhistan's Ismaili towns were Persian-speaking.
result_basis: Tun was taken after a week-long siege and sacked, and nearly all its people killed.
sources: Juvayni; Rashid al-Din; en.wikipedia Mongol campaign against the Nizaris
note: Kitbuqa had already pillaged Tun in July 1253. Hulagu's army is treated as the Mongol Empire's (the invader).
qbasis: Nizari Ismailis: an Iranian-led state

name: Mount Siyalan
label: Mount Siyalan
persian_force: Nizari fighters of the Rudbar of Alamut, Daylamite highlanders.
iranian_note: The Rudbar Ismailis were local Daylamite highlanders.
result_basis: The Nizaris of Rudbar beat back Yasur's force on the mountain, though it stayed in the district to raid.
borderline: a small action
doubt: Borderline: a small action.
sources: Juvayni; en.wikipedia Mongol campaign against the Nizaris
qbasis: Nizari Ismailis: an Iranian-led state

name: Alamut (siege, 1256)
label: Alamut (siege, 1256)
persian_force: The garrison of Alamut under its sipahsalar, who at first refused the Imam's order to surrender.
iranian_note: The Rudbar fortresses were held by local Daylamite Ismailis.
result_basis: The commander of Alamut capitulated in December 1256 after a short investment, and the castle was dismantled.
borderline: surrendered after a brief investment, with little recorded fighting
doubt: Borderline: surrendered after a brief investment, with little recorded fighting.
sources: Juvayni; en.wikipedia Mongol campaign against the Nizaris; en.wikipedia Timeline of the Ilkhanate
note: Georgian-Armenian units under David VII Ulu took part (en.wikipedia David Ulu). The Timeline of the Ilkhanate dates the capture to 20 November.
qbasis: Nizari Ismailis: an Iranian-led state

name: Maymun-Diz (siege)
label: Maymun-Diz (siege)
commanders_a: Hulagu, Kitbuqa, Guo Kan, Balaghai and others
persian_force: The Imam's garrison of Maymun-Diz, with its own mangonels; heavily outnumbered.
iranian_note: The Rudbar fortresses were held by local Daylamite Ismailis.
strength_a: about 80,000 and 1,000 squads of siege engineers (Chinese, Khitan and Muslim)
result_basis: After three days of bombardment and a repulsed assault Khurshah surrendered on 19 November; the last defenders in the qubba were killed.
sources: Juvayni; Rashid al-Din; en.wikipedia Siege of Maymun-Diz
note: Hulagu's army is treated as the Mongol Empire's (the invader); if counted as the Ilkhanate (from 1256), the Nizari battles of 1256 would be civil.
qbasis: Nizari Ismailis: an Iranian-led state

name: Lambsar (siege)
label: Lambsar (siege)
persian_force: The Nizari garrison of Lambsar, which refused Khurshah's order to surrender.
iranian_note: The Rudbar fortresses were held by local Daylamite Ismailis.
result_basis: Lambsar fell in January 1257 after cholera broke out in the garrison.
sources: Juvayni; en.wikipedia Mongol campaign against the Nizaris
qbasis: Nizari Ismailis: an Iranian-led state

name: Mayyafariqin (siege)
label: Mayyafariqin (siege)
war: Mongol invasion of Syria and the Jazira
commanders_a: Yoshmut, Prosh Khaghbakian, Shahnshah Zakarian, al-Salih Isma'il ibn Lu'lu'
persian_force: A small Mongol detachment under Yoshmut and a much larger Georgian-Armenian force under Prosh and Shahnshah, with Cilician Armenian units and Mosul siege engineers.
iranian_note: The sources name Mongols, Georgians, Armenians and Mosul troops only.
losses_a: unknown (the Armenian prince Sevata of Kachen killed)
result_basis: Mayyafariqin fell to the besiegers on 7 April 1260 after a siege of about ten months.
sources: Kirakos; Rashid al-Din; en.wikipedia Siege of Mayyafariqin
note: Persian role kept as principal: the Georgians and Armenians fought as vassals under Mongol command.
qbasis: The city was defended by its Ayyubid ruler al-Kamil Muhammad, of the Kurdish-descended Ayyubid line, against Yoshmut's Mongols and a Georgian-Armenian force (Wikipedia, Siege of Mayyafariqin; Humphreys).

name: Aleppo (siege, 1260)
label: Aleppo (siege, 1260)
date: 18-24 January 1260 (citadel surrendered about a month later)
commanders_a: Hulagu, Kitbuqa, Hethum I, Bohemond VI
persian_force: Hulagu's Mongol army with Kitbuqa's vanguard, and the troops of Hethum I of Cilician Armenia and Bohemond VI of Antioch.
iranian_note: Hulagu's army had Persian auxiliaries and engineers, but the fighting force was Mongol and Turkic with Armenian and Frankish allies.
losses_b: heavy; the Muslim and Jewish inhabitants massacred
result_basis: Aleppo fell after six days of bombardment and the citadel surrendered about a month later.
sources: Rashid al-Din; Ibn Shaddad; en.wikipedia Siege of Aleppo (1260)
note: Bohemond VI's Antioch is 'Crusaders' (Principality of Antioch).
qbasis: an Ayyubid (Kurdish by descent) held the city

name: Ain Jalut
label: Ain Jalut
place: Ain Jalut (Ma'ayan Harod), Jezreel Valley, Israel & Palestine
persian_force: One Mongol tumen (10,000-12,000 men in all), Georgian and Cilician Armenian battalions (about 500 Armenians), the troops of the Ayyubid princes al-Ashraf Musa and al-Sa'id Hasan, and Syrian levies.
iranian_note: No Iranian units are named; the Ayyubid contingents may have included Kurds.
result_basis: The Mamluks held the field; Kitbuqa was killed and his army fled towards Baysan, where its rally was broken.
sources: al-Maqrizi; Rashid al-Din; Abu'l-Fida; en.wikipedia Battle of Ain Jalut
qbasis: The Mongol side included contingents of the Ayyubid princes al-Ashraf Musa and al-Sa'id Hasan (Kurdish-descended dynasty) and Qutuz's army included the Shahrazuriyya, usually described as Kurdish (Wikipedia, Battle of Ain Jalut; Amitai-Preiss).

name: Homs (1260)
label: Homs (1260)
place: near the tomb of Khalid ibn al-Walid, Homs, Syria
commanders_a: al-Ashraf Musa of Homs, al-Mansur of Hama
persian_force: About 6,000 Mongol horsemen sent by Hulagu after Ain Jalut, in eight formations.
iranian_note: A Mongol raiding force; no Iranian units are named.
result_basis: The Muslim princes' small army routed the Mongol force, which fled the field.
sources: Abu'l-Fida; al-Maqrizi; en.wikipedia First Battle of Homs
note: Wikipedia title: 'First Battle of Homs'.
qbasis: The army that met Baydara's Mongols was led by the Ayyubid princes al-Ashraf Musa of Homs and al-Mansur II of Hama, of the Kurdish-descended Ayyubid dynasty, with Mamluk emirs (Maqrizi; Amitai-Preiss).

name: Kazerun (1264)
label: Kazerun (1264)
commanders_a: Ilkhanid commanders (unnamed here), with the troops of the atabegs of Yazd and Luristan
persian_force: Ilkhanid Mongol troops with levies of the subject atabegs of Yazd and Luristan, against the Salghurid atabeg's Turkmen and Persian troops of Fars.
iranian_note: Both sides drew on Iranian levies (Fars, Yazd, Luristan) beside Mongol and Salghurid Turkic horsemen.
result_basis: The Ilkhanid army defeated Seljuk-Shah, who had killed the Mongol governors, and took him at Kazerun.
borderline: known from Vassaf and Rashid al-Din; commanders and site not verified on the web
