doubt: Borderline: known from Vassaf and Rashid al-Din; commanders and site not verified on the web.
sources: Vassaf; Rashid al-Din
note: Civil: the Salghurids of Fars and the Ilkhanate are both Persian states in this set.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Herat (1270)
label: Herat (1270)
place: Qara Su plain near Ghurian, west of Herat, Afghanistan
commanders_a: Abaqa, Yoshmut, Tubshin, Arghun Aqa, Samaghar, Abatai
persian_force: Abaqa's Mongol tumens, with contingents from Kerman and Yazd on the left wing and a Georgian contingent under King David in the vanguard.
iranian_note: Rashid al-Din names the Kerman and Yazd contingents (Persian-speaking) beside the Mongol tumens and Georgians.
result_basis: Baraq's army broke and fled towards the Oxus, leaving the field to Abaqa.
sources: Rashid al-Din; Vassaf; en.wikipedia Battle of Herat (1270); en.wikipedia Timeline of the Ilkhanate ('Battle of Qara-Su')
note: Also called the battle of Qara Su. The Kartid ruler of Herat, Shams al-Din, had submitted to Baraq earlier that year.
qbasis: Rashid al-Din names Kirman and Yazd contingents on Yoshmut's left wing in Abaqa's army, and the Atabegs of Yazd were ethnically Persian (Wikipedia, Battle of Herat (1270) and Atabegs of Yazd).

name: Alamut (1275-1276)
label: Alamut (1275-1276)
faction_b: Nizari rebels (a son of Khurshah and a Khwarazmshah descendant)
commanders_b: Naw Dawlat (or Abu Dawlat), son of Khurshah
persian_force: An Ilkhanid force against Nizari partisans of Rudbar and Daylam.
iranian_note: The rebels were Daylamite Ismailis; the Ilkhanid besiegers were mainly Mongol and Turkic.
result_basis: The Ilkhanid army retook Alamut in 1276, about a year after the Nizari restoration force had seized it.
borderline: a rising, not a state
doubt: Borderline: a rising, not a state.
sources: Rashid al-Din; en.wikipedia Mongol campaign against the Nizaris
note: One entry for the Nizari seizure (1275) and the Ilkhanid siege that ended it (1276).
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Siege of Changzhou (1275)
label: Siege of Changzhou
date: Autumn-winter 1275 (the city, which had rebelled after submitting, resisted for five months before Bayan stormed it)
war: Yuan conquest of the Southern Song
result_basis: Bayan stormed Changzhou and massacred its people (Song shi, Yuan shi; Yule on Polo).
sources: Yuanshi; Songshi; Marco Polo (Yule, Book of Ser Marco Polo, notes on Alans and Chang-chou); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayan_of_the_Baarin
note: The Alan link is the weak point. Polo (and Pauthier) tie a massacre of Alans to Changzhou, but Yule argues the Alan episode belongs to Zhenzhou (see next entry). Asud troops did serve in Bayan's army, so a contingent is likely but not shown for this siege.

name: Zhenzhou (Yizheng), Asud garrison massacre
label: Zhenzhou, Asud garrison massacre
date: 4th lunar month 1275 (about May 1275); Polo says 1274, Tu Chi 1276
war: Yuan conquest of the Southern Song
result_basis: Songshi: Hong Fu retook the city in April-May 1275; Polo's tale is that the Alan troops billeted there were killed in the night.
doubt: Traditional: known only from a doubtful tradition.
sources: Marco Polo (the Alans of 'Chang-chou'); Yule, Book of Ser Marco Polo, vol. 1 notes (dsr.nii.ac.jp/toyobunko/III-2-F-c-104/V-1/page/0037.html.en); Songshi
note: Known mainly from Polo's story of Alans killed after a feast, which Yule places at Chen-chou rather than Changzhou. Polo's '30,000 Alans' is not credible as a number.

name: Siege of Dedyakov
label: Siege of Dedyakov
date: Winter 1277-78; Russian chronicles give February 1278 (some works say 1277)
war: Golden Horde suppression of the Alan revolt (Dedyakov uprising)
place: Dedyakov, an Alan town, usually placed near Vladikavkaz, North Ossetia (Russia)
result_basis: Russian chronicles (Nikon and related) say the Tatars with the Rus' princes took Dedyakov and burned it in February 1278.
sources: Nikon Chronicle and related Russian chronicles (s.a. 6786); Klaproth; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongol_invasion_of_Alania; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alans
note: The last big Alan revolt against the Horde. The Wikipedia text on the Dedyakov events is partly tagged 'citation needed'.

name: Aq Khwaja
label: Aq Khwaja
war: Ilkhanid succession war (Arghun against Ahmad Tekuder)
place: Aq Khwaja, south of Qazvin, Iran
persian_force: Arghun's Khorasan army of Mongol and Turkic cavalry against Alinaq's 15,000 Ilkhanid troops; the Sufi Ala al-Dawla Simnani rode with Arghun.
iranian_note: Both armies were Ilkhanid nomad cavalry; Persian notables served on both sides but not as units.
result_basis: Arghun's army defeated Alinaq's 15,000, though Arghun then fell back to Khorasan before Tekuder's main army.
sources: Rashid al-Din; Iranica 'Argun Khan'; en.wikipedia Arghun
note: Some accounts make Alinaq the victor; Rashid al-Din and Iranica give the battle to Arghun. Arghun was captured at Kalat in July and freed by Buqa, who killed Alinaq; Tekuder was executed on 10 August 1284.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Marqab (siege, 1285)
label: Marqab
commanders_a: Qalawun; al-Muzaffar II Mahmud of Hama (Hama contingent)
result_basis: The Mamluks took Marqab by mining and the Hospitallers surrendered on terms on 25 May 1285.
sources: Wikipedia, Abu al-Fida (fetched): he was present at the attack on a Hospitaller stronghold; Abu'l-Fida, al-Mukhtasar
note: Qualifies only by the Hama contingent under the Ayyubid prince; the Hama Ayyubids were allies not leaders of the Mamluk army.

name: Tripoli (siege, 1289)
label: Tripoli
commanders_a: Qalawun; al-Muzaffar II Mahmud of Hama (Hama contingent)
result_basis: Qalawun's army stormed the city, killed the garrison and razed Tripoli.
sources: Wikipedia, Abu al-Fida (fetched): he took part in the sieges of Tripoli and Acre; Abu'l-Fida, al-Mukhtasar
note: Qualifies only by the Hama contingent under the Ayyubid prince.

name: Acre (siege, 1291)
label: Acre
commanders_a: al-Ashraf Khalil; al-Muzaffar II Mahmud of Hama (Hama contingent); Abu al-Fida
commanders_b: Jean de Grailly; Guillaume de Beaujeu (killed); Peter of Sevrey
result_basis: The Mamluks stormed Acre on 18 May 1291, the last Crusader stronghold on the mainland.
sources: Wikipedia, Abu al-Fida (fetched); Abu'l-Fida, al-Mukhtasar; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: Abu al-Fida records his own presence and the Hama catapult force. Qualifies only by the Ayyubid prince's contingent; likely to be judged marginal.

name: Qazvin (1295)
label: Qazvin (1295)
persian_force: Ghazan's Khorasan army (Nawruz's Oirat and Mongol horse) against Baydu's advance guard.
iranian_note: Both forces were Ilkhanid nomad cavalry.
result_basis: Ghazan's commanders beat Baydu's advance guard, though Ghazan then withdrew on finding Baydu's main army ahead.
borderline: an advance-guard action with no standard name
doubt: Borderline: an advance-guard action with no standard name.
sources: Rashid al-Din; en.wikipedia Ghazan
note: Baydu was deposed after mass defections and executed on 4 October 1295.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Nishapur (1297)
label: Nishapur (1297)
persian_force: Ghazan's army under Qutlugh-Shah against Nawruz's Oirat and Mongol followers in Khorasan.
iranian_note: Both forces were Ilkhanid nomad cavalry.
result_basis: Ghazan's army defeated Nawruz near Nishapur; he fled to Herat, where the Kartid Fakhr al-Din handed him over.
borderline: named only by place in Ghazan's biography
doubt: Borderline: named only by place in Ghazan's biography.
sources: Rashid al-Din; en.wikipedia Ghazan; en.wikipedia Kart dynasty
note: No siege of Herat followed: Fakhr al-Din Kart surrendered Nawruz when the Ilkhanid army approached.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Erzincan (1299)
label: Erzincan (1299)
persian_force: Qutlugh-Shah's Ilkhanid army against Sulamish's 20,000 Oirat, Mongol and Turkmen troops of Anatolia.
iranian_note: Both forces were Ilkhanid nomad cavalry with Anatolian Turkmen.
result_basis: Qutlugh-Shah defeated Sulamish's army and Sulamish fled to Mamluk Syria.
sources: Rashid al-Din; Aqsara'i; en.wikipedia Ghazan; en.wikipedia Chupan
note: Civil: a revolt of the Ilkhanate's own army in Anatolia (not of the Anatolians). Sulamish returned with Mamluk help, was beaten again and burnt in Tabriz on 27 September 1299.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Bapheus
label: Bapheus
place: Plain of Bapheus (Koyunhisar), near Nicomedia (Izmit), Turkey; exact field unknown
result_basis: Ottoman cavalry broke the Roman line and Mouzalon withdrew into Nicomedia (Pachymeres).
sources: Pachymeres, Historia, book 4; Bartusis, The Late Roman Army (1997); Inalcik, 'Osman Ghazi's Siege of Nicaea and the Battle of Bapheus' (1994); Treiyer (2017); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Bapheus
note: About half of Mouzalon's roughly 2,000 men were newly hired Alans, who are said to have covered the retreat rather than fought hard. Alans crossed into Roman service in 1301-02, which supports the 1302 date over 1299.

name: Apros
label: Apros
place: Apros, near modern Kermeyan, eastern Thrace (Turkey); exact field unknown
commanders_b: Michael IX Palaiologos; Girgon (Alan chief, in Roman service in 1305; his part at Apros is not attested here)
result_basis: The Catalans broke the Roman line, Michael IX was unhorsed and carried off, and the camp was looted.
sources: Pachymeres, Historia; Muntaner, Chronicle; Bartusis, The Late Roman Army (1997); Jessee and Isaenko, 'The military effectiveness of Alan mercenaries in Constantinople, 1301-1306', J. Medieval Military History 12 (2014); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Apros
note: Alan cavalry held the Roman left and withdrew almost at once, which disrupted the line (Wikipedia, from Pachymeres). Whether Alans were a fifth of the army is not given.

name: Catalans v Alans and Turcopoles at the Balkan foothills
label: Catalans v Alans and Turcopoles at the Balkan foothills
date: Spring 1306 (Muntaner; the Wikipedia summary of Apros places an annihilation of the Alans after Apros)
place: Foot of the Balkan mountains near the Bulgarian frontier, Thrace (Bulgaria/Turkey); site unknown
result_basis: Muntaner (via Jessee and Isaenko): a hard fight on the Bulgarian frontier went to the Catalan almogavars, who destroyed the Alan contingent.
sources: Muntaner, Chronicle; Pachymeres; Jessee and Isaenko (2014); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Apros
note: Muntaner puts Girgon's and Melik's horse at about 8,000 together. Place, date and exact order of events are poorly fixed, so this is an uncertain entry.

name: Herat (siege, 1306-1307)
label: Herat (siege, 1306-1307)
date: 1306 (Danishmend killed) - June 1307 (citadel taken; Wikipedia gives 5 February - 24 June 1306)
commanders_b: Fakhr al-Din Kart and his garrison commanders
persian_force: Danishmend's 10,000 Ilkhanid troops, then Bujai's besieging army with a Frankish mangonel corps, against the Kartid garrison of Herat (Tajik and Ghurid troops).
iranian_note: The Kartid defenders were Persian-speaking (the dynasty was Tajik and Ghurid in origin); the Ilkhanid besiegers were Mongol and Turkic.
result_basis: After the Kartids destroyed Danishmend's force inside Herat, Bujai's army besieged and took the citadel.
sources: Sayfi Haravi; Rashid al-Din; en.wikipedia Oljaitu; en.wikipedia Kart dynasty
note: Civil: the Kartids and the Ilkhanate are both Persian states in this set.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Gilan (1307)
label: Gilan (1307)
persian_force: Qutlugh-Shah's Ilkhanid column (one of four armies, others under Chupan, Sutai, Esen Qutluq, Irinjin) against the Gilaki highland and forest levies.
iranian_note: The victors were Gilaki-speaking local levies; the Ilkhanid column was Mongol and Turkic.
losses_b: Qutlugh-Shah and much of his column
result_basis: The Gilaks defeated Qutlugh-Shah's column and killed him, though the other Ilkhanid columns forced Gilan's submission.
borderline: civil only if the Gilaki lords count as an Iran-seated local power; otherwise an Ilkhanid defeat by local rebels
doubt: Borderline: civil only if the Gilaki lords count as an Iran-seated local power; otherwise an Ilkhanid defeat by local rebels.
sources: Kashani; Rashid al-Din; en.wikipedia Oljaitu; en.wikipedia Chupan
note: The campaign as a whole ended with Gilan's submission (tributized June 1307).
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Erbil (siege, 1310)
label: Erbil (siege, 1310)
persian_force: Ilkhanid troops with Kurdish tribesmen (and Arabs, per the Timeline of the Ilkhanate).
iranian_note: The sources name Kurdish tribesmen beside the Ilkhan's troops; their share is not known.
result_basis: Ilkhanid troops and Kurdish tribesmen took the citadel on 1 July 1310 and massacred its defenders.
borderline: the defenders were Christian (Assyrian) townsmen and militia, part rebellion, part refuge from persecution
doubt: Borderline: the defenders were Christian (Assyrian) townsmen and militia, part rebellion, part refuge from persecution.
sources: Bar Hebraeus (continuation); History of Mar Yahballaha; en.wikipedia Oljaitu; en.wikipedia Citadel of Erbil
note: New opponent name 'Christian rebels (Erbil)'.
qbasis: The sources name Kurdish tribesmen beside the Ilkhan's troops; their share is not known.

name: Herat (siege, 1319)
label: Herat (siege, 1319)
faction_b: Yasa'ur (rebel Chagatayid prince holding an Ilkhanid appanage)
persian_force: The Kartid garrison and people of Herat against Yasa'ur's Chagatayid Mongol followers.
iranian_note: The Kartid defenders were Persian-speaking; Yasa'ur's besiegers were Mongol and Turkic nomads.
result_basis: Herat held and Yasa'ur raised the siege as Ilkhanid armies approached.
borderline: civil only if Yasa'ur counts as a rebel Ilkhanid vassal (he held Khorasan lands from Oljaitu); otherwise a Kartid defence against a Chagatai prince
doubt: Borderline: civil only if Yasa'ur counts as a rebel Ilkhanid vassal (he held Khorasan lands from Oljaitu); otherwise a Kartid defence against a Chagatai prince.
sources: Sayfi Haravi; Hafiz-i Abru; en.wikipedia Kart dynasty; en.wikipedia Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan
note: Yasa'ur was killed by Kebek's men in 1320.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Zanjan-Rud
label: Zanjan-Rud
date: 20 June 1319 (13 July in the Timeline of the Ilkhanate)
persian_force: The young Ilkhan's army with Chupan's following against the rebels' 40,000 (Keraite and other Mongol troops under Irinjin and the governor of Georgia, Qurumishi).
iranian_note: Both forces were Ilkhanid nomad cavalry.
result_basis: The Ilkhan's army decisively defeated the rebel emirs, and thirty-six of them were executed.
sources: Hafiz-i Abru; en.wikipedia Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan; en.wikipedia Chupan; en.wikipedia Timeline of the Ilkhanate
note: Also called the battle near Mianeh.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Mubariz al-Din's campaign against the Nikudaris
label: Mubariz al-Din's campaign against the Nikudaris
date: c. 1320 (first battle; the campaign lasted 13-14 years)
persian_force: Mubariz al-Din's 60 horsemen of Yazd, then reinforcements from the town; he was the Ilkhan's governor of Yazd.
iranian_note: A local force raised in Yazd and Maybod, Persian-speaking.
result_basis: Mubariz al-Din's horsemen, once reinforced from Yazd, broke Nawruz's Negudaris and pursued them to Bafq.
borderline: a campaign of some twenty small fights; only the first battle is described, and its date is not given
doubt: Borderline: a campaign of some twenty small fights; only the first battle is described, and its date is not given.
sources: Mahmud Kutubi, Tarikh-i Al-i Muzaffar; en.wikipedia Mubariz al-Din's campaign against the Nikudaris; en.wikipedia Muzaffarids (Iran)
note: New opponent name 'Negudaris' (Nikudari, Qara'unas Mongol tribes of Sistan and Afghanistan).
qbasis: Muzaffarids, of Arab descent: counted through their Persian troops

name: Philippopolis (siege)
label: Philippopolis
war: War with Bulgaria (George Terter II and Michael Shishman), 1322-1324
commanders_a: Ivan the Russian, his deputy Inas; the Alan chiefs Itil and Temir
commanders_b: Andronikos III; the Bulgarian despot Voysil of Kopsis (ally)
result_basis: As in Battles of the Romans: The defenders had about 1,000 Alan horse and 2,000 foot, with Bulgarian (perhaps also Hungarian) troops. The siege failed, but the city was taken soon afterwards when pro-imperial citizens opened the
sources: Kantakouzenos book 1; Gregoras book 8; en.wikipedia Ivan the Russian
note: The Alan chiefs Itil and Temir with their men in the Bulgarian garrison (Kantakouzenos 1.37)
qbasis: The Alan chiefs Itil and Temir with their men in the Bulgarian garrison (Kantakouzenos 1.37)

name: Hisn Kayfa (1334)
label: Hisn Kayfa
commanders_a: Ayyubid emir of Hisn Kayfa (name not given in the source seen)
result_basis: An Artuqid force attacked Hisn Kayfa and was decisively defeated; the Ayyubids gained land on the left bank of the Tigris.
sources: Wikipedia, Hasankeyf (fetched): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasankeyf
note: Known only from a summary; the commanders and the exact place are not named in the source seen.

name: Jaghatu (1336)
label: Jaghatu (1336)
war: Disintegration of the Ilkhanate (succession war after Abu Sa'id)
side_b: Arpa Ke'un and the vizier Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad
faction_b: Arpa Ke'un and the vizier Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad
persian_force: Ali Padshah's Oirat tribesmen and their allies against Arpa's larger army of Mongol and Persian regiments, including Akrunj's mostly Uyghur contingent, which defected before the fighting.
iranian_note: Both armies were drawn from the Mongol and Turkic tribes of the Ilkhanate; only Arpa's side is said to have had Persian regiments.
result_basis: Arpa's army fell into disarray when the Uyghur contingent of Akrunj changed sides, and Ali Padshah held the field; Arpa was captured in flight and executed.
sources: Hafiz-i Abru; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Chobanids; en.wikipedia Battle of Jaghatu
note: Iranica's Chobanids article prints the date as 18 Ramadan 735 / 10 April 1336; the Hijri year must be 736, which gives about 29-30 April 1336, the date in Wikipedia's Qara Darra article.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Qara Darra
label: Qara Darra
war: Disintegration of the Ilkhanate (succession war after Abu Sa'id)
place: Qara Darra (Zilan valley) near Erciş, Turkey
commanders_a: Hasan Buzurg, Hajji Taghay, Surghan, Botso Tsmedisdze (Georgian vanguard, died of wounds)
persian_force: Hasan Buzurg's Jalayirs with the Sutayids of Diyarbakir, Chobanid troops under Surghan and a Georgian vanguard under Botso Tsmedisdze; against them the Oirats of Ali Padshah and the Uyghur emir Ogrunch.
iranian_note: The units named are Mongol tribes (Jalayir, Oirat), Uyghurs and Georgians; no Iranian contingent is named.
losses_b: unknown; Ali Padshah killed or executed
result_basis: Hasan Buzurg's charge broke Musa's centre and Ali Padshah was captured; Musa fled and Hasan held the field.
sources: Hafiz-i Abru; Sharaf Khan Bidlisi; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Chobanids; en.wikipedia Battle of Qara Darra
note: Muhammad Khan was proclaimed Ilkhan on 20 July and installed at Tabriz on 25 July 1336, with Hasan Buzurg holding real power.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Soltaniyeh (1337)
label: Soltaniyeh (1337)
war: Disintegration of the Ilkhanate (succession war after Abu Sa'id)
side_b: Togha Temur with Musa Khan and the Oirats
faction_b: Togha Temur (Khorasan) with Musa Khan and the Oirats
commanders_b: Togha Temur, Shaykh Ali Ke'un, Musa Khan
persian_force: Hasan Buzurg's Jalayir and allied tribal cavalry against Togha Temur's Khorasani army (the Jauni Qurban Oirats and other Mongol tribes of Khorasan) and the remaining Oirats of Musa.
iranian_note: Inferred: both claimants led the Turco-Mongol tribal cavalry of the Ilkhanate.
result_basis: Togha Temur and Musa were defeated and driven from the region, Togha Temur back to Khorasan.
borderline: no separate article; named by its place in the Wikipedia article on Togha Temur
doubt: Borderline: no separate article; named by its place in the Wikipedia article on Togha Temur.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Chobanids; en.wikipedia Togha Temur
note: Musa was captured and executed in July 1337.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Alataq (1338)
label: Alataq (1338)
place: Ala Tagh (Alataq) north of Lake Van, Turkey
persian_force: The Chobanid (Suldus) following and allied Mongol and Turkic tribal cavalry against the Jalayir and allied tribes of Hasan Buzurg.
iranian_note: Inferred: both sides were Turco-Mongol amirs leading their tribal cavalry.
result_basis: Desertions by Pir Husayn and Surghan broke Hasan Buzurg's army and the Chobanids held the field; Muhammad Khan was captured and executed.
borderline: no separate article; named by its place in Iranica and Wikipedia
doubt: Borderline: no separate article; named by its place in Iranica and Wikipedia.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Chobanids; en.wikipedia Hasan Kuchak
note: After the battle the Chobanids held Tabriz and Azerbaijan; Hasan Buzurg kept Iraq.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Jaghatu (1340)
label: Jaghatu (1340)
persian_force: Chobanid and allied Turco-Mongol cavalry assembled at Ujan against the Jalayirid army from Iraq.
iranian_note: Inferred: tribal cavalry on both sides, with troops from Iraq on the Jalayirid side.
result_basis: The Jalayirid army was defeated and Hasan Buzurg withdrew to Baghdad, leaving the Chobanids masters of the field.
borderline: no separate article; named by its place in Iranica
doubt: Borderline: no separate article; named by its place in Iranica.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Chobanids; en.wikipedia Hasan Kuchak
note: Jahan Temur was deposed after the defeat. Wikipedia names the site the Zarrinarud valley near Maragha, which is the same river.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Zava
label: Zava
faction_b: Sarbadars (Wajih al-Din Mas'ud, Shaykh Hasan Juri)
commanders_b: Wajih al-Din Mas'ud, Shaykh Hasan Juri (killed)
persian_force: The Kartid army of Herat (Tajik and Ghuri troops with Turkic retainers) against the Sarbadar army of Bayhaq: Persian peasant and townsmen soldiers and the Shi'i dervishes of Hasan Juri.
iranian_note: Both armies were raised in Persian-speaking Khorasan; the Sarbadar dervish militia was local.
losses_b: Hasan Juri killed; the poet Ibn Yamin captured
result_basis: The Sarbadars had the upper hand until Hasan Juri was killed, when his dervish followers left the field and the Kartids held it.
sources: Hafiz-i Abru; J. M. Smith, The History of the Sarbadar Dynasty; en.wikipedia Battle of Zava, Sarbadars
note: The Sarbadars believed Mas'ud's men had murdered Hasan Juri, which caused the withdrawal.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Shiraz (1342)
label: Shiraz (1342)
persian_force: Abu Ishaq's Injuid followers and the townsmen of Shiraz against Pir Husayn's Chobanid troops of Mongol and Turkic origin.
iranian_note: Inferred: the Injuid side rested on the Persian townsmen of Shiraz, the Chobanid side on Turco-Mongol troops.
result_basis: Abu Ishaq's partisans defeated Pir Husayn and drove the Chobanids out of Shiraz.
borderline: a fight for the city known from Iranica's summary; no separate article
doubt: Borderline: a fight for the city known from Iranica's summary; no separate article.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Chobanids
note: Pir Husayn had taken Shiraz from Mas'ud Shah Inju in 1340 with Muzaffarid help; he was later poisoned at Tabriz.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Amol (1344)
label: Amol (1344)
place: forest route between Sari and Amol, Mazandaran, Iran
side_a: Togha Temur's vassal Hasan II, Bavandid ispahbad of Mazandaran
faction_a: Togha Temur's vassal Hasan II, Bavandid ispahbad of Mazandaran
persian_force: The Mazandarani forces of the Bavandid ispahbad, Togha Temur's vassal, against the Sarbadar army of western Khorasan.
iranian_note: Inferred: Caspian highlanders and lowlanders on one side, Persian-speaking Khorasanis on the other.
losses_b: most of the army; Mas'ud killed
result_basis: The Sarbadar army was caught in a pincer in the forests of Mazandaran and destroyed; Mas'ud was captured and executed.
borderline: no standard name: the defeat of Mas'ud the Sarbadar in Mazandaran
doubt: Borderline: no standard name: the defeat of Mas'ud the Sarbadar in Mazandaran.
sources: J. M. Smith, The History of the Sarbadar Dynasty; en.wikipedia Sarbadars, Togha Temur
note: Wikipedia's Sarbadars article places the ambush on the Sari-Amol route; its Togha Temur article in a valley south of Amol.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Baghdad (siege, 1347)
label: Baghdad (siege, 1347)
persian_force: Hasan Buzurg's Jalayir troops and the garrison of Baghdad against Malek Ashtar's Chobanid army of Turco-Mongol cavalry.
iranian_note: Inferred: Turco-Mongol tribal armies, with Arabic-speaking townsmen in Baghdad.
result_basis: The Chobanid attack on Baghdad was repelled with heavy losses and the attempt was given up.
borderline: Jalayirid seat at Baghdad (seat rule); counted here as part of the Ilkhanid succession war, which lasted to 1357
doubt: Borderline: Jalayirid seat at Baghdad (seat rule); counted here as part of the Ilkhanid succession war, which lasted to 1357.
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Chobanids; en.wikipedia Malek Ashraf
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Daulatabad (Hasan Gangu's rising, 1347)
label: Daulatabad
date: July-August 1347 (Hasan Gangu was crowned on 3 or 12 August 1347)
war: Rise of the Bahmani Sultanate (rebellion of the Deccan amirs against Muhammad bin Tughluq)
commanders_a: Hasan Gangu (Zafar Khan), with Isma'il Mukh
commanders_b: Malik Jauhar and Shaikh Burhan al-Din Bilgrami
result_basis: The imperial forces left in the Deccan were put to flight and Hasan Gangu was crowned (Wikipedia 'Bahmani Sultanate').
doubt: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Wikipedia 'Bahmani Sultanate' (fetched 1 Nov 2026); Ferishta; Isami, Futuh us-Salatin
note: Descent of the dynasty is disputed: Wikipedia ('Bahmani Sultanate') cites Esami and Andre Wink for an Afghan origin of Hasan Gangu and Encyclopaedia Iranica for a 'Khorasani adventurer who claimed descent from Bahram Gur' (Ferishta calls the Persian pedigree flattery). Either way Iranian, so both peoples are marked uncertain. The Delhi army under Muhammad bin Tughluq took Daulatabad earlier in 1347 and then left for Gujarat; this entry is the rebels' recovery of the citadel.

name: Yazd (siege, 1350)
label: Yazd (siege, 1350)
persian_force: The Muzaffarid troops of Yazd and Kerman against Abu Ishaq's army of Fars.
iranian_note: Inferred: Persian townsmen and retainers with Mongol tribesmen of Kerman (Awghani, Jurma'i) and Turkic troops.
result_basis: Abu Ishaq's siege of Yazd failed and was given up.
borderline: no separate article and little detail on the fighting
doubt: Borderline: no separate article and little detail on the fighting.
sources: en.wikipedia Muzaffarids (Iran), Mubariz al-Din Muhammad
note: An Injuid army sent against Kerman about the same time was also defeated.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Herat (siege, 1351)
label: Herat (siege, 1351)
persian_force: The Kartid troops of Herat: Tajik townsmen and Ghuri hillmen with Turkic retainers (the normal Kartid army; the sources give no detail).
iranian_note: Inferred from the Kartid state's base in Persian-speaking Herat and Ghur.
result_basis: Herat was taken and sacked by Qazaghan's coalition and Mu'izz al-Din submitted.
borderline: date and course uncertain
doubt: Borderline: date and course uncertain.
sources: B. F. Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane; en.wikipedia Qazaghan, Kart dynasty
note: Qazaghan led the tribes of the southern Chagatai ulus after Kartid raids on the Arlat and Apardi; Wikipedia's Kart dynasty article dates the sack to c. 1358, most accounts to 1351-52.
qbasis: Kartids: an Iranian-led state

iranian_note: Both armies were Aq Qoyunlu tribal Turkmen forces (Iranica, Aq Qoyunlu).
result_basis: Khalil broke Ya'qub's right wing but was surrounded and killed, and his army fled.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Khoy (1478); en.wikipedia Yaqub (Aq Qoyunlu); Iranica, Aq Qoyunlu
note: Ya'qub entered Tabriz in September 1478 and was proclaimed sultan.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Rapri
label: Rapri
date: 1479 (one of a series of engagements of 1478-1479; exact date uncertain)
war: Bahlul Lodi's wars against the Sharqis of Jaunpur
place: Rapri, Doab, near Firozabad (Uttar Pradesh, India)
result_basis: Husain Shah was beaten at Rapri, as in the other engagements of the war, and lost Kampil, Patiali, Shamsabad, Suket, Koil, Marhara and Jalesar.
sources: Wikipedia, Husain Shah of Jaunpur: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Husain_Shah_of_Jaunpur; Nizamuddin Ahmad, Tabaqat-i Akbari; Ferishta
note: The war of 1478-1479 is a chain of defeats at Senha, Rapri, Raigaon Khaga and the Yamuna; the chronology of the individual fights is not secure, so Rapri stands for the series.

name: Kondapalli (Bahmani siege, c. 1480-1481)
label: Kondapalli
date: c. 1480-early 1481 (Ferishta's 885-886 AH; sources disagree on the year and on Kondapalli versus Kondavidu)
war: Bahmani-Gajapati wars (Bahmani invasion of Orissa's Andhra possessions)
place: Kondapalli fort near Vijayawada, Andhra Pradesh
commanders_a: Muhammad Shah III Lashkari (sultan); Mahmud Gawan (Persian-speaking Afaqi from Gilan; minister, with the army)
commanders_b: Hamvira Deva (Gajapati governor; brother of Purushottama)
result_basis: Ferishta has the Bahmani army take Kondapalli after a siege and then send Gawan on the expedition to Kanchi, but the Wikipedia articles on Kondapalli and the Bahmani invasion of Orissa put the fall of Kondavidu or Kondapalli differently (one has Purushottama retaking Kondapalli in 1481).
sources: Muhammad Qasim Ferishta, Tarikh-i Firishta (trans. J. Briggs, History of the Rise of the Mahomedan Power in India, vol. 2); H. K. Sherwani, Mahmud Gawan, the Great Bahmani Wazir (1942); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bahmani_invasion_of_Orissa; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kondapalli_Fort
note: Gawan was executed in April 1481 at the end of this campaign, on the sultan's return. the chronology (Kondapalli versus Kondavidu, 1478/1480/1481) is conflicting and the sultan, not Gawan, directed the army.

name: Chirciq River
label: Chirciq River
place: Chirchiq river, southeast of Tashkent, Uzbekistan
commanders_a: Sultan Mahmud Khan of Moghulistan; Muhammad Shaybani (defected from the Timurid side)
commanders_b: Sultan Ahmad Mirza, Mir Abdul Ali Tarkhan, Muhammad Majid Tarkhan
persian_force: Sultan Ahmad Mirza's army of Samarkand and Bukhara (reportedly 150,000), with infantry, Mir Abdul Ali's contingent and Shaybani's 3,000 Uzbeks, who defected.
iranian_note: The army included infantry, in Transoxiana normally Tajik levies, beside Chagatai cavalry and 3,000 Uzbeks; proportions are not recorded.
losses_b: heavy; many drowned in the river
result_basis: Shaybani's Uzbeks turned and fled at the critical moment, the Timurid army broke, and many drowned in the river.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of the Chirciq River
note: Moghulistan = the eastern Chagatai Khanate. Peace followed; Mahmud Khan gave Turkistan to Shaybani.
qbasis: The army included infantry, in Transoxiana normally Tajik levies, beside Chagatai cavalry and 3,000 Uzbeks; proportions are not recorded.

name: Tabasaran (1488)
label: Tabasaran (1488)
place: outside Bayqird castle, Tabasaran, Dagestan, Russia
side_a: Aq Qoyunlu with Shirvanshah Farrukh Yasar
faction_a: Aq Qoyunlu (Sultan Ya'qub) with Shirvanshah Farrukh Yasar
commanders_a: Shirvanshah Farrukh Yasar; Aq Qoyunlu troops sent by Ya'qub
persian_force: An Aq Qoyunlu Turkmen force sent by Ya'qub with Farrukh Yasar's Shirvan army, against Haydar's Qizilbash Sufi followers (Turkmen tribesmen).
iranian_note: Both the Aq Qoyunlu troops and the Safavid order's ghazis were Turkmen tribal cavalry.
result_basis: Haydar and his men were cornered in a pitched battle, defeated and killed.
borderline: the Safavid order before the Safavid state; civil because both the Aq Qoyunlu and the order (an Iranian religious faction) fought as principals
doubt: Borderline: the Safavid order before the Safavid state; civil because both the Aq Qoyunlu and the order (an Iranian religious faction) fought as principals.
sources: en.wikipedia Shaykh Haydar; Iranica, Aq Qoyunlu
note: Haydar had sacked Shamakhi on his way north; his sons were captured afterwards and his head buried at Tabriz.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Darguzin
label: Darguzin
date: 1490-1491 (during Sufi Khalil's regency; no date given)
side_a: Sufi Khalil Beg Mawsilu, regent for Baysunghur
side_b: Mahmud ibn Ughurlu Muhammad and Shah-Ali Beg Purnak
faction_a: Sufi Khalil Beg Mawsilu, regent for Baysunghur
faction_b: Mahmud ibn Ughurlu Muhammad and Shah-Ali Beg Purnak
commanders_b: Mahmud ibn Ughurlu Muhammad (captured, executed), Shah-Ali Beg Purnak (killed)
persian_force: Aq Qoyunlu Turkmen factions: the Mawsillu-led regency against a Purnak-backed claimant.
iranian_note: Both sides were Aq Qoyunlu Turkmen tribal forces.
result_basis: Sufi Khalil's forces won; Shah-Ali was killed and Mahmud captured.
borderline: date not given
doubt: Borderline: date not given.
sources: en.wikipedia Baysunghur (Aq Qoyunlu)
note: Sufi Khalil himself was defeated and killed by Sulayman Beg Bijan on 29 July 1491 on the way to Tabriz (an unnamed battle).
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Banaras (1494)
label: Banaras
war: Sikandar Lodi's conquest of the remaining Sharqi lands
result_basis: Sikandar defeated Husain Shah, who fled to Bihar and then Bengal, ending Sharqi resistance.
sources: Nizamuddin Ahmad, Tabaqat-i Akbari; Ferishta, Tarikh-i Firishta; Cambridge History of India, vol. 3 (Lodis)
note: Known mainly from Ferishta and Nizamuddin; recorded here from general knowledge and not confirmed on Wikipedia.

name: Shamasbi
label: Shamasbi
war: Aq Qoyunlu succession wars; Safavid order's wars
persian_force: Rustam's pursuing Aq Qoyunlu Turkmen force against Ali Mirza's small retinue of Sufis.
iranian_note: Both the Aq Qoyunlu troops and the Safavid order's followers were Turkmen tribesmen.
result_basis: The pursuing Aq Qoyunlu troops caught Ali Mirza's small band and killed him.
borderline: described as a pursuit and killing rather than a battle; the Safavid order before the state
doubt: Borderline: described as a pursuit and killing rather than a battle; the Safavid order before the state.
sources: en.wikipedia Ali Mirza Safavi; Iranica, Aq Qoyunlu
note: Ali Mirza had helped Rustam defeat Baysunghur in 1493 (an unnamed battle); his brother Ismail escaped to Lahijan.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Samarkand (siege, 1496)
label: Samarkand (siege, 1496)
side_b: Babur, Sultan Ali Mirza, Sultan Masud Mirza
faction_b: Babur (Fergana), Sultan Ali Mirza (Bukhara), Sultan Masud Mirza (Hissar)
commanders_b: Babur, Sultan Ali Mirza, Sultan Masud Mirza
persian_force: Three Timurid princely armies (Fergana, Bukhara, Hissar) against Baysonqor's garrison of Samarkand.
iranian_note: Chagatai and Moghul cavalry on the attacking side, a Persian-speaking city on the defending side; proportions are not recorded.
result_basis: The three uncoordinated besieging armies withdrew as winter came, and the city did not fall.
borderline: no fighting is recorded
doubt: Borderline: no fighting is recorded.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Samarkand (1490s)
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Aras (1497)
label: Aras (1497)
place: on the Aras (Araxes) river; exact site unknown
faction_a: Ahmad Beg (Gövde Ahmad), with Ottoman troops
persian_force: Ahmad's Aq Qoyunlu partisans with Ottoman troops, against Rustam's Turkmen tribal army.
iranian_note: Both sides were Aq Qoyunlu Turkmen forces, one with Ottoman help.
result_basis: Ahmad defeated Rustam and took the throne.
sources: en.wikipedia Aq Qoyunlu; Iranica, Aq Qoyunlu
note: Rustam was put to death after his defeat. The country is uncertain: the Aras forms the Iran-Azerbaijan-Armenia border.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Samarkand (siege, 1497)
label: Samarkand (siege, 1497)
commanders_b: Baysonqor Mirza; Muhammad Shaybani (Uzbek relief force, withdrew without fighting)
persian_force: Babur's Fergana army (Chagatai begs and Moghul horse) and Ali Mirza's Bukharan troops, against Baysonqor's garrison and the citizens of Samarkand, who made sorties.
iranian_note: Babur's Moghul horse and Chagatai followers are named; the citizen sortie shows Persian-speaking townsmen fighting; proportions are not recorded.
losses_a: considerable (Babur's best men killed or captured in an ambush at the Lovers' Cave)
losses_b: considerable (many citizens killed or captured in a sortie)
result_basis: After seven months Baysonqor abandoned the city and Babur entered Samarkand at the end of November 1497.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Samarkand (1497); en.wikipedia Babur
note: Wikipedia's lead says the city fell in May; its body and the seven-month length give late November. Babur held Samarkand for about 100 days.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Isfahan (1497)
label: Isfahan (1497)
side_a: Aq Qoyunlu emirs led by Ayba Sultan
faction_a: Aq Qoyunlu emirs led by Ayba Sultan
persian_force: Aq Qoyunlu Turkmen tribal factions (the Purnak and Qajar under Ayba Sultan) against Ahmad's followers.
iranian_note: Both sides were Aq Qoyunlu Turkmen tribal forces.
result_basis: Ahmad was defeated and killed by the revolting emirs.
sources: Iranica, Aq Qoyunlu
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Herat (siege, 1499)
label: Herat (siege, 1499)
war: Revolts of Badi' al-Zaman against Husayn Bayqara
persian_force: Badi' al-Zaman's army of Balkh against Husayn's garrison and army of Herat.
iranian_note: Timurid armies had a Chagatai Turkic core with Tajik levies and town garrisons; proportions are not recorded.
result_basis: Badi' al-Zaman did not take Herat, which Husayn held until his death in 1506.
borderline: the course of the siege is not described
doubt: Borderline: the course of the siege is not described.
sources: en.wikipedia Badi' al-Zaman Mirza; en.wikipedia Husayn Bayqara
note: Wikipedia gives no outcome; failure is inferred from Husayn's unbroken rule at Herat.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Samarkand (1500)
label: Samarkand (1500)
persian_force: Babur's band of about 240 Chagatai and Moghul followers, joined by the Persian-speaking townspeople of Samarkand.
iranian_note: Babur's own men were Chagatai Turks and Moghuls (Baburnama); the Tajik townsmen who rose against the garrison are not counted in the force.
losses_b: many of the garrison killed in the streets
result_basis: Babur's night escalade took the city and the townspeople rose and killed the Uzbek garrison.
borderline: a surprise capture with fighting in the streets rather than a battle or siege
doubt: Borderline: a surprise capture with fighting in the streets rather than a battle or siege.
sources: Babur, Baburnama; en.wikipedia Babur; en.wikipedia Siege of Samarkand (1497)
note: Shaybani had taken Samarkand from Sultan Ali Mirza without a battle earlier in 1500; he beat Babur at Sar-i Pul and besieged him in Samarkand in 1501.
qbasis: the Persian-speaking townsmen of Samarkand rose and fought

name: Jabani
label: Jabani
persian_force: About 7,000 Qizilbash of the Ustajlu, Rumlu, Takkalu, Dhu'l-Qadar, Afshar, Qajar and Varsaq tribes, gathered at Erzincan in summer 1500.
iranian_note: All the named tribes were Turkmen; Iranian Sufis from Gilan and Ardabil were few.
result_basis: The Qizilbash routed Farrukh Yasar's army and the Shirvanshah was killed.
borderline: fought before Ismail's coronation at Tabriz (1501)
doubt: Borderline: fought before Ismail's coronation at Tabriz (1501).
sources: en.wikipedia Ismail I
note: Ismail then took Baku; the Shirvanshahs ruled on as Safavid vassals until 1538.
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Baku (siege, 1501)
label: Baku (siege, 1501)
commanders_a: Ismail I (his emirs conducted the siege)
commanders_b: the Shirvanshah's garrison (commander not named in the sources used)
persian_force: Ismail's Qizilbash, about 7,000 Turkmen tribal warriors (Ustajlu, Rumlu, Shamlu, Takkalu, Dhu'l-Qadar, Afshar, Qajar) who had joined him at Erzincan in 1500.
iranian_note: Ismail's first army was the Turkoman Qizilbash of Anatolia and Syria, with only a few Talish and Gilani followers from his years in Lahijan (Savory).
result_basis: Baku fell to Ismail's besiegers in 1501.
borderline: no separate article; known from the Safavid chronicles as summarised in the Ismail I articles
doubt: Borderline: no separate article; known from the Safavid chronicles as summarised in the Ismail I articles.
sources: en.wikipedia Ismail I and Campaigns of Ismail I (Siege of Baku in the infobox); Savory, Iran under the Safavids
note: Fought after Ismail's victory over Shirvanshah Farrukh Yassar at Jabani or Gulistan (December 1500) and before Sharur.
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Sharur
label: Sharur
date: summer 1501 (July or August per Farrokh; day unknown)
war: Safavid-Aq Qoyunlu war (rise of Ismail I)
persian_force: Ismail's 7,000 Qizilbash from the Ustajlu, Rumlu, Takkalu, Dhu'l-Qadar, Afshar, Qajar and Varsaq tribes, against Alvand's Aq Qoyunlu Turkmen army of Azerbaijan and Armenia.
iranian_note: Both armies were Turkmen tribal cavalry; the Qizilbash tribes are named in the sources (Savory; en.wikipedia Battle of Sharur).
strength_b: more than four times Ismail's army (Savory)
losses_b: up to 18,000 killed (Alam-ara-ye Safavi, a late and inflated figure)
result_basis: Alvand fled the field, which Ismail's army held; he was driven out of Azerbaijan.
sources: Hasan Beg Rumlu, Ahsan al-tawarikh; Savory, Iran under the Safavids; Farrokh, Iran at War; en.wikipedia Battle of Sharur
note: Some accounts place the battle late in 1501; Ismail entered Tabriz and was proclaimed shah after it.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Tabriz (siege, 1501)
label: Tabriz (siege, 1501)
war: Safavid-Aq Qoyunlu war (rise of Ismail I)
commanders_b: Alvand Beg, Osman Sultan Torkaman; Dulkadirid troops sent by Ala al-Dawla Bozkurt
persian_force: Ismail's qurchis and Qizilbash; about 500 men under Khalvachi-oghlu defended the palace with bows and muskets (Alam-ara-ye Safavi).
iranian_note: The qurchis were drawn from the Turkmen Qizilbash tribes.
strength_b: 10,000-40,000 Aq Qoyunlu and about 20,000 Dulkadirids (infobox, after the Alam-ara)
result_basis: Ismail kept Tabriz: in the Alam-ara account the palace garrison held out and Alvand's force was then defeated and dispersed.
borderline: a capture whose fighting rests on one doubtful source
doubt: Traditional: The fighting is known only from the anonymous popular romance Alam-ara-ye Safavi; Hasan Beg Rumlu says the notables of Tabriz received Ismail without resistance, and Ibn Kemal's violent account is hostile to the Safavids. Borderline: a capture whose fighting rests on one doubtful source.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Tabriz (1501); Alam-ara-ye Safavi; Hasan Beg Rumlu
note: The article places Alvand's counter-attack in the context of his moves of 1502-1503; date and scale are uncertain.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Hamadan (1503)
label: Hamadan (1503)
war: Safavid-Aq Qoyunlu war (rise of Ismail I)
commanders_a: Ismail I; Khulafa Beg, Qipchaq Mansur Beg, Qarapiri Beg Qajar, Yegan Beg Tekelu, Bayram Beg Qaramanlu
commanders_b: Sultan Murad; Ali Beg Turkman, Islamish Beg
persian_force: About 12,000 Qizilbash horse, with Qarapiri Beg Qajar's 1,500 cavalry in reserve and Tekelu and Qaramanlu emirs on the wings, against Sultan Murad's Aq Qoyunlu Turkmen cavalry.
iranian_note: The commanders named are all Qizilbash Turkmen emirs; Murad's army was Turkmen cavalry.
result_basis: Sultan Murad's army broke and he fled; the Safavids held the field.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Hamadan (1503); Savory, Iran under the Safavids
note: Opened Iraq-i Ajam and Fars to Ismail.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Usta (siege)
label: Usta (siege)
war: Ismail I's conquest of Iran (Mazandaran campaign)
persian_force: Ismail's Qizilbash army; no unit details are given, so this is the normal Turkmen tribal army of the first Safavid campaigns.
iranian_note: Ismail's army of 1504 was still essentially the Turkmen Qizilbash tribes; Husayn Kiya's men were local Iranian highlanders.
losses_b: garrison taken; Husayn Kiya died in captivity
result_basis: The fortress fell after its water supply was cut, and Husayn Kiya was taken prisoner.
borderline: no Wikipedia battle article; a siege known from the Safavid chronicles
doubt: Borderline: no Wikipedia battle article; a siege known from the Safavid chronicles.
sources: Savory, Iran under the Safavids; Cambridge History of Iran vol. 6 (Savory); en.wikipedia Campaigns of Ismail I (conquest of Mazandaran, 1504)
note: In the same campaign Ismail took the fortresses of Gulkhandan and Firuzkuh. The exact site of Usta is not securely located; coordinates are for the Firuzkuh district.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Yazd (siege, 1504)
label: Yazd (siege, 1504)
persian_force: Ismail's Qizilbash army (no unit details in the sources used).
iranian_note: Normal composition of Ismail's early army: Turkmen Qizilbash tribal cavalry.
result_basis: Yazd fell to Ismail after a siege and Muhammad Karra was captured.
borderline: no Wikipedia battle article
doubt: Borderline: no Wikipedia battle article.
sources: Savory, Iran under the Safavids; en.wikipedia Campaigns of Ismail I (conquest of Yazd, 1504)
note: Muhammad Karra, a former Aq Qoyunlu officer and lord of Abarquh, had seized Yazd; Wikipedia's campaign list counts the conquest against the Aq Qoyunlu. Ismail then sacked Tabas.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Trabzon (1505)
label: Trabzon (1505)
place: Trabzon province, with the pursuit to Erzincan, Turkey
persian_force: A Qizilbash raiding force of about 3,000 horsemen.
iranian_note: Raids on the Anatolian frontier were made by Turkmen Qizilbash horsemen.
result_basis: Selim drove off the raiders and pursued them to Erzincan, taking their arms and supplies.
borderline: a frontier raid known from Ottoman chronicles
doubt: Borderline: a frontier raid known from Ottoman chronicles.
sources: en.wikipedia Trabzon Expedition (1505); Ottoman-Persian War (1505-1517)
note: Bayezid II kept the captured arms but answered Ismail's complaint with gifts.
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Gwalior (siege, 1505-1506)
label: Gwalior
result_basis: Hit-and-run attacks and crop destruction forced Sikandar to lift the siege; the fort was not taken.
sources: Wikipedia, Sikandar Lodi: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sikandar_Lodi; Ferishta; K. S. Lal on the Tomars
note: The Lodi army was largely Afghan; Sikandar was a Lodi Afghan by descent. Sikandar was ambushed at Jatwar on the retreat in 1506.

name: Erzincan (1507)
label: Erzincan (1507)
persian_force: About 10,000 Qizilbash, partly Turkmen recruited among Ottoman subjects.
iranian_note: The article notes the Safavids recruited Turkmen warriors who were Ottoman subjects.
result_basis: Selim defeated the Safavid force and it withdrew.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Erzincan (1507); Ottoman-Persian War (1505-1517)
note: Fought while Ismail's army of about 20,000 crossed Ottoman land to attack the Dulkadirids; Selim acted without his father's approval.
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Hormuz (1507)
label: Hormuz (1507)
war: Portuguese campaigns in the Persian Gulf (Albuquerque's first expedition)
commanders_b: Khwaja Ata (Cogeatar), vizier of the young King Sayf al-Din; Rais Nur al-Din Fali
persian_force: The Hormuzi fleet: 50-60 large armed merchantmen and 120-200 light oared craft carrying hired Persian bowmen.
iranian_note: The oared craft carried Persian mercenary archers; the ships and crews were Arab, Gujarati and other Indian Ocean seafarers.
losses_b: 2 large ships and about a dozen light craft sunk, most of the fleet captured or burnt
result_basis: Portuguese gunfire sank or disabled much of the Hormuzi fleet and the vizier raised a white flag and accepted tribute.
borderline: the Kingdom of Hormuz was an Iran-seated island kingdom independent of the Safavids and not one of this set's Persian states
doubt: Borderline: the Kingdom of Hormuz was an Iran-seated island kingdom independent of the Safavids and not one of this set's Persian states.
sources: en.wikipedia Capture of Ormuz (1507); Portuguese-Safavid wars
note: Albuquerque could not hold Hormuz in 1507-08; the Portuguese took it in 1515 (by a palace coup, no battle).

label: Narwar
war: Sikandar Lodi's campaigns in Malwa and Gwalior
commanders_b: Tomara ruler of Narwar (name not secure)
result_basis: The fort fell after a year-long siege.
sources: Wikipedia, Sikandar Lodi: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sikandar_Lodi; Ferishta
note: Minor siege; included for the Lodi sultan as Pashtun leader.

label: Diyarbakır (siege, 1509)

persian_force: About 800 Safavid troops, the Ustajlu Qizilbash of the governor of Diyarbakir.
iranian_note: Mohammad Khan's following was drawn from his Ustajlu Turkmen tribe.
result_basis: The Safavids retook Diyarbakir from its Dulkadirid defenders and executed the two princes.
borderline: a recapture described in one article; the scale of the fighting is unclear
doubt: Borderline: a recapture described in one article; the scale of the fighting is unclear.

name: Diyarbakır (1510)
label: Diyarbakır (1510)
commanders_b: Shahruh and Ahmed, sons of Ala al-Dawla Bozkurt
persian_force: The Ustajlu Qizilbash of the Safavid governor of Diyarbakir (size not given).
iranian_note: Mohammad Khan's army was his Ustajlu Turkmen tribal following.
losses_b: Shahruh, Ahmed and about forty others beheaded
result_basis: The Safavid attack routed the Dulkadirid army, whose leaders were captured and beheaded.

sources: en.wikipedia Trabzon Expedition (1510); Ottoman-Persian War (1505-1517)

name: Merv
label: Merv
persian_force: About 17,000 Qizilbash cavalry under the shah.
iranian_note: The army was the Qizilbash tribal cavalry; Persian (Tajik) officials and Khorasani levies were a small element.
result_basis: Ismail's feigned retreat drew the Uzbeks into an ambush; they were routed and Shaybani was killed in the flight.

name: Qarshi (siege)

persian_force: Najm-e Sani's army (said to be 60,000): the Qizilbash emirs of Khorasan, the governor of Herat, Biram Khan Qaramanlu from Balkh and Abdal Beg Talish, with Babur's Chagatai Turks.

name: Ghazdewan
label: Ghazdewan

iranian_note: The contingents named are Qizilbash Turkmen and Babur's Turks under a Persian (Tajik) vizier, with a Talish emir.
result_basis: The Safavid army broke within about an hour after Biram Khan fell, and fled across the Amu Darya.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Ghazdewan; Baburnama; Savory; Iranica, Ghojdovan

name: Chaldiran

persian_force: Ismail's Qizilbash cavalry (Ustajlu, Shamlu, Rumlu, Takkalu, Dhu'l-Qadar and others), without artillery or infantry; Persian (Tajik) grandees such as the vakil Abd al-Baqi Yazdi and the sadr Sharif al-Din Shirazi fought and fell.
iranian_note: The army was mostly Turkmen tribal levies (cited in en.wikipedia); Tajik notables held commands but brought few troops.

name: Isfahan (Alqas Mirza's attack, 1548)

result_basis: Islam Shah defeated the Niazi rebels, who fled to the hills and then to Kashmir.

note: Afghan against Afghan. The Wikipedia article calls the place Sambla near Dinkot; older histories say Ambala, so the location is not secure.

name: Banihal Pass (1552)
label: Banihal Pass
war: Niazi revolt against Islam Shah Suri: flight to Kashmir
place: Banihal Pass, Jammu and Kashmir, India
commanders_a: Haibat Khan Niazi; Said Khan; Shahbaz Khan
result_basis: The Kashmiris blocked the pass, captured the Niazi chiefs and killed Haibat Khan, Shahbaz Khan and Said Khan.
sources: Wikipedia, Haibat Khan Niazi: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haibat_Khan_Niazi; Abbas Khan Sarwani
note: More an ambush of fugitives than a pitched battle; included because the Niazi Afghans had fought their way to the pass.

name: Erzurum (1552)
label: Erzurum (1552)
commanders_a: Ismail Mirza (later Ismail II), Shahverdi Sultan Ziyad-oghlu, Badr Khan Ustajlu, Muhammad Khan Turkman
persian_force: Qizilbash contingents (Ziyad-oghlu Qajar, Ustajlu, Turkman) with 1,000 Tehran and 600 Nakhchivan guards.
iranian_note: The commanders named are Qizilbash emirs; the Tehran guards may have been Persian.
strength_b: unknown (Turks and Kurds of eastern Anatolia)
losses_b: 2,576 killed besides those drowned, several begs captured
result_basis: Iskender Pasha's army was routed outside Erzurum, many dying in the fortress ditch.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Erzurum (1552); Iranica, Tahmasp I
note: Wikipedia's Tahmasp I dates Ismail Mirza's victory to May 1554.
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Farah
label: Farah
place: Farah, between Mathura and Agra, Uttar Pradesh, India
persian_state: Sikandar Shah Suri v Ibrahim Shah Suri
result_basis: Sikandar defeated Ibrahim near Agra and took Delhi and Agra; Ibrahim fled east.
sources: Wikipedia, Muhammad Adil Shah (died 1557): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Adil_Shah_(died_1557); Nizamuddin Ahmad, Tabaqat-i Akbari
note: Sur against Sur. The name Farah and the date come from the later chronicles and the Wikipedia article only says 'near Agra'.

name: Machhiwara
label: Machhiwara
result_basis: The Sur army was defeated and the Mughals gained the Sutlej line and the Punjab.
sources: Wikipedia, List of battles involving the Mughal Empire: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_battles_involving_the_Mughal_Empire; Abul Fazl, Akbarnama; Wikipedia, Mughal-Afghan Wars
note: Sikandar Shah Suri was a Sur Afghan by descent; the commanders for the Sur army are from memory.

name: Sirhind
label: Sirhind
result_basis: The Sur army was routed, and Humayun re-entered Delhi in July 1555.
sources: Wikipedia, List of battles involving the Mughal Empire: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_battles_involving_the_Mughal_Empire; Abul Fazl, Akbarnama
note: The decisive battle of Humayun's restoration.

name: Garisi
label: Garisi
commanders_a: Shahverdi Sultan Ziyad-oghlu Qajar, beglarbeg of Karabakh (killed)
commanders_b: Luarsab I of Kartli (mortally wounded), Simon
persian_force: About 25,000 Qizilbash placed under Shahverdi Sultan by Tahmasp.
iranian_note: The army is described as Qizilbash under the Ziyad-oghlu Qajar of Karabakh.
losses_a: more than 10,000 killed or wounded (Georgian figure)
result_basis: In a pitched battle the Georgians beat off the Qizilbash, whose commander Shahverdi Sultan fell, though Luarsab I was killed.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Garisi; Luarsab I of Kartli; Tahmasp I
note: Kingdom of Kartli.
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Tughlaqabad
label: Tughlaqabad
result_basis: After a day's fighting Hemu defeated Tardi Beg Khan and took Delhi.
sources: Wikipedia, Second Battle of Panipat: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Battle_of_Panipat; Abul Fazl, Akbarnama; Badauni
note: Hemu was a Hindu general, but the army he led for the Sur sultan was mainly Afghan horse; no Afghan leader is named for this battle.

name: Second Battle of Panipat
label: Second Battle of Panipat
commanders_a: Ali Quli Khan Shaibani; Bairam Khan (behind the line)
result_basis: Hemu was struck in the eye by an arrow, his army broke and fled, and he was captured and killed.
sources: Wikipedia, Second Battle of Panipat: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Battle_of_Panipat; Abul Fazl, Akbarnama
note: Hemu's army is described as mostly Afghan horse (about 30,000) with Shadi Khan Kakar, a Pashtun, commanding one wing.

name: Chhapparghatta
label: Chhapparghatta
persian_state: Muhammad Shah Sur's Bengal v Adil Shah Suri
commanders_a: Khizr Khan Sur (Bahadur Shah of Bengal)
result_basis: Adil Shah was defeated and killed by Khizr Khan of Bengal.
sources: Wikipedia, Muhammad Adil Shah (died 1557): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Adil_Shah_(died_1557); Nizamuddin Ahmad, Tabaqat-i Akbari
note: Sur against Sur. The name and exact place are not given in the Wikipedia article and are taken from the later chronicles.

name: Kandahar (siege, 1557-1558)
label: Kandahar (siege, 1557-1558)
commanders_a: Ali Sultan Tati-oghlu Dhu'l-Qadar; Soltan Hosayn Mirza
persian_force: A Qizilbash army under Ali Sultan Dhu'l-Qadar, fighting with bows and muskets (no numbers).
iranian_note: Khorasan's Qizilbash (Dhu'l-Qadar, Shamlu) formed the army; local levies are not recorded.
result_basis: After six months of fighting Shah Muhammad surrendered the fort on terms and left for India.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Kandahar (1557-1558); Mughal-Persian wars; Soltan Hosayn Mirza Safavi
note: Akbar, under the regent Bairam Khan, could send no relief. The Safavids held Kandahar until 1595.
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Mankot (siege, 1556-1557)
label: Mankot
date: January to 25 July 1557 (the siege began in late 1556 in some accounts)
result_basis: Sikandar surrendered after about six months, on terms, once Adil Shah was dead.
sources: Wikipedia, List of battles involving the Mughal Empire: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_battles_involving_the_Mughal_Empire; Wikipedia, Muhammad Adil Shah (died 1557); Abul Fazl, Akbarnama
note: The last stand of the Sur dynasty in the north.

name: Sarangpur (1561)
label: Sarangpur
result_basis: Baz Bahadur was defeated and fled, and the Mughals took Malwa.
sources: Abul Fazl, Akbarnama; Wikipedia, Baz Bahadur: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baz_Bahadur
note: Baz Bahadur was the son of Shuja'at Khan Sur, Sher Shah's governor of Malwa, so a Sur Afghan by descent.

name: Tsikhedidi
label: Tsikhedidi
commanders_a: the Persian garrison commanders of Tbilisi (not named)
commanders_b: Simon I of Kartli, Prince George of Kakheti (killed)
persian_force: The Qizilbash garrison and field troops holding Tbilisi (no details).
iranian_note: Safavid forces in Georgia were Qizilbash.
result_basis: Simon was defeated and his ally George of Kakheti was killed.
borderline: the opponent is not named in the Wikipedia article; Simon was campaigning to retake Persian-held Tbilisi
doubt: Borderline: the opponent is not named in the Wikipedia article; Simon was campaigning to retake Persian-held Tbilisi.
sources: en.wikipedia Simon I of Kartli
note: Kingdoms of Kartli and Kakheti.
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Chauragarh (siege, 1564)
label: Chauragarh
date: 1564, soon after Narrai (exact dates not fixed)
place: Chauragarh fort, Narsinghpur district, Madhya Pradesh, India
commanders_a: Asaf Khan I (Abdul Majid Asaf Khan)
commanders_b: Vir Narayan (killed); the garrison and the Rani's household
result_basis: Vir Narayan was killed, the women committed jauhar and Asaf Khan took the fort and its treasure.
sources: Wikipedia, Mughal conquest of Garha (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mughal_conquest_of_Garha); Wikipedia, Asaf Khan I; Akbarnama
note: Same weak origin evidence as Narrai (the nisba Harawi). Asaf Khan kept most of the loot, including 800 elephants, and rebelled in 1565.

name: Narrai
label: Narrai
place: Narrai, between the Gaur and Narmada rivers, near Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh, India
commanders_a: Asaf Khan I (Abdul Majid Asaf Khan, governor of Kara)
commanders_b: Rani Durgavati (died by suicide in the battle); Vir Narayan (pushed the Mughals back three times and was wounded)
result_basis: The Rani's army was broken and she killed herself; Asaf Khan went on to Chauragarh.
sources: Wikipedia, Mughal conquest of Garha (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mughal_conquest_of_Garha); Wikipedia, Asaf Khan I (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asaf_Khan_I); Abu'l-Fazl, Akbarnama (Beveridge trans.)
note: The origin of Asaf Khan I is thin: the Wikipedia articles do not state it; he is called Harawi (of Herat) in the Akbarnama, which makes him Persian-speaking Khurasani by origin, but this rests on the nisba. Also called the Battle of Damoh in Wikipedia's infobox.

name: Digomi
label: Digomi
commanders_b: Daud Khan (David XI), Tahmasp's appointee in Tbilisi
persian_force: The Persian garrison of Tbilisi under the converted Georgian prince Daud Khan: Qizilbash troops with his Georgian followers.
iranian_note: Qizilbash garrison with Georgian partisans of Daud Khan; no breakdown in the sources.
result_basis: Daud Khan's sortie was routed on the Digomi plain, though the Georgians could not take the Tbilisi fortress.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Digomi; Simon I of Kartli
note: The campaign failed and the fortress stayed in Persian hands; the field fight is scored.
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Partskhisi (1569)
label: Partskhisi (1569)
place: near Partskhisi castle, Kvemo Kartli, Georgia
commanders_a: Persian commanders supporting Daud Khan (not named)
persian_force: Persian (Qizilbash) troops backing Daud Khan's rule in Kartli (no details).
iranian_note: Qizilbash troops with Daud Khan's Georgian partisans.
result_basis: Simon was defeated and taken prisoner.
borderline: the opponent is implied in the source (Simon was captured by Persian forces)
doubt: Borderline: the opponent is implied in the source (Simon was captured by Persian forces).
sources: en.wikipedia Simon I of Kartli
note: Earlier in 1569 Simon won at Samadlo against an opponent the source does not name (not listed). Simon was held in Alamut until 1578.
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Hajipur and Patna (siege, 1574)
label: Hajipur and Patna
war: Mughal conquest of Bengal and Bihar
commanders_a: Akbar; Munim Khan; Todar Mal; Man Singh
commanders_b: Daud Khan Karrani; Katlu Lohani; Gujar Khan Karrani
result_basis: The Afghan garrison nearly won at Hajipur but Akbar took the supply fort, and Daud fled from Patna into Bengal.
sources: Wikipedia, Daud Khan Karrani: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daud_Khan_Karrani; Abul Fazl, Akbarnama; Banglapedia, Karrani Rule
note: Hajipur and Patna fell within days of each other; recorded as one siege.

name: Tukaroi
label: Tukaroi
war: Mughal conquest of Bengal and Bihar
place: Tukaroi (Mughalmari), Balasore/Midnapore border, Odisha/West Bengal, India
commanders_a: Munim Khan Khan-i-Khanan; Khan Jahan (Husain Quli Khan)
commanders_b: Daud Khan Karrani; Gujar Khan Karrani
result_basis: The Afghans withdrew to Cuttack and the Mughals took Tanda; Wikipedia's article on Daud Khan records the battle as a draw.
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Tukaroi: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Tukaroi; Wikipedia, Daud Khan Karrani: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daud_Khan_Karrani; Abul Fazl, Akbarnama
note: Daud withdrew to Cuttack and made peace, ceding Bengal and Bihar to the Mughals; the Mughal commanders are not named in the Wikipedia article and are given from memory.

name: Rajmahal
label: Rajmahal
war: Mughal conquest of Bengal and Bihar
commanders_a: Khan Jahan Quli; Muzaffar Khan Turbati
commanders_b: Daud Khan Karrani; Junaid; Qutlu Khan; Ismail Khan Lodi
result_basis: After a long battle Daud was defeated, captured and executed.
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Rajmahal: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Rajmahal; Wikipedia, Daud Khan Karrani: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daud_Khan_Karrani; Banglapedia, Rajmahal, The battle of
note: The end of the Karrani Sultanate of Bengal.

name: Uzbek invasion of Khorasan (1578)
label: Uzbek invasion of Khorasan (1578)
commanders_a: Mortaza Qoli Khan Pornak Turkman (beglarbeg of Mashhad), Ommat Beg Ustajlu
commanders_b: Jalal Khan Uzbek, governor of Merv (killed)
persian_force: About 3,000 men of the Mashhad governor, Turkman and Ustajlu Qizilbash.
iranian_note: Khorasan's governor led his Qizilbash tribesmen with some local levies.
result_basis: After an evening fight that ended level, Jalal Khan was killed and the Uzbeks withdrew to their own territory, leaving the Safavids in possession.
borderline: the article names the fight inconsistently (it mentions Ashgabat and Jam); listed under the article's title
doubt: Borderline: the article names the fight inconsistently (it mentions Ashgabat and Jam); listed under the article's title.
sources: en.wikipedia Uzbek invasion of Khorasan (1578)
note: Jalal Khan had plundered the Mashhad and Jam districts after Tahmasp's subsidy stopped.
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Çıldır
label: Çıldır
commanders_a: Lala Mustafa Pasha (main army), Ozdemiroglu Osman Pasha, Dervis Pasha
commanders_b: Mohammad Khan Tokhmaq Ustajlu (Erivan), Imam Quli Khan Qajar (Ganja), Qara Khan (wounded)
persian_force: Tokhmaq Khan's army of north-western Iran, 15,000-30,000 Qizilbash (Ustajlu of Erivan, Qajar of Ganja), with about 7,000 Georgians.
iranian_note: The governors and tribes named are Qizilbash Turkmen; the Georgian allies were a large separate contingent.
strength_a: unknown (Iskandar Beg Munshi claimed 100,000 for the Ottoman army)
losses_b: 5,000-7,000 killed and about 3,000 captured and beheaded
result_basis: The Safavid-Georgian army was routed and thousands of prisoners were executed on the field the next day.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Çıldır; Lala Mustafa Pasha's Caucasian campaign; Mohammad Khan Tokhmaq Ustajlu
note: Opened Tbilisi to the Ottomans (taken by 24 August 1578).
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Koyun Geçidi
label: Koyun Geçidi
place: Koyun Geçidi ford on the Kanik (Alazani) river, Azerbaijan
commanders_a: Lala Mustafa Pasha (overall); Osman Pasha, Mehmed Pasha, Mustafa Pasha
commanders_b: Amir Khan Turkman, Murad Khan (killed), Sharaf Khan Bitlisi
persian_force: Qizilbash cavalry of Karabakh and Shirvan (no details in the sources used).
iranian_note: The Safavid border armies of 1578 were Qizilbash tribal cavalry.
result_basis: The Ottomans crossed the Alazani (Qanikh) in force and drove the Safavid army into the river with heavy loss, holding the field (9 September 1578).
borderline: named only in an infobox; date, site and result not checked against a detailed online source for this file
doubt: Borderline: named only in an infobox; date, site and result not checked against a detailed online source for this file.
sources: en.wikipedia Lala Mustafa Pasha (infobox: Battle of Koyun Geçidi); Ottoman chronicles (Mustafa Ali, Nusretname)
note: The site and the details given here are uncertain; the Turkish Wikipedia page could not be fetched.
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Mollahasanli
label: Mollahasanli
date: 28 November 1578 (24 or 30 November in some accounts)
place: Mollahasanli on the Agsu river, near Pirgasanli, Azerbaijan
commanders_a: Hamza Mirza (nominal), Mirza Salman Jaberi, Mohammad Khan Turkman, Mohammad Khan Ustajlu, Sharaf al-Din Takkalu, Imam Quli Khan Qajar
persian_force: About 20,000 Qizilbash cavalry under the tribal emirs, led in fact by the vizier Mirza Salman.
iranian_note: The emirs named lead Turkman, Ustajlu, Takkalu and Qajar Qizilbash; the vizier Mirza Salman was Persian.
losses_b: about 2,000 captured, including some 30 nobles and the Ottoman sanjak-bey Piyale Beg
result_basis: The surprise attack routed the Tatars, who had scattered to guard their booty, and Adil Giray was captured.

note: Adil Giray was executed at Qazvin. The war article's body places the battle in a 1579 context.

persian_force: About 20,000 Qizilbash of Shirvan and Karabakh under Aras Khan.
iranian_note: Provincial Qizilbash forces; no breakdown in the sources.

sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Shamakhi (1578); Ottoman-Safavid War (1578-1590)

qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Shamakhi (1581)
label: Shamakhi (1581)
commanders_a: Piri Muhammad Beg, Imam Quli Khan Qajar
persian_force: Qizilbash of Karabakh and Shirvan under Imam Quli Khan Qajar and Piri Muhammad Beg (no numbers).
iranian_note: Provincial Qizilbash forces.
result_basis: The Ottoman-Crimean force was decisively defeated and Gazi Giray was taken prisoner.
borderline: described in two articles but not given a battle name
doubt: Borderline: described in two articles but not given a battle name.
sources: en.wikipedia Ottoman-Safavid War (1578-1590); Gazi II Giray
note: Osman Pasha then withdrew to Derbent, leaving a garrison in Baku.

label: Herat (siege, 1582-1583)

persian_force: Khodabanda's army of about 80,000, Turkman, Takkalu and other Qizilbash of the west, against the Shamlu and Ustajlu of Khorasan.
iranian_note: A war between Qizilbash factions; the Herat side had the support of the Persian-speaking city.

sources: en.wikipedia Ali-Qoli Khan Shamlu; Abbas the Great; Savory

qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Torches
label: Torches
commanders_a: Ozdemiroglu Osman Pasha, Cafer Pasha, Haydar Pasha

persian_force: Imam Quli Khan Qajar's army of 50,000 or more, the Qizilbash of Karabakh, Shirvan and Azerbaijan, with Georgian irregulars.
iranian_note: A provincial Qizilbash army under the Qajar beglarbeg of Ganja-Karabakh; no breakdown.

sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Torches; Ottoman-Safavid War (1578-1590)
note: Meşaleler Savaşı, so called because fighting went on by torchlight. Ottoman allies: the Crimean Khanate, the Shamkhalate of Tarki and the Nogais. Some accounts place the battle near the Samur river.
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Tabriz (siege, 1585-1586)
label: Tabriz (siege, 1585-1586)
commanders_a: Cafer Pasha (governor of the new Ottoman fortress)
persian_force: Hamza Mirza's Qizilbash army (no details).

sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Tabriz (disambiguation: Siege of Tabriz (1585-1586), a red link); Capture of Tabriz (1585); Hamza Mirza; Savory
note: Hamza Mirza was murdered in his camp in Karabakh on 6 December 1586, after which the Safavid effort collapsed.

name: Alvar
label: Alvar

commanders_a: Ozdemiroglu Osman Pasha, Cigalazade Yusuf Sinan Pasha, Mehmed Pasha

losses_a: 500-1,000 casualties on one side (unassigned in the source)
result_basis: Hamza Mirza's ambush was beaten off and he fell back to the main army; the Ottomans went on to Tabriz, which surrendered on 25 September.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Alvar; Capture of Tabriz (1585)
note: Capture of Tabriz (1585), 23-25 September, followed without a separate battle and is not listed.

note: Akbar's worst defeat; Todar Mal's punitive expedition followed on 19 February. Khafi Khan's figure of 40,000 dead is much higher than Badauni's 8,000.

label: Herat (siege, 1587-1589)

sources: en.wikipedia Ali-Qoli Khan Shamlu; Abbas the Great; Savory

name: Bahrain (1602)

note: Asaf Khan was the son of Mirza Ghiyas Beg, a Persian from Tehran, and Nur Jahan's brother. The fight itself was small and the date is recalled from memory, not fetched; Nur Jahan, also Persian, stood behind the other side.

persian_force: Imam Quli Khan's Fars army (no details).

result_basis: The Safavids took outlying forts but not the city and abandoned the siege after Abbas's death in January 1629.
sources: en.wikipedia Safavid invasions of Basra
note: Basra was ruled by the autonomous Afrasiyab pashas, nominally Ottoman; the campaign followed a rising against Ali Pasha led by Ibn Ilayan.

name: Mahidasht
label: Mahidasht

iranian_note: Safavid field armies of Shah Safi's reign combined Turkic Qizilbash cavalry, Caucasian ghulams and Persian musketeers; proportions unknown.
result_basis: Husrev Pasha's army routed the Persians and held the field, then marched on and sacked Hamadan.
borderline: no separate Wikipedia article; named in the war article
doubt: Borderline: no separate Wikipedia article; named in the war article.
sources: en.wikipedia Ottoman-Safavid War (1623-1639); Encyclopaedia Iranica (Safi I)

label: Baghdad (siege, 1630)

iranian_note: No breakdown of the garrison is given; Safavid garrisons of the period mixed Persian tufangchis, Qizilbash and Caucasian ghulams.

name: Sihonda
label: Sihonda

sources: Wikipedia, Khan Jahan Lodi: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khan_Jahan_Lodi; Britannica, battle of Shihonda
note: Khan Jahan Lodi (Pir Khan) was an Afghan Lodi who had risen under Jahangir. The source gives the date as 1 February in the text and 3 February in the infobox.

name: Hooghly (siege, 1632)
label: Hooghly

note: Ya'rubid Oman. Persians and Portuguese each held a fort at Julfar and are listed together as defenders, though they were not allies.

label: Daulatabad

label: Erivan (siege, 1636)

sources: en.wikipedia Fall of Kandahar (1638); Mughal-Safavid War (1637-1638)
note: Ali Mardan Khan had handed the fortress to the Mughals without a fight on 11 March 1638; this entry is the field battle a month later.
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

result_basis: The Mughals mined and stormed the walls and Mihrab Khan surrendered the citadel on 3 September.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Bost (1638)

losses_b: more than 20,000 killed, many in the massacre after the fall

note: Rostom was a Muslim Georgian of the Safavid court installed by the shah in Kartli. Kingdoms of Kartli and Kakheti.

iranian_note: Garrison make-up unrecorded; the Safavid gunners are singled out in the accounts.

commanders_b: Prince Aurangzeb, Sadullah Khan, Jai Singh I

name: Khajwa

note: Aurangzeb was in overall command, but Mir Jumla (born Isfahan) led the decisive advance and Shaista Khan (Persian origin, grandson of Mirza Ghiyas Beg) held the reserve. Persian generals were thus among the principal commanders; the troops were mostly Hindustani and Deccani.

borderline: assaults on forts within a revolt, not a field battle

persian_force: The Shirvan army of Hajji Manuchehr Khan, 15,000-30,000 strong, with artillery and musketeers (no breakdown).
