commanders_b: Aimal Khan Mohmand; Darya Khan Afridi
result_basis: The Mughal army was ambushed in the gorge and largely destroyed; Muhammad Amin Khan escaped with a few followers.
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Ali Masjid (1672): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Ali_Masjid_(1672); Wikipedia, Aimal Khan Mohmand: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aimal_Khan_Mohmand; Sarkar, History of Aurangzib, vol. 3
note: The casualty and force figures on Wikipedia (240,000 Mughals, 40,000 killed) are inflated and are not used.

name: Kohat (1674)
label: Kohat
persian_state: Afridi Pashtuns v Bangash garrison of Kohat
commanders_a: Darya Khan Afridi; Tatar Khan Afridi (killed)
result_basis: The Afridi assault on the fort was repulsed with the loss of over 100 men and Tatar Khan.
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Kohat: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Kohat; Wikipedia, Darya Khan Afridi
note: Pashtun against Pashtun; Darya Khan attacked before Khushal Khan could join him.

name: Langarkot (c. 1674)
label: Langarkot
place: Langarkot fort, near Panjpir (Swabi), Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
result_basis: Khushal Khan's men surrounded and took the fort and the garrison commander was killed.
doubt: Traditional: known only from a doubtful tradition.
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Langarkot: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Langarkot
note: Known only from a thin Pashtun tradition; the Wikipedia article's casualty figures are inconsistent.

name: Nowshera (1674)
label: Nowshera
commanders_b: Khushal Khan Khattak; Darya Khan Afridi; Aimal Khan Mohmand
result_basis: The fort was plundered, the commander killed and the garrison suffered heavy losses.
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Nowshera (1674): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Nowshera_(1674); Wikipedia, Mughal-Afghan Wars
note: Khushal Khan Khattak, long a Mughal servant, joined the revolt here. Sources are thin and the date is not secure.

name: Gandab (Karapa Pass, 1674)
label: Gandab
place: Gandab valley and Karapa Pass, Mohmand country, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
allies_a: Rathor contingent sent by Jaswant Singh
result_basis: Shuja'at Khan was killed and his army was cut up in the pass; the Rathors saved the remnant.
sources: Wikipedia, Aimal Khan Mohmand: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aimal_Khan_Mohmand; Military Wiki, Sixth Afghan-Mughal War: https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Sixth_Afghan-Mughal_War_(1667%E2%80%931678); pashtunhistory.com, Karapa disaster
note: Shuja'at Khan was sent in November 1673 and the disaster was in February 1674, not 1673; Gandab and Karapa are two names for one campaign.

name: Jagdalak (1675)
label: Jagdalak
place: Jagdalak, between Kabul and Jalalabad, Afghanistan
commanders_b: not named in the sources seen
result_basis: The Afghans defeated Fidai Khan on his way to Peshawar until Aghar Khan relieved him.
sources: Military Wiki, Sixth Afghan-Mughal War: https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Sixth_Afghan-Mughal_War_(1667%E2%80%931678); Wikipedia, Aimal Khan Mohmand
note: The sources seen do not say which tribes fought; they are recorded only as Afghan tribal forces on the Kabul-Peshawar road.

name: Khapush (1675)
label: Khapush
side_b: Pashtun lashkar of Aimal Khan and Darya Khan
persian_state: Pashtun lashkar of Aimal Khan and Darya Khan
commanders_b: Aimal Khan Mohmand; Darya Khan Afridi
result_basis: The Mughal column was ambushed, Shamsher Khan was killed and Mukarram Khan retreated wounded to Bajaur.
sources: Wikipedia, Aimal Khan Mohmand: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aimal_Khan_Mohmand; Khushal Khan Khattak's verse (as cited by pashtunhistory.com)
note: The date and the exact identity of the battle (Khapush or Karapa) differ between sources.

name: Golconda (siege, 1687)
label: Golconda
date: c. January-21/22 September 1687 (about eight months; the fort fell when Abul Hasan surrendered)
war: Mughal conquest of Golconda (Aurangzeb's Deccan wars)
commanders_a: Aurangzeb; Prince Muhammad Azam; Ghazi ud-Din Khan Firuz Jang
commanders_b: Abdur Razzaq Lari (Persian from Lar; commander of the Golconda army and fort); Abul Hasan Qutb Shah (Tana Shah)
result_basis: Golconda fell to the Mughals when Abul Hasan surrendered in September 1687 after the fort's gate was opened by traitors, while Abdur Razzaq Lari fought on to the end (J. Sarkar, History of Aurangzib, vol. 5).
sources: J. Sarkar, History of Aurangzib, vol. 5; R. M. Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan, 1300-1761 (2005); Maasir-i Alamgiri (Saqi Mustaid Khan)
note: Abdur Razzaq Lari defended the Fateh Darwaza and was left for dead; Aurangzeb is said to have had him treated and offered him service, which he refused. His Persian origin (Lar in Fars) comes from his nisba and from Mughal accounts; I could not fetch a dedicated page. The Qutb Shahi dynasty itself was Qara Qoyunlu Turkmen (not Iranian).

name: Raigarh (siege, 1689)
label: Raigarh
date: siege from spring 1689; the fort fell about 3 November 1689 (dates not re-checked)
commanders_b: Suryaji Pisal (betrayed the fort); Yesubai (Sambhaji's widow, captured); Rajaram escaped before the end
result_basis: Zulfiqar Khan captured the fort and took Sambhaji's family, including the boy Shahu (Wikipedia, Zulfiqar Khan).
sources: Wikipedia, Zulfiqar Khan Nusrat Jung (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zulfiqar_Khan_Nusrat_Jung); Wikipedia list of battles involving the Mughal Empire; Sarkar, History of Aurangzib, vol. 5
note: Same origin question as for Jinji: an Iranian lineage by Wikipedia, but possibly Qaramanlu Turkmen. Dates from memory.

name: Khurma (1697)
label: Khurma (1697)
commanders_a: Shaykh Mani ibn Mughamis (Muntafiq), with Musha'sha' defectors
persian_force: A large Safavid force from Basra (no breakdown; the Basra garrison was largely Lur and Kohgiluyeh troops).
iranian_note: The Safavid troops in Basra came from Lorestan and Kohgiluyeh; inferred.
result_basis: Shaykh Mani defeated a large Safavid force and captured its general.
borderline: described in one sentence; site uncertain
doubt: Borderline: described in one sentence; site uncertain.
sources: en.wikipedia Safavid occupation of Basra
note: The Safavids evacuated Basra by sea on 9 March 1701 under blockade and mutiny, before an Ottoman army arrived (no battle).
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Basra (1697)
label: Basra (1697)
date: early 1697 (Basra occupied for the Shah on 26 March 1697)
persian_force: The Arab followers of the Musha'sha' vali of Arabestan (Khuzestan), a Safavid governor.
iranian_note: The fighters were Arabs of Khuzestan under the Safavid vali; Lur troops under Ali Mardan Khan came only afterwards.
result_basis: Farajollah Khan's Musha'sha' fighters defeated Shaykh Mani and drove him out of Basra, which was then held for the Shah.
borderline: the victor was a Safavid vassal vali with his own Arab tribesmen; the fight is not separately named
doubt: Borderline: the victor was a Safavid vassal vali with his own Arab tribesmen; the fight is not separately named.
sources: en.wikipedia Safavid occupation of Basra
note: The Muntafiq had held Basra since 1695. Ali Mardan Khan, chief of the Fayli Lurs, then came as governor with an army from Lorestan.
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Jinji (siege, 1690-98)
label: Jinji
commanders_a: Zulfiqar Khan Nusrat Jung (main commander throughout); Kam Bakhsh; Asad Khan; Daud Khan Panni; Dalpat Rao Bundela
commanders_b: Rajaram I; Dhanaji Jadhav; Santaji Ghorpade
result_basis: The fortress capitulated on 8 January 1698 (renamed Nusratgarh), though Rajaram had escaped.
sources: Wikipedia, Siege of Jinji (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Jinji); Zulfiqar Khan Nusrat Jung (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zulfiqar_Khan_Nusrat_Jung); Irvine, Later Mughals
note: The origin is disputed: Wikipedia calls Zulfiqar Khan's patrilineal line Iranian (great-grandfather beglar begi of Safavid Shirvan, executed c. 1600 by Shah Abbas; grandfather Khanlar moved to India), but the Safavid Zulfiqar family is usually placed in the Qaramanlu tribe, a Turkmen Qizilbash tribe, which BRIEF3 does not count as Iranian.

name: Kandahar (1709)
label: Kandahar (1709)
commanders_b: Gurgin Khan (Giorgi XI of Kartli, killed)
persian_force: Gurgin Khan's escort and the Georgian garrison of Kandahar; most of the Georgian troops were away on campaign.
iranian_note: The Safavid force at Kandahar was mainly Georgian soldiers of Gurgin Khan.
result_basis: Mirwais's Ghilzai killed Gurgin Khan in his camp outside the city and destroyed the Georgian garrison left in Kandahar.
borderline: a surprise attack and massacre more than a battle
doubt: Borderline: a surprise attack and massacre more than a battle.
sources: en.wikipedia Hotak revolt; Lockhart, The Fall of the Safavi Dynasty
note: Ghilzai (Hotak) Afghans of Kandahar; the start of the Hotaki state.
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Kandahar (siege, 1711)
label: Kandahar (siege, 1711)
commanders_b: Kay Khosrow (Kaikhosro of Kartli, killed), Prince Alexander of Kartli (killed)
persian_force: About 30,000 Georgian and Persian troops with contingents from Khorasan, Herat and Kerman.
iranian_note: The Khorasan, Herat and Kerman contingents were largely Persian-speaking, beside Kay Khosrow's Georgians; no figures.
losses_b: almost the whole army; only about 700 escaped
result_basis: The besiegers, harassed by the Baloch, retreated on 26 October 1711 and the Afghans destroyed the retreating army.
sources: en.wikipedia Kaikhosro of Kartli; Lockhart, The Fall of the Safavi Dynasty
note: Kay Khosrow had campaigned against Kandahar since November 1709; his death is dated 27 September or 26 October 1711.
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Shamakhi (siege, 1711)
label: Shamakhi (siege, 1711)
commanders_b: Haji Davud, Ali Sultan of Elisu, Ahmed Khan of Kaytag, Surkhay Khan
persian_force: The Safavid garrison of Shamakhi (no details).
iranian_note: Shirvan's garrisons were drawn from the mainly Turkic-speaking province; inferred.
result_basis: Haji Davud's siege of Shamakhi failed, although he had beaten Safavid garrisons in the field.
borderline: no separate article; briefly described
doubt: Borderline: no separate article; briefly described.
sources: en.wikipedia Lezgin campaign into Shirvan
note: Lezgin and other Sunni highlanders of Dagestan and northern Shirvan. A second attempt in 1712 is described contradictorily and is not listed; a first raid stormed Shamakhi in 1707.
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Bahrain (1717)
label: Bahrain (1717)
date: 1717 (third Omani attempt; the first two had failed)
war: Omani-Safavid conflict in the Persian Gulf
persian_force: The Safavid garrison and the islanders; a later Persian relief army with many Bedouins was destroyed.
iranian_note: The defenders were mostly the Arab (Baharna) islanders with a small Safavid garrison; inferred.
losses_b: unknown (heavy killing and plunder, per al-Bahrani)
result_basis: The Omanis blockaded the island and took the fortress by force.
sources: en.wikipedia 1717 Omani invasion of Bahrain
note: Ya'rubid Oman (Sultan ibn Saif II); Wikipedia names Al Bin Ali mercenaries. Bahrain returned to Persian rule by treaty after a payment; the year is sometimes given as 1717-1718.
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Kafir Qala (1719)
label: Kafir Qala (1719)
war: Afghan rebellions (1709-1726): Abdali revolt of Herat
commanders_a: Mohammad Zaman Khan, Asadullah Khan (Abdali of Herat)
persian_force: Safi Quli Khan's army of Khorasan, 30,000-35,000 strong, with an artillery train under European officers.
iranian_note: A Khorasan provincial army: Persian musketeers, Qizilbash and Kurdish tribal horse; inferred, no breakdown in the sources used.
result_basis: The Abdali routed the Persian army, killed its commander and took its baggage train.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kafir Qala (1719); Lockhart, The Fall of the Safavi Dynasty
note: Abdali (Sadozai) Afghans of Herat. The battle secured Herat's independence from the Safavids.
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Dilaram
label: Dilaram
persian_state: Hotak dynasty v Abdali Afghans of Herat
result_basis: Asadullah Khan was shot in the back and about 3,000 of his Abdali men were killed; Mahmud Hotak's Ghilzais held the field.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Dilaram; Axworthy, M., Sword of Persia (2006); Lockhart, L., The Fall of the Safavi Dynasty (1958)
note: A Pashtun against Pashtun battle between the two great tribal confederations of the day, the Ghilzai Hotaks and the Abdalis (later Durranis); it left Mahmud free to invade Kerman in 1721. The Wikipedia infobox calls Asadullah's side the Sadozai Sultanate of Herat, but the article text says Abdali.
qbasis: Both armies were Pashtun: Mahmud Hotak's Ghilzais of Kandahar and Asadullah's Abdalis (Wikipedia 'Battle of Dilaram').

name: Kerman (siege, 1721)
label: Kerman (siege, 1721)
date: 1721 (town taken; citadel held out by October 1721)
war: Afghan rebellions (1709-1726): Mahmud Hotak's invasion of Persia
commanders_a: the Safavid commander of the citadel (unnamed in the sources used)
persian_force: The Safavid garrison of Kerman citadel (no breakdown).
iranian_note: A local garrison of Kerman, a Persian-speaking province; inferred.
result_basis: The Ghilzai took the town but failed to storm the citadel, losing about 1,500 men, and moved on.
borderline: no separate article
doubt: Borderline: no separate article.
sources: en.wikipedia Mahmud Hotak; Lockhart, The Fall of the Safavi Dynasty
note: Ghilzai (Hotak) Afghans of Kandahar. Mahmud had occupied Kerman town before, in 1719-1720. A further attempt on the reinforced city late in 1721 or early in 1722 also failed (included here).
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Kura River (1721)
label: Kura River (1721)
commanders_b: the beglerbegis of Ganja and Erivan
persian_force: The provincial armies of Ganja and Erivan, about 30,000 men (60,000 in the infobox).
iranian_note: Ganja and Erivan levies were mainly Turkic-speaking Qizilbash tribesmen; inferred.
result_basis: Haji Davud's night attack on the Safavid camp routed the relief army, much of which fled.
borderline: no separate article; site not identified
doubt: Borderline: no separate article; site not identified.
sources: en.wikipedia Lezgin campaign into Shirvan
note: Haji Davud then took Barda and besieged Ganja, withdrawing as Vakhtang VI of Kartli marched to its relief (no battle, not listed).
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Shamakhi (siege, 1721)
label: Shamakhi (siege, 1721)
commanders_a: Haji Davud, Surkhay Khan of Ghazikumukh
persian_force: The governor's garrison and the Shia townsmen of Shamakhi (no breakdown).
iranian_note: Shirvan's Shia population and garrisons were mainly Turkic-speaking, with some Persian (Tat) speakers; inferred.
losses_b: 4,000-5,000 Shia inhabitants killed, with the governor; also Russian merchants
result_basis: Shamakhi fell when its Sunni inhabitants opened a gate to the besiegers, and the city was sacked.
sources: en.wikipedia Sack of Shamakhi; Lezgin campaign into Shirvan
note: Lezgins and other Dagestani highlanders. The killing of Russian merchants was Peter the Great's pretext for the war of 1722-1723.
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Yazd (1722)
label: Yazd (1722)
date: early 1722 (between the Kerman siege and Gulnabad)
war: Afghan rebellions (1709-1726): Mahmud Hotak's invasion of Persia
persian_force: The garrison and townsmen of Yazd (no details).
iranian_note: A local garrison of a Persian-speaking city; inferred.
result_basis: The garrison of Yazd beat off Mahmud's attack and he marched on towards Isfahan.
borderline: a brief repulse, no separate article
doubt: Borderline: a brief repulse, no separate article.
sources: en.wikipedia Mahmud Hotak; Lockhart, The Fall of the Safavi Dynasty
note: Ghilzai (Hotak) Afghans. Yazd beat off a second Hotaki attempt later in the 1720s (date not given; not listed).
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Gulnabad
label: Gulnabad
war: Afghan rebellions (1709-1726): Mahmud Hotak's invasion of Persia
commanders_a: Mahmud Hotak, Ashraf Hotak, Amanullah Khan, Nasrullah
commanders_b: Mohammad Qoli Khan (grand vizier), Ali Mardan Khan (vali of Lorestan), Rustam Khan (killed), Philippe Colombe (killed), Sayyid Abdollah (vali of Arabistan)
persian_force: 42,000-50,000 men with 24 guns: the royal guard and ghulams (Rustam Khan), Fayli Lur horse under Ali Mardan Khan, the Arab horse of the vali of Arabistan, Persian musketeers and the artillery under the French gunner Colombe.
iranian_note: The wings were led by the vali of Lorestan (Lur cavalry) and the vali of Arabistan (Arab cavalry); the centre held Persian infantry and the royal ghulams (Lockhart).
strength_a: 10,000-11,000 (up to 18,000 in some accounts), with 100 zamburaks
result_basis: The Afghans routed the Persian army, which fled back to Isfahan leaving its guns.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Gulnabad; Lockhart, The Fall of the Safavi Dynasty; Axworthy, The Sword of Persia
note: Ghilzai (Hotak) Afghans of Kandahar; Mahmud was not yet ruler of Iran, so the battle is not civil.
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Isfahan (siege, 1722)
label: Isfahan (siege, 1722)
commanders_b: Shah Sultan Husayn, Ahmad Agha (commander of the defence), Tahmasp Mirza (escaped to raise relief)
persian_force: The remnants of the Gulnabad army, the royal guard and ghulams, and the armed townsmen of Isfahan; relief attempts failed and Vakhtang VI of Kartli refused to come.
iranian_note: The defenders were mostly the people and militia of Isfahan with the remains of the royal army; inferred.
losses_b: about 80,000 or more inhabitants died, mostly of famine
result_basis: Famine forced Shah Sultan Husayn to capitulate on 23 October 1722 and Mahmud entered Isfahan.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Isfahan; Mahmud Hotak; Lockhart, The Fall of the Safavi Dynasty
note: Ghilzai (Hotak) Afghans. The shah abdicated in Mahmud's favour; Mahmud entered the city on 25 October. Tahmasp escaped with about 600 men to Qazvin.
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Julfa (1722)
label: Julfa (1722)
persian_force: Several hundred armed Armenian townsmen of Julfa, loyal to the Shah, who had been largely disarmed by the Persian authorities.
iranian_note: The defenders were the Armenian townsmen of New Julfa.
result_basis: After hours of resistance the Armenian quarter fell to the Afghans and was plundered.
borderline: the defenders were loyal townsmen rather than Safavid troops
doubt: Borderline: the defenders were loyal townsmen rather than Safavid troops.
sources: en.wikipedia Capture of Julfa
note: Ghilzai (Hotak) Afghans. Julfa paid an indemnity of 70,000 tomans; Farahabad was then abandoned without a fight.
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Qazvin (1723)
label: Qazvin (1723)
war: Hotaki rule in Iran: risings against the Afghans
persian_force: Side A: the armed population of Qazvin; side B: the Ghilzai garrison Mahmud had sent after Tahmasp.
iranian_note: Persian- and Turkic-speaking townsmen against Pashto-speaking Ghilzai; both sides were mostly Iranian-speaking.
result_basis: The townsmen rose, killed many of the Afghan garrison and drove the rest out of the city.
borderline: an urban rising against a garrison
doubt: Borderline: an urban rising against a garrison.
sources: en.wikipedia Mahmud Hotak; Lockhart, The Fall of the Safavi Dynasty
note: Civil because the Hotaki were ruling Iran from Isfahan after October 1722. Tahmasp II had fled before the Afghans arrived.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Rasht (1723)
label: Rasht (1723)
persian_force: About 15,000 men, mostly untrained and poorly armed peasant levies raised by the governor of Gilan.
iranian_note: The levies were Gilani peasants (Gilaki speakers).
result_basis: A Russian sortie broke the Persian force besieging the Russian barracks and the Russians held Rasht.
sources: en.wikipedia Peter the Great's capture of Rasht; Russo-Persian War (1722-1723)
note: The Russians had entered Rasht in late 1722 as nominal helpers; the date may be Julian (Old Style).
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Baku (siege, 1723)
label: Baku (siege, 1723)
date: July 1723 (the city capitulated on 26 July Julian, 6 August Gregorian)
persian_force: The garrison and townsmen of Baku (no details).
iranian_note: Baku's population was Tat (Persian-speaking) and Turkic; inferred.
result_basis: After a naval bombardment and landing the garrison capitulated and the Russians took Baku.
borderline: no separate article
doubt: Borderline: no separate article.
sources: en.wikipedia Russo-Persian War (1722-1723); Lockhart, The Fall of the Safavi Dynasty
note: Wikipedia's war article dates the capture to 26 June 1723 (7 July N.S.); Russian accounts give the capitulation as 26 July 1723 (Old Style). Derbent (August 1722) surrendered without a fight and is excluded.
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Shiraz (siege, 1723-1724)
label: Shiraz (siege, 1723-1724)
war: Hotaki rule in Iran: conquest of Fars
persian_force: Side A: Ghilzai Afghans with Sunni Dargazini settlers from Isfahan; side B: the Safavid garrison and people of Shiraz.
iranian_note: Pashto-speaking Afghans against Persian-speaking Shirazis.
losses_b: up to 100,000 inhabitants said to have died, mostly of famine (an exaggerated figure)
result_basis: Shiraz was starved into surrender after a nine-month siege and sacked.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Shiraz
note: Civil because the Hotaki were ruling Iran from Isfahan. The capitulation is also put in mid-1724.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Erivan (siege, 1724)
label: Erivan (siege, 1724)
date: spring to summer 1724 (the city fell on 7 June and the citadel by 28 September at the latest)
commanders_a: Ahmed Pasha (the Ottoman serasker, as given in Wikipedia)
persian_force: The Safavid garrison of Erivan with the Armenian and Muslim townsmen (no breakdown).
iranian_note: The defenders were mostly Armenian and Turkic-speaking inhabitants and Qizilbash garrison troops; inferred.
result_basis: Erivan capitulated after a siege of more than three months.
sources: en.wikipedia Ottoman-Hotaki War (1726-1727); Armenian liberation struggle (1722-1730); Abraham of Erevan, History of the Wars
note: Defended in the name of Tahmasp II's remnant Safavid state. Dates differ: Wikipedia gives 28 September 1724, Abraham of Erevan 7 June (city) and 20 August (citadel).
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Hamadan (siege, 1724)
label: Hamadan (siege, 1724)
date: 1724 (the city fell after a siege of about two months)
persian_force: The garrison and armed townsmen of Hamadan, loyal to Tahmasp II (no details).
iranian_note: Townsmen of Hamadan, Persian- and Turkic-speaking; inferred.
result_basis: Hamadan was stormed by the Ottomans after a hard siege and many of its defenders were killed.
borderline: no Wikipedia article; dates not verified
doubt: Borderline: no Wikipedia article; dates not verified.
sources: Lockhart, The Fall of the Safavi Dynasty; Longrigg, Four Centuries of Modern Iraq
note: Kermanshah had fallen to the Ottomans in 1723 without a recorded battle (excluded).
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Tabriz (siege, 1724)
label: Tabriz (siege, 1724)
commanders_a: unnamed (the townsmen and Safavid loyalists of Tabriz)
persian_force: The armed townsmen of Tabriz with local Safavid loyalist troops (no details).
iranian_note: Tabriz was largely Turkic-speaking by the 18th century; inferred.
result_basis: The Ottomans failed to take the city and retreated to Tasuj at the end of September.
sources: en.wikipedia Ottoman-Hotaki War (1726-1727)
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Tabriz (siege, 1725)
label: Tabriz (siege, 1725)
commanders_b: unnamed (the townsmen and Safavid loyalists of Tabriz)
persian_force: The armed townsmen of Tabriz with local Safavid loyalist troops (no details).
iranian_note: Tabriz was largely Turkic-speaking; inferred.
result_basis: The reinforced Ottoman army took Tabriz after hard fighting.
sources: en.wikipedia Ottoman-Hotaki War (1726-1727); Lockhart, The Fall of the Safavi Dynasty
note: The commander is named from Lockhart; Wikipedia gives none.
qbasis: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

name: Mashhad (siege, 1726)
label: Mashhad (siege, 1726)
war: Rise of Nader: Tahmasp II's recovery of Khorasan
persian_force: Side A: Nader's Afshar and Kurdish tribesmen of northern Khorasan with Tahmasp's Qajar and other Qizilbash followers; side B: Malik Mahmud's Sistani and Khorasani troops.
iranian_note: Nader's early following was Afshar (Turkic) and Kurdish; Malik Mahmud's men were Persian-speaking Sistanis and Khorasanis.
result_basis: Mashhad fell to the besiegers when a commander of the garrison opened a gate.
borderline: no separate article
doubt: Borderline: no separate article.
sources: en.wikipedia Persian-Afghan Wars; Axworthy, The Sword of Persia
note: Malik Mahmud, who claimed descent from the Saffarids, had ruled Khorasan from Mashhad since 1722; counted as civil (an Iran-seated local ruler).

name: Anjudan
label: Anjudan
persian_force: Ashraf's Ghilzai Afghan army of 12,000 (Axworthy) to 17,000 (Lockhart), with camel-mounted zamburak swivel guns but no artillery.
iranian_note: The Hotaki field army was a Ghilzai (Pashto-speaking) tribal force.
losses_b: about 12,000 killed (18,000 dead and 20,000 deserted in the infobox)
result_basis: Ottoman assaults failed, the Kurdish contingent defected and Ahmad Pasha withdrew, abandoning his guns and baggage.
sources: en.wikipedia Ottoman-Hotaki War (1726-1727); Lockhart; Axworthy, The Sword of Persia
note: Wikipedia places the battle near Khorramabad; Turkish sources call it Ancidan (Anjudan), between Hamadan and Isfahan. About 20,000 Kurds under Bebek Suleiman Oglu changed sides; a 6,000-strong Ottoman scouting force had been destroyed before the battle.
qbasis: Hotaki: an Iranian-led state

name: Sangan
label: Sangan

iranian_note: The sources name Kurdish, Afghan and Qizilbash units; Axworthy stresses the Afghan and Persian musketeer element. The Iranian-speaking share may have been a majority.
strength_b: about 75,000 on the field (up to 300,000 with camp followers), 2,000 elephants
losses_a: about 1,100 (400 killed, 700 wounded); up to 2,500 killed in other figures
result_basis: In under three hours Nader's army destroyed the Mughal forces that attacked it, and Muhammad Shah surrendered.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Karnal; Nader Shah's invasion of India; Axworthy, The Sword of Persia
note: Heraclius (Erekle) II of Kakheti served with a Georgian contingent. The massacre in Delhi on 22 March 1739 followed a riot and is excluded.
qbasis: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian

name: Bukhara (1740)
label: Bukhara (1740)
commanders_a: Nader Shah, Reza Qoli Mirza, Lotf Ali Khan
persian_force: Nader's guard of 3,000 and the main army with artillery (no breakdown); 8,000 under Reza Qoli Mirza were sent to Charjuy.
iranian_note: Inferred.
result_basis: Nader's guard and artillery broke Abu'l-Fayz Khan's army, which fell back on Bukhara, and the khan sued for peace.
borderline: a series of fights (Qatartut, near Bukhara) grouped as one entry; dates not given
doubt: Borderline: a series of fights (Qatartut, near Bukhara) grouped as one entry; dates not given.

note: Bukhara Khanate (Ashtarkhanid). Lotf Ali Khan also beat a 20,000-strong force of Samarkand, Bukhara and Kokand; Samarkand was then taken almost unopposed (not listed). About 30,000 Uzbeks were enrolled in Nader's army.
qbasis: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian

name: Khanqah (siege, 1740)
label: Khanqah (siege, 1740)
persian_force: Nader's army with mortars, howitzers and jazayerchi (no breakdown).
iranian_note: Inferred.
result_basis: Besieged in Khanqah, Ilbars Khan surrendered and was executed with more than twenty of his amirs.
sources: en.wikipedia Nader Shah's Central Asian campaign; Battle of Pitnak
note: Khiva itself then submitted without a fight.
qbasis: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian

name: Pitnak
label: Pitnak

iranian_note: The named units (Afshar, Marv and Atak horse) were mostly Turkic-speaking tribesmen of Khorasan; the share is uncertain and may have been larger.
strength_b: about 30,000 Uzbek and Turkmen horsemen (including 6,000 Yomut)
result_basis: Nader's cavalry routed the Khivan army, killing or capturing many in the pursuit.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Pitnak; Nader Shah's Central Asian campaign

name: Andalal
label: Andalal
date: late August to 28 September 1741 (Aimaki gorge ambush on 12 September)
place: Andalal and the Aimaki gorge, Gunib district, Dagestan, Russia
commanders_a: Murtazali Khan (son of Surkhay), Ahmed Khan Mekhtuly, Qadi Pir Muhammad
commanders_b: Nader Shah, Lotf Ali Khan, Haydar Bek
persian_force: Nader's army of 100,000-150,000 at its height in Dagestan: levies from all Iran, Uzbek and Tatar auxiliaries, mounted and foot tofangchi musketeers, Georgian and other vassal contingents; the units destroyed were Haydar Bek's 4,000 and Lotf Ali Khan's 6,000.
iranian_note: Wikipedia names levies from all Iran with Uzbek, Tatar and Georgian contingents; no proportions.
losses_b: 30,000 men, 33,000 animals and 79 guns (infobox); about 9,000 of the two ambushed contingents

borderline: a withdrawal under harassment rather than a single battle
doubt: Traditional: The great set-piece battle of Dagestani tradition is not described in contemporary sources, which show a harried withdrawal with an ambush in the Aimaki gorge; the losses (30,000 men, 79 guns) rest on weak sourcing. Borderline: a withdrawal under harassment rather than a single battle.
sources: en.wikipedia Withdrawal through Andalal (1741); Gazikumukh Khanate; Nader Shah's Dagestan campaign
note: Avars and Laks of Andalal and Gazi-Kumukh. Fights at Sogratl, Megeb, Chokh and Oboch are part of this entry. Surkhay Khan had surrendered to Nader in August 1741.
qbasis: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian

name: Sohar (siege, 1742-1743)
label: Sohar (siege, 1742-1743)

commanders_b: Ahmad bin Said al-Busaidi (governor of Sohar); Imam Sultan bin Murshid (mortally wounded under the walls)

iranian_note: Troops from Fars and the Gulf coast; inferred.
result_basis: After about nine months Ahmad bin Said came to terms, keeping Sohar as governor under Persian tribute without the town being taken.
sources: en.wikipedia Ahmad bin Said al-Busaidi; Saif bin Sultan II
note: Ya'rubid Oman. Sources differ: one says the Persians took neither Sohar nor Muscat, another that Ahmad negotiated a surrender. The Persians took the Muscat forts by a ruse in 1743 (no battle, excluded); the killing of the last Persians at Barka (1747) was a massacre at a banquet (excluded).
qbasis: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian

label: Basra (siege, 1743)

iranian_note: Inferred.
result_basis: The siege was still in progress after Mosul and ended with the peace negotiated with Ahmad Pasha of Baghdad, the city untaken.
borderline: mentioned only in passing; extent of fighting unknown
doubt: Borderline: mentioned only in passing; extent of fighting unknown.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Mosul (1743); Longrigg, Four Centuries of Modern Iraq

label: Kirkuk (siege, 1743)

borderline: listed only in the war article; details of the fighting not given

iranian_note: Nader's army of 1743; proportions unknown.

commanders_b: Ali Muhammad Khan Rohilla; Rohilla generals including Hafiz Rahmat Khan
result_basis: The Rohilla invaders were beaten by the combined Kumaon and Garhwal armies and had to sue for peace after sacking Almora.

note: Ali Muhammad Khan was a Hindu-born adoptee of the Pashtun Daud Khan Barech and his army was mainly Pashtun (Rohilla) mercenaries; the site and exact year are weakly sourced (one Wikipedia summary).
qbasis: The Rohilla army was drawn from Pashtun (Afghan) settlers of Rohilkhand under Ali Muhammad Khan (Wikipedia 'Rohilla'; Iqbal Husain).

label: Shah Bagh (1744)

faction_b: Mohammad Taqi Khan Shirazi (rebel governor of Fars)
persian_force: Side A: about 30,000 royal troops under Allahverdi Khan; side B: 10,000-12,000 of Taqi Khan's Fars army.
iranian_note: Fars troops on the rebel side were largely Persian-speaking; the loyal army was mixed; inferred.
result_basis: After several hours' fighting Taqi Khan's force, with heavy losses, retreated into the fortress of Shiraz.
sources: en.wikipedia Afsharid conquests in the Persian Gulf and Oman; Mohammad Taqi Khan Shirazi's Rebellion
note: Before this, Taqi Khan had ambushed Muhammad Husain Khan Qirkhli's 7,000 men in the streets of Shiraz after two or three indecisive fights (not listed).
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

label: Shiraz (siege, 1744)

commanders_a: Allahverdi Khan Kirkhli, with reinforcements sent by Nader
persian_force: Side A: Allahverdi Khan's royal army with reinforcements; side B: Taqi Khan's Fars troops and the townsmen.
iranian_note: Inferred.
losses_b: unknown (20,000 casualties in the infobox, side unclear)
result_basis: A defending commander opened a gate, Shiraz fell and was sacked, and Taqi Khan fled.
sources: en.wikipedia Afsharid conquests in the Persian Gulf and Oman; Mohammad Taqi Khan Shirazi's Rebellion
note: Taqi Khan was later caught and mutilated. The revolt had begun at Bandar Abbas, where the fleet commander Rustam Khan was killed by his own officers late in 1743 (a mutiny, excluded).
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Kars (siege, 1744)
label: Kars (siege, 1744)
persian_force: Nader's army with 16 heavy guns (no breakdown).
iranian_note: Nader's army of 1744; proportions unknown.
losses_b: about 1,700 killed; nine field guns abandoned
result_basis: After 73 days and a successful Ottoman sortie on 18-19 September, Nader raised the siege on 9 October.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Kars (1744)
note: Nader withdrew to deal with a revolt in Dagestan.
qbasis: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian

name: Aghsu (1745)
label: Aghsu (1745)

persian_force: Nasrollah Mirza's army of Shirvan and Azerbaijan (no breakdown).
iranian_note: A provincial army of the Turkic-speaking Caucasus provinces; inferred.
result_basis: Muhammad Khan retreated to Gazi-Kumukh and the Persians recovered Derbent and the Kura country.

sources: en.wikipedia Gazikumukh Khanate

name: Bangarh (siege, 1745)
label: Bangarh

war: Mughal expedition against Ali Muhammad Khan Rohilla (1745)
place: Bangarh fort, Rohilkhand, Uttar Pradesh, India
commanders_a: Muhammad Shah; Qamar-ud-Din Khan; Safdar Jang
result_basis: Ali Muhammad Khan, blockaded in Bangarh, surrendered, was taken to Delhi, then pardoned and made governor of Sirhind.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rohilla; Husain, Iqbal, The Rise and Decline of the Ruhela Chieftaincy in 18th Century India (1994)
note: The emperor took the field himself against the rising Rohilla state; the site (Bangarh) and the length of the siege are from memory and a single summary, so the entry is uncertain.
qbasis: Ali Muhammad Khan's Rohilla army was Pashtun (Afghan) in composition and tradition (Iqbal Husain; Wikipedia 'Rohilla').

name: Kars (1745)
label: Kars (1745)
persian_force: About 60,000, including 40,000 elite cavalry of the Khorasan army (savaran-e sepah-e Khorasan), jazayerchi musketeers, artillery and fowj infantry.
iranian_note: The Khorasan cavalry was largely Turkic and Kurdish tribesmen with Afghans; proportions unknown.
result_basis: After ten days of fighting Nader's jazayerchi and cavalry broke the Ottoman army, which disintegrated and lost its commander.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kars (1745); Ottoman-Persian War (1743-1746); Axworthy, The Sword of Persia
note: Named after Kars, the Ottoman base; Wikipedia's account places both camps near Yeghevard, where the battle of 1735 was also fought, so the site is uncertain. The Treaty of Kerden (4 September 1746) followed.
qbasis: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian

name: Mosul (1745)
label: Mosul (1745)
persian_force: Nasrollah Mirza's detached army (no breakdown).
iranian_note: Inferred.
result_basis: Nasrollah Mirza inflicted a crushing defeat on Abdullah Pasha's army and its Kurdish auxiliaries.
borderline: described in passing; site not named
doubt: Borderline: described in passing; site not named.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kars (1745)
note: Abdullah Pasha had been joined by local Ottoman troops and Kurdish tribal auxiliaries. Nasrollah's letter reporting the victory reached Nader on the last day of the battle of Kars.
qbasis: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian

name: Lahore (Shalimar Gardens, 1748)
label: Lahore
date: 11 January 1748 (Wikipedia, Ahmad Shah Durrani; older accounts give 12 January)
war: Ahmad Shah Durrani's first invasion of India (1747-1748)
commanders_a: Ahmad Shah Durrani; Jahan Khan Popalzai
result_basis: Shah Nawaz Khan was beaten at the Shalimar Gardens; his own Afghan regiments went over to Ahmad Shah and he fled to Delhi.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Shah_Durrani; Ganda Singh, Ahmad Shah Durrani: Father of Modern Afghanistan (1959); Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: Opening battle of Ahmad Shah's first invasion; the governor's Afghan regiments (a Pashtun contingent on B) defected during the fight.
qbasis: Ahmad Shah Abdali, a Pashtun (Popalzai Durrani) ruler, led an army of Durrani and Ghilzai Afghans (Ganda Singh; Wikipedia 'Ahmad Shah Durrani').

name: Manupur
label: Manupur
date: 11 March 1748 (Wikipedia/Sarkar; some accounts place the fighting between late February and early March)
war: Ahmad Shah Durrani's first invasion of India (1747-1748)
commanders_a: Ahmad Shah Durrani; Jahan Khan Popalzai; Shah Wali Khan
commanders_b: Wazir Qamar-ud-Din Khan (killed); Safdar Jang; Mu'in al-Mulk (Mir Mannu); Prince Ahmad Shah Bahadur
result_basis: A powder explosion in the Afghan camp killed about 1,000 men and Ahmad Shah, outnumbered about five to one, withdrew toward the Indus while the Mughals held the field.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Shah_Durrani; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34); Ganda Singh, Ahmad Shah Durrani: Father of Modern Afghanistan (1959)
note: Mughal wazir Qamar-ud-Din was killed by a cannonball during the battle; Mir Mannu's pursuit of the retreating Afghans won him Lahore. Ahmad Shah's army was about 12,000 against 60,000-70,000 (Wikipedia).
qbasis: Ahmad Shah Abdali (Pashtun) led an almost wholly Afghan army (Sarkar; Ganda Singh).

name: Soltaniyeh (1748)
label: Soltaniyeh (1748)

persian_force: Both armies were remnants of Nader Shah's host: Afshar and other Turkic Qizilbash tribesmen with Kurdish horse and Afghan and Uzbek contingents; Ebrahim drew on the Afshar troops of Azerbaijan.
iranian_note: Nader's successor armies were led by Turkic (Afshar, Qajar) tribal khans with Kurdish, Afghan and Uzbek contingents; proportions are not recorded.

borderline: no article and no conventional name; the encounter is described only as Adel Shah's defeat by Ebrahim
doubt: Borderline: no article and no conventional name; the encounter is described only as Adel Shah's defeat by Ebrahim.
sources: en.wikipedia Adel Shah; Ebrahim Afshar; Perry in Cambridge History of Iran vol. 7
note: The site is not named in the Wikipedia articles; Zanjan-Soltaniyeh is the usual placing of Adel's defeat in the older literature and is given as approximate.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

label: Herat (siege, 1749-50)
commanders_b: the Afsharid governor of Herat (not named in the sources used)
persian_force: The Persian garrison left by Nader Shah's successors in Herat; its composition is not recorded (Afsharid garrisons were Qizilbash Turkic and Kurdish troops with local levies).
iranian_note: Inferred from the usual make-up of Afsharid garrisons; the sources used say nothing on this garrison.
result_basis: Herat fell to Ahmad Shah after a long siege.
borderline: the Persian character of the Herat garrison after Nader's death is not well documented
doubt: Borderline: the Persian character of the Herat garrison after Nader's death is not well documented.

name: Semnan (1749)
label: Semnan (1749)

iranian_note: Shahrokh was raised by Turkic, Kurdish and Arab chiefs at Mashhad; Ebrahim's Afghan and Uzbek troops are named in the sources.
result_basis: Ebrahim withdrew from the field when his army fell into turmoil and part of it deserted to Shahrokh; he was later captured at Qal'a-ye Qalapur.
borderline: no article; known only as the fighting near Semnan
doubt: Borderline: no article; known only as the fighting near Semnan.
sources: en.wikipedia Ebrahim Afshar; Adel Shah
note: Ebrahim was blinded by Musa Khan and died on the way to Mashhad.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Daunri (Badaun, 1749)
label: Daunri
place: Daunri (Dauri), near Badaun, Uttar Pradesh, India
persian_state: Rohilla chiefs v Bangash Nawabs of Farrukhabad
commanders_a: Dunde (Dundi) Khan; Hafiz Rahmat Khan; Sa'dullah Khan
result_basis: Qaim Khan Bangash was killed in the battle and his army broke, after which Farrukhabad was annexed to Awadh and plundered.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Khan_Bangash; Husain, Iqbal, The Rise and Decline of the Ruhela Chieftaincy in 18th Century India (1994); Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: A Pashtun against Pashtun battle: the Rohillas against the Bangash Nawab of Farrukhabad, a conflict Safdar Jang of Awadh exploited to seize Farrukhabad. Wikipedia's Ahmad Khan Bangash article calls it the Battle of Badaun and does not use 'Daunri'.
qbasis: Both armies were Pashtun: Rohilla Barech and Yusufzai chiefs against Qaim Khan Bangash, a Pashtun (Iqbal Husain; Wikipedia 'Ahmad Khan Bangash').

label: Turbat-i-Shaikh Jam

sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Turbat-i-Shaikh Jam
note: The Khanate of Kalat (Baloch) fought as Ahmad Shah's vassal; recorded as 'Kalat' (a new short name). The fortress of Nun surrendered after Mir Alam's death.
qbasis: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian

label: Golpayegan (1750)

faction_a: Karim Khan Zand and Zakariya Khan
persian_force: Karim Khan's Zand and Lak tribesmen and Zakariya Khan's men against Bakhtiari tribesmen.
iranian_note: Both sides were Lak, Lur and Bakhtiari tribal forces.
result_basis: Karim Khan and Zakariya Khan defeated the Bakhtiaris and took the town, though Ali Mardan recovered it soon after.
borderline: no article; mentioned in the campaign article
doubt: Borderline: no article; mentioned in the campaign article.
sources: en.wikipedia Zand campaigns in Western Iran

label: Murcheh Khort (1750)

faction_a: Abu'l-Fath Khan Bakhtiari, Afsharid governor of Isfahan
persian_force: The army of Isfahan (largely Haft Lang Bakhtiari) against Ali Mardan's Chahar Lang Bakhtiari tribesmen.
iranian_note: Both sides were Bakhtiari tribal forces with townsmen of Isfahan.
result_basis: Ali Mardan Khan was defeated and driven off in his first attempt on Isfahan.
borderline: mentioned as a battle only in the background of the Isfahan articles
doubt: Borderline: mentioned as a battle only in the background of the Isfahan articles.
sources: en.wikipedia Fall of Isfahan (1750); Zand campaigns in Western Iran
note: Ali Mardan then allied with Karim Khan Zand and Zakariya Khan and took Isfahan in May 1750.

name: Isfahan (siege, 1750)
label: Isfahan (siege, 1750)
side_a: Coalition of Ali Mardan Khan Bakhtiari, Karim Khan Zand and Zakariya Khan
faction_a: Coalition of Ali Mardan Khan Bakhtiari, Karim Khan Zand and Zakariya Khan
commanders_a: Ali Mardan Khan, Karim Khan Zand, Zakariya Khan, Shahbaz (Qaraguzlu)
persian_force: Ali Mardan's Chahar Lang Bakhtiari (about 20,000), Karim Khan's Zand and other Lak and Lur tribesmen (about 12,000) and 2,000 Qaraguzlu, against the Haft Lang Bakhtiari and Afshar troops of the Isfahan garrison.
iranian_note: The attackers were Bakhtiari and Zand (Lak) tribesmen with a Turkic Qaraguzlu contingent; the defenders were mostly Haft Lang Bakhtiari with Afshars.

note: The coalition set up the Safavid prince Ismail III as puppet shah; Karim Khan later ousted Ali Mardan.

name: Mashhad (siege, 1750)
label: Mashhad (siege, 1750)
persian_force: About 8,000 Afsharid troops of the 'Persian garrison' of Mashhad, with the armed townsmen.
iranian_note: Shahrokh's regime rested on the Turkic (Afshar, Jalayir), Kurdish and Arab chiefs of Khorasan and on the Persian-speaking city; the garrison is not broken down in the sources.

name: Khudaganj
label: Khudaganj
place: Khudaganj, near Farrukhabad, Uttar Pradesh, India

name: Ram Chatauni (1750)
label: Ram Chatauni
