result_basis: Ahmad Khan defeated Safdar Jang in a pitched battle (Wikipedia, Ahmad Khan Bangash).
sources: Wikipedia, Ahmad Khan Bangash (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Khan_Bangash); Wikipedia, Safdar Jang; Irvine, Later Mughals
note: Safdar Jang is conventionally a Persian (the Nishapuri Sayyid house of Awadh). The family also claims descent from Qara Yusuf of the Qara Qoyunlu (Wikipedia, Safdar Jang), which would make it Turkmen, so the Persian label is contested. I recall an earlier Ram Chatauni fight in 1748 between the Rohillas and Qaim Khan Bangash; it is a different battle.

name: Chaman Zaghan
label: Chaman Zaghan
commanders_b: Mohammad Hussain Khan (Kurdish chief, killed), with two nephews of Nader Shah
persian_force: A relief army raised by Mohammad Hussain Khan from the Kurdish and Turkic tribes of Khorasan and other Khorasani elements, with two nephews of Nader Shah.
iranian_note: The sources name Kurdish and Turkic tribal contingents of Khorasan.
result_basis: The relief army was destroyed and its survivors fled to the mountains.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Chaman Zaghan; Siege of Mashhad (1750)
note: The defeat led to the surrender of Mashhad.
qbasis: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian

name: Nishapur (siege, 1750-51)
label: Nishapur (siege, 1750-51)
commanders_a: Jafar Khan Bayat (killed), then his nephew Abbas Qoli Khan
persian_force: A garrison of 'only a few thousand men' of the Qara Bayat amirs of Nishapur with the townsmen.
iranian_note: The Bayat were a Turkic tribe ruling a Persian-speaking city; the share of townsmen in the defence is not recorded.
losses_b: about 12,000 dead and thousands wounded (as given)
result_basis: The garrison threw back the assault through the breaches and Ahmad Shah retreated to Herat.
borderline: the Qara Bayat amirdom of Nishapur was a local Iran-seated power nominally under the Afsharids
doubt: Borderline: the Qara Bayat amirdom of Nishapur was a local Iran-seated power nominally under the Afsharids.
sources: en.wikipedia Durrani Campaign to Khorasan (1749-1751)
note: The Afghan loss figure is high and comes from a single account.
qbasis: Qara Bayat (Nishapur): an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian

name: Allahabad (siege, 1750-51)
label: Allahabad
date: autumn 1750 to early 1751 (the siege was raised when Safdar Jang's allies arrived)
war: Safdar Jang's war with the Bangash Nawab of Farrukhabad (1750-51)
result_basis: Ahmad Khan was close to taking the city when Safdar Jang's Maratha, Jat and Rohilla allies came up; the Bangash were defeated and fell back.
sources: Wikipedia, Ahmad Khan Bangash (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Khan_Bangash); Irvine, Later Mughals; Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire, vol. 1
note: Dates and the exact fighting are loose in the sources I could use; counted as a siege that was raised. Same Persian/Qara Qoyunlu caveat for Safdar Jang as above.

name: Chaharmahal (1751)
label: Chaharmahal (1751)
persian_force: Karim Khan's Zand, Lak and Lur tribesmen against Ali Mardan's Bakhtiari.
iranian_note: Karim Khan's soldiers were mainly Laks, Lurs and Kurds (Perry); Ali Mardan's were Bakhtiari.
result_basis: Karim Khan completely defeated Ali Mardan, whose captured leaders were blinded or executed and whose foot-soldiers were taken into the Zand army.
borderline: no article; described as a decisive defeat in the campaign article
doubt: Borderline: no article; described as a decisive defeat in the campaign article.
sources: en.wikipedia Zand campaigns in Western Iran; Karim Khan Zand
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Kirkhbulakh
label: Kirkhbulakh
persian_force: Azad Khan's army of Azerbaijan: a core of Afghan (Ghilzai) cavalry with the Kurdish and Turkic chiefs of Azerbaijan allied to him.
iranian_note: Azad Khan's core was Ghilzai Afghan cavalry (Pashto, an Iranian language) with Turkic and Kurdish allies; the force at Kirkhbulakh is not broken down.
result_basis: The Georgians routed Azad Khan's army and pursued it for about 30 km, and the siege of Erivan was lifted.
borderline: Azad Khan was an Iran-seated warlord (Azerbaijan, Urmia and Tabriz) rather than a dynasty
doubt: Borderline: Azad Khan was an Iran-seated warlord (Azerbaijan, Urmia and Tabriz) rather than a dynasty.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kirkhbulakh; Azad Khan Afghan
note: Kingdoms of Kartli and Kakheti under Erekle II. The Khan of Erivan then paid tribute to the Georgian kings.
qbasis: Azad Khan (Azerbaijan): an Iranian-led state

name: Kermanshah (siege, 1752-53)
label: Kermanshah (siege, 1752-53)
side_b: Garrison of Kermanshah for Ali Mardan Khan and the pretender Soltan Hoseyn II
faction_b: Garrison of Kermanshah for Ali Mardan Khan and the pretender Soltan Hoseyn II
commanders_a: Karim Khan Zand, Mohammad Khan Zand, Sadeq Khan Zand, Shaykh Ali Khan Zand, Najaf Qoli Khan
commanders_b: Abd ol-Ali Khan Mishmast, Mirza Mohammad Taqi Golestaneh; relief under Ali Mardan Khan and Esma'il Khan Feyli
persian_force: Zand regulars with mortars and Kalhor and Zangana Kurdish tribesmen under Najaf Qoli Khan, against a garrison of Afsharid-era troops supported by Haft Lang Bakhtiari and Feyli Lurs.
iranian_note: Kalhor and Zangana Kurds fought for Karim Khan; the garrison's allies were Bakhtiari and Feyli Lurs.
losses_b: the whole garrison surrendered; the relief force was destroyed
result_basis: The garrison surrendered in 1753 when Ali Mardan's promised relief failed to break through.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Kermanshah; Zand campaigns in Western Iran
note: A Zand attempt under Mohammad Khan to intercept Ali Mardan's relief force in spring 1752 was repelled with heavy losses.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Lahore (1752)
label: Lahore
war: Ahmad Shah Durrani's third invasion of India (1751-1752)
commanders_a: Ahmad Shah Durrani; Jahan Khan Popalzai
result_basis: Mir Mannu was defeated outside Lahore, surrendered and was kept as Ahmad Shah's governor; Lahore was plundered.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Shah_Durrani; Ganda Singh, Ahmad Shah Durrani: Father of Modern Afghanistan (1959); Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: Ahmad Shah, after a siege-like blockade of Lahore from late 1751, defeated Mir Mannu's army and secured the Punjab by treaty; Kashmir was then annexed without a battle.
qbasis: Ahmad Shah Abdali, a Pashtun, led the Durrani and Ghilzai army (Ganda Singh).

name: Nahavand (1752)
label: Nahavand (1752)
side_b: Ali Mardan Khan Bakhtiari, with Al-Kathir Arabs and Lurs
faction_b: Ali Mardan Khan Bakhtiari, with Al-Kathir Arabs and Lurs
persian_force: Karim Khan's Zand, Lak, Lur and Kurdish tribesmen against Ali Mardan's Bakhtiari with Khuzestani Arab (Al-Kathir) and Lur support.
iranian_note: Both armies were mainly Lur, Bakhtiari and Kurdish tribesmen; Ali Mardan had Arab allies.
result_basis: Karim Khan defeated Ali Mardan, who fled west into Ottoman territory towards Baghdad.
borderline: no article; described as a battle in the campaign article
doubt: Borderline: no article; described as a battle in the campaign article.
sources: en.wikipedia Zand campaigns in Western Iran
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Astarabad (siege, 1752)
label: Astarabad (siege, 1752)
side_b: Karim Khan Zand, with Ismail III
faction_b: Karim Khan Zand, with Ismail III
commanders_a: Mohammad Hasan Khan Qajar, Mohammad Mirza
commanders_b: Karim Khan Zand, Musa Khan Afshar, Zakariya Khan
persian_force: Mohammad Hasan's Qajar tribesmen and Yomut Turkmen (about 35,000, 'mainly Turkmen') against Karim Khan's Zand, Lur and Kurdish army with siege artillery (about 45,000).
iranian_note: The defenders were Qajar and Yomut Turkmen (Turkic); the Zand besiegers were mainly Lak, Lur and Kurdish tribesmen.
result_basis: The Zands failed to take Astarabad and retreated with heavy losses; the puppet Ismail III fell into Qajar hands.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Astarabad; Zand campaigns in Western Iran; Mohammad Hasan Khan Qajar
note: The Mohammad Hasan Khan Qajar article dates the Zand failure at Astarabad to 1751.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Pari (1753)
label: Pari (1753)
place: near the fortress of Pari, by Malayer, Iran
persian_force: Azad Khan's Afghan cavalry with Kurdish and Turkic allies of Azerbaijan, against Karim Khan's Zand and Lur tribesmen.
iranian_note: Azad's Ghilzai core spoke Pashto and the Zand army was mainly Lak, Lur and Kurdish; Turkic allies were a minority on each side as far as known.
result_basis: Azad Khan turned on the pursuing Zand army, inflicted a heavy defeat and took Karim Khan's fortress of Pari.
borderline: no article and no conventional name; named here after the fortress taken
doubt: Borderline: no article and no conventional name; named here after the fortress taken.
sources: en.wikipedia Azad Khan Afghan
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Qomsheh (1753)
label: Qomsheh (1753)
side_a: Azad Khan Afghan, with Fath-Ali Khan Afshar
faction_a: Azad Khan Afghan, with Fath-Ali Khan Afshar
commanders_b: Karim Khan Zand, Eskandar Khan Zand (killed)
persian_force: Azad Khan's Afghans and Fath-Ali Khan's Afshar Turks against the Zand tribesmen.
iranian_note: Fath-Ali Khan's Afshars were Turkic; Azad's Afghans and the Zands spoke Iranian languages.
result_basis: The Zands withdrew after Karim Khan's half-brother Eskandar Khan was killed, and Azad's forces went on to take Shiraz.
borderline: no article; described in the biographies
doubt: Borderline: no article; described in the biographies.
sources: en.wikipedia Fath-Ali Khan Afshar; Azad Khan Afghan
note: The Fath-Ali Khan Afshar article dates the attack to 1753, the Azad Khan article to 1754.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Delhi (siege, 1753)
label: Delhi
date: 26 March to 7 November 1753 (major assault on the walls failed on 5 June)
war: Safdar Jang's rebellion (the Plunder of Old Delhi, 1753)
commanders_a: Safdar Jang; Rajendra Gossain (killed); Suraj Mal
result_basis: Safdar Jang's assault failed, his men defected, and on 7 November he was pushed back to Ballabgarh and made peace.
sources: Wikipedia, Plunder of Old Delhi (Safdarjung's rebellion) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plunder_of_Old_Delhi); Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire, vol. 1; Irvine, Later Mughals
note: A months-long investment with skirmishes rather than one battle. Najib Khan is a Rohilla (Pashtun). Safdar Jang's Persian/Qara Qoyunlu question applies as above.

name: Tabas (1754)
label: Tabas (1754)
commanders_a: Sardar Jahan Khan, Nasir Khan of Kalat
commanders_b: Ali Murad Khan, governor of Tabas (killed)
persian_force: The levies of the governor of Tabas; composition not recorded.
iranian_note: The sources used do not describe the Tabas force.
result_basis: The Persian army was routed and its commander killed; Tabas and Tun were then taken.
borderline: no article; a local governor nominally under the Afsharids
doubt: Borderline: no article; a local governor nominally under the Afsharids.
sources: en.wikipedia Durrani Campaign to Khorasan (1754-1755)
note: Kalat (Baloch) fought as Ahmad Shah's vassal, recorded as 'Kalat' (a new short name).
qbasis: Tabas (local rulers): an Iranian-led state

name: Mashhad (siege, 1754)
label: Mashhad (siege, 1754)
persian_force: Shahrokh's garrison and the townsmen of Mashhad; composition not recorded.
iranian_note: Inferred from the Turkic, Kurdish and Persian-speaking supporters of Shahrokh's regime.
result_basis: Shahrokh surrendered the city on 1 December after a four-month siege.
sources: en.wikipedia Durrani Campaign to Khorasan (1754-1755)
note: Ahmad Shah's name was read in the Friday sermon on 4 December; Shahrokh was reinstated as a protected ruler on 9 May 1755.
qbasis: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian

name: Kamarej
label: Kamarej
faction_b: Azad Khan Afghan (Fath-Ali Khan Afshar in the field)
commanders_a: Karim Khan Zand, Mirza Ali Beg Khurmuji, Ra'is Ahmad Shah Tangestani
persian_force: Karim Khan's Zand troops, Kazerun townsmen and Dashtestan levies, reinforced by about 4,000 Tangestani and Khesht musketeers; against Azad Khan's main army of Afghans and Afshars under Fath-Ali Khan.
iranian_note: The Zand side was Zand tribesmen with Persian-speaking townsmen and musketeers of southern Fars; the losers included Turkic Afshars and Afghans.
result_basis: Fath-Ali Khan's army was ambushed in the pass, lost heavily and fled, and Azad's forces left Kazerun and then Fars.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kamarej; Fath-Ali Khan Afshar
note: The turning point of Karim Khan's war with Azad Khan; Karim then retook Shiraz.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Sabzevar (1755)
label: Sabzevar (1755)
commanders_b: an Abdali regiment (Shah Pasand Khan's force, as probably meant)
persian_force: Mohammad Hasan Khan's Qajar tribesmen and Yomut Turkmen allies with Mazandarani levies.
iranian_note: Mohammad Hasan's field army was mainly Qajar and Turkmen horse; Mazandarani musketeers were a smaller part.
result_basis: Mohammad Hasan Khan is said to have defeated the Abdali regiment.
borderline: poorly documented; the Durrani campaign article reports only an unconfirmed defeat of Shah Pasand Khan by the Qajars
doubt: Borderline: poorly documented; the Durrani campaign article reports only an unconfirmed defeat of Shah Pasand Khan by the Qajars.
sources: en.wikipedia Mohammad Hasan Khan Qajar; Durrani Campaign to Khorasan (1754-1755)
note: The Durrani article also says Ahmad Shah defeated the Qajars after Nishapur, without place or date.
qbasis: Qajars of Astarabad: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian

name: Nishapur (siege, 1755)
label: Nishapur (siege, 1755)
commanders_b: Abbas Qoli Khan Bayat and the elders of Nishapur
persian_force: The townsmen of Nishapur under the Bayat amirs.
iranian_note: The defence was by the citizens of a Persian-speaking city who rose after the Bayat khan had first submitted.
result_basis: Bombarded with a great Armenian-cast cannon, the elders opened the gates after about a week and the city was plundered and largely razed.
sources: en.wikipedia Durrani Campaign to Khorasan (1754-1755)
note: The city had revolted on a rumour that Shah Pasand Khan had been beaten by the Qajars.
qbasis: Qara Bayat (Nishapur): an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian

name: Gulnabad (1756)
label: Gulnabad (1756)
persian_force: Qajar and Turkmen cavalry with Mazandarani musketeers, against Zand, Lur and Kurdish tribesmen.
iranian_note: Inferred from the usual composition of the two armies.
result_basis: Mohammad Hasan defeated Karim Khan's forces and went on to occupy Isfahan.
borderline: no article; listed among Mohammad Hasan's battles
doubt: Borderline: no article; listed among Mohammad Hasan's battles.
sources: en.wikipedia Mohammad Hasan Khan Qajar
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Kazzaz
label: Kazzaz
place: Sanjan, near Kazzaz, northwest of Isfahan (near Arak), Iran
commanders_b: Shaykh Ali Khan Zand, Mohammad Khan Zand (captured)
persian_force: Mohammad Hasan's veteran Qajar army with musketeers levied in Astarabad, against a weakened Zand force whose Arab musketeers had mutinied.
iranian_note: The Qajar army was Turkic tribal horse with Astarabad musketeers; the Zand force was Lak, Lur and Kurdish.
losses_b: unknown (Mohammad Khan Zand and four officers captured)
result_basis: The outnumbered Zand force was broken; Mohammad Khan Zand was captured and Shaykh Ali Khan escaped with fifteen men.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kazzaz
note: Karim Khan abandoned Isfahan for Shiraz.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Delhi (occupation and sack, 1757)
label: Delhi
date: late January 1757 (Ahmad Shah entered Delhi about 28 January)
war: Ahmad Shah Durrani's fourth invasion of India (1756-1757)
commanders_a: Ahmad Shah Durrani; Jahan Khan Popalzai; Najib ad-Dawla (Rohilla)
result_basis: The Mughal court submitted, Delhi was occupied and sacked for weeks, and Alamgir II was left on the throne as a vassal.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Shah_Durrani; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34); Ganda Singh, Ahmad Shah Durrani: Father of Modern Afghanistan (1959)
note: Little organised fighting: included because the capture and sack of Delhi is a named event of the invasion. Najib ad-Dawla, a Yusufzai Rohilla, had invited Ahmad Shah and was made his agent in Delhi.
qbasis: Ahmad Shah (Pashtun) led the Afghan army, with Najib ad-Dawla's Rohilla Pashtuns.

name: Narela
label: Narela
war: Ahmad Shah Durrani's fourth invasion of India (1756-1757)
result_basis: The Afghan vanguard drove back about 3,400 Marathas of Antaji Mankeshwar, who withdrew and left Delhi open.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Shah_Durrani; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: A skirmish-sized action on the road into Delhi, known mainly from Sarkar and the Maratha letters; the date and numbers rest on a single summary of Wikipedia's account.
qbasis: Ahmad Shah's army was Afghan (Wikipedia 'Ahmad Shah Durrani').

name: Chaumuhan
label: Chaumuhan
date: about 28 February 1757 (the day before the sack of Mathura)
war: Ahmad Shah Durrani's fourth invasion of India (1756-1757)
place: Chaumuhan (Chaumuha), near Mathura, Uttar Pradesh, India
commanders_b: Jawahar Singh; Suraj Mal (ruler of Bharatpur)
result_basis: The Jats resisted at Chaumuhan with heavy losses on both sides (10,000-12,000 combined), after which the Afghans went on to sack Mathura.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Shah_Durrani; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: The outcome is not stated outright in the sources I could check; A is inferred from the Afghan advance to Mathura next day.
qbasis: The Afghan column was drawn from Ahmad Shah's Durrani army (Wikipedia 'Ahmad Shah Durrani').

name: Agra (siege, 1757)
label: Agra
war: Ahmad Shah Durrani's fourth invasion of India (1756-1757)
result_basis: The Afghans plundered the town but could not take Agra Fort, and cholera in their camp forced the withdrawal to Afghanistan.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Shah_Durrani; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: Limit of the 1757 advance; over 2,000 townspeople were killed.
qbasis: The besiegers were Ahmad Shah's Afghan army (Wikipedia 'Ahmad Shah Durrani').

name: Ballabhgarh
label: Ballabhgarh
war: Ahmad Shah Durrani's fourth invasion of India (1756-1757)
commanders_b: Jawahar Singh; Balram Singh (Jat chief of Ballabhgarh)
result_basis: The Afghans seized Ballabhgarh on about 4 March and Jawahar Singh withdrew.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Shah_Durrani; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: Ahmad Shah's Afghans cleared the Jat forts south of Delhi on the way to Mathura and Agra.
qbasis: The attackers were Ahmad Shah's Durrani army (Wikipedia 'Ahmad Shah Durrani').

name: Gokul
label: Gokul
war: Ahmad Shah Durrani's fourth invasion of India (1756-1757)
place: Gokul, near Mathura, Uttar Pradesh, India
commanders_b: Naga sadhu leaders (not named in the sources checked)
result_basis: About 2,000 died on both sides and the Afghans withdrew without sacking Gokul.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Shah_Durrani; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: A rare check to the Afghan advance, remembered chiefly in Hindu tradition; the fighting itself is also noted by Sarkar.
qbasis: The attackers were Ahmad Shah's Afghan troops (Wikipedia 'Ahmad Shah Durrani').

name: Urmia (1757)
label: Urmia (1757)
side_b: Azad Khan Afghan, with Fath-Ali Khan Afshar of Urmia
faction_b: Azad Khan Afghan, with Fath-Ali Khan Afshar of Urmia
persian_force: Mohammad Hasan's Qajar army against Azad Khan's Afghans and the Afshars of Urmia.
iranian_note: Both armies were led by Turkic tribal forces, with Azad's Afghan core the main Iranian-speaking element.
result_basis: Azad Khan fled to Ottoman territory and Urmia and Tabriz passed to the Qajars.
borderline: the infobox of the Mohammad Hasan article lists a 'Battle of Urmiya', but its text and the Fath-Ali Khan Afshar article say Urmia surrendered without a fight
doubt: Borderline: the infobox of the Mohammad Hasan article lists a 'Battle of Urmiya', but its text and the Fath-Ali Khan Afshar article say Urmia surrendered without a fight.
sources: en.wikipedia Mohammad Hasan Khan Qajar; Fath-Ali Khan Afshar
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Delhi (Maratha siege of Najib ad-Dawla, 1757)
label: Delhi
date: August-September 1757 (Marathas entered about 11 August; Najib left Delhi in September)
side_b: Najib ad-Dawla and the Rohilla garrison of Delhi
persian_state: Najib ad-Dawla and the Rohilla garrison of Delhi
result_basis: The Marathas, with Imad al-Mulk, invested Najib in Delhi and forced him to give up the capital's government and retire to his jagir.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Shah_Durrani; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: Najib ad-Dawla (Yusufzai Rohilla), left as Ahmad Shah's agent in Delhi, was dislodged by Raghunathrao's Marathas; the fighting was brief and the date within 1757 is not fixed.
qbasis: Najib ad-Dawla, a Pashtun (Yusufzai) Rohilla chief, led the defence (Sarkar).

name: Amritsar (Gohalwar, 1757)
label: Amritsar
date: 11-13 November 1757 (Diwali; Baba Deep Singh killed 13 November)
war: Afghan-Sikh Wars: Durrani occupation of the Punjab
commanders_a: Jahan Khan Popalzai; Prince Timur Shah
result_basis: Baba Deep Singh's Sikhs were beaten near Gohalwar on the way to Amritsar and he was killed; the Afghans desecrated the Harmandir Sahib.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Shah_Durrani; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan%E2%80%93Sikh_Wars; Ganda Singh, Ahmad Shah Durrani: Father of Modern Afghanistan (1959)
note: Prince Timur Shah, Ahmad Shah's son and viceroy at Lahore, and the general Jahan Khan commanded; Sikh accounts hold that Baba Deep Singh fought on after being wounded.
qbasis: Jahan Khan Popalzai and Timur Shah, Pashtun Durranis, commanded an Afghan army (Wikipedia 'Afghan-Sikh Wars').

name: Kalat (siege, 1758)
label: Kalat
persian_state: Durrani Empire v Khanate of Kalat
result_basis: The siege of about forty days failed and a treaty confirmed Nasir Khan as governor under Durrani suzerainty.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Shah_Durrani; Axworthy / Noelle-Karimi on Kalat (not consulted in full)
note: Ended with a treaty rather than a storm, and Nasir Khan later served Ahmad Shah with a Baloch-Brahui contingent.
qbasis: Ahmad Shah (Pashtun) led the besiegers while the defenders included Baloch levies (Wikipedia 'Ahmad Shah Durrani').

name: Mastung (1758)
label: Mastung
persian_state: Durrani Empire v Khanate of Kalat
commanders_a: Ahmad Shah Durrani; Shah Wali Khan
result_basis: Nasir Khan's forces were defeated at Mastung, after which he withdrew to Kalat.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Shah_Durrani; Axworthy / Noelle-Karimi on Kalat (not consulted in full)
note: Follows Shah Wali Khan's defeat at Pringuez; Nasir Khan's army was mostly Brahui with Baloch tribal levies, so the Baloch share is a guess.
qbasis: Ahmad Shah (Pashtun) led the Durrani army, while Kalat's army included Baloch levies (Wikipedia 'Ahmad Shah Durrani').

name: Sirhind (siege, 1758)
label: Sirhind
result_basis: After about two weeks the garrison of some 15,000 Afghans surrendered and the town was sacked.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan%E2%80%93Maratha_War; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: Dal Khalsa Sikhs under Jassa Singh Ahluwalia and Ala Singh and Adina Beg Khan fought alongside the Marathas.
qbasis: The garrison was an Afghan force of about 15,000 (Wikipedia 'Afghan-Maratha War').

name: Attock (1758)
label: Attock
place: Attock fort on the Indus, Punjab, Pakistan
commanders_a: Raghunathrao (overall); Mahadji Shinde; Tukoji (Holkar/Shinde; Wikipedia's infobox says Scindia)
commanders_b: Karim Shah; Wazirullah Khan (named in Wikipedia's infobox; their roles are not explained)
result_basis: The Marathas took Attock and raised their flag over the fort, the farthest point of their advance up the Indus.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Attock_(1758); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan%E2%80%93Maratha_War; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: The Durrani garrisons of the Punjab were pushed out in 1758 by Raghunathrao's army with Sikh help; the garrison was Afghan, but I did not find a source naming its commanders' tribes.
qbasis: The defenders were Ahmad Shah Durrani's Afghan garrison (Wikipedia 'Afghan-Maratha War').

name: Peshawar (1758)
label: Peshawar
commanders_b: Durrani garrison commander (not identified in the sources checked)
result_basis: The Marathas defeated the Durrani force and took Peshawar, the farthest Maratha conquest.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Attock_(1758); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan%E2%80%93Maratha_War; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: Sabaji Shinde held Peshawar until Ahmad Shah's general Jahan Khan retook the fort in 1759. The Maratha commanders' names are from memory of Sarkar, not checked here.
qbasis: The garrison was Ahmad Shah's Afghan force (Wikipedia 'Afghan-Maratha War').

name: Shiraz (siege, 1758)
label: Shiraz (siege, 1758)
side_b: Mohammad Hasan Khan Qajar, with Fath-Ali Khan Afshar and Nasir Khan Lari
faction_b: Mohammad Hasan Khan Qajar, with Fath-Ali Khan Afshar and Nasir Khan Lari
commanders_a: Karim Khan Zand, Shaykh Ali Khan Zand, Nadr Khan Zand
commanders_b: Mohammad Hasan Khan Qajar, Ebrahim Khan Boghayeri, Fath-Ali Khan Afshar, Abu'l-Qasem Khan (captured), Nasir Khan Lari
persian_force: About 10,000 Zand defenders behind fortified ramparts, against at least 27,000 Qajar troops of many peoples (many of them defectors from Azad Khan's army: Afghans, Uzbeks, Azeri Turks) with the Afshar contingent of Urmia.
iranian_note: The Zand garrison was Lak, Lur and Kurdish with Shirazi townsmen; the Qajar army was mostly Turkic with Afghan and Uzbek defectors.
result_basis: The Qajars failed to take Shiraz and withdrew after Uzbek and Afghan defectors raided their camp on the night of 3 July.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Shiraz (1758); Mohammad Hasan Khan Qajar
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Astarabad (1759)
label: Astarabad (1759)
commanders_a: Shaykh Ali Khan Zand, Hoseyn Khan Develu
commanders_b: Mohammad Hasan Khan Qajar (killed), Agha Mohammad Khan (captured)
persian_force: A larger Zand army under Shaykh Ali Khan with Develu Qajar and Kurdish defectors, against a smaller Qajar army of 'fickle Kurdish and Turkic tribesmen'.
iranian_note: The Qajar army is described as Kurdish and Turkic tribesmen; the Zand army was mainly Lak, Lur and Kurdish.
losses_b: unknown (Mohammad Hasan killed, Agha Mohammad captured)
result_basis: The Qajar army broke and Mohammad Hasan Khan was killed in flight; Astarabad passed to the Zands.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Astarabad (1759); Mohammad Hasan Khan Qajar
note: Also called the battle of Ashraf. The Mohammad Hasan article dates his death to 13 February.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Barari Ghat
label: Barari Ghat
place: Barari (Burari) Ghat on the Yamuna, north of Delhi, India
commanders_b: Ahmad Shah Durrani; Najib ad-Dawla; Qutb Shah (Rohilla religious leader)
result_basis: Dattaji Shinde was killed on the Yamuna bank and his army fell back, ending Maratha control of the Doab north of Delhi.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan%E2%80%93Maratha_War; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: Dattaji was ambushed (some accounts say struck down when he rode forward to meet Qutb Shah); Ahmad Shah's Afghans and Najib's Rohillas were present.
qbasis: Ahmad Shah (Pashtun) and Najib ad-Dawla's Rohilla Pashtuns fought the Marathas (Sarkar).

name: Sikandarabad (1760)
label: Sikandarabad
place: near Sikandarabad, Bulandshahr district, Uttar Pradesh, India
commanders_a: Ahmad Shah Durrani; Jahan Khan Popalzai; Najib ad-Dawla
result_basis: Ahmad Shah's vanguard caught and destroyed the Maratha advance guard and Holkar retreated toward Agra.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Sikandarabad; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan%E2%80%93Maratha_War; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: Najib ad-Dawla advised the Afghans to prepare for a fresh Maratha army from the Deccan, which Holkar's defeat preceded.
qbasis: Ahmad Shah (Pashtun) and Jahan Khan led the Durrani army, with Najib's Rohillas (Wikipedia 'Battle of Sikandrabad').

name: Tabriz (siege, 1760)
label: Tabriz (siege, 1760)
persian_force: Fath-Ali Khan's Afshar and Shahsevan Turkic tribesmen and the townsmen of Tabriz, against Karim Khan's Zand, Lur and Kurdish army.
iranian_note: Inferred from the usual make-up of the two armies: Turkic Afshars and Shahsevan against Lak, Lur and Kurdish Zands.
result_basis: Karim Khan could not take Tabriz, which Fath-Ali Khan defended, and withdrew to Tehran.
borderline: no article; Karim Khan briefly occupied Maragheh before the failure at Tabriz
doubt: Borderline: no article; Karim Khan briefly occupied Maragheh before the failure at Tabriz.
sources: en.wikipedia Fath-Ali Khan Afshar
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Delhi (Maratha capture, 1760)
label: Delhi
date: 22-23 July 1760 (the fort besieged until a negotiated surrender in early August)
place: Delhi and the Red Fort, India
commanders_a: Sadashivrao Bhau; Malharrao Holkar; Jankoji Shinde; Balwantrao Mehendale
result_basis: The Marathas took the city; the Afghan garrison held the fort for a few days, then left safely with its property under a negotiated settlement and Naro Shankar became subahdar.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capture_of_Delhi_(1760); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan%E2%80%93Maratha_War
note: About 100 Maratha soldiers who entered the fort were killed by the Afghan guards before the siege and bombardment began.
qbasis: The fort was held by Yakub Ali Khan's Afghan troops of Ahmad Shah's army (Wikipedia 'Capture of Delhi (1760)').

name: Kunjpura
label: Kunjpura
commanders_a: Sadashivrao Bhau; Ibrahim Khan Gardi; Mahadji Shinde; Jankoji Shinde; Malharrao Holkar
commanders_b: Najabat Khan (died of wounds); Abdus Samad Khan (governor of Sirhind, killed); Mian Qutb Shah (wounded, later executed)
result_basis: The Marathas encircled the fort overnight, bombarded it, and stormed in when the garrison forced a gate; the Afghan commanders were killed.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Kunjpura; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan%E2%80%93Maratha_War; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: About 10,000 Afghans inside and 5,000 outside under Abdus Samad Khan and Qutb Shah; the Marathas took a very large booty. Ahmad Shah crossed the Yamuna in revenge, which led to Panipat.
qbasis: The garrison is described as Afghans and Rohillas (Wikipedia 'Battle of Kunjpura').

name: Samalkha
label: Samalkha
result_basis: The Afghans lost about 1,000 men and the Marathas over 2,000 and retreated slowly for days.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Samalkha_(1760); Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: A cavalry action in the manoeuvres before Panipat; Ahmad Shah took part in person.
qbasis: Ahmad Shah Durrani (Pashtun) commanded the Afghan army (Wikipedia 'Battle of Samalkha (1760)').

name: Meerut (1760)
label: Meerut
result_basis: Atai Khan's 14,000 Afghans destroyed Govind Pant's foragers and killed him, cutting the Maratha supplies from the Doab.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Meerut_(1760); Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: The destruction of Govind Pant's force (Wikipedia gives about 12,000 horse on the Maratha side) left Bhau short of supplies and led to Panipat. The summary I checked calls the attackers only 'Afghans'; Atai Khan was a nephew of the Durrani wazir Shah Wali Khan (Sarkar, from memory).
qbasis: The attackers were a 14,000-strong Afghan contingent of Ahmad Shah's army under Atai Khan (Wikipedia 'Battle of Meerut (1760)').

name: Shusha (siege, 1761)
label: Shusha (siege, 1761)
persian_force: Fath-Ali Khan's Afshar and allied Turkic and Kurdish tribal forces of Azerbaijan.
iranian_note: Fath-Ali Khan's confederation was mainly Turkic (Afshar, Shahsevan) with Donboli Kurds.
result_basis: The siege ended by agreement while Shusha was still invested: Panah Ali Khan gave his son Ibrahim Khalil Khan as a hostage and Fath-Ali Khan withdrew.
borderline: no article; the Karabakh khanate was outside present-day Iran
doubt: Borderline: no article; the Karabakh khanate was outside present-day Iran.
sources: en.wikipedia Fath-Ali Khan Afshar
note: Karabakh Khanate (Panah Ali Khan Javanshir).
qbasis: Afshars of Urmia: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian

name: Third Battle of Panipat
label: Third Battle of Panipat
commanders_a: Ahmad Shah Durrani; Shuja-ud-Daula (Nawab of Awadh); Najib ad-Dawlah; Hafiz Rahmat Khan
commanders_b: Sadashivrao Bhau; Vishwasrao; Ibrahim Khan Gardi; Malharrao Holkar; Jankoji Scindia
result_basis: The Durrani coalition destroyed the Maratha army; Vishwasrao and Bhau were killed.
sources: Wikipedia, Shuja-ud-Daula (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuja-ud-Daula); Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire, vol. 2; Kashi Raj Pandit, Account of the Battle of Panipat
note: Counted for the Awadh army under Shuja-ud-Daula, a Persian by descent (Nishapuri Sayyid house; also a claimed Qara Qoyunlu descent, see Ram Chatauni). the Persian share is a named allied army, not a fifth proved.

name: Gujranwala (1761)
label: Gujranwala
war: Afghan-Sikh Wars: Sikh rising after Panipat
commanders_a: Charat Singh Sukerchakia; Jassa Singh Ahluwalia (named in Sikh tradition)
commanders_b: Khwaja Ubaid Khan (Afghan governor of Lahore)
result_basis: The Durrani governor of Lahore was defeated by the Sikhs near Gujranwala and fell back to Lahore, which the Sikhs then held.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan%E2%80%93Sikh_Wars; Ganda Singh, Ahmad Shah Durrani: Father of Modern Afghanistan (1959)
note: The first big Sikh victory after Panipat; Wikipedia's Afghan-Sikh Wars article names a Gujranwala fight in September 1761 and another in 1762 against Jahan Khan, and I have kept only the first. The commanders are from memory.
qbasis: The Durrani army of the Lahore governor was Afghan (Wikipedia 'Afghan-Sikh Wars').

name: Kup (Vadda Ghallughara)
label: Kup (Vadda Ghallughara)
war: Afghan-Sikh Wars: Ahmad Shah's sixth invasion
commanders_a: Ahmad Shah Durrani; Shah Wali Khan; Jahan Khan Popalzai
commanders_b: Jassa Singh Ahluwalia; Charat Singh; Ala Singh
result_basis: Ahmad Shah's cavalry caught the Sikh families and warriors on the march and killed between 10,000 and 30,000 of them.
sources: Ganda Singh, Ahmad Shah Durrani: Father of Modern Afghanistan (1959); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Shah_Durrani
note: The Great Holocaust of Sikh memory: a surprise attack, not a pitched battle; the Sikhs regrouped within months. The Pashtun nawabs of Malerkotla and the faujdar of Sirhind joined the Afghans.
qbasis: Ahmad Shah (Pashtun) led the Afghan army, with the Pashtun Nawab of Malerkotla (Ganda Singh).

name: Qara Chaman
label: Qara Chaman
place: Qara Chaman (Qareh Chaman), about 80 km southeast of Tabriz, Iran
side_b: Fath-Ali Khan Afshar of Urmia, with Donboli Kurds and Karabakh troops
faction_b: Fath-Ali Khan Afshar of Urmia, with Donboli Kurds and Karabakh troops
commanders_a: Karim Khan Zand, Shaykh Ali Khan Zand, Lotf Ali Khan (artillery), Ebrahim Boghayeri, Rafi' Khan Qajar
commanders_b: Fath-Ali Khan Afshar, Najaf Qoli Khan (captured), Amir Guna Khan Afshar, Shahbaz Khan Donboli (captured)
persian_force: Karim Khan's army with artillery in front and musketeers on the flanks, 300 gholams, Kurdish (Amarlu) and Shamlu and Shahsevan tribesmen and Georgian gunners; against Fath-Ali Khan's 35,000 Afshars and Shahsevan with Donboli Kurds and 1,600 Karabakh troops.
iranian_note: The Zand army combined its Lak, Lur and Kurdish core with Turkic Shamlu and Shahsevan and Georgian gunners; the losers were mostly Turkic.
losses_b: baggage train lost; many officers and men captured and executed
result_basis: Fath-Ali Khan's baggage was overrun by a final charge of Zand gholams and he fled the field to Urmia.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Qara Chaman; Zand campaigns in Western Iran
note: Also called Siah Chaman. Karabakh Khanate troops guarded Fath-Ali's baggage.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Urmia (siege, 1762-63)
label: Urmia (siege, 1762-63)
persian_force: Karim Khan's Zand, Lur and Kurdish army against the Afshar garrison of Urmia, harried by Kurdish raids during a harsh winter.
iranian_note: Inferred from the usual make-up of the two sides.
result_basis: Urmia fell to the Zands in February 1763 after a seven-month siege, and Fath-Ali Khan was captured.
sources: en.wikipedia Fath-Ali Khan Afshar; Zand campaigns in Western Iran
note: Fath-Ali Khan was executed near Isfahan in July 1764.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Amritsar (Diwali, 1762)
label: Amritsar
date: 17 October 1762 (Diwali); some accounts date the attack on the Sikh gathering earlier in the autumn
war: Afghan-Sikh Wars: Ahmad Shah's sixth invasion
result_basis: Ahmad Shah's attack on the Sikh gathering at Amritsar was fought off in a night action and he left the Punjab soon after.
sources: Ganda Singh, Ahmad Shah Durrani: Father of Modern Afghanistan (1959); Latif, S. M., History of the Panjab (1891)
note: Follows the Harmandir Sahib's destruction in April 1762; accounts of the result differ (Sikh sources claim a victory, Afghan sources a withdrawal after a successful attack), so the result is recorded as a draw.
qbasis: Ahmad Shah (Pashtun) led the Afghan army (Ganda Singh).

name: Kasur (1763)
label: Kasur
war: Afghan-Sikh Wars: Sikh conquests in the Bari Doab
commanders_a: Dal Khalsa chiefs (Jassa Singh Ahluwalia and Hari Singh Bhangi are named in Sikh tradition)
result_basis: The Dal Khalsa stormed and plundered Kasur and its Pashtun ruler fell.
sources: Ganda Singh, Ahmad Shah Durrani: Father of Modern Afghanistan (1959); Latif, S. M., History of the Panjab (1891)
note: Tradition says the raid was provoked by the Kasur Pashtuns' seizure of a Brahmin's wife; the Khweshgi Pashtuns of Kasur were Ahmad Shah's supporters in the Bari Doab. The commanders' names are from tradition, not checked.
qbasis: Kasur was ruled by the Pashtun Khweshgi family and defended by their followers (Latif; Ganda Singh).

name: Hindon (Suraj Mal's death, 1763)
label: Hindon
place: Hindon river near Shahdara, Delhi, India
side_b: Najib ad-Dawla and the Mughal imperial army
persian_state: Najib ad-Dawla and the Mughal imperial army
commanders_b: Najib ad-Dawla; Musa Khan Baloch; Sayyid Muhammad Khan Baloch
result_basis: Suraj Mal was ambushed and killed on the Hindon and the Jat army withdrew to Bharatpur.
sources: Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: Suraj Mal rode out with a small escort to reconnoitre and ran into a Rohilla and Baloch force; it was less a battle than a skirmish with great consequences. The Baloch commanders' names are from memory of Sarkar.
qbasis: Najib ad-Dawla, a Yusufzai Pashtun Rohilla, led the imperial forces with Baloch commanders (Sarkar).

name: Sirhind (1764)
label: Sirhind
war: Afghan-Sikh Wars: Sikh conquest of Sirhind
commanders_a: Jassa Singh Ahluwalia; Ala Singh; Charat Singh
result_basis: Zain Khan Sirhindi was killed and his army routed, and the Sikhs sacked Sirhind.
sources: Ganda Singh, Ahmad Shah Durrani: Father of Modern Afghanistan (1959); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan%E2%80%93Sikh_Wars
note: The Sikhs' revenge for the Vadda Ghallughara; Sirhind was sacked and its territory divided among the Dal Khalsa chiefs. Whether Zain Khan was himself Pashtun or an Afghan appointee is not settled in the sources I used.
qbasis: Sirhind was held for Ahmad Shah by an Afghan force under Zain Khan (Ganda Singh).

name: Buxar
label: Buxar
commanders_b: Shuja-ud-Daula; Shah Alam II; Mir Qasim; Mirza Najaf Khan (in Shah Alam's service)
result_basis: The Company's army routed the allied army; Shuja withdrew to Awadh and Shah Alam came to terms (Treaty of Allahabad, 1765).
sources: Wikipedia, Shuja-ud-Daula (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuja-ud-Daula); Mir Qasim; Mirza Najaf Khan; Dalrymple, The Anarchy; Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire, vol. 2
note: Iranian element: Shuja-ud-Daula (Persian by descent; Qara Qoyunlu claim noted at Ram Chatauni) and Mirza Najaf Khan (Safavid lineage, born in Iran). Mir Qasim's 'Najafi' Sayyid house is not securely Persian, so he is not counted.

name: Delhi (siege, 1764-1765)
label: Delhi
side_b: Najib ad-Dawla and the Rohilla garrison of Delhi
persian_state: Najib ad-Dawla and the Rohilla garrison of Delhi
result_basis: Jawahar Singh withdrew from Delhi on 16 February 1765 after spending about two crore rupees without taking the city.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Delhi_(1764); Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: Jawahar Singh came to avenge his father Suraj Mal with about 65,000 Jat, Maratha and Sikh troops (Wikipedia), and Najib ad-Dawla saved Delhi by generalship, famine-bound trench defence and bribing Holkar; Najib asked Ahmad Shah for help but none came in time.
qbasis: Najib ad-Dawla, a Yusufzai Pashtun Rohilla, led the Rohilla defence (Wikipedia 'Battle of Delhi (1764)').

name: Amritsar (1764)
label: Amritsar
date: December 1764 (Ahmad Shah's seventh invasion; March 1765 withdrawal)
war: Afghan-Sikh Wars: Ahmad Shah's seventh invasion
commanders_a: Ahmad Shah Durrani; Jahan Khan Popalzai
commanders_b: Jassa Singh Ahluwalia; Charat Singh; Ala Singh
result_basis: Ahmad Shah's Afghans and the Dal Khalsa fought around Amritsar without a decision and the Afghans left the Punjab in March 1765, partly through mutiny in their own ranks.
sources: Ganda Singh, Ahmad Shah Durrani: Father of Modern Afghanistan (1959); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan%E2%80%93Sikh_Wars
note: Ahmad Shah's last invasion; the Sikhs avoided a pitched battle and harassed the Afghans. I have a thin source for the actual engagement and its date, hence the low confidence.
qbasis: Ahmad Shah (Pashtun) led the Afghan army (Ganda Singh).

name: Kora
label: Kora
place: Kora (Jahanabad), Fatehpur district, Uttar Pradesh, India
result_basis: Carnac defeated Shuja's and Holkar's army, after which Shuja negotiated the Treaty of Allahabad.
sources: Wikipedia, Shuja-ud-Daula (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuja-ud-Daula); Dalrymple, The Anarchy
note: The Kora fighting is only lightly covered in what I fetched; the main weakness is the date and place, and the Persian-by-descent label on Shuja (Qara Qoyunlu claim).

name: Kharg (1765)
label: Kharg (1765)
commanders_a: Mir Mahna (Mir Muhanna) of Bandar Rig
commanders_b: the Dutch East India Company officers at Kharg (Baron Kniphausen's successors)
persian_force: Mir Mahna's dhows and fighters of Bandar Rig (Arab and Persian sailors of the Gulf coast).
iranian_note: Mir Mahna's followers were the Arab (Za'abi) and Persian coastal people of Bandar Rig; proportions are not recorded.
strength_b: 2 galliots and a cargo ship; over 40 Europeans and 18 local sailors
result_basis: Mir Mahna's men captured a Dutch cargo ship and both Dutch galliots sent to escort it, with their crews.
borderline: Mir Mahna was a local lord of Bandar Rig, often at war with Karim Khan; the article presents him as acting for the Zands
doubt: Borderline: Mir Mahna was a local lord of Bandar Rig, often at war with Karim Khan; the article presents him as acting for the Zands.
sources: en.wikipedia Persian-Dutch War
note: Dutch East India Company (VOC); 'Netherlands' is a new opponent name. The article's dates are garbled (1 or 22 December 1765; other accounts put the fall of Kharg on 1 January 1766).
qbasis: Bandar Rig (Mir Mahna): an Iranian-led state

name: Kharg (siege, 1765-66)
label: Kharg (siege, 1765-66)
commanders_b: the Dutch commander of Fort Mosselstein (not named in the source)
persian_force: Mir Mahna's men of Bandar Rig, landed near the Armenian quarter out of range of the Dutch guns.
iranian_note: As for the naval action: the coastal Arab and Persian followers of Mir Mahna.
result_basis: Mir Mahna's men besieged Fort Mosselstein and took it, expelling the Dutch from Kharg.
borderline: as for Kharg (1765): Mir Mahna's relation to the Zand state is disputed
doubt: Borderline: as for Kharg (1765): Mir Mahna's relation to the Zand state is disputed.
sources: en.wikipedia Persian-Dutch War
note: Dutch East India Company (VOC). The end of the Dutch presence in the Persian Gulf.
qbasis: Bandar Rig (Mir Mahna): an Iranian-led state

name: Mashhad (siege, 1769-70)
label: Mashhad (siege, 1769-70)
persian_force: Shahrokh's garrison, with sorties; Nasrollah Mirza raised a relief army from the Kurds at Chenaran.
iranian_note: Kurds of northern Khorasan supported Nasrollah; the garrison is not described.
result_basis: Ahmad Shah did not storm the city (out of respect for the shrine of Imam Reza) and the siege ended in negotiations, Shahrokh submitting again while Mashhad was still invested.
sources: en.wikipedia Durrani campaign in Khorasan (1769-1770)
note: After submitting, Shahrokh furnished troops to the Afghan army.
qbasis: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian

name: Gonabad (first, 1770)
label: Gonabad (first, 1770)
commanders_a: Nader Mirza and Ali Mardan Khan of Tabas (reinforcements)
persian_force: Afsharid reinforcements under Nader Mirza with the troops of Ali Mardan Khan, chief of Tabas.
iranian_note: Inferred from the Khorasani and Tabasi following of the commanders; not described.
result_basis: The Afghan contingent was repelled.
borderline: no article
doubt: Borderline: no article.
sources: en.wikipedia Durrani campaign in Khorasan (1769-1770)
qbasis: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian

name: Gonabad (second, 1770)
label: Gonabad (second, 1770)
place: near Gonabad, with the pursuit to Soltanabad, Iran
commanders_a: Jahan Khan, Nasir Khan Ahmadzai of Kalat
commanders_b: Ali Mardan Khan of Tabas (killed), Nader Mirza
persian_force: Nader Mirza's Afsharid troops and the forces of Tabas.
iranian_note: As for the first battle of Gonabad.
result_basis: The Persians were defeated, Ali Mardan Khan was killed and Nader Mirza was pursued as far as Soltanabad.
borderline: no article
doubt: Borderline: no article.
sources: en.wikipedia Durrani campaign in Khorasan (1769-1770)
note: Khanate of Kalat (Baloch) as Ahmad Shah's vassal.
qbasis: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian

name: Pathargarh (siege, 1772)
label: Pathargarh
date: 1772 (the Maratha invasion began at the turn of 1771-72; the fort's fall is not dated precisely here)
place: Pathargarh fort, Najibabad, Uttar Pradesh, India
commanders_a: Mahadji Shinde; Tukoji Holkar; Visaji Krishna Biniwale
commanders_b: Zabita Khan (son of Najib ad-Dawla); Sa'adat Khan (killed); Sayyid Khan
result_basis: The Marathas stormed Pathargarh and Najibabad, Saadat Khan was killed and Zabita Khan fled to Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rohilla; Husain, Iqbal, The Rise and Decline of the Ruhela Chieftaincy in 18th Century India (1994)
note: The Marathas, after retaking Delhi in 1771, plundered Najib's old jagir in revenge for Panipat; the Rohillas withdrew to the Terai, and Hafiz Rahmat Khan's promise of money to Shuja-ud-Daula for protection (the treaty of June 1772) was the root of the Rohilla War of 1774. The date of the fort's fall is from memory and not fixed.
qbasis: Najib ad-Dawla's jagir was defended by his son Zabita Khan with Pashtun Yusufzai Rohillas (Wikipedia 'Rohilla').

name: Agra (siege, 1773-74)
label: Agra
date: late 1773 to 18 February 1774, when Najaf Khan retook the city (start date not fixed)
war: Najaf Khan's campaign against the Jats of Bharatpur
commanders_b: Jat garrison commanders under Nawal Singh (not named in the source consulted)
result_basis: Najaf Khan retook Agra on 18 February 1774, ending thirteen years of Jat rule (Wikipedia, Capture of Agra).
sources: Wikipedia, Capture of Agra (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capture_of_Agra); Wikipedia, Mirza Najaf Khan (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirza_Najaf_Khan); K. R. Qanungo, History of the Jats
note: Najaf Khan is described by Wikipedia as of 'Safavid lineage', born in Iran about 1723 and arriving at Delhi about 1740. The fighting at Agra is thinly described in what I could read.

name: Miranpur Katra
label: Miranpur Katra
place: Miranpur Katra, Shahjahanpur district, Uttar Pradesh, India
result_basis: Hafiz Rahmat Khan was killed and the Rohilla army broke; Awadh and the Company then overran Rohilkhand.
sources: Wikipedia, Shuja-ud-Daula (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuja-ud-Daula); Dalrymple, The Anarchy; Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire, vol. 3
note: Both armies are partly Iranian peoples: Awadh under a Persian-descended Nawab, and the Rohillas (Pashtuns). The Company brigade did much of the fighting.

name: Chamchamal
label: Chamchamal
commanders_a: Ahmad Pasha Baban, reinforced by Omar Pasha of Baghdad
persian_force: About 10,000 troops sent by Karim Khan with some 2,000 Kurds loyal to the fugitive Baban pasha Mehmed Pasha.
iranian_note: Karim Khan's armies were mainly Lak, Lur and Kurdish tribesmen, and the 2,000 recruits were Baban Kurds.
losses_b: 4,000-5,000 dead; 10-12 officers captured besides the commander
result_basis: The Persian army lost cohesion when Ali-Morad Khan was unhorsed and captured, and its retreat became a rout.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Chamchamal; Ottoman-Persian War (1775-1779)
note: Baban emirate forces under Ottoman suzerainty. Ali-Morad was taken to Baghdad and later released.
qbasis: Zands: an Iranian-led state

name: Hella
label: Hella
commanders_a: Shaykh Ahmad and Shaykh Soltan of the Khaza'il
commanders_b: unknown (a Mamluk relief force from Baghdad)
persian_force: The Khaza'il Arab tribe acting as Zand allies; no Zand unit is described.
iranian_note: The fighting is credited to the Khaza'il Arabs.
result_basis: The relief force sent from Baghdad towards Basra was intercepted and driven back.
borderline: the article lists 'Zand Iran' as a belligerent but describes only the Khaza'il fighting
doubt: Borderline: the article lists 'Zand Iran' as a belligerent but describes only the Khaza'il fighting.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Hella; Siege of Basra (1775-1776)
note: Khaza'il tribe of the middle Euphrates.
qbasis: Zands: an Iranian-led state

name: Khanaqin (1775)
label: Khanaqin (1775)
persian_force: A Zand detachment; composition not recorded (Zand field forces were Lak, Lur and Kurdish horse).
iranian_note: Inferred from the recruitment of Zand field forces on the western frontier.
result_basis: Nazar Ali Khan defeated Abdollah Pasha's force, inflicting heavy losses and taking much livestock.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Khanaqin (1775)
note: The article places Khanaqin in Iran; it lies in Iraq today.
qbasis: Zands: an Iranian-led state

name: Ashar Creek
label: Ashar Creek
commanders_a: Shaykh Naser of Bushehr (fleet), under Sadeq Khan Zand
commanders_b: Soleyman Aqa (mutasallim of Basra), Henry Moore (East India Company)
persian_force: The Bushehr fleet of Shaykh Naser (14 gallivats and about 50 small craft, later 16 ships including the captured Tyger), with Banu Ka'b boats, supporting Sadeq Khan's army.
iranian_note: The ships were manned by the Arab and Persian seamen of Bushehr and the Banu Ka'b; proportions are not recorded.
strength_a: 14 gallivats and about 50 smaller ships (31 March); 16 ships (8 April)
strength_b: 2 gallivats, the ships Eagle and Success, 200 janissaries and Ottoman vessels
result_basis: Naser's ships broke the British chain boom and the British broke off and withdrew to Bushehr and Bombay, leaving the Zand blockade of Basra in place.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Ashar Creek; Siege of Basra (1775-1776)
note: East India Company (recorded as 'England'). Arab allies: Banu Ka'b and the Arabs of Bushehr.
qbasis: Zands: an Iranian-led state

name: Basra (siege, 1775-76)
label: Basra (siege, 1775-76)
commanders_a: Sadeq Khan Zand, Ali Mohammad Khan Zand, Shaykh Naser of Bushehr
commanders_b: Soleyman Aqa, Abd ol-Rahman, Shaykh Mohanna of the Muntafiq; Ahmad bin Said of Oman; Henry Moore
persian_force: Sadeq Khan's army of 30,000-60,000, broken down in one account as about 24,000 Lurs and Kurds, 3,000 Bakhtiari, 4,000 other Lurs, 12,000 from 'Ajam' (Iraq-e Ajam) and 6,000 Farsis; with the Bushehr fleet and Banu Ka'b and Khaza'il Arab allies.
iranian_note: The source breakdown is almost entirely Lur, Kurdish, Bakhtiari and Persian-speaking troops, with Arab allies outside it.
strength_b: about 15,000 levies and tribesmen, 1,500 janissaries, 300 Muntafiq, about 58 guns
losses_a: unknown (about 100 killed in the night raid of 9 April; Basran claims of 2,000 in one assault)
losses_b: unknown; the city devastated by war and plague
result_basis: Basra surrendered to Sadeq Khan on 20 April 1776 after a year-long siege.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Basra (1775-1776); Ottoman-Persian War (1775-1779); Perry, Karim Khan Zand
note: An Omani fleet broke into Basra on 14 October 1775 and fought indecisive sorties before withdrawing in early 1776. The Zands held Basra until Karim Khan's death in 1779.
qbasis: Zands: an Iranian-led state

name: Sunukhar
label: Sunukhar
date: 18 May 1775 (17 Rabi I 1189 AH, from Qanungo)
war: Najaf Khan's campaign against the Jats of Bharatpur
place: Sunukhar (Sankar), near Kama and Barsana, on the Rajasthan-Uttar Pradesh border, India
commanders_a: Mirza Najaf Khan; Najaf Quli Khan; Somru (Walter Reinhardt)
result_basis: The Jat and Rajput army was beaten and fled to Deeg (Qanungo).
sources: K. R. Qanungo, History of the Jats (jatland.com, 'Decline of the House of Bharatpur'); Wikipedia, Najaf Quli Khan (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Najaf_Quli_Khan)
note: Wikipedia's Najaf Quli Khan article calls the same campaign season the Battle of Barsana (1775) and credits Najaf Quli with the command; Qanungo gives the command to Najaf Khan. Najaf Khan's Iranian descent is as for the Agra entry.

name: Deeg (siege, 1775-76)
label: Deeg
war: Najaf Khan's campaign against the Jats of Bharatpur
commanders_a: Mirza Najaf Khan; Najaf Quli Khan; Muhammad Beg Khan Hamadani; Somru; Himmat Bahadur
commanders_b: Nawal Singh and Ranjit Singh (the latter slipped out at night to Kumher)
result_basis: Famine forced the town to yield and Najaf Khan entered it on 29 April 1776; the last defenders were killed in the citadel.
sources: K. R. Qanungo, History of the Jats (jatland.com, 'Decline of the House of Bharatpur'); Wikipedia, Mirza Najaf Khan (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirza_Najaf_Khan)
note: Najaf Khan led a charge in person against the Naga and Jat army outside the town. Muhammad Beg Hamadani (Persian origin, his kinsman) was one of his captains; Najaf Quli Khan was a Rajput convert, so not counted.

name: Shahrezur (1777)
label: Shahrezur (1777)
commanders_a: Ali-Morad Khan Zand, Zulfaqar Khan Zand, Kalb Ali Khan
persian_force: Three Zand armies under Ali-Morad Khan, Zulfaqar Khan and Kalb Ali Khan; composition not described.
iranian_note: Inferred from the recruitment of Zand field armies.
result_basis: The Zands routed the Ottoman army and pursued it back towards Baghdad.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Shahrezur
note: The article places the plain in Iran; its coordinates lie in Iraq.
qbasis: Zands: an Iranian-led state

name: Baneh (1777)
label: Baneh (1777)
commanders_b: Saleh Khan, Zand governor of Baneh
persian_force: The provincial army of Baneh and Ardalan (Kurdish levies).
iranian_note: A provincial army raised in the Kurdish districts of Baneh and Ardalan.
result_basis: After a three-hour battle the Ottoman force defeated the Iranian provincial army and occupied Baneh.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Baneh (1777); Ottoman-Persian War (1775-1779)
note: Baban forces under Ottoman suzerainty.
qbasis: Zands: an Iranian-led state

name: Sanandaj
label: Sanandaj
persian_force: The Ardalan army, mainly cavalry with swords, muskets and spears.
iranian_note: The vali of Ardalan's army was raised from the Kurds of Ardalan.
result_basis: Khosrow Khan was wounded and fled and the Iranian army was routed.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Sanandaj; Ottoman-Persian War (1775-1779)
note: Also called the battle of Marivan and Sanandaj.
qbasis: Zands: an Iranian-led state

name: Panipat (1777)
label: Panipat
war: Najaf Khan's campaign against Zabita Khan
commanders_a: Mirza Najaf Khan (with 5,000 troops and artillery)
result_basis: The Sikh allies fled to Sirhind and Zabita Khan made peace (Wikipedia, Najaf Quli Khan).
sources: Wikipedia, Najaf Quli Khan (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Najaf_Quli_Khan); Wikipedia, Mirza Najaf Khan; Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire, vol. 3
note: Whether real fighting took place beyond a demonstration is not clear from the one source I could read; Najaf Khan is the Persian leader and Zabita Khan a Rohilla (Pashtun).

name: Shatt al-Arab (1778)
label: Shatt al-Arab (1778)
place: west bank of the Shatt al-Arab near Fudhailah, Iraq
persian_force: 6,000-7,000 cavalry and 6,000 infantry from the Zand garrison of Basra, with 18 gunboats and boats taken from Persian-shore ports.
iranian_note: Inferred from the make-up of Sadeq Khan's army that had taken Basra.
result_basis: The Muntafiq beat the Iranian force that had crossed the river and the survivors were evacuated by ship.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Shatt al-Arab (1778)
note: Al-Muntafiq tribe, Ottoman-backed. The infobox calls Ali Mohammad Khan killed; the text says he escaped.
qbasis: Zands: an Iranian-led state

name: Shiraz (siege, 1780-81)
label: Shiraz (siege, 1780-81)
persian_force: Rival Zand armies of Lak, Lur and Kurdish tribesmen with Persian townsmen of Shiraz.
iranian_note: Both factions drew on the same Zand tribal following.
result_basis: Ali-Morad's men stormed the Bagh-e Shah gate and took Shiraz in February 1781.
borderline: no article
doubt: Borderline: no article.
sources: en.wikipedia Zand campaigns in Western Iran; Perry in Cambridge History of Iran vol. 7
note: Sadeq Khan and most of his sons were put to death after the fall of the city.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Multan (siege, 1780)
label: Multan
commanders_a: Timur Shah Durrani; Muzaffar Khan Sadozai (installed as governor afterwards)
commanders_b: Bhangi Misl garrison (chief not itemised in the sources checked)
result_basis: Multan fort fell on about 18 February 1780 after the defeat of the Sikh relief force, ending Bhangi rule there; Timur Shah installed Muzaffar Khan Sadozai as governor.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan%E2%80%93Sikh_Wars; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timur_Shah_Durrani; Latif, S. M., History of the Panjab (1891)
note: Timur Shah's reconquest of the lower Punjab from the Bhangi Misl; the Afghan-Sikh Wars article dates the siege 8-18 February, Wikipedia's Timur Shah article gives January.
qbasis: Timur Shah, a Pashtun, led the Durrani army (Wikipedia 'Timur Shah Durrani').

name: Shujabad
label: Shujabad
commanders_b: Bhangi Misl chiefs (not itemised in the sources checked)
result_basis: Timur Shah's army beat the Sikh relief force at Shujabad and Multan fell ten days later.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan%E2%80%93Sikh_Wars; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timur_Shah_Durrani; Ganda Singh, Ahmad Shah Durrani (1959; for the context)
note: The Yusufzai Pashtun contingent is singled out in the Afghan-Sikh Wars article for the 1780 Multan campaign; the Sikh commanders are not named in the source I used.
qbasis: Timur Shah Durrani, a Pashtun, led the army, with Yusufzai troops (Wikipedia 'Afghan-Sikh Wars').

name: Halani
label: Halani
war: Talpur overthrow of the Kalhora dynasty of Sindh
place: Halani, near Naushahro Feroze, Sindh, Pakistan
allies_a: Leghari, Nizamani, Marri, Khatian, Khokhar and Khaskheli tribes
allies_b: Khosa, Jatoi, Numria, Juneja, Lekhi and Khuhawar tribes
persian_state: Talpur Baloch of Sindh v Kalhora Mians of Sindh
commanders_a: Mir Fateh Ali Khan Talpur; Mir Ghulam Ali Khan Talpur; Allahyar Khan Talpur; Thara Khan Talpur
commanders_b: Mian Abdul Nabi Khan Kalhora; Muhammad Hasan Khuhawar
result_basis: Abdul Nabi's army was beaten and Talpur rule replaced Kalhora rule in Sindh (Wikipedia 'Battle of Halani').
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Halani (fetched); H. T. Lambrick, Sind: A General Introduction (1964); Sindh Gazetteer
note: The Talpurs were Baloch (Talpur tribe of the Baloch), and most of the tribes on both sides (Leghari, Marri, Nizamani; Khosa, Jatoi) were Baloch tribes. The Kalhoras themselves were Sindhi.

name: Bahrain (1782)
label: Bahrain (1782)
commanders_a: the Al Khalifa and Bani Utbah of Zubarah
commanders_b: the Persian garrison of Bahrain (for Nasr Al-Madhkur of Bushehr)
persian_force: The garrison of Nasr Al-Madhkur, the Persian-appointed ruler of Bushehr and Bahrain; composition not recorded.
iranian_note: The Bushehr regime's troops were Arab and Persian Gulf-coast men; this garrison is not described.
result_basis: The raiders plundered and burned Manama and returned to Zubarah after three days with a captured Persian gallivat.
borderline: a raid; Nasr Al-Madhkur governed Bushehr and Bahrain for the Zand state
doubt: Borderline: a raid; Nasr Al-Madhkur governed Bushehr and Bahrain for the Zand state.
sources: en.wikipedia Bani Utbah invasion of Bahrain
note: Bani Utbah (Al Khalifa).
qbasis: Zands: an Iranian-led state

name: Tehran (siege, 1783)
label: Tehran (siege, 1783)
commanders_a: the Zand governor of Tehran (not named)
persian_force: Agha Mohammad's Qajar tribesmen and Turkmen and Mazandarani levies against a Zand garrison.
iranian_note: Inferred: the early Qajar army was Qajar and Turkmen horse with Mazandarani foot; the Zand garrison was Lur and Persian.
result_basis: Agha Mohammad lifted the siege when plague spread from the town into his camp.
borderline: no article
doubt: Borderline: no article.
sources: en.wikipedia Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar
note: Tehran became Agha Mohammad's capital in 1786.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Zubarah (1783)
label: Zubarah (1783)
date: May 1783 (the final battle is dated December 1783 in the article)
commanders_a: Ahmad bin Muhammad Al Khalifa and the Qatari tribes (Al-Maadeed of Freiha)
commanders_b: Nasr Al-Madhkur; his nephew Sheikh Muhammad bin Khalifa (killed); Madan Al-Jidhafsi
persian_force: About 2,000 troops sent from the Persian mainland at the order of Ali-Morad Khan Zand, with Nasr Al-Madhkur's fleet and Bahraini levies.
iranian_note: Troops from the Persian mainland (Bushehr and Dashtestan) with Nasr's Arab followers; proportions not recorded.
result_basis: After a month's siege of Zubarah the Persian army was routed in the field by the Utub and Qatari tribes and withdrew.
sources: en.wikipedia Bani Utbah invasion of Bahrain
note: Bani Utbah (Al Khalifa) and Qatari tribes. Ahmad bin Muhammad Al Khalifa then took Bahrain (1783) and expelled the Persians.
qbasis: Zands: an Iranian-led state

name: Astarabad (siege, 1784)
label: Astarabad (siege, 1784)
persian_force: Agha Mohammad's Qajar garrison with Yomut Turkmen allies, against 8,000 Zand troops.
iranian_note: The Qajar side was Turkic (Qajar and Yomut), the Zand besiegers Lur and Kurdish.
result_basis: The besiegers were worn down by Agha Mohammad's raids and stored provisions and Zahir Khan fled, to be killed by Yomut Turkmen.
borderline: no article
doubt: Borderline: no article.
sources: en.wikipedia Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Ashraf (1784)
label: Ashraf (1784)
persian_force: Qajar and Turkmen horse with Mazandarani foot, against the Zand army that had invaded Mazandaran (reportedly 60,000 at the start of the campaign).
iranian_note: Inferred from the make-up of the two armies.
strength_b: unknown (60,000 reported for the whole Zand invasion)
result_basis: The Zand force was defeated and Sheikh Veis Khan fled to Tehran.
borderline: no article
doubt: Borderline: no article.
sources: en.wikipedia Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Kashan (1785)
label: Kashan (1785)
persian_force: Qajar tribal cavalry and Mazandarani musketeers against a Zand army of Lurs and Kurds.
iranian_note: Inferred from the make-up of the two armies.
result_basis: Agha Mohammad defeated the larger Zand army and Ja'far Khan fled to Shiraz; Agha Mohammad entered Isfahan on 2 May 1785.
borderline: no article
doubt: Borderline: no article.
sources: en.wikipedia Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Baramulla (Azad Khan's revolt, 1786)
label: Baramulla
commanders_a: Azad Khan (Afghan governor of Kashmir); Pahlawan Khan
commanders_b: Mir Muhammad Ali Khan; Madad Khan; Payandah Khan (Durrani commanders)
result_basis: Azad Khan won the first two clashes but then lost his supporters and was handed over by Raja Rustam Khan; he shot himself and Kashmir returned to Durrani rule.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timur_Shah_Durrani; Hasan, M., Kashmir under the Sultans / Pandit, 'Afghan rule in Kashmir' (not consulted)
note: Both sides were Afghan armies; Azad Khan, the rebel governor, won the early fighting at the Kishanganga and near Baramulla, so the field result is recorded as B (the royal side) only on the strength of the final outcome. Evidence thin: one Wikipedia summary.
qbasis: Azad Khan and the Durrani commanders both led Afghan forces (Wikipedia 'Timur Shah Durrani').

name: Lalsot
label: Lalsot
war: Maratha-Rajput war of 1787 (Mahadji Scindia against Jaipur and Jodhpur)
allies_b: Mughal contingent of Muhammad Beg Hamadani
commanders_a: Mahadji Scindia; Benoit de Boigne; Khande Rao Hari; Ambaji Ingle
commanders_b: Pratap Singh of Jaipur; Bhim Singh (Jodhpur); Muhammad Beg Hamadani (killed by a cannon shot)
result_basis: The battle was indecisive; both sides lost heavily and the Marathas withdrew on 1 August leaving the situation unchanged (Wikipedia).
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Lalsot (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lalsot); Wikipedia, Ismail Beg (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ismail_Beg); Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire, vol. 3
note: Muhammad Beg Hamadani belonged to the Persian-origin family of Najaf Khan's kinsmen (Wikipedia on Ismail Beg: family fled Persia after Nader Shah; the nisba is Hamadani). The battle article does not call him Persian itself.

name: Chaksana
label: Chaksana
war: Mughal civil war of 1788 (Ismail Beg and Ghulam Qadir against Scindia)
place: Chaksana, Uttar Pradesh, India (site not firmly identified)
side_b: Mughal army of Ismail Beg Hamadani
persian_state: Mughal army of Ismail Beg Hamadani
commanders_a: Maratha generals of Mahadji Scindia (Rane Khan and others)
commanders_b: Ismail Beg Hamadani (Wikipedia: 'general of the Mughal army')
result_basis: After a long, fierce fight the Marathas retreated (Wikipedia, Battle of Chaksana).
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Chaksana (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Chaksana); Wikipedia, Ismail Beg (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ismail_Beg); Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire, vol. 3
note: Ismail Beg Hamadani was a Mughal commander 'of Persian origin', son of Mirza Munim Beg and kinsman of Najaf Khan (Wikipedia). The battle article gives little detail and no month.

name: Delhi (Ghulam Qadir's seizure, 1788)
label: Delhi
date: July-August 1788 (Rohillas in the Red Fort from about 30 July; Shah Alam II blinded 10 August)
place: Delhi and the Red Fort, India
side_b: Mughal Empire and the Delhi court
commanders_a: Ghulam Qadir Khan; Ismail Beg Hamadani (Persian, ally)
result_basis: Ghulam Qadir's Rohilla troops seized the Red Fort and the person of Shah Alam II, plundered the palace and blinded him on 10 August.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rohilla; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34); Compton, H., A Particular Account of the European Military Adventurers of Hindustan (1892)
note: Little fighting: the Maratha garrison had been drawn off by Mahadji's absence and the court was seized; Ghulam Qadir held Delhi until October, when Mahadji Shinde's army drove him out. Ismail Beg, a Persian-born Mughal noble, was his ally in the early stages.
qbasis: Ghulam Qadir Khan, a Rohilla of Najib's Pashtun (Yusufzai) house, led the Rohilla troops (Wikipedia 'Rohilla'; Compton).

name: Shiraz (1789)
label: Shiraz (1789)
persian_force: The Qajar army (Qajar and other Turkic tribal cavalry with Mazandarani and Iraqi musketeers) against Lotf Ali's Zand cavalry.
iranian_note: Inferred from the make-up of the two armies.
result_basis: Lotf Ali Khan was beaten in the field (camels were used to frighten the Zand horses) and withdrew into Shiraz.
borderline: no article
doubt: Borderline: no article.
sources: en.wikipedia Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar; Lotf Ali Khan
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

label: Shiraz (siege, 1789)
persian_force: Lotf Ali's Zand troops and the townsmen of Shiraz against the Qajar army.
iranian_note: Inferred from the make-up of the two sides.
result_basis: The siege ended without the city being taken and Agha Mohammad returned to Tehran.
borderline: no article
doubt: Borderline: no article.
sources: en.wikipedia Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar

name: Patan (1790)
label: Patan
date: 20 June 1790 (from memory; Wikipedia's Ismail Beg article gives no date)
war: Maratha-Rajput war of 1790 (Mahadji Scindia against Jaipur and Jodhpur)
side_b: Mughal troops of Ismail Beg Hamadani
persian_state: Jaipur and Jodhpur Rajputs & Mughal troops of Ismail Beg Hamadani
commanders_a: Benoit de Boigne; Mahadji Scindia's generals
commanders_b: Ismail Beg Hamadani (defected from the Marathas to the Rajputs); Rajput captains of Jaipur and Jodhpur
result_basis: De Boigne's disciplined brigades beat the Rajput and Mughal army; Ismail Beg fled to Jaipur and then Jodhpur.
sources: Wikipedia, Ismail Beg (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ismail_Beg); Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire, vol. 3; Compton, A Particular Account of the European Military Adventurers of Hindustan
note: Persian origin of Ismail Beg Hamadani as above. The date and site are from memory; the Wikipedia Patan article was not found.

name: Shiraz (1791)
label: Shiraz (1791)
side_b: Hajji Ebrahim Shirazi, with Qajar reinforcements
faction_b: Hajji Ebrahim Shirazi, with Qajar reinforcements
commanders_b: Hajji Ebrahim's forces; Mostafa Qoli Khan Qajar
persian_force: Lotf Ali's small army of Zand loyalists and local levies of Bandar Rig and the Gulf coast, against the forces of Shiraz and 7,000 Qajar horse.
iranian_note: Inferred: Lotf Ali's following was Zand and southern Persian; the Qajar horse were Turkic.
result_basis: Lotf Ali defeated the combined army of Hajji Ebrahim and the 7,000 horsemen sent by Agha Mohammad.
borderline: no article; the Lotf Ali Khan article speaks of two Zand victories at Shiraz over Qajar armies under Mostafa Qoli Khan and another commander
doubt: Borderline: no article; the Lotf Ali Khan article speaks of two Zand victories at Shiraz over Qajar armies under Mostafa Qoli Khan and another commander.
sources: en.wikipedia Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar; Lotf Ali Khan
note: Hajji Ebrahim had shut Shiraz against Lotf Ali in 1791.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Persepolis (1792)
label: Persepolis (1792)
persian_force: Agha Mohammad's army of 30,000-40,000 (Qajar and Turkic tribal cavalry, musketeers), against Lotf Ali's much smaller force of Zand loyalists.
iranian_note: Inferred from the make-up of the two armies.
result_basis: Lotf Ali's night raid broke into the Qajar camp, but Agha Mohammad held his ground and the Zands withdrew at dawn when the Qajars rallied.
borderline: no article and no settled name
doubt: Borderline: no article and no settled name.
sources: en.wikipedia Lotf Ali Khan; Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar
note: Lotf Ali fled to Tabas; Agha Mohammad entered Shiraz on 21 July 1792.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Kerman (siege, 1794)
label: Kerman (siege, 1794)
date: spring to 24 October 1794 (about four months of siege)
persian_force: Agha Mohammad's 'large army' against Lotf Ali's Zand followers and the citizens of Kerman, reinforced by about 1,000 horsemen from Bam and Narmashir and the Afghan chiefs of Bam.
iranian_note: The Qajar army was led by Turkic tribal cavalry; the defenders were Kermanis with Afghan and Baloch horse from Bam and Narmashir.
strength_b: unknown, with about 1,000 horse from Bam and Narmashir
losses_b: unknown; tens of thousands of inhabitants killed, blinded or enslaved
result_basis: Disaffected troops opened the citadel gates, and after a three-hour fight Lotf Ali fled by night to Bam; the city fell on 24 October.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Kerman; Lotf Ali Khan; Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar
note: Lotf Ali had retaken Kerman on 30 March 1794; Agha Mohammad marched on 14 May. The Agha Mohammad article implies 1793, against the usual 1794. The Afghan chiefs of Bam fought for Lotf Ali.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Bitaura
label: Bitaura
side_a: Rohilla party of Ghulam Muhammad Khan
side_b: British East India Company and Awadh
persian_state: Rohilla party of Ghulam Muhammad Khan
commanders_a: Ghulam Muhammad Khan (son of Faizullah Khan)
result_basis: The Company and Awadh army under Abercromby defeated Ghulam Muhammad Khan's Rohilla force and he was driven out of Rampur.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rohilla; Husain, Iqbal, The Rise and Decline of the Ruhela Chieftaincy in 18th Century India (1994); Mill, J., The History of British India (1817)
note: Fought after the death of Faizullah Khan of Rampur: his younger son Ghulam Muhammad Khan killed his brother, the Nawab Muhammad Ali Khan, and seized Rampur; Muhammad Ali's son Ahmad Ali Khan was then installed with Company and Awadh backing. The site is placed only to the Rohilkhand region.
qbasis: Ghulam Muhammad Khan, son of Faizullah Khan and so of Ali Muhammad Khan's Rohilla house, led a Rohilla army of Pashtun settlers (Iqbal Husain).

name: Shusha (siege, 1795)
label: Shusha (siege, 1795)
persian_force: The main body of Agha Mohammad's expedition of about 60,000 cavalry and infantry: Qajar and other Turkic tribal horse, Mazandarani and Iraqi musketeers (tofangchi) and royal ghulams.
iranian_note: Qajar armies of the 1790s were led by Turkic tribal cavalry with musketeers from Mazandaran and Iraq-e Ajam (Persian-speaking); proportions not recorded.
strength_a: part of an expedition of about 60,000
result_basis: Meeting stiff resistance, Agha Mohammad accepted the khan's formal submission and hostages instead of taking the town, so the siege ended by agreement with Shusha still unconquered.
sources: en.wikipedia Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar
note: Karabakh Khanate (Ibrahim Khalil Khan Javanshir). Agha Mohammad entered Shusha without a fight in 1797, shortly before his murder.
qbasis: Qajars: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian

name: Krtsanisi
label: Krtsanisi
commanders_b: Heraclius II (Erekle II); Solomon II of Imereti's auxiliaries
persian_force: About 35,000 (some say 40,000) of Agha Mohammad's army: Qajar and Turkic tribal cavalry with musketeers and royal ghulams, and contingents of the submitted Caucasian khans (Ganja, Erivan).
iranian_note: No breakdown is given; inferred from the recruitment of the early Qajar army (Turkic tribal horse, Persian and Mazandarani foot).
result_basis: The Georgian army was broken and Agha Mohammad took and sacked Tbilisi.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Krtsanisi; Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar
note: Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti with Imereti. About 15,000 captives were taken from Tbilisi.
qbasis: Qajars: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian

name: Qazvin (1797)
label: Qazvin (1797)
persian_force: Fath-Ali Shah's Qajar army against about 15,000 tribesmen of Azerbaijan led by Sadeq Khan of the Shaqaqi (a Kurdish-origin tribe of Azerbaijan).
iranian_note: Sadeq Khan's following was Shaqaqi and other Azerbaijani tribesmen (Kurdish and Turkic); the royal army was led by Qajar Turkic cavalry.
result_basis: Fath-Ali Shah defeated Sadeq Khan's army as it marched on Qazvin, ending his bid for the throne.
borderline: no article; place and date of the decisive encounter are given only generally
