war: First Anglo-Afghan War (Army of the Indus, Balochistan)
side_a: Army of the Indus, Bombay column
result_basis: The fort was stormed within about an hour, Mehrab Khan was killed and the city sacked.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khanate_of_Kalat (fetched: 'The British sacked the city', 13 Nov 1839); Havelock, Narrative of the War in Affghanistan (1840), from memory; Kaye (1851), from memory
note: The Khan was a Brahui of the Ahmadzai house; his garrison was Brahui with Baloch tribal levies, and British writers and Wikipedia's Kalat article call his people Baloch, so it counts as a Baloch contingent on that wording. The Baloch share is a guess.

name: Yazd (1840)
label: Yazd (1840)
side_b: Bahman Mirza Baha al-Dawla, governor of Yazd
faction_b: Bahman Mirza Baha al-Dawla, governor of Yazd
persian_force: The Aga Khan's relatives and Ismaili followers against the provincial troops of Yazd.
iranian_note: Both sides were raised in central Iran; not described.
result_basis: Bahman Mirza's forces were defeated by the Aga Khan.
borderline: no article
doubt: Borderline: no article.
sources: en.wikipedia Aga Khan I
note: persian_state set to Qajars for both sides, since the Aga Khan held no state of his own.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Kahun (siege, 1840)
label: Kahun
date: 16 May to 25 September 1840 (the garrison capitulated 25 or 28 September)
commanders_a: Mir Sharbat Khan Marri; Sardar Doda Khan Marri
commanders_b: Captain Lewis Brown; Lieutenant Walpole Clarke (killed in the convoy ambush)
result_basis: Brown's garrison, left with about 140 men after the convoy was destroyed on 16 May, capitulated and marched out with the honours of war.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Kahun (fetched); Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851)
note: About 2,000 Marri besieged the post; Clibborn's relief column was beaten back at Nafusk Pass on 31 August (already in the dataset). The Marri are Baloch tribesmen under their own chiefs.

name: Nafusk Pass
label: Nafusk Pass
war: First Anglo-Afghan War (1839-1842): Marri revolt on the Baloch front
place: Nafusk Pass on the road to Kahan, Marri country, Balochistan, Pakistan
result_basis: Clibborn's supply column, bound for the beleaguered post at Kahan, was ambushed in the pass, lost its guns and baggage and fell back to Dadhar.
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); Wikipedia 'Kahan' and 'Marri (tribe)' (not fetched)
note: A minor but well-known British reverse on the Kachhi side of the war; the date and the commander's name are from memory of Kaye and need checking.
qbasis: The attackers were Marri Baloch tribesmen under their chief; the Baloch are Iranian-speakers (Wikipedia and Kaye on the Kahan expeditions).

name: Dadur (Dhadar, 1840)
label: Dadur
war: First Anglo-Afghan War (1839-1842): Brahui revolt in Kalat
place: Dhadar (Dadur), at the mouth of the Bolan Pass, Balochistan, Pakistan
commanders_b: Mir Nasir Khan II of Kalat
result_basis: Boscawen defeated Nasir Khan's attempt to drive the British from the road between Shikarpur and Quetta (FIBIS 'Battle of Dadur').
sources: https://wiki.fibis.org/w/Battle_of_Dadur (fetched); Kaye (1851)
note: Weak on the Baloch share: FIBIS calls the enemy 'Brahui tribesmen', and the Khan was a Brahui. British writers of the time lumped the Khan's Brahui and Baloch levies together; the Baloch contingent is inferred.

name: Parwan Darra
label: Parwan Darra
place: Parwan Darra, near Charikar, Parwan Province, Afghanistan
commanders_a: Sir Robert Sale (per Kaye); Lt. Col. William Dennie (infantry)
result_basis: The 2nd Bengal Cavalry broke and fled and two British officers were killed, so Dost Mohammad kept the field, though he surrendered at Kabul the next evening.
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); W. Dalrymple, Return of a King: The Battle for Afghanistan (2013); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: Dost Mohammad's tactical victory, followed at once by his surrender to Macnaghten at Kabul; he was exiled to India.
qbasis: Dost Mohammad, the Barakzai ruler of Kabul, led a force of Afghans and Kohistanis in his last field action (Kaye; Wikipedia 'First Anglo-Afghan War').

name: Kotra (Dhadar, 1840)
label: Kotra
war: First Anglo-Afghan War (1839-1842): Brahui revolt in Kalat
place: Kotra, Kachhi plain near Dhadar, Balochistan, Pakistan (site approximate)
commanders_b: Mir Nasir Khan II of Kalat
result_basis: Marshall and Teasdale attacked the Brahui camp from two sides and broke it; British loss 5 killed and 30 wounded, tribal loss about 500 killed (FIBIS).
sources: https://wiki.fibis.org/w/Battle_of_Kotra (fetched); Kaye (1851)
note: Weak on the Baloch share, as at Dadur: FIBIS names only Brahui tribesmen. Included because the Khanate's levies were Brahui and Baloch together and the Brief counts them as Baloch when the sources do.

name: Rigan (1841)
label: Rigan (1841)
persian_force: A government army (24,000 had driven him out of Bam) against the Aga Khan's followers.
iranian_note: Inferred from the setting.
result_basis: The Aga Khan suffered a decisive defeat and fled to Afghanistan.
borderline: no article
doubt: Borderline: no article.
sources: en.wikipedia Aga Khan I
note: The Aga Khan went on to Kandahar and later Sind and Bombay.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Dashtab (1841)
label: Dashtab (1841)
persian_force: The Aga Khan's Ismaili and tribal followers against 4,000 government troops.
iranian_note: Inferred from the Kerman setting.
result_basis: The Aga Khan defeated a government force of 4,000.
borderline: no article
doubt: Borderline: no article.
sources: en.wikipedia Aga Khan I
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Khurd Kabul Pass (1841)
label: Khurd Kabul Pass
date: 9-12 October 1841 (Khurd Kabul, 9 Oct; Tezin and the night attacks, 10-12 Oct)
war: First Anglo-Afghan War (1839-1842): Ghilzai rising of October 1841
place: Khurd Kabul Pass, between Kabul and Jalalabad, Afghanistan
result_basis: Sale's brigade forced the pass and fought through to Gandamak, though with heavy losses.
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: The Ghilzai rising that preceded the Kabul uprising by three weeks; Sale's brigade then went on to Jalalabad.
qbasis: The Eastern Ghilzai, a Pashtun tribal confederacy, closed the passes after the cut in their subsidies (Kaye; Wikipedia 'First Anglo-Afghan War').

name: Behmaru Heights
label: Behmaru Heights
place: Behmaru (Bemaru) Heights, north of the Kabul cantonment, Kabul, Afghanistan
commanders_b: Mohammad Akbar Khan (arrived 22 Nov); Abdullah Khan Achakzai; Mohammad Shah Khan
result_basis: Shelton's column on the heights was driven off, losing its gun, and the British never again left the cantonment in strength.
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); W. Dalrymple, Return of a King: The Battle for Afghanistan (2013)
note: The decisive failure of the winter; Akbar Khan, Dost Mohammad's son, had reached Kabul the day before.
qbasis: The Afghan force that took the heights was drawn from the Kabul Pashtun chiefs and their followers under Akbar Khan, a Barakzai Pashtun (Kaye; Dalrymple).

name: Charikar (1841)
label: Charikar
result_basis: The garrison was overwhelmed and cut to pieces as it broke out; only a handful, including Haughton and Dr Grant, reached Kabul.
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); W. Dalrymple, Return of a King: The Battle for Afghanistan (2013)
note: Kohistan (north of Kabul) was Tajik country; names of the garrison officers are from Kaye and need checking.
qbasis: The Kohistani Tajiks rose under their chief and destroyed the Gurkha garrison (Kaye; Dalrymple).

name: Jalalabad (siege, 1841-1842)
label: Jalalabad
date: 12 November 1841 to 7 April 1842 (Sale's brigade invested from mid-November; Akbar Khan joined in January)
commanders_b: Sir Robert Sale; Capt. George Broadfoot; Maj. Henry Havelock
result_basis: The garrison held through the winter and earthquake (19 Feb) and was relieved by Pollock's advance after Sale's successful sortie.
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); W. Dalrymple, Return of a King: The Battle for Afghanistan (2013); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: Entered with its 7 April sortie as a separate battle.
qbasis: The besiegers were Pashtun tribal levies under Dost Mohammad's son Akbar Khan (Kaye; Wikipedia 'First Anglo-Afghan War').

name: Kabul (uprising and siege of the cantonment, 1841)
label: Kabul
date: 2 November 1841; the cantonment was invested until the capitulation of 23 December and the evacuation of 6 January 1842
side_a: Afghan insurgents of Kabul and Kohistan
allies_b: Shah Shuja's government and his own troops in the Bala Hissar
persian_state: Afghan insurgents of Kabul and Kohistan v East India Company
faction_a: Afghan insurgents of Kabul and Kohistan
commanders_a: Abdullah Khan Achakzai; Mohammad Zaman Khan Barakzai (figurehead); Mohammad Akbar Khan (from 22 Nov)
commanders_b: Maj.-Gen. William Elphinstone; Brig. John Shelton; Sir William Macnaghten (envoy, murdered 23 Dec); Shah Shuja ul-Mulk
result_basis: After repeated failures to break out, the British envoy was killed and the cantonment's garrison agreed to evacuate Kabul.
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); W. Dalrymple, Return of a King: The Battle for Afghanistan (2013); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: Treated as one entry covering the street fighting from Burnes's murder, the loss of the commissariat fort (9 Nov) and the investment of the cantonment; Behmaru Heights is entered separately.
qbasis: The rising was led by Pashtun chiefs (Achakzai, Barakzai, Ghilzai) with the Kabul and Kohistan Tajiks, while Shah Shuja, a Sadozai Pashtun, ruled in the Bala Hissar under British protection (Kaye; Dalrymple).

name: Ghazni (siege, 1841-1842)
label: Ghazni
date: late 1841 to about 6 March 1842 (the garrison capitulated; the exact start and end dates vary between accounts)
commanders_a: Shams ud-Din Khan (Barakzai, former governor of Ghazni)
result_basis: The garrison surrendered the citadel on terms, which were then broken, and was destroyed or enslaved.
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: Dates approximate; Palmer's surrender is usually put in the first week of March 1842.
qbasis: The investing force was Pashtun tribal and Barakzai levies under Shams ud-Din Khan (Kaye; Wikipedia 'First Anglo-Afghan War').

name: Gandamak (1842)
label: Gandamak
commanders_a: Local Ghilzai chiefs; Mohammad Akbar Khan nearby
commanders_b: Brig. Thomas Anquetil; Col. Thain (44th Foot)
result_basis: The remaining 20 officers and 45 men of the 44th Foot were killed or captured on the hill.
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); W. Dalrymple, Return of a King: The Battle for Afghanistan (2013); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: Dr William Brydon reached Jalalabad on 13 January as the only man to arrive on horseback.
qbasis: The last stand was against Ghilzai Pashtun tribesmen who first parleyed, then closed in (Kaye; Dalrymple).

name: Jugdulluk (retreat from Kabul, 1842)
label: Jugdulluk
place: Jagdalak (Jugdulluk) Pass, Surobi District, Kabul Province, Afghanistan
result_basis: The remnant of the column was surrounded on the hill at Jugdulluk and broken up in the night; Elphinstone and Johnson became hostages.
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); W. Dalrymple, Return of a King: The Battle for Afghanistan (2013)
note: Entered separately from the September 1842 fighting at the same pass.
qbasis: Ghilzai Pashtuns blocked the pass with barricades and held the hills above it (Kaye; Dalrymple).

name: Kandahar (siege, 1842)
label: Kandahar
date: January to March 1842 (blockade and sorties; Safdar Jang's attack in early March)
side_a: Durrani and Ghilzai insurgents of the Kandahar region
persian_state: Durrani and Ghilzai insurgents of the Kandahar region
commanders_a: Prince Safdar Jang (Sadozai); Aktar Khan (Durrani chief of Zamindawar)
result_basis: Nott repulsed the Afghan assaults and the blockade was lifted; he held Kandahar until he marched to Kabul in August.
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: Wikipedia treats the whole of 1841-42 as a siege; the actions were mostly sorties against loose investment, and the names of the Afghan leaders are from Kaye and need checking.
qbasis: The investing forces were Pashtun Durrani and Ghilzai levies, with Shah Shuja's son Safdar Jang as figurehead (Kaye; Wikipedia 'First Anglo-Afghan War').

name: Khurd Kabul Pass (retreat from Kabul, 1842)
label: Khurd Kabul Pass
place: Khurd Kabul Pass, east of Kabul, Afghanistan
side_a: Ghilzai tribesmen and Akbar Khan's followers
persian_state: Ghilzai tribesmen and Akbar Khan's followers
result_basis: Some 3,000 of the column were killed in the pass.
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); W. Dalrymple, Return of a King: The Battle for Afghanistan (2013); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: First and bloodiest of the ambushes on the retreat.
qbasis: Pashtun Ghilzai tribesmen fired down on the column in the pass under the general direction of Akbar Khan, a Barakzai (Kaye; Dalrymple).

name: Tezin (retreat from Kabul, 1842)
label: Tezin
date: 9-10 January 1842 (the 'Tunghee Tareekee', the Dark Defile, 10 January)
place: Tezin valley and the Tunghee Tareekee defile, Kabul-Jalalabad road, Afghanistan
side_a: Ghilzai tribesmen and Akbar Khan's followers
persian_state: Ghilzai tribesmen and Akbar Khan's followers
result_basis: The column lost most of its remaining fighting men and followers in the defile.
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); W. Dalrymple, Return of a King: The Battle for Afghanistan (2013); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: The exact location of the Tunghee Tareekee relative to Tezin is approximate.
qbasis: Ghilzai Pashtuns ambushed the column in the defile (Kaye; Wikipedia 'First Anglo-Afghan War').

name: Jalalabad (7 April 1842)
label: Jalalabad
commanders_a: Sir Robert Sale; Capt. Henry Havelock
result_basis: The garrison marched out in three columns, routed Akbar Khan's camp and captured his guns.
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); W. Dalrymple, Return of a King: The Battle for Afghanistan (2013); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: The sortie that ended the siege a week before Pollock's relief force arrived.
qbasis: Akbar Khan, a Barakzai Pashtun, led the besieging Afghan army (Kaye; Wikipedia 'First Anglo-Afghan War').

name: Khyber Pass (Pollock, 1842)
label: Khyber Pass
place: Khyber Pass (Ali Masjid), Khyber District, Pakistan
result_basis: Pollock turned the Afridi stockades by flank marches over the hills and cleared the pass, relieving Jalalabad on 16 April.
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: Distinct from the Second War's Ali Masjid (1878) and the Afridi capture of the Khyber forts (1897).
qbasis: The defenders of the pass were Afridi Pashtuns (Kaye; Wikipedia 'First Anglo-Afghan War').

name: Kalat-i-Ghilzai (1842)
label: Kalat-i-Ghilzai
result_basis: The garrison beat off the assault with heavy Afghan loss, and was withdrawn on Nott's orders a few weeks later.
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: One of the few clear British successes of the dark months of spring 1842.
qbasis: The assault was made by Ghilzai Pashtun tribesmen (Kaye; Wikipedia 'First Anglo-Afghan War').

name: Ghoaine (1842)
label: Ghoaine
place: Ghoaine (Goaine), on the road from Kandahar to Ghazni, Afghanistan
result_basis: Nott's brigades stormed the Afghan position and cleared the road to Ghazni.
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: The site is placed only to the region between Mukur and Ghazni.
qbasis: Shams ud-Din Khan, a Barakzai Pashtun, led some 10,000 Afghans against Nott (Kaye; Wikipedia 'First Anglo-Afghan War').

name: Ghazni (Nott's recapture, 1842)
label: Ghazni
result_basis: The Afghans were beaten outside the walls, and the British entered the town and demolished the citadel.
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: Nott's column then marched to Kabul by Maidan, fighting a further action there on 14 September.
qbasis: The city was held by Afghan Pashtun levies under the same Shams ud-Din Khan (Kaye; Wikipedia 'First Anglo-Afghan War').

name: Istalif (1842)
label: Istalif
side_b: Kohistani Tajiks and Pashtuns of Istalif
persian_state: Kohistani Tajiks and Pashtuns of Istalif
result_basis: McCaskill stormed the town and it was sacked and burnt.
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: Part of the reprisal for the destruction of the Charikar garrison; Mir Masjidi's presence at Istalif is from Kaye.
qbasis: Istalif was a Tajik town of Kohistan and its defenders were under the Kohistani leader Mir Masjidi (Kaye; Wikipedia 'First Anglo-Afghan War' mentions the Tajik rising at Istalif).

name: Jugdulluk (Pollock, 1842)
label: Jugdulluk
place: Jagdalak (Jugdulluk) Pass, Surobi District, Kabul Province, Afghanistan
result_basis: Pollock's flanking parties took the heights and the army forced the pass where the retreating column had perished.
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: Date from memory of the despatches; needs checking.
qbasis: The pass was held by Ghilzai Pashtun tribesmen (Kaye; Wikipedia 'First Anglo-Afghan War').

name: Tezin (Pollock, 1842)
label: Tezin
place: Tezin, between Jagdalak and Kabul, Afghanistan
result_basis: Pollock's army carried the heights and Akbar Khan fled north; Kabul was reoccupied on 15 September.
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: Akbar Khan's force is given as 15,000-16,000 in the sources.
qbasis: Akbar Khan, a Barakzai Pashtun, made his last stand with some 16,000 Afghans, mostly Ghilzai levies (Kaye; Wikipedia 'First Anglo-Afghan War').

name: Tiyari and Tkhuma (1843)
label: Tiyari and Tkhuma
war: Bedir Khan's campaign against the Hakkari Assyrians
place: Tiyari and Tkhuma, Hakkari highlands, Turkey
commanders_a: Bedir Khan Beg; Nurullah Bey of Hakkari
commanders_b: Shimun XVII Abraham (Mar Shimun) and the maliks
result_basis: Bedir Khan broke Assyrian resistance and Mar Shimun fled to Mosul.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedir_Khan_Beg; Eppel, A People Without a State (2016)
note: Nurullah Bey called Bedir Khan in after failing alone. It was a campaign of several assaults and massacres rather than a single battle, so the date and the point are approximate.

name: Hyderabad Residency (Outram's defence, 1843)
label: Hyderabad Residency
commanders_a: Major James Outram; Captain Conway (steamer Planet)
commanders_b: Mir Nasir Khan Talpur and Baloch tribal chiefs
result_basis: Outram's guard of about 100 beat off repeated assaults for some hours, then withdrew with its guns to the river steamers and the Baloch burned the Residency.
sources: Outram, Conquest of Scinde (1846), from memory; W. Napier, History of General Sir Charles Napier's Administration of Scinde (1851), from memory; Dalrymple/Lambrick on the conquest of Sindh, from memory
note: The attack by the Mirs' Baloch followers two days before Miani opened the fighting of the 1843 war. Numbers are from British accounts (about 8,000 attackers).

name: Miani
label: Miani
commanders_b: Mir Nasir Khan Talpur; Mir Muhammad Khan Talpur; Mir Shahdad Khan Talpur
result_basis: Napier's disciplined sepoys broke the Baloch lines after hours of close fighting, and Hyderabad fell to him a few days later.
sources: C. J. Napier, The Conquest of Scinde (1845); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Miani (not fetched); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talpur_dynasty (not fetched; from memory)
note: Amir names are from memory.
qbasis: The Talpur Amirs were Baloch by descent and their army was largely Baloch tribal levies (Wikipedia 'Talpur dynasty' and 'Battle of Miani'; Napier).

name: Hyderabad (Dubba, 1843)
label: Hyderabad
commanders_b: Mir Sher Muhammad Talpur of Mirpur; Hosh Muhammad Sidi (Siddi Sindhi general, killed)
result_basis: Napier's brigade stormed the nullah position and Sher Muhammad fled, ending organised Baloch resistance.
sources: C. J. Napier, The Conquest of Scinde (1845); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hyderabad_(1843) (not fetched); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talpur_dynasty (not fetched; from memory)
note: Included for the Baloch Talpur dynasty; the Sidi general Hosh Muhammad ('Hoshu') was a Siddi, not Baloch.
qbasis: Sher Muhammad Talpur, the 'Lion of Mirpur', was a Baloch Talpur chief commanding a Baloch tribal army (Wikipedia 'Conquest of Sindh'; Napier).

name: Shahdadpur (1843)
label: Shahdadpur
commanders_a: Captain John Jacob (Scinde Horse), under Sir Charles Napier
result_basis: Sher Muhammad's force was routed and he fled to the desert border, which ended organised Talpur resistance.
sources: W. Napier, Administration of Scinde (1851), from memory; not confirmed in any source I fetched (Wikipedia 'British conquest of Sindh' does not mention it)
note: Weak entry: date, commander and result are from memory and I could not fetch a source for the engagement. Sher Muhammad was the Talpur Mir of Mirpur Khas, a Baloch.

name: Trukki (Truckee, 1845)
label: Trukki
war: Napier's campaign against the hill Baloch of the Sindh border (Jakrani, Dombki and Bugti)
place: Trukki (Truckee) fortress in the hills north of Jacobabad, on the Sindh-Kachhi border, Pakistan
side_b: Jakrani, Dombki and Bugti Baloch tribes
persian_state: Jakrani, Dombki and Bugti Baloch tribes
commanders_a: Major-General Sir Charles Napier; Major Beatson (blockade of the north entrance)
result_basis: The tribes submitted by 19 March 1845 after Napier's columns invested the stronghold.
sources: https://wiki.fibis.org/w/Truckee_Campaign (fetched); W. Napier, Administration of Scinde (1851), from memory
note: A frontier expedition against Baloch tribal strongholds; the amount of actual fighting at Trukki is not clear from the page I reached, so keep it as a minor entry.

name: Zeitun (Cizre, 1847)
label: Zeitun
date: 1847, before 4 July (the source gives no day)
commanders_a: Omer Pasha (Latas) per Wikipedia; Osman Pasha in other accounts
result_basis: The Ottoman army of about 12,000 beat Bedir Khan's Kurds in the field and he withdrew to Evreh castle.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedir_Khan_Beg; Jwaideh, The Kurdish National Movement (2006)
note: Yezdanser's defection decided the war. The name of the Ottoman field commander differs between accounts.

name: Evreh Castle (siege, 1847)
label: Evreh Castle
date: ended 4 July 1847 with Bedir Khan's surrender (start uncertain; Wikipedia says months)
commanders_a: Omer Pasha (Latas) per Wikipedia; Osman Pasha in other accounts
result_basis: Bedir Khan surrendered the castle on 4 July 1847 and was exiled.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedir_Khan_Beg; Jwaideh, The Kurdish National Movement (2006)
note: The end of the emirate of Bohtan. The length of the siege is uncertain and the coordinates are for Eruh.

name: Mayamey (1847)
label: Mayamey (1847)
commanders_a: Muhammad Qoli Khan, Muhammad Ali Khan Maku'i, Ebrahim Khalil Khan
persian_force: Four government regiments with 10 guns and Ebrahim Khalil Khan's 6,000, against Salar's 24,000-25,000 including 12,000 Khorasani cavalry, Turkmen and Kurdish (Shadlu) allies.
iranian_note: Government regiments of Azerbaijan, Maku and Bayat (largely Turkic) faced Salar's Turkmen, Kurdish and Khorasani horse.
strength_a: 4 regiments and 10 guns, with about 6,000 men
result_basis: Salar's army was routed and fled to Joveyn.
borderline: no separate article
doubt: Borderline: no separate article.
sources: en.wikipedia Revolt of Hasan Khan Salar
note: Salar, a Develu Qajar noble, rebelled in Khorasan from 1846.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Kal Yaquti (1848)
label: Kal Yaquti (1848)
place: Kal Yaquti, a suburb of Mashhad, Iran
persian_force: Government regiments of the Khorasan garrison against Salar's 8,000 Khorasani, Kurdish and Turkmen followers.
iranian_note: As for Mayamey (1847).
result_basis: Salar's 8,000 men were routed.
borderline: no separate article
doubt: Borderline: no separate article.
sources: en.wikipedia Revolt of Hasan Khan Salar
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Qarabaqa'ah (1848)
label: Qarabaqa'ah (1848)
place: Qarabaqa'ah, about 5 farsangs from Mashhad, Iran
persian_force: Government regiments against Salar's followers and Sarakhs Turkmen.
iranian_note: As for Mayamey (1847).
result_basis: Salar was defeated again and the Sarakhs Turkmen defected.
borderline: no separate article
doubt: Borderline: no separate article.
sources: en.wikipedia Revolt of Hasan Khan Salar
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Mashhad (1848)
label: Mashhad (1848)
side_a: Hasan Khan Salar and the rising of Mashhad
side_b: Qajar garrison under Hamzeh Mirza, with Yar Mohammad Khan of Herat
faction_a: Hasan Khan Salar and the rising of Mashhad
faction_b: Qajar garrison under Hamzeh Mirza, with Yar Mohammad Khan of Herat

result_basis: Roberts turned the Afghan left by a night march up the Spingawi ravine and the Afghans abandoned the pass and their guns.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Afghan_War; B. Robson, The Road to Kabul: The Second Afghan War 1878-1881 (1986); H. B. Hanna, The Second Afghan War, 3 vols. (1899-1910)
note: Karim Khan's name is from memory of Roberts's despatch; the British had Turi (Kurram Pashtun) auxiliaries.
qbasis: The Afghan army on the Peiwar Kotal was made up of regulars and Pashtun tribesmen of the Khost border under Karim Khan (Robson; Wikipedia 'Second Anglo-Afghan War').

name: Kabul Residency (siege, 1879)
label: Kabul Residency
side_a: Mutinous Afghan regiments and the Kabul crowd
persian_state: Mutinous Afghan regiments and the Kabul crowd
commanders_a: Daud Shah (reported leader of the Herati regiments)
commanders_b: Sir Louis Cavagnari (envoy, killed); Lt. Walter Hamilton, V.C. (Guides escort, killed)
result_basis: After a day-long defence the Residency was burned and Cavagnari, his staff and the escort were all killed.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Afghan_War; B. Robson, The Road to Kabul: The Second Afghan War 1878-1881 (1986); H. B. Hanna, The Second Afghan War, 3 vols. (1899-1910)
note: The Herati regiments' ethnic make-up (Durrani Pashtun and Persian-speaking Herati) is not broken down in the sources; the Guides' Pathan companies on the other side are not counted.
qbasis: The attackers were Afghan regular regiments from Herat with the city's people; the Guides escort included Pathan companies on the British side (Robson; Wikipedia 'Second Anglo-Afghan War').

name: Charasiab (1879)
label: Charasiab
place: Charasiab (Char Asiab), south of Kabul, Afghanistan
commanders_b: Nek Muhammad Khan (name from memory); Mohammad Jan Khan Wardak (with the reserves)
result_basis: Roberts's two columns carried the Sang-i-Nawishta heights and the Afghan army broke and dispersed.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Afghan_War; B. Robson, The Road to Kabul: The Second Afghan War 1878-1881 (1986); H. B. Hanna, The Second Afghan War, 3 vols. (1899-1910)
note: The way into Kabul; Roberts entered the city on 12 October.
qbasis: The Afghan force was the Kabul regular regiments with Wardak, Logari and Ghilzai tribesmen (Robson; Wikipedia 'Second Anglo-Afghan War').

name: Asmai Heights
label: Asmai Heights
commanders_a: Brig.-Gen. Baker; Maj.-Gen. Sir Frederick Roberts
commanders_b: Mohammad Jan Khan Wardak; Mullah Din Muhammad (Mushk-i-Alam)
result_basis: The Afghans took the Asmai Heights and drove the British back into Sherpur, which was invested.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Afghan_War; B. Robson, The Road to Kabul: The Second Afghan War 1878-1881 (1986); H. B. Hanna, The Second Afghan War, 3 vols. (1899-1910)
note: The Afghans held the heights from 14 to 22 December.
qbasis: The Afghan army on the heights was the tribal host under Mohammad Jan Wardak (Robson; Wikipedia 'Second Anglo-Afghan War').

name: Chardeh Valley (1879)
label: Chardeh Valley
place: Chardeh Valley, west of Kabul, Afghanistan
commanders_a: Brig.-Gen. Macpherson; Brig.-Gen. Baker; Brig.-Gen. Massy (cavalry)
commanders_b: Mohammad Jan Khan Wardak; Mullah Din Muhammad (Mushk-i-Alam)
result_basis: Massy's cavalry was routed and lost four guns, and Roberts ordered the withdrawal of all outlying forces into the Sherpur cantonment.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Afghan_War; B. Robson, The Road to Kabul: The Second Afghan War 1878-1881 (1986); H. B. Hanna, The Second Afghan War, 3 vols. (1899-1910)
note: Wikipedia lists neighbouring actions (Karez Mir, Takht-i-Shah, Shajui) which may overlap with this entry.
qbasis: The rising was led by Mohammad Jan Wardak and the Ghazni mullah Mushk-i-Alam, with Wardak, Logari, Ghilzai and Kohistani levies (Robson; Wikipedia 'Second Anglo-Afghan War').

name: Sherpur (siege, 1879)
label: Sherpur
date: 15-23 December 1879 (the Afghan assault failed on the morning of 23 December)
commanders_a: Mohammad Jan Khan Wardak; Mullah Din Muhammad (Mushk-i-Alam)
result_basis: The Afghan assault on the cantonment was repulsed on 23 December and the besiegers dispersed.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Afghan_War; B. Robson, The Road to Kabul: The Second Afghan War 1878-1881 (1986); H. B. Hanna, The Second Afghan War, 3 vols. (1899-1910)
note: Roberts's decisive defence of Kabul; the Afghan numbers vary between 10,000 and 100,000 in different accounts.
qbasis: Mohammad Jan Khan Wardak, a Wardak Pashtun, commanded the besiegers, a force of about 10,000 (Wikipedia 'Second Anglo-Afghan War', fetched).

name: Mahabad (1880)
label: Mahabad
date: autumn 1880 (the rebels held the town for some days before the Qajar army came from Tabriz)
allies_a: Local Kurdish tribes loyal to the shah
persian_state: Qajar Iran v Kurdish rebels of Sheikh Ubeydullah
commanders_a: Qajar commanders from Tabriz (not named in the source consulted)
result_basis: The rebels retreated from Mahabad when the Qajar force arrived, and the whole rising collapsed after eight weeks.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uprising_of_Sheikh_Ubeydullah; Jwaideh, The Kurdish National Movement (2006)
note: The Urmia siege of the same rising is already in the dataset. Whether a real fight took place at Mahabad is not clear from the source; the result is the town changing hands.

name: Ahmed Khel
label: Ahmed Khel
place: Ahmed Khel, on the road from Ghazni to Kabul, Afghanistan
commanders_b: Mullah Din Muhammad (Mushk-i-Alam); Ghilzai and Hazara chiefs
result_basis: Stewart's division beat off the ghazi charges and held the field; the tribal host dispersed.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Afghan_War; H. B. Hanna, The Second Afghan War, 3 vols. (1899-1910); B. Robson, The Road to Kabul: The Second Afghan War 1878-1881 (1986)
note: The 'Ghazni 1880' of the span list is most probably this battle, fought in the Ghazni country; the battlefield is placed approximately.
qbasis: The attackers were some 15,000 Ghilzai and other Pashtun tribesmen with a Hazara following of the Ghazni mullah Mushk-i-Alam (Wikipedia 'Second Anglo-Afghan War'; Hanna).

name: Kandahar (siege, 1880)
label: Kandahar
result_basis: The garrison held until Roberts's relief force arrived on 31 August, and Ayub was routed the next day.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Afghan_War; B. Robson, The Road to Kabul: The Second Afghan War 1878-1881 (1986)
note: The Deh Khwaja sortie and the battle of 1 September are entered separately.
qbasis: Ayub Khan's Pashtun army invested the city after Maiwand (Wikipedia 'Mohammad Ayub Khan'; Robson).

name: Maiwand
label: Maiwand
allies_b: Levies of the Wali of Kandahar
commanders_a: Mohammad Ayub Khan; Mullah Mohammad Ghazi (ghazi leader)
result_basis: Burrows's brigade was routed and lost about half its strength, Afghan gunners and ghazis overrunning the line.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Afghan_War; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammad_Ayub_Khan_(Afghanistan); B. Robson, The Road to Kabul: The Second Afghan War 1878-1881 (1986)
note: Ayub's Afghan victory; the Wali's levies on the British side mostly deserted before or during the fight.
qbasis: Ayub Khan, a Barakzai Pashtun prince of Herat, led an army of regulars and tens of thousands of ghazi tribesmen, while the Wali of Kandahar's Afghan levies were on the British side (Wikipedia 'Mohammad Ayub Khan'; Robson).

name: Deh Khwaja
label: Deh Khwaja
place: Deh Khwaja (Deh Khoja), near Kandahar, Afghanistan
result_basis: The sortie was driven back with heavy loss and Brooke was killed.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Afghan_War; B. Robson, The Road to Kabul: The Second Afghan War 1878-1881 (1986)
note: Date and Brooke's death are from memory of the siege narratives.
qbasis: The village was held by Ayub Khan's besieging Pashtun army (Wikipedia 'Second Anglo-Afghan War', which lists the action as an Afghan victory).

name: Kandahar (1 September 1880)
label: Kandahar
place: Kandahar (Baba Wali and Pir Paimal), Kandahar Province, Afghanistan
result_basis: Roberts stormed Ayub's camp and drove the Afghans from the field; Ayub fled to Herat and then to Persia.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Afghan_War; B. Robson, The Road to Kabul: The Second Afghan War 1878-1881 (1986)
note: The last battle of the war.
qbasis: Ayub Khan, a Barakzai Pashtun, commanded the Afghan army (Wikipedia 'Battle of Kandahar (1880)'; Wikipedia 'Second Anglo-Afghan War', fetched).

name: Urmia (siege, 1880)
label: Urmia (siege, 1880)
commanders_a: the Persian governor and garrison of Urmia (not named in the source)
persian_force: The garrison and armed townspeople of Urmia, later relieved by Qajar forces from Tabriz.
iranian_note: Urmia's Shia population was Azerbaijani Turkic-speaking; the garrison is not described.
strength_b: part of a rising claimed at 80,000
result_basis: The Shia townspeople and garrison refused to surrender and the Kurds could not take the city.
sources: en.wikipedia Uprising of Sheikh Ubeydullah
note: Kurdish rebels of Sheikh Ubeydullah (from Ottoman Hakkari). His columns took Mahabad and Maragheh and failed before Tabriz; the rising collapsed after about eight weeks.
qbasis: Qajars: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian

name: Maiwand (1881)
label: Maiwand
date: July 1881 (Wikipedia 'Mohammad Ayub Khan' dates the reign in Kandahar from 20 July; the battle is said to coincide with the anniversary of 27 July 1880)
war: Ayub Khan's bid for the throne (1881)
persian_state: Mohammad Ayub Khan's army v Abdur Rahman's governor of Kandahar
result_basis: Ayub Khan won and took Kandahar, ruling it briefly in 1881.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammad_Ayub_Khan_(Afghanistan); M. Ewans, Afghanistan: A Short History of Its People and Politics (2002)
note: Details are thin and the Wikipedia article gives no date or numbers; it may be the same action some sources place at Karez-i-Atta.
qbasis: Both armies were Afghan under Barakzai Pashtun leaders, Ayub against Abdur Rahman's governor (Wikipedia 'Mohammad Ayub Khan', fetched).

name: Kandahar (Ayub Khan's defeat, 1881)
label: Kandahar
date: 22 September 1881 (the end of Ayub's reign in Kandahar, per Wikipedia 'Mohammad Ayub Khan'; the battle is usually called Gundigan after a village near Kandahar)
war: Ayub Khan's bid for the throne (1881)
persian_state: Emirate of Afghanistan v Mohammad Ayub Khan's army
commanders_a: Abdur Rahman Khan (advanced from Kabul with British support); Abdul Quddus Khan (field commander, from memory)
result_basis: Ayub Khan was defeated outside Kandahar and fled to Persia, leaving Abdur Rahman master of the country.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammad_Ayub_Khan_(Afghanistan); M. Ewans, Afghanistan: A Short History of Its People and Politics (2002)
note: The battle name 'Gundigan', the date and Abdul Quddus's role are from memory and need checking.
qbasis: Afghan Pashtun armies under Abdur Rahman and Ayub Khan, both Barakzai, fought on either side (Wikipedia 'Mohammad Ayub Khan', fetched; Ewans).

name: Panjdeh (1885)
label: Panjdeh
commanders_b: Naib Salar Ghaus ud-Din Khan (Yate's account) / Naib Salar Teimour Shah (Wikipedia infobox)
result_basis: Komarov's Russians routed the Afghans, took their guns and convoy and occupied Panjdeh.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panjdeh_incident; C. E. Yate, Northern Afghanistan (1888); T. Barfield, Afghanistan: A Cultural and Political History (2010)
note: The sources do not give the ethnic make-up of the Afghan troops, so the Pashtun share is unknown; the Afghan force is put at 600 to 4,700 in different accounts.
qbasis: The Afghan force was the regular army of the Herat border command, whose officers were Afghan (Pashtun and Herati) and whose men included Sariq Turkmen irregulars (Wikipedia 'Panjdeh incident', fetched; Yate).

name: Ghaznigak
label: Ghaznigak
place: Ghaznigak, near Tashkurghan (Khulm), Samangan Province, Afghanistan
persian_state: Emirate of Afghanistan v Mohammad Ishaq Khan's Turkestan army
commanders_a: Ghulam Haidar Khan Charkhi; Abdur Rahman Khan (directing from Kabul)
result_basis: Ishaq's army was beaten, many of his troops deserting, and he fled across the Oxus to Russian territory.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghulam_Haidar_Khan_Charkhi; Encyclopaedia Britannica 11th ed., 'Abdur Rahman Khan'; T. Barfield, Afghanistan: A Cultural and Political History (2010)
note: Date and place from memory (the Wikipedia article on Charkhi, fetched, dates the Turkestan revolt to 1892 and does not name Ghaznigak); the Turkestan army was mixed Pashtun, Uzbek and Tajik.
qbasis: Abdur Rahman and his cousin Ishaq Khan were both Barakzai Pashtun, and the Amir's field commander Ghulam Haidar Charkhi was a Yusufzai Pashtun (Wikipedia 'Ghulam Haidar Khan Charkhi', fetched; Britannica 'Abdur Rahman Khan').

name: Black Mountain (1888)
label: Black Mountain
date: October to November 1888 (after the murder of Major Battye and Captain Urmston in June)
place: Black Mountain (Tor Ghar), Hazara, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
commanders_b: Hasanzai and Akazai maliks (names not verified)
result_basis: The expeditionary force marched through the clans' country, burned villages and the tribes submitted.
sources: H. D. Nevill, Campaigns on the North-West Frontier (1912)
note: Details from memory of Nevill; the 1868 expedition is entered separately.
qbasis: The opponents were the Yusufzai Pashtun clans of the Black Mountain (Nevill; Wikipedia 'Black Mountain Expedition').

name: Uruzgan (first battle, 1892)
label: Uruzgan
persian_state: Emirate of Afghanistan v Hazara rebels of Uruzgan
commanders_a: Brig. Zabardast Khan; Faiz Mohammad Khan (brother)
result_basis: Zabardast Khan's force was destroyed and Faiz Mohammad Khan surrendered after a month-long siege, the Hazaras then massacring the fort's garrison.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Battle_of_Uruzgan; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazara_Uprisings
note: The Hazaras are counted here as Persian-speakers; the only source consulted is Wikipedia, which is thin.
qbasis: Abdur Rahman's army was a Pashtun-led Afghan force fighting Persian-speaking Hazara rebels (Wikipedia 'First Battle of Uruzgan', fetched; both sides Iranian under the span ruling on Hazaras).

name: Uruzgan (1893)
label: Uruzgan
date: 1893 (later in the year; exact date not given in Wikipedia 'Battle of Uruzgan')
place: Uruzgan (now Uruzgan and Daikundi Provinces), Afghanistan
persian_state: Emirate of Afghanistan v Hazara rebels
commanders_a: Abdur Rahman Khan; Ghulam Haidar Khan Charkhi; Abdul Quddus Khan
commanders_b: Hussain Khan Hazara; Rasul Khan; Tajei Khan
result_basis: The three Hazara leaders were captured and the rising ended, followed by massacre and displacement of the Hazaras.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Uruzgan; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazara_Uprisings
note: Wikipedia's figure of 100,000 troops for the Emirate is unsourced; the final action took place in what is now Daikundi.
qbasis: The Emirate's army under Pashtun commanders crushed Persian-speaking Hazara rebels in the final battle of the war (Wikipedia 'Battle of Uruzgan', fetched).

name: Sasun (1894)
label: Sasun
date: August to September 1894 (the Ottoman assault on the Sasun mountains)
commanders_b: Armenian village leaders and Hunchak organisers
result_basis: The Fourth Army with the Kurdish tribal horse overran the Armenian positions on Mount Andok and the villages were sacked.
sources: Klein, The Margins of Empire: Kurdish Militias in the Ottoman Tribal Zone (2011); Kieser; Hovannisian (ed.), The Armenian People from Ancient to Modern Times vol. 2 (1997)
note: The sources single out the Kurdish tribes as active partners of the army; how formally the Hamidiye regiments were involved in 1894 is debated, and the numbers on each side are not firm.

name: Wana (1894)
label: Wana
commanders_a: Escort commander of the Waziristan Delimitation Commission (name not verified)
commanders_b: Mullah Powindah (from memory); Wazir and Mahsud maliks
result_basis: The attack was repulsed with heavy tribal losses, though the camp suffered about 45 killed, and a punitive expedition followed.
sources: H. D. Nevill, Campaigns on the North-West Frontier (1912); A. Swinson, North-West Frontier (1967)
note: Casualties, the commander's name and Mullah Powindah's role are from memory.
qbasis: The night attackers were Waziri and Mahsud Pashtuns (Nevill; Wikipedia 'Waziristan campaign (1894-1895)').

name: Malakand Pass (1895)
label: Malakand Pass
place: Malakand Pass, Malakand District, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
side_b: Pashtun tribes of Swat, Bajaur and Jandol
persian_state: Pashtun tribes of Swat, Bajaur and Jandol
commanders_b: Umra Khan of Jandol (directing the coalition; not named on the field)
result_basis: Low's brigades stormed the heights and forced the pass in a day, and the force went on to the Panjkora.
sources: G. S. Robertson, Chitral: The Story of a Minor Siege (1898); H. D. Nevill, Campaigns on the North-West Frontier (1912)
note: Numbers and the tribal composition are from memory of Robertson and Nevill.
qbasis: The pass was held by some 12,000 Pashtun tribesmen of the Umra Khan coalition (Robertson, Chitral: The Story of a Minor Siege; Wikipedia 'Chitral Expedition').

name: Maizar
label: Maizar
place: Maizar, Tochi Valley, North Waziristan, Pakistan
commanders_b: Mr. Gee (political officer); Lt.-Col. Bunny (escort commander, killed)
result_basis: The escort was overwhelmed during a halt, losing its commander and several officers, and fell back to Datta Khel.
sources: H. D. Nevill, Campaigns on the North-West Frontier (1912); A. Swinson, North-West Frontier (1967)
note: The opening of the 1897 frontier rising in Waziristan; the details of the officers killed are from memory.
qbasis: The attackers were Madda Khel Wazirs, a Pashtun (Darwesh Khel) clan (Nevill).

name: Chakdara (siege, 1897)
label: Chakdara
war: Frontier uprising of 1897 (Malakand, Mohmand and Tirah campaigns)
place: Chakdara Fort, Lower Dir District, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
side_a: Pashtun tribes of Swat and Dir
persian_state: Pashtun tribes of Swat and Dir
commanders_b: Chakdara garrison (45th Sikhs), relieved by Sir Bindon Blood's cavalry on 2 Aug
result_basis: The garrison held the fort and the lashkar was cut up by the relieving cavalry on 2 August.
sources: W. S. Churchill, The Story of the Malakand Field Force (1898); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Chakdara
note: The Guides cavalry charge of 2 August broke the besiegers.
qbasis: Chakdara was besieged by the same Swat Pashtun lashkar (Churchill; Wikipedia 'Siege of Chakdara').

name: Malakand (siege, 1897)
label: Malakand
war: Frontier uprising of 1897 (Malakand, Mohmand and Tirah campaigns)
place: Malakand Pass, Malakand District, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
side_a: Pashtun tribes of Swat and Dir
persian_state: Pashtun tribes of Swat and Dir
commanders_b: Brig.-Gen. William Meiklejohn; Brig.-Gen. Sir Bindon Blood (arrived 1 Aug)
result_basis: The garrison held the pass through six nights of attack and the lashkar withdrew when the relief columns arrived.
sources: W. S. Churchill, The Story of the Malakand Field Force (1898); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Malakand
note: Churchill served in the relieving Malakand Field Force and wrote the standard account.
qbasis: The besiegers were Pashtun Yusufzai and other Swat tribesmen led by Mullah Sadullah, a Pashtun of Swat (Churchill; Wikipedia 'Siege of Malakand').

name: Khyber forts (Afridi attack, 1897)
label: Khyber forts
war: Frontier uprising of 1897 (Malakand, Mohmand and Tirah campaigns)
place: Khyber Pass (Landi Kotal, Fort Maude, Ali Masjid), Khyber District, Pakistan
side_b: British posts of the Khyber Rifles
persian_state: Afridi lashkar v British posts of the Khyber Rifles
faction_b: British posts of the Khyber Rifles
commanders_a: Mullah Sayyid Akbar (Aka Khel); Afridi maliks (names not verified)
commanders_b: British officers of the Khyber Rifles (names not verified)
result_basis: The Afridis occupied the Khyber forts, which were re-taken without opposition only in December.
sources: H. D. Nevill, Campaigns on the North-West Frontier (1912); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirah_campaign
note: A named Pashtun unit (the Afridi Khyber Rifles) on the British side as well as the Afridi lashkar; the day-by-day dates are from memory.
qbasis: The lashkar was Afridi tribesmen and the Khyber Rifles garrisons, who were themselves Afridi levies, mostly gave up their posts (Nevill; Wikipedia 'Tirah campaign').

name: Shabqadar (1897)
label: Shabqadar
war: Frontier uprising of 1897 (Malakand, Mohmand and Tirah campaigns)
place: Shabqadar Fort, Charsadda District, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
result_basis: A cavalry charge and the relief column drove off the Mohmands, who lost heavily, and the fort held.
sources: W. S. Churchill, The Story of the Malakand Field Force (1898); H. D. Nevill, Campaigns on the North-West Frontier (1912)
note: The Mohmand Field Force's later punitive operations (Landakai and others) are not entered.
qbasis: The lashkar was Mohmand Pashtun tribesmen raised by the Hadda Mullah (Churchill; Nevill).

name: Mamund Valley (1897)
label: Mamund Valley
date: September to October 1897 (Agrah, Shahi Tangi and Bilot, mid to late September)
war: Frontier uprising of 1897 (Malakand, Mohmand and Tirah campaigns)
place: Mamund Valley, Bajaur Agency, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
commanders_a: Brig.-Gen. Edmond Jeffreys; Maj.-Gen. Sir Bindon Blood
result_basis: Jeffreys's brigades burned the valley's villages against stubborn resistance and the Mamunds submitted in October.
sources: W. S. Churchill, The Story of the Malakand Field Force (1898); H. D. Nevill, Campaigns on the North-West Frontier (1912)
note: Treated as one entry for the valley campaign; Churchill's account describes the fights at Agrah and Bilot.
qbasis: The Mamunds are a Pashtun (Tarkani) tribe of Bajaur (Churchill, who served in the campaign).

name: Saragarhi
label: Saragarhi
war: Frontier uprising of 1897 (Malakand, Mohmand and Tirah campaigns): Samana
place: Saragarhi, Samana Ridge, Kohat District, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
result_basis: The tribesmen overran the post after hours of fighting and killed all 21 defenders.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirah_campaign; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Saragarhi
note: Lockhart and Gulistan forts were also attacked on the same day; Gulistan is entered separately.
qbasis: The attackers were Orakzai and Afridi Pashtun tribesmen under Gul Badshah (Wikipedia 'Tirah campaign', fetched; Wikipedia 'Battle of Saragarhi').

name: Dargai Heights
label: Dargai Heights
date: 18 and 20 October 1897 (taken and given up on the 18th, stormed on the 20th)
place: Dargai Heights, near Shinawari, Kohat-Orakzai border, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
commanders_a: Gen. Sir William Lockhart; Maj.-Gen. Yeatman-Biggs; Brig.-Gen. Kempster
commanders_b: Mullah Sayyid Akbar (Aka Khel Afridi); Orakzai and Afridi maliks
result_basis: The Gordon Highlanders, with the 3rd Sikhs and Derbyshires, stormed the heights on 20 October at a cost of 199 killed and wounded.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirah_campaign; H. D. Nevill, Campaigns on the North-West Frontier (1912); A. Swinson, North-West Frontier (1967)
note: Piper Findlater's piping under fire made the second assault famous; the Afridi leader's name is from memory and the site is placed to the region.
qbasis: The Dargai Heights were held by about 12,000 Afridi and Orakzai Pashtun tribesmen (Wikipedia 'Tirah campaign', fetched; Nevill).

name: Saran Sar
label: Saran Sar
date: 9 and 11 November 1897 (Westmacott's first attack, Gaselee's second)
place: Saran Sar, Tirah, Khyber Agency, Pakistan
commanders_a: Brig.-Gen. Richard Westmacott; Brig.-Gen. Alfred Gaselee
commanders_b: Afridi and Orakzai maliks (names not verified)
result_basis: The position was taken on both occasions, but the first retirement was hard-pressed with 64 British casualties.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirah_campaign
note: Wikipedia's table gives the first attack as 'before 11 Nov'; 9 November is from memory.
qbasis: The Saran Sar ridge was held by Afridi Pashtun tribesmen (Wikipedia 'Tirah campaign', fetched).

name: Tseri Kandao
label: Tseri Kandao
place: Tseri Kandao Pass and the Waran Valley, Tirah, Khyber Agency, Pakistan
result_basis: Kempster's brigade destroyed the Waran villages but the rearguard was heavily engaged on the way back, with 72 casualties.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirah_campaign
note: A punitive raid on the Waran valley.
qbasis: The opposition on the Waran expedition was Afridi Pashtun tribesmen (Wikipedia 'Tirah campaign', fetched).

name: Bara Valley (1897)
label: Bara Valley
commanders_a: Gen. Sir William Lockhart; Maj.-Gen. Yeatman-Biggs
result_basis: The Afridis inflicted heavy casualties on the retiring columns in four days of snow and ice, but the columns reached the Peshawar column and the Khyber forts on 14 December.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirah_campaign; H. D. Nevill, Campaigns on the North-West Frontier (1912)
note: Kuki Khel and other Afridi clans; the Afridis later paid fines and gave up rifles, so the campaign ended in a British victory overall.
qbasis: The tribesmen who harassed the withdrawal through the Bara Valley were Afridi Pashtuns (Wikipedia 'Tirah campaign', fetched).

name: Bazar Valley campaign (Zakka Khel expedition)
label: Bazar Valley campaign
place: Bazar Valley, Khyber Agency (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan)
commanders_a: Zakka Khel maliks and mullahs (names not recorded here)
result_basis: Willcocks's columns swept the Bazar Valley, destroyed towers and held the valley until the Zakka Khel submitted and paid a fine.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bazar_Valley_campaign (title seen in search; not fetched)
note: Short expedition against the Zakka Khel section of the Afridis after raids on Peshawar; the Afridi were Pashtun tribesmen and so the lashkar qualifies.

name: Mohmand expedition of 1908
label: Mohmand expedition of 1908
place: Mohmand hills near Matta and the Karapa pass, Mohmand Agency (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan)
commanders_a: Mullah Najmuddin (the Hadda Mullah); Mohmand chiefs

note: Doubtful entry: my sources record a campaign and a defeat but no named engagement or date, and the fighting may have been slight. Reza Shah was Mazandarani; Jahanbani was of the Qajar family, so the Iranian-army rule rests on Reza Shah's leadership.

name: First Battle of Kabul (1928-1929)
label: First Battle of Kabul
result_basis: Kalakani entered the city, the army largely mutinied, and he held Murad Beg Fort until Amanullah abdicated on 14 January.

name: Fall of Kabul (January 1929)

persian_state: Saqqawists v Government of Inayatullah Khan
result_basis: Inayatullah abdicated and left Kabul and the Saqqawists took the Arg.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1928–1929)

note: Fuzail Maksum, a mullah of Karategin (Gharm), is described in Soviet and later literature as a Tajik leader of the Basmachi; the Wikipedia page fetched does not state his ethnicity. Famous in Soviet military history for the airlift of Red Army troops to the Gharm area. Size of his band not established here.

sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1928–1929)

doubt: Borderline: an engagement within the invasion; no separate article.
