result_basis: The government forces took the Afshar neighbourhood, though they failed to capture Mazari.
sources: Wikipedia, Afghan Civil War (1992-1996): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1992%E2%80%931996)
note: A military attack on Wahdat positions in a Hazara neighbourhood that turned into the Afshar massacre (Amnesty International). Borderline for a battle entry because the massacre of civilians dominates the record; kept as a named operation with real fighting.

name: Iraqi Kurdistan incursion (1993)
label: Iraqi Kurdistan incursion (1993)
date: April-May 1993 (a second cross-border attack on 9 August 1993)
persian_state: Islamic Republic of Iran v Kurdish rebels
persian_force: Iranian troops with artillery and aircraft (units not named; artillery and air strikes continued through 1993).
iranian_note: The IRGC and Artesh were raised from every province of Iran, so the force mirrored Iran's population, about three-quarters Iranian-speaking.
result_basis: Iranian forces crossed the border and occupied a 'security zone' of over 100 sq km against the Kurdish opposition forces.
borderline: a thinly documented cross-border incursion without a separate article
doubt: Borderline: a thinly documented cross-border incursion without a separate article.
sources: en.wikipedia KDPI insurgency (1989-1996)
qbasis: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state

name: Camp Ashraf air raid (1993)
label: Camp Ashraf air raid (1993)
place: Camp Ashraf (Diyala) and Jalat near Sulaymaniyah, Iraq
side_a: Islamic Republic of Iran Air Force
faction_a: Islamic Republic of Iran Air Force
persian_force: Government side: 12 IRIAF aircraft (MEK statement); MEK side: the NLA garrisons.
iranian_note: Both sides were Iranians.
result_basis: Twelve aircraft struck the two MEK camps according to the MEK, but no damage, casualties or losses are reported.
borderline: an air raid on camps known from one side's statement, without a separate article
doubt: A strike operation (air, missile or drone attacks): listed and mapped but not scored, because its result is judged by damage claims rather than by a held field. Borderline: an air raid on camps known from one side's statement, without a separate article.
sources: en.wikipedia Camp Ashraf
note: Iranian state media called it retaliation for MEK attacks on military personnel and oil pipelines in Khuzestan.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: 12th border post (Moscow Border Detachment, 1993)
label: 12th border post
date: 13 July 1993 (fight lasting more than eleven hours)
place: 12th outpost of the Moscow Border Detachment on the Tajik-Afghan frontier (Pyanj river, Khatlon); exact site not established
commanders_a: Not identified (one Russian account names a Tabarov among the planners)
result_basis: The post held after an 11-hour fight; 25 border guards were killed and the attack was repelled (TASS).
sources: Asia-Plus https://asiaplus.news/?p=15505 (fetched: about 250 fighters in 14 groups from Afghanistan; 48 defenders; 25 killed); TASS https://tass.com/world/697435 (fetched: 'Tajik gunmen'); Moscow Times archive 1993; RBTH 'Black Tuesday' (blocked)
note: Qualifies as an opposing Iranian force: the attackers are called Tajik gunmen of the opposition operating from Afghanistan (probably with Afghan mujahideen), but their composition and commander are not given in the sources fetched. The Russian post commander's name is from memory and unverified.

name: Kabul (1994)
label: Kabul
date: 1 January to about June 1994 (heaviest fighting January-February)
side_a: Supreme Coordination Council: Hezb-i Islami Gulbuddin, Junbish-i Milli, Hezb-i Wahdat and allies
persian_state: Supreme Coordination Council: Hezb-i Islami Gulbuddin, Junbish-i Milli, Hezb-i Wahdat and allies v Islamic State of Afghanistan
faction_a: Supreme Coordination Council: Hezb-i Islami Gulbuddin, Junbish-i Milli, Hezb-i Wahdat and allies
commanders_a: Gulbuddin Hekmatyar; Abdul Rashid Dostum (Uzbek); Abdul Ali Mazari
commanders_b: Burhanuddin Rabbani (president); Ahmad Shah Massoud (defence minister); Abdul Rasul Sayyaf
result_basis: The government held the core of Kabul, and Dostum's Junbish withdrew north after the heavy fighting, while HiG and Junbish held some districts in the centre for a time.
sources: Wikipedia, Afghan Civil War (1992-1996): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1992%E2%80%931996)
note: The worst fighting of the 1992-96 civil war in the capital; the Afghanistan Justice Project cites about 25,000 killed between January and June 1994. The Uzbek Junbish is not counted.

name: Spin Boldak (1994)
label: Spin Boldak
place: Spin Boldak, on the Pakistan border (Kandahar Province, Afghanistan)
commanders_b: Local Hezb-i Islami commander (not verified here)
result_basis: The Taliban took the town and the large Hezb-i Islami arms depot after a short fight, which gave them their first stock of heavy weapons.
sources: Wikipedia, Afghan Civil War (1992-1996): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1992%E2%80%931996)
note: The first notable Taliban action; fighting was short and the numbers are not firmly recorded, so the entry is weak. Both sides were Pashtun.

name: Kandahar (1994)
label: Kandahar
side_b: Kandahar commanders and Hezb-i Islami forces
persian_state: Taliban v Kandahar commanders and Hezb-i Islami forces
faction_b: Kandahar commanders and Hezb-i Islami forces
result_basis: The Taliban took the city and its airport and arsenal on 5 November, and the rival commanders fled or submitted.
sources: Wikipedia, Afghan Civil War (1992-1996): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1992%E2%80%931996)
note: The Taliban's take-over of their home city: some real fighting at the airport and the Kandahar garrison, but mostly negotiated surrender of the warlords.

name: Charasiab (1995)
label: Charasiab
place: Charasiab and the southern approaches of Kabul (Kabul Province, Afghanistan)
persian_state: Islamic State of Afghanistan v Taliban
result_basis: Massoud's offensive retook Charasiab on 19 March and drove the Taliban back from Kabul, their first major defeat.
sources: Wikipedia, Afghan Civil War (1992-1996): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1992%E2%80%931996)
note: Followed the Taliban's capture of Ghazni (January) and Maidan Shahr (10 February) and the killing of Wahdat's Mazari in Taliban custody on 13 March; the Taliban went on to retreat to Maidan Shahr and Ghazni.

name: Operation Steel (1995)
label: Operation Steel
place: Zap, Haftanin and Metina areas of northern Iraq (Duhok and Erbil Governorates)
result_basis: Turkish troops overran PKK camps in northern Iraq and then withdrew after six weeks, without breaking the PKK.
sources: Wikipedia 'Turkish military operations in Iraq' and 'Kurdish-Turkish conflict' (fetches failed; from memory); McDowall (2004); Marcus, Blood and Belief: the PKK and the Kurdish Fight for Independence (2007)
note: The largest Turkish operation of its time, with air support and the passive consent of the KDP. Both sides' casualty claims differ greatly.

name: Farah (1995)
label: Farah
date: 4 April to 11 May 1995 (Taliban attack 4 April; Ismail Khan recaptured the town 11 May)
persian_state: Taliban v Islamic State of Afghanistan
result_basis: The Taliban took Farah after killing about 800 government soldiers, but Ismail Khan recaptured the town on 11 May and held the west until the Taliban attacked again in September.
sources: Wikipedia, Afghan Civil War (1992-1996): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1992%E2%80%931996)
note: The two-step fight is merged into one entry; the exact dates come from the Wikipedia summary of the civil war.

name: Herat (1995)
label: Herat
persian_state: Taliban v Islamic State of Afghanistan
result_basis: The Taliban took Shindand air base and then entered Herat on 5 September, and Ismail Khan fled to Mashhad.
sources: Wikipedia, Afghan Civil War (1992-1996): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1992%E2%80%931996)
note: The Taliban's first conquest of a Persian-speaking city. Some accounts credit an informal Dostum-Taliban understanding for the collapse of Ismail Khan's front.

name: Tavildara (May 1996)
label: Tavildara
persian_state: United Tajik Opposition v Government of Tajikistan
result_basis: The opposition took the district centre, killing scores of government soldiers and capturing many, and seized arms and ammunition.
sources: Jamestown Monitor, 'Tajik opposition captures Tavildara', 13 May 1996 https://jamestown.org/program/tajik-opposition-captures-tavildara (fetched)
note: Both sides Tajik. Part of the opposition's spring 1996 offensive; the government later held it again until the opposition recaptured it in August 1996.

name: Koysanjaq incursion (1996)
label: Koysanjaq incursion (1996)
persian_state: Islamic Republic of Iran v Kurdish rebels
commanders_a: IRGC commanders (not named in the sources used)
persian_force: About 2,000-3,000 Iranian troops (IRGC ground forces with artillery support), allowed through PUK-held territory by Jalal Talabani.
iranian_note: IRGC units of the 1990s were raised by national conscription and volunteering, mostly Persian speakers with Azeri Turkic and Kurdish minorities; the sources give no unit breakdown.
strength_a: about 3,000 (KDPI insurgency article); 2,000 (Iraqi Kurdish Civil War infobox)
result_basis: The Iranian column reached and shelled the KDPI camps around Koysanjaq, killing about 20 guerrillas and scattering some 2,000 refugees, and withdrew unopposed; the KDPI announced a halt to cross-border attacks a week later (a strategic consequence).
borderline: no separate article; a cross-border incursion described by date and place in the KDPI insurgency and Iraqi Kurdish Civil War articles
doubt: Borderline: no separate article; a cross-border incursion described by date and place in the KDPI insurgency and Iraqi Kurdish Civil War articles.
sources: en.wikipedia KDPI insurgency (1989-1996) and Iraqi Kurdish Civil War
note: Iran called it self-defence against KDPI raids. On 4 August 1996 the KDPI declared a unilateral halt to cross-border attacks, ending its 1989-1996 insurgency. The incursion prompted Masoud Barzani to call in the Iraqi army against the PUK (Erbil, 31 August 1996).
qbasis: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state

name: Erbil (1996)
label: Erbil
persian_state: Iraq v Patriotic Union of Kurdistan
faction_b: Patriotic Union of Kurdistan, Iraqi National Congress
commanders_a: Masoud Barzani (KDP); Iraqi Republican Guard armoured division (about 30,000 Iraqi troops)
commanders_b: Kosrat Rasul Ali (PUK Peshmerga, about 3,000); Jalal Talabani
result_basis: The Iraqi Republican Guard and the KDP took Erbil in a day, and the PUK and INC fighters withdrew.
sources: Wikipedia 'Iraqi Kurdish Civil War' (fetched); McDowall, A Modern History of the Kurds (2004); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraqi_Kurdish_Civil_War
note: The KDP asked Baghdad for help after an Iranian incursion on the PUK side in July 1996. Both Kurdish parties fought, so Kurds are on both sides. About 700 INC and PUK prisoners were reportedly executed afterwards.

name: Tavildara (August 1996)
label: Tavildara
date: 16 August 1996 (confirmed by the government on 20 August)
persian_state: United Tajik Opposition v Government of Tajikistan
commanders_a: Mirzo Ziyoyev's command (not named in the source)
result_basis: The opposition retook Tavildara and several villages; military officials admitted 30 government dead.
sources: Jamestown Monitor, 20 Aug 1996 https://jamestown.org/program/tajik-oppositions-recapture-of-tavildara-confirmed-russia-warns-afghanistan (fetched)
note: Both sides Tajik. The government had tried to hide the defeat; Rahmonov then reshuffled his security chiefs. Commander attribution to Ziyoyev is inferred from his command of the Tavildara front.

name: Kabul (1996)
label: Kabul
persian_state: Taliban v Islamic State of Afghanistan
commanders_a: Mullah Mohammad Omar (supreme leader); Mullah Mohammad Rabbani
commanders_b: Ahmad Shah Massoud; Burhanuddin Rabbani; Gulbuddin Hekmatyar (prime minister; withdrew)
result_basis: After the Taliban took Sarobi on 25 September, Massoud judged his forces nearly encircled and withdrew north, and the Taliban entered Kabul and proclaimed the Islamic Emirate.
sources: Wikipedia, Afghan Civil War (1992-1996): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1992%E2%80%931996)
note: Massoud pulled out rather than fight it to a finish, so the real combat was at Sarobi and on the eastern approaches. Najibullah was taken from the UN compound and killed.

name: Sulaymaniyah (1996)
label: Sulaymaniyah (1996)
persian_force: Alleged Iranian support for the PUK (Iran is credited with 2,000 troops in Iraqi Kurdistan in 1996); no Iranian units are named.
iranian_note: No Iranian unit is identified; the PUK fighters themselves were Kurdish-speaking.
result_basis: The PUK retook Sulaymaniyah from the KDP on 13 October 1996.
borderline: Iranian participation is only alleged ('allegedly with support of Iranian forces'); both principals were Iraqi Kurdish parties (PUK as side_a, KDP as side_b, both under 'Kurdish rebels')
doubt: Borderline: Iranian participation is only alleged ('allegedly with support of Iranian forces'); both principals were Iraqi Kurdish parties (PUK as side_a, KDP as side_b, both under 'Kurdish rebels').
sources: en.wikipedia Iraqi Kurdish Civil War
note: Listed as contingent only; the KDP had taken Sulaymaniyah in September 1996 with Iraqi army help.
qbasis: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state

name: Mazar-i-Sharif (1997)
label: Mazar-i-Sharif
date: 24-28 May 1997 (Taliban entered 24-25 May; driven out by 28 May)
side_a: Junbish forces of Abdul Malik Pahlawan, Hezb-i Wahdat and local Jamiat forces
persian_state: Junbish forces of Abdul Malik Pahlawan, Hezb-i Wahdat and local Jamiat forces v Taliban
faction_a: Junbish forces of Abdul Malik Pahlawan, Hezb-i Wahdat and local Jamiat forces
commanders_a: Abdul Malik Pahlawan (Uzbek); Haji Mohammad Mohaqiq (Wahdat)
commanders_b: Mullah Abdul Razzaq; Mullah Mohammad Ghaus
result_basis: After Malik let the Taliban in, his men and the Wahdat Hazaras turned on them and drove them out, killing or capturing thousands (Wikipedia estimates about 3,000 killed).
sources: Wikipedia, Afghan Civil War (1996-2001): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1996%E2%80%932001)
note: Dostum's Junbish (Uzbek) split when Malik turned on him; the Taliban's defeat here was one of the largest of the war. Leaders' names are from memory and uncertain.

name: Operation Hammer (1997)
label: Operation Hammer
place: Zakho, Amadiya and the Haftanin-Zap area of northern Iraq
commanders_a: Turkish General Staff (about 50,000 troops); Masoud Barzani (KDP)
result_basis: Turkish troops and KDP Peshmerga forced the PKK out of the border zone and took heavy casualties on the PKK, but the PKK kept its main camps.
sources: Wikipedia 'Iraqi Kurdish Civil War' (fetched; names Operation Hammer, May 1997) and 'Operation Hammer'; McDowall (2004); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraqi_Kurdish_Civil_War
note: The KDP fought on the Turkish side because of its war with the PUK, which was allied with the PKK. The end date is approximate.

name: Operation Dawn (1997)
label: Operation Dawn
place: Northern Iraq (PUK- and PKK-held areas east of Rawandiz and Sidakan)
faction_b: Kurdistan Workers' Party, Patriotic Union of Kurdistan
commanders_a: Turkish General Staff (about 15,000 troops); Masoud Barzani (KDP)
result_basis: Turkish forces with KDP help struck PKK and PUK positions and caused heavy casualties among both, then withdrew.
sources: Wikipedia 'Iraqi Kurdish Civil War' (fetched: 25 September 1997 Turkish re-entry); McDowall (2004); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraqi_Kurdish_Civil_War
note: A shorter sequel to Operation Hammer, aimed at the PUK-PKK alliance. Details of the Turkish force and end date are approximate.

name: Mazar-i-Sharif (1998)
label: Mazar-i-Sharif
side_b: Junbish forces, Hezb-i Wahdat and Jamiat
persian_state: Taliban v Junbish forces, Hezb-i Wahdat and Jamiat
faction_b: Junbish forces, Hezb-i Wahdat and Jamiat
commanders_a: Mullah Mohammad Omar (supreme leader); Mullah Abdul Manan Niazi (later governor)
commanders_b: Abdul Malik Pahlawan (Uzbek); Karim Khalili (Wahdat); Atta Muhammad Nur (Jamiat)
result_basis: The Taliban took Mazar-i-Sharif on 8 August, the northern alliance's main city, and went on to seize Hairatan and the rest of the north.
sources: Wikipedia, Afghan Civil War (1996-2001): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1996%E2%80%932001)
note: Followed by the massacre of Hazara civilians (about 4,000 killed) and the killing of Iranian diplomats; the Uzbek Junbish is not counted.

name: Bamyan (1998)
label: Bamyan
result_basis: The Taliban took Bamyan after the fall of Mazar-i-Sharif, with the Hazara forces withdrawing into the highlands.
sources: Wikipedia, Afghan Civil War (1996-2001): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1996%E2%80%932001) (the page notes Bamyan in 1998 only in passing)
note: Weakly documented: the capture followed Mazar and seems to have involved little set-piece fighting, though the Hazara retreat was contested. A weak entry; the Hazara guerrilla war that continued is not covered.

name: Khujand (November 1998)
label: Khujand
place: Khujand and Chkalovsk (Buston), Sughd (Leninabad) region, Tajikistan
commanders_a: Tajik government commanders (Defence Minister Sherali Khayrulloyev); UTO field commander Mirzo Ziyoyev assisted
result_basis: Government forces repelled the rebels, who withdrew to Uzbekistan after several days of fighting around Khujand.
sources: Wikipedia 'Mirzo Ahmadovich Ziyoev' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirzo_Ahmadovich_Ziyoev (fetched: he assisted government forces in suppressing Khudoiberdiev's rebellion, Nov 1998); HRW 1998 Leninabad report; Nourzhanov and Bleuer (2013)
note: Government army and former UTO fighters on one side (Tajik); the rebels were a mixed force of former Popular Front and Hissari fighters led by an ethnic Uzbek colonel, so Iranian status of the rebel side is not counted. Rebel numbers and dates are from memory of standard accounts; Wikipedia fetched gives only the fact of the suppression. WEAK on detail.

name: Shomali Plain (1999)
label: Shomali Plain
place: Shomali Plain north of Kabul, Bagram, Charikar and Istalif (Parwan and Kabul provinces, Afghanistan)
side_b: United Front forces of Ahmad Shah Massoud
persian_state: Taliban v United Front forces of Ahmad Shah Massoud
faction_b: United Front forces of Ahmad Shah Massoud
result_basis: The Taliban overran the Shomali Plain, burned villages and drove the population out, and Massoud's forces fell back to the Panjshir and Salang approaches.
sources: Wikipedia, Afghan Civil War (1996-2001): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1996%E2%80%932001)
note: The Taliban kept the plain until the American air campaign of late 2001. Fighting involved large numbers on both sides; the Wikipedia civil-war page does not give details, so day-level dating is approximate.

name: Taloqan (2000)
label: Taloqan
date: 5 September 2000 (siege and offensive from about late July 2000; start date not verified)
side_b: United Front forces of Ahmad Shah Massoud
persian_state: Taliban v United Front forces of Ahmad Shah Massoud
faction_b: United Front forces of Ahmad Shah Massoud
result_basis: The Taliban captured Taloqan, Massoud's headquarters town, on 5 September 2000 after a siege, and the United Front held the line north and east of the city.
sources: Wikipedia, Taloqan: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taloqan; Wikipedia, Afghan Civil War (1996-2001): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1996%E2%80%932001)
note: The last major city to fall to the Taliban before 2001 (the fetched page says the siege killed hundreds of civilians); the Taliban were joined by the IMU in the siege according to the civil-war article.

name: Scud strikes on MEK camps (2001)
label: Scud strikes on MEK camps (2001)
place: MEK camps in Iraq (Camp Ashraf and others), Iraq
persian_force: Government side: IRGC ballistic-missile units firing Scud-B missiles from western Iran; MEK side: the NLA camps.
iranian_note: Both sides were Iranians.
result_basis: Dozens of Scud-B missiles were fired at MEK bases across Iraq, but no reliable account of hits or damage is available.
borderline: strike operation; not verified in Wikipedia; number of missiles uncertain
doubt: A strike operation (air, missile or drone attacks): listed and mapped but not scored, because its result is judged by damage claims rather than by a held field. Borderline: strike operation; not verified in Wikipedia; number of missiles uncertain.
sources: contemporary press reports (Reuters, BBC, April 2001); not covered by the Wikipedia articles fetched
note: Recorded from contemporary reports; the date and scale should be checked.
qbasis: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Herat (uprising, 2001)
label: Herat (uprising, 2001)
commanders_a: Ismail Khan (Northern Alliance); Tommy Franks; Yahya Rahim Safavi and Qasem Soleimani (IRGC)
persian_force: IRGC Quds Force agents in Herat, directed by Safavi and Soleimani, who were to enter the city covertly and start the uprising; the fighting force was about 5,000 Northern Alliance militiamen.
iranian_note: Only the Quds Force agents are counted; Iranian, Persian-speaking (the Herati militia also spoke Dari Persian).
result_basis: The city fell to Ismail Khan's forces on 12 November 2001 and the Taliban fled toward the mountains.
sources: en.wikipedia 2001 uprising in Herat
note: 'Afghans' here is the Northern Alliance of Ismail Khan.
qbasis: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state

name: Kandahar (2001)
label: Kandahar
date: late November to 7 December 2001 (negotiated surrender announced 6 December; city entered 7 December)
side_a: Pashtun forces of Hamid Karzai and Gul Agha Sherzai
persian_state: Pashtun forces of Hamid Karzai and Gul Agha Sherzai v Taliban
faction_a: Pashtun forces of Hamid Karzai and Gul Agha Sherzai
result_basis: The Taliban agreed a surrender on 6 December, Sherzai's men took the airport and city on 7 December, and Mullah Omar left.
sources: Wikipedia, United States invasion of Afghanistan: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_invasion_of_Afghanistan
note: The fall of the Taliban's capital after air attacks and the fights at Shin-Narai, Sayyd Alma Kalay and Camp Rhino; the surrender rather than a final assault ended it. Pashtuns on both sides.

name: Kunduz (siege, 2001)
label: Kunduz
date: 11-26 November 2001 (siege; surrender negotiated 21-23 November; city taken 25-26 November)
persian_state: Northern Alliance v Taliban garrison of Kunduz
commanders_a: General Mohammad Daud Daud (Tajik); Abdul Rashid Dostum (Uzbek)
commanders_b: Taliban and volunteer commanders in Kunduz (not individually verified)
result_basis: After about two weeks of siege and air attack, the Taliban and foreign fighters surrendered in stages on 23-26 November and the Northern Alliance took the city.
sources: Wikipedia, United States invasion of Afghanistan: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_invasion_of_Afghanistan (the page treats the surrender briefly)
note: The last Taliban stronghold in the north. Numbers in the garrison vary widely (perhaps 10,000) and the foreign volunteers were a large share. The captives from Kunduz were taken to Qala-i-Jangi.

name: Mazar-i-Sharif (2001)
label: Mazar-i-Sharif
date: 5-10 November 2001 (Baluch 5 November; Tangi Pass 8-9 November; city entered 10 November)
place: Mazar-i-Sharif and the Tangi Pass (Balkh Province, Afghanistan)
persian_state: Northern Alliance v Taliban garrison of the north
commanders_a: Atta Muhammad Nur (Tajik); Mohammad Mohaqiq (Hazara); Abdul Rashid Dostum (Uzbek)
commanders_b: Taliban commanders of Balkh (Mullah Nurullah Nuri, governor)
result_basis: The Northern Alliance forced the Tangi Pass on 9 November and entered Mazar-i-Sharif on 10 November as the Taliban retreated, the first major city to fall.
sources: Wikipedia, United States invasion of Afghanistan: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_invasion_of_Afghanistan
note: The first great success of the US-Northern Alliance campaign, helped by American special forces (ODA 595 and 534) and B-52 strikes. Dostum's Junbish (Uzbek) is not counted as Iranian. The Taliban were mostly Pashtun.

name: Qala-i-Jangi (2001)
label: Qala-i-Jangi
date: 25 November to 1 December 2001 (prisoner revolt and its suppression)
place: Qala-i-Jangi fortress, west of Mazar-i-Sharif (Balkh Province, Afghanistan)
side_a: Northern Alliance guards of Dostum's Junbish
result_basis: Dostum's forces, with AC-130 and aircraft support, crushed the revolt over six days; of the prisoners (estimates range from about 300-500 up to 1,000) only 86 survived, and about 50 Northern Alliance soldiers died (Wikipedia).
sources: Wikipedia, United States invasion of Afghanistan: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_invasion_of_Afghanistan
note: Doubtful for the Iranian rule: the prisoners were mostly Pakistanis, Uzbeks, Arabs and Chechens, with an unmeasured number of Afghan Taliban (Pashtun), and the guards were mainly Dostum's Uzbeks. Kept because it is a famous battle in the assigned span; qualification uncertain.

name: Taloqan (2001)
label: Taloqan
commanders_b: Taliban commanders of Takhar (not recorded here)
result_basis: The Northern Alliance took Taloqan in a quick infantry assault on 11 November, before the first planned bomb was dropped.
sources: Wikipedia, United States invasion of Afghanistan: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_invasion_of_Afghanistan; Wikipedia, Taloqan: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taloqan
note: Retaking Massoud's old headquarters town; the Taliban garrison gave way quickly.

name: Tarin Kowt (2001)
label: Tarin Kowt
side_a: Pashtun anti-Taliban militia of Hamid Karzai
persian_state: Pashtun anti-Taliban militia of Hamid Karzai v Taliban of Uruzgan
faction_a: Pashtun anti-Taliban militia of Hamid Karzai
commanders_b: Taliban commanders of Uruzgan (not recorded here)
result_basis: Karzai's force held Tarin Kowt after the town rose against the Taliban, and the Taliban counter-attack was beaten off with American close air support.
sources: Wikipedia, United States invasion of Afghanistan: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_invasion_of_Afghanistan
note: The first Pashtun uprising in the south. Pashtuns fought on both sides; the Taliban counter-attack came from Kandahar and was destroyed by air power.

name: Sayyd Alma Kalay (2001)
label: Sayyd Alma Kalay
date: about 3-5 December 2001 (bridge battle; friendly-fire bombing 5 December; the Wikipedia invasion article dates it only to late November)
place: Sayyd Alma Kalay bridge over the Arghandab, near Shawali Kot (Kandahar Province, Afghanistan)
side_a: Pashtun anti-Taliban force of Hamid Karzai
persian_state: Pashtun anti-Taliban force of Hamid Karzai v Taliban
faction_a: Pashtun anti-Taliban force of Hamid Karzai
result_basis: Karzai's force took the bridge, opening the road to Kandahar, and the Taliban then entered the surrender talks.
sources: Wikipedia, United States invasion of Afghanistan: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_invasion_of_Afghanistan
note: Fought two days; the 5 December friendly-fire bombing killed American soldiers and Afghans and wounded Karzai. The exact dates are uncertain.

name: Tora Bora (2001)
label: Tora Bora
date: air attacks from mid-November; main ground fighting 12-17 December 2001
place: Tora Bora cave complex, White Mountains (Nangarhar Province, Afghanistan)
persian_state: Eastern Alliance v Al-Qaeda and Taliban remnants
commanders_a: Hazrat Ali (Pashtun); Haji Zaman Ghamsharik (Pashtun); Haji Zahir (Pashtun)
result_basis: The Eastern Alliance and American air power took the cave complex by 17 December, but bin Laden and a number of fighters escaped into Pakistan.
sources: Wikipedia, United States invasion of Afghanistan: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_invasion_of_Afghanistan
note: The anti-Taliban militias were Pashtun and did most of the ground fighting; the defenders were largely Arab al-Qaeda fighters with some Afghan Taliban and local tribesmen, so the Iranian share on side B is small.

name: Operation Anaconda (Shah-i-Kot)
label: Operation Anaconda
place: Shah-i-Kot Valley and Arma Ghar, near Gardez, Paktia (Afghanistan)
persian_state: United States-led coalition v Al-Qaeda, Taliban and Haqqani-network fighters
commanders_a: Maj. Gen. Franklin Hagenbeck (CJTF Mountain); Zia Lodin (Pashtun commander of the Afghan Interim Administration militia); Zakim Khan; Kamal Khan
commanders_b: Saif ur-Rahman Mansur (Zadran Pashtun, Haqqani network); Tohir Yuldashev (IMU, not Iranian)
result_basis: After two weeks of air strikes and ground sweeps the coalition and Afghan militia held the valley and ridges while most of the enemy slipped away into Pakistan.
sources: Wikipedia, Operation Anaconda: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Anaconda; Wikipedia, List of military operations in the war in Afghanistan (2001-2021)
note: The first large set-piece battle after Tora Bora. About a thousand Afghan militiamen under Zia Lodin (Pashtun) fought on the coalition side, and the enemy included local Pashtun Taliban and Haqqani fighters alongside the foreign fighters, so both sides had an Iranian element; the enemy's share of Pashtuns is a guess.

name: Operation Viking Hammer
label: Operation Viking Hammer
place: Khurmal, Sargat and the Ansar al-Islam enclave near Halabja, Sulaymaniyah Governorate, Iraqi Kurdistan
faction_a: United States, Patriotic Union of Kurdistan
commanders_a: Col. Charles Cleveland (US 10th SFG); PUK Peshmerga commanders
result_basis: US special forces and about 1,000-plus PUK Peshmerga drove Ansar al-Islam out of its mountain strongholds in three days.
sources: Wikipedia 'Operation Viking Hammer' and 'Peshmerga'; Briscoe et al., Weapon of Choice (2003); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peshmerga
note: Ansar al-Islam was itself mostly Kurdish (with Arab volunteers), so Kurds were on both sides. The Peshmerga formed the bulk of the ground force.

name: Operation Mountain Viper
label: Operation Mountain Viper
allies_a: Afghan Militia Forces and early Afghan National Army
commanders_a: US task force commanders (not named in the sources consulted)
commanders_b: Local Taliban commanders (Mullah Dadullah's network; individuals not named in the sources consulted)
result_basis: The coalition forces killed over a hundred Taliban and the group dispersed from the Daychopan valleys, though they returned in 2004.
sources: Wikipedia, List of military operations in the war in Afghanistan (2001-2021): Operation Mountain Viper (30 Aug-Sep 2003, Dey Chopan, Zabul)
note: One of the first big engagements with the regrouped Taliban in the south. Taliban fighters in Zabul were Pashtun (Tokhi, Hotak and Kakar tribesmen); commander names not checked, so the commander list is a placeholder.

name: Battle of Wana (2004)
label: Wana
date: 16 March to April 2004 (main fighting 16-18 March; Shakai agreement 24 April)
war: Insurgency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (War in North-West Pakistan)
side_b: Ahmadzai Wazir tribal militants of Nek Muhammad Wazir
persian_state: Ahmadzai Wazir tribal militants of Nek Muhammad Wazir
result_basis: The army failed to capture or destroy the militants and ended the operation with the Shakai agreement (24 April 2004) with Nek Muhammad, which many Pakistani commentators called a militant success.
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Wana: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Wana; Wikipedia, War in North-West Pakistan
note: The first major Pakistani army operation in the tribal areas after 2001, against the Wazir militants sheltering Uzbek and Arab fighters. The Frontier Corps also fought on the government side (a Pashtun force), but the main Iranian side is the militants.

name: Dera Bugti (March 2005)
label: Dera Bugti
place: Dera Bugti and the Sui gas field, Balochistan, Pakistan
commanders_b: Frontier Corps Balochistan (Major-General Shujaat Zamir Dar, IG FC)
result_basis: Several days of shelling and gun battles ended in a ceasefire with the Frontier Corps still in the town and the Bugti militia in the hills.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insurgency_in_Balochistan (fetched: Bugti uprising 2005-06); BBC and Dawn reports, March 2005, from memory
note: The Bugti are Baloch under a hereditary Baloch chief. Casualty figures (dozens killed, including civilians) are disputed and from memory.

name: Operation Red Wings
label: Operation Red Wings
date: 27 June to mid-July 2005 (main battle 28 June, Abbas Ghar)
place: Korengal and Pech area near Asadabad, Kunar Province (Afghanistan)
commanders_a: Lt. Michael Murphy (SEAL team leader); Cdr. Erik Kristensen
result_basis: A four-man SEAL team was compromised and three killed, a rescue helicopter was shot down with 16 more US dead, and only Marcus Luttrell survived, sheltered by villagers; the militia lost an estimated 30-35.
sources: Wikipedia, Operation Red Wings: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Red_Wings
note: Famous for the book and film Lone Survivor. The enemy were Kunar mountain fighters; Ahmad Shah's own origin (Pashtun or Nuristani/Pashai) is not firmly settled in the sources, so qualification is doubtful.

name: April 2006 Iran-Iraq cross-border raids
label: April 2006 Iran-Iraq cross-border raids
date: 3 April 2006 (PJAK attacks); Iranian shelling and incursion near Mount Qandil 21-28 April 2006
theatre: Iranian Kurdistan and the Qandil mountains
place: Iran-Iraq border near Mount Qandil, Iraq and north-western Iran
persian_state: Islamic Republic of Iran v Kurdish rebels
persian_force: Iranian border garrisons and security forces, then IRGC artillery and troops in a brief cross-border incursion (units not named).
iranian_note: Iranian security forces in the Kurdish border provinces were national conscripts and IRGC regulars, mostly Persian speakers with Kurdish and Azeri Turkic minorities; no breakdown in the sources.
losses_b: about 10 militants killed in the Iranian shelling (reports)
result_basis: PJAK's three raids of early April and Iran's retaliatory shelling and brief incursion near Mount Qandil each struck and withdrew, and Wikipedia records the result as indecisive.
borderline: a series of raids and shelling rather than one battle
doubt: Borderline: a series of raids and shelling rather than one battle.
sources: en.wikipedia April 2006 Iran-Iraq cross-border raids; Iran-PJAK conflict
note: PJAK said its raids avenged the killing of 10 Kurdish demonstrators at Maku in February 2006. The Iraqi defence ministry reported nearly 100 Iranian shells on the Qandil area.
qbasis: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state

name: Operation Mountain Thrust
label: Operation Mountain Thrust
place: Kandahar, Helmand, Uruzgan, Zabul and Paktika provinces (Afghanistan)
persian_state: ISAF and Operation Enduring Freedom v Taliban
result_basis: The coalition reported over a thousand Taliban killed and pushed them from several districts, but the Taliban regrouped in Panjwayi within weeks.
sources: Wikipedia, List of military operations in the war in Afghanistan (2001-2021); Wikipedia, Operation Mountain Thrust
note: The largest offensive since 2001 at the time; Pashtun Taliban on one side and Afghan National Army units fighting beside the coalition. Reported enemy losses are coalition claims.

name: Battle of Musa Qala (2006 siege)
label: Musa Qala
side_b: Taliban and local tribal fighters of Upper Helmand
persian_state: ISAF v Taliban and local tribal fighters of Upper Helmand
faction_b: Taliban and local tribal fighters of Upper Helmand
commanders_a: Brig. Ed Butler (UK Task Force Helmand); Lt. Col. Stuart Tootal (3 PARA)
commanders_b: Local Taliban commanders (Mullah Salaam and others)
result_basis: The British garrison in the district centre was withdrawn under the 17 October 2006 agreement with the elders, and the Taliban soon took the town (February 2007).
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Musa Qala: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Musa_Qala
note: A long siege of the district centre including Operation Snakebite (August 2006). The Afghan police posted there fought beside the British; the Taliban side was Pashtun (Alizai and Ishaqzai).

name: Tarateni (Kohlu, death of Akbar Bugti, 2006)
label: Tarateni
place: Tarateni, mountains of Kohlu district, Balochistan, Pakistan (cave site approximate)
commanders_a: Pakistan Army field commanders (not named in my sources)
result_basis: Akbar Bugti, aged 79, was killed in the operation; the army also lost several officers and soldiers (Wikipedia gives at least 60 soldiers and 7 officers dead; official figures were lower).
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insurgency_in_Balochistan (fetched); Dawn and BBC, 27 August 2006, from memory
note: An armed assault on a hideout, not a field battle, but it is the best-documented single fight of the 2005-06 war and triggered the wider insurgency.

name: Operation Medusa (Battle of Panjwaii)
label: Operation Medusa
place: Pashmul, Panjwayi and Zhari districts, Kandahar Province (Afghanistan)
commanders_a: Brig. Gen. David Fraser (Canadian, Task Force Orion)
result_basis: After several days of heavy fighting and air strikes ISAF cleared the Pashmul pocket and the Taliban withdrew, although they later returned to the area.
sources: Wikipedia, Operation Medusa: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Medusa
note: The biggest NATO ground battle in Afghanistan up to that date. About 1,000-1,500 Taliban stood to fight; Afghan National Army units were part of the assault force.

name: September 2006 Sardasht incident
label: September 2006 Sardasht incident
place: Iran-Iraq border near Sardasht, West Azerbaijan, Iran
persian_state: Islamic Republic of Iran v Kurdish rebels
persian_force: Iranian border and security forces of the IRGC (units not named).
iranian_note: Inferred from IRGC recruitment in this period; the sources give no breakdown.
result_basis: By the Iranian account, Iranian security forces killed over 30 PJAK fighters and wounded 40 in the clash; PJAK did not contest the field and then declared a unilateral ceasefire.
borderline: a small border clash known mainly from one side's claims
doubt: Borderline: a small border clash known mainly from one side's claims.
sources: en.wikipedia September 2006 Sardasht incident; Iran-PJAK conflict
note: Only the Iranian casualty claim is reported; the outcome rests on it. Iran rejected PJAK's ceasefire offer.
qbasis: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state

name: 2007 West Azerbaijan clashes
label: 2007 West Azerbaijan clashes
place: Khoy and the Turkish border districts of West Azerbaijan, Iran
persian_state: Islamic Republic of Iran v Kurdish rebels
commanders_a: IRGC commander Said Qahari (killed in the helicopter crash of 24 February); other commanders not named
persian_force: IRGC ground forces and the regular army's 3rd Corps in West Azerbaijan, with IRGC helicopters.
iranian_note: IRGC and army units in West Azerbaijan drew on national conscripts and local Azeri Turkic and Kurdish recruits; no breakdown in the sources.
losses_a: 17 soldiers killed (25 February-1 March), plus 8-20 IRGC killed in the helicopter crash (Iranian and PJAK figures)
losses_b: 47 killed (Iranian figure, 25 February-1 March); 17 killed 22-24 February (unsourced)
result_basis: After the loss of an IRGC helicopter near Khoy, the IRGC counter-offensive killed 47 rebels for 17 soldiers by its own count, but neither side drove the other from the area and Wikipedia gives the result as indecisive.
sources: en.wikipedia 2007 West Azerbaijan clashes; Iran-PJAK conflict
note: The Wikipedia infobox misdates the clashes to 2006; the text and the Iran-PJAK article give 2007. Iran blamed the helicopter crash on weather; PJAK claimed to have shot it down.
qbasis: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state

name: Operation Achilles
label: Operation Achilles
place: Sangin and Kajaki districts, Helmand Province (Afghanistan)
commanders_a: Brig. John Lorimer (UK Task Force Helmand)
commanders_b: Mullah Dadullah (southern commander, killed 12 May 2007); Mullah Mansour Dadullah
result_basis: ISAF secured the Kajaki dam area and Sangin valley and the Taliban lost ground and several commanders, though the Taliban held much of northern Helmand.
sources: Wikipedia, List of military operations in the war in Afghanistan (2001-2021): Operation Achilles
note: At the time the largest NATO operation of the war (about 4,500 troops). Real fighting around Sangin and Kajaki; outcome claimed as a success by ISAF.

name: Battle of Chora
label: Chora
side_a: Netherlands, Australia and the Afghan National Army
persian_state: Netherlands, Australia and the Afghan National Army v Taliban
faction_a: Netherlands, Australia and the Afghan National Army
commanders_a: Dutch Task Force Uruzgan and Australian task group commanders (not named in the sources consulted)
result_basis: Dutch, Australian and Afghan forces, with air support, held the Chora district centre against a Taliban assault and the attackers withdrew.
sources: Wikipedia, List of military operations in the war in Afghanistan (2001-2021): Battle of Chora (15-19 Jun 2007)
note: Taliban attempted to take the Chora district centre; the Dutch fought their first major action in Uruzgan. Commander names were not checked.

name: Daglica (2007)
label: Daglica
result_basis: The PKK overran the Turkish army post, killing about 12 soldiers and taking 8 prisoners, and withdrew into Iraq.
sources: Wikipedia 'Kurdish-Turkish conflict'; press reports (BBC, Reuters, Oct 2007); from memory
note: The attack led Turkey to win parliamentary approval for the cross-border operations of December 2007 and Operation Sun in 2008. The Turkish counter-attack in the area claimed dozens of PKK dead.

name: First Battle of Swat (Operation Rah-e-Haq)
label: First Battle of Swat
date: 25 October to December 2007 (mopping up into early 2008)
war: Insurgency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (War in North-West Pakistan)
place: Swat Valley (Matta, Kabal, Imam Dheri, Khwazakhela), Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (Pakistan)
side_a: Pakistan Army, Special Service Group and Frontier Corps
side_b: Tehrik-e Nifaz-e Shariat-e Mohammadi and Swat Taliban of Maulana Fazlullah
persian_state: Tehrik-e Nifaz-e Shariat-e Mohammadi and Swat Taliban of Maulana Fazlullah
commanders_b: Maulana Fazlullah (Swati Yusufzai); Muslim Khan; Maulana Shah Dauran
result_basis: The army retook Matta, Khwazakhela and Fazlullah's headquarters at Imam Dheri by December, though Fazlullah escaped and the Taliban returned in force in 2008.
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Swat (2007) / Operation Rah-e-Haq: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Swat_(2007)
note: The first major army operation in Swat after the 2007 uprising of Fazlullah's followers. The Pakistan Army is not counted as Iranian; the Frontier Corps also fought on the government side.

name: Second Battle of Musa Qala
label: Second Battle of Musa Qala
commanders_a: Brig. Andrew Mackay; General Mahayadin Ghori (Afghan National Army)
commanders_b: Abdul-Mannan; Abdul-Rahim; Abdul-Matin Akhund; Abdul-Bari Akhund
result_basis: The coalition and Afghan army advanced into the town, the Taliban withdrew north on 10 December and Afghan troops entered the centre on 12 December.
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Musa Qala: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Musa_Qala
note: Operation Snakepit/Mar Lek: about 4,500 ISAF and Afghan troops against 200-2,000 Taliban (figures differ). Mullah Salaam's later defection made the town a government base.

name: Operation Zalzala (South Waziristan, 2008)
label: Operation Zalzala
war: Insurgency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (War in North-West Pakistan)
place: Ladha, Sararogha and Makeen, South Waziristan (Pakistan)
commanders_a: Pakistani XII Corps and 14th Division commanders (not named in the sources consulted)
result_basis: The army relieved besieged forts and retook Ladha, but Baitullah Mehsud kept control of the Mehsud heartland and a peace agreement followed in February 2008.
sources: Wikipedia, Operation Zalzala (2008): recalled from memory; not fetched
note: Fighting around Fort Ladha and Sararogha in the winter of 2007-2008 after the TTP's formation. Dates and outcome come from memory and are weak.

name: Operation Sun (2008)
label: Operation Sun
place: Zap, Avashin and Hakurk areas of northern Iraq
result_basis: Turkey withdrew after eight days, claiming hundreds of PKK dead against 27 Turkish soldiers, while the PKK kept its bases and claimed victory.
sources: Wikipedia 'Operation Sun (2008)' (from memory); press reports (BBC, 29 Feb 2008)
note: The first Turkish ground operation in Iraq since 1997 and the only one stopped by US and Iraqi pressure and winter weather. Casualty claims on both sides conflict.

name: Battle of Garmsir (2008)
label: Garmsir
date: 29 April to 8 September 2008 (also given as April-September)
persian_state: United States and Britain v Taliban
result_basis: The Marines pushed the Taliban out of Garmsir district and held the district centre; the offensive ended on schedule in September.
sources: Wikipedia, List of military operations in the war in Afghanistan (2001-2021): Battle of Garmsir (Apr-8 Sep 2008)
note: A Marine battalion landing team cleared the southern Helmand river valley. Start date given loosely.

name: Battle of Shok Valley
label: Shok Valley
persian_state: United States with Afghan commandos v Hizb-i Islami fighters
result_basis: After six hours of fighting and heavy air support the team and the Afghan commandos broke out of the valley with the wounded; the insurgent force was driven off with heavy losses.
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Shok Valley: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Shok_Valley
note: Qualifies only through the Afghan commando contingent (about a hundred men beside 12 Americans); the Hizb-i Islami fighters in Nuristan were largely Nuristani/Pashai, so their qualification is not claimed.

name: Battle of Wanat
label: Wanat
side_b: Taliban, Hizb-i Islami and local Waygal valley fighters
commanders_a: Capt. Matthew Myer; Lt. Jonathan Brostrom
result_basis: The US and Afghan soldiers held the vehicle patrol base after being overrun in part, losing nine US dead, and the attackers withdrew after air strikes.
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Wanat: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Wanat
note: Qualifies only through the Afghan National Army platoon (about two dozen men beside about 48 Americans); the attackers were largely Nuristani, who are not Iranian. The Army's ethnic composition (Pashtun and Tajik) is not given in the sources.

name: Battle of Bajaur (Operation Sher Dil)
label: Bajaur
war: Insurgency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (War in North-West Pakistan)
place: Bajaur Agency (Khar, Loi Sam, Charmang), Federally Administered Tribal Areas (Pakistan)
side_a: Pakistan Army and Frontier Corps with pro-government tribal lashkars
side_b: Tehrik-i Taliban Pakistan and TNSM fighters of Maulana Faqir Muhammad
persian_state: Pakistan Army and Frontier Corps with pro-government tribal lashkars v Tehrik-i Taliban Pakistan and TNSM fighters of Maulana Faqir Muhammad
faction_a: Pakistan Army and Frontier Corps with pro-government tribal lashkars
faction_b: Tehrik-i Taliban Pakistan and TNSM fighters of Maulana Faqir Muhammad
commanders_a: Maj. Gen. Tariq Khan (Inspector General, Frontier Corps)
result_basis: The army and Frontier Corps cleared Loi Sam, Charmang and Khar and the militants accepted a ceasefire in February 2009, losing their stronghold in the agency.
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Bajaur: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Bajaur
note: A six-month operation in Bajaur; the Frontier Corps and the Pashtun tribal lashkars were singled out in the fighting on the government side, the militants were Tarkani Pashtun.

name: Liakhvi Gorge (August 2008)
label: Liakhvi Gorge
date: 7-9 August 2008 (Roki Tunnel, Java and Gufta Bridge, before and into the battle of Tskhinvali)
place: Liakhvi Gorge, Java and the Gufta Bridge, South Ossetia (Georgia)
persian_state: Russia & South Ossetian militia and volunteers
commanders_a: Col. Kazachenko (693rd regiment), Taymuraz Mamsurov (South Ossetian leader in the first convoy from Java)
commanders_b: Georgian commanders not named in the source
result_basis: Georgia failed to block the Roki Tunnel and Gufta, the Russian and Ossetian column got through and the battle of Tskhinvali began.
sources: Wikipedia 'Battle in the Liakhvi Gorge' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_in_the_Liakhvi_Gorge (fetched)
note: Qualifies through the South Ossetian militia and volunteers (Alans), singled out in the source, fighting beside Russian regulars; the Battle of Tskhinvali itself is already in the dataset. Fighting for the Georgian-held villages (Kekhvi, Kurta, Achabeti, Tamarasheni) is not itemized in the source.

name: Tskhinvali (2008)
label: Tskhinvali
place: Tskhinvali, South Ossetia (Georgia, de facto South Ossetia)
commanders_a: Mikheil Saakashvili; Mamuka Kurashvili; Zaza Gogava
commanders_b: Eduard Kokoity (South Ossetian president); Marat Kulakhmetov (Joint Peacekeeping Force); Anatoly Khrulyov (58th Army)
result_basis: Georgian forces took most of the town on 8 August and were driven out by 10 August after the Russian 58th Army arrived.
sources: Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on the Conflict in Georgia (Tagliavini Report, 2009); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Tskhinvali
note: For the first two days the South Ossetian militia and a small peacekeeping force were the only defenders; Russian regulars then took over most of the fighting.

name: Uzbin Valley (ambush and battle, 2008)
label: Uzbin Valley
place: Uzbin Valley, Surobi District, Kabul Province (Afghanistan)
side_b: Taliban and Hizb-i Islami fighters of Surobi
persian_state: France v Taliban and Hizb-i Islami fighters of Surobi
faction_b: Taliban and Hizb-i Islami fighters of Surobi
commanders_a: French task force commanders (not named in the sources consulted)
commanders_b: Local Taliban and Hizb-i Islami commanders (unnamed)
result_basis: A French patrol was ambushed with ten killed, and the survivors were relieved only after heavy air and ground reinforcement; the insurgents kept the heights.
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Uzbin Valley (Embuscade d'Uzbin)
note: The most costly action for the French army since 1983. Afghan National Army troops accompanied the patrol and the attackers came from the Pashtun communities of Surobi. Commander names are not confirmed.

name: Aktutun (2008)
label: Aktutun
place: Aktutun border post near Cukurca, Hakkari Province, Turkey
result_basis: The PKK overran the border post and killed 17 soldiers before Turkish forces and aircraft drove them off.
sources: Press reports (BBC, Reuters, 3-6 Oct 2008); from memory
note: One of the deadliest PKK attacks of the 2000s. The post's name and exact place are as reported by the press.

name: Battle of Buner (Operation Black Thunderstorm)
label: Buner
date: 26 April to June 2009 (Buner cleared by mid-May)
war: Insurgency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (War in North-West Pakistan)
place: Buner District (Daggar, Pir Baba) and Lower Dir, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (Pakistan)
result_basis: The army pushed the Taliban out of Buner and Lower Dir in about three weeks and then moved into Swat.
sources: Wikipedia, Operation Black Thunderstorm: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Black_Thunderstorm
note: Launched after the Taliban advanced into Buner, within 100 km of Islamabad. The Frontier Corps was involved, but the Army is the main force.

name: Ravansar and Sanandaj police station attacks
label: Ravansar and Sanandaj police station attacks
place: Ravansar (Kermanshah province) and Sanandaj (Kurdistan province), Iran
persian_state: Kurdish rebels v Islamic Republic of Iran
persian_force: The Law Enforcement Force (police) garrisons of the two stations, reinforced by security forces.
iranian_note: Police in Kermanshah and Kurdistan provinces were national conscripts and locally recruited Kurdish and Persian speakers; no breakdown in the sources.
result_basis: PJAK raided the two police stations and killed 10-24 policemen while losing 8-10 or more men, but the sources do not say whether the stations fell or the raiders were driven off.
borderline: two insurgent raids on police stations rather than a battle
doubt: Borderline: two insurgent raids on police stations rather than a battle.
sources: en.wikipedia Ravansar and Sanandaj police station attacks; Iran-PJAK conflict
note: About a week later Iranian helicopter gunships struck Kurdish villages around Panjwin in Iraq, displacing over 800 people (ICRC). Side_a is PJAK only because the outcome is unknown; no victor is implied.
qbasis: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state

name: Second Battle of Swat (Operation Rah-e-Rast)
label: Second Battle of Swat
date: 5 May to mid-July 2009 (Mingora retaken about 30 May)
war: Insurgency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (War in North-West Pakistan)
place: Swat Valley (Mingora, Matta, Peochar), Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (Pakistan)
side_a: Pakistan Army, Special Service Group and Frontier Corps
commanders_a: Lt. Gen. Masood Aslam (XI Corps); Gen. Ashfaq Pervez Kayani (Chief of Army Staff)
result_basis: The army retook Mingora at the end of May and cleared the valley by July; Fazlullah fled to Afghanistan and around two million people were displaced.
sources: Wikipedia, Second Battle of Swat: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Battle_of_Swat
note: The largest counter-insurgency offensive in Pakistan to that point, following the collapse of the Swat peace deal. The XI Corps commander named is from memory.

name: Operation Panther's Claw
label: Operation Panther's Claw
place: Babaji and Chah-e Anjir, near Lashkar Gah, Helmand Province (Afghanistan)
side_a: United Kingdom with Danish and Estonian troops and the Afghan National Army
persian_state: United Kingdom with Danish and Estonian troops and the Afghan National Army v Taliban
faction_a: United Kingdom with Danish and Estonian troops and the Afghan National Army
commanders_a: Brig. Tim Radford (UK Task Force Helmand)
commanders_b: Local Taliban commanders of central Helmand (unnamed)
result_basis: British and Afghan forces cleared the Babaji and Chah-e Anjir area and secured the Highway One approaches to Lashkar Gah, though Taliban resistance went on beyond the cleared zone.
sources: Wikipedia, List of military operations in the war in Afghanistan (2001-2021); Wikipedia, Operation Panther's Claw
note: The main British offensive of 2009; real fighting with 3-4 hundred Taliban expected and heavy British losses (about 20 killed).

name: Operation Khanjar
label: Operation Khanjar
place: Helmand River valley (Nawa, Garmsir, Khan Neshin, Dahaneh), Helmand Province (Afghanistan)
result_basis: The Marines occupied the objective districts in the southern Helmand valley and the Taliban left or dispersed, though the area stayed contested.
sources: Wikipedia, List of military operations in the war in Afghanistan (2001-2021): Operation Khanjar
note: About 4,000 Marines and 650 Afghan soldiers; the largest Marine heliborne operation since Vietnam. Part of the Helmand offensive that preceded the Afghan presidential election.

name: Battle of Ganjgal
label: Ganjgal
place: Ganjgal village, Shigal (Narang) District, Kunar Province (Afghanistan)
side_b: Hizb-i Islami and Taliban fighters of Kunar
allies_a: Afghan National Army and Afghan Border Police
persian_state: United States v Hizb-i Islami and Taliban fighters of Kunar
faction_b: Hizb-i Islami and Taliban fighters of Kunar
commanders_a: Capt. William Swenson; 1st Lt. Michael Johnson; Cpl. Dakota Meyer (Medal of Honor)
commanders_b: Local insurgent commanders (unnamed in the sources consulted)
result_basis: The ambushed column lost four Americans and eight Afghan soldiers and could not relieve its pinned-down elements for hours; the insurgents melted away with the dead recovered.
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Ganjgal: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Ganjgal
note: A dawn ambush of a joint patrol into a village; Afghan soldiers were the larger part of the patrol (several dozen Afghan soldiers and border police beside about a dozen Americans). Medal of Honor (Meyer, Swenson).

name: Battle of Kamdesh (Combat Outpost Keating)
label: Kamdesh
side_b: Taliban, Hizb-i Islami and local fighters of Kamdesh
allies_a: Afghan National Police and Border Police
commanders_a: Capt. Robert Yllescas (Bull Troop, 3-61 Cavalry); Staff Sgt. Clinton Romesha (Medal of Honor)
result_basis: The outpost was not overrun, and heavy air support drove off about 300 attackers, but eight US soldiers were killed and the base was evacuated and destroyed within days.
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Kamdesh: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Kamdesh
note: Qualifies only through the Afghan soldiers and police at the outpost (some two dozen men beside 53 Americans); the attackers were chiefly Nuristani and so not Iranian. Commander names for the attackers are not given in English sources.

name: Operation Rah-e-Nijat (South Waziristan campaign)
label: Operation Rah-e-Nijat
war: Insurgency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (War in North-West Pakistan)
place: South Waziristan (Sararogha, Ladha, Makeen, Kaniguram), Federally Administered Tribal Areas (Pakistan)
side_b: Tehrik-i Taliban Pakistan with Uzbek fighters
persian_state: Tehrik-i Taliban Pakistan with Uzbek fighters
commanders_a: Gen. Ashfaq Pervez Kayani (Chief of Army Staff)
commanders_b: Hakimullah Mehsud; Qari Hussain; Waliur Rehman Mehsud
result_basis: The army took the main Mehsud towns and by 12 December announced the end of the main phase, although most of the TTP leaders escaped into North Waziristan.
sources: Wikipedia, Operation Rah-e-Nijat: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Rah-e-Nijat
note: The army's largest ground offensive in the tribal areas. TTP strength estimates range from 10,000 to 20,000. The Frontier Corps also fought on the government side.

name: Battle of Marjah (Operation Moshtarak)
label: Marjah
date: 13 February to about 25 February 2010 (Moshtarak continued to December)
